entries.joshua 9:1: News of Israel's victories spread, and many local kings heard about it. It shows how quickly word travels when God does something powerful.
entries.joshua 9:2: These kings joined forces to fight Joshua and Israel. People often unite against what God is doing rather than turn to him.
entries.joshua 9:3: The people of Gibeon heard how Joshua had destroyed Jericho and Ai. Hearing what God had done made them think hard about their own safety.
entries.joshua 9:4: They decided to trick Israel by pretending to be travelers from far away, packing worn-out supplies. Their plan was deception, not honesty.
entries.joshua 9:5: They wore old shoes and clothes and carried stale, crumbly food to look like they had traveled a long distance. Everything about them was staged to mislead.
entries.joshua 9:6: They went to Joshua's camp and claimed to come from a distant land, asking for a peace agreement. They wanted a treaty based on a lie.
entries.joshua 9:7: Israel's leaders were suspicious and pointed out that the visitors might actually live nearby, which would forbid a treaty. They were right to be cautious.
entries.joshua 9:8: The visitors flattered Joshua by calling themselves his servants, and he asked them plainly who they were and where they came from. He was trying to get at the truth.
entries.joshua 9:9: They claimed to have come a long way because of the fame of Israel's God and what he had done in Egypt. They used true stories of God's power to cover their lie.
entries.joshua 9:10: They also mentioned God's victories over the two Amorite kings east of the Jordan. They knew the facts about God's deeds but used them to deceive.
entries.joshua 9:11: They said their leaders had sent them with food to offer themselves as servants and ask for a treaty. The whole story was carefully crafted to win trust.
entries.joshua 9:12: They showed bread that was fresh when they left home but now dry and crumbled, as proof of a long journey. It was evidence designed to fool Israel.
entries.joshua 9:13: They pointed to cracked wineskins and worn-out clothes and shoes as proof of their long trip. Every detail was meant to make the lie convincing.
entries.joshua 9:14: The men examined the food but did not ask the Lord what to do. They relied on their own judgment instead of seeking God's guidance.
entries.joshua 9:15: Joshua made peace with them and the leaders swore an oath not to kill them. They made a serious promise without knowing the full truth.
entries.joshua 9:16: Three days later Israel learned the visitors were actually neighbors living nearby. The deception was exposed, but too late to undo the agreement.
entries.joshua 9:17: Israel set out and reached the towns of these people on the third day. The Gibeonites were close by all along, just as Israel had feared.
entries.joshua 9:18: Israel did not attack them because the leaders had sworn an oath before the Lord. The people were angry at their leaders, but the promise had to be kept.
entries.joshua 9:19: The leaders insisted they could not harm the Gibeonites because they had sworn an oath by the Lord. Keeping a promise made before God mattered more than convenience.
entries.joshua 9:20: The leaders decided to spare them so that God's anger would not fall on them for breaking their oath. They chose to honor their word even though they had been tricked.
entries.joshua 9:21: The leaders ruled that the Gibeonites would live but serve as woodcutters and water carriers for the people. The curse of their deception became a life of service.
entries.joshua 9:22: Joshua confronted them for lying about being from far away when they actually lived nearby. He named their deceit directly.
entries.joshua 9:23: Because of their lie, Joshua declared they would always be servants, cutting wood and carrying water for God's house. Their deception brought lasting consequences.
entries.joshua 9:24: They explained they had heard God had commanded Israel to take the land and destroy its people, so they feared for their lives and resorted to trickery. Fear drove them to deceive.
entries.joshua 9:25: They accepted whatever Joshua decided was fair and right. They surrendered completely to his judgment.
entries.joshua 9:26: Joshua protected them from the Israelites and did not let them be killed. He honored the oath that had been made.
entries.joshua 9:27: From that day on, Joshua made them woodcutters and water carriers for the people and for the Lord's altar. Their deception led to a permanent role of service in Israel's worship.
entries.joshua 8:1: God tells Joshua not to be afraid and promises that the city of Ai and its king are already as good as defeated. It means the reader can face a hard task knowing God goes ahead of them.
entries.joshua 8:2: This time the Israelites are allowed to keep the city's animals and goods, and God gives Joshua a battle plan involving a hidden ambush behind the town. It shows God's instructions can differ from one situation to the next, so we should listen each time.
entries.joshua 8:3: Joshua gets the army ready and sends thirty thousand fighting men out at night. It means careful planning and preparation are part of doing what God asks.
entries.joshua 8:4: Joshua tells the hidden soldiers to stay close behind the town and be fully ready. It means waiting in the right place and staying alert is part of following orders well.
entries.joshua 8:5: Joshua explains that he and the main army will approach the town and then pretend to run away when the enemy comes out. It means the plan depends on the enemy reacting the way they expect.
entries.joshua 8:6: The enemy will chase them, thinking Israel is running away again, which will pull the defenders away from the town. It means the plan uses the enemy's own confidence against them.
entries.joshua 8:7: Once the enemy is drawn away, the hidden soldiers are to rush in and take the town, because God will give it to them. It means the victory comes from God, but the people still have to act.
entries.joshua 8:8: Joshua orders them to set the town on fire after capturing it, just as God commanded. It means obedience to God's specific instructions matters down to the details.
entries.joshua 8:9: The ambush force takes its position west of Ai, and Joshua stays with the main camp that night. It means the plan is now in motion and the leader stays with his people.
entries.joshua 8:10: Early the next morning Joshua gets the people organized and leads them up toward Ai with the leaders. It means good leadership means being up early, organized, and out in front.
entries.joshua 8:11: The main army takes its position north of the town with a valley in between. It means the setup for the battle is now complete on that side.
entries.joshua 8:12: Joshua places about five thousand men in hiding west of Ai as well. It means he uses a second force to make sure the trap works.
entries.joshua 8:13: The army is north of the town and the hidden force is west, and Joshua goes down into the valley that night. It means the leader puts himself in the risky place with his troops.
entries.joshua 8:14: The king of Ai sees the Israelites and rushes out to attack them, not knowing about the hidden soldiers behind the town. It means pride and overconfidence can blind people to danger.
entries.joshua 8:15: Joshua and the Israelites pretend to be beaten and run away toward the desert. It means the plan is a deliberate deception to draw the enemy out.
entries.joshua 8:16: All the men of Ai chase after the Israelites, leaving the town behind. It means the trap is working exactly as planned.
entries.joshua 8:17: Every man in Ai and Bethel goes after Israel, leaving the town wide open and unguarded. It means the enemy's whole defense is gone in one wrong move.
entries.joshua 8:18: God tells Joshua to point his spear toward Ai as a signal, and Joshua does it. It means a simple act of obedience becomes the signal for God's promised victory.
entries.joshua 8:19: The hidden soldiers see the signal, rush into the town, capture it, and set it on fire. It means timing and obedience turn a waiting plan into success.
entries.joshua 8:20: The men of Ai look back, see their town burning, and are trapped between the two Israelite forces. It means there is no way out once the trap closes.
entries.joshua 8:21: When Joshua and the main army see the smoke, they turn around and attack the men of Ai. It means the fleeing army becomes the attacking army at the right moment.
entries.joshua 8:22: The soldiers from the town join the fight, so the men of Ai are attacked from both sides and none escape. It means the ambush is complete and total.
entries.joshua 8:23: The king of Ai is captured alive and brought to Joshua. It means even the leader of the enemy falls into Israel's hands.
entries.joshua 8:24: Israel kills all the people of Ai, both in the field and in the town. It means the whole population is destroyed, which is a harsh reality of this war account.
entries.joshua 8:25: Twelve thousand men and women of Ai die that day. It means the scale of the destruction is enormous and should not be softened.
entries.joshua 8:26: Joshua keeps his spear raised until the destruction of Ai is finished. It means he stays committed to the task until it is complete.
entries.joshua 8:27: Israel keeps the animals and goods of the town, just as God had told Joshua. It means the people are allowed to benefit from the victory in the way God permitted.
entries.joshua 8:28: Joshua burns Ai and turns it into a permanent pile of ruins. It means the city is destroyed so completely that it stays that way.
entries.joshua 8:29: The king of Ai is executed and hung on a tree until evening, then buried under a pile of stones. It means the king's defeat is made public and final.
entries.joshua 8:30: Joshua builds an altar to the Lord on Mount Ebal. It means after the battle, the people turn back to worship God.
entries.joshua 8:31: The altar is built from uncut stones, as Moses commanded, and they offer burnt and peace offerings on it. It means they worship God exactly the way he instructed, not however they like.
entries.joshua 8:32: Joshua writes a copy of Moses' law on the stones in front of all the Israelites. It means God's word is put on public display for everyone to see.
entries.joshua 8:33: All the people, including foreigners living among them, stand on both sides of the ark facing the two mountains, as Moses had ordered. It means everyone in the community, insiders and outsiders alike, is included in this covenant ceremony.
entries.joshua 8:34: Joshua reads out all the words of the law, including the blessings and the curses. It means the people hear the whole thing, both the good and the warning.
entries.joshua 8:35: Joshua reads every word of Moses' commands to the whole assembly, including women, children, and foreigners. It means no one is left out of hearing God's word.
entries.joshua 4:1: After everyone had crossed the Jordan River, God spoke to Joshua. This shows God was guiding the whole event and had more to say once the people were safe on the other side.
entries.joshua 4:2: God told Joshua to pick twelve men, one from each tribe of Israel. Each tribe would have a representative in what happened next.
entries.joshua 4:3: Each man was to lift a stone from the dry riverbed where the priests stood and carry it to the place they would camp that night. These stones would become a lasting reminder of what God did.
entries.joshua 4:4: Joshua called the twelve men he had already chosen, one from each tribe. He was putting God's instructions into action right away.
entries.joshua 4:5: Joshua told the men to walk into the middle of the riverbed in front of the ark and each carry a stone on his shoulder. The stones were heavy reminders of a real, physical event.
entries.joshua 4:6: The stones were meant to be a sign the people would see and ask about. When children asked what the stones meant, parents would have a chance to tell the story.
entries.joshua 4:7: The answer would be that the river stopped flowing when the ark of the Lord crossed it. The stones were to keep that miracle fresh in Israel's memory for good.
entries.joshua 4:8: The Israelites obeyed Joshua exactly, taking twelve stones from the riverbed and setting them down at their camp. Obedience to God's instructions was central to this moment.
entries.joshua 4:9: Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the riverbed where the priests had stood. Those stones remained there as a witness to where God had held back the water.
entries.joshua 4:10: The priests stayed in the riverbed until everything God commanded through Moses was finished, then the people hurried across. God's timing and Moses' authority were both honored.
entries.joshua 4:11: Once everyone was across, the ark of the Lord and the priests also crossed while the people watched. God himself, represented by the ark, went with his people.
entries.joshua 4:12: The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh crossed over armed, just as Moses had arranged. They kept their promise to lead the way in battle.
entries.joshua 4:13: About forty thousand armed soldiers crossed over before the Lord toward the plains of Jericho. This was a real military force ready for what lay ahead.
entries.joshua 4:14: That day God made Joshua highly respected in the eyes of all Israel, and they feared him as they had Moses. God publicly confirmed Joshua as the new leader.
entries.joshua 4:15: Then the Lord spoke to Joshua again. God was still directing each step of this event.
entries.joshua 4:16: God told Joshua to command the priests carrying the ark to come up out of the riverbed. The sign was complete, and it was time to move on.
entries.joshua 4:17: Joshua passed the command to the priests to come up out of the Jordan. He acted promptly on what God said.
entries.joshua 4:18: As soon as the priests' feet touched dry ground, the river returned to its normal flow and overflowed its banks as before. The miracle ended exactly when God intended.
entries.joshua 4:19: The people came out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and camped at Gilgal, east of Jericho. This date and place would be remembered as the start of their new life in the land.
entries.joshua 4:20: Joshua set up the twelve stones from the riverbed at Gilgal. The memorial was placed where the people were living, so they would see it regularly.
entries.joshua 4:21: Joshua told the Israelites that when their children asked what the stones meant, they should be ready to explain. Parents were responsible for passing the story on.
entries.joshua 4:22: They were to tell their children plainly that Israel crossed the Jordan River on dry ground. The story was simple and true, and it needed to be told.
entries.joshua 4:23: God dried up the Jordan just as he had dried up the Red Sea for their ancestors. The same God who rescued the previous generation was acting for this one.
entries.joshua 4:24: The purpose was for all nations to see how strong the Lord's hand is and for Israel to fear him always. The miracle pointed beyond Israel to God's power over all the earth.
entries.joshua 11:1: A powerful king named Jabin heard what Israel had done and started gathering other kings to fight back. It shows that success often brings new opposition, so readers shouldn't be surprised when trouble follows a victory.
entries.joshua 11:2: He also called the kings from the northern hills and the valleys and plains around them. The point is that the opposition was widespread, coming from many directions at once.
entries.joshua 11:3: He reached out to all the different people groups across the land, from east to west and north to south. This shows how many nations banded together against Israel.
entries.joshua 11:4: They came with a huge army, as countless as sand on the shore, along with many horses and chariots. The odds looked overwhelming, which sets up the need for God's help.
entries.joshua 11:5: All these kings joined forces and camped together to attack Israel. The reader sees that the threat was real and unified, not scattered.
entries.joshua 11:6: God told Joshua not to be afraid because he would hand the whole army over to Israel the next day, and he told them to cripple the horses and burn the chariots. The message for the reader is that God's promise is stronger than any military advantage.
entries.joshua 11:7: Joshua and his soldiers launched a sudden attack on the enemy camp. Acting promptly on God's word is the example here.
entries.joshua 11:8: God gave Israel the victory, and they chased the enemy far in several directions until none escaped. It shows that the outcome depended on God giving them the win.
entries.joshua 11:9: Joshua did exactly what God had commanded about the horses and chariots. Obedience to God's specific instructions is the lesson for the reader.
entries.joshua 11:10: Joshua captured Hazor and killed its king, since Hazor had been the most important of those kingdoms. Defeating the leader mattered because it was the center of the opposition.
entries.joshua 11:11: They killed everyone in the city and burned it down. This is a harsh wartime account; the reader should see it as part of the severe judgment described in this chapter, not a model for how to treat people today.
entries.joshua 11:12: Joshua captured all the other royal towns and killed their kings, just as Moses had commanded. The emphasis is on carrying out the instructions that had been handed down.
entries.joshua 11:13: Israel did not burn the towns built on mounds, except Hazor, which Joshua burned. This detail shows that the destruction was not random but followed specific orders.
entries.joshua 11:14: The Israelites kept the livestock and goods for themselves but killed all the people. Again this reflects the extreme judgment language of the conquest story, and readers should take it as a historical report rather than a pattern to copy.
entries.joshua 11:15: Everything the Lord commanded Moses, Moses passed to Joshua, and Joshua carried it out completely. The reader sees the value of passing on instructions faithfully and finishing what was entrusted to you.
entries.joshua 11:16: Joshua took control of the whole land, from the hills to the southern desert to the plains. The summary shows that the promise was being fulfilled across the entire territory.
entries.joshua 11:17: The conquered land stretched from Mount Halak in the south to Baal-gad near Mount Hermon in the north, and all those kings were defeated. It highlights how complete the victory was.
entries.joshua 11:18: The fighting went on for a long time. The reader learns that big goals often take sustained effort, not a quick win.
entries.joshua 11:19: No town made peace with Israel except the Gibeonites, who made a treaty; the rest were taken by force. This shows that most of the land resisted rather than welcomed Israel.
entries.joshua 11:20: The Lord allowed those peoples to harden themselves against Israel so that they would be destroyed without mercy, as he had told Moses. This is a difficult verse about God's judgment; the reader should see it as describing that judgment, not as permission to harden their own heart against others.
entries.joshua 11:21: Joshua wiped out the Anakim, a famously tall people, from the hill country of Judah and Israel and destroyed their towns. It shows that even the most feared enemies were not beyond God's power.
entries.joshua 11:22: No Anakim were left in Israel's land, though some remained in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. The reader sees that the victory was real but not absolutely total.
entries.joshua 11:23: Joshua took the whole land as the Lord had promised Moses, divided it among the tribes, and the land finally had rest from war. The chapter ends with the promise kept and peace restored, encouraging the reader to trust that God finishes what he starts.
entries.joshua 12:1: This starts a list of the kings Israel defeated east of the Jordan River and the land they took. It reminds the reader that God kept his promise and gave his people real, specific territory.
entries.joshua 12:2: This describes the territory of Sihon, an Amorite king, stretching from the Arnon valley up to the Jabbok River. It shows how large and defined the land was that Israel captured from him.
entries.joshua 12:3: This continues marking out Sihon's land, from the Sea of Galilee down to the Dead Sea and the slopes of Pisgah. It gives the reader a clear picture of the region's borders.
entries.joshua 12:4: This introduces Og, the king of Bashan, one of the last of the Rephaim, a group of very tall people. It sets up the account of another powerful king Israel defeated.
entries.joshua 12:5: This describes Og's large territory in Bashan and around Mount Hermon. It shows the reader that even a strong king with wide lands could not stop Israel.
entries.joshua 12:6: Moses and the Israelites defeated these kings, and Moses gave their land to three tribes as their inheritance. It shows that the land was passed on fairly to specific families.
entries.joshua 12:7: This begins the list of kings Joshua and Israel defeated west of the Jordan, from Lebanon down toward Seir. It shows that the whole promised land, not just part of it, was being taken.
entries.joshua 12:8: This lists the different kinds of terrain and the peoples who lived there. It tells the reader that Israel's victory covered every region and every group in the land.
entries.joshua 12:9: This begins a simple count of defeated kings, starting with Jericho and Ai. The repeated 'one' makes clear each victory was real and counted.
entries.joshua 12:10: The kings of Jerusalem and Hebron are added to the list. It shows that even well-known, strong cities fell to Israel.
entries.joshua 12:11: Jarmuth and Lachish are named next in the count. Each name is a reminder of another real place where God gave victory.
entries.joshua 12:12: Eglon and Gezer are added to the list of defeated kings. The reader sees the victories piling up one after another.
entries.joshua 12:13: Debir and Geder are counted here. The list keeps showing that no single city could stand against Israel.
entries.joshua 12:14: Hormah and Arad are named next. Each entry quietly records another enemy overcome.
entries.joshua 12:15: Libnah and Adullam are added to the tally. The steady count shows how thorough the conquest was.
entries.joshua 12:16: Makkedah and Beth-el are counted here. The reader is meant to see that the victories kept coming across the land.
entries.joshua 12:17: Tappuah and Hepher are named in the list. Each one stands for a real place and a real defeat.
entries.joshua 12:18: Aphek and Lassharon are added to the count. The list keeps building a picture of complete victory.
entries.joshua 12:19: Madon and Hazor are named here. Hazor was a major city, so its defeat shows how significant these victories were.
entries.joshua 12:20: Shimron-meron and Achshaph are counted next. The reader sees that even lesser-known places were part of the same story.
entries.joshua 12:21: Taanach and Megiddo are added to the list. These were important strongholds, and their fall shows the scope of Israel's success.
entries.joshua 12:22: Kedesh and Jokneam in Carmel are named here. The count continues across different parts of the land.
entries.joshua 12:23: Dor and Goiim in Gilgal are counted next. Each name marks another place where Israel won.
entries.joshua 12:24: The list ends with Tirzah and a total of thirty-one kings. The reader is left with a clear summary of how much God gave Israel.
entries.joshua 14:1: The land of Canaan was officially divided up and handed out to Israel's tribes by the priest Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal leaders. It shows that God's promise was being fulfilled in an organized, public way.
entries.joshua 14:2: The land was assigned by God's own decision, passed down through Moses, for the nine tribes and the half-tribe. The reader sees that this was not a random land grab but something God himself directed.
entries.joshua 14:3: Two and a half tribes had already received their land east of the Jordan, and the Levites were not given a share of territory like the others. God's plan made room for each group in a different way.
entries.joshua 14:4: Joseph's family counted as two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, and the Levites only received towns and pastureland rather than a full territory. This explains how the land could still be divided fairly among the remaining tribes.
entries.joshua 14:5: The Israelites did exactly what God had commanded through Moses when they divided the land. Obedience to God's instructions is the pattern here for the reader to notice.
entries.joshua 14:6: Caleb reminded Joshua of what God had promised about the two of them back at Kadesh-barnea. He was respectfully asking Joshua to honor a promise made decades earlier.
entries.joshua 14:7: Caleb recalled being forty when Moses sent him to scout out the land, and he brought back an honest, encouraging report. His faithfulness then is the basis for his request now.
entries.joshua 14:8: The other scouts scared the people and drained their courage, but Caleb stayed fully loyal to the Lord. One person's wholehearted trust can stand out even when others give in to fear.
entries.joshua 14:9: Moses swore that day that the very land Caleb had walked on would belong to him and his descendants forever, because he followed God wholeheartedly. God remembers and rewards lasting faithfulness.
entries.joshua 14:10: Caleb pointed out that God had kept him alive for forty-five years since that promise, through all the wilderness years, and now he was eighty-five. God's promises can take a long time, but he does not forget them.
entries.joshua 14:11: Caleb claimed he was still as strong at eighty-five as he had been at forty, ready for war and daily work. His vigor is presented as evidence of God's care over his long life.
entries.joshua 14:12: Caleb asked for the hill country where the giant Anakim lived in large fortified cities, trusting God to help him take it. He was not asking for something easy but for a challenge he believed God would see him through.
entries.joshua 14:13: Joshua blessed Caleb and gave him Hebron as his inheritance. The promise made long ago was now officially kept.
entries.joshua 14:14: Hebron became Caleb's family inheritance and remained so, because he had followed the Lord with his whole heart. The reader sees that wholehearted loyalty leaves a lasting legacy.
entries.joshua 14:15: Hebron used to be called Kiriath-arba after Arba, the greatest of the giants, and after this the land finally had rest from war. A place once named for a fearsome enemy became part of God's people's inheritance, and peace followed.
entries.joshua 10:1: News reached the king of Jerusalem that Joshua had destroyed Ai and that the people of Gibeon had made peace with Israel. This made him worried because a strong nearby city had now sided with the enemy.
entries.joshua 10:2: He and his people were terrified because Gibeon was a large, important city with brave fighting men. A powerful ally joining Israel was a serious threat.
entries.joshua 10:3: So the king of Jerusalem asked four other kings to join him. He was building a coalition because he knew one city alone could not handle the situation.
entries.joshua 10:4: He urged them to help him attack Gibeon for switching sides and making peace with Joshua and Israel. Their plan was to punish Gibeon for its alliance.
entries.joshua 10:5: The five Amorite kings gathered their armies and surrounded Gibeon to attack it. This was a united front against both Gibeon and Israel.
entries.joshua 10:6: The people of Gibeon sent an urgent message to Joshua asking for help, reminding him they were now his servants and that all the Amorite kings had come against them. They needed rescue quickly.
entries.joshua 10:7: Joshua responded immediately, marching up from Gilgal with his whole army and fighting men. He kept his promise to protect the people who had made peace with him.
entries.joshua 10:8: God told Joshua not to be afraid because he would give him victory over these enemies. This reassurance came before the battle, strengthening Joshua's confidence.
entries.joshua 10:9: Joshua traveled all night from Gilgal and launched a surprise attack on the enemy. The element of surprise was part of his strategy.
entries.joshua 10:10: The Lord threw the enemy into panic before Israel, who defeated many of them at Gibeon and chased the rest toward Beth-horon and beyond. God was actively fighting on Israel's side.
entries.joshua 10:11: As the enemy fled, the Lord sent large hailstones from the sky that killed more of them than Israel's swords did. God's direct intervention was decisive in the victory.
entries.joshua 10:12: On that day Joshua prayed publicly before all Israel, asking the sun to stand still over Gibeon and the moon over the valley of Aijalon. He was asking God for more daylight to finish the battle.
entries.joshua 10:13: The sun and moon stayed in place until Israel had defeated its enemies, and this event was recorded in the Book of Jashar. The sun remained in the sky for about a full day, which was unprecedented.
entries.joshua 10:14: No day like that had ever happened before or since, when the Lord answered a man's request so dramatically, because the Lord was fighting for Israel. This shows how directly God was involved in this battle.
entries.joshua 10:15: After the battle, Joshua and all Israel returned to their camp at Gilgal. This was their base of operations.
entries.joshua 10:16: The five kings ran away and hid in a cave at Makkedah. They were trying to escape the defeat.
entries.joshua 10:17: Someone reported to Joshua that the five kings had been found hiding in the cave. Their hiding place was discovered.
entries.joshua 10:18: Joshua ordered large stones rolled over the cave entrance and guards posted to keep the kings trapped inside. He wanted to deal with them later while pursuing the rest of the army.
entries.joshua 10:19: Joshua told his men not to delay but to chase the enemy army from behind and prevent them from reaching their fortified towns, because God had given them into Israel's hands. The priority was finishing the battle.
entries.joshua 10:20: Joshua and Israel finished destroying the enemy, except for a small group who escaped into walled cities. The victory was nearly complete.
entries.joshua 10:21: All the people returned safely to Joshua at Makkedah, and no one dared to speak against Israel. The victory was total and Israel's reputation was secure.
entries.joshua 10:22: Joshua ordered the stones removed from the cave so the five kings could be brought out to him. It was time to deal with the captured leaders.
entries.joshua 10:23: The five kings were brought out of the cave and presented to Joshua. They were now completely in his power.
entries.joshua 10:24: Joshua called all Israel together and had his military commanders put their feet on the kings' necks, a symbol of total victory and dominance. This was a public demonstration that the enemy was completely defeated.
entries.joshua 10:25: Joshua told his men not to be afraid or discouraged but to be strong and courageous, because God would do the same to all their future enemies. This was meant to build their confidence for the battles ahead.
entries.joshua 10:26: Joshua had the five kings executed and their bodies hung on trees until evening. This was a public display of their defeat.
entries.joshua 10:27: At sunset, Joshua ordered the bodies taken down and thrown back into the cave, which was then sealed with large stones that remained there. This marked the final end of these kings.
entries.joshua 10:28: That same day Joshua captured Makkedah, killed its king and everyone in it, and treated its king as he had treated the king of Jericho. The city was completely destroyed.
entries.joshua 10:29: Joshua and Israel moved on from Makkedah to Libnah and attacked it. The campaign continued from town to town.
entries.joshua 10:30: The Lord gave Libnah and its king into Israel's hands, and they destroyed everyone in it, doing to its king as they had done to Jericho's king. God continued to give them victory.
entries.joshua 10:31: Joshua and Israel moved on to Lachish, set up camp against it, and attacked. The advance continued southward.
entries.joshua 10:32: The Lord gave Lachish to Israel, and on the second day of fighting they captured it and destroyed everyone in it, just as they had done to Libnah. God was directing the victories.
entries.joshua 10:33: Horam, king of Gezer, came to help Lachish, but Joshua defeated him and his army, killing all of them. Even reinforcements could not stop Israel.
entries.joshua 10:34: Joshua and Israel moved on from Lachish to Eglon, surrounded it, and attacked. The campaign pressed forward.
entries.joshua 10:35: They captured Eglon that same day and destroyed everyone in it, just as they had done to Lachish. The pattern of total victory continued.
entries.joshua 10:36: Joshua and Israel went up from Eglon to Hebron and attacked it. They were moving through the hill country.
entries.joshua 10:37: They captured Hebron and destroyed its king, its towns, and everyone in them, just as they had done to Eglon. The city was completely wiped out.
entries.joshua 10:38: Joshua and Israel turned to attack Debir. The conquest continued without pause.
entries.joshua 10:39: They captured Debir, its king, and all its towns, destroying everyone in them, just as they had done to Hebron and Libnah. The same total destruction was carried out.
entries.joshua 10:40: Joshua conquered the entire land—the hill country, the southern region, the lowlands, and the slopes—and killed all their kings, destroying every living thing as the Lord had commanded. This summarizes the whole southern campaign as complete obedience to God's orders.
entries.joshua 16:1: This verse starts describing the border of the land given to Joseph's descendants, beginning at the Jordan River near Jericho and heading up into the hills toward Bethel. It shows that God's gift of land was specific and carefully measured out for each family.
entries.joshua 16:2: The boundary line continues from Bethel toward Luz and then to the territory of the Archites at Ataroth. These details helped the Israelites know exactly which land belonged to them.
entries.joshua 16:3: The border then runs down westward past the Japhletites and lower Beth-horon, ending at the Mediterranean Sea near Gezer. The land was real, physical ground with clear edges the people could see and walk.
entries.joshua 16:4: The tribes of Manasseh and Ephraim, both descended from Joseph, received their share of the land. Each tribe got its own inheritance, just as God had promised.
entries.joshua 16:5: This begins listing the borders of Ephraim's land by clan, running from Ataroth-addar to upper Beth-horon on the east side. It shows the land was divided fairly among family groups.
entries.joshua 16:6: The boundary goes west to Michmethath and then turns east toward Taanath-shiloh, passing by Janoah. These place names marked the actual edges of Ephraim's territory.
entries.joshua 16:7: The line continues from Janoah down through Ataroth and Naarah, touches Jericho, and reaches the Jordan River. The description traces the land like a map so the people knew their boundaries.
entries.joshua 16:8: From Tappuah the border runs west along the Kanah river and ends at the sea, completing Ephraim's inheritance by clan. This closed off the description of the land Ephraim's families would live in.
entries.joshua 16:9: Ephraim also received some towns located inside Manasseh's territory, along with their surrounding villages. This shows the allotment wasn't perfectly neat but was arranged to meet each tribe's needs.
entries.joshua 16:10: The people of Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer, so those Canaanites stayed among them and were put to forced labor. This is a reminder that incomplete obedience left a lasting problem for Israel.
entries.joshua 10:41: Joshua defeated his enemies across a wide stretch of land, from the desert in the south to the coast and up to Gibeon. The point is that the victory covered a large area, not just one small battle.
entries.joshua 10:42: Joshua captured all these kings and their territory in one campaign because God himself was fighting on Israel's side. The reader should see that the success came from God's help, not just from Joshua's skill or strength.
entries.joshua 10:43: After the fighting, Joshua and the army returned to their camp at Gilgal. This shows the campaign had ended and the people went back to their base to rest.
entries.joshua 13:1: Joshua had grown very old, yet God pointed out that much of the land was still unconquered. Age is no excuse to stop working—there is always more to do, and God still expects faithfulness to the end.
entries.joshua 13:2: God listed the regions still remaining to be taken, starting with the Philistine and Geshurite territory. The task was not finished, so the people needed to keep pressing forward rather than settling early.
entries.joshua 13:3: This verse describes the Philistine coastland from Egypt's border up to Ekron, naming the five Philistine rulers and the Avvim. It shows the specific, real places that still stood outside Israel's control.
entries.joshua 13:4: The remaining land included Canaanite areas in the south and Sidonian territory up to Aphek. God was spelling out exactly what still needed to be claimed.
entries.joshua 13:5: This covers the Gebalite land and all of Lebanon from Baal-gad near Mount Hermon up to Hamath. The scope of the promise was large, far beyond what Israel had yet occupied.
entries.joshua 13:6: God promised to drive out the hill-country peoples and Sidonians himself, and told Joshua to assign the land to Israel anyway. We can act on God's promise even before we see it fulfilled.
entries.joshua 13:7: Joshua was commanded to divide the land among the nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh. Leadership meant organizing and passing on the inheritance, not just fighting battles.
entries.joshua 13:8: The Reubenites and Gadites had already received their land east of the Jordan through Moses. Different tribes received different portions, but all by God's direction.
entries.joshua 13:9: This verse marks the southern boundary of Reuben's territory from Aroer by the Arnon valley across the plateau to Medeba and Dibon. It anchors the inheritance in real geography.
entries.joshua 13:10: The land included all the towns of Sihon, the Amorite king at Heshbon, up to the Ammonite border. Israel received territory that had belonged to defeated kings.
entries.joshua 13:11: This adds Gilead, the Geshurite and Maacathite lands, Mount Hermon, and Bashan as far as Salecah. The inheritance was extensive and varied.
entries.joshua 13:12: This was the kingdom of Og in Bashan, one of the last of the Rephaim, whom Moses had defeated and dispossessed. God had already given Israel victory over powerful enemies.
entries.joshua 13:13: Israel failed to drive out the Geshurites and Maacathites, so they lived among Israel to that day. Incomplete obedience leaves lasting consequences.
entries.joshua 13:14: The tribe of Levi received no land inheritance; their share was the offerings made to God. Those who serve God are sustained by him and by the gifts of his people.
entries.joshua 13:15: Moses had assigned land to the Reubenites according to their family groups. Each clan received its own portion.
entries.joshua 13:16: Reuben's territory ran from Aroer by the Arnon valley across the plateau to Medeba. These boundary markers defined what belonged to them.
entries.joshua 13:17: This lists towns on the plateau, including Heshbon, Dibon, and Beth-baal-meon. The inheritance was made up of specific, named places.
entries.joshua 13:18: Jahaz, Kedemoth, and Mephaath are named as part of Reuben's inheritance. Even small towns mattered in God's allocation of land.
entries.joshua 13:19: Kiriathaim, Sibmah, and Zereth-shahar in the hill country of the valley are included. The list shows the fullness of what Reuben received.
entries.joshua 13:20: Beth-peor, the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth were also part of the territory. These places carried history from Israel's journey through the wilderness.
entries.joshua 13:21: This covers the plateau towns and all of Sihon's kingdom, along with the Midianite chiefs whom Moses defeated. God gave Israel victory over both kings and their allies.
entries.joshua 13:22: Balaam, the prophet who tried to curse Israel, was killed by the Israelites in battle. Those who set themselves against God's people do not prevail.
entries.joshua 13:23: Reuben's boundary was the edge of the Jordan, and this was their inheritance with its towns and villages. The description closes with a clear, settled boundary.
entries.joshua 13:24: Moses gave the tribe of Gad its inheritance according to their family groups. Like Reuben, Gad received land east of the Jordan.
entries.joshua 13:25: Gad's territory included Jazer, the towns of Gilead, and half the Ammonite land up to Aroer near Rabbah. Their portion was sizable and strategically placed.
entries.joshua 13:26: The boundary ran from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the edge of Debir. These markers defined Gad's land.
entries.joshua 13:27: In the valley they held Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of Sihon's kingdom, with the Jordan as their border up to the Sea of Chinnereth. Their land reached a major body of water.
entries.joshua 13:28: This summarizes Gad's inheritance with its towns and villages. The record confirms that the assignment was complete and specific.
entries.joshua 13:29: Moses also gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh by their families. Even a partial tribe received a defined share.
entries.joshua 13:30: Their territory ran from Mahanaim through all Bashan, Og's kingdom, including the sixty towns of Havvoth-Jair. The portion was large and included many settlements.
entries.joshua 13:31: Half of Gilead, plus Ashtaroth and Edrei in Og's kingdom, went to the Machirites within Manasseh. The land was divided down to clan level.
entries.joshua 13:32: These are the inheritances Moses distributed in the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan across from Jericho. The record ties the allotment to a specific time and place.
entries.joshua 13:33: Levi received no land inheritance because the Lord himself was their inheritance, as he had promised. God himself is the greatest portion anyone can receive.
entries.joshua 17:1: This describes the land assigned to Manasseh, Joseph's firstborn, with part going to Machir because he was a proven warrior. It shows that God's promises were being fulfilled in real, specific places.
entries.joshua 17:2: The rest of Manasseh's descendants also received their share of land, divided by family groups. Each family had its own place, showing that everyone had a rightful inheritance.
entries.joshua 17:3: Zelophehad had no sons, only five daughters named here. In that culture this mattered because land usually passed to sons, setting up the next verses.
entries.joshua 17:4: The daughters boldly asked the leaders for land, reminding them that God had told Moses to give them an inheritance. They were granted land among their relatives, showing that God's command protected them.
entries.joshua 17:5: Manasseh received ten shares of land, plus the territory of Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan. This shows the tribe's inheritance was large and carefully divided.
entries.joshua 17:6: The daughters received land alongside the sons, and Gilead belonged to the other families of Manasseh. This confirms that the daughters were not left out of the family inheritance.
entries.joshua 17:7: This verse marks the boundary of Manasseh's land, running from Asher toward Shechem and on to En-tappuah. It shows the land was measured out with real borders.
entries.joshua 17:8: The town of Tappuah's land belonged to Manasseh, but the town itself on the border belonged to Ephraim. This shows how closely the two tribes' lands were intertwined.
entries.joshua 17:9: The border followed the Kanah stream, with some towns inside Manasseh's area belonging to Ephraim, and Manasseh's line ending at the sea. It describes a practical, shared landscape.
entries.joshua 17:10: Ephraim's land was to the south and Manasseh's to the north, with the sea as their western edge and Asher and Issachar as neighbors. This maps out where each tribe actually lived.
entries.joshua 17:11: Manasseh also held several towns within Issachar and Asher, including Beth-shean, Megiddo, and Dor with their surrounding villages. These were important, strategic places.
entries.joshua 17:12: The people of Manasseh could not drive out the Canaanites from those towns, so the Canaanites stayed living there. It shows that the conquest was incomplete and not everything went as planned.
entries.joshua 17:13: Once the Israelites grew stronger, they made the Canaanites do forced labor instead of removing them. They chose control and profit over full obedience.
entries.joshua 17:14: The tribes of Joseph complained to Joshua that their one share of land was too small for how numerous God had made them. They wanted more territory because of their growth.
entries.joshua 17:15: Joshua told them that if they were so numerous, they should clear the forest land in the hill country themselves. He turned their complaint into a challenge to work for more room.
entries.joshua 17:16: They replied that the hill country wasn't enough, and the Canaanites in the valley had iron chariots, which made them hard to defeat. They were afraid of the stronger enemy forces.
entries.joshua 17:17: Joshua repeated that they were a great and powerful people, so one share of land was not going to be their only portion. He encouraged them to expect more.
entries.joshua 17:18: Joshua told them the forested hill country would be theirs if they cleared it, and they should drive out the Canaanites despite their iron chariots. He called them to trust God and act boldly rather than fear.
entries.joshua 20:1: God is speaking directly to Joshua, the leader who took over after Moses. This shows that God was still guiding his people through their leader.
entries.joshua 20:2: God tells Joshua to set aside special towns as safe places, just as he had already instructed through Moses. God keeps his earlier promises and plans.
entries.joshua 20:3: These towns were for someone who killed another person by accident, not on purpose. The person could run there and be protected from the family member seeking revenge.
entries.joshua 20:4: When the person arrived, they would explain their case to the town leaders at the entrance area. If accepted, the leaders gave them a place to stay and kept them safe.
entries.joshua 20:5: If the relative seeking revenge chased after them, the town leaders were not allowed to hand the person over, because the death was accidental and not done out of hatred.
entries.joshua 20:6: The person had to stay in that safe town until a public trial was held and until the current high priest died. After that, they could go back home safely.
entries.joshua 20:7: The people chose three safe towns west of the Jordan River: Kedesh, Shechem, and Hebron. These were spread across the land so help was never too far away.
entries.joshua 20:8: They also chose three safe towns east of the Jordan: Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan. This made sure people on both sides of the river had a place to run to.
entries.joshua 20:9: These towns were open to Israelites and to foreigners living among them, so anyone who killed someone by accident could find protection and get a fair hearing before being judged.
entries.joshua 15:1: This verse starts describing the land assigned to the tribe of Judah, beginning at its southern border near Edom and the desert of Zin. It shows that God's people received specific, real territory, and that God keeps his promises in concrete ways.
entries.joshua 15:2: Judah's southern border began at the southern end of the Dead Sea. This is simply a boundary marker, showing the land was carefully defined.
entries.joshua 15:3: The border line ran past a mountain pass, through the desert of Zin, and down past Kadesh-barnea and several other places. These details show the land was real and measured out piece by piece.
entries.joshua 15:4: The southern border continued to the stream that marked Egypt's edge and ended at the sea. This fixed the southern limit of Judah's land.
entries.joshua 15:5: The eastern border was the Dead Sea up to where the Jordan River flows into it, and the northern border started from that same point. The land was surrounded by clear natural boundaries.
entries.joshua 15:6: The northern border went up past Beth-hoglah and Beth-arabah to a landmark called the stone of Bohan. These were real places people could see and use to know where the land ended.
entries.joshua 15:7: The border continued up from the valley of Achor toward Gilgal and on to two springs near Jerusalem. Each landmark helped the people know exactly where their land began and ended.
entries.joshua 15:8: The line went up through the valley of Hinnom, past the south side of Jerusalem, and along a mountain ridge to the west. This shows Jerusalem sat right on the edge of Judah's territory.
entries.joshua 15:9: From that mountain the border ran to a spring and on through towns to Kiriath-jearim. The land was divided carefully so each family knew what was theirs.
entries.joshua 15:10: The border turned west from Baalah, passed Mount Seir and Mount Jearim, and went down past Beth-shemesh and Timnah. These were towns and hills the people knew well.
entries.joshua 15:11: The line went out to the north side of Ekron and on to Mount Baalah, ending at the sea. This marked the western edge of Judah's land.
entries.joshua 15:12: The western border was the coastline of the Great Sea, the Mediterranean. This verse sums up the whole boundary of the land given to Judah's families.
entries.joshua 15:13: Joshua gave Caleb a special share of land, the town of Hebron, just as the Lord had commanded. This shows God honors faithful people and keeps his word to them.
entries.joshua 15:14: Caleb drove out the three giant descendants of Anak who lived in Hebron. With God's help, even fearsome enemies could not stop his people from taking the land.
entries.joshua 15:15: Caleb then moved against the town of Debir, which used to be called Kiriath-sepher. He kept pressing forward to take the land promised to him.
entries.joshua 15:16: Caleb offered his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever could capture the town. This was a common way in that culture to reward bravery and secure the family's future.
entries.joshua 15:17: Othniel, Caleb's nephew, captured the town, so Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah as his wife. Othniel later became a leader of Israel, and this shows how courage was rewarded.
entries.joshua 15:18: Achsah urged her new husband to ask her father for a field, and when she came to Caleb he asked what she wanted. She was bold in asking for what her family needed.
entries.joshua 15:19: Achsah asked her father for a blessing, since the land she had was dry, and asked for springs of water; so he gave her both upper and lower springs. It is fine to ask God and others for what we truly need.
entries.joshua 15:20: This verse introduces the full list of land given to the tribe of Judah, divided among their families. Each family received its own share of the promised land.
entries.joshua 15:21: This begins a list of the towns in the far south of Judah's territory, near the border of Edom. The list shows the land was actually settled town by town.
entries.joshua 15:22: This verse continues naming towns in the southern part of Judah's land. These were real places where families lived.
entries.joshua 15:23: More towns in the south are listed here. The detailed record shows the people carefully kept track of what God had given them.
entries.joshua 15:24: The list of southern towns continues. Each name represents a community that received its place in the land.
entries.joshua 15:25: This verse adds more towns to the southern list, including one also called Hazor. The record keeps growing as the territory is described.
entries.joshua 15:26: Three more southern towns are named here. The list shows the land was divided fairly and thoroughly.
entries.joshua 15:27: The list of towns in the south continues with three more names. These were homes and places of work for Judah's families.
entries.joshua 15:28: This verse names more southern towns, including Beer-sheba, a well-known place in Israel's story. The land was filled with real communities.
entries.joshua 15:29: Three more towns in the southern territory are listed. The careful naming shows the people valued every part of what they received.
entries.joshua 15:30: The list continues with more southern towns. Each one had its own place and people.
entries.joshua 15:31: More towns are named, including Ziklag, which later mattered in David's story. The record shows the land was fully accounted for.
entries.joshua 15:32: This verse ends the southern list, counting twenty-nine towns plus their surrounding villages. The exact count shows the division was organized and complete.
entries.joshua 15:33: This begins a new list of towns in the lowland hills of Judah. The land had different regions, and each was settled.
entries.joshua 15:34: More lowland towns are named here. These were farming communities in the flatter part of Judah's territory.
entries.joshua 15:35: The list continues with towns in the lowlands, including Adullam and Azekah. These places were part of Judah's everyday life.
entries.joshua 15:36: This verse ends the first lowland group, counting fourteen towns with their villages. The careful count shows the land was divided in an orderly way.
entries.joshua 15:37: A new group of lowland towns begins here. The list keeps showing how much real territory Judah received.
entries.joshua 15:38: Three more lowland towns are named. Each one was a place where people lived and worked.
entries.joshua 15:39: This verse names more towns, including Lachish and Eglon. These were significant places in Judah's territory.
entries.joshua 15:40: The list of lowland towns continues with three more names. The record shows the land was settled town by town, family by family.
entries.joshua 23:1: After years of peace from their enemies, Joshua had grown very old. It reminds the reader that God's rest is a gift worth remembering as life moves on.
entries.joshua 23:2: Joshua gathered Israel's leaders and told them plainly that he was old and near the end of his life. It shows the value of leaders passing on what they have learned before they go.
entries.joshua 23:3: Joshua reminded the people that they had seen God fight for them against their enemies. What God has done in the past is reason to trust him now.
entries.joshua 23:4: Joshua had already assigned the remaining land to the tribes as their inheritance. It means God's promises are secure even when the work is not yet finished.
entries.joshua 23:5: God himself would drive out the remaining nations and give the land to Israel. The reader can rely on God to complete what he has promised.
entries.joshua 23:6: Joshua urged the people to be strong and carefully follow everything written in God's law, without drifting off course. Staying faithful to God's word takes deliberate effort.
entries.joshua 23:7: They were not to mix with the remaining nations or adopt their gods in any way. The point for the reader is to keep clear of influences that pull you away from God.
entries.joshua 23:8: Instead of turning away, they were to stay close to the Lord as they had done so far. Loyalty to God is something to keep up, not just start.
entries.joshua 23:9: God had already driven out great and strong nations ahead of them. It shows that no obstacle is too big when God is the one clearing the way.
entries.joshua 23:10: One Israelite could chase a thousand enemies because God was fighting for them. The reader is reminded that real strength comes from God, not numbers.
entries.joshua 23:11: Joshua told them to watch themselves carefully and keep loving the Lord. Loving God is something you guard and nurture, not something you take for granted.
entries.joshua 23:12: If they turned back and joined themselves to the remaining nations through marriage and close ties, trouble would follow. It warns the reader that small compromises can lead you away from God.
entries.joshua 23:13: God would then stop driving out those nations, and they would become traps, whips, and thorns to Israel until they lost the land. Disobedience brings real harm, not just a slap on the wrist.
entries.joshua 23:14: Joshua said he was about to die, and he reminded them that every good thing God promised had come true. It encourages the reader to trust God's record of keeping his word.
entries.joshua 23:15: Just as God kept every good promise, he would also bring the promised judgment if they turned away. God is faithful in both blessing and warning.
entries.joshua 23:16: If they broke their agreement with God and served other gods, his anger would burn against them and they would quickly lose the land. It is a serious warning that turning from God has serious consequences.
entries.joshua 18:1: The whole nation gathered at Shiloh and set up the tent where they worshiped God, and the land was now under their control. For the reader, it shows a moment of unity and rest after years of struggle.
entries.joshua 18:2: Seven tribes still had not received their own land. It means some of God's people were lagging behind while others had already settled.
entries.joshua 18:3: Joshua asks the people why they are waiting so long to go and claim the land God has already given them. It's a nudge to stop hesitating and act on what God has promised.
entries.joshua 18:4: Joshua tells them to pick three men from each tribe to survey the land and write down what they find so it can be divided up. It's a practical step to get the job done fairly.
entries.joshua 18:5: The surveyors are to split the land into seven parts, with Judah staying in the south and Joseph's tribes in the north. It keeps everyone's territory clear and organized.
entries.joshua 18:6: Once the land is mapped in seven parts, the people bring the record back to Joshua, and he will assign the pieces by God's direction. It shows the distribution was done prayerfully, not by favoritism.
entries.joshua 18:7: The Levites get no land because their role as priests is their inheritance, and three tribes already received land east of the Jordan. It reminds the reader that some people's share is serving God rather than property.
entries.joshua 18:8: The men set out to survey the land, and Joshua repeats his instructions to map it and return so he can divide it before the Lord at Shiloh. It shows careful obedience to a clear plan.
entries.joshua 18:9: The surveyors traveled through the land, listed the towns in seven sections in a book, and came back to Joshua at the camp. It shows the work was done thoroughly and honestly.
entries.joshua 18:10: Joshua divided the land among the tribes at Shiloh, making the decisions before the Lord. It means the allocation was done in God's presence, not just by human choice.
entries.joshua 18:11: The first share went to the tribe of Benjamin, whose land lay between Judah and Joseph. It shows God's order in giving each tribe its place.
entries.joshua 18:12: This verse describes Benjamin's northern border, running from the Jordan up past Jericho and through the hills to the wilderness. It's a boundary marker showing exactly where their land began.
entries.joshua 18:13: The border continued south past Bethel and down toward the mountain south of lower Beth-horon. It's more detail fixing the shape of Benjamin's territory.
entries.joshua 18:14: The western border curved around from the mountain south of Beth-horon to Kiriath-jearim, a town belonging to Judah. It marks the edge of Benjamin's land on the west.
entries.joshua 18:15: The southern border started from the far side of Kiriath-jearim and ran out to the spring called Nephtoah. It's another boundary line defining the tribe's land.
entries.joshua 18:16: The line dropped down past the valley of Hinnom, along the Jebusite hill on the south, as far as En-rogel. It traces the southern edge in detail.
entries.joshua 18:17: The border went on past En-shemesh and Geliloth, opposite the road up to Adummim, down to the stone of Bohan. It keeps marking the outline of the territory.
entries.joshua 18:18: It continued along the slope facing the Arabah on the north and down into the Arabah valley. It's part of the same boundary description.
entries.joshua 18:19: The border ran to the north side of Beth-hoglah and ended at the northern tip of the Salt Sea where the Jordan empties in. That was Benjamin's southern limit.
entries.joshua 18:20: The Jordan River formed Benjamin's eastern border. This verse sums up that the whole territory was marked out on every side for their families.
entries.joshua 18:21: This begins a list of the towns belonging to Benjamin's families, starting with Jericho, Beth-hoglah, and Emek-kezziz. It shows the actual places the tribe would live in.
entries.joshua 18:22: The list continues with Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, and Bethel. These were towns within Benjamin's allotted land.
entries.joshua 18:23: The towns of Avvim, Parah, and Ophrah are added to Benjamin's list. It's a record of the places they received.
entries.joshua 18:24: Chephar-Ammoni, Ophni, and Geba are listed, making twelve towns plus their surrounding villages. It shows the tribe's holdings were concrete and counted.
entries.joshua 18:25: Gibeon, Ramah, and Beeroth are named next among Benjamin's towns. The list keeps track of each place they were given.
entries.joshua 18:26: Mizpeh, Chephirah, and Mozah are added to the list. These were more towns in Benjamin's territory.
entries.joshua 18:27: Rekem, Irpeel, and Taralah are named. The record continues town by town.
entries.joshua 18:28: The list ends with Zela, Eleph, the Jebusite city (Jerusalem), Gibeath, and Kiriath, making fourteen towns with their villages. This closes the account of Benjamin's inheritance by family groups.
entries.joshua 15:41: This verse lists four towns in the lowlands that belonged to Judah, along with the small villages around them. It shows that God's gift of land included many ordinary places, not just famous ones.
entries.joshua 15:42: This verse names three more towns in Judah's territory. It is part of a long record showing that the land was carefully divided and each family received its share.
entries.joshua 15:43: Three more town names are listed here as part of Judah's inheritance. The detail reminds the reader that God kept his promise down to the smallest place.
entries.joshua 15:44: This verse finishes a group of nine towns and notes the villages around them. It shows the land was organized and settled, not left vague.
entries.joshua 15:45: Ekron was a larger Philistine city that came under Judah's control, along with its surrounding villages. It marks how far Judah's territory reached toward the coast.
entries.joshua 15:46: This describes the coastal area from Ekron toward the sea, including towns near Ashdod. It shows Judah's land stretched all the way to the Mediterranean shore.
entries.joshua 15:47: Ashdod and Gaza, with their villages, formed the southern coastal border down to the stream of Egypt. The Great Sea marked the western edge of the land God gave them.
entries.joshua 15:48: This begins a new section listing towns in the hill country of Judah. It shows the inheritance included the highlands as well as the plains.
entries.joshua 15:49: This verse names more hill-country towns, noting that Kiriath-sannah was also called Debir. The double name helps connect the list to places mentioned elsewhere in the story.
entries.joshua 15:50: Three more towns in the hill country are named here. Each name is a small piece of the larger picture of Judah's settled land.
entries.joshua 15:51: This verse closes a group of eleven hill-country towns and mentions their surrounding villages. The count shows the list was careful and complete.
entries.joshua 15:52: This starts another group of towns in the hill country. It continues the detailed record of where Judah's families lived.
entries.joshua 15:53: Three more town names appear in this hill-country list. The reader sees again how thoroughly the land was mapped out.
entries.joshua 15:54: This verse names towns including Hebron, earlier called Kiriath-arba, and closes a group of nine. Hebron was a significant city in Judah's history.
entries.joshua 15:55: This begins a list of towns in the southern hill country. These places were part of the land assigned to Judah's clans.
entries.joshua 15:56: Three more towns are named in this southern group. The list keeps showing the breadth of Judah's territory.
entries.joshua 15:57: This verse completes a group of ten towns with their villages. The careful counting shows the record was meant to be trusted.
entries.joshua 15:58: This starts another short group of hill-country towns. It is part of the same orderly account of Judah's inheritance.
entries.joshua 15:59: This verse closes a group of six towns and their villages. The small number shows not every group was large, but each was recorded.
entries.joshua 15:60: Only two towns are listed here, including Kiriath-jearim, another name for Kiriath-baal. Even small portions of the land were noted and given.
entries.joshua 15:61: This begins a list of towns in the desert or wilderness area. It shows Judah's land included harsh, empty regions too.
entries.joshua 15:62: This verse names six wilderness towns, including En-gedi near the Dead Sea. The list ends with the wilder edges of Judah's territory.
entries.joshua 15:63: Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem, so they lived alongside Judah's people. This honest note shows that Israel's possession of the land was not complete, and it sets up later events in the story.
entries.joshua 19:1: Simeon's share of the land was assigned second, and it sat inside the territory already given to Judah. This shows that God's promise to give each tribe land was being carried out in an orderly way.
entries.joshua 19:2: This begins a list of the towns that belonged to Simeon's tribe. The reader sees that their inheritance was made up of real, named places, not just a vague promise.
entries.joshua 19:3: More towns in Simeon's territory are named here. Each name shows the land was carefully divided and recorded for the families who would live there.
entries.joshua 19:4: The list of Simeon's towns continues. These details remind the reader that God's gift of land was specific and concrete.
entries.joshua 19:5: Simeon's towns keep being listed, including Ziklag. The careful record shows the tribe's inheritance was real and accounted for.
entries.joshua 19:6: This verse totals the towns so far and notes the villages around them. It shows the inheritance included both towns and the farmland and settlements nearby.
entries.joshua 19:7: Four more towns are added to Simeon's list, along with their surrounding villages. The reader sees the full extent of what the tribe received.
entries.joshua 19:8: This wraps up Simeon's territory, including the villages around the towns. It confirms that the whole inheritance was settled and complete.
entries.joshua 19:9: Simeon's land came out of Judah's larger portion because Judah had more than they needed. This shows generosity and cooperation between tribes rather than selfishness.
entries.joshua 19:10: Zebulun's share was assigned third, and its boundary started at a place called Sarid. The reader sees the land being divided tribe by tribe, just as planned.
entries.joshua 19:11: This describes the western edge of Zebulun's land, running past several landmarks. The boundaries were marked out clearly so everyone knew what belonged to them.
entries.joshua 19:12: The boundary line turns east and passes through several towns. These details show the land was measured and defined with care.
entries.joshua 19:13: The border continues eastward through more towns to its endpoint. The reader sees that Zebulun's territory was a specific, bounded area.
entries.joshua 19:14: The line curves around on the north side and ends at a valley. This completes the picture of Zebulun's borders.
entries.joshua 19:15: Five towns are named, with a total of twelve towns plus their villages. The list shows the inheritance was substantial and well recorded.
entries.joshua 19:16: This summarizes Zebulun's inheritance as these towns and their surrounding villages. It confirms the tribe's share was fully assigned.
entries.joshua 19:17: Issachar's share was assigned fourth, given to their families. The reader sees each tribe receiving its own place in turn.
entries.joshua 19:18: This starts the list of towns within Issachar's territory. The names show the land was real and specific.
entries.joshua 19:19: More towns in Issachar's area are named. The careful listing shows the inheritance was recorded for the families who would live there.
entries.joshua 19:20: The list of Issachar's towns continues. Each name marks part of the land God gave them.
entries.joshua 19:21: Four more towns are added to Issachar's territory. The reader sees the tribe's inheritance taking shape town by town.
entries.joshua 19:22: This describes the boundary reaching the Jordan River and totals sixteen towns with their villages. It shows Issachar's land was clearly defined and complete.
entries.joshua 19:23: This summarizes Issachar's inheritance as these towns and villages. It confirms their share was fully settled.
entries.joshua 19:24: Asher's share was assigned fifth, given to their families. The division of the land continues in an orderly way.
entries.joshua 19:25: This begins listing the towns in Asher's territory. The names show the land was concrete and carefully recorded.
entries.joshua 19:26: The boundary stretches to Mount Carmel on the west. This shows Asher's land reached the coast and included valuable areas.
entries.joshua 19:27: The border turns east and passes through several places, reaching as far as Cabul. The reader sees the land was measured out with clear landmarks.
entries.joshua 19:28: More towns are named, extending as far as the great city of Sidon. This shows Asher's territory reached into the northern region.
entries.joshua 19:29: The boundary loops around to Tyre and ends at the sea. This confirms Asher's land included a stretch of coastline.
entries.joshua 19:30: Three more towns are named, with a total of twenty-two towns plus their villages. The list shows the inheritance was sizable and complete.
entries.joshua 19:31: This summarizes Asher's inheritance as these towns and villages. It confirms their share was fully assigned.
entries.joshua 19:32: Naphtali's share was assigned sixth, given to their families. The land division continues tribe by tribe.
entries.joshua 19:33: This describes Naphtali's boundary starting from a large tree and running to the Jordan. The reader sees the land was marked out with clear landmarks.
entries.joshua 19:34: The border turns west and touches the lands of Zebulun, Asher, and Judah. This shows Naphtali's territory bordered several other tribes.
entries.joshua 19:35: This begins listing the fortified towns in Naphtali's territory. The names show the land included strong, defensible cities.
entries.joshua 19:36: More towns in Naphtali's area are named, including Hazor. The careful record shows the inheritance was real and specific.
entries.joshua 19:37: Three more towns are added to Naphtali's list. Each name marks part of the land given to the tribe.
entries.joshua 19:38: This ends the list with a total of nineteen towns plus their villages. It shows Naphtali's inheritance was fully recorded.
entries.joshua 19:39: This summarizes Naphtali's inheritance as these towns and villages. It confirms their share was completely settled.
entries.joshua 19:40: Dan's share was assigned seventh, given to their families. The reader sees the last of these tribes receiving its land.
entries.judges 1:1: After Joshua died, the Israelites asked God which tribe should lead the fight against the Canaanites first. It shows them looking to God for direction before acting.
entries.judges 1:2: God answered that Judah should go first and promised them victory over the land. The reader sees that God gives clear guidance and backs it with his promise.
entries.judges 1:3: Judah asked their brother tribe Simeon to fight alongside them, promising to help Simeon in return. It's a picture of tribes working together instead of going it alone.
entries.judges 1:4: Judah attacked and God gave them victory, defeating ten thousand enemy soldiers at Bezek. The success is credited to God, not just to their military strength.
entries.judges 1:5: They met King Adoni-zedek in battle and defeated his Canaanite and Perizzite forces. The story continues to show God handing their enemies over to them.
entries.judges 1:6: The king ran away, but they caught him and cut off his thumbs and big toes. This was a brutal act that crippled him, common in ancient warfare.
entries.judges 1:7: Adoni-zedek admitted he had done the same thing to seventy kings, and now it had happened to him. He was taken to Jerusalem, where he died, showing that cruel treatment often comes back on the one who does it.
entries.judges 1:8: Judah's men attacked Jerusalem, killed its people, and burned the city. This was total warfare as practiced in that era.
entries.judges 1:9: After that, Judah fought the Canaanites in the hills, the southern area, and the lowlands. They kept pressing the campaign into different regions.
entries.judges 1:10: Caleb attacked the Canaanites in Hebron, formerly called Kiriath-arba, and defeated three enemy leaders there. Caleb is shown as a faithful fighter carrying out what was promised to him.
entries.judges 1:11: From Hebron, Caleb moved on to attack the people of Debir, which used to be called Kiriath-sepher. The advance continues town by town.
entries.judges 1:12: Caleb offered his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever could capture Kiriath-sepher. This was a common way in that culture to reward a brave warrior.
entries.judges 1:13: Othniel, Caleb's nephew, captured the town and so received Achsah as his wife. He becomes an important figure later in the book.
entries.judges 1:14: On the way, Othniel urged Achsah to ask her father for a field, and she got off her donkey to speak with Caleb. It sets up her request for something valuable.
entries.judges 1:15: Achsah asked her father for a blessing, since the land he gave her was dry, and requested springs of water. Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs, showing a father's generosity.
entries.judges 1:16: The Kenites, relatives of Moses' father-in-law, left the city of palms and settled among the people of Judah in the desert near Arad. It shows other groups joining Israel's life.
entries.judges 1:17: Judah and Simeon together defeated the Canaanites in Zephath and completely destroyed the town, renaming it Hormah. The name means destruction, marking what happened there.
entries.judges 1:18: Judah captured Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron along with the land around them. These were major Philistine cities on the coast.
entries.judges 1:19: God was with Judah, and they took the hill country, but they couldn't drive out the people in the valleys because those enemies had iron chariots. Even with God's help, some obstacles proved too strong for them at that time.
entries.judges 1:20: Hebron was given to Caleb as Moses had promised, and he drove out the three giant descendants of Anak living there. It shows a promise from long ago finally being kept.
entries.judges 1:21: The tribe of Judah failed to remove the Jebusites from Jerusalem, so they lived there alongside the people of Benjamin. This is the first of several failures to fully clear the land.
entries.judges 1:22: The tribes of Joseph attacked Bethel, and God was with them. Their campaign begins with God's support.
entries.judges 1:23: They sent spies to scout out Bethel, which used to be called Luz. They wanted information before attacking.
entries.judges 1:24: The spies saw a man leaving the town and offered to spare him if he showed them a way in. It was a bargain made in the middle of war.
entries.judges 1:25: The man showed them the entrance, and they killed everyone in the town but let him and his family go free. They kept their promise to him.
entries.judges 1:26: The man moved to the land of the Hittites, built a town, and named it Luz after his old home. The name stuck, the text notes.
entries.judges 1:27: The tribe of Manasseh failed to drive out the Canaanites from several towns, including Beth-shean and Megiddo, so those people stayed in the land. This is another incomplete victory.
entries.judges 1:28: Later, when Israel grew stronger, they forced the Canaanites to work for them but still didn't remove them. They chose advantage over full obedience.
entries.judges 1:29: Ephraim also failed to remove the Canaanites living in Gezer, so they lived side by side. The pattern of incomplete conquest keeps repeating.
entries.judges 1:30: Zebulun didn't drive out the people of Kitron and Nahalol either, but made them forced laborers. Again, the enemy stayed in the land.
entries.judges 1:31: Asher failed to take several coastal towns, including Acco and Sidon, and didn't drive their people out. Their territory remained partly in enemy hands.
entries.judges 1:32: So the people of Asher ended up living among the Canaanites instead of replacing them. The two peoples shared the land.
entries.judges 1:33: Naphtali didn't remove the people of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath but lived among them and forced them to work. The same compromise shows up again.
entries.judges 1:34: The Amorites pushed the tribe of Dan back into the hills and wouldn't let them come down into the valley. Dan was squeezed out of its lowland territory.
entries.judges 1:35: The Amorites stayed in several hill towns, but when Joseph's tribes grew stronger they forced them to work. The enemy remained but was subdued.
entries.judges 1:36: The boundary of the Edomites ran from the slope of Akrabbim up from Sela. This verse marks the southern edge of the land being described.
entries.joshua 19:41: This verse starts listing the towns that marked the border of the land given to the tribe of Dan. It reminds the reader that God's gift of land was specific and real, not vague.
entries.joshua 19:42: This continues the list of towns in Dan's territory. Each name shows that the land was carefully divided and assigned, town by town.
entries.joshua 19:43: More towns are named as part of Dan's inheritance. The reader sees that the allocation was detailed and orderly.
entries.joshua 19:44: The list of Dan's towns keeps going. These names show that the land was actually handed over to real families and places.
entries.joshua 19:45: The verse adds more towns to Dan's share of the land. It shows the territory was made up of many small communities.
entries.joshua 19:46: This describes the western edge of Dan's land, near the sea opposite Joppa. It shows the territory had clear boundaries on the coast.
