entries.judges 16:7: Samson gave her a false answer, saying fresh bowstrings would make him weak. He was playing a game with her instead of being honest, and that game would cost him dearly.
entries.judges 16:8: The Philistine rulers brought the bowstrings to Delilah, and she tied Samson up with them. The trap was being set exactly as she planned, and Samson let it happen.
entries.judges 16:9: Men were hiding in the room, and when Delilah shouted that the Philistines were coming, Samson snapped the cords like thread. His strength was still with him, but he did not seem to realize how dangerous this game was.
entries.judges 16:10: Delilah complained that Samson had lied to her and demanded the real answer. She kept pressing him, and he kept making up stories instead of walking away.
entries.judges 16:11: Samson gave another false answer, saying new unused ropes would make him weak. He was still toying with her, not taking seriously the danger he was in.
entries.judges 16:12: Delilah tied him with new ropes, and again men were hiding nearby, and again Samson broke free. The pattern repeated, and Samson kept ignoring the warning signs.
entries.judges 16:13: Delilah complained again and asked for the truth, and Samson gave a third false answer about weaving his hair into cloth. He was getting closer to the truth but still not honest.
entries.judges 16:14: While Samson slept, Delilah wove his hair into the cloth and pinned it, then shouted that the Philistines were coming, and he pulled it all loose. He was sleeping through a trap that was closing in on him.
entries.judges 16:15: Delilah accused Samson of not really loving her because he kept his secret from her. This is a common way to pressure someone, and Samson was starting to give in.
entries.judges 16:16: She nagged him day after day until he was worn out and miserable. Constant pressure can wear down even a strong person, so we should be aware of people who won't let us alone.
entries.judges 16:17: Samson finally told her the truth: his hair had never been cut because he was set apart to God from birth, and cutting it would take away his strength. He gave away the one thing that marked him as God's special servant.
entries.judges 16:18: Delilah saw he had finally told the truth, so she called the Philistine rulers to come with the money. She had gotten what she wanted, and Samson had handed her the key to his downfall.
entries.judges 16:19: Delilah put Samson to sleep on her lap and had his hair cut off, and his strength left him. The very thing that set him apart for God was taken from him while he slept.
entries.judges 16:20: Samson woke up and thought he could shake himself free as before, not realizing the Lord had left him. We can get so used to God's help that we stop noticing when it is gone.
entries.judges 16:21: The Philistines captured Samson, blinded him, chained him in bronze, and made him grind grain in prison. His foolish choices led to terrible suffering, a sober warning about the cost of sin.
entries.judges 16:22: Even in prison, Samson's hair began to grow back. God had not completely abandoned him, and there was still hope for what would come next.
entries.judges 16:23: The Philistine rulers gathered to offer a great sacrifice to their god Dagon and celebrate, saying their god had handed Samson over to them. They gave credit to a false god for what had happened.
entries.judges 16:24: When the people saw Samson, they praised their god for giving them victory over the man who had fought against them and killed many of them. People often celebrate a victory without understanding the real story behind it.
entries.judges 16:25: While everyone was celebrating, they brought Samson out of prison to entertain them, and he stood between the pillars of the building. He was being mocked and humiliated in front of his enemies.
entries.judges 16:26: Samson asked the boy leading him to let him lean his hands on the pillars that held up the building. Even blind and weak, he was thinking about what he could do.
entries.judges 16:27: The building was packed with men and women, including all the Philistine rulers, and about three thousand more were on the roof watching Samson. A huge crowd had gathered to laugh at him.
entries.judges 16:28: Samson prayed and asked God to remember him and give him strength one more time, so he could pay back the Philistines for his eyes. Even after all his failures, he turned to God in his last moment.
entries.judges 16:29: Samson put his arms around the two middle pillars that held up the building, leaning on them with his right and left hands. He was positioning himself to bring the whole structure down.
entries.judges 16:30: Samson asked to die with the Philistines, then pushed with all his strength and the building collapsed on everyone, killing more in his death than he had killed in his life. God answered his prayer, but it cost him his own life.
entries.judges 16:31: Samson's family came and buried him in his father's tomb, and he had judged Israel for twenty years. His story ends with both his failures and God's mercy, a reminder that God can still use flawed people.
entries.judges 9:41: Abimelech stayed in Arumah while Zebul forced Gaal and his relatives out of Shechem, refusing to let them live there. This shows that the challenge to Abimelech's power was crushed and his rivals were expelled from the city.
entries.judges 9:42: The next day the people of Shechem went out into the fields, and Abimelech was told about it. Their ordinary activity gave Abimelech the chance he was waiting for.
entries.judges 9:43: Abimelech split his men into three groups and hid them in the fields, then attacked when he saw the people leaving the town. He used a planned ambush rather than an open fight, catching the townspeople off guard.
entries.judges 9:44: Abimelech's group rushed to block the town gate while the other two groups attacked everyone out in the fields and defeated them. The town was trapped and its people outside were cut off.
entries.judges 9:45: Abimelech fought the town all day, captured it, killed its people, and destroyed it, scattering salt over it. Spreading salt was a sign that the place was meant to stay ruined and unusable.
entries.judges 9:46: When the people at the tower of Shechem heard what happened to the town, they crowded into the inner room of the temple of El-berith. They ran to a place they thought was safe, a strong building tied to their worship.
entries.judges 9:47: Abimelech was told that all the men of the tower of Shechem had gathered in one place. Their hiding place became known to him, setting up what he did next.
entries.judges 9:48: Abimelech went up Mount Zalmon, cut branches with an axe, carried them on his back, and told his men to copy him quickly. He was preparing a mass attack using wood as fuel.
entries.judges 9:49: Every man cut a branch, and they piled the wood against the inner room and set it on fire, burning about a thousand men and women inside. The people who sought safety in the temple died there.
entries.judges 9:50: Abimelech then went to Thebez, set up his army against it, and captured it. His campaign of conquest continued to the next town.
entries.judges 9:51: In the middle of Thebez was a strong tower, and all the men and women fled into it, locked themselves in, and went up on its roof. They hoped the tower would protect them from the attack.
entries.judges 9:52: Abimelech came to the tower and attacked it, getting close to its door so he could set it on fire. He was about to repeat the burning tactic that had worked before.
entries.judges 9:53: A woman dropped a heavy upper millstone on Abimelech's head and cracked his skull. The mighty attacker was brought down by an unexpected person in a single blow.
entries.judges 9:54: Abimelech quickly told his servant to run him through with a sword so people would not say a woman killed him, and the servant did so. His concern for his reputation mattered to him even as he was dying.
entries.judges 9:55: When the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they all went home. His death ended the campaign and scattered his army.
entries.judges 9:56: In this way God repaid Abimelech for the evil he did to his father by killing his seventy brothers. The story presents his downfall as God's justice for his crimes.
entries.judges 9:57: God also brought back on the men of Shechem the evil they had done, and Jotham's curse came true on them. The passage says both the cruel ruler and the treacherous city got what their actions deserved.
entries.judges 14:1: Samson traveled to a Philistine town and noticed a woman there. This sets up a choice that will cause trouble, showing how a strong person can still be led by what looks good to him.
entries.judges 14:2: He went home and told his parents to arrange a marriage with this Philistine woman. He expected them to simply do what he wanted because he liked her.
entries.judges 14:3: His parents objected, asking why he couldn't marry a woman from his own people instead of from a group they considered outsiders. Samson ignored their concerns and insisted, because he only cared that she pleased him.
entries.judges 14:4: His parents didn't realize God was using this situation for his own plan against the Philistines, who were ruling over Israel at the time. Even when people make selfish choices, God can still work through them.
entries.judges 14:5: Samson went down to Timnah with his parents and, near the vineyards, a young lion suddenly charged at him. Trouble came at him unexpectedly on an ordinary trip.
entries.judges 14:6: God's Spirit gave Samson sudden strength, and he killed the lion with his bare hands. He kept it a secret from his parents, showing he was already keeping parts of his life hidden from them.
entries.judges 14:7: He continued on and talked with the woman, and he still found her pleasing. His attraction to her remained strong even after the dangerous encounter.
entries.judges 14:8: Later, on his way back to marry her, he turned aside to look at the lion's carcass and found bees and honey inside it. Something sweet had come from something dead and dangerous.
entries.judges 14:9: He scooped up the honey, ate some as he walked, and shared it with his parents without telling them where it came from. He gave them a gift but kept the truth about it to himself.
entries.judges 14:10: Samson went to the woman and held a wedding feast, as young men customarily did. This was a normal celebration that would soon turn into a contest.
entries.judges 14:11: Thirty men were brought in to be with him at the feast. These companions would become the opponents in his riddle.
entries.judges 14:12: Samson proposed a bet: if they could answer his riddle within the seven days of the feast, he would give them thirty sets of clothes. He turned the celebration into a challenge with a costly stake.
entries.judges 14:13: He told them that if they couldn't solve it, they would owe him thirty sets of clothes instead. They agreed and asked to hear the riddle.
entries.judges 14:14: His riddle described food coming from a eater and sweetness coming from something strong, pointing to the honey and the lion. After three days, they still had no answer.
entries.judges 14:15: On the fourth day they threatened Samson's wife, saying they would burn her and her family if she didn't get the answer for them. They were willing to harm her to avoid losing the bet.
entries.judges 14:16: His wife cried and accused him of not loving her because he wouldn't tell her the answer. He pointed out that he hadn't even told his own parents.
entries.judges 14:17: She kept crying about it for the rest of the seven days, and finally he told her because she wouldn't let up. She then passed the answer on to her people.
entries.judges 14:18: Before the wedding night, the men gave him the answer, revealing they had gotten it through his wife. Samson replied that they would never have solved it without using her to pressure him.
entries.judges 14:19: God's Spirit gave Samson power again, and he went to another Philistine city, killed thirty men, and gave their clothes to the men who had answered. Furious, he went back to his father's house.
entries.judges 14:20: Samson's wife was then given to one of the men who had been his companion at the wedding. His marriage ended in betrayal and loss.
entries.judges 18:1: At this time Israel had no king, so everyone did what seemed right to them. The tribe of Dan still had no land of their own to settle in, so they went looking for a place to live.
entries.judges 18:2: The Danites sent five brave men to explore the land and find a good place. On their journey they stopped for the night at Micah's house in the hill country of Ephraim.
entries.judges 18:3: The men recognized the voice of the young Levite and were curious about him. They stopped to ask how he ended up living there.
entries.judges 18:4: The Levite explained that Micah had hired him and paid him to serve as his personal priest.
entries.judges 18:5: The men asked the priest to ask God whether their journey would succeed.
entries.judges 18:6: The priest told them to go in peace and said the Lord would guide their way.
entries.judges 18:7: The five men came to Laish and found a people living carelessly and feeling safe, with plenty of everything and no nearby allies to protect them.
entries.judges 18:8: The men returned home to their fellow Danites, who asked them what they had found.
entries.judges 18:9: The spies urged their people to attack Laish right away, saying the land was excellent and there was no reason to delay.
entries.judges 18:10: They described a people who felt safe and a wide, rich land that God had put within their reach.
entries.judges 18:11: So six hundred Danite men from Zorah and Eshtaol set out ready for battle.
entries.judges 18:12: They camped near Kiriath-jearim in Judah, and the place was called Mahaneh-dan, meaning Dan's camp, from that day on.
entries.judges 18:13: From there they traveled into the hill country of Ephraim and arrived at Micah's house.
entries.judges 18:14: The five spies reminded their companions that Micah's house held religious objects, including an ephod and idols, and hinted they should take them.
entries.judges 18:15: The men turned aside to Micah's house and greeted the young Levite, asking if all was well with him.
entries.judges 18:16: The six hundred armed Danites stood guard at the entrance of the house.
entries.judges 18:17: The five spies went inside and took the idols and the ephod while the priest stood at the door with the armed men.
entries.judges 18:18: When the men came out carrying Micah's religious objects, the priest asked them what they were doing.
entries.judges 18:19: They told him to be quiet and come with them, arguing it was better to be priest for a whole tribe than for one man's household.
entries.judges 18:20: The priest was pleased with this offer, so he took the religious objects and joined the Danites.
entries.judges 18:21: The Danites continued on their way, placing their children, livestock, and possessions in front for safety.
entries.judges 18:22: After they had traveled some distance from Micah's house, Micah and his neighbors caught up with them.
entries.judges 18:23: The Danites turned and asked Micah why he had gathered men and come after them.
entries.judges 18:24: Micah said they had taken his gods and his priest, leaving him with nothing, so he had good reason to be upset.
entries.judges 18:25: The Danites warned Micah to stop complaining, or angry men might attack and kill him and his people.
entries.judges 18:26: The Danites went on their way, and Micah, seeing they were too strong for him, turned back home.
entries.judges 18:27: The Danites took Micah's idols and his priest, then attacked the peaceful people of Laish with the sword and burned their town.
entries.judges 18:28: No one came to help Laish because it was far from Sidon and had no allies, so the Danites rebuilt the town and settled there.
entries.judges 18:29: They renamed the town Dan after their ancestor Dan, son of Israel, though it had formerly been called Laish.
entries.judges 18:30: The Danites set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan, a descendant of Moses, and his sons served as priests for the tribe of Dan until the ark was captured.
entries.judges 18:31: They kept Micah's carved image set up for themselves the whole time God's house was at Shiloh.
entries.ruth 1:1: A famine hit Israel during the time of the judges, so a man from Bethlehem took his wife and two sons to live in Moab to survive. Hard times can push ordinary families to make difficult moves.
entries.ruth 1:2: The man was Elimelech, his wife Naomi, and their sons Mahlon and Chilion, and they settled in Moab for a while. This introduces the family whose story the book will follow.
entries.ruth 1:3: Elimelech died, leaving Naomi alone with her two sons. A family's plans can be shattered by loss, and Naomi's hardship is only beginning.
entries.ruth 1:4: The sons married Moabite women named Orpah and Ruth, and the family stayed there about ten years. These marriages set up the loyalty and love that will matter later in the story.
entries.ruth 1:5: Both sons also died, so Naomi was left with no husband and no sons. She lost nearly everything that gave her security, and her grief is real.
entries.ruth 1:6: Naomi heard that God had blessed his people with food again, so she prepared to return home with her daughters-in-law. News of hope gave her a reason to go back.
entries.ruth 1:7: Naomi left the place where she had been living, and her two daughters-in-law went with her toward Judah. The journey home begins with all three women together.
entries.ruth 1:8: Naomi urged her daughters-in-law to return to their mothers' homes and asked God to bless them for their kindness to her and to the dead. She put their welfare ahead of her own need for company.
entries.ruth 1:9: Naomi prayed that God would give each of them rest and security in a new marriage, then kissed them, and they all wept loudly. Saying goodbye to people you love is deeply painful.
entries.ruth 1:10: Both women insisted they would go back with Naomi to her people. Their love for her made them willing to leave their own homeland.
entries.ruth 1:11: Naomi told them to go back and asked whether she could possibly have more sons who could become their husbands. She was pointing out honestly that she had nothing left to offer them.
entries.ruth 1:12: Naomi said she was too old to marry again, and even if she remarried and had sons that very night, it would not help. She was being realistic about her age and situation.
entries.ruth 1:13: Naomi asked whether the women would wait for sons who might be born, which would be absurd, and said she was sadder for them than for herself because God's hand had gone against her. She felt her suffering was also hurting those who loved her.
entries.ruth 1:14: They wept again, and Orpah kissed Naomi goodbye, but Ruth refused to leave her. The two women made different choices, and Ruth's choice shows deep loyalty.
entries.ruth 1:15: Naomi told Ruth that Orpah had gone back to her people and her gods, and urged Ruth to follow her. She was giving Ruth a free way out.
entries.ruth 1:16: Ruth begged Naomi not to make her leave, promising to go where Naomi goes, stay where she stays, and adopt Naomi's people and God as her own. This is a powerful promise of loyalty that puts relationship above comfort.
entries.ruth 1:17: Ruth vowed that she would die and be buried where Naomi dies, and called on the Lord to punish her if anything but death separated them. She made an unbreakable commitment.
entries.ruth 1:18: When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped arguing. Sometimes the right response to someone's firm love is to accept it.
entries.ruth 1:19: The two women traveled to Bethlehem, and the whole town was stirred up about them, asking if this was really Naomi. Her return drew attention because people remembered her.
entries.ruth 1:20: Naomi told them not to call her Naomi but Mara, meaning bitter, because God had made her life very hard. She was honest about her pain instead of pretending everything was fine.
entries.ruth 1:21: Naomi said she left with plenty and came back empty, and asked why they would still call her Naomi when the Lord had brought sorrow on her. She felt God had turned against her, and she said so plainly.
entries.ruth 1:22: Naomi returned from Moab with Ruth, and they arrived in Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest. The timing matters because the harvest will provide food and a way forward for these two poor women.
entries.judges 21:1: The Israelites had sworn a solemn promise not to let their daughters marry any man from the tribe of Benjamin. That oath later trapped them, because it left Benjamin with no way to keep its families going.
entries.judges 21:2: The people went to Bethel and sat crying bitterly before God until evening. Their grief shows how deeply the near-destruction of one tribe hurt the whole nation.
entries.judges 21:3: They asked God why Israel had come to this point, with one whole tribe now missing. They were bewildered that such a loss had happened among God's own people.
entries.judges 21:4: Early the next day they built an altar and offered sacrifices to God. They were turning to worship while still trying to deal with the damage they had caused.
entries.judges 21:5: They asked who had failed to show up at the national gathering, because they had sworn to put to death anyone who stayed away. That oath set up the next tragic step.
entries.judges 21:6: The Israelites felt sorry for Benjamin, their fellow tribe, and grieved that one tribe had been lost from Israel. Their pity shows they knew something precious had been nearly wiped out.
entries.judges 21:7: They were stuck: the surviving Benjaminite men needed wives, but the Israelites had sworn not to give them their own daughters. Their own promise now stood in the way of fixing the problem.
entries.judges 21:8: They checked which tribe had not come to the gathering at Mizpah, and found that no one from Jabesh-gilead had shown up. That discovery gave them a way to find wives without breaking their oath.
entries.judges 21:9: When the people were counted, none of Jabesh-gilead was there. Their absence made them the target of the oath's penalty.
entries.judges 21:10: The assembly sent twelve thousand fighting men with orders to kill everyone in Jabesh-gilead, including women and children. This was a brutal act done to solve a problem the Israelites had created themselves.
entries.judges 21:11: They were told to kill every male and every woman who had been with a man, but to spare the virgins. The command treated the young women as survivors to be taken.
entries.judges 21:12: They found four hundred young women who had never been with a man and brought them to the camp at Shiloh. These women were taken to become wives for the surviving Benjaminites.
entries.judges 21:13: The whole assembly sent word to the Benjaminite men hiding at the rock of Rimmon, offering them peace. They were trying to bring the surviving tribe back into the nation.
entries.judges 21:14: Benjamin came back, and the four hundred women from Jabesh-gilead were given to them as wives. But there were still not enough women for all the men.
entries.judges 21:15: The people felt sorry for Benjamin because the Lord had allowed disaster to fall on the tribes of Israel. Their pity came after great violence had already been done.
entries.judges 21:16: The leaders asked what could be done for the remaining Benjaminite men, since the women of Benjamin were dead. They still needed a way to keep the tribe from dying out.
entries.judges 21:17: They wanted the survivors of Benjamin to have children so the tribe would not disappear from Israel. Keeping the tribe alive had become their main concern.
entries.judges 21:18: They could not give their own daughters to Benjamin because of the oath they had sworn. So they looked for another way around their promise.
entries.judges 21:19: They pointed out that a yearly festival of the Lord was held at Shiloh, and they described where it was located. That festival would become the setting for their plan.
entries.judges 21:20: They told the Benjaminite men to hide in the vineyards. This was the start of a scheme to get wives without formally breaking the oath.
entries.judges 21:21: They were to watch for the young women of Shiloh coming out to dance, then seize one each and take her home to Benjamin. The plan used force and surprise rather than a proper marriage arrangement.
entries.judges 21:22: If the women's fathers or brothers complained, the leaders would ask them to let it go, arguing that the men had not been given wives in war and that the families would not be guilty of breaking the oath. This was a convenient excuse to cover the wrongdoing.
entries.judges 21:23: The Benjaminites did as told, each grabbing a wife from the dancers, then returned to rebuild their towns and settle there. The tribe survived, but through kidnapping rather than honorable means.
entries.judges 21:24: The Israelites then went home, each to his own tribe and family and inherited land. The national crisis ended and everyone returned to normal life.
entries.judges 21:25: There was no king in Israel at that time, and everyone did whatever seemed right to himself. This explains why so much confusion and wrongdoing happened, and it warns against a life guided only by personal opinion.
entries.ruth 3:1: Naomi wants to find a safe, secure home for Ruth, her widowed daughter-in-law. It shows that love in a family means actively looking out for the other person's future and security.
entries.ruth 3:2: Naomi points out that Boaz, a relative who could protect them, is working at the threshing floor that night. She is making a careful plan based on what she knows about him and the situation.
entries.ruth 3:3: Naomi tells Ruth to wash, put on perfume and her best clothes, then go to Boaz but stay out of sight until he has finished eating. This was a practical way to prepare for a serious, respectful approach to him.
entries.ruth 3:4: Naomi tells Ruth to notice where Boaz lies down, then uncover his feet and lie there, and he will tell her what to do. Ruth is being asked to trust her mother-in-law's guidance and to let Boaz take the lead.
entries.ruth 3:5: Ruth simply agrees to do everything Naomi has told her. Her answer shows her trust in Naomi and her willingness to follow a plan that could change her whole life.
entries.ruth 3:6: Ruth goes to the threshing floor and carries out Naomi's instructions exactly. Her obedience shows she is serious about seeking a secure future and is willing to act on good advice.
entries.ruth 3:7: After Boaz has eaten and drunk and is in good spirits, he lies down by the grain, and Ruth quietly comes and lies at his feet. She is following the plan carefully and discreetly.
entries.ruth 3:8: In the middle of the night Boaz wakes with a start and is startled to find a woman lying at his feet. The scene shows how unexpected and bold Ruth's action was.
entries.ruth 3:9: Boaz asks who she is, and Ruth identifies herself and asks him to take her as his wife because he is a close relative. She is openly asking him to accept the responsibility of protecting and providing for her.
entries.ruth 3:10: Boaz blesses Ruth and praises her for choosing to seek a family protector rather than chasing after younger men, rich or poor. He recognizes her loyalty and good character.
entries.ruth 3:11: Boaz tells Ruth not to be afraid and promises to do whatever she asks, because everyone in town knows she is a woman of good character. He reassures her that her reputation and request are respected.
entries.ruth 3:12: Boaz admits he is a close relative, but there is an even closer one who has the first right to act. He is being honest and fair rather than rushing to take what was not yet his to take.
entries.ruth 3:13: Boaz tells Ruth to stay the night, and in the morning he will let the closer relative do his duty if he will; if not, Boaz swears before God that he himself will marry her. He promises to settle the matter properly and without delay.
entries.ruth 3:14: Ruth stays at his feet until morning and leaves before it is light enough for people to recognize each other, and Boaz asks that her visit be kept quiet. He is protecting her reputation while the matter is still unresolved.
entries.ruth 3:15: Boaz tells Ruth to hold out her cloak, and he pours six measures of grain into it for her to carry back to town. This is a generous gift that shows his care for her and for Naomi.
entries.ruth 3:16: When Ruth gets home, Naomi asks how things went, and Ruth tells her everything Boaz had done. The two women share the outcome openly and honestly.
entries.ruth 3:17: Ruth explains that Boaz gave her the grain so she would not return to Naomi empty-handed. The gift is a sign of his kindness and a pledge that he is taking the situation seriously.
entries.ruth 3:18: Naomi tells Ruth to wait quietly and see what happens, because Boaz will not rest until he has settled the matter that day. She is confident that Boaz will keep his word and act quickly.
entries.ruth 4:1: Boaz went to the town gate, where business was done, and called over the closer relative and some witnesses. He wanted to settle the family matter publicly and fairly.
entries.ruth 4:2: Boaz gathered ten town leaders to sit as official witnesses. This made the agreement legal and public, so no one could dispute it later.
entries.ruth 4:3: Boaz told the closer relative that Naomi was selling the family land that had belonged to Elimelech. He was explaining the deal before offering it to him.
entries.ruth 4:4: Boaz offered the relative the first chance to buy the land, as the law required, and the man agreed to do it. Boaz was being fair by letting the closer relative decide first.
entries.ruth 4:5: Boaz added that whoever bought the land also had to marry Ruth and keep her dead husband's family name alive. The deal came with a responsibility, not just property.
entries.ruth 4:6: The closer relative backed out because taking on Ruth and the land could harm his own family's inheritance. He gave up his right to Boaz.
entries.ruth 4:7: In those days, a man took off his sandal and gave it to the other person to seal a deal. It was the public way of making an agreement official.
entries.ruth 4:8: The closer relative told Boaz to take the land and handed over his sandal as proof. He was officially giving up his claim.
entries.ruth 4:9: Boaz announced to the witnesses that he had legally bought all the property that had belonged to Elimelech and his sons. He made the purchase public and official.
entries.ruth 4:10: Boaz also announced that he was marrying Ruth to keep her dead husband's name and memory alive. The witnesses were there to confirm both the land deal and the marriage.
entries.ruth 4:11: The people and leaders agreed to be witnesses and blessed the couple. They prayed that Ruth would be like Rachel and Leah, the mothers of Israel, and that Boaz would prosper.
entries.ruth 4:12: They prayed that Boaz's family would be as great as Perez's family, which came from Tamar and Judah. They were asking God to bless the children Boaz and Ruth would have.
entries.ruth 4:13: Boaz married Ruth, and God gave her a son. This was the happy result of her loyalty and Boaz's kindness.
entries.ruth 4:14: The women praised God for giving Naomi a grandson and a family line to carry on. They saw this as God's kindness to her after her loss.
entries.ruth 4:15: They told Naomi the child would bring her new life and care for her in old age. They praised Ruth, whose love for Naomi was worth more than seven sons.
entries.ruth 4:16: Naomi took the baby and held him close, caring for him as her own. Her emptiness and grief were replaced with joy and purpose.
entries.ruth 4:17: The neighbor women named the baby Obed, which means servant or worshiper, and he became the grandfather of King David. This ordinary family became part of God's plan for Israel's greatest king.
entries.ruth 4:18: The book ends with a family list starting with Perez. This shows the family line that led from the past to the present.
entries.ruth 4:19: The list continues through Hezron, Ram, and Amminadab. Each name shows the family line moving forward through the generations.
entries.ruth 4:20: The family line goes on through Nahshon and Salmon. These names connect the earlier generations to Boaz.
entries.ruth 4:21: Salmon was Boaz's father, and Boaz was Obed's father. This ties Boaz and Ruth directly into the family line.
entries.ruth 4:22: Obed was Jesse's father, and Jesse was David's father. The story ends by showing that Ruth, a foreigner, became the great-grandmother of King David.
entries.ruth 2:1: Naomi had a wealthy relative on her husband's side named Boaz. This matters because he will become the key person who helps the two women survive.
entries.ruth 2:2: Ruth asks Naomi for permission to go into the fields and pick up leftover grain behind the workers. This was a humble way for a poor person to get food, and Ruth is willing to do it.
entries.ruth 2:3: Ruth went out and happened to end up in a field owned by Boaz, a relative of her father-in-law. What looked like chance was really the start of God's help for them.
entries.ruth 2:4: Boaz arrived and greeted his workers with a blessing, and they blessed him back. This shows he was a kind and respectful boss.
entries.ruth 2:5: Boaz noticed Ruth and asked his foreman who she was. He was paying attention to a stranger in his field.
entries.ruth 2:6: The foreman told him she was the Moabite woman who had come back from Moab with Naomi. Everyone knew her story.
entries.ruth 2:7: The foreman said Ruth had politely asked to gather grain and had worked hard all morning without a break. She was humble and diligent.
entries.ruth 2:8: Boaz tells Ruth to stay in his field and keep close to his young women workers. He is offering her safety and protection.
entries.ruth 2:9: Boaz tells her to follow the women cutting grain, promises the men won't bother her, and says she can drink from the water his workers have. He is looking out for her needs.
entries.ruth 2:10: Ruth bows down and asks why Boaz would notice her, since she is a foreigner. She is surprised by his kindness.
entries.ruth 2:11: Boaz says he has heard how Ruth left her own parents and homeland to stay with Naomi after her husband died. He respects her loyalty and sacrifice.
entries.ruth 2:12: Boaz asks God to reward Ruth and says she has come under God's protection. He is praying that God will bless her for what she has done.
entries.ruth 2:13: Ruth thanks Boaz and says his kind words have comforted her, even though she isn't one of his own servants. She feels encouraged and valued.
entries.ruth 2:14: At mealtime Boaz invites Ruth to eat with his workers and even gives her extra roasted grain. She eats until she is full, showing his generosity.
entries.ruth 2:15: When Ruth went back to work, Boaz told his men to let her gather grain even among the bundles and not to embarrass her. He quietly made her work easier.
entries.ruth 2:16: Boaz also told the men to pull out some grain and leave it for her, and to speak kindly to her. He went out of his way to provide for her.
entries.ruth 2:17: Ruth gathered grain until evening, then threshed it, and it came to about a full ephah, a large amount. Her hard work paid off with enough food for many days.
entries.ruth 2:18: Ruth carried the grain home, showed Naomi what she had gathered, and gave her the food she had left over. She shared generously with her mother-in-law.
entries.ruth 2:19: Naomi asked where Ruth had worked and asked God to bless the man who helped her. When Ruth said it was Boaz, Naomi recognized his name.
entries.ruth 2:20: Naomi praised God for his kindness and told Ruth that Boaz is a close relative, one of their family guardians. This was very good news for their future.
entries.ruth 2:21: Ruth told Naomi that Boaz had invited her to stay close to his workers until the whole harvest was finished. That meant steady food and safety for weeks.
entries.ruth 2:22: Naomi agreed it was safer for Ruth to stay with Boaz's servant girls than to go to another field where she might be harmed. She was protecting her daughter-in-law.
entries.ruth 2:23: Ruth stayed with Boaz's workers through the barley and wheat harvests and kept living with Naomi. She worked steadily and remained loyal to her mother-in-law.
entries.1 samuel 1:1: This introduces Elkanah, a man from the hill country of Ephraim, and lists his family line. It reminds the reader that this story is about a real, ordinary family with a history.
entries.1 samuel 1:2: Elkanah had two wives, and one of them, Peninnah, had children while Hannah had none. In that culture, having no children was a deep sorrow, so this sets up Hannah's pain.
entries.1 samuel 1:3: Elkanah faithfully went to Shiloh each year to worship and offer sacrifices to God, where Eli's sons served as priests. It shows his devotion, but also hints that the priesthood there had problems.
entries.1 samuel 1:4: When Elkanah offered his sacrifice, he shared the meat with Peninnah and all her children. This was a joyful family meal connected to worship.
entries.1 samuel 1:5: Elkanah gave Hannah a special portion because he loved her, even though God had not given her children. His love did not erase her sorrow, but he showed her kindness.
entries.1 samuel 1:6: Peninnah deliberately provoked Hannah to make her miserable about being childless. It shows how one person's cruelty can deepen another's grief.
entries.1 samuel 1:7: This happened year after year, and Peninnah's taunting at worship time left Hannah weeping and unable to eat. The place meant for worship became a place of pain for her.
entries.1 samuel 1:8: Elkanah asked Hannah why she was crying and reminded her that he loved her more than many sons could. He meant well, but his words could not fully heal her longing.
entries.1 samuel 1:9: After the family meal at Shiloh, Hannah got up while Eli the priest was sitting by the doorway of the Lord's temple. The scene shifts to her private moment with God.
entries.1 samuel 1:10: Deeply grieved and crying, Hannah poured out her prayer to the Lord. She brought her pain honestly to God rather than hiding it.
entries.1 samuel 1:11: Hannah made a vow: if God gave her a son, she would dedicate him to the Lord for life as a Nazirite. She was willing to give back to God what she most longed for.
entries.1 samuel 1:12: Hannah prayed for a long time, and Eli watched her mouth. Her long prayer drew the attention of the priest.
entries.1 samuel 1:13: Hannah was praying silently from her heart, with only her lips moving, so Eli assumed she was drunk. He misread her deep devotion as misbehavior.
entries.1 samuel 1:14: Eli told her to sober up and put away her wine. He judged her wrongly without knowing what was really happening.
entries.1 samuel 1:15: Hannah respectfully explained that she was not drunk but was pouring out her broken heart to the Lord. She defended herself calmly and honestly.
entries.1 samuel 1:16: She asked Eli not to think of her as a worthless woman, since her words came from great sorrow and pain. She wanted to be understood rather than condemned.
entries.1 samuel 1:17: Eli blessed her and prayed that Israel's God would grant her request. His words turned from accusation to encouragement.
entries.1 samuel 1:18: Hannah accepted his blessing, went back to eat, and her face was no longer sad. The priest's kindness and her trust in God lifted her spirits.
entries.1 samuel 1:19: The family worshiped early in the morning and returned home, and God remembered Hannah. The phrase means God acted on her behalf at the right time.
entries.1 samuel 1:20: Hannah became pregnant and gave birth to a son, naming him Samuel because she had asked the Lord for him. The name reflects her prayer being answered.
entries.1 samuel 1:21: Elkanah went up with his family for the yearly sacrifice and to keep his vow. He continued his regular pattern of worship.
entries.1 samuel 1:22: Hannah chose to stay home until the child was weaned, then planned to bring him to the Lord permanently. She took her vow seriously and waited for the right time.
entries.1 samuel 1:23: Elkanah agreed to let her wait until the child was weaned and encouraged her to keep her promise to God. He supported her decision rather than pressuring her.
entries.1 samuel 1:24: Once Samuel was weaned, Hannah brought him to Shiloh with an ox, flour, and wine for sacrifice. She came prepared to fulfill her vow.
entries.1 samuel 1:25: After offering the ox, they brought the young child to Eli the priest. The moment of dedication had arrived.
entries.1 samuel 1:26: Hannah reminded Eli that she was the woman he had seen praying there before. She connected her present joy to that earlier painful moment.
entries.1 samuel 1:27: She explained that this child was the answer to her prayer. She gave God the credit for what she had asked and received.
entries.1 samuel 1:28: Hannah gave Samuel to the Lord for his whole life, and they worshiped there. Her gift back to God came from gratitude for the gift he had given her.
entries.judges 19:1: This sets the scene in a time when Israel had no king, so everyone did as they pleased. It introduces a Levite and his concubine, and the lack of leadership hints that trouble is coming.
entries.judges 19:2: The woman was unfaithful to him and left to stay with her father for four months. Her leaving sets off the chain of events that follows.
entries.judges 19:3: Her husband went to win her back and speak kindly to her, bringing supplies and a servant. Her father welcomed him warmly, showing the man meant to make peace.
entries.judges 19:4: His father-in-law urged him to stay three days, and they ate, drank, and rested together. The hospitality was generous and relaxed.
entries.judges 19:5: On the fourth day the man tried to leave early, but his father-in-law pressed him to eat first for strength. The repeated delays show how much the father wanted him to stay.
entries.judges 19:6: They sat down to eat and drink together, and the father-in-law invited him to stay another night and enjoy himself. The man's plans to leave kept getting pushed back.
entries.judges 19:7: The man got up to go, but his father-in-law persuaded him to stay one more night. The pressure to linger was strong.
entries.judges 19:8: On the fifth day the man tried again, but the father-in-law urged him to eat, and they did not leave until midday. The delays were wearing on, and the day was slipping away.
entries.judges 19:9: The father-in-law pointed out that evening was near and urged one more night's rest before an early start. He kept finding reasons for them to stay.
entries.judges 19:10: This time the man refused to stay and left with his concubine and donkeys, heading toward Jebus (Jerusalem). His decision to leave late set them up to be on the road at nightfall.
entries.judges 19:11: As they neared Jebus, the servant suggested stopping there for the night. It seemed like a sensible plan.
entries.judges 19:12: The master refused to stay in a non-Israelite town and insisted on going on to Gibeah. His choice of where to stop would prove fateful.
entries.judges 19:13: He suggested they press on to Gibeah or Ramah to spend the night. They kept moving as darkness came.
entries.judges 19:14: They continued and reached the area of Gibeah in Benjamin's territory just as the sun set. They were now far from home with night falling.
entries.judges 19:15: They stopped in Gibeah and sat in the town square, but no one offered them a place to stay. Being left outside at night was a sign of danger and cold hospitality.
entries.judges 19:16: An old man from Ephraim, living among the Benjamites, came in from his field and saw them. He was an outsider in that town, which may explain his kindness.
entries.judges 19:17: The old man asked the traveler where he was going and where he came from. A simple question opened the way for hospitality.
entries.judges 19:18: The man explained he was traveling home from Bethlehem to Ephraim and that no one would take him in. His words show he was a stranger with nowhere to go.
entries.judges 19:19: He assured the old man they had everything they needed for themselves and their animals. They were not asking for supplies, only shelter.
entries.judges 19:20: The old man welcomed him and promised to take care of all his needs, insisting he not sleep in the street. This was the kindness the traveler had been waiting for.
entries.judges 19:21: He brought them into his house, fed the donkeys, washed their feet, and gave them food and drink. The old man showed full hospitality.
entries.judges 19:22: While they were enjoying the meal, worthless men of the town surrounded the house and pounded on the door, demanding the guest be sent out so they could abuse him. The scene turns from welcome to terror.
entries.judges 19:23: The old man went out and pleaded with them not to do this wicked thing, reminding them the man was his guest. He tried to protect him.
entries.judges 19:24: In a shocking offer, the old man proposed sending out his virgin daughter and the man's concubine instead, begging them not to shame his guest. This shows how badly women were treated in that culture.
entries.judges 19:25: The men refused to listen, so the man pushed his concubine out to them, and they abused her all night until morning. This is a horrifying act of cruelty and betrayal.
entries.judges 19:26: At dawn the woman crawled back to the door of the house where her master was and collapsed there until daylight. She had nowhere else to go and was left broken.
entries.judges 19:27: In the morning her master got up to leave and found her lying at the door with her hands on the threshold. He expected to find her ready to travel.
entries.judges 19:28: He told her to get up so they could go, but she did not answer, so he put her on the donkey and went home. The text leaves it unclear whether she was dead or unconscious.
entries.judges 19:29: At home he cut her body into twelve pieces and sent them throughout Israel. This gruesome act was meant to shock the nation into responding to the crime.
entries.judges 19:30: He told the messengers to ask all Israel whether such a thing had ever happened since they left Egypt, and to consider what should be done. The question demanded a response to the horror, and the story shows how far Israel had fallen without good leadership.
entries.judges 20:41: The Israelites had tricked the Benjaminites by circling back, and suddenly the Benjaminites realized they were trapped and doomed. It shows how quickly a situation can turn when you think you are winning.
entries.judges 20:42: The Benjaminites ran toward the desert to escape, but the fighting caught up with them and other Israelites came out of the town to cut them off. There was no safe way out for them.
entries.judges 20:43: The Israelites surrounded and crushed the Benjaminites, chasing them from Nohah toward the east of Gibeah. The pursuit was relentless and gave them no rest.
entries.judges 20:44: Eighteen thousand of Benjamin's best soldiers died in that battle. The loss was enormous for a small tribe.
entries.judges 20:45: The survivors fled toward a rocky place called Rimmon, but the Israelites caught and killed five thousand along the roads and two thousand more near Geba. Even the escape route became a place of death.
entries.judges 20:46: In total, twenty-five thousand Benjaminite soldiers died that day. It was a devastating defeat that nearly wiped out the tribe's fighting force.
entries.judges 20:47: Only six hundred men survived by hiding at the rock of Rimmon, where they stayed for four months. A whole tribe was reduced to a small remnant hiding in fear.
entries.judges 20:48: The Israelites then went through Benjamin's towns, killing people and animals and burning everything. The punishment went far beyond the battlefield and left the tribe's homeland in ruins.
entries.1 samuel 3:1: God rarely spoke to people in those days, and young Samuel served God by helping the priest Eli. It reminds us that God can still speak even when things seem quiet.
entries.1 samuel 3:2: Eli was old and his eyesight was failing, so he was lying down to rest. It shows that even the leaders of God's people grow weak.
entries.1 samuel 3:3: The lamp in God's house was still lit and Samuel was sleeping near the ark, the special chest that stood for God's presence. God often speaks in ordinary, quiet moments.
entries.1 samuel 3:4: God called Samuel by name, and Samuel answered right away. God knows each person by name and invites us to respond.
entries.1 samuel 3:5: Samuel ran to Eli because he thought the old priest had called him, but Eli sent him back to bed. It shows how easy it is to mistake God's voice for someone else's.
entries.1 samuel 3:6: God called again and Samuel again went to Eli, who still said he had not called. God is patient and keeps calling even when we don't understand at first.
entries.1 samuel 3:7: Samuel did not yet know God personally, and God's word had not yet been revealed to him. Knowing about God is not the same as knowing him, and that knowledge can grow.
entries.1 samuel 3:8: After the third call, Eli realized it was God speaking to the boy. Sometimes we need someone older or wiser to help us recognize what God is doing.
entries.1 samuel 3:9: Eli told Samuel to answer the next call by saying he was listening as God's servant. We can prepare our hearts to listen and respond when God speaks.
entries.1 samuel 3:10: God came and called Samuel twice by name, and Samuel answered as Eli had taught him. God speaks personally, and we can answer him with open ears.
entries.1 samuel 3:11: God told Samuel he was about to do something in Israel so shocking that everyone who heard it would be stunned. God's judgment is real and should be taken seriously.
entries.1 samuel 3:12: God said he would carry out everything he had warned about Eli's family. God keeps his word, both his promises and his warnings.
entries.1 samuel 3:13: God was punishing Eli's family because his sons were cursing God and Eli did not stop them. Leaders are responsible for correcting serious wrong in those they oversee.
entries.1 samuel 3:14: God swore that no sacrifice could ever remove the guilt of Eli's family. Some choices have consequences that cannot be undone by religious rituals.
entries.1 samuel 3:15: Samuel stayed in bed until morning and was afraid to tell Eli what God had said. It is natural to fear delivering hard news, but honesty matters.
entries.1 samuel 3:16: Eli called Samuel his son, and Samuel answered him respectfully. A relationship of trust and respect makes hard conversations possible.
entries.1 samuel 3:17: Eli demanded to hear everything God said and warned Samuel not to hide anything. We should be willing to hear the whole truth, even the parts we don't like.
entries.1 samuel 3:18: Samuel told Eli everything, and Eli accepted it, saying God should do what seems right to him. Trusting God means accepting his will even when it is painful.
entries.1 samuel 3:19: As Samuel grew, God was with him and made everything he said come true. God backs up the words of those who faithfully serve him.
entries.1 samuel 3:20: Everyone in Israel, from one end of the land to the other, recognized Samuel as a true prophet of God. A faithful life earns trust and recognition over time.
entries.1 samuel 3:21: God continued to appear at Shiloh and gave Samuel his messages there. God keeps speaking to his people through those he has chosen.
entries.1 samuel 4:1: The Philistines gathered their army to fight Israel, and both sides set up camp facing each other. This sets the scene for a battle the Israelites were about to lose.
entries.1 samuel 4:2: The Philistines attacked, the fighting was fierce, and Israel was beaten, losing about four thousand soldiers. A defeat like this would have shaken the people's confidence.
entries.1 samuel 4:3: The Israelite leaders asked why God had let them lose, then decided to bring the ark of the covenant from Shiloh, hoping it would protect them and give them victory. They treated the ark like a lucky charm instead of trusting God himself.
entries.1 samuel 4:4: The people sent for the ark, which was kept at Shiloh and was associated with God's presence, and Eli's two sons Hophni and Phinehas came with it. These sons were known for doing evil, so carrying the ark did not make them right with God.
entries.1 samuel 4:5: When the ark arrived at the camp, the Israelites shouted so loudly that the ground shook. They were confident the ark would save them.
entries.1 samuel 4:6: The Philistines heard the loud shouting and realized the ark of the Lord had been brought into the Israelite camp. They understood something unusual was happening.
entries.1 samuel 4:7: The Philistines were terrified and said God had come into the Israelite camp, and they feared disaster because nothing like this had happened before. They were afraid of the God of Israel.
entries.1 samuel 4:8: The Philistines asked who could save them from these mighty gods, remembering how those gods had struck the Egyptians with plagues in the wilderness. They were recalling Israel's history and feared the same power.
entries.1 samuel 4:9: The Philistines urged each other to be strong and fight bravely so they would not become servants of the Hebrews as the Hebrews had been to them. They chose courage over fear.
entries.1 samuel 4:10: The Philistines fought, Israel was defeated, and every man fled to his tent, with thirty thousand foot soldiers killed. It was a devastating loss for Israel.
entries.1 samuel 4:11: The ark of God was captured, and Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas were killed. The very things Israel trusted in were taken away.
entries.1 samuel 4:12: A man from Benjamin ran from the battle to Shiloh that same day, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head as signs of grief. He came to bring terrible news.
entries.1 samuel 4:13: Eli was sitting by the road watching, worried about the ark of God, and when the man arrived and told the news, the whole town cried out loudly. Eli's greatest fear was losing the ark.
entries.1 samuel 4:14: Eli heard the noise and crying and asked what it meant, and the man hurried over to tell him. Eli was anxious to know what had happened.
entries.1 samuel 4:15: Eli was ninety-eight years old and his eyes were so weak he could not see. He was old and blind, which made the news even harder for him.
entries.1 samuel 4:16: The man told Eli he had fled from the battle that day, and Eli asked him how things had gone. Eli was eager for news.
entries.1 samuel 4:17: The messenger reported that Israel had fled, many had died, Eli's two sons were dead, and the ark of God had been captured. This was the worst possible news for Eli.
entries.1 samuel 4:18: When Eli heard that the ark had been taken, he fell backward off his seat by the town gate, broke his neck, and died, since he was old and heavy; he had judged Israel for forty years. The loss of the ark hit him hardest.
entries.1 samuel 4:19: Phinehas's wife, who was pregnant and about to give birth, went into labor suddenly when she heard the ark was taken and her husband and father-in-law were dead. The shock brought on her delivery.
entries.1 samuel 4:20: As she was dying, the women attending her told her not to fear because she had given birth to a son, but she did not answer or pay attention. She was too overcome by grief to respond.
entries.1 samuel 4:21: She named the baby Ichabod, meaning the glory has gone from Israel, because the ark of God had been taken and because of her father-in-law and husband. The name was a sad reminder of what Israel had lost.
entries.1 samuel 4:22: She repeated that the glory had gone from Israel because the ark of God had been taken. For her, losing the ark meant losing God's presence and honor among the people.
entries.1 samuel 5:1: The Philistines had captured Israel's sacred chest, the ark, and carried it from the battlefield to their own city of Ashdod. It shows that winning a battle did not mean they had power over Israel's God.
entries.1 samuel 5:2: They placed the ark inside the temple of their god Dagon, setting it beside the idol as if Dagon had defeated Israel's God. They were treating the true God as one god among many.
entries.1 samuel 5:3: The next morning they found their idol Dagon fallen face down in front of the ark, like a servant bowing to a master. They set it back up, not realizing their god was being shown to be powerless.
entries.1 samuel 5:4: The following morning Dagon had fallen again, and this time its head and hands were broken off, leaving only the stump. This pictured their god as completely helpless before the God of Israel.
entries.1 samuel 5:5: Because of this, the priests of Dagon and visitors to the temple would not step on that doorway threshold. The story explains a custom that lasted long after.
entries.1 samuel 5:6: God brought a painful disease on the people of Ashdod and the surrounding area. The ark they thought was a trophy was actually bringing judgment on them.
entries.1 samuel 5:7: The people of Ashdod realized the ark was bringing trouble on them and their god, so they wanted it gone. They began to see that Israel's God was stronger than they had assumed.
entries.1 samuel 5:8: The Philistine rulers decided to move the ark to another city, Gath, hoping to escape the trouble. But moving the problem elsewhere did not solve it.
entries.1 samuel 5:9: Once the ark arrived in Gath, God's judgment struck that city too, and people of every age and rank broke out in disease. The trouble followed the ark wherever it went.
entries.1 samuel 5:10: The ark was then sent to Ekron, and the people there panicked, fearing it had been sent to kill them. They understood by now that the ark meant danger, not victory.
entries.1 samuel 5:11: The Philistine rulers finally agreed to send the ark back to Israel so it would stop causing death among them. Fear of death had spread through the whole city because God's hand was so heavy on them.
entries.1 samuel 5:12: Those who survived the disease were still suffering terribly, and the city's cry of distress rose up to heaven. The whole episode shows that no one can treat the living God lightly.
entries.1 samuel 6:1: God's sacred chest had been captured by Israel's enemies and stayed in their land for seven months. Even when God's people lose, God is still at work among those who don't know him.
entries.1 samuel 6:2: The Philistines called in their priests and fortune-tellers to ask how to get rid of the ark properly. When people are frightened by God's power, they often look for advice from the wrong sources.
entries.1 samuel 6:3: The advisers said to send the ark back with a gift to make up for wrong, and then they would be healed and understand why trouble had come. Admitting you were wrong and making things right is the first step toward peace.
entries.1 samuel 6:4: They were told to send five gold models of the tumors and five gold mice, one for each Philistine ruler, because the disease had hit everyone. The gift matched the harm done, showing they took the damage seriously.
entries.1 samuel 6:5: Making these gold models and honoring Israel's God might stop the sickness on them, their gods, and their land. Honoring God, even when you don't fully understand him, is wiser than ignoring him.
entries.1 samuel 6:6: They were warned not to be stubborn like Pharaoh, who only let Israel go after being humbled. Stubbornness against God only makes things harder for yourself in the end.
entries.1 samuel 6:7: They were told to build a new cart and hitch two cows that had never been used for work, then take their calves away from them. Setting up a test like this would show whether God or chance was behind the trouble.
entries.1 samuel 6:8: They were to put the ark and the gold gifts on the cart and send it off on its own. Leaving the outcome to God was a way of letting him show what he wanted.
entries.1 samuel 6:9: If the cart went toward Israel, they would know God had caused the disaster; if not, it was just bad luck. Watching what happens can help you see whether God is involved.
entries.1 samuel 6:10: The men did exactly as they were told, hitching the cows and penning up their calves. Obeying good advice, even when it seems strange, is often the right move.
entries.1 samuel 6:11: They loaded the ark of the Lord and the chest of gold gifts onto the cart. The gifts and the ark traveled together as a package back to Israel.
entries.1 samuel 6:12: The cows went straight down the road toward Beth-shemesh without turning aside, lowing as they went, and the Philistine rulers followed to the border. God can guide even animals to do his will, which is a comfort when you feel powerless.
entries.1 samuel 6:13: The people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat when they looked up, saw the ark, and were thrilled. Seeing God's presence return brings real joy to those who have missed it.
entries.1 samuel 6:14: The cart stopped in Joshua's field by a large stone, and the people broke up the cart for firewood and sacrificed the cows to the Lord. Responding to God's arrival with worship is the right reaction.
entries.1 samuel 6:15: The Levites, the priests' helpers, took down the ark and the gold chest and set them on the big stone, and the people offered sacrifices and worshiped that day. God's people are to handle holy things with care and honor.
entries.1 samuel 6:16: The five Philistine rulers watched all this and then went home to Ekron that same day. Once they saw God's power at work, they knew to leave it alone.
entries.1 samuel 6:17: The gold tumors were a guilt offering, one for each of the five Philistine cities: Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. Each city's gift showed that every place had been affected and needed to make things right.
entries.1 samuel 6:18: The gold mice matched every Philistine town, both walled cities and open country, and the large stone where the ark was set down was still there when this was written. Remembering where God acted in the past helps later generations trust him.
entries.1 samuel 6:19: God struck down seventy men of Beth-shemesh because they looked inside the ark, and the people mourned deeply. God is holy, and treating him casually has serious consequences even for his own people.
entries.1 samuel 6:20: The people asked who could stand before such a holy God and where the ark could go next. Realizing God's holiness makes us humble and careful about how we approach him.
entries.1 samuel 6:21: They sent word to the people of Kiriath-jearim to come and take the ark to their town. When you don't know how to handle something holy, it's wise to ask others who can help you honor God properly.
entries.1 samuel 2:1: Hannah is praying out of deep joy because God answered her prayer and helped her. It means you can be honest and glad before God when he lifts you up, even if others opposed you.
entries.1 samuel 2:2: Hannah says there is no one and nothing like God—he alone is holy and completely reliable. It means you can trust God as a solid rock when everything else feels shaky.
entries.1 samuel 2:3: She warns people to stop bragging and talking big, because God knows everything and judges what people do. It means watch your proud words, since God sees and weighs your actions.
entries.1 samuel 2:4: God can break the power of strong warriors and give strength to the weak. It means human strength is not what decides things—God can reverse who is strong and who is not.
entries.1 samuel 2:5: People who had plenty can end up begging, while the needy find rest, and a childless woman can become a mother of many. It means God can turn around anyone's situation, so don't assume things will stay as they are.
entries.1 samuel 2:6: God is the one who decides life and death, bringing people down to the grave and raising them up. It means your life and death are in God's hands, not just chance.
entries.1 samuel 2:7: God gives wealth and can take it away, and he can bring people low or lift them high. It means don't put your security in money, since God is the one who really controls it.
entries.1 samuel 2:8: God lifts the poor and needy from the dust and gives them a place of honor with rulers. It means no one is too low for God to raise up and treat with dignity.
entries.1 samuel 2:9: God protects the steps of those who belong to him, but wicked people will be silenced in darkness, because strength alone won't save anyone. It means you can rely on God's protection rather than your own power.
entries.1 samuel 2:10: Those who fight against God will be shattered, and God will judge the whole earth and strengthen his chosen king. It means opposing God is a losing battle, and he is the final judge over everyone.
entries.1 samuel 2:11: Elkanah goes home to Ramah, and young Samuel stays to serve the Lord under the priest Eli. It means Samuel's life of service began early, showing that even a child can be given to God's work.
entries.1 samuel 2:12: Eli's sons were wicked men who had no real knowledge of the Lord. It means being religious by position doesn't mean knowing God—character matters more than role.
entries.1 samuel 2:13: The priests had a custom of sending a servant with a three-pronged hook to take meat from people's offerings. It means the priests were taking what was meant for worship, which sets up the problem of greed.
entries.1 samuel 2:14: Whatever meat came up on the hook, the priest's servant took for the priests, and this happened to everyone bringing offerings at Shiloh. It means the priests were grabbing their share in a way that treated people's offerings as fair game.
entries.1 samuel 2:15: Even before the fat was burned, the priest's servant demanded raw meat for the priest instead of the boiled portion. It means they were greedy and disrespectful of how God's offerings were supposed to work.
entries.1 samuel 2:16: If the worshiper asked them to burn the fat first, the servant refused and threatened to take the meat by force. It means the priests were bullying people and ignoring God's rules for worship.
entries.1 samuel 2:17: The sin of these young men was very serious before the Lord because they treated his offerings with contempt. It means disrespecting God in worship is not a small thing—it is serious in his eyes.
entries.1 samuel 2:18: Samuel, still a child, served in the Lord's house wearing a linen ephod. It means even a young person can faithfully serve God, and his example stands out against the corruption around him.
entries.1 samuel 2:19: His mother made him a small robe and brought it each year when she came with her husband for the annual offering. It means small, faithful acts of care can support someone's service to God year after year.
entries.1 samuel 2:20: Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife, asking God to give them children in place of the son they gave to the Lord. It means God honors those who give sacrificially, and blessing can come through faithful priests.
entries.1 samuel 2:21: God showed mercy to Hannah and she had three more sons and two daughters, while Samuel grew up before the Lord. It means God can restore what was given up, and he was watching over Samuel's growth.
entries.1 samuel 2:22: Eli was very old and kept hearing reports of what his sons were doing to all Israel. It means a leader's failure to stop wrongdoing eventually becomes known and affects everyone.
entries.1 samuel 2:23: Eli confronted his sons, asking why they were doing these things, since he heard about their evil from all the people. It means it's right to confront wrongdoing, though words alone aren't enough.
entries.1 samuel 2:24: Eli told his sons that the reports spreading among the Lord's people were not good. It means a bad reputation among God's people is a serious warning sign that something is deeply wrong.
entries.1 samuel 2:25: Eli said that if someone sins against another person, God can judge it, but sinning against the Lord is far worse—yet his sons wouldn't listen, because God had decided to bring them down. It means ignoring correction hardens you, and sin against God is the most serious kind.
entries.1 samuel 2:26: Young Samuel grew and was liked by both the Lord and people. It means a life that pleases God also tends to earn the respect of others.
entries.1 samuel 2:27: A man of God came to Eli and reminded him that the Lord had revealed himself to his ancestors when they were slaves in Egypt. It means God's past faithfulness makes it worse when his chosen servants betray him.
entries.1 samuel 2:28: God says he chose Eli's ancestors from all the tribes to be priests, to serve at the altar and wear the ephod, and he gave them the offerings of Israel. It means Eli's family had been given a great privilege, which made their failure more serious.
entries.1 samuel 2:29: God asks why Eli treated his offerings with contempt by honoring his sons above God and fattening himself on the best parts of Israel's offerings. It means putting family above God and profiting from worship is a serious betrayal.
entries.1 samuel 2:30: God had promised Eli's family a lasting place before him, but now says that will not happen—he honors those who honor him and treats with contempt those who despise him. It means God's promises don't excuse disobedience, and honoring him is what really matters.
entries.1 samuel 2:31: God says the time is coming when Eli's strength and his family's strength will be cut off. It means a family that abuses a sacred role will lose the power and place it had.
entries.1 samuel 2:32: God says there will never again be an old man in Eli's family. It means the family line will not enjoy the long, honored old age that a blessing would bring.
entries.1 samuel 2:33: One man from Eli's family will not be cut off, but his eyes will grow dim and his heart will grieve, and the rest of the family will die by the sword. It means judgment will bring ongoing sorrow, not just a single loss.
entries.1 samuel 2:34: God gives Eli a sign: his two sons Hophni and Phinehas will both die on the same day. It means God's warning is specific and certain, so it can be trusted as a real sign.
entries.1 samuel 2:35: God says he will raise up a faithful priest who will do what God wants, and God will give him a lasting family line to serve before his chosen one forever. It means God will replace corrupt leadership with someone who truly follows him.
entries.1 samuel 2:36: The remaining members of Eli's family will come and kneel before that faithful priest, asking for a bit of silver or bread and begging for a place among the priests just to have food. It means those who once had honor will end up humbled and dependent, showing how far they fall.
entries.1 samuel 7:1: The people moved the sacred chest to a man's house in a nearby town and set apart his son to guard it. It shows that God's presence was treated with serious respect and needed someone trustworthy to care for it.
entries.1 samuel 7:2: The chest stayed there about twenty years, and during that time the whole nation was grieving and looking for the Lord. Long seasons of waiting can still be times when people turn their hearts back to God.
entries.1 samuel 7:3: Samuel told the people that if they truly wanted to return to God, they had to throw out their false gods and serve only him. Real turning to God means removing the things that compete with him and trusting him to rescue you.
entries.1 samuel 7:4: The Israelites stopped worshiping the false gods Baal and Astarte and worshiped only the Lord. Obeying God's call means actually letting go of the old loyalties, not just saying we will.
entries.1 samuel 7:5: Samuel gathered all Israel at one place so he could pray to the Lord for them. It helps to come together and ask God's help through someone who prays for the whole group.
entries.1 samuel 7:6: The people fasted, poured out water as a sign of sorrow, and openly admitted they had sinned against the Lord, while Samuel led them. Honest confession and humility before God are the right response when we realize we have done wrong.
entries.1 samuel 7:7: When the Philistines heard Israel had gathered, they came to attack, and the Israelites were terrified. Doing the right thing can still bring trouble, and fear is a normal reaction when danger appears.
entries.1 samuel 7:8: The people begged Samuel to keep praying that God would rescue them from the Philistines. It is good to ask others to pray for us when we are afraid and need help.
entries.1 samuel 7:9: Samuel offered a whole lamb to the Lord and prayed for Israel, and God answered him. God listens when his people pray and responds to their need.
entries.1 samuel 7:10: While Samuel was still offering the sacrifice, the Philistines attacked, but God sent loud thunder that threw them into panic and they were defeated. God can rescue his people in ways no one expected, even in the middle of the crisis.
entries.1 samuel 7:11: The Israelites chased the Philistines from Mizpah and struck them down as far as Beth-car. When God gives the victory, his people still have to step out and do their part.
entries.1 samuel 7:12: Samuel set up a stone as a memorial and named it 'stone of help,' saying the Lord had helped them up to that point. Remembering God's past help builds trust for the future.
entries.1 samuel 7:13: The Philistines were defeated and did not invade Israel again, and God kept them down throughout Samuel's lifetime. God's help was not a one-time event but lasting protection for his people.
entries.1 samuel 7:14: The towns the Philistines had captured were returned to Israel, and there was peace with the Amorites too. God's rescue restored what had been lost and brought peace on every side.
entries.1 samuel 7:15: Samuel served as judge over Israel for the rest of his life. Faithful, steady service over many years is a real gift to God's people.
entries.1 samuel 7:16: Samuel traveled each year to several towns in turn to settle disputes and lead the people. Good leadership often means going to where people are rather than waiting for them to come to you.
entries.1 samuel 7:17: Samuel's home base was Ramah, where he judged Israel and built an altar to the Lord. Having a settled place of worship and service helps anchor a life of faith.
entries.1 samuel 8:1: Samuel was getting old, so he appointed his sons to serve as judges over Israel. It shows how leadership gets passed on, and it sets up the trouble that follows.
entries.1 samuel 8:2: Samuel's sons were named Joel and Abijah, and they served as judges in Beer-sheba. This tells us where they worked and who they were.
entries.1 samuel 8:3: Samuel's sons did not follow his example; they took bribes because they loved money and judged unfairly. It reminds us that good parents can have children who choose wrong.
entries.1 samuel 8:4: The elders of Israel gathered and came to Samuel at Ramah. The leaders of the people were bringing a serious concern to the man in charge.
entries.1 samuel 8:5: They told Samuel he was old and his sons were not like him, and they demanded a king to rule them like other nations have. They had a real problem, but their solution was to copy the nations around them.
entries.1 samuel 8:6: Samuel was upset by their request for a king, so he prayed to the Lord. It is good to bring our hurt and confusion to God instead of reacting on our own.
entries.1 samuel 8:7: God told Samuel to do what the people asked, because they were not rejecting Samuel but rejecting God as their king. The real issue was deeper than a leadership problem.
entries.1 samuel 8:8: God said the people had been turning away from him and worshiping other gods since he brought them out of Egypt, and now they were treating Samuel the same way. Their pattern of rejection went back a long way.
entries.1 samuel 8:9: God told Samuel to listen to the people but also to warn them clearly and describe what kind of king would rule over them. God wanted them to know the cost before they got what they asked for.
entries.1 samuel 8:10: Samuel told the people who wanted a king everything the Lord had said. He delivered God's message honestly, even though it was not what they wanted to hear.
entries.1 samuel 8:11: Samuel warned that a king would take their sons to serve in his army, as horsemen and chariot drivers running ahead of his chariots. Their families would pay a price for having a king.
entries.1 samuel 8:12: The king would appoint some of their sons as military officers and put others to work plowing his fields, harvesting his crops, and making weapons and chariots. Their sons' lives would be used for the king's purposes.
entries.1 samuel 8:13: The king would take their daughters to make perfumes, cook, and bake bread for him. Their daughters would be pulled into serving the royal household.
entries.1 samuel 8:14: He would take their best fields, vineyards, and olive groves and give them to his own officials. Their best land and hard-won property would not be safe.
entries.1 samuel 8:15: He would take a tenth of their grain and grape harvest and give it to his servants. A king would tax what they worked to produce.
entries.1 samuel 8:16: He would take their male and female servants, and their best oxen and donkeys, and put them to his own work. Even their workers and animals would be conscripted.
entries.1 samuel 8:17: He would take a tenth of their flocks, and they themselves would become his servants. In the end, having a king would mean serving him, not just being led by him.
entries.1 samuel 8:18: When that day comes, they will cry out because of the king they chose, but the Lord will not answer them then. God was warning them that some choices cannot be easily undone.
entries.1 samuel 8:19: The people refused to listen to Samuel and insisted they wanted a king anyway. They were determined to get what they wanted, no matter the warning.
entries.1 samuel 8:20: They wanted to be like the other nations, with a king to judge them and lead them into battle. Their reason was about status and military security rather than trusting God.
entries.1 samuel 8:21: Samuel listened to everything the people said and reported it to the Lord. He kept the lines of communication open with God even in a hard situation.
entries.1 samuel 8:22: The Lord told Samuel to do as the people asked and give them a king, so Samuel sent everyone back to their towns. God allowed them to have what they demanded, and the story moved forward from there.
entries.1 samuel 11:1: An enemy king named Nahash surrounded an Israelite town and offered a deal: surrender and serve him. It shows how God's people were vulnerable and needed a rescuer.
entries.1 samuel 11:2: Nahash's terms were cruel—he wanted to gouge out their right eyes to humiliate all Israel. It shows that some offers are traps meant to shame and harm you.
entries.1 samuel 11:3: The town elders asked for seven days to find help, and Nahash agreed. It shows they were buying time and hoping someone would come to their rescue.
entries.1 samuel 11:4: Messengers brought the news to Saul's hometown, and everyone wept. It shows how deeply the threat affected ordinary people.
entries.1 samuel 11:5: Saul was out working with his oxen when he heard the crying and asked why. It shows he was an ordinary farmer who got drawn into a crisis.
