entries.2 samuel 12:8: God had given David great wealth, power, and family, and would have given even more. David had no excuse for taking what belonged to someone else.
entries.2 samuel 12:9: Nathan asked why David had ignored God's word and done evil by having Uriah killed and taking his wife. The sin was not just against a man but against God himself.
entries.2 samuel 12:10: Because David showed contempt for God and took another man's wife, violence would never leave his family. Sin brings consequences that reach beyond the moment.
entries.2 samuel 12:11: God announced that trouble would rise from within David's own household, and his wives would be taken publicly. The judgment would match the secret wrong he had done.
entries.2 samuel 12:12: David acted in secret, but God said the consequences would happen openly before all Israel. Hidden sin does not stay hidden from God.
entries.2 samuel 12:13: David admitted his sin, and Nathan told him God had forgiven him so he would not die. Confession brings real mercy, though it does not erase every result.
entries.2 samuel 12:14: Even though David was forgiven, his contempt for God would still cost the child's life. Forgiveness and consequences can both be real at the same time.
entries.2 samuel 12:15: Nathan went home, and God struck the child David had with Uriah's wife so that he became very sick. The story turns from confrontation to grief.
entries.2 samuel 12:16: David pleaded with God for the child, fasting and lying on the ground all night. He poured out his desperate hope that God might spare the boy.
entries.2 samuel 12:17: His senior servants tried to get him up and to eat with them, but he refused. His grief was so deep that he would not be comforted.
entries.2 samuel 12:18: On the seventh day the child died, and the servants were afraid to tell David because they feared what he might do to himself. They had watched how intensely he had grieved.
entries.2 samuel 12:19: David noticed the servants whispering and guessed the child was dead, and they confirmed it. He read the truth from their behavior.
entries.2 samuel 12:20: David got up, washed, changed clothes, worshiped at the house of the Lord, and then ate. His grief turned into trust and acceptance of God's will.
entries.2 samuel 12:21: The servants asked why he fasted and wept while the child lived but ate once the child died. They did not understand the change in his behavior.
entries.2 samuel 12:22: David explained that while the child was alive he fasted and wept because he hoped God might show mercy and let the child live. He had prayed as long as there was hope.
entries.2 samuel 12:23: Now that the child was dead, fasting could not bring him back; David said he would go to the child one day, but the child would not return. He accepted death as final and looked ahead to reunion.
entries.2 samuel 12:24: David comforted Bathsheba, and she bore a son named Solomon, whom the Lord loved. God brought new life and hope after the grief.
entries.2 samuel 12:25: God sent word through Nathan to give the child the name Jedidiah, meaning loved by the Lord. This confirmed God's special favor on Solomon.
entries.2 samuel 12:26: Joab was fighting against Rabbah, the Ammonite city, and captured its water supply. The war moved forward while David's personal story unfolded.
entries.2 samuel 12:27: Joab sent messengers to tell David he had taken the water-town. He reported progress and asked for the king's next move.
entries.2 samuel 12:28: Joab urged David to gather the rest of the troops and finish taking the city himself, so the victory would be credited to the king rather than to Joab. He was protecting David's honor.
entries.2 samuel 12:29: David gathered all the people, went to Rabbah, fought against it, and captured it. He completed the victory Joab had started.
entries.2 samuel 12:30: David took the crown of Milcom from the king's head, a heavy gold crown set with precious stones, and it was placed on David's head, and he carried off much plunder. The victory brought wealth and symbolized the defeat of the Ammonite god.
entries.2 samuel 12:31: David put the people of the city to forced labor with saws, iron picks, axes, and brickmaking, and did the same to other Ammonite towns, then returned to Jerusalem. This shows the harsh reality of ancient warfare and the total subjection of the defeated.
entries.2 samuel 14:1: Joab could tell that King David was starting to miss his son Absalom and wanted him back. It shows that even when someone has been wronged, love can soften over time.
entries.2 samuel 14:2: Joab found a clever woman from Tekoa and told her to dress and act like someone in deep mourning for the dead. He was setting up a story to get the king to change his mind.
entries.2 samuel 14:3: Joab gave the woman the exact words to say to the king. He was using her to make his case without speaking to David directly.
entries.2 samuel 14:4: The woman came to the king, bowed low to show respect, and begged him for help. She was playing the part of a desperate widow.
entries.2 samuel 14:5: The king asked what was wrong, and she told him she was a widow whose husband had died. She was drawing him into her story step by step.
entries.2 samuel 14:6: She claimed her two sons fought in a field with no one to stop them, and one killed the other. This was a made-up story designed to mirror David's own situation with Absalom.
entries.2 samuel 14:7: She said her whole family wanted the surviving son put to death for killing his brother, which would leave her with no one to carry on the family name. The story was meant to make David see his own family situation.
entries.2 samuel 14:8: The king told her to go home and promised he would give orders to protect her. He was responding to her story without realizing it was really about him.
entries.2 samuel 14:9: She said if there was any guilt in sparing the son, let it fall on her and her family, not on the king. She was making it easier for him to show mercy.
entries.2 samuel 14:10: The king promised that if anyone bothered her about it, he would make sure they left her alone. He was committing himself to protect her case.
entries.2 samuel 14:11: She pressed him to swear before God that no one would harm her son, and the king swore that not a hair on his head would be hurt. She had gotten him to promise mercy in a case of killing.
entries.2 samuel 14:12: She asked for permission to say one more thing, and the king told her to go ahead. She was about to turn the story toward his own situation.
entries.2 samuel 14:13: She pointed out that the king was being unfair to God's people by not bringing back the son he had sent away, since he had just promised mercy in her made-up case. She was gently showing him his inconsistency.
entries.2 samuel 14:14: She reminded him that everyone dies eventually and can't be brought back, and that God doesn't want a banished person cut off forever. She was urging David to bring Absalom home while there was still time.
entries.2 samuel 14:15: She said she came to speak because she was afraid of the people, and she hoped the king would grant her request. She was wrapping up her appeal.
entries.2 samuel 14:16: She said the king would listen and rescue her and her son from those who wanted to destroy them and cut them off from God's people. She was flattering him as a protector.
entries.2 samuel 14:17: She praised the king, saying his judgment was like that of an angel of God, able to tell good from bad. She was building him up so he would act on her words.
entries.2 samuel 14:18: The king asked her to answer honestly and hold nothing back, and she agreed to speak. He was starting to suspect something.
entries.2 samuel 14:19: The king asked if Joab was behind all this, and she admitted that Joab had told her what to say. She couldn't deny it once he asked directly.
entries.2 samuel 14:20: She said Joab did this to change the situation, and she praised the king's wisdom as being like an angel's, knowing everything on earth. She was still flattering him even while admitting the plot.
entries.2 samuel 14:21: The king told Joab he would do it and told him to go bring the young man Absalom back. David finally gave in and allowed his son to return.
entries.2 samuel 14:22: Joab bowed down and blessed the king, saying he was glad to know he had the king's favor because his request was granted. He was relieved his plan had worked.
entries.2 samuel 14:23: Joab went to Geshur and brought Absalom back to Jerusalem. Absalom was finally allowed to come home.
entries.2 samuel 14:24: The king said Absalom could go to his own house but must not come to see him. So Absalom was back in the city but still cut off from his father.
entries.2 samuel 14:25: Absalom was the best-looking man in all Israel, praised for his appearance from head to foot. His good looks made him stand out among the people.
entries.2 samuel 14:26: He cut his hair once a year because it got so heavy, and it weighed about two hundred shekels by the king's standard. This detail shows how remarkable his hair was.
entries.2 samuel 14:27: Absalom had three sons and a daughter named Tamar, who was very beautiful. He had a family of his own.
entries.2 samuel 14:28: Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years without ever seeing his father's face. He was home but still shut out from the king.
entries.2 samuel 14:29: Absalom sent for Joab to ask him to take a message to the king, but Joab wouldn't come, even when he sent a second time. Joab was ignoring him.
entries.2 samuel 14:30: So Absalom told his servants to set Joab's barley field on fire, and they did. He was forcing Joab to pay attention to him.
entries.2 samuel 14:31: Joab came to Absalom's house and asked why his servants had burned his field. Absalom had gotten the reaction he wanted.
entries.2 samuel 14:32: Absalom said he had called for Joab so he could send him to the king to ask why he had been brought back if he still couldn't see his father, and he offered to be put to death if he had done wrong. He wanted a real answer from David.
entries.2 samuel 14:33: Joab told the king, and when David sent for Absalom, Absalom came and bowed low before him, and the king kissed him. Father and son were finally reconciled, at least on the surface.
entries.2 samuel 16:1: Ziba, who served Mephibosheth, met David as he fled with donkeys loaded with food and wine. It shows someone bringing supplies to a king in a desperate moment.
entries.2 samuel 16:2: David asked why he had brought all this, and Ziba said the donkeys were for riding and the food and drink were for his tired men. The gifts were meant to help the king's group survive their journey.
entries.2 samuel 16:3: David asked where Mephibosheth was, and Ziba claimed he had stayed in Jerusalem hoping to get his father's kingdom back. Ziba was accusing his master of betrayal.
entries.2 samuel 16:4: David believed Ziba and gave him everything that belonged to Mephibosheth, and Ziba bowed in thanks. It shows how quickly a king under pressure could make a costly decision based on one report.
entries.2 samuel 16:5: As David reached Bahurim, a man from Saul's family named Shimei came out and cursed him. Someone from the family of the king David had replaced was publicly wishing him harm.
entries.2 samuel 16:6: Shimei threw stones at David, his officials, and his soldiers on both sides. He was attacking the king openly while the king's men stood around him.
entries.2 samuel 16:7: Shimei cursed David and called him a man of blood and a worthless man. He was accusing David of being violent and evil.
entries.2 samuel 16:8: Shimei said God was punishing David for the blood of Saul's family and had given the kingdom to Absalom, so David was caught in his own evil. He was claiming David's troubles were deserved.
entries.2 samuel 16:9: Abishai offered to go over and cut off Shimei's head for cursing the king. He wanted to defend David's honor by force.
entries.2 samuel 16:10: David refused, telling the sons of Zeruiah to leave Shimei alone, since he believed the Lord had told Shimei to curse him. David chose to accept the insult rather than fight back.
entries.2 samuel 16:11: David told his men that if his own son wanted him dead, a man from Saul's family cursing him was no surprise, so they should let him continue. He saw the cursing as something God had allowed.
entries.2 samuel 16:12: David hoped the Lord would see his suffering and repay him with good for the curses he received that day. He was trusting God to notice his pain and respond.
entries.2 samuel 16:13: David and his men kept traveling while Shimei walked along the hillside nearby, cursing and throwing stones and dust at him. The harassment continued as they moved on.
entries.2 samuel 16:14: The king and his people arrived at the Jordan River exhausted and rested there. After the stress and travel, they finally got a chance to stop and recover.
entries.2 samuel 16:15: Absalom and the men of Israel came into Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him. The rebellion had now taken over the capital city.
entries.2 samuel 16:16: Hushai, David's friend, came to Absalom and greeted him with shouts of long life to the king. He appeared to switch sides, though he was really still loyal to David.
entries.2 samuel 16:17: Absalom asked Hushai why he had not gone with his friend David. He was testing whether Hushai was really on his side.
entries.2 samuel 16:18: Hushai said he would be loyal to the man whom the Lord and the people had chosen as king, and he would stay with him. He was giving Absalom a reason to trust him.
entries.2 samuel 16:19: Hushai added that just as he had served Absalom's father, he would now serve Absalom. He was making his loyalty to the new king sound natural.
entries.2 samuel 16:20: Absalom asked Ahithophel for advice on what they should do next. The new king was looking for a plan to secure his position.
entries.2 samuel 16:21: Ahithophel told Absalom to sleep with his father's wives who were left in charge of the house, so all Israel would hear that he was hated by his father and his supporters would be encouraged. The advice was meant to make the break between father and son permanent.
entries.2 samuel 16:22: They set up a tent on the roof for Absalom, and he went in to his father's women in front of all Israel. This publicly shamed David and showed everyone that Absalom had taken over.
entries.2 samuel 16:23: In those days Ahithophel's advice was treated as if it came from God himself, and both David and Absalom valued it that way. People regarded his counsel as extremely reliable.
entries.2 samuel 13:1: Amnon, one of King David's sons, became obsessed with his half-sister Tamar, who was very beautiful. This sets up a story of desire that turns destructive, warning us how unchecked longing can lead to terrible harm.
entries.2 samuel 13:2: Amnon's obsession made him physically sick, and because Tamar was off-limits to him, he felt trapped and frustrated. It shows how wanting what we cannot rightly have can eat away at us.
entries.2 samuel 13:3: Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, described as clever or shrewd. His cleverness turns out to be the kind that helps someone do wrong, reminding us that bad advice from friends can lead us into disaster.
entries.2 samuel 13:4: Jonadab noticed Amnon looked worse each day and asked what was wrong, and Amnon admitted he wanted Tamar. Being honest about a wrong desire is only the first step; what we do with it next matters most.
entries.2 samuel 13:5: Jonadab told Amnon to fake illness and ask his father to send Tamar to prepare food for him. This was a sneaky plan to get her alone, showing how a trusted friend can help set up a terrible wrong.
entries.2 samuel 13:6: Amnon followed the plan, pretending to be sick and asking the king to send Tamar to make him food. He used his father's trust to get what he wanted, which is a warning about how deception often hides behind normal-seeming requests.
entries.2 samuel 13:7: David, unaware of the plot, sent Tamar to Amnon's house to care for her sick brother. An innocent person was sent straight into danger because the king trusted his son's story.
entries.2 samuel 13:8: Tamar went to Amnon's house and made cakes for him right in front of him as he lay in bed. She was doing a kind, family duty, with no idea what he was planning.
entries.2 samuel 13:9: When she brought the food, Amnon refused it and told everyone else to leave the room. He was clearing the way to be alone with her, a sign that his intentions were not about food at all.
entries.2 samuel 13:10: Amnon asked Tamar to bring the food into his bedroom so he could eat from her hand, and she went in. She trusted him as her brother, which makes what follows a betrayal of that trust.
entries.2 samuel 13:11: When she came close to give him the food, Amnon grabbed her and told her to come to bed with him. This is the moment his hidden plan became an open assault.
entries.2 samuel 13:12: Tamar pleaded with him, saying this was shameful and evil and must not be done in Israel. She named the wrong clearly and tried to stop it, showing courage even when she was in danger.
entries.2 samuel 13:13: Tamar pointed out that both of them would be disgraced, and suggested he ask the king instead. She was trying to reason her way out of danger, but the person hurting her was not willing to listen.
entries.2 samuel 13:14: Amnon ignored her words, overpowered her, and forced himself on her. The text is blunt about what happened: this was rape, a serious crime and a deep betrayal of his sister.
entries.2 samuel 13:15: Right after the assault, Amnon hated Tamar even more intensely than he had wanted her before, and he told her to get out. This shows that lust is not love; it can turn into hatred once the desire is satisfied.
entries.2 samuel 13:16: Tamar said that sending her away now was an even greater wrong than what he had already done, and he still refused to listen. She was left with no protection and no justice from the one who had hurt her.
entries.2 samuel 13:17: Amnon called his servant and ordered him to throw her out and lock the door behind her. He treated her like something to be discarded, adding humiliation to the harm he had already done.
entries.2 samuel 13:18: Tamar was wearing the special long robe that the king's unmarried daughters wore, and the servant pushed her out and locked the door. The robe marked her as a royal virgin, so being cast out in it made her shame public.
entries.2 samuel 13:19: Tamar put ashes on her head and her hand on her head and went away crying loudly, which were traditional signs of deep grief and shame. She did not hide what had happened; she mourned openly because she had been deeply wronged.
entries.2 samuel 13:20: Absalom asked if Amnon had been with her, told her to stop crying and not to take it to heart, and she lived on in his house, still desolate. His words tried to quiet the matter rather than bring justice, and Tamar was left without comfort.
entries.2 samuel 13:21: When David heard what had happened he was very angry, but he did nothing to punish Amnon because he loved him as his firstborn. A father's anger without action left the wrong unaddressed and set the stage for more trouble.
entries.2 samuel 13:22: Absalom said nothing to Amnon, good or bad, but he hated him for what he had done to Tamar. Silence can hide deep anger that is waiting for a chance to strike.
entries.2 samuel 13:23: Two years later, Absalom held a sheep-shearing feast near Ephraim and invited all the king's sons. The long delay shows his hatred had not faded; he was waiting for the right moment.
entries.2 samuel 13:24: Absalom invited the king and his servants to the feast. On the surface it looked like a normal, generous invitation, but Absalom had a hidden purpose.
entries.2 samuel 13:25: The king declined, saying too many people would be a burden, and blessed him. David had no idea what Absalom was really planning.
entries.2 samuel 13:26: Absalom then asked that Amnon go instead, and the king wondered why Amnon in particular should go. This question shows David sensed something odd but did not stop it.
entries.2 samuel 13:27: Absalom kept pressing until the king let Amnon and all his sons go with him, and Absalom prepared a great feast. The trap was now set with the king's own permission.
entries.2 samuel 13:28: Absalom told his servants to strike Amnon down when he was drunk and cheerful, and to be brave about it. He used a celebration as cover for murder, turning a feast into a killing.
entries.2 samuel 13:29: Absalom's servants killed Amnon as ordered, and all the other king's sons jumped on their animals and fled. One act of revenge sent the whole royal family into panic.
entries.2 samuel 13:30: While they were still traveling, a false report reached David that Absalom had killed all his sons and none were left. Rumors in a crisis can multiply fear far beyond the truth.
entries.2 samuel 13:31: The king rose in grief, lay on the ground, and all his servants stood by with their clothes torn. This was the customary way to show overwhelming sorrow, and David believed the worst had happened.
entries.2 samuel 13:32: Jonadab, the same shrewd friend from before, told David not to believe all the sons were dead, since only Amnon was killed and Absalom had planned it since the day Amnon violated Tamar. He correctly explained the cause, showing that the earlier wrong had been left to fester.
entries.2 samuel 13:33: Jonadab urged the king not to think all his sons were dead, because only Amnon had died. His words were meant to calm the king, though the news was still terrible.
entries.2 samuel 13:34: Absalom fled, and a watchman saw a large group coming down the hillside and reported it to the king. The approaching crowd turned out to be the surviving sons, not an army.
entries.2 samuel 13:35: Jonadab told the king that the king's sons were arriving just as he had said. His prediction was confirmed, which showed he understood the situation better than the panicked king.
entries.2 samuel 13:36: As he finished speaking, the king's sons arrived weeping loudly, and the king and all his servants wept bitterly too. The whole family was overwhelmed with grief over Amnon's death and the chaos in their house.
entries.2 samuel 13:37: Absalom fled to Talmai, king of Geshur, and stayed there three years. He escaped punishment but lived in exile, separated from his family and his home.
entries.2 samuel 13:38: David mourned for his son the whole time Absalom was away. Even though Absalom had done wrong, David's grief shows how deeply family love can ache.
entries.2 samuel 13:39: David's heart longed for Absalom, and he was eventually comforted over Amnon's death. The story shows a father torn between grief, anger, and love, with no easy way to make things right.
entries.2 samuel 17:1: Ahithophel offers to take a large force and chase David down that same night. It shows how quickly David's enemies wanted to strike while he was weak.
entries.2 samuel 17:2: Ahithophel plans to attack David while he is exhausted and catch him off guard, so his followers will scatter and only the king will be killed. The plan aims to end the conflict by targeting one man.
entries.2 samuel 17:3: Ahithophel promises that once David is dead, everyone will come back to Absalom peacefully. He frames the whole war as being about one man's life.
entries.2 samuel 17:4: Absalom and his advisors liked this plan. It seemed like a smart and quick way to win.
entries.2 samuel 17:5: Absalom decides to get a second opinion before acting. He calls for Hushai to hear what he thinks.
entries.2 samuel 17:6: Absalom tells Hushai the plan and asks whether they should follow it or hear another idea. He is weighing his options.
entries.2 samuel 17:7: Hushai says Ahithophel's plan is not wise this time. He is about to argue against it.
entries.2 samuel 17:8: Hushai warns that David and his men are experienced fighters and are furious, like a mother bear robbed of her cubs. He also notes David won't be sleeping among the troops, so he'll be hard to surprise.
entries.2 samuel 17:9: Hushai says David is probably hiding in a cave or some secret spot. If Absalom's men get beaten at first, rumors will spread that his side is losing.
entries.2 samuel 17:10: Even brave soldiers would lose their nerve, because everyone knows David and his men are fierce fighters. Fear would spread through the army.
entries.2 samuel 17:11: Hushai advises gathering the whole nation into one huge army and having Absalom lead it himself. He wants a massive show of force rather than a quick raid.
entries.2 samuel 17:12: With that many men, they could find David wherever he hides and overwhelm him completely. Hushai promises total victory.
entries.2 samuel 17:13: Even if David hides in a walled town, Hushai says the whole army could drag the town into the valley until nothing is left. He paints a picture of overwhelming force.
entries.2 samuel 17:14: Absalom and his men prefer Hushai's plan over Ahithophel's. But the real reason is that God was working to defeat Absalom by making the smarter plan fail.
entries.2 samuel 17:15: Hushai tells the priests Zadok and Abiathar both plans—what Ahithophel advised and what he himself advised. He is passing on information to David's allies.
entries.2 samuel 17:16: Hushai urges them to send word to David right away: don't camp across the river, cross it immediately or you'll be destroyed. He wants David to escape while there's time.
entries.2 samuel 17:17: Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting at a spring outside the city, and a servant girl carried messages back and forth. They couldn't be seen entering the town without danger.
entries.2 samuel 17:18: A boy spotted them and told Absalom, so the two men fled quickly to a house in Bahurim that had a well in its courtyard, and they climbed down into it.
entries.2 samuel 17:19: The woman of the house spread a covering over the well and scattered grain on top so no one would suspect anything. She hid them well.
entries.2 samuel 17:20: When Absalom's men came asking where the two were, the woman said they had gone on across the stream. The soldiers searched, found nothing, and returned to Jerusalem.
entries.2 samuel 17:21: Once the soldiers were gone, Jonathan and Ahimaaz climbed out and brought David the warning. They told him to get up and cross the water quickly because of Ahithophel's plan against him.
entries.2 samuel 17:22: David and everyone with him crossed the Jordan River, and by dawn they were all safely on the other side. The escape was complete.
entries.2 samuel 17:23: When Ahithophel saw his advice was ignored, he went home, got his affairs in order, and hanged himself. He died and was buried with his ancestors.
entries.2 samuel 17:24: David reached Mahanaim, and Absalom and his army crossed the Jordan too. The two sides were moving toward a confrontation.
entries.2 samuel 17:25: Absalom made Amasa commander of his army instead of Joab. Amasa was related to Joab through his mother's side of the family.
entries.2 samuel 17:26: Absalom and the Israelites set up camp in the region of Gilead. They were preparing for battle.
entries.2 samuel 17:27: When David arrived at Mahanaim, three men came to help him: Shobi, Machir, and Barzillai. They were wealthy and loyal supporters.
entries.2 samuel 17:28: They brought beds, bowls, pots, grain, flour, and all kinds of dried food. They were supplying David's group with practical necessities.
entries.2 samuel 17:29: They also brought honey, butter, sheep, and cheese for David and his people, because they knew the group was tired, hungry, and thirsty in the wilderness. Their kindness met real needs.
entries.2 samuel 15:1: Absalom started acting like a king by getting a chariot, horses, and fifty men to run ahead of him. He was building his own importance and popularity, which is a warning about pride and self-promotion.
entries.2 samuel 15:2: Absalom got up early and stood by the city gate, where people came for legal cases, and asked each visitor where they were from. He was deliberately meeting people and gaining their attention for his own purposes.
entries.2 samuel 15:3: Absalom told each person their case was good and right, but claimed the king had no one to hear them. He was flattering people and making the king look neglectful so they would side with him.
entries.2 samuel 15:4: Absalom wished out loud that he were the judge, promising he would give everyone justice. He was offering people what they wanted in order to win their loyalty.
entries.2 samuel 15:5: When people came to bow to him, Absalom took them by the hand and kissed them. He acted warm and familiar to make people feel important and draw them to himself.
entries.2 samuel 15:6: Absalom did this to everyone who came to the king for judgment, and in this way he stole the loyalty of the people of Israel. He was quietly turning the nation against David.
entries.2 samuel 15:7: After four years Absalom asked the king for permission to go to Hebron to fulfill a vow. He used a religious excuse to cover what he was really planning.
entries.2 samuel 15:8: Absalom explained that while he lived in Geshur he had promised to worship the Lord in Hebron if he was allowed back in Jerusalem. His words sounded devout, but they were part of his scheme.
entries.2 samuel 15:9: The king told him to go in peace, and Absalom left for Hebron. David trusted him and did not see the danger behind the request.
entries.2 samuel 15:10: Absalom secretly sent messengers through all the tribes to announce, at a signal, that he was now king in Hebron. He was organizing a rebellion while pretending to be loyal.
entries.2 samuel 15:11: Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom without knowing anything about his plan. They were innocent people caught up in his scheme.
entries.2 samuel 15:12: Absalom sent for Ahithophel, one of David's advisers, while he was offering sacrifices, and his conspiracy grew as more people joined him. A trusted adviser turning against David made the rebellion much stronger.
entries.2 samuel 15:13: A messenger came to David and told him that the hearts of the men of Israel had turned to Absalom. David learned that his own son had won over the nation.
entries.2 samuel 15:14: David told his servants they must flee at once or none of them would be safe from Absalom, who might attack the city quickly. He chose to leave rather than risk a massacre in Jerusalem.
entries.2 samuel 15:15: The king's servants told him they were ready to do whatever he decided. They showed their loyalty to David in a moment of crisis.
entries.2 samuel 15:16: The king left with all his household, except ten of his concubines, who were left to take care of the house. David had to abandon his home and most of his possessions.
entries.2 samuel 15:17: The king and all his servants went out and stopped at a place called the Far House. This was the beginning of David's flight from Jerusalem.
entries.2 samuel 15:18: All the people passed by him, including the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and six hundred men from Gath who had come with him. These were loyal soldiers who stayed with David.
entries.2 samuel 15:19: The king asked Ittai from Gath why he was coming along, since he was a foreigner far from his own land. David was giving him a chance to go back to safety.
entries.2 samuel 15:20: David told Ittai he had only just arrived and should not have to wander with him, and he wished him mercy and faithfulness from the Lord. David showed kindness and did not want to drag a newcomer into his trouble.
entries.2 samuel 15:21: Ittai swore by the living Lord and by the king's life that wherever David went, whether to life or death, he would stay with him. He showed remarkable loyalty and courage.
entries.2 samuel 15:22: David told Ittai to go forward, and Ittai went on with all his men and the little ones with them. David accepted his loyalty and let him join the journey.
entries.2 samuel 15:23: Everyone wept loudly as the people passed by, and the king stood in the Kidron Valley while the people went toward the wilderness. The whole scene was one of grief and loss.
entries.2 samuel 15:24: Zadok and Abiathar came with the ark of God and set it down until all the people had passed by. The priests brought the most sacred object to be with David in his flight.
entries.2 samuel 15:25: David told Zadok to take the ark back into the city, saying that if the Lord was pleased with him, he would return to see it again. David trusted God's will rather than using the ark as a good-luck charm.
entries.2 samuel 15:26: David said that if the Lord had no delight in him, he was still ready to accept whatever God chose to do. He submitted himself to God's decision, whether good or bad for him.
entries.2 samuel 15:27: The king told Zadok the priest to go back to the city in peace with his son Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan. David arranged for loyal men to stay behind in Jerusalem.
entries.2 samuel 15:28: David said he would wait at the crossing in the wilderness until he received news from them. He set up a way to get information while he was away.
entries.2 samuel 15:29: So Zadok and Abiathar took the ark back to Jerusalem and stayed there. They obeyed David and remained in the city as he had asked.
entries.2 samuel 15:30: David went up the Mount of Olives weeping, with his head covered and his feet bare, and all the people with him wept too. These were signs of deep sorrow and humiliation as he fled.
entries.2 samuel 15:31: David was told that Ahithophel was among Absalom's supporters, and he prayed that the Lord would turn Ahithophel's advice into foolishness. David turned to God for help against a clever enemy.
entries.2 samuel 15:32: When David reached the top of the slope where people worshiped God, Hushai the Archite came to him in grief with dust on his head. Hushai came as a loyal friend in a time of distress.
entries.2 samuel 15:33: David told Hushai that if he went with him he would only be a burden. David was thinking practically about what would help him most.
entries.2 samuel 15:34: David told Hushai to go back and pretend to serve Absalom, saying he would be Absalom's servant just as he had been his father's, so he could work against Ahithophel's plans. David set up a secret plan to protect himself.
entries.2 samuel 15:35: David reminded Hushai that Zadok and Abiathar the priests were in the city, and told him to report anything he heard from the king's house to them. David built a network of trusted people to pass information.
entries.2 samuel 15:36: David pointed out that the two priests had their sons with them, Ahimaaz and Jonathan, and said Hushai could send messages to David through them. This gave David a reliable way to receive news.
entries.2 samuel 15:37: So Hushai, David's friend, went into the city just as Absalom arrived in Jerusalem. Hushai went back to do the dangerous work David had asked of him.
entries.2 samuel 20:1: A troublemaker named Sheba blew a trumpet and told Israel they had no share in David, urging everyone to abandon the king. It shows how quickly loyalty can be broken by a loud, divisive voice.
entries.2 samuel 20:2: Most of Israel turned away from David and followed Sheba, but the men of Judah stayed loyal and escorted the king back toward Jerusalem. It reminds us that people divide in a crisis, and faithfulness matters.
entries.2 samuel 20:3: David put the ten women who had been with Absalom into a separate house and provided for them but never lived with them again, so they remained like widows until they died. It shows the lasting damage sin causes, even to innocent people.
entries.2 samuel 20:4: David ordered Amasa to gather the men of Judah and report back within three days. It was a clear, urgent command meant to deal with the rebellion quickly.
entries.2 samuel 20:5: Amasa went to gather the troops but took longer than the deadline David had set. Even a simple task can go wrong, and delays can create bigger problems.
entries.2 samuel 20:6: David told Abishai that Sheba could do more harm than Absalom, so he should chase him before he could hide in fortified cities. It shows the wisdom of acting fast before a threat grows worse.
entries.2 samuel 20:7: Joab, the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the fighting men left Jerusalem with Abishai to chase Sheba. The king's forces moved together to stop the rebellion.
entries.2 samuel 20:8: When the army reached a large stone at Gibeon, Amasa met them, and Joab's sword slipped out of its sheath as he walked. The scene sets up a moment of danger that Amasa did not notice.
entries.2 samuel 20:9: Joab greeted Amasa warmly as a brother and took him by the beard to kiss him. It looked friendly, but it was a trap.
entries.2 samuel 20:10: Amasa did not see the sword in Joab's other hand, and Joab stabbed him in the stomach, killing him with one blow; then Joab and Abishai continued after Sheba. It shows how jealousy and betrayal can hide behind a friendly greeting.
entries.2 samuel 20:11: One of Joab's men stood by Amasa's body and called out that anyone on Joab's side and David's side should follow Joab. He used the moment to rally support for Joab's leadership.
entries.2 samuel 20:12: Amasa lay in a pool of blood on the road, and when the man saw that everyone stopped to look, he moved the body into a field and covered it. He did this so the army would keep moving.
entries.2 samuel 20:13: Once Amasa's body was off the road, all the people followed Joab in pursuit of Sheba. The distraction was removed and the mission continued.
entries.2 samuel 20:14: Sheba traveled through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maacah, and the Bichrites gathered and followed him there. His rebellion drew a following, but it also cornered him in one place.
entries.2 samuel 20:15: Joab's army surrounded Sheba in Abel of Beth-maacah and built a siege ramp against the wall, trying to break it down. The town was in serious danger of being destroyed.
entries.2 samuel 20:16: A wise woman stood on the wall and called out, asking to speak with Joab. One brave, thoughtful person stepped forward to try to stop the destruction.
entries.2 samuel 20:17: Joab came close, and the woman asked if he was Joab; he said yes and agreed to listen to her. A conversation began that could save the town.
entries.2 samuel 20:18: She reminded him of an old saying about seeking counsel in Abel, implying that this town was known for wise, faithful answers. She was appealing to its good reputation.
entries.2 samuel 20:19: She accused Joab of trying to destroy a peaceful mother-town in Israel and asked why he would wipe out part of the Lord's inheritance. She appealed to his sense of justice and respect for God's people.
entries.2 samuel 20:20: Joab answered that he had no desire at all to kill or destroy the town. He clarified that his target was not the city itself.
entries.2 samuel 20:21: Joab explained that Sheba, a man from the hill country of Ephraim, had rebelled against King David, and he only wanted Sheba handed over; the woman promised his head would be thrown over the wall. The demand was narrow, and she agreed to meet it.
entries.2 samuel 20:22: The woman persuaded the town, and they cut off Sheba's head and threw it to Joab; he blew the trumpet, dismissed the army, and returned to the king in Jerusalem. Wise words ended the siege and saved the town.
entries.2 samuel 20:23: Joab was in charge of the whole army, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada commanded the Cherethites and Pelethites. This lists the key military leaders under David.
entries.2 samuel 20:24: Adoram was over the forced labor, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder. These were important officials who kept the kingdom running.
entries.2 samuel 20:25: Sheva was the scribe, and Zadok and Abiathar were the priests. The list shows the administrative and religious leaders serving alongside the king.
entries.2 samuel 20:26: Ira the Jairite also served as a priest to David. This closes the list of David's officials with one more trusted servant.
entries.2 samuel 21:1: A famine lasted three years, and when David asked God why, God said Saul's family was guilty of killing the Gibeonites. It shows that wrongs done to others can have long consequences, and it's right to ask God for answers.
entries.2 samuel 21:2: The Gibeonites were outsiders Israel had promised to protect, but Saul had tried to wipe them out in his zeal for Israel. It reminds us that breaking a serious promise, even with good motives, is still wrong.
entries.2 samuel 21:3: David asked the Gibeonites what he could do to make things right so they would bless God's people. It shows that real repair of a wrong means asking the harmed people what they need.
entries.2 samuel 21:4: The Gibeonites said money wouldn't fix it and they had no right to kill anyone in Israel, so David asked them to name their terms. It shows that justice isn't always about payment and that the wronged should have a say.
entries.2 samuel 21:5: They reminded David of the man who had tried to destroy them completely from the land. It shows how deeply Saul's attack had hurt them and that their grievance was real.
entries.2 samuel 21:6: They asked for seven of Saul's male descendants to be executed publicly before the Lord in Gibeon, and David agreed. It reflects the harsh justice of that time, where a family's guilt was shared.
entries.2 samuel 21:7: David spared Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, because he had sworn a promise to Jonathan before the Lord. It shows that keeping a solemn promise matters, even when other obligations pull the other way.
entries.2 samuel 21:8: David handed over two sons of Saul's wife Rizpah and five sons of Saul's daughter Merab. It shows the painful cost of Saul's wrongdoing falling on his family.
entries.2 samuel 21:9: The Gibeonites executed the seven men on a mountain before the Lord at the start of the barley harvest. It shows the grim seriousness with which the wrong was treated in that culture.
entries.2 samuel 21:10: Rizpah spread sackcloth on a rock and guarded the bodies day and night from birds and wild animals until rain came. Her loyal grief is a striking picture of a mother's love and dignity in the face of horror.
entries.2 samuel 21:11: David was told what Rizpah had done. It shows that acts of faithful love get noticed and can move even a king to act.
entries.2 samuel 21:12: David retrieved the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had taken them from where the Philistines had displayed them. It shows David honoring the dead and repairing a past dishonor.
entries.2 samuel 21:13: David gathered the bones of Saul and Jonathan along with the bones of the seven who had been hanged. It shows him giving proper burial to all involved and bringing the matter to a close.
entries.2 samuel 21:14: They buried the bones in the family tomb of Kish in Zela, and afterward God answered prayers for the land. It shows that when wrongs are dealt with and the dead are honored, healing can follow.
entries.2 samuel 21:15: The Philistines went to war with Israel again, and David's forces fought them at Gob. It shows that even after earlier troubles, conflict and danger keep coming.
entries.2 samuel 21:16: A giant descendant of the Rephaim with a heavy bronze spear and a new sword tried to kill David. It shows that leaders face real danger and can't always protect themselves.
entries.2 samuel 21:17: Abishai rescued David by killing the giant, and David's men swore he would never go into battle again so Israel's light wouldn't be put out. It shows the value of protecting those whose loss would be devastating to everyone.
entries.2 samuel 21:18: Another battle at Gob followed, and Sibbecai killed Saph, another descendant of the giants. It shows that David's men, not just David, were capable of defeating these fearsome enemies.
entries.2 samuel 21:19: In another battle at Gob, Elhanan killed Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was as thick as a weaver's beam. It shows that other soldiers also won great victories against giants.
entries.2 samuel 21:20: At Gath there was a very tall man with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, also a descendant of the giants. It shows the unusual and intimidating enemies Israel faced.
entries.2 samuel 21:21: When this man taunted Israel, Jonathan, David's nephew, killed him. It shows that standing up to those who mock God's people can come from unexpected members of the family.
entries.2 samuel 21:22: These four giants from Gath were all killed by David and his men. It shows that with skilled and loyal fighters, even the most frightening enemies were defeated.
entries.2 samuel 19:1: Someone told Joab that King David was crying and grieving over Absalom. Even a king's victory can feel empty when he has lost a son.
entries.2 samuel 19:2: The day that should have been a celebration turned into mourning, because everyone heard the king was devastated over his son. The people's joy was swallowed up by the king's sadness.
entries.2 samuel 19:3: The soldiers slipped back into the city quietly, like people sneaking home ashamed after losing a battle. Their win felt like a defeat because of the king's grief.
entries.2 samuel 19:4: The king hid his face and cried out loudly for Absalom, repeating his name over and over. His sorrow was so raw he couldn't stop.
entries.2 samuel 19:5: Joab went to the king and told him bluntly that he was shaming the very men who had just saved his life and his family's lives. Joab was saying the king's public grief was insulting his loyal troops.
entries.2 samuel 19:6: Joab accused the king of acting as if he loved his enemies and hated his friends, and said David would have been happier if Absalom lived and all the soldiers died. It was a harsh way of pointing out that David's grief was hurting the people who had risked everything for him.
entries.2 samuel 19:7: Joab told the king to get up and speak kindly to his men, swearing that if he didn't, he would lose every one of them that night, which would be worse than anything he had suffered before. Sometimes leaders have to set aside their own pain to care for the people who depend on them.
entries.2 samuel 19:8: The king got up and sat at the city gate, and when people heard he was there, they all came to him. Meanwhile the men of Israel had scattered back to their homes.
entries.2 samuel 19:9: People across Israel were arguing with each other, remembering how David had saved them from enemies but had then fled the land because of Absalom. They were confused about what to do next.
entries.2 samuel 19:10: They pointed out that Absalom, the man they had made ruler, was now dead in battle, so they wondered why no one was talking about bringing the king back. Word of this discussion reached David.
entries.2 samuel 19:11: King David sent a message to the priests Zadok and Abiathar, telling them to ask the leaders of Judah why they were the last to act on bringing him back home. He was urging his own tribe to take the lead.
entries.2 samuel 19:12: David reminded the men of Judah that they were his own relatives, his flesh and blood, and asked why they were dragging their feet about restoring him. Family loyalty should have made them the first to welcome him back.
entries.2 samuel 19:13: David told them to say to Amasa that he was his flesh and blood too, and he swore before God that he would make Amasa the commander of his army in place of Joab. David was offering a former rebel leader a top position to win back loyalty.
entries.2 samuel 19:14: The men of Judah were united in their response, and they sent word to the king to come back with all his servants. Their hearts turned toward David as one.
entries.2 samuel 19:15: So the king started back and reached the Jordan River, and the men of Judah came to Gilgal to meet him and escort him across. The return was finally underway.
entries.2 samuel 19:16: Shimei, a Benjamite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David. This was the same man who had cursed David earlier, so his appearance was significant.
entries.2 samuel 19:17: With Shimei came a thousand men of Benjamin, plus Ziba, Saul's servant, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, all rushing to the Jordan ahead of the king. It was a large show of support.
entries.2 samuel 19:18: They crossed the river to bring the king's household over and to do whatever he wanted, and Shimei fell face down in the dust before the king as he was about to cross the Jordan. Shimei was humbling himself before the man he had wronged.
entries.2 samuel 19:19: Shimei begged the king not to count his sin against him or hold onto the wrong he had done on the day David left Jerusalem. He was asking for mercy for his past betrayal.
entries.2 samuel 19:20: Shimei said he knew he had sinned, and that he had come today as the first of all the sons of Joseph to meet the king. He was trying to show his repentance by being the first to welcome David back.
entries.2 samuel 19:21: Abishai, son of Zeruiah, asked whether Shimei shouldn't be put to death for cursing the Lord's anointed king. He thought Shimei's insult deserved the death penalty.
entries.2 samuel 19:22: David rebuked the sons of Zeruiah, asking what business they had opposing him today, and said no one should be put to death on a day like this, because he knew he was king over Israel again. David chose mercy over revenge on a day of celebration.
entries.2 samuel 19:23: The king told Shimei he would not die, and he swore an oath to him. David spared his enemy's life and sealed the promise with a vow.
entries.2 samuel 19:24: Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, came down to meet the king, and he hadn't cared for his feet, cut his hair, or washed his clothes from the day the king left until he returned in peace. His neglected appearance showed he had been mourning the whole time.
entries.2 samuel 19:25: When Mephibosheth came from Jerusalem to see the king, David asked him why he hadn't gone with him. The king wanted an explanation for his absence.
entries.2 samuel 19:26: Mephibosheth explained that his servant had deceived him, because he had told the servant to saddle a donkey so he could ride with the king, since he couldn't walk. He was crippled and had been misled.
entries.2 samuel 19:27: Mephibosheth said his servant had lied about him, but he trusted the king to do whatever seemed right, comparing the king to an angel of God. He was putting himself entirely in David's hands.
entries.2 samuel 19:28: He said all his father's family deserved death before the king, yet the king had still given him a place at his table, so he had no right to ask for anything more. He was expressing humble gratitude.
entries.2 samuel 19:29: The king told him to stop talking about it and decided to divide the land between Ziba and Mephibosheth. David settled the dispute with a compromise.
entries.2 samuel 19:30: Mephibosheth said Ziba could take it all, now that the king had come home in peace. He cared more about the king's safe return than about the property.
entries.2 samuel 19:31: Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim and went with the king as far as the Jordan to see him across. He was one of the loyal supporters who helped David during his exile.
entries.2 samuel 19:32: Barzillai was a very old man, about eighty years old, and he had provided everything the king needed while he was at Mahanaim, because he was a wealthy and important man. He had used his resources to support David in a time of need.
entries.2 samuel 19:33: The king invited Barzillai to come with him to Jerusalem, promising to take care of him there. David wanted to reward the old man's kindness.
entries.2 samuel 19:34: Barzillai asked the king how many years he had left that he should go up to Jerusalem with him. He was gently declining the offer because of his age.
entries.2 samuel 19:35: He said at eighty, good and bad no longer made much difference to him, food and drink had lost their taste, and he couldn't enjoy singers anymore, so why should he be a burden to the king? He was honestly explaining that he was too old to enjoy court life.
entries.2 samuel 19:36: Barzillai said his only wish was to escort the king across the Jordan, and asked why the king would give him such a reward. He felt he had already received enough honor.
entries.2 samuel 19:37: He asked to go back home so he could die in his own town, near the graves of his father and mother, and he offered his servant Chimham to go with the king instead, asking David to do for him whatever seemed good. He chose to spend his last days at home and passed the honor to a younger man.
entries.2 samuel 19:38: The king agreed that Chimham would go with him, and promised to do for him whatever Barzillai wanted, and to grant Barzillai whatever he desired. David honored the old man's request and his wishes.
entries.2 samuel 19:39: All the people crossed the Jordan, and the king crossed too, then he kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai went back to his own place. It was a warm farewell between the king and his loyal friend.
entries.2 samuel 19:40: The king went on to Gilgal with Chimham, and all the people of Judah and half the people of Israel escorted him along the way. The king's return was marked by widespread public support.
entries.2 samuel 22:1: David sang this song to God on the day God rescued him from all his enemies, including Saul. It reminds readers to thank God when he brings them through hard times.
entries.2 samuel 22:2: David calls the Lord his rock, his fortress, and the one who saves him. For the reader, it means God is a solid, safe place to depend on.
entries.2 samuel 22:3: David piles up pictures of God as his protector, shield, and hiding place. It means you can trust God to keep you safe from people who mean you harm.
entries.2 samuel 22:4: David says he will call out to the Lord, who deserves praise, and God will save him from his enemies. It encourages the reader to pray to God when others are against them.
entries.2 samuel 22:5: David describes feeling surrounded by death and evil, like waves and seas closing in on him. It shows that even overwhelming fear is a place where you can still cry out to God.
entries.2 samuel 22:6: David felt trapped by death, like ropes and nets had caught him. It means death and danger can feel inescapable, but God is still able to reach you.
entries.2 samuel 22:7: In his distress David called to God, and God heard him from his temple. It tells the reader that God listens when you pray in trouble.
entries.2 samuel 22:8: David pictures the earth shaking and the foundations of heaven moving because God was angry. It shows how seriously God takes the rescue of his people.
entries.2 samuel 22:9: Smoke and fire come from God's presence, showing his fierce anger. It means God's response to evil is powerful and not something to take lightly.
entries.2 samuel 22:10: David imagines God bending the heavens and coming down, with darkness under his feet. It pictures God stepping into the situation personally to help.
entries.2 samuel 22:11: God rides on a storm cloud and flies on the wind. It means God is not distant; he moves powerfully to act on behalf of his people.
entries.2 samuel 22:12: Darkness, water, and thick clouds surround God like a tent. It shows that God's ways are often hidden, yet he is still present and working.
entries.2 samuel 22:13: Bright light breaks through the dark clouds, with hail and fire falling. It means God's presence is both dazzling and fearsome.
entries.2 samuel 22:14: The Lord thunders from heaven and the Most High speaks. It reminds the reader that God's voice is powerful and demands attention.
entries.2 samuel 22:15: God shoots arrows and flashes fire, scattering his enemies. It means God actively fights against those who oppose his purposes.
entries.2 samuel 22:16: The sea floor and the world's foundations are laid bare by God's anger and breath. It shows that nothing is hidden or safe from God's power.
entries.2 samuel 22:17: God reached down from above and pulled David out of deep waters. It means God himself rescues people from situations too deep for them to escape.
entries.2 samuel 22:18: God freed David from enemies who were stronger than he was. It encourages the reader that God can save them even when the odds are against them.
entries.2 samuel 22:19: David's enemies attacked him when he was in trouble, but the Lord held him up. It means God supports you when you feel overwhelmed.
entries.2 samuel 22:20: God brought David out into an open, safe place because he delighted in him. It means God's rescue comes from his love, not just his power.
entries.2 samuel 22:21: David says God rewarded him because he had done right and kept his hands clean. It shows that God honors a life lived honestly before him.
entries.2 samuel 22:22: David kept following the Lord's ways and did not turn away from God into sin. It encourages the reader to stay faithful to God in daily choices.
entries.2 samuel 22:23: David kept God's rules in front of him and did not throw them away. It means remembering and obeying God's instructions matters.
entries.2 samuel 22:24: David says he was blameless before God and kept himself from sin. It shows the value of personal integrity in how you live.
entries.2 samuel 22:25: Because David lived rightly, God gave him the reward of his righteousness. It reminds the reader that God sees and responds to how we live.
entries.2 samuel 22:26: God shows mercy to those who show mercy and is straightforward with the upright. It means the way you treat others shapes how you experience God.
entries.2 samuel 22:27: God is holy to the holy but opposes those who twist their ways. It warns the reader that God deals honestly with people according to how they live.
entries.2 samuel 22:28: God saves people who are in trouble but brings down the proud. It encourages the humble and warns those who think too highly of themselves.
entries.2 samuel 22:29: David says the Lord is his light and turns his darkness bright. It means God can bring hope and clarity into the darkest parts of life.
entries.2 samuel 22:30: With God's help David got through walls that blocked him. It means God can help you overcome obstacles that seem impossible.
entries.2 samuel 22:31: God's way is perfect, his word is proven, and he shields those who trust him. It encourages the reader to rely on God's trustworthy character.
entries.2 samuel 22:32: David asks who else is God or a rock like our God. It means there is no one and nothing as reliable as the Lord.
entries.2 samuel 22:33: God gives David strength and keeps him on a straight path. It means God provides both the power and the direction to live well.
entries.2 samuel 22:34: God makes David's feet sure like a deer's and sets him on high places. It means God gives stability and safety even on difficult ground.
entries.2 samuel 22:35: God trains David's hands for battle and makes him strong enough to bend a bronze bow. It means God equips people for the challenges they face.
entries.2 samuel 22:36: God gives David his saving shield, and his mercy makes David great. It means God's kindness, not just strength, lifts people up.
entries.2 samuel 22:37: God makes the path wide under David so his feet do not slip. It means God gives room to move and keeps you from falling.
entries.2 samuel 22:38: David chases his enemies and does not stop until they are defeated. It shows God giving complete victory over those who oppose him.
entries.2 samuel 22:39: David strikes down his enemies so they cannot rise again. It pictures total victory, showing that God brings an end to the threat.
entries.2 samuel 22:40: God arms David with strength for battle and brings his opponents down. It means God is the one who gives the ability to face and overcome opposition.
entries.2 samuel 19:41: The northern tribes felt left out because Judah had quietly brought the king back across the river without including them. It means people can feel hurt when they're excluded from something important, even if no harm was intended.
entries.2 samuel 19:42: Judah answered that the king was their close relative, so they had a natural reason to help him, and they insisted they had gained nothing personally from it. It shows how quickly people defend themselves when accused, and reminds us to check whether our own motives are really clean.
entries.2 samuel 19:43: The northern tribes argued they had a bigger share in the king and had been the first to want him back, so they felt insulted; the argument then turned harsh. It shows how pride and hurt feelings can turn a disagreement into a bitter fight that does real damage.
entries.2 samuel 24:1: God was angry with Israel, and he caused David to order a count of the people. This shows that even a leader's wrong choice can be part of a bigger situation God is dealing with.
entries.2 samuel 24:2: David told his army commander to go through the whole country and count the people so he would know how many there were. He wanted to measure his strength by numbers.
entries.2 samuel 24:3: Joab warned the king that this counting was a bad idea, even wishing God would multiply the people far beyond what they were. It's a friend's honest warning to stop before doing something unwise.
entries.2 samuel 24:4: The king overruled Joab, and the commanders went out to count the people as ordered. Sometimes a leader's insistence wins the day even when others see the danger.
entries.2 samuel 24:5: The counting team crossed the Jordan and moved through the towns on the eastern side. This is just the record of where they traveled to do the job.
entries.2 samuel 24:6: They continued north through Gilead and the region near Hermon, then looped around toward Sidon. The count was covering the whole land step by step.
entries.2 samuel 24:7: They reached the fortified city of Tyre and passed through the Canaanite towns, ending up in the south at Beersheba. The survey reached the far edges of the country.
entries.2 samuel 24:8: After traveling the whole land in every direction, they returned to Jerusalem about nine months and twenty days later. The task took a long time to finish.
entries.2 samuel 24:9: Joab reported the totals: eight hundred thousand fighting men in Israel and five hundred thousand in Judah. David now had the number he wanted.
entries.2 samuel 24:10: After the count, David's conscience struck him and he confessed to God that he had sinned greatly and acted foolishly. Doing something wrong can leave us uneasy until we admit it to God.
entries.2 samuel 24:11: The next morning, God spoke to the prophet Gad, who served as David's seer. God was about to respond to David's sin through a messenger.
entries.2 samuel 24:12: God told Gad to offer David a choice among three consequences, and David would pick which one would happen. God was letting David choose the form of the judgment.
entries.2 samuel 24:13: Gad laid out the options: three years of famine, three months of fleeing from enemies, or three days of severe disease. David had to think carefully and give an answer.
entries.2 samuel 24:14: David said the choice was hard, but he would rather fall into God's hands than into human hands, because God is merciful. It's better to trust God's mercy than to face people's cruelty.
entries.2 samuel 24:15: David chose the disease, and it struck the people during the grain harvest, killing seventy thousand across the land. The consequence of his choice fell on the nation.
entries.2 samuel 24:16: As the angel was about to destroy Jerusalem, the Lord stopped him and said it was enough. God's mercy limited the destruction, and the angel stood by a threshing floor.
entries.2 samuel 24:17: When David saw the angel striking the people, he admitted the fault was his and asked that the punishment fall on him and his family instead of the people. A true leader takes responsibility for his own wrong.
entries.2 samuel 24:18: That same day Gad told David to go up and build an altar to the Lord on Araunah's threshing floor. God was giving David a specific step to take.
entries.2 samuel 24:19: David went up and did exactly what Gad said, just as the Lord had commanded. Obedience to God's instruction was David's response.
entries.2 samuel 24:20: Araunah saw the king and his men approaching and bowed low before him. He showed respect to the king who had come to him.
entries.2 samuel 24:21: Araunah asked why the king had come, and David explained he wanted to buy the threshing floor to build an altar so the disease would stop. David was seeking a way to end the suffering.
entries.2 samuel 24:22: Araunah offered to give David the threshing floor, the oxen for the offering, and the wooden equipment for fuel. He was generous and wanted to help.
entries.2 samuel 24:23: Araunah gave everything to the king and wished that God would accept David's offering. His generosity came with a blessing.
entries.2 samuel 24:24: David refused to take it for nothing, saying he would not offer God something that cost him nothing, and he bought the floor and oxen for fifty shekels of silver. Real worship involves personal cost.
entries.2 samuel 24:25: David built the altar and offered burnt and peace offerings, and the Lord answered his prayer for the land, and the disease ended. God responded to sincere prayer and sacrifice with mercy.
entries.2 samuel 18:1: David organized his followers into fighting units and appointed officers over them. It shows that even in a crisis, careful planning and order matter for the reader.
entries.2 samuel 18:2: David split his army into three groups under three commanders and said he would march out with them himself. This shows a leader willing to share his people's danger rather than send them alone.
entries.2 samuel 18:3: The people urged David to stay behind because his life was worth more to them than many soldiers. It reminds the reader that sometimes the wisest help is to stay safe where you can still support others.
entries.2 samuel 18:4: David agreed to do what his people thought best and stood by the town gate as the army marched out. It shows a leader who listens to good advice instead of insisting on his own way.
entries.2 samuel 18:5: David publicly ordered his commanders to deal gently with Absalom for his sake. Even after being betrayed, David still loved his son, showing how deep a parent's love can be.
entries.2 samuel 18:6: The battle took place in the forest region of Ephraim. The setting matters because the terrain would shape how the fighting went.
entries.2 samuel 18:7: David's men defeated the Israelite army there, and a great many died that day. It shows the heavy cost of the rebellion that Absalom had started.
entries.2 samuel 18:8: The fighting spread across the whole countryside, and the forest itself killed more men than the sword did. It reminds the reader that war's destruction goes beyond direct combat.
entries.2 samuel 18:9: Absalom, riding a mule, got his head caught in the branches of a large tree and was left hanging while the mule ran on. It shows how quickly a powerful man can be brought down and left helpless.
entries.2 samuel 18:10: A soldier saw Absalom hanging in the tree and reported it to Joab. The reader sees that the moment of Absalom's downfall had a witness.
entries.2 samuel 18:11: Joab scolded the man for not killing Absalom on the spot and offered him money and a reward for doing it. It shows how Joab valued victory over the king's clear command.
entries.2 samuel 18:12: The soldier refused, saying no amount of silver would make him harm the king's son, since he had heard David's order to protect Absalom. It shows courage to obey a leader's command even when a superior pressures you to break it.
entries.2 samuel 18:13: The soldier pointed out that if he had killed Absalom, the king would find out and Joab would not defend him. It shows that doing wrong to please someone rarely ends well for the one who does it.
entries.2 samuel 18:14: Joab dismissed the man's concerns, took three spears, and drove them into Absalom while he hung in the tree. It shows Joab taking justice, and the king's wishes, into his own hands.
entries.2 samuel 18:15: Ten of Joab's young soldiers surrounded Absalom and finished him off. It shows that once the commander decided Absalom must die, others joined in.
entries.2 samuel 18:16: Joab blew the trumpet to stop the pursuit and call the troops back. It shows the fighting was ended once Absalom was dead.
entries.2 samuel 18:17: They threw Absalom's body into a large pit in the forest and piled stones over it, and the Israelite soldiers fled home. It shows the rebellion collapsing and Absalom buried without honor.
entries.2 samuel 18:18: Absalom had built a monument for himself because he had no son to carry on his name. It shows a man trying to secure his memory, yet his legacy ended in disgrace.
entries.2 samuel 18:19: Ahimaaz wanted to run and tell David that God had given him victory over his enemies. It shows a loyal man eager to bring good news to the king.
entries.2 samuel 18:20: Joab told Ahimaaz not to bring news that day because the king's son was dead. It shows that even a victory message would be painful news for David.
entries.2 samuel 18:21: Joab sent a foreign servant, a Cushite, to report what he had seen, and the man bowed and ran off. It shows Joab choosing someone else to deliver the hard news.
entries.2 samuel 18:22: Ahimaaz insisted on running too, even though Joab warned he would get no reward for his news. It shows determination to serve the king even without personal gain.
entries.2 samuel 18:23: Ahimaaz would not be talked out of it, so Joab let him go, and he ran a faster route and passed the Cushite. It shows persistence paying off in getting there first.
entries.2 samuel 18:24: David sat between the town gates while a watchman on the wall saw a lone runner approaching. It shows the tense waiting of a father and king for news from the battle.
entries.2 samuel 18:25: The watchman told the king, who said a lone runner must be bringing news, and the man came closer. It shows David reading the signs and bracing for the report.
entries.2 samuel 18:26: The watchman spotted a second runner, and the king again said he must be bringing news. It shows the growing anticipation as more messengers arrive.
entries.2 samuel 18:27: The watchman recognized the first runner's style as Ahimaaz's, and David said he was a good man bringing good news. It shows David hoping for the best from a trusted messenger.
entries.2 samuel 18:28: Ahimaaz called out that all was well, bowed low, and praised God for giving David victory over his enemies. It shows gratitude to God for the outcome of the battle.
entries.2 samuel 18:29: David asked whether Absalom was safe, and Ahimaaz said he saw a commotion but did not know what it was. It shows Ahimaaz avoiding the painful truth, or at least not knowing it.
entries.2 samuel 18:30: David told Ahimaaz to step aside and wait, and he did. It shows the king turning to the next messenger for the answer he really wanted.
entries.2 samuel 18:31: The Cushite arrived and announced that God had given the king victory over all who rebelled against him. It shows the full report of victory finally reaching David.
entries.2 samuel 18:32: David asked if Absalom was safe, and the Cushite answered by wishing all the king's enemies would end up like that young man. It was a blunt way of saying Absalom was dead.
entries.2 samuel 18:33: David was deeply shaken, went up to the room over the gate, and wept, wishing he could have died in Absalom's place. It shows a father's grief overwhelming even his relief at victory, and how love and sorrow can mix.
entries.2 samuel 22:41: God made David's enemies run away, so they were defeated. It means God can give you victory over those who oppose you.
entries.2 samuel 22:42: David's enemies cried for help, even to God, but no one rescued them. It shows that help comes too late for those who fight against God's chosen leader.
entries.2 samuel 22:43: David's enemies were completely crushed, like dust or trash underfoot. It means his victory was total, and God can fully defeat what threatens you.
entries.2 samuel 22:44: God freed David from conflict among his own people and made him ruler over other nations he had never known. It means God can raise you above strife and give you influence you never expected.
entries.2 samuel 22:45: Foreigners would pretend to submit to David as soon as they heard of him. It means people may obey you out of fear rather than real loyalty, so don't trust flattery.
entries.2 samuel 22:46: These foreigners would lose their courage and come trembling out of their hiding places. It means those who resist God's plan will eventually be humbled and afraid.
entries.2 samuel 22:47: David praises the living God, calling him his rock and savior. It means you can honor God as the solid, living foundation you can depend on.
entries.2 samuel 22:48: God is the one who punishes David's enemies and brings nations under his authority. It means justice and victory come from God, not from your own strength.
entries.2 samuel 22:49: God rescued David from his enemies and violent men and lifted him above his attackers. It means God can protect you from people who are stronger or more cruel than you.
entries.2 samuel 22:50: Because God saved him, David promises to praise God publicly among other nations. It means your gratitude to God should be spoken openly, not kept private.
entries.2 samuel 22:51: God gives great victory to his king and shows lasting mercy to David and his descendants. It means God keeps his promises to his chosen leader and to the family line that follows him.
entries.1 kings 5:1: Hiram, the king of Tyre, heard that Solomon had become king after his father David, so he sent messengers to him because he had always been a friend of David. It shows that good relationships can carry over from one generation to the next.
entries.1 kings 5:2: Solomon sent a message back to Hiram. This simply sets up the reply that follows.
entries.1 kings 5:3: Solomon reminds Hiram that David could not build a temple for God because he was surrounded by wars until God gave him victory over his enemies. It shows that some good plans have to wait for the right time.
entries.1 kings 5:4: Solomon says that God has now given him peace on every side, with no trouble or danger. It reminds the reader to be grateful when life is calm and to use peaceful times well.
entries.1 kings 5:5: Solomon explains that he intends to build a temple for God, just as God had promised David that his son would do it. It shows that God keeps his promises and that we can take part in what he promised.
entries.1 kings 5:6: Solomon asks Hiram to have cedar trees cut from Lebanon and offers to pay whatever wages he sets, since his own people are not skilled woodcutters like the men of Sidon. It shows the wisdom of asking skilled help and paying fairly for it.
entries.1 kings 5:7: Hiram was glad to hear Solomon's message and praised the Lord for giving David such a wise son to rule over this great people. It shows that wisdom is a gift worth thanking God for.
entries.1 kings 5:8: Hiram replied that he had received Solomon's message and would do everything he wanted with the cedar and cypress wood. It shows a friend keeping his word and helping with the task.
entries.1 kings 5:9: Hiram explains how his men will bring the wood down from Lebanon to the sea, float it to wherever Solomon says, and have it ready there, asking only for food for his people as payment. It shows a fair and practical agreement between friends.
entries.1 kings 5:10: Hiram supplied Solomon with all the cedar and cypress wood he needed. It shows that a promise made was fully kept.
entries.1 kings 5:11: Solomon gave Hiram large amounts of grain and clear oil as food for his household, year after year. It shows that fair payment was made and the partnership was kept up.
entries.1 kings 5:12: The Lord had given Solomon wisdom as he promised, and Hiram and Solomon lived in peace and made an agreement together. It shows that God's gift of wisdom helped build good relationships.
entries.1 kings 5:13: Solomon gathered thirty thousand men from all Israel for forced labor. It shows how large the building project was and that many people were needed to do it.
entries.1 kings 5:14: He sent them to Lebanon in groups of ten thousand each month, so they worked one month there and spent two months at home, with Adoniram in charge. It shows that even hard work was organized so people got time at home.
entries.1 kings 5:15: Solomon also had seventy thousand men carrying loads and eighty thousand men cutting stone in the mountains. It shows the huge scale of the work needed to build the temple.
entries.1 kings 5:16: Besides these workers, there were three thousand three hundred foremen appointed by Solomon to supervise the work. It shows that good leadership and oversight were needed alongside the laborers.
entries.1 kings 5:17: By the king's command, large and costly stones were cut and squared to form the foundation of the temple. It shows that the house of God was built with care and the best materials.
entries.1 kings 5:18: Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders cut and shaped the stones and prepared the wood and stone for building the temple. It shows people working together to get everything ready for God's house.
entries.1 kings 2:1: David knew he was about to die, so he called his son Solomon to give him final instructions. It's a reminder that wise people prepare the next generation before they go.
entries.1 kings 2:2: David says he is dying, as everyone does, and urges Solomon to be brave and act like a man. Facing death honestly and encouraging others to be strong is part of leaving a good legacy.
entries.1 kings 2:3: David tells Solomon to obey God's commands and follow his ways as written in Moses' law. Obedience to God is the path to doing well in life, wherever you go.
entries.1 kings 2:4: God had promised David that if his descendants stayed faithful, there would always be a king from his line. This shows that God's promises come with the call to live faithfully before him.
entries.1 kings 2:5: David reminds Solomon of how Joab had treacherously killed two army commanders during peacetime. It's a warning that past violence and betrayal cannot simply be ignored.
entries.1 kings 2:6: David tells Solomon to use his wisdom and not let Joab die peacefully in old age. He is handing over the responsibility of justice to his son.
entries.1 kings 2:7: David asks Solomon to be kind to the sons of Barzillai, who had helped him when he was fleeing from Absalom. Kindness shown to you should be repaid with kindness to others.
entries.1 kings 2:8: David recalls how Shimei had cursed him bitterly, though Shimei later came to meet him and David had sworn not to kill him. David is passing on an unresolved matter to his son.
entries.1 kings 2:9: David tells Solomon not to let Shimei go unpunished and to deal with him wisely. He trusts Solomon's judgment to settle an old wrong.
entries.1 kings 2:10: David died and was buried in the city of David. Even a great king ends up in the grave like everyone else.
entries.1 kings 2:11: David ruled Israel for forty years, seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem. It's a summary of a long reign that shaped the nation.
entries.1 kings 2:12: Solomon took his father's place as king, and his rule became firmly established. God's promise to David continued through his son.
