entries.1 kings 2:13: Adonijah, Solomon's older half-brother, came to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, and she asked if he came in peace. His visit sets up a request that turns out to be dangerous.
entries.1 kings 2:14: Adonijah said he had something to tell Bathsheba, and she told him to speak. He is approaching her with a hidden purpose.
entries.1 kings 2:15: Adonijah admits the kingdom had seemed his and that everyone expected him to be king, but God gave it to Solomon instead. He acknowledges God's choice, even while he clearly still wants power.
entries.1 kings 2:16: Adonijah asks Bathsheba for one favor and begs her not to refuse. He is trying to use her influence for his own advantage.
entries.1 kings 2:17: Adonijah asks Bathsheba to request that Solomon give him Abishag as a wife. In that culture, taking a king's woman was a way of claiming the throne.
entries.1 kings 2:18: Bathsheba agrees to take Adonijah's request to the king. She doesn't seem to realize what Adonijah is really after.
entries.1 kings 2:19: Bathsheba went to Solomon, who honored her by rising, bowing, and having a seat placed for her at his right hand. Solomon shows proper respect for his mother.
entries.1 kings 2:20: Bathsheba tells Solomon she has one small request and asks him not to refuse. She presents Adonijah's request as something minor.
entries.1 kings 2:21: Bathsheba asks Solomon to give Abishag to Adonijah as his wife. She is asking for something that sounds small but carries huge political meaning.
entries.1 kings 2:22: Solomon sees through the request, saying it's really a bid for the kingdom since Adonijah is his older brother and has Joab and Abiathar on his side. What looked like a small favor was actually a threat to the throne.
entries.1 kings 2:23: Solomon swears by the Lord that Adonijah will pay for this request with his life. Solomon treats the request as a serious act of rebellion.
entries.1 kings 2:24: Solomon declares that, since God put him on David's throne as promised, Adonijah will be put to death that very day. He is defending the kingdom God gave him.
entries.1 kings 2:25: Solomon sent Benaiah, who struck Adonijah down and killed him. The threat to Solomon's throne was removed.
entries.1 kings 2:26: Solomon tells Abiathar the priest to go to his fields in Anathoth and spares his life because he had carried the ark and shared David's hardships. Mercy is shown where there had been loyal service.
entries.1 kings 2:27: Solomon removed Abiathar from being priest, which fulfilled God's earlier word against Eli's family in Shiloh. God's long-standing word came true.
entries.1 kings 2:28: Joab heard what happened; he had backed Adonijah, so he fled to the Lord's tent and grabbed the horns of the altar, hoping for safety. He was looking for protection he didn't deserve.
entries.1 kings 2:29: When Solomon heard Joab was at the altar, he sent Benaiah to strike him down. Solomon did not accept the altar as a shield for a guilty man.
entries.1 kings 2:30: Benaiah told Joab the king ordered him to come out, but Joab refused and said he would die there. Joab chose to stay rather than face the king.
entries.1 kings 2:31: Solomon told Benaiah to strike Joab there and bury him, so that the guilt of innocent blood would be removed from Solomon and his family. Justice had to be carried out to clear the kingdom.
entries.1 kings 2:32: Solomon says the Lord will bring Joab's blood guilt on his own head, because he killed two men better than himself without David's knowledge. Wrongdoing eventually comes back on the one who did it.
entries.1 kings 2:33: The guilt for that blood will stay on Joab and his descendants, but David's family and throne will have peace from the Lord. God's justice and blessing are both at work.
entries.1 kings 2:34: Benaiah struck Joab down and buried him at his home in the wilderness. Joab's long career of violence ended in judgment.
entries.1 kings 2:35: Solomon put Benaiah over the army in Joab's place and Zadok as priest in Abiathar's place. New leaders were appointed to keep the kingdom running.
entries.1 kings 2:36: Solomon called Shimei and told him to build a house in Jerusalem and stay there, never leaving. He was given a restricted but safe place to live.
entries.1 kings 2:37: Solomon warned Shimei that if he ever crossed the Kidron stream, he would die and be responsible for his own death. The condition was clear and the consequence was serious.
entries.1 kings 2:38: Shimei agreed to the king's terms and lived in Jerusalem for a long time. He kept the agreement, at least for a while.
entries.1 kings 2:39: After three years, two of Shimei's servants ran away to Achish, king of Gath, and Shimei was told where they had gone. Trouble came when he least expected it.
entries.1 kings 2:40: Shimei got up, saddled his donkey, and went to Gath to find his servants. He broke the king's command for the sake of his runaway slaves.
entries.1 kings 3:1: Solomon made a political marriage alliance with Egypt by marrying Pharaoh's daughter, housing her temporarily until his building projects were finished. This shows Solomon's early compromises, reminding readers that even wise people can make choices that quietly pull them away from full devotion.
entries.1 kings 3:2: The people still sacrificed at local shrines called high places because the temple hadn't been built yet. It explains why worship was scattered, and it warns readers that good intentions can drift into habits God never intended.
entries.1 kings 3:3: Solomon loved the Lord and followed his father David's example, but he still offered sacrifices at the high places. This shows a mixed heart: real devotion alongside practices that would later cause trouble, reminding readers to watch for small inconsistencies in their own faith.
entries.1 kings 3:4: Solomon went to Gibeon, the most important high place, and offered a huge number of sacrifices there. His generosity in worship shows sincerity, but the location hints that his worship wasn't yet fully centered where God wanted it.
entries.1 kings 3:5: At Gibeon God appeared to Solomon in a dream and invited him to ask for whatever he wanted. It shows God's kindness in approaching Solomon personally, and it invites readers to consider what they would ask God for if given the chance.
entries.1 kings 3:6: Solomon thanked God for the great kindness shown to his father David, who had lived faithfully, and for giving David a son to succeed him. It models gratitude by recalling God's past faithfulness, encouraging readers to remember what God has already done.
entries.1 kings 3:7: Solomon admitted he felt like a young, inexperienced boy who didn't know how to lead. His honesty about his inadequacy shows that admitting weakness is the first step toward receiving help, and it invites readers to be honest about their own limits.
entries.1 kings 3:8: Solomon noted that he was responsible for God's chosen people, a nation so large it couldn't be counted. It shows the weight of his responsibility, reminding readers that leadership over others is a serious trust from God.
entries.1 kings 3:9: Solomon asked for a wise and discerning heart so he could judge the people well and tell right from wrong. His request shows that wisdom to do one's job well matters more than personal gain, and it encourages readers to ask God for wisdom in their own responsibilities.
entries.1 kings 3:10: God was pleased that Solomon asked for this. It shows that God delights in requests that serve others rather than selfish desires, encouraging readers to examine what motivates their prayers.
entries.1 kings 3:11: God noted that Solomon hadn't asked for long life, wealth, or revenge on his enemies, but for wisdom to judge fairly. It highlights the unselfishness of his request, showing readers that God notices what we value most.
entries.1 kings 3:12: God granted Solomon a wise and understanding heart unlike anyone before or after him. It shows God generously answers prayers for wisdom, assuring readers that asking for wisdom is a prayer God loves to answer.
entries.1 kings 3:13: God also gave Solomon wealth and honor, things he hadn't asked for. It shows God's generosity goes beyond what we request, encouraging readers to trust that God may add blessings we never thought to ask for.
entries.1 kings 3:14: God promised Solomon long life if he kept walking in God's ways and obeying his commands like David did. It shows that God's gifts come with the call to stay faithful, reminding readers that blessings and obedience are connected.
entries.1 kings 3:15: Solomon woke and realized it was a dream, then went to Jerusalem to worship before the ark and held a feast for his servants. His response of worship and celebration shows gratitude in action, encouraging readers to respond to God's goodness with worship and generosity.
entries.1 kings 3:16: Two prostitutes came and stood before the king for a legal case. It shows that Solomon's wisdom was available even to the poorest and most marginalized, reminding readers that God's justice cares for everyone, not just the powerful.
entries.1 kings 3:17: One woman explained that she and the other woman lived in the same house, and she gave birth while the other was there. It sets up the story by showing how closely their lives were intertwined, drawing readers into a real dispute between real people.
entries.1 kings 3:18: She explained that three days after her own baby was born, the other woman also gave birth, and no one else was in the house. It establishes that there were no witnesses, which is why the case was so hard to settle and why wisdom was needed.
entries.1 kings 3:19: The other woman accidentally smothered her own child during the night while sleeping on it. It describes a tragic accident, showing how the dispute began and helping readers understand the grief and confusion behind the conflict.
entries.1 kings 3:20: The woman got up in the middle of the night, took the living baby from beside the sleeping mother, and swapped it with her dead child. It reveals the deception at the heart of the case, showing readers how far someone might go to avoid loss.
entries.1 kings 3:21: When the mother got up to nurse her baby, she found it dead, but on closer look in the morning she realized it wasn't her child. It shows her shock and growing realization, drawing readers into her distress and the urgency of the case.
entries.1 kings 3:22: The two women argued back and forth in front of the king, each claiming the living child was hers. It shows the impossible situation with no witnesses, highlighting why Solomon needed God-given wisdom to find the truth.
entries.1 kings 3:23: Solomon summarized the dispute: each woman claimed the living child and said the dead one belonged to the other. It shows him carefully listening and restating the facts, modeling how wise leaders pay attention before deciding.
entries.1 kings 3:24: Solomon ordered a sword to be brought to him. It's a startling move that sets up his test, showing readers that wisdom sometimes involves unconventional methods to uncover the truth.
entries.1 kings 3:25: Solomon proposed cutting the living child in half so each woman could have a share. It sounds cruel, but it was a test designed to reveal who truly loved the child, showing that wisdom can expose what's really in people's hearts.
entries.1 kings 3:26: The real mother begged for the child to be given to the other woman rather than killed, while the other woman agreed to cut it in two. Her willingness to give up her child to save its life reveals true love, showing readers that genuine love sacrifices itself for the good of another.
entries.1 kings 3:27: Solomon ordered the child given to the woman who begged for its life, because she was the real mother. It shows his test worked, revealing that true motherhood is proven by selfless love, and it encourages readers to value sacrificial love over claims and rights.
entries.1 kings 3:28: News of the verdict spread through Israel, and the people stood in awe of the king because they saw God's wisdom in him. It shows that God-given wisdom earns respect and points people toward God, reminding readers that wise, fair decisions have a powerful impact on those around us.
entries.2 samuel 23:1: These are David's final recorded words, and he introduces himself as a man God raised up, chosen and anointed, and loved in Israel's songs. It reminds the reader that God can lift an ordinary person to a high place and make their life matter.
entries.2 samuel 23:2: David says that God's Spirit spoke through him and put God's words on his tongue. It means the reader can trust that God can speak through people and that his words are worth listening to.
entries.2 samuel 23:3: God, the solid Rock of Israel, told David that a ruler who does right and respects God is what a good king looks like. It tells the reader that leaders who honor God and act fairly are the kind God approves of.
entries.2 samuel 23:4: A good ruler is compared to the clear morning sunlight that makes grass grow. It means good leadership brings life and freshness to the people under it, and the reader should value and pray for that kind of leadership.
entries.2 samuel 23:5: David asks whether his family stands right with God, and he rests on God's permanent, well-ordered promise to him. It means the reader can hold on to God's promises even when things look imperfect, trusting him to keep and complete what he promised.
entries.2 samuel 23:6: Wicked people are compared to thorns that get thrown away because you can't safely grab them. It tells the reader that evil will not last or be kept, so it is foolish to cling to it.
entries.2 samuel 23:7: Anyone who handles those thorns needs iron tools and a spear, and in the end they are burned up. It means dealing with hardened evil takes serious effort, and evil finally comes to nothing.
entries.2 samuel 23:8: This begins a list of David's mighty warriors, starting with one who struck down eight hundred men at once. It shows that God gave David remarkable fighters, and the reader sees that great deeds are remembered.
entries.2 samuel 23:9: Eleazar was one of the three great fighters who stood with David when the Philistines gathered for battle and the Israelites ran away. It reminds the reader that courage often means staying when others flee.
entries.2 samuel 23:10: Eleazar kept fighting until his hand stuck to his sword, and God gave a great victory that day. It means God can use plain hard work and persistence to win big things, and the reader should not give up too soon.
entries.2 samuel 23:11: Shammah was another fighter; when the Philistines gathered and the people ran, he was there in a field of lentils. It sets up the reader to see another example of standing firm when everyone else leaves.
entries.2 samuel 23:12: Shammah stood his ground in the middle of the field, fought off the enemy, and God gave a great victory. It tells the reader that holding your position, even in a small place, can matter greatly and God honors it.
entries.2 samuel 23:13: Three of the thirty leading warriors came down to David at the stronghold of Adullam while Philistines held the valley. It shows the loyalty of David's men and how they risked much to be near him.
entries.2 samuel 23:14: David was hiding in the stronghold while a Philistine force occupied Bethlehem. It reminds the reader that even a great leader has times of danger and hiding.
entries.2 samuel 23:15: David longed out loud for a drink of water from the well by the gate of Bethlehem. It shows he was human with simple desires, and the reader sees that even heroes have ordinary longings.
entries.2 samuel 23:16: The three men broke through the enemy lines to get that water, but David refused to drink it and poured it out to the Lord. It means David treated their sacrifice as too precious for himself and honored God with it, teaching the reader to value others' sacrifice.
entries.2 samuel 23:17: David said he could not drink what was like the lifeblood of men who risked their lives, so he poured it out to God. It shows deep respect for those who risk everything, and the reader learns to honor sacrifice rather than use it selfishly.
entries.2 samuel 23:18: Abishai, Joab's brother, led the thirty and killed three hundred men with his spear, gaining a name for himself. It shows that skill and bravery earn respect, and the reader sees that courage is worth noting.
entries.2 samuel 23:19: Abishai was the most honored of the thirty and became their captain, though he was not equal to the top three. It means being highly respected is real honor even if you are not the very best, and the reader can be content with their place.
entries.2 samuel 23:20: Benaiah from Kabzeel did great deeds, killing two Moabite warriors and a lion in a pit on a snowy day. It shows remarkable courage and strength, and the reader sees that bravery shows up in surprising, difficult situations.
entries.2 samuel 23:21: Benaiah also killed a huge Egyptian by taking his own spear from him and using it. It means quick thinking and courage can overcome a stronger opponent, and the reader is encouraged to be resourceful.
entries.2 samuel 23:22: These were Benaiah's deeds, and he became famous among the thirty warriors. It reminds the reader that brave actions are remembered and build a good reputation.
entries.2 samuel 23:23: Benaiah was honored above the thirty but not equal to the top three, and David put him in charge of his bodyguard. It shows that trustworthy, brave people get important responsibilities, and the reader sees the value of reliability.
entries.2 samuel 23:24: This starts the longer list of the thirty warriors, beginning with Asahel and Elhanan. It shows that many people played a part in David's success, and the reader learns that a great leader needs a team.
entries.2 samuel 23:25: Shammah and Elika are named among David's warriors. It reminds the reader that even people we know little about were part of something important.
entries.2 samuel 23:26: Helez and Ira are listed among the warriors. It shows the reader that the list includes many faithful men whose names still matter.
entries.2 samuel 23:27: Abiezer and Sibbecai are named among the fighting men. It reminds the reader that each person's contribution is recorded and valued.
entries.2 samuel 23:28: Zalmon and Maharai are listed among the warriors. It shows that many ordinary-sounding people made up David's strong support.
entries.2 samuel 23:29: Heldai and Ittai are named, one from Benjamin. It reminds the reader that people from different backgrounds worked together for a common cause.
entries.2 samuel 23:30: Benaiah and Hiddai are listed among the fighting men. It shows the reader that the list keeps going because many people were needed.
entries.2 samuel 23:31: Abiel and Azmaveth are named among the warriors. It reminds the reader that faithfulness in a supporting role still counts.
entries.2 samuel 23:32: Eliahba and Jashen are listed among David's men. It shows that even those with brief mention were part of the team.
entries.2 samuel 23:33: Jonathan and Ahiam are named among the warriors. It reminds the reader that courage was shared among many, not just a few famous names.
entries.2 samuel 23:34: Eliphelet and Eliam are listed, one connected to Ahithophel. It shows the reader that family connections and loyalties ran through David's fighting men.
entries.2 samuel 23:35: Hezrai and Paarai are named among the warriors. It reminds the reader that many quiet, faithful people helped David succeed.
entries.2 samuel 23:36: Igal and Bani are listed among the fighting men. It shows that people from different places served together in David's army.
entries.2 samuel 23:37: Zelek and Naharai are named, with Naharai carrying Joab's weapons. It reminds the reader that even behind-the-scenes jobs were important to the whole effort.
entries.2 samuel 23:38: Ira and Gareb are listed among the warriors. It shows the reader that the record of faithful service continues to the end.
entries.2 samuel 23:39: The list ends with Uriah the Hittite, making thirty-seven in all. It reminds the reader that even a foreigner was counted among David's loyal men, and that every name in the list mattered.
entries.1 kings 2:41: Solomon was told that Shimei had left Jerusalem and gone to Gath and then come back. This mattered because Shimei had promised never to leave the city.
entries.1 kings 2:42: Solomon reminded Shimei of the oath he had sworn before the Lord: the day he left Jerusalem, he would die, and Shimei had agreed to it. The king was pointing out that Shimei had broken his own solemn promise.
entries.1 kings 2:43: Solomon asked why Shimei had broken his oath to the Lord and disobeyed the king's command. It shows that a promise made before God is serious and cannot be ignored.
entries.1 kings 2:44: Solomon told Shimei that he knew all the evil he had done to David, and that God was now paying him back for it. It reminds us that wrongs done to others do not go unnoticed by God.
entries.1 kings 2:45: Solomon said that blessing would be on him and David's kingdom would stand firm before the Lord forever. It shows the king's confidence that God was establishing his rule.
entries.1 kings 2:46: Solomon ordered Benaiah to execute Shimei, and after that the kingdom was firmly in Solomon's hands. The story shows that justice was carried out and Solomon's rule was made secure.
entries.1 kings 4:1: Solomon was now the undisputed king over the whole nation of Israel. It reminds the reader that God had established his rule over all the people, not just part of them.
entries.1 kings 4:2: The writer begins listing the top officials who served under Solomon, starting with Azariah the priest. This shows that a wise king surrounded himself with capable, trusted leaders.
entries.1 kings 4:3: Two men named Elihoreph and Ahijah handled the king's written records, and Jehoshaphat kept the official records of events. Good government needs people who keep careful track of what happens.
entries.1 kings 4:4: Benaiah commanded the army, and Zadok and Abiathar served as priests. This shows that Solomon organized both the military and the spiritual life of the nation.
entries.1 kings 4:5: Azariah supervised the regional officials, and Zabud served as a priest and a close personal advisor to the king. A wise leader needs both administrators and trusted friends.
entries.1 kings 4:6: Ahishar managed the king's household, and Adoniram oversaw the forced labor. This shows how the daily running of the palace and the workforce was carefully organized.
entries.1 kings 4:7: Solomon appointed twelve men to supply food for the king and his household, each taking one month a year. Spreading the work out this way kept the burden fair and the supplies steady.
entries.1 kings 4:8: The list of officials begins with a man from the hill country of Ephraim, whose father was named Hur. Each region had its own person responsible for providing for the king.
entries.1 kings 4:9: This official was responsible for several towns in the area of Makaz and Beth-shemesh. Each district had a specific person accountable for its supply of food.
entries.1 kings 4:10: Another official managed Arubboth along with Socoh and the land of Hepher. The kingdom was divided into districts so that each one could contribute its share.
entries.1 kings 4:11: This official governed the region of Naphath-dor and was married to Solomon's daughter Taphath. Marrying into the royal family likely strengthened loyalty to the king.
entries.1 kings 4:12: Baana was responsible for a large area including Taanach, Megiddo, and Beth-shean. Some officials had much bigger districts than others, depending on the region.
entries.1 kings 4:13: This official governed Ramoth-gilead and the towns of Jair, including sixty fortified cities with bronze bars on their gates. This shows the kingdom included strong, well-defended towns.
entries.1 kings 4:14: Ahinadab was in charge of the district of Mahanaim. Each official had a clearly assigned area to manage.
entries.1 kings 4:15: Ahimaaz governed Naphtali and was also married to Solomon's daughter Basemath. Family ties like this helped keep the regional leaders loyal to the king.
entries.1 kings 4:16: Baana was responsible for the districts of Asher and Aloth. The work of supplying the king was shared among many officials across the land.
entries.1 kings 4:17: Jehoshaphat was in charge of the region of Issachar. Each tribe's territory had someone accountable for its contributions.
entries.1 kings 4:18: Shimei managed the district of Benjamin. The organization reached every part of the country.
entries.1 kings 4:19: Geber governed the land of Gilead, the old territory of kings Sihon and Og, and one official supervised all the others. A clear chain of command kept the whole system running.
entries.1 kings 4:20: The people of Judah and Israel grew as numerous as the sand on the seashore, and they ate and drank happily. This pictures a nation blessed with abundance and joy.
entries.1 kings 4:21: Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt, and they brought him tribute and served him. His kingdom was large and powerful, and the surrounding nations honored him.
entries.1 kings 4:22: Solomon's household used a huge amount of grain and meal every single day. This shows how large his court was and how wealthy the kingdom had become.
entries.1 kings 4:23: The daily food included many cattle and sheep, plus deer, gazelles, and fowl. The king's table was supplied with rich and varied food, showing great prosperity.
entries.1 kings 4:24: Solomon controlled all the land west of the Euphrates, from Tiphsah to Gaza, and he had peace on every side. God had given the nation security and rest from its enemies.
entries.1 kings 4:25: Throughout Solomon's reign, the people of Judah and Israel lived safely, each person under their own vine and fig tree, from Dan to Beer-sheba. This is a picture of ordinary families enjoying peace and plenty.
entries.1 kings 4:26: Solomon had four thousand stalls for his chariot horses and twelve thousand horsemen. His military strength was enormous, a sign of the kingdom's power.
entries.1 kings 4:27: The twelve officials each made sure, during their month, that food was provided for Solomon and everyone at his table, so nothing was missing. Careful planning meant the king's household never went without.
entries.1 kings 4:28: The officials also brought grain and dry grass for the horses and chariot teams, each doing his assigned part. Even the needs of the animals were carefully provided for.
entries.1 kings 4:29: God gave Solomon great wisdom, good sense, and a mind as broad as the sand on the seashore. His remarkable understanding was a gift from God, not something he earned.
entries.1 kings 4:30: Solomon's wisdom surpassed that of all the people of the East and of Egypt. God made him wiser than the most famous wise men of his time.
entries.1 kings 4:31: He was wiser than everyone, including well-known wise men like Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Darda, and his fame spread among all the surrounding nations. His reputation for wisdom reached far beyond his own country.
entries.1 kings 4:32: Solomon composed three thousand wise sayings and a thousand and five songs. His wisdom was not just in his head; he put it into writing for others.
entries.1 kings 4:33: He spoke about all kinds of plants, from the great cedar of Lebanon to the tiny hyssop on a wall, and about animals, birds, fish, and small creatures. His understanding covered the whole natural world.
entries.1 kings 4:34: People from every nation came to listen to Solomon's wisdom, sent by kings who had heard about it. His God-given wisdom drew the attention of the whole world.
entries.1 kings 1:1: King David had grown very old, and even with blankets piled on him he could not get warm. It shows that even a great king becomes weak and frail with age.
entries.1 kings 1:2: His servants suggested finding a young woman to care for him and keep him warm by lying close to him. They were trying to help the aging king in a practical way.
entries.1 kings 1:3: They searched the whole country and found a beautiful young woman named Abishag, and brought her to the king. She was chosen to serve and care for him.
entries.1 kings 1:4: Abishag was very beautiful and looked after the king constantly, but they were not intimate. She was his caretaker, not his wife.
entries.1 kings 1:5: Adonijah, one of David's sons, proudly decided he would be the next king and got chariots, horses, and fifty men to run ahead of him. He was trying to seize the throne for himself.
entries.1 kings 1:6: His father David had never corrected him or asked why he did things, and he was handsome and born after Absalom. His parents' lack of discipline left him spoiled and self-centered.
entries.1 kings 1:7: Adonijah got Joab the army commander and Abiathar the priest on his side to support his bid for the throne. He was building a power base to make himself king.
entries.1 kings 1:8: But several important leaders—Zadok the priest, Benaiah, the prophet Nathan, and others—refused to join Adonijah. Not everyone was fooled by his grab for power.
entries.1 kings 1:9: Adonijah held a big sacrificial feast near a spring outside Jerusalem and invited all his brothers and the king's officials. It looked religious but was really a political rally for himself.
entries.1 kings 1:10: He deliberately left out Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the loyal soldiers, and his brother Solomon. He knew these people would not support his takeover.
entries.1 kings 1:11: Nathan the prophet went to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, and asked if she knew that Adonijah had made himself king without David's knowledge. He alerted her to the danger.
entries.1 kings 1:12: Nathan told her he had a plan to save her life and her son Solomon's life. The situation was serious enough that their lives were at risk.
entries.1 kings 1:13: Nathan told Bathsheba to remind David of his promise that Solomon would be king after him, and to ask why Adonijah was acting as king. She was to appeal to the king's own word.
entries.1 kings 1:14: Nathan said he would come in while she was still speaking and confirm her story. Two witnesses made the case stronger.
entries.1 kings 1:15: Bathsheba went to the king's room, where he was very old and Abishag was attending him. She came to make her urgent appeal.
entries.1 kings 1:16: Bathsheba bowed low before the king in respect, and he asked what she wanted. She approached him with proper honor.
entries.1 kings 1:17: She reminded him that he had sworn by the Lord that Solomon would be king after him. She was holding him to his solemn promise.
entries.1 kings 1:18: She told him that Adonijah had made himself king without David even knowing about it. The takeover was happening behind the king's back.
entries.1 kings 1:19: Adonijah had held a huge feast and invited the king's sons, the priest, and the army commander—but not Solomon. He was gathering support while excluding the rightful heir.
entries.1 kings 1:20: She said all Israel was watching the king, waiting for him to announce who would succeed him. The whole nation needed his clear decision.
entries.1 kings 1:21: She warned that if the king died without settling this, she and Solomon would be treated as criminals. Their safety depended on David acting now.
entries.1 kings 1:22: While she was still speaking, Nathan the prophet arrived. His timing confirmed her words.
entries.1 kings 1:23: The king was told Nathan had come, and Nathan bowed low before him. He showed proper respect as he entered.
entries.1 kings 1:24: Nathan asked the king directly whether he had decided that Adonijah would be the next king. He was testing whether this was really David's choice.
entries.1 kings 1:25: Nathan reported that Adonijah had thrown a great feast, invited the king's sons and officials, and people were shouting long live King Adonijah. The celebration was happening without the king's approval.
entries.1 kings 1:26: Nathan pointed out that he, Zadok, Benaiah, and Solomon had not been invited. This proved Adonijah was acting on his own.
entries.1 kings 1:27: Nathan asked whether the king had really authorized this without telling his trusted servants who should succeed him. He was pressing David to clarify the truth.
entries.1 kings 1:28: David called for Bathsheba to come back, and she came and stood before him. He was ready to respond to her appeal.
entries.1 kings 1:29: The king swore an oath by the living Lord, who had rescued him from every trouble. He called on God as his witness.
entries.1 kings 1:30: David confirmed that just as he had sworn to Bathsheba, Solomon would be king after him that very day. He kept his promise without delay.
entries.1 kings 1:31: Bathsheba bowed low in honor and wished the king long life. She showed gratitude and respect for his decision.
entries.1 kings 1:32: David summoned Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah to carry out his orders. He moved quickly to put Solomon on the throne.
entries.1 kings 1:33: David told them to take his own royal animal and have Solomon ride it down to Gihon. Riding the king's mount was a public sign that Solomon was the chosen successor.
entries.1 kings 1:34: He instructed Zadok and Nathan to anoint Solomon with oil as king over Israel and to blow the horn and shout long live King Solomon. The anointing and public proclamation made it official.
entries.1 kings 1:35: David said they should come back up with Solomon, who would sit on the throne and rule in his place over Israel and Judah. He gave clear orders about the succession.
entries.1 kings 1:36: Benaiah agreed and prayed that the Lord would confirm the king's word. He supported the decision wholeheartedly.
entries.1 kings 1:37: Benaiah prayed that the Lord would be with Solomon as he had been with David and make his throne even greater. He honored both the old king and the new one.
entries.1 kings 1:38: So the priest, the prophet, Benaiah, and the royal guards went down and put Solomon on David's animal and took him to Gihon. They carried out the king's command exactly.
entries.1 kings 1:39: Zadok took the sacred oil from the tent and anointed Solomon, and when the horn blew, all the people shouted long live King Solomon. The anointing and the people's response confirmed him as king.
entries.1 kings 1:40: The whole crowd followed him playing flutes and celebrating so loudly that the ground shook with the sound. The people joyfully accepted Solomon as their king.
entries.1 kings 6:1: This dates the start of the temple building to 480 years after Israel left Egypt, in Solomon's fourth year as king. It shows God's long plan was still moving forward, and that big things for God often come after long waiting.
entries.1 kings 6:2: The temple was a long, narrow, tall building, about 90 feet by 30 by 45. The exact size matters less than the fact that it was built carefully and generously for God.
entries.1 kings 6:3: A covered porch stood at the front of the temple, matching the building's width. It gave people a place to approach the entrance, showing that coming to God's house was meant to be a deliberate step.
entries.1 kings 6:4: The temple had windows with lattice work, letting in light while keeping the inside enclosed. Even God's house was designed to be practical and livable, not just decorative.
entries.1 kings 6:5: Side rooms were built all around the outside walls of the temple and its inner room. These gave the temple practical storage and work space, showing that serving God involves ordinary arrangements too.
entries.1 kings 6:6: The side rooms got wider on each higher floor, and they rested on ledges rather than being built into the temple walls. The design protected the sacred walls from being cut into.
entries.1 kings 6:7: The stones were cut and finished at the quarry, so no hammer or iron tool was heard at the building site. The quiet construction suggests that God's house was to be built with care and reverence.
entries.1 kings 6:8: A door on the right side led into the lowest side rooms, with winding stairs up to the middle and top floors. Even the access was thought through so the temple could be used and maintained.
entries.1 kings 6:9: Solomon finished the main structure and roofed it with cedar boards. The work was completed step by step, showing that finishing what we start for God matters.
entries.1 kings 6:10: The side rooms around the temple were fifteen cubits high and attached with cedar beams. They were part of the whole complex, supporting the temple's daily use.
entries.1 kings 6:11: This introduces a message from God to Solomon in the middle of the building project. It reminds us that God speaks while we are busy working, not only after we finish.
entries.1 kings 6:12: God told Solomon that if he obeyed God's laws, God would keep the promise he made to David. The temple mattered, but Solomon's obedience mattered more.
entries.1 kings 6:13: God promised to live among Israel and never abandon his people. The temple was a sign of God's presence, but the promise was about relationship, not just a building.
entries.1 kings 6:14: Solomon completed the building of the temple. The verse marks the end of the main construction, showing that the work God gave him was finished.
entries.1 kings 6:15: Inside, the walls were lined with cedar from floor to ceiling, and the floor was covered with cypress wood. The inside was finished with care and beauty for God's house.
entries.1 kings 6:16: A separate inner room, twenty cubits deep, was walled off at the back of the temple. This was the most sacred space, set apart for God's presence.
entries.1 kings 6:17: The main hall in front of the inner room was forty cubits long. The layout separated the ordinary worship area from the most holy place.
entries.1 kings 6:18: The cedar interior was carved with buds and flowers, and no stone was visible inside. The temple was made beautiful inside, showing that God's house deserved careful craftsmanship.
entries.1 kings 6:19: Solomon prepared the inner room to hold the ark of the Lord's covenant. This room was the heart of the temple, where God's agreement with Israel was remembered.
entries.1 kings 6:20: The inner room was a cube twenty cubits each way, overlaid with pure gold, and it held a cedar altar covered in gold. The most sacred space was also the most richly decorated.
entries.1 kings 6:21: Solomon covered the inside of the temple with gold and hung gold chains in front of the inner room. The gold showed how precious and set apart this place was for God.
entries.1 kings 6:22: Gold covered the whole interior, including the altar in the inner room. Nothing was left plain, showing total dedication of the space to God.
entries.1 kings 6:23: Two large winged figures made of olive wood, ten cubits high, were placed in the inner room. They stood as guardians of the most holy place.
entries.1 kings 6:24: Each figure had wings stretching five cubits, with a ten-cubit span from wingtip to wingtip. Their size and symmetry made the inner room feel awe-inspiring.
entries.1 kings 6:25: Both winged figures were the same size and shape, ten cubits high. The matching pair showed order and balance in God's house.
entries.1 kings 6:26: This repeats that both figures were ten cubits high, emphasizing their equal size. The detail underscores that the inner room was designed with precision.
entries.1 kings 6:27: The figures stood inside the inner room with their wings touching the walls and each other in the middle. Their spread wings filled the space, pointing to God's presence covering the whole room.
entries.1 kings 6:28: The winged figures were covered with gold. Even these guardians were made precious, matching the glory of the inner room.
entries.1 kings 6:29: All the temple walls, inside and out, were carved with winged figures, palm trees, and open flowers. The decoration filled the house with symbols of life and God's heavenly court.
entries.1 kings 6:30: The floor of the temple was covered with gold inside and out. Even what people walked on was treated as precious because the whole house belonged to God.
entries.1 kings 6:31: The entrance to the inner room had olive-wood doors with a five-sided frame. The doorway was designed with care because it led to the most sacred place.
entries.1 kings 6:32: The olive-wood doors were carved with winged figures, palm trees, and flowers, then covered with gold. Beauty and reverence marked the way into God's presence.
entries.1 kings 6:33: Olive-wood pillars with square frames were made for the entrance to the main temple hall. The entryways were solid and carefully built.
entries.1 kings 6:34: The temple doors were made of cypress wood in two folding panels. Practical design and craftsmanship served the worship life of God's people.
entries.1 kings 6:35: The doors were carved with winged figures, palm trees, and flowers, and overlaid with gold. Even the doors were made beautiful, showing that every part of God's house mattered.
entries.1 kings 6:36: An inner courtyard was built with three courses of cut stone and one of cedar beams. The temple complex had boundaries that set it apart from ordinary space.
entries.1 kings 6:37: The foundation of the temple was laid in Solomon's fourth year, in the month Ziv. The exact date is recorded because this was a real, historical project.
entries.1 kings 6:38: The temple was finished in Solomon's eleventh year, in the month Bul, taking seven years in all. The work was completed exactly as designed, showing faithful follow-through on a long task.
entries.1 kings 1:41: Adonijah and his guests had just finished eating when they heard the noise of a big celebration in the city, and Joab asked what all the commotion was about. It reminds us that trouble can arrive right when we feel most secure.
entries.1 kings 1:42: Jonathan, a priest's son, arrived and Adonijah welcomed him, assuming he brought good news because he was a trustworthy man. We should be careful not to assume news will be good just because we want it to be.
entries.1 kings 1:43: Jonathan told Adonijah plainly that his hope was wrong: David had made Solomon king instead. The truth can overturn our plans in a single sentence.
entries.1 kings 1:44: Jonathan explained that David had sent the priest, the prophet, the army commander, and the royal guard to put Solomon on the king's own mule. This showed the new king had full official backing.
entries.1 kings 1:45: The priest and prophet anointed Solomon with oil at Gihon, and the joyful crowd that followed is the noise Adonijah had heard. The celebration was for someone else's coronation, not his.
entries.1 kings 1:46: Jonathan stated the simple fact that Solomon was now sitting on the throne. The matter was settled and could not be undone.
entries.1 kings 1:47: David's servants blessed him and prayed that Solomon would be even greater than he was, and David bowed in worship on his bed. A humble leader can rejoice when his successor is honored.
entries.1 kings 1:48: David praised God for letting him live to see his own son take the throne. It is a gift to see good come to those who follow us.
entries.1 kings 1:49: Adonijah's guests were suddenly afraid and scattered, each going home. People who gather around a self-seeking leader often vanish when his cause fails.
entries.1 kings 1:50: Adonijah was terrified of Solomon and grabbed the horns of the altar, a place where a person could seek protection. Fear drove him to cling to the one safe place he knew.
entries.1 kings 1:51: Solomon was told that Adonijah was hiding at the altar and asking for a promise that he would not be killed. He was bargaining for his life out of fear.
entries.1 kings 1:52: Solomon said that if Adonijah proved loyal he would not be harmed, but any further wrongdoing would cost him his life. Mercy was offered, but it came with real accountability.
entries.1 kings 1:53: Solomon had Adonijah brought down from the altar, and after Adonijah bowed in respect, Solomon sent him home. The new king showed restraint instead of taking revenge.
entries.1 kings 9:1: Solomon finished building both the Lord's temple and his own palace, completing everything he had planned. It shows that a long project can finally be finished, and God notices our completed work.
entries.1 kings 9:2: God appeared to Solomon a second time, just as he had earlier at Gibeon. God sometimes speaks again to people he has already spoken to, so we can expect him to keep guiding us.
entries.1 kings 9:3: God told Solomon he had heard his prayers and had set apart the temple as his own, promising to watch over it always. This means God listens when we pray and cares about the places where people worship him.
entries.1 kings 9:4: God's promise came with a condition: Solomon had to keep following God faithfully, as his father David did. The same is true for us—God's blessings go together with our staying faithful to him.
entries.1 kings 9:5: If Solomon stayed faithful, God promised his family would always have a king on Israel's throne. God keeps the promises he made long ago, even across generations.
entries.1 kings 9:6: God warned that if Solomon or his descendants turned away and worshiped other gods, the good things would be lost. It is a serious warning that turning from God has real consequences.
entries.1 kings 9:7: God said that if his people turned away, he would remove them from the land and let the temple be destroyed, making them an example to others. This shows that God's patience has limits when people keep rejecting him.
entries.1 kings 9:8: The temple would become a pile of ruins, and passersby would be shocked and ask why God let this happen. Even impressive things can fall when people abandon God.
entries.1 kings 9:9: People would answer that it happened because the Israelites turned from the Lord who rescued them and worshiped other gods instead. The lesson is that forgetting the God who helped us leads to ruin.
entries.1 kings 9:10: After twenty years, Solomon had finished both the temple and his palace. Big accomplishments often take a long time, and it is good to see them through.
entries.1 kings 9:11: Hiram, the king of Tyre, had supplied Solomon with wood and gold, so Solomon gave him twenty towns in Galilee in return. This shows how leaders made deals and traded favors to get things done.
entries.1 kings 9:12: When Hiram came to look at the towns, he was not happy with them. Even a generous gift can disappoint, and it is okay to be honest when something does not meet expectations.
entries.1 kings 9:13: Hiram asked what kind of towns these were, and they were nicknamed the land of Cabul, which suggests they were worthless. A bad deal can leave a lasting bad name.
entries.1 kings 9:14: Hiram sent Solomon a large amount of gold. This reminds us that the help Solomon received came with real value, and generosity between people should be remembered.
entries.1 kings 9:15: Solomon used forced labor to build the temple, his palace, the Millo, Jerusalem's wall, and the towns of Megiddo and Gezer. Great building projects often came at a cost to ordinary workers.
entries.1 kings 9:16: The king of Egypt had captured Gezer, burned it, and killed its people, then gave it to his daughter when she married Solomon. This shows how marriages between royal families were used to make political deals.
entries.1 kings 9:17: Solomon rebuilt Gezer and the lower town of Beth-horon. Rebuilding what was ruined is a practical way to make a place strong again.
entries.1 kings 9:18: Solomon also built Baalath and Tamar out in the desert land. Leaders often build in hard places to secure their borders and help people live there.
entries.1 kings 9:19: Solomon built storage towns, towns for his chariots and horses, and anything else he wanted in Jerusalem, Lebanon, and across his kingdom. A powerful king can get a lot done, but his plans were mostly about his own glory.
entries.1 kings 9:20: There were still other peoples in the land who were not Israelites. These groups had been there before Israel arrived and had not been fully removed.
entries.1 kings 9:21: Solomon made the descendants of these peoples do forced labor, and they were still doing it at the time this was written. This shows how one group of people was treated as less than another, which is a hard part of the story.
entries.1 kings 9:22: Solomon did not force Israelites to do that labor; instead they served as soldiers, officials, and officers. He treated his own people differently from the others, which reminds us to notice unfair treatment.
entries.1 kings 9:23: There were 550 foremen in charge of the workers on Solomon's projects. Large projects need many supervisors, and the people in charge carry real responsibility.
entries.1 kings 9:24: Solomon moved Pharaoh's daughter from the old city area to a house he built for her, and then he built the Millo. He was organizing his capital and making room for his wife.
entries.1 kings 9:25: Three times a year Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar he had built to the Lord. Regular worship was part of his life, and setting aside regular times for God is a good habit for us too.
entries.1 kings 9:26: Solomon built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, a port on the Red Sea in Edom. He used his country's location to build trade and wealth.
entries.1 kings 9:27: Hiram sent experienced sailors to work with Solomon's men on the ships. Good results often come when people with different skills work together.
entries.1 kings 9:28: The ships sailed to Ophir and brought back a huge amount of gold for Solomon. The voyage paid off, showing that careful planning and skilled people can bring great returns.
entries.1 kings 10:1: A foreign queen heard reports about Solomon's wisdom and traveled to test whether it was real. It reminds readers that genuine wisdom invites honest questions and scrutiny.
entries.1 kings 10:2: She arrived with a huge caravan of camels carrying spices, gold, and jewels, then discussed everything on her mind with him. It shows she came seriously prepared to seek answers, not just to sightsee.
entries.1 kings 10:3: Solomon answered every question she raised, and nothing was too difficult for him to explain. It shows that his God-given wisdom held up under hard questioning.
entries.1 kings 10:4: After seeing his wisdom and the palace he had built, she was deeply impressed. What she observed matched and exceeded what she had heard.
entries.1 kings 10:5: The food, the orderly servants in fine robes, the cupbearers, and his worship at the temple left her breathless. The sheer scale and order of his court overwhelmed her.
entries.1 kings 10:6: She admitted that the reports she had heard back home about his achievements and wisdom were accurate. Seeing for herself confirmed the truth of what others had said.
entries.1 kings 10:7: She confessed she had doubted the reports until she saw it herself, and now realized the reality was far greater than the story. It teaches that firsthand experience can surpass even high expectations.
entries.1 kings 10:8: She called his wives and servants fortunate because they could regularly hear his wisdom. She recognized that being near wise teaching is a real privilege.
entries.1 kings 10:9: She praised the Lord for placing Solomon on Israel's throne out of his lasting love for the nation, to rule with justice. She saw Solomon's reign as evidence of God's faithfulness, not just human achievement.
entries.1 kings 10:10: She gave him an enormous amount of gold, spices, and jewels, more spices than had ever been seen. Her generosity matched her gratitude for what she had received.
entries.1 kings 10:11: Hiram's fleet also brought back large amounts of sandalwood and jewels along with gold from Ophir. It shows how trade and international connections added to the kingdom's riches.
entries.1 kings 10:12: Solomon used the sandalwood for temple and palace pillars and for musical instruments, and such wood was never seen again in that quantity. Valuable resources were put to use for worship and beauty.
entries.1 kings 10:13: Solomon gave the queen everything she asked for and more from his own generosity, and then she returned home with her servants. Their meeting ended with mutual respect and generous giving.
entries.1 kings 10:14: The gold that came to Solomon in a single year weighed six hundred sixty-six talents. This highlights the extraordinary scale of his annual income.
entries.1 kings 10:15: On top of that came revenue from traders, Arabian kings, and regional governors. His wealth came from many sources, not just one.
entries.1 kings 10:16: He made two hundred large gold shields, each using six hundred shekels of gold. These were ceremonial displays of royal wealth and power.
entries.1 kings 10:17: He made three hundred smaller gold shields and stored them in a palace hall called the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Even his ceremonial armor was made of gold.
entries.1 kings 10:18: He built a large throne out of ivory and covered it with fine gold. It was designed to display his status as a great king.
entries.1 kings 10:19: The throne had six steps, a rounded back, armrests, and two lions beside the armrests. Every detail was crafted to convey majesty and authority.
entries.1 kings 10:20: Twelve more lions stood on the steps, six on each side, and no other kingdom had anything like it. His throne was unique in the ancient world.
entries.1 kings 10:21: All his drinking cups and palace vessels were gold, and silver was considered too ordinary to bother with. His wealth was so great that common metals lost their value.
entries.1 kings 10:22: He had a fleet of trading ships that returned every three years with gold, silver, ivory, monkeys, and peacocks. Long-distance trade brought exotic goods and great profit.
entries.1 kings 10:23: Solomon became richer and wiser than any other king on earth. His reputation stood above all others in his time.
entries.1 kings 10:24: People came from everywhere to hear the wisdom God had placed in his heart. His gift drew the attention of the whole world.
entries.1 kings 10:25: Visitors brought him gifts year after year: silver, gold, robes, weapons, spices, horses, and mules. His court received a steady stream of tribute from those who came.
entries.1 kings 10:26: Solomon gathered fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, stationed in chariot cities and with him in Jerusalem. He built up a large military force.
entries.1 kings 10:27: Silver became as common as stone in Jerusalem, and cedar as plentiful as sycamore trees in the lowlands. His wealth made rare materials ordinary.
entries.1 kings 10:28: His horses were imported from Egypt and Kue, bought through royal traders at set prices. He depended on international trade for his military resources.
entries.1 kings 10:29: A chariot could be bought from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver and a horse for a hundred fifty, and the traders resold them to Hittite and Aramean kings. Solomon's kingdom was a hub in the horse and chariot trade.
entries.1 kings 7:1: Solomon took thirteen years to finish building his own palace, which was longer than the temple took. It's a reminder that even a wise king could pour huge time and effort into his own comfort.
entries.1 kings 7:2: He built a large hall called the Forest of Lebanon, made of cedar pillars and beams. This showed the wealth and grandeur of his kingdom.
entries.1 kings 7:3: The roof over the pillars was made of cedar, supported by rows of beams. The details show careful, costly construction.
entries.1 kings 7:4: The windows were set in three rows so they lined up opposite each other. Good design and order marked his building.
entries.1 kings 7:5: All the doorways and windows had square frames and matched each other in three rows. The building was carefully planned and symmetrical.
entries.1 kings 7:6: He made a pillared porch with steps leading up to it. It was a grand entrance for a grand palace.
entries.1 kings 7:7: He built a special room with a throne where he judged legal cases, paneled in cedar. It reminds us that leaders are meant to give fair decisions.
entries.1 kings 7:8: His own living quarters and a separate house for Pharaoh's daughter were built the same way. His many marriages brought separate households and complexity.
entries.1 kings 7:9: All these buildings were made of expensive, specially cut stone from foundation to top. No expense was spared on the king's buildings.
entries.1 kings 7:10: The foundations were huge, costly stones, some over ten feet across. A strong foundation was needed for such grand structures.
entries.1 kings 7:11: Above the foundations were more costly cut stones and cedar wood. The finest materials were used throughout.
entries.1 kings 7:12: The outer courtyard was walled with layers of stone and cedar, matching the temple courtyard. The king's grounds were built to the same high standard as the temple area.
entries.1 kings 7:13: Solomon sent for a craftsman named Hiram from Tyre. He knew to bring in skilled experts for the temple work.
entries.1 kings 7:14: Hiram was a skilled bronze worker with a mixed background, and he came to do all the work Solomon needed. God can use people of any background for important work.
entries.1 kings 7:15: He made two large bronze pillars, each about twenty-seven feet tall and eighteen feet around. These stood as impressive markers at the temple entrance.
entries.1 kings 7:16: He made decorative tops for the pillars, each about seven and a half feet high. The temple was adorned with beauty, not just bare function.
entries.1 kings 7:17: He made lattice networks to decorate the tops of the pillars. Fine craftsmanship was part of honoring God's house.
entries.1 kings 7:18: He added rows of decorative fruit shapes around the tops of the pillars. Small details were carefully attended to in the temple.
entries.1 kings 7:19: The pillar tops were decorated with lily designs and were about six feet across. The temple's beauty reflected care and devotion.
entries.1 kings 7:20: Two hundred decorative fruit shapes went around each pillar top. The work was lavish and detailed.
entries.1 kings 7:21: He set the pillars at the temple entrance and named them Jachin and Boaz, names suggesting God establishes and gives strength. They stood as a reminder of God's firm foundation.
entries.1 kings 7:22: The pillar tops were finished with lily designs, completing that work. The craftsman finished what he started.
entries.1 kings 7:23: He made a huge round bronze basin, about fifteen feet across and seven and a half feet high. It was a major feature for the temple's water needs.
entries.1 kings 7:24: Decorative bud shapes circled the basin, cast as one piece with it. Even a functional object was made beautiful.
entries.1 kings 7:25: The great basin rested on twelve bronze oxen facing outward in four directions. The number twelve echoes the tribes of Israel.
entries.1 kings 7:26: The basin was about a hand's width thick, shaped like a lily, and held about two thousand baths of water. It was huge, meant for washing and ritual cleansing.
entries.1 kings 7:27: He made ten bronze stands on wheels, each about six feet square and four and a half feet high. These movable stands held smaller basins for washing.
entries.1 kings 7:28: The stands were built with square panels set in frames. Careful structure went into each one.
entries.1 kings 7:29: The panels were decorated with lions, oxen, and winged creatures, with wreaths around them. The temple furnishings were richly ornamented.
entries.1 kings 7:30: Each stand had four bronze wheels and axle fittings, with decorative plates at the corners. These stands were both useful and finely made.
entries.1 kings 7:31: The opening on top of each stand was round, about a cubit and a half across, with carvings on the square sides. Practical design and decoration went together.
entries.1 kings 7:32: The four wheels sat under the frames, each about two and a quarter feet high. The stands could be moved where needed.
entries.1 kings 7:33: The wheels were made like chariot wheels, all cast from bronze. The work was sturdy and well engineered.
entries.1 kings 7:34: Four corner plates were attached to each stand as part of its structure. The stands were solidly built.
entries.1 kings 7:35: On top of each stand was a round piece about nine inches high. This held the basin in place.
entries.1 kings 7:36: He carved winged creatures, lions, and palm trees on the panels, with decorative borders. The temple's equipment was covered in meaningful art.
entries.1 kings 7:37: All ten stands were identical in design, size, and shape. Consistency and order marked the temple work.
entries.1 kings 7:38: He made ten bronze basins, each holding about forty baths, one for each stand. These were for washing at the temple.
entries.1 kings 7:39: Five stands went on each side of the temple, and the great basin was placed at the southeast corner. Everything had its proper place in God's house.
entries.1 kings 7:40: Hiram finished making the pots, shovels, and bowls, completing all his work for the temple. Faithful, skilled work done for God's house is worth finishing well.
entries.1 kings 7:41: This lists the two bronze pillars with decorative bowl-shaped tops and the lattice work around them. It reminds the reader that even small details of the temple were carefully made for God's house.
entries.1 kings 7:42: There were four hundred pomegranate-shaped ornaments arranged in rows on the lattice around the pillar tops. The reader can see that beauty and order were part of honoring God.
entries.1 kings 7:43: This names the ten bronze stands and the ten basins that sat on them. These were practical items used in the temple's worship.
entries.1 kings 7:44: This describes the large bronze water basin called the sea, held up by twelve bronze oxen. It shows the scale and craftsmanship of the temple furnishings.
entries.1 kings 7:45: All the pots, shovels, and bowls Hiram made for Solomon's temple were made of polished bronze. The reader sees that ordinary tools for temple service were made with care.
entries.1 kings 7:46: These bronze items were cast in clay molds in the Jordan Valley between Succoth and Zarethan. It shows the work was done at a real place by real craftsmen.
entries.1 kings 7:47: No one weighed the bronze because there was simply too much of it. The abundance points to how richly the temple was supplied.
entries.1 kings 7:48: Solomon also had the gold altar and the gold table for the sacred bread made for the temple. These were central pieces for worship in God's house.
entries.1 kings 7:49: Ten gold lampstands stood in front of the inner room, five on each side, along with gold flowers and lamps. The reader sees that light and beauty were built into the place of worship.
entries.1 kings 7:50: Even the cups, snuffers, bowls, spoons, fire pans, and door hinges were made of gold. This shows that everything connected with the temple was treated as special.
entries.1 kings 7:51: When all the work was finished, Solomon stored his father David's dedicated silver, gold, and vessels in the temple treasuries. It marks the completion of the temple and the honoring of what had been set apart for God.
entries.1 kings 11:1: Solomon loved many foreign women from nations God had warned Israel about. Loving people from these nations would pull his heart away from God, which is exactly what happened.
entries.1 kings 11:2: God had told Israel not to marry people from these nations because they would lead them to worship other gods. Solomon ignored that warning and married them anyway.
entries.1 kings 11:3: Solomon had 700 wives who were princesses and 300 other wives. His many wives turned his heart away from God.
entries.1 kings 11:4: When Solomon was old, his wives led him to worship other gods. His heart was no longer fully devoted to the Lord as his father David's had been.
entries.1 kings 11:5: Solomon followed Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Zidonians, and Milcom, the god of the Ammonites. These were false gods, not the true God.
entries.1 kings 11:6: Solomon did what was evil in the Lord's sight. He did not follow the Lord with his whole heart as his father David had done.
entries.1 kings 11:7: Solomon built places of worship for Chemosh, the god of Moab, and Molech, the god of Ammon, on a mountain near Jerusalem. He set up shrines for false gods in the land God had given him.
entries.1 kings 11:8: Solomon did this for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and offered sacrifices to their gods. He allowed idol worship to spread because of his marriages.
entries.1 kings 11:9: The Lord was angry with Solomon because his heart had turned away from the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice. God had shown him great favor, and Solomon turned from him anyway.
entries.1 kings 11:10: God had specifically commanded Solomon not to follow other gods, but Solomon disobeyed. He knew what God wanted and chose to do otherwise.
entries.1 kings 11:11: God told Solomon that because he had broken his covenant and laws, the kingdom would be torn from him and given to one of his servants. Sin had consequences for Solomon's whole kingdom.
entries.1 kings 11:12: God said he would not take the kingdom away during Solomon's lifetime, out of respect for David his father. The judgment would fall on Solomon's son instead.
entries.1 kings 11:13: God would not take the whole kingdom from Solomon's son but would leave him one tribe. He did this for the sake of David and Jerusalem, the city he had chosen.
entries.1 kings 11:14: God raised up Hadad the Edomite as an adversary to trouble Solomon. He was a member of Edom's royal family.
entries.1 kings 11:15: This recalls when David defeated Edom and Joab, his army commander, stayed to bury the dead and kill every male in Edom. It sets the background for Hadad's escape.
entries.1 kings 11:16: Joab and all Israel stayed in Edom for six months until every male there was killed. This was a harsh military campaign.
entries.1 kings 11:17: Hadad was still a young boy when he fled to Egypt with some of his father's Edomite servants. He escaped the slaughter.
entries.1 kings 11:18: They traveled through Midian and Paran, picking up men along the way, and came to Pharaoh king of Egypt. Pharaoh gave Hadad a house, food, and land.
entries.1 kings 11:19: Hadad pleased Pharaoh so much that Pharaoh gave him the sister of his wife, Queen Tahpenes, as a wife. Hadad was treated like family in Egypt.
entries.1 kings 11:20: Tahpenes' sister bore Hadad a son named Genubath, and Tahpenes raised him in Pharaoh's palace among Pharaoh's own sons. Hadad's family was fully accepted in Egypt.
entries.1 kings 11:21: When Hadad heard that David and Joab were dead, he asked Pharaoh to let him return to his own country. With his enemies gone, he wanted to go home.
entries.1 kings 11:22: Pharaoh asked Hadad what he lacked in Egypt that made him want to leave, and Hadad said nothing, but still asked to go. He wanted to return despite having been treated well.
entries.1 kings 11:23: God raised up another adversary, Rezon son of Eliada, who had fled from his master Hadadezer king of Zobah. God used him too to oppose Solomon.
entries.1 kings 11:24: Rezon gathered a band of outlaws and became their leader, then went to Damascus and made himself king there. He built his own power base.
entries.1 kings 11:25: Rezon was a trouble to Israel throughout Solomon's reign, and Hadad also caused damage, being hostile to Israel while ruling over Edom. Solomon faced opposition from multiple enemies.
entries.1 kings 11:26: Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite from Zeredah whose mother was a widow named Zeruah, was a servant of Solomon who rebelled against the king. He would become a key figure in the kingdom's division.
entries.1 kings 11:27: This is how Jeroboam came to rebel against Solomon: Solomon was building the Millo and repairing the broken parts of the city of David. The building projects were part of the setting for Jeroboam's rise.
entries.1 kings 11:28: Jeroboam was a capable and responsible man, and Solomon saw he was a good worker, so he put him in charge of all the labor assigned to the tribes of Joseph. Jeroboam was given real authority.
entries.1 kings 11:29: At that time Jeroboam was leaving Jerusalem, and the prophet Ahijah from Shiloh met him on the road. Ahijah was wearing a new robe, and the two were alone in the open country.
entries.1 kings 11:30: Ahijah took his new robe and tore it into twelve pieces. This was a visual sign of what God was about to do to the kingdom.
entries.1 kings 11:31: Ahijah told Jeroboam to take ten pieces, because the Lord said he would tear the kingdom from Solomon and give ten tribes to Jeroboam. God was announcing a major change in leadership.
entries.1 kings 11:32: One tribe would remain with Solomon's line, for the sake of God's servant David and Jerusalem, the city God had chosen out of all Israel's tribes. God kept a remnant for David's sake.
entries.1 kings 11:33: God gave this judgment because the people had turned to worship Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Milcom. They had not walked in God's ways or kept his laws as David had.
entries.1 kings 11:34: God would not take the kingdom from Solomon himself but would let him remain king for his whole life, because of David, who delighted God by keeping his commands. God honored his promise to David.
entries.1 kings 11:35: God would take the kingdom from Solomon's son and give it to Jeroboam. The judgment would fall on the next generation.
entries.1 kings 11:36: God would give one tribe to Solomon's son so that David would always have a lamp burning before God in Jerusalem, the city God chose for his name. God preserved a line for David.
entries.1 kings 11:37: God told Jeroboam that he would take him and make him king over Israel, and Jeroboam would rule over whatever he desired. God was offering Jeroboam the throne.
entries.1 kings 11:38: If Jeroboam listened to God's commands, walked in his ways, and did what was right, God would be with him and build him a lasting house as he did for David, and give Israel to him. The promise was conditional on obedience.
entries.1 kings 11:39: God said he would bring trouble on David's descendants because of this, but not forever. The discipline would be temporary, not the end of David's line.
entries.1 kings 11:40: Solomon tried to find a way to kill Jeroboam, but Jeroboam fled to Egypt to Shishak king of Egypt and stayed there until Solomon died. The conflict drove Jeroboam into exile.
entries.1 kings 11:41: The rest of Solomon's acts, including all he did and his wisdom, are written in the book of the acts of Solomon. The writer points readers to another record for more details.
entries.1 kings 11:42: Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years. His reign was long, but it ended with his kingdom under judgment.
entries.1 kings 11:43: Solomon died and was buried in the city of David his father, and his son Rehoboam became king in his place. The throne passed to the next generation, where the promised division would happen.
entries.1 kings 12:1: Rehoboam, Solomon's son, traveled to Shechem where the people of Israel had gathered to crown him king. This was the moment he would take power, and everyone was watching what kind of ruler he would be.
entries.1 kings 12:2: Jeroboam had fled to Egypt to escape Solomon and was living there. When he heard what was happening, he returned from Egypt to his hometown in the hill country.
entries.1 kings 12:3: The people of Israel sent for Jeroboam and then came together to speak to Rehoboam. They wanted to present their concerns to the new king as a group.
entries.1 kings 12:4: The people told Rehoboam that his father Solomon had made their lives very hard. They asked him to lighten the burden, and in return they would serve him loyally.
entries.1 kings 12:5: Rehoboam told the people to go away for three days and then come back for his answer. He wanted time to think about what to say.
entries.1 kings 12:6: Rehoboam asked the older men who had advised his father Solomon what answer he should give the people. He was looking for wise counsel from experienced advisors.
entries.1 kings 12:7: The old men told him that if he served the people and spoke kindly to them now, they would be loyal to him forever. Their advice was to lead with humility and care.
entries.1 kings 12:8: Rehoboam ignored the advice of the older men and instead turned to the young men he had grown up with. He chose to listen to people his own age instead of those with experience.
entries.1 kings 12:9: Rehoboam asked the young men what answer he should give to the people who wanted their burden lightened. He was looking for their opinion on how to respond.
entries.1 kings 12:10: The young men told him to answer the people harshly, saying his little finger was thicker than his father's waist. They wanted him to show he would be even tougher than Solomon.
entries.1 kings 12:11: The young men told him to say his father used whips but he would use scorpions, meaning he would be far harsher. This was a threat of even heavier treatment, not a promise of relief.
entries.1 kings 12:12: The people came back to Rehoboam on the third day, just as he had told them to. They were expecting his answer to their request.
entries.1 kings 12:13: Rehoboam answered the people harshly and ignored the wise advice of the older men. He chose to be tough instead of kind.
entries.1 kings 12:14: Rehoboam repeated the young men's words, telling the people he would make their burden heavier and punish them more severely. He threatened them instead of listening to their pain.
entries.1 kings 12:15: The king refused to listen to the people, and this happened because God was carrying out what he had planned. God had already said through the prophet Ahijah that Jeroboam would take part of the kingdom.
entries.1 kings 12:16: When the people saw the king would not listen, they rejected the family of David and went home. They declared they had no share in David's dynasty and would no longer follow Rehoboam.
entries.1 kings 12:17: Rehoboam still ruled over the Israelites who lived in the towns of Judah. His kingdom was now limited to the southern territory.
entries.1 kings 12:18: Rehoboam sent Adoniram, who was in charge of forced labor, to the people, and they stoned him to death. Rehoboam quickly fled in his chariot to Jerusalem to save his life.
entries.1 kings 12:19: From that day on, the people of Israel have been separated from the family of David. The kingdom split, and the northern tribes no longer belonged to David's line.
entries.1 kings 12:20: When the people heard Jeroboam had returned, they called him to the assembly and made him king over Israel. Only the tribe of Judah stayed loyal to the family of David.
entries.1 kings 12:21: Rehoboam gathered the fighting men of Judah and Benjamin, about 180,000 strong, to go to war against Israel and win back the kingdom. He was preparing for a civil war.
entries.1 kings 12:22: God spoke to Shemaiah, a man of God, giving him a message. God was about to intervene in the situation.
entries.1 kings 12:23: God told Shemaiah to deliver the message to Rehoboam, the king of Judah, and to all the people of Judah and Benjamin. The message was for the whole southern kingdom.
entries.1 kings 12:24: God said they must not go to war against their fellow Israelites, because this division was his plan. The people obeyed God and went home instead of fighting.
entries.1 kings 12:25: Jeroboam built up the town of Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there, and he also strengthened Penuel. He was securing his new kingdom.
entries.1 kings 12:26: Jeroboam began to worry that his kingdom would go back to the family of David. He was afraid of losing the people's loyalty.
entries.1 kings 12:27: Jeroboam feared that if the people kept going to Jerusalem to worship at the Lord's temple, they would turn back to Rehoboam and kill him. He saw worship in Jerusalem as a threat to his rule.
entries.1 kings 12:28: After thinking it over, Jeroboam made two golden calves and told the people these were the gods who brought them out of Egypt. He set up idols to keep the people from going to Jerusalem.
entries.1 kings 12:29: Jeroboam placed one golden calf in Bethel and the other in Dan. He set up these idols at two locations in his kingdom.
entries.1 kings 12:30: This became a sin for Israel, because the people went to worship the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Jeroboam led the nation into idol worship.
entries.1 kings 12:31: Jeroboam built shrines at the high places and appointed priests from ordinary people, not from the tribe of Levi. He changed how worship was done and ignored God's instructions.
entries.1 kings 12:32: Jeroboam set up a festival in the eighth month, copying the feast in Judah, and he went to the altar in Bethel to offer sacrifices to the golden calves. He created his own religious celebration to compete with Jerusalem.
entries.1 kings 12:33: Jeroboam went to the altar he had built in Bethel on the day he had chosen himself, and he offered sacrifices and burned incense. He was inventing his own form of worship rather than following God's commands.
entries.1 kings 13:1: God sent a prophet from Judah to the altar at Bethel, where King Jeroboam was offering sacrifices. It shows God speaks directly into places where worship has gone wrong.
entries.1 kings 13:2: The prophet announced that a future king named Josiah would one day destroy this false altar and its priests. God was warning that judgment was coming, even if it took years.
entries.1 kings 13:3: The prophet gave a sign to prove his message was from God: the altar would split and its ashes would spill out. God backs up his words with evidence so people can trust them.
entries.1 kings 13:4: Jeroboam tried to arrest the prophet, but his outstretched hand froze and he could not pull it back. Opposing God's messenger left the king powerless.
entries.1 kings 13:5: The altar broke apart and the ashes poured out, exactly as the prophet had said. The sign came true, confirming God's word.
entries.1 kings 13:6: The king begged the prophet to pray for his hand to be healed, and it was restored. Even a rebellious king could receive mercy when he asked.
entries.1 kings 13:7: The king invited the prophet home for a meal and a reward. He wanted to soften the prophet and perhaps control him.
entries.1 kings 13:8: The prophet refused, saying he would not take even half the king's wealth. He was loyal to God's command above any reward.
entries.1 kings 13:9: God had told him not to eat, drink, or return the same way in that place. Obedience meant following God's instructions exactly.
entries.1 kings 13:10: So the prophet left by a different road than the one he came on. He kept the command he had been given.
entries.1 kings 13:11: An old prophet living in Bethel heard from his sons what the man of God had done and said. News of God's work spread quickly.
entries.1 kings 13:12: The old prophet asked which road the man had taken, and his sons told him. He was curious enough to pursue the visitor.
entries.1 kings 13:13: The old prophet had his sons saddle a donkey and set off. He was determined to catch up with the man of God.
entries.1 kings 13:14: He found the man of God resting under an oak tree and confirmed he was the one from Judah. The two prophets met on the road.
entries.1 kings 13:15: The old prophet invited him back to his house for a meal. It seemed like ordinary hospitality.
