entries.1 kings 13:16: The man of God refused, repeating that God had forbidden him to eat or drink there. He was still trying to obey.
entries.1 kings 13:17: He explained that God had told him not to eat, drink, or return by the same road. His refusal was based on God's clear command.
entries.1 kings 13:18: The old prophet lied, claiming an angel had told him to bring the man back for a meal. The man of God was deceived by a false claim.
entries.1 kings 13:19: So the man of God went back and ate and drank in the old prophet's house. He trusted a lie over what God had already told him.
entries.1 kings 13:20: While they were at the table, God gave the old prophet a message. God still spoke, even through the man who had lied.
entries.1 kings 13:21: The old prophet announced that because the man of God had disobeyed God's command, judgment would come. Disobedience had serious consequences.
entries.1 kings 13:22: He would die and not be buried with his ancestors. His body would be dishonored because he broke God's word.
entries.1 kings 13:23: After the meal, the old prophet saddled the donkey for the man of God to leave. He sent him back on his way.
entries.1 kings 13:24: A lion attacked and killed him on the road, and his body lay there with the donkey and the lion beside it. The judgment God announced came true.
entries.1 kings 13:25: Passersby saw the body and the lion and reported it in the town where the old prophet lived. The news spread to the community.
entries.1 kings 13:26: The old prophet recognized it as God's judgment on the man who disobeyed. He understood the death as a fulfillment of God's word.
entries.1 kings 13:27: He told his sons to saddle his donkey, and they did. He was going to retrieve the body.
entries.1 kings 13:28: He found the body untouched by the lion, and the donkey also unharmed. The lion had killed but not eaten, which was unusual and showed God's hand.
entries.1 kings 13:29: The old prophet took the body, laid it on the donkey, and brought it back to bury it with mourning. He honored the man of God in death.
entries.1 kings 13:30: He buried the body in his own tomb and wept over it, calling him brother. Even in judgment, there was grief and respect.
entries.1 kings 13:31: He told his sons to bury him beside the man of God when he died, so their bones would rest together. He wanted to be associated with the true prophet.
entries.1 kings 13:32: He was sure the prophecy against the altars in Bethel and Samaria would come true. God's word against false worship would not fail.
entries.1 kings 13:33: Jeroboam did not change his ways; he kept appointing priests for the false altars from anyone who wanted the job. He hardened his heart despite the warning.
entries.1 kings 13:34: This became a sin that led to the destruction of Jeroboam's family. Persistent disobedience brought ruin on his house.
entries.1 kings 15:1: Abijam became king of Judah in the eighteenth year of Jeroboam's reign over Israel. This dates the change of ruler in the southern kingdom.
entries.1 kings 15:2: Abijam ruled in Jerusalem for three years, and his mother was Maacah. The text notes his family background.
entries.1 kings 15:3: Abijam repeated the same sins his father had committed, and his heart was not fully devoted to God like David's was. His example warns us that following a bad family pattern can pull us away from God.
entries.1 kings 15:4: Even so, God kept a descendant on the throne in Jerusalem because of his promise to David, keeping the city secure. God's faithfulness to his promises does not depend on our goodness.
entries.1 kings 15:5: David did what was right before God and obeyed him throughout his life, except in the matter of Uriah. This shows that even a faithful person can fail badly, yet God still remembers the overall direction of a life.
entries.1 kings 15:6: This verse is missing from the text provided, so there is nothing to explain here.
entries.1 kings 15:7: The rest of Abijam's deeds are recorded in the official history of Judah's kings, and there was ongoing war between him and Jeroboam. The record reminds us that conflict marked this period.
entries.1 kings 15:8: Abijam died and was buried in the city of David, and his son Asa became king. One king's death makes way for the next.
entries.1 kings 15:9: Asa became king of Judah in the twentieth year of Jeroboam's reign over Israel. This places Asa's rise within the timeline of the northern kingdom.
entries.1 kings 15:10: Asa ruled in Jerusalem for forty-one years, and his mother was Maacah. His long reign gave him time to make lasting changes.
entries.1 kings 15:11: Asa did what was right in God's eyes, following the example of David. His life shows that a person can choose to follow a good example rather than a bad family pattern.
entries.1 kings 15:12: Asa removed the men involved in shrine prostitution and destroyed the idols his ancestors had made. He took real action to clean up the worship of his nation.
entries.1 kings 15:13: Asa even removed his own mother from her position as queen because she had made an obscene image for Asherah, and he destroyed it. Doing right may mean confronting people close to us, even family.
entries.1 kings 15:14: The local worship sites were not removed, but Asa's heart stayed true to God throughout his life. A person can be genuinely devoted to God while still leaving some things unfinished.
entries.1 kings 15:15: Asa brought the silver, gold, and sacred objects dedicated by his father and himself into the Lord's house. He honored God with valuable gifts.
entries.1 kings 15:16: There was war between Asa and Baasha, king of Israel, throughout their reigns. The two kingdoms remained in conflict.
entries.1 kings 15:17: Baasha attacked Judah and fortified Ramah to cut off all movement in and out of Asa's territory. This was a serious threat to Asa's kingdom.
entries.1 kings 15:18: Asa took the silver and gold from the Lord's house and his own palace and sent them to Ben-hadad, king of Aram, in Damascus. He used sacred treasure to buy help.
entries.1 kings 15:19: Asa proposed a treaty with Ben-hadad, offering silver and gold to persuade him to break his agreement with Baasha and stop the attacks. He relied on money and foreign alliances rather than on God.
entries.1 kings 15:20: Ben-hadad agreed and sent his armies against towns in Israel, conquering territory as far as Naphtali. Asa's plan worked, but it came at a cost.
entries.1 kings 15:21: When Baasha heard what happened, he stopped building Ramah and withdrew to Tirzah. The pressure on Judah eased.
entries.1 kings 15:22: Asa gathered all Judah and used the stones and wood from Ramah to build Geba and Mizpah. He turned the enemy's abandoned materials into defenses for his own land.
entries.1 kings 15:23: The rest of Asa's deeds and building projects are recorded in Judah's royal history, and in old age he suffered from a disease in his feet. Even a long, mostly good reign ends with weakness and death.
entries.1 kings 15:24: Asa died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, and his son Jehoshaphat became king. The throne passed to the next generation.
entries.1 kings 15:25: Nadab, Jeroboam's son, became king of Israel in the second year of Asa's reign in Judah and ruled for two years. His time in power was short.
entries.1 kings 15:26: Nadab did evil in God's eyes, following his father's sinful ways and leading Israel into the same sin. He repeated his father's mistakes instead of learning from them.
entries.1 kings 15:27: Baasha plotted against Nadab and struck him down at Gibbethon, a Philistine town, while Nadab and Israel's army were besieging it. Even in the middle of a military campaign, betrayal was close at hand.
entries.1 kings 15:28: Baasha killed Nadab in the third year of Asa's reign and took the throne in his place. This was a violent takeover, not a rightful succession.
entries.1 kings 15:29: As soon as Baasha became king, he killed every member of Jeroboam's family, fulfilling what the Lord had spoken through the prophet Ahijah. God's word proved true, even through a ruthless man.
entries.1 kings 15:30: This happened because of Jeroboam's sins and the sins he led Israel into, which provoked the Lord's anger. Persistent sin brought judgment on his whole family.
entries.1 kings 15:31: The rest of Nadab's deeds are recorded in the official history of Israel's kings. His story is preserved in the records.
entries.1 kings 15:32: There was war between Asa and Baasha, king of Israel, throughout their reigns. The conflict between the two kingdoms continued.
entries.1 kings 15:33: Baasha became king over all Israel in Tirzah in the third year of Asa's reign and ruled for twenty-four years. His reign was long, but it was marked by the same sins.
entries.1 kings 15:34: Baasha did evil in God's eyes, following Jeroboam's sinful ways and leading Israel into the same sin. A new king did not mean a new direction.
entries.1 kings 17:1: Elijah tells King Ahab that because Israel has turned from God, there will be no rain until Elijah says so. It shows that God's word, spoken through an ordinary man, controls even the weather.
entries.1 kings 17:2: God speaks directly to Elijah to guide him. It reminds the reader that God still gives personal direction to those who serve him.
entries.1 kings 17:3: God tells Elijah to leave and hide by a stream east of the Jordan. Sometimes God's protection means stepping away from the public eye and waiting on him.
entries.1 kings 17:4: God promises Elijah that the stream will supply his water and that ravens will bring him food. It shows God can provide in surprising, even unlikely, ways.
entries.1 kings 17:5: Elijah simply obeys and goes to the stream as God commanded. Trusting God's word enough to act on it is the heart of faith.
entries.1 kings 17:6: The ravens actually bring Elijah bread and meat each morning and evening, and he drinks from the stream. God keeps his promise in a way no one would expect.
entries.1 kings 17:7: Eventually the stream dries up because the drought Elijah announced has taken hold. Even when God's provision changes, he is still in control of the circumstances.
entries.1 kings 17:8: God speaks to Elijah again after the stream dries up. God's guidance often comes just when the previous plan runs out.
entries.1 kings 17:9: God sends Elijah to a foreign town and says a widow there will feed him. God's care reaches beyond Israel, and he uses ordinary, needy people to provide.
entries.1 kings 17:10: Elijah arrives and asks a widow gathering firewood for a drink of water. It's a simple request that opens the door to a much bigger story of God's provision.
entries.1 kings 17:11: Elijah also asks her for a piece of bread. He is asking someone who has almost nothing, which sets up a test of trust.
entries.1 kings 17:12: The widow swears she has only a handful of flour and a little oil left, and she is preparing a final meal for herself and her son before they starve. Her honesty shows how desperate her situation is.
entries.1 kings 17:13: Elijah tells her not to be afraid and asks her to feed him first, then make food for herself and her son. It's a bold request that calls her to trust God's promise before seeing the result.
entries.1 kings 17:14: God promises that her flour and oil will not run out until the rain comes. The promise is specific and tied to God's timing, not hers.
entries.1 kings 17:15: The widow does what Elijah says, and she, Elijah, and her household eat for many days. Her obedience, though risky, leads to survival for everyone.
entries.1 kings 17:16: The flour and oil keep lasting exactly as God promised through Elijah. It confirms that God's word through his prophet can be trusted.
entries.1 kings 17:17: Later the widow's son becomes so sick that he stops breathing. Even after a miracle, life still brings pain and loss.
entries.1 kings 17:18: The widow blames Elijah, thinking her son's death is punishment for some sin. Grief often makes people look for someone or something to blame.
entries.1 kings 17:19: Elijah calmly takes the boy from her, carries him upstairs, and lays him on his own bed. He responds to her panic with action rather than argument.
entries.1 kings 17:20: Elijah cries out to God, asking why this tragedy has come to the widow who took him in. He brings his confusion and pain honestly to God in prayer.
entries.1 kings 17:21: Elijah stretches himself over the child three times and pleads with God to bring the boy back to life. It shows persistent, earnest prayer for something only God can do.
entries.1 kings 17:22: God hears Elijah's prayer, and the boy's life returns and he revives. God is shown to have power over death itself.
entries.1 kings 17:23: Elijah brings the living boy back downstairs and gives him to his mother. The miracle restores not just the child but the mother's hope.
entries.1 kings 17:24: The widow declares that she now knows Elijah is truly a man of God and that his words are true. Seeing God act in her own home moved her from doubt to confidence.
entries.1 kings 16:1: God sent the prophet Jehu to deliver a message of judgment against King Baasha. It shows that God sees and speaks against those in power who do wrong.
entries.1 kings 16:2: God reminds Baasha that he raised him from nothing to become king, but Baasha followed Jeroboam's bad example and led Israel into sin. Being given power by God means being accountable to him for how you use it.
entries.1 kings 16:3: God declares that Baasha's whole family line will be wiped out, just like Jeroboam's was. Persistent sin brings ruin, even on a family.
entries.1 kings 16:4: Baasha's family members will die shamefully, with their bodies left unburied for dogs and birds. This was a sign of total disgrace in that culture.
entries.1 kings 16:5: The writer notes that Baasha's other deeds and achievements are recorded in the official royal records. His story is history, but his legacy is judged by his disobedience.
entries.1 kings 16:6: Baasha died and was buried in Tirzah, and his son Elah took the throne. Death comes to every king, and the throne passes on.
entries.1 kings 16:7: God's judgment on Baasha came through the prophet Jehu because of his evil, his idolatry, and his killing of Jeroboam's family. God holds people responsible even when they repeat sins others started.
entries.1 kings 16:8: Elah became king of Israel during Asa's reign in Judah and ruled only two years. His short reign hints at how unstable a kingdom built on sin can be.
entries.1 kings 16:9: Elah's own servant Zimri, a military commander, plotted against him while Elah was drinking heavily at a official's house. Drunkenness and carelessness left him vulnerable to betrayal.
entries.1 kings 16:10: Zimri attacked and killed Elah, then took the throne himself. This was a violent coup, not a legitimate succession.
entries.1 kings 16:11: As soon as Zimri took power, he killed every member of Baasha's family and their friends. This fulfilled God's judgment, but Zimri's cruelty was still his own doing.
entries.1 kings 16:12: Zimri's massacre of Baasha's family fulfilled what God had said through the prophet Jehu. God's word proved true, even through a wicked man's actions.
entries.1 kings 16:13: The sins of Baasha and Elah, and the way they led Israel into idolatry, provoked God's anger. Leaders who cause others to sin bear a heavy responsibility.
entries.1 kings 16:14: Elah's other deeds are recorded in the official royal records. His brief reign is summed up and closed.
entries.1 kings 16:15: Zimri became king for only seven days while the army was away attacking a Philistine town. His reign was short because the army was elsewhere and would soon turn on him.
entries.1 kings 16:16: When the army heard that Zimri had murdered the king, they proclaimed their commander Omri as king right there in the camp. Loyalty shifted quickly in a crisis.
entries.1 kings 16:17: Omri marched the army back and surrounded Tirzah to take the city from Zimri. Zimri's coup was doomed from the start.
entries.1 kings 16:18: When Zimri saw the city was lost, he set the palace on fire and died in the flames. His rebellion ended in self-destruction.
entries.1 kings 16:19: Zimri died because of his own sin and because he followed Jeroboam's idolatry and led Israel into it. His death was a judgment on his evil.
entries.1 kings 16:20: Zimri's other deeds and his plot are recorded in the official royal records. His brief, violent reign is remembered as a warning.
entries.1 kings 16:21: Israel split into two factions, half supporting Tibni and half supporting Omri. Political division followed the chaos of repeated coups.
entries.1 kings 16:22: Omri's supporters defeated Tibni's side, and Tibni and his brother died, leaving Omri as king. Power was settled by force, not by God's choice.
entries.1 kings 16:23: Omri became king over Israel during Asa's reign and ruled twelve years, six of them in Tirzah. His reign was longer and more stable than the kings just before him.
entries.1 kings 16:24: Omri bought a hill from Shemer for silver and built a city there, naming it Samaria after the seller. This city became the new capital of the northern kingdom.
entries.1 kings 16:25: Omri did more evil than any king before him. Even a strong, successful ruler can be judged by God for his disobedience.
entries.1 kings 16:26: Omri copied Jeroboam's idolatry and led Israel into the same sins, making God angry. Following a bad example multiplies the harm.
entries.1 kings 16:27: Omri's other deeds and his military strength are recorded in the official royal records. His accomplishments are noted, but so is his evil.
entries.1 kings 16:28: Omri died and was buried in Samaria, and his son Ahab became king. The throne passed to a son who would be even worse.
entries.1 kings 16:29: Ahab became king over Israel during Asa's reign and ruled twenty-two years in Samaria. His long reign would bring deep spiritual decline.
entries.1 kings 16:30: Ahab did more evil than any king before him. Each generation that ignores God's warnings tends to sink further.
entries.1 kings 16:31: Ahab treated Jeroboam's sins as minor and then married Jezebel, a foreign princess, and began to worship and serve the false god Baal. Marrying into idolatry pulled him and the nation further from God.
entries.1 kings 16:32: Ahab built a temple and altar for Baal in Samaria. He officially established idol worship in the capital of Israel.
entries.1 kings 16:33: Ahab made an idol for the goddess Asherah and provoked God more than any king before him. He didn't just tolerate idolatry; he promoted it.
entries.1 kings 16:34: During Ahab's reign, a man named Hiel rebuilt Jericho and lost his oldest and youngest sons in the process, just as Joshua had prophesied. God's word spoken long before came true, showing that his warnings are not empty.
entries.1 kings 14:1: Jeroboam's son Abijah got sick. Even a king's family is not safe from illness and worry.
entries.1 kings 14:2: Jeroboam told his wife to disguise herself and go to the prophet Ahijah, hoping to get an answer without being recognized. He was trying to hide from the truth he already knew.
entries.1 kings 14:3: She was to bring simple gifts of bread and honey to the prophet and ask what would happen to the sick boy. People often brought gifts when asking a prophet for God's word.
entries.1 kings 14:4: She did as her husband said and went to Ahijah's house, but the prophet was now very old and blind. Her disguise might have fooled a blind man, but not God.
entries.1 kings 14:5: God had already told Ahijah she was coming and that she would pretend to be someone else, and He told him what to say. God sees through every disguise.
entries.1 kings 14:6: As soon as she came in, Ahijah called her by name and asked why she was pretending, then told her his news was bad. You cannot hide your real self from God.
entries.1 kings 14:7: God reminded Jeroboam through the prophet that He had raised him from an ordinary man to be ruler over Israel. God's message begins by recalling what He had done for him.
entries.1 kings 14:8: God said Jeroboam had not been faithful like David, who obeyed God with his whole heart. Being given a position does not excuse unfaithfulness.
entries.1 kings 14:9: Jeroboam had done more evil than those before him by making other gods and turning his back on the Lord. His sin was serious because he knew better.
entries.1 kings 14:10: Because of this, God said Jeroboam's whole family line would be cut off and swept away like trash. A leader's sin can bring ruin on his whole household.
entries.1 kings 14:11: Those of Jeroboam's family who die in the city will be eaten by dogs, and those who die in the country by birds. This was a picture of total disgrace, with no proper burial.
entries.1 kings 14:12: The prophet sent her home, saying the child would die the moment she entered the town. The answer she came for was the hardest one to hear.
entries.1 kings 14:13: All Israel would mourn this boy and bury him, because he alone in Jeroboam's family had something good in him before God. Even in judgment, God showed mercy to this child.
entries.1 kings 14:14: God would soon raise up a new king over Israel who would destroy Jeroboam's family. The judgment would come through a real person at a real time.
entries.1 kings 14:15: God would shake Israel like a reed in water and uproot them from the land, scattering them beyond the river because of their idols. Persistent idolatry leads to losing what God gave.
entries.1 kings 14:16: God would give Israel over to trouble because of Jeroboam's sins and because he led the nation into sin. Leaders are accountable for the way they lead others.
entries.1 kings 14:17: Jeroboam's wife went home to Tirzah, and as she crossed the doorway the child died, just as the prophet said. God's word came true exactly as spoken.
entries.1 kings 14:18: All Israel buried the boy and mourned him, just as the Lord had said through Ahijah. Even a hard prophecy proved completely reliable.
entries.1 kings 14:19: The rest of Jeroboam's reign, his wars and his rule, were written in the official records of the kings of Israel. His story is remembered in history.
entries.1 kings 14:20: Jeroboam ruled twenty-two years, then died and was buried, and his son Nadab became king. No king, however powerful, rules forever.
entries.1 kings 14:21: Rehoboam, Solomon's son, became king of Judah at forty-one and ruled seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city God had chosen for His name. His mother was Naamah, an Ammonite.
entries.1 kings 14:22: Judah did evil in God's eyes and made Him angrier than their ancestors had by their sins. Being God's chosen people did not protect them from the results of sin.
entries.1 kings 14:23: They built shrines, sacred stones, and wooden poles on every high hill and under every green tree. They copied the worship of the nations around them instead of worshiping God.
entries.1 kings 14:24: There were even people in the land practicing ritual sex in worship of false gods, doing the same disgusting things as the nations God had driven out. Sin had spread into the whole culture.
entries.1 kings 14:25: In Rehoboam's fifth year, Shishak king of Egypt attacked Jerusalem. Judah's sin brought real trouble from a powerful enemy.
entries.1 kings 14:26: Shishak took all the treasures from the Lord's temple and the king's palace, including the gold shields Solomon had made. The wealth built up in better days was gone in one attack.
entries.1 kings 14:27: Rehoboam replaced the gold shields with bronze ones and gave them to the guards at the palace door. The replacement showed how far the kingdom's glory had fallen.
entries.1 kings 14:28: Whenever the king went to the temple, the guards carried the bronze shields and then returned them to their room. It became a routine reminder of what had been lost.
entries.1 kings 14:29: The rest of Rehoboam's deeds are written in the official records of the kings of Judah. His reign too is part of the recorded history.
entries.1 kings 14:30: There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their lifetimes. A divided nation meant constant conflict between the two kingdoms.
entries.1 kings 14:31: Rehoboam died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, and his son Abijam became king in his place. His mother's name is mentioned again, and his reign ended like all others.
entries.1 kings 19:1: Ahab told his wife Jezebel everything Elijah had done, including how he had killed all the prophets of Baal. This shows that the powerful people in charge now knew what Elijah had done and would react to it.
entries.1 kings 19:2: Jezebel sent a message to Elijah swearing that by the next day she would kill him, just as he had killed her prophets. She was threatening his life directly and making it clear she meant it.
entries.1 kings 19:3: Elijah was afraid and ran for his life, traveling all the way to Beersheba in Judah, where he left his servant behind. Even a brave prophet can be scared enough to flee when someone threatens to kill him.
entries.1 kings 19:4: Elijah went alone into the desert, sat under a bush, and asked God to let him die, saying he had had enough and was no better than his ancestors. He was deeply discouraged and worn out, and he told God exactly how he felt.
entries.1 kings 19:5: He lay down and fell asleep, and an angel touched him and told him to get up and eat. God cared for Elijah's physical needs before dealing with his despair.
entries.1 kings 19:6: Elijah looked and saw bread baked on hot stones and a jar of water beside his head, so he ate and drank and lay down again. God gave him simple, practical help right where he was.
entries.1 kings 19:7: The angel came back a second time, touched him, and told him to eat because the journey ahead would be too much for him. God knew Elijah needed more rest and food before he could keep going.
entries.1 kings 19:8: Elijah got up, ate and drank, and then traveled forty days and nights to Horeb, the mountain of God, strengthened by that food. God can sustain a tired person for a long and difficult road.
entries.1 kings 19:9: At the mountain Elijah spent the night in a cave, and God spoke to him, asking what he was doing there. God invites Elijah to explain himself and starts a conversation with him.
entries.1 kings 19:10: Elijah said he had been completely devoted to God, but the Israelites had broken their covenant, destroyed God's altars, and killed his prophets, leaving him alone and now hunted. He felt like the only faithful person left and was afraid for his life.
entries.1 kings 19:11: God told Elijah to stand on the mountain, and a powerful wind tore the rocks apart, then an earthquake came, but God was not in either one. God's presence was not shown through dramatic, destructive forces.
entries.1 kings 19:12: After the earthquake came a fire, but God was not in the fire either; then came a quiet, gentle sound. God often speaks in a still, small way rather than through loud and frightening events.
entries.1 kings 19:13: When Elijah heard the gentle sound, he covered his face with his cloak and stood at the cave entrance, and a voice asked him again what he was doing there. Elijah responded with reverence to God's quiet presence.
entries.1 kings 19:14: Elijah gave the same answer as before: he had been devoted to God, but the people had broken their covenant, destroyed the altars, and killed the prophets, and now he was alone and they wanted to kill him. He still felt isolated and afraid, even after encountering God.
entries.1 kings 19:15: God told Elijah to go back through the desert to Damascus and anoint Hazael as king over Aram. God gave Elijah a clear job to do instead of letting him stay stuck in despair.
entries.1 kings 19:16: God also told him to anoint Jehu as king over Israel and Elisha as prophet to take Elijah's place. God was providing for the future and making sure the work would continue after Elijah.
entries.1 kings 19:17: God said that those who escaped Hazael's sword would be killed by Jehu, and those who escaped Jehu's sword would be killed by Elisha. God was telling Elijah that judgment on the unfaithful would surely come through these leaders.
entries.1 kings 19:18: God told Elijah that he had kept seven thousand people in Israel who had never bowed to Baal or kissed his image. Elijah was not alone after all; God had many faithful people he did not know about.
entries.1 kings 19:19: Elijah left and found Elisha plowing with twelve pairs of oxen, and Elijah threw his cloak over him. This was a sign that Elisha was being called to follow and eventually take Elijah's place.
entries.1 kings 19:20: Elisha left the oxen, ran after Elijah, and asked to say goodbye to his parents first; Elijah told him to go back, since he had not forced him. Elisha was allowed to settle things at home before beginning his new calling.
entries.1 kings 19:21: Elisha went back, slaughtered the oxen, cooked them over the wooden plows, and fed the people, then followed Elijah and served him. He left his old life completely and committed himself to the work God had called him to.
entries.1 kings 18:1: After a long drought, God told Elijah it was time to show himself to King Ahab because God was about to send rain. It reminds the reader that God keeps his timing and his promises.
entries.1 kings 18:2: Elijah obeyed and went to meet Ahab, even though the famine in Samaria was severe. It shows that doing what God says can mean stepping into hard situations.
entries.1 kings 18:3: Ahab called for Obadiah, the man who managed his palace, who deeply respected and feared the Lord. It shows that faith in God can exist even inside a corrupt king's household.
entries.1 kings 18:4: When Queen Jezebel was killing God's prophets, Obadiah hid a hundred of them in caves and fed them. It shows quiet courage and loyalty to God when it was dangerous to be faithful.
entries.1 kings 18:5: Ahab told Obadiah they should search the whole land for water and grass to keep their horses and animals alive. It shows how desperate the drought had made everyone, even the king.
entries.1 kings 18:6: The two men split up and searched the country in different directions. It simply sets the scene for Obadiah's unexpected meeting with Elijah.
entries.1 kings 18:7: Obadiah ran into Elijah and fell face down in respect, asking if it was really him. It shows how greatly Elijah was respected, and how startling his sudden appearance was.
entries.1 kings 18:8: Elijah confirmed it was him and told Obadiah to go tell Ahab that he had arrived. It was a simple but risky instruction that put Obadiah in a hard spot.
entries.1 kings 18:9: Obadiah asked what he had done wrong to be sent on an errand that could get him killed. It shows his very real fear of the king's anger.
entries.1 kings 18:10: Obadiah swore that Ahab had searched every nation for Elijah and made people swear they hadn't seen him. It shows how determined the king was to find Elijah.
entries.1 kings 18:11: Obadiah pointed out that Elijah was now asking him to simply announce his arrival to the king. He was worried about what would happen next.
entries.1 kings 18:12: Obadiah feared that God's Spirit would whisk Elijah away and Ahab would blame and kill him, despite his lifelong devotion to God. It shows how fear can make even faithful people hesitate.
entries.1 kings 18:13: Obadiah reminded Elijah that he had hidden a hundred prophets from Jezebel and fed them. He was pleading his own record of faithfulness as proof he deserved not to be put in danger.
entries.1 kings 18:14: Obadiah repeated his fear that telling Ahab would cost him his life. It shows how heavy the pressure felt to him.
entries.1 kings 18:15: Elijah swore by the living God that he would definitely show himself to Ahab that very day. His firm promise was meant to calm Obadiah's fear.
entries.1 kings 18:16: Obadiah went and told Ahab, and Ahab went out to meet Elijah. The long-awaited confrontation was finally about to happen.
entries.1 kings 18:17: When Ahab saw Elijah, he accused him of being the one who brought trouble on Israel. It shows how people often blame God's messengers for problems their own choices caused.
entries.1 kings 18:18: Elijah shot back that the trouble came from Ahab and his family, because they had abandoned God's commands and followed false gods. It shows that the real cause of Israel's trouble was their own unfaithfulness.
entries.1 kings 18:19: Elijah told Ahab to gather all Israel and the 450 prophets of Baal at Mount Carmel for a showdown. It was a public challenge to settle who really was God.
entries.1 kings 18:20: Ahab did as Elijah said and gathered the people and the prophets at Mount Carmel. The stage was set for a dramatic test.
entries.1 kings 18:21: Elijah asked the crowd how long they would keep wavering between two loyalties, and told them to choose plainly whether God or Baal was real. The people stayed silent, showing their confusion or unwillingness to decide.
entries.1 kings 18:22: Elijah pointed out that he stood alone as God's prophet while Baal had 450 prophets. The odds looked completely against him, which made what followed even more striking.
entries.1 kings 18:23: Elijah proposed a test: each side would prepare an ox on wood but light no fire. It was a fair and simple setup that would let the true God reveal himself.
entries.1 kings 18:24: Each side would pray to their god, and whichever one answered with fire would prove to be the real God, and the people agreed this was fair. It put the question of who is truly God to a clear test.
entries.1 kings 18:25: Elijah let the many prophets of Baal go first and call on their god, with no fire lit under the offering. It gave them every chance to prove their god was real.
entries.1 kings 18:26: The prophets of Baal cried out to him from morning until noon and danced around the altar, but nothing happened. Their god gave no answer at all.
entries.1 kings 18:27: At midday Elijah mocked them, suggesting their god might be thinking, busy, traveling, or asleep and needed waking. It highlighted how powerless a made-up god really is.
entries.1 kings 18:28: They shouted louder and cut themselves with knives and swords until blood flowed, as their custom was. It shows how frantic and empty their worship had become.
entries.1 kings 18:29: They kept praying until the time of the evening offering, but there was still no voice, no answer, and no one paying attention. Their god simply could not respond.
entries.1 kings 18:30: Elijah called the people to come close and rebuilt the altar of the Lord that had been torn down. He was restoring proper worship before asking God to act.
entries.1 kings 18:31: Elijah used twelve stones, one for each tribe of Jacob's sons, whom God had named Israel. It was a visual reminder that all twelve tribes belonged to God.
entries.1 kings 18:32: He built the altar in the Lord's name and dug a deep trench around it. The trench would make the coming miracle even more unmistakable.
entries.1 kings 18:33: Elijah arranged the wood, laid the cut-up ox on it, and told them to pour four jars of water over the offering and wood. He was making it impossible for anyone to claim he secretly started a fire.
entries.1 kings 18:34: He told them to do it a second and then a third time, and they did. The offering was now thoroughly soaked.
entries.1 kings 18:35: The water ran all around the altar and filled the trench. Everything was drenched, setting up an even more dramatic display of God's power.
entries.1 kings 18:36: At the time of the evening offering, Elijah prayed to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, asking him to show that he is God and that Elijah acted on his orders. He wanted the glory to go to God, not himself.
entries.1 kings 18:37: Elijah begged God to answer so the people would see that he is God and that he was turning their hearts back to him. His prayer was focused on the people's restoration.
entries.1 kings 18:38: Fire from the Lord fell and burned up the offering, the wood, the stones, the dust, and even the water in the trench. It was an overwhelming answer that left no doubt about God's power.
entries.1 kings 18:39: When the people saw it, they fell on their faces and declared that the Lord is God. The miracle brought them to acknowledge the truth openly.
entries.1 kings 18:40: Elijah ordered that none of Baal's prophets escape, and they were taken to the Kishon stream and put to death there. It was a harsh act of removing the false worship that had led Israel astray.
entries.1 kings 18:41: Elijah tells King Ahab to go eat and drink because he can hear the sound of heavy rain coming. It means God was about to keep his promise, so the reader can trust that God's word comes true even before we see anything.
entries.1 kings 18:42: Ahab goes off to eat, but Elijah climbs to the top of Mount Carmel and bends down with his face to the ground to pray. It shows that the one who spoke about the rain now humbly waits on God for it, and it invites the reader to pray with humble persistence.
entries.1 kings 18:43: Elijah sends his servant to look toward the sea for rain, and the servant reports nothing, so Elijah keeps sending him back seven times. It means real faith keeps waiting even when nothing appears yet, and it encourages the reader not to give up too soon.
entries.1 kings 18:44: On the seventh look the servant sees a tiny cloud the size of a hand, and Elijah immediately tells Ahab to hitch up his chariot and leave before the rain traps him. It shows that God's answer can start very small, and the reader is reminded to act on what God begins.
entries.1 kings 18:45: Soon the sky turns black with wind and clouds and a huge rainstorm pours down, and Ahab rides off to Jezreel. It means the drought really ended just as God said, showing the reader that God's promises are fulfilled completely.
entries.1 kings 18:46: God's power comes on Elijah, and he tucks up his robe and runs ahead of Ahab's chariot all the way to Jezreel. It shows God giving unusual strength for the moment, reminding the reader that God equips people to do what he asks.
entries.2 kings 1:1: After King Ahab died, the country of Moab stopped obeying Israel and broke away. It shows how a change in leadership can shake loose old loyalties.
entries.2 kings 1:2: King Ahaziah fell through a window and was hurt, so he sent men to ask a foreign idol whether he would recover. He looked for answers in the wrong place instead of turning to God.
entries.2 kings 1:3: God told the prophet Elijah to intercept the king's messengers and ask why they were consulting a foreign god. God was pointing out that his own people had stopped asking him.
entries.2 kings 1:4: God declared that the injured king would not recover but would die in his bed. Elijah delivered the message and left.
entries.2 kings 1:5: The messengers came back early, and the king wanted to know why. Their return set up the moment when he would learn what God had said.
entries.2 kings 1:6: The messengers repeated the prophet's words: because the king consulted a foreign god instead of Israel's God, he would die from his injury. The warning was clear and direct.
entries.2 kings 1:7: The king asked what the man who gave the message looked like. He was trying to figure out who had dared to speak against him.
entries.2 kings 1:8: They described a man in a hairy coat with a leather belt, and the king knew at once it was Elijah. His distinctive clothing made him easy to identify.
entries.2 kings 1:9: The king sent a captain with fifty soldiers to order Elijah to come down. They treated the prophet as someone the king could simply command.
entries.2 kings 1:10: Elijah called on God to prove he was a true prophet, and fire fell and killed the captain and his men. It was a serious warning against treating God's messenger with contempt.
entries.2 kings 1:11: The king sent a second captain and fifty men with the same demand, this time telling Elijah to hurry. The king was still not willing to humble himself.
entries.2 kings 1:12: Elijah again called on God, and fire came down and killed the second group too. The same defiance brought the same result.
entries.2 kings 1:13: A third captain came, but he knelt before Elijah and begged for mercy for himself and his men. He showed the respect the first two lacked.
entries.2 kings 1:14: He reminded Elijah that fire had already destroyed the first two groups and pleaded for his own life. He was asking for mercy rather than making demands.
entries.2 kings 1:15: God's angel told Elijah to go with the captain and not be afraid, so Elijah went down to the king. God's command overruled Elijah's fear.
entries.2 kings 1:16: Elijah told the king face to face that because he had asked a foreign god about his illness, he would not recover but would die. The judgment was repeated directly to him.
entries.2 kings 1:17: The king died just as the Lord had said through Elijah, and his brother Jehoram took the throne because Ahaziah had no son. God's word proved true.
entries.2 kings 1:18: The writer notes that the rest of Ahaziah's deeds are recorded in the official royal records. It is a standard closing note pointing readers to the fuller history.
entries.1 kings 21:1: Naboth owned a vineyard right next to King Ahab's palace in Jezreel. It was his family's land, and it mattered because it sat close to the king's property.
entries.1 kings 21:2: Ahab offered Naboth a fair deal—a better vineyard or cash—so he could turn the land into a vegetable garden near his house. It sounds reasonable, but Ahab was used to getting what he wanted.
entries.1 kings 21:3: Naboth refused because the land was his family's inherited property, which in Israel was not supposed to be sold permanently. He chose loyalty to his family and God's law over pleasing the king.
entries.1 kings 21:4: Ahab went home sulking, angry that he didn't get his way, and lay in bed refusing to eat. A grown king acted like a spoiled child because one man said no.
entries.1 kings 21:5: Jezebel, Ahab's wife, noticed he was sulking and asked why he wouldn't eat. She was about to take charge of the situation.
entries.1 kings 21:6: Ahab explained that Naboth had refused to sell or trade the vineyard. He left out that Naboth had a legitimate reason rooted in his family's inheritance.
entries.1 kings 21:7: Jezebel basically said, "You're the king—act like it," and promised to get the vineyard for him herself. She was willing to use royal power to take what was not hers.
entries.1 kings 21:8: Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab's name and sealed them with his official seal, sending them to the town leaders where Naboth lived. She used the king's authority to set a trap.
entries.1 kings 21:9: She told the leaders to call a public fast and put Naboth in a place of honor at the front. The setup made it look like a solemn religious occasion.
entries.1 kings 21:10: She arranged for two worthless men to falsely accuse Naboth of cursing God and the king, a crime punishable by stoning. It was a deliberate, calculated plot to kill an innocent man.
entries.1 kings 21:11: The town leaders did exactly what Jezebel's letters said, without questioning or objecting. They went along with an evil plan because it came from the palace.
entries.1 kings 21:12: They proclaimed a fast and gave Naboth a prominent seat, making the coming accusation look official and serious. The whole town was drawn into the scheme.
entries.1 kings 21:13: The two false witnesses accused Naboth of cursing God and the king, and he was dragged outside town and stoned to death. An innocent man died because of lies and corrupt leaders.
entries.1 kings 21:14: They reported back to Jezebel that Naboth was dead. The murder was complete, and she had gotten what she wanted.
entries.1 kings 21:15: Jezebel told Ahab to go and take the vineyard now that Naboth was dead. She presented the murder as good news and a done deal.
entries.1 kings 21:16: Ahab went straight to the vineyard to claim it, showing he was willing to benefit from the crime. He took the land without a word of concern for the man who died.
entries.1 kings 21:17: God spoke to the prophet Elijah, setting up a confrontation with Ahab. God had seen what happened and was not silent.
entries.1 kings 21:18: God told Elijah to go find Ahab in Naboth's vineyard, where he had gone to take possession. Ahab thought he had gotten away with it, but God knew exactly where he was.
entries.1 kings 21:19: God's message was blunt: Ahab had murdered a man to take his land, and he would pay with his own life—dogs would lick his blood in the same place. The judgment matched the crime.
entries.1 kings 21:20: Ahab greeted Elijah with hostility, calling him an enemy, and Elijah answered that Ahab had brought this on himself by doing evil. Ahab's real problem was not Elijah but his own choices.
entries.1 kings 21:21: God announced that Ahab's entire family line would be wiped out—every male descendant would be cut off. The judgment was total because Ahab's evil was persistent.
entries.1 kings 21:22: God said Ahab's family would end like the families of Jeroboam and Baasha, earlier kings whose dynasties were destroyed for their sins. Ahab had made God angry and led Israel into evil.
entries.1 kings 21:23: God also pronounced judgment on Jezebel: she would be eaten by dogs in Jezreel. The one who plotted murder would meet a shameful end.
entries.1 kings 21:24: Any member of Ahab's family who died in the city would be eaten by dogs, and any who died in the country would be eaten by birds. This meant none of them would get a proper burial—a sign of disgrace.
entries.1 kings 21:25: The writer notes that no one was as thoroughly evil as Ahab, and that Jezebel pushed him into it. Ahab was not just weak; he willingly gave himself over to evil.
entries.1 kings 21:26: Ahab did disgusting things by worshiping false gods, copying the wicked practices of the Amorites whom God had driven out. He sank lower than the nations around him.
entries.1 kings 21:27: When Ahab heard the judgment, he genuinely humbled himself—wearing rough cloth, fasting, and walking around quietly. He showed real grief and repentance, at least outwardly.
entries.1 kings 21:28: God spoke to Elijah again after Ahab's humble response. God noticed the change in Ahab's behavior.
entries.1 kings 21:29: God told Elijah that because Ahab had humbled himself, the disaster would not come during his lifetime but during his son's reign. God showed mercy in delaying judgment, though the evil was not left unpunished.
entries.1 kings 20:1: Ben-hadad, the king of Aram, gathered a huge army with many allies and attacked Samaria, the capital of Israel, and surrounded it. It means the people of Israel were facing a powerful enemy with no easy way out.
entries.1 kings 20:2: Ben-hadad sent messengers into the city to deliver his demands to King Ahab. It means the threat was not distant; it came right to the king's door.
entries.1 kings 20:3: Ben-hadad demanded Ahab's silver, gold, wives, and children as his own. It means he was not just asking for tribute but for total surrender of everything Ahab valued.
entries.1 kings 20:4: Ahab answered that he accepted Ben-hadad's terms and would give him everything he had. It means Ahab was willing to give up almost anything to avoid a fight.
entries.1 kings 20:5: Ben-hadad's messengers returned with a stronger demand, repeating the claim on Ahab's wealth and family. It means the first concession was not enough; the enemy wanted more.
entries.1 kings 20:6: Ben-hadad said his men would come the next day and search through the houses, taking anything they found valuable. It means the threat had moved from a demand to an actual plan to plunder the city.
entries.1 kings 20:7: Ahab called the elders of the land and pointed out that Ben-hadad was looking for trouble, since he had already agreed to give up his family and wealth. It means Ahab recognized the demand was a trap and wanted the leaders to see it too.
entries.1 kings 20:8: The elders and the people told Ahab not to listen to Ben-hadad or do what he asked. It means the leaders of Israel stood with their king and refused to surrender further.
entries.1 kings 20:9: Ahab told Ben-hadad's messengers that he would keep the first agreement but could not accept this new demand. It means Ahab drew a line and refused to give in completely.
entries.1 kings 20:10: Ben-hadad replied with a boast that he would reduce Samaria to dust, swearing by his gods. It means he was threatening total destruction and mocking Israel's ability to resist.
entries.1 kings 20:11: Ahab answered that a man should not boast while still putting on his armor, but only after the battle is won. It means Ahab was saying Ben-hadad should not brag before the fight even started.
entries.1 kings 20:12: Ben-hadad heard the answer while drinking with his allied kings and ordered his men to get ready to attack the city. It means the boast turned into action, and the battle was about to begin.
entries.1 kings 20:13: A prophet came to Ahab and told him that God would give the huge enemy army into his hands that day, so Ahab would know that God is the Lord. It means God was going to act on Israel's behalf even though Ahab had not been faithful.
entries.1 kings 20:14: Ahab asked who would do the fighting, and the prophet said it would be the young servants of the district leaders, with Ahab leading them. It means God would use unlikely, ordinary people to win the battle.
entries.1 kings 20:15: Ahab gathered the 232 young servants of the district leaders and then the rest of the army, seven thousand men. It means Israel's force was small compared to the enemy, making the coming victory clearly God's doing.
entries.1 kings 20:16: Israel's men went out at midday while Ben-hadad was still drinking in his tent with his thirty-two allied kings. It means the enemy was caught off guard and unprepared.
entries.1 kings 20:17: The young servants of the district leaders went out first, and Ben-hadad sent scouts who reported that men were coming out of Samaria. It means the attack began with a small advance group.
entries.1 kings 20:18: Ben-hadad ordered his men to capture the attackers alive, whether they came for peace or for war. It means he underestimated them and wanted prisoners rather than a real fight.
entries.1 kings 20:19: The young servants went out of the city with the rest of the army following behind them. It means Israel advanced in force, not just a small raiding party.
entries.1 kings 20:20: Each Israelite soldier killed his opponent, and the Arameans fled with Israel chasing them, while Ben-hadad escaped on horseback with his cavalry. It means the battle turned into a rout, and the enemy king barely got away.
entries.1 kings 20:21: The king of Israel went out and captured the enemy's horses and chariots and struck down many Arameans. It means Israel won a decisive victory and took the enemy's military equipment.
entries.1 kings 20:22: The prophet told Ahab to strengthen himself and be careful, because a year later the king of Aram would attack again. It means the victory was not the end; trouble was coming back.
entries.1 kings 20:23: Ben-hadad's servants said Israel's god was a god of the hills, which is why Israel won, but if they fought in the lowlands they would win. It means they misunderstood God as limited to certain places.
entries.1 kings 20:24: They advised Ben-hadad to remove the kings from their command positions and replace them with trained captains. It means they wanted a more professional army for the next battle.
entries.1 kings 20:25: They told him to raise another army just like the one that was destroyed, with the same number of horses and chariots, and fight Israel in the lowlands where they expected to win. It means they planned to try again on their own terms.
entries.1 kings 20:26: A year later Ben-hadad gathered the Arameans and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel. It means the predicted attack happened exactly as the prophet said.
entries.1 kings 20:27: Israel gathered and prepared food, then went out against them; Israel's camp looked like two small flocks of goats compared to the land full of Arameans. It means Israel was badly outnumbered.
entries.1 kings 20:28: A man of God told Ahab that because the Arameans said the Lord is only a god of the hills and not the valleys, God would give the whole army into Israel's hands, so they would know He is the Lord. It means God would prove He rules everywhere, not just in one kind of place.
entries.1 kings 20:29: The two armies faced each other for seven days, and on the seventh day Israel killed a hundred thousand Aramean foot soldiers in one day. It means the battle was a massive defeat for the enemy.
entries.1 kings 20:30: The rest fled into Aphek, where a wall fell on twenty-seven thousand of them, and Ben-hadad hid in an inner room in the city. It means the enemy's refuge became a death trap, and their king was left hiding.
entries.1 kings 20:31: Ben-hadad's servants suggested they wear rough cloth and ropes and surrender to Israel's king, since they had heard the kings of Israel were merciful, hoping he would spare Ben-hadad's life. It means they were desperate and appealing for mercy.
entries.1 kings 20:32: They came to Ahab in mourning clothes and ropes and asked him to spare Ben-hadad's life, and Ahab replied that Ben-hadad was still alive and called him his brother. It means Ahab was ready to treat his enemy as a friend.
entries.1 kings 20:33: The men seized on Ahab's word and confirmed that Ben-hadad was his brother, so Ahab ordered him brought out and had him come up into his chariot. It means Ahab welcomed his defeated enemy with honor.
entries.1 kings 20:34: Ben-hadad offered to return towns his father had taken and let Ahab set up trading streets in Damascus, and Ahab made a treaty with him and let him go. It means Ahab made a deal with the enemy instead of treating him as God's defeated foe.
entries.1 kings 20:35: A member of the prophets' group told his neighbor, by the word of the Lord, to strike him, but the man refused. It means the man disobeyed a direct command from God given through a prophet.
entries.1 kings 20:36: The prophet told him that because he did not obey the Lord's voice, a lion would kill him as soon as he left, and that is what happened. It means disobeying God's word brought serious consequences.
entries.1 kings 20:37: The prophet met another man and asked him to strike him, and this man did, wounding him. It means this time the command was obeyed.
entries.1 kings 20:38: The prophet went and covered his face with his headband and stood by the road waiting for the king to pass. It means he disguised himself to deliver a message to Ahab.
entries.1 kings 20:39: As the king passed, the prophet called out a story about a soldier who was given a prisoner to guard, with his own life or a large amount of silver as the penalty if the prisoner escaped. It means he was setting up a lesson for the king to judge.
entries.1 kings 20:40: The prophet said that while he was busy looking around, the prisoner got away, and the king replied that he had judged himself guilty and must pay the penalty. It means Ahab pronounced the verdict without realizing it applied to him.
entries.1 kings 20:41: The prophet dropped his disguise and let the king see who he really was. It means the truth we try to hide from eventually gets shown to us, so it's better to face it honestly.
entries.1 kings 20:42: God says the king will pay with his own life and his people's lives because he spared the enemy God had condemned. It means disobeying God's clear command has real consequences, even for powerful people.
entries.1 kings 20:43: The king went home sullen and furious about the sentence against him. It means he was angry at the outcome rather than sorry for what he did, and that stubborn anger kept him from God.
entries.1 kings 22:1: For three years the two kingdoms stayed at peace instead of fighting. Quiet seasons are part of the story too, not just the battles.
entries.1 kings 22:2: In that third year, Judah's king Jehoshaphat traveled to visit Israel's king. This visit sets up a partnership between the two kings.
entries.1 kings 22:3: Israel's king pointed out that a border town belonged to them but they had done nothing to take it back. He was stirring up his officials to act.
entries.1 kings 22:4: The king asked Jehoshaphat to join the fight, and Jehoshaphat agreed to share everything he had. It's generous loyalty, though he commits before asking God.
entries.1 kings 22:5: Jehoshaphat wisely said they should first ask God what to do. Even when plans seem obvious, it's right to seek God's direction.
entries.1 kings 22:6: The king gathered about four hundred prophets, and they all said to go and that God would give victory. A crowd agreeing doesn't prove they speak for God.
entries.1 kings 22:7: Jehoshaphat wasn't satisfied with the crowd and asked if there was another prophet of the Lord. He wanted a genuine word from God, not just confirmation.
entries.1 kings 22:8: The king admitted there was one prophet, Micaiah, but he hated him because he never predicted good. Jehoshaphat gently corrected him, showing we shouldn't reject truth just because it's unwelcome.
entries.1 kings 22:9: The king sent an official to bring Micaiah quickly. Despite his dislike, he still summoned the prophet.
entries.1 kings 22:10: The two kings sat in royal robes at the city gate while all the prophets performed before them. It was an impressive display of royal power and religious excitement.
entries.1 kings 22:11: One prophet made iron horns and declared that with them the king would crush the enemy completely. It was a dramatic, confident prediction of victory.
entries.1 kings 22:12: All the prophets echoed the same message: go and succeed, because God will give victory. Their unity made the advice seem certain.
entries.1 kings 22:13: The messenger urged Micaiah to agree with the other prophets and speak favorably. He was pressuring him to go along with the crowd.
entries.1 kings 22:14: Micaiah promised to say only what the Lord told him, no matter what others said. That's the mark of a true prophet: loyalty to God's word over popularity.
entries.1 kings 22:15: Micaiah first repeated the prophets' words, likely in a mocking tone. The king sensed he wasn't being serious and demanded the truth.
entries.1 kings 22:16: The king made Micaiah swear to tell him only the truth in God's name. He wanted honesty, even if he wouldn't like it.
entries.1 kings 22:17: Micaiah described Israel scattered like sheep with no shepherd, meaning the king would die and the people would go home. The picture spelled disaster for the king.
entries.1 kings 22:18: The king turned to Jehoshaphat and said this proved Micaiah only ever predicted bad things for him. He heard the warning but only complained about the messenger.
entries.1 kings 22:19: Micaiah then described a vision of the Lord on his throne with all heaven's army around him. He was claiming a direct, authoritative word from God.
entries.1 kings 22:20: In the vision, the Lord asked how Ahab could be drawn into going to his death at Ramoth-gilead, and various spirits offered ideas. The scene shows God sovereignly directing events.
entries.1 kings 22:21: A spirit stepped forward before the Lord and volunteered to trick Ahab. Even deceptive plans are shown as under God's control.
entries.1 kings 22:22: The spirit proposed to be a lying influence in the mouths of Ahab's prophets, and the Lord permitted it. Ahab's own preference for flattery left him open to deception.
entries.1 kings 22:23: Micaiah concluded that God had allowed a lying spirit in these prophets and had decreed disaster for Ahab. The false comfort was itself part of the judgment.
entries.1 kings 22:24: Zedekiah slapped Micaiah and mocked him, asking where God's spirit had gone. The false prophet responded to truth with violence.
entries.1 kings 22:25: Micaiah warned that Zedekiah would see the truth when he hid in an inner room for safety. His confidence would collapse when events proved Micaiah right.
entries.1 kings 22:26: The king ordered Micaiah taken back to the city officials. He was silencing the prophet rather than listening to the warning.
entries.1 kings 22:27: Micaiah was to be jailed and fed meager prison rations until the king returned safely. The king was betting his own safety against God's word.
entries.1 kings 22:28: Micaiah said that if the king returned safely, God had not spoken through him. He staked his credibility on the prophecy coming true.
entries.1 kings 22:29: Both kings went up to Ramoth-gilead to fight, ignoring the warning. They proceeded with the plan despite the clear word from God.
entries.1 kings 22:30: Ahab disguised himself as an ordinary soldier while Jehoshaphat wore royal robes. Ahab tried to dodge the prophecy by hiding his identity.
entries.1 kings 22:31: The enemy king ordered his chariot commanders to target only the king of Israel. The battle was aimed squarely at Ahab.
entries.1 kings 22:32: The chariot commanders mistook Jehoshaphat for Ahab and surrounded him, but he cried out. He was in danger only because he had joined a fight God had warned against.
entries.1 kings 22:33: When they realized Jehoshaphat wasn't the king of Israel, they stopped chasing him. God spared him, though he had put himself in harm's way.
entries.1 kings 22:34: A soldier shot an arrow at random, and it struck Ahab in a gap in his armor. The disguised king was hit anyway, showing no disguise can escape God's word.
entries.1 kings 22:35: The battle raged on while Ahab was propped up in his chariot, bleeding into it, until he died by evening. The prophecy came true despite all his precautions.
entries.1 kings 22:36: At sunset a cry went through the army telling everyone to go home because the king was dead. The scattered sheep of Micaiah's vision went back to their towns.
entries.1 kings 22:37: They brought Ahab's body to Samaria and buried him there. The king who tried to avoid his fate was laid to rest in his own city.
entries.1 kings 22:38: When his chariot was washed at a pool in Samaria, dogs licked up his blood, just as the Lord had said. The prophecy was fulfilled down to the smallest detail.
entries.1 kings 22:39: The writer notes that the rest of Ahab's achievements, including his ivory palace and building projects, are recorded in the royal records. His impressive legacy is summed up in a history book.
entries.1 kings 22:40: Ahab died and was buried with his ancestors, and his son Ahaziah became king. One king's story ended and the next began, as God's word had foretold.
entries.2 kings 2:1: God was about to take Elijah to heaven in a powerful wind, so Elijah and his student Elisha traveled together from Gilgal. It reminds us that God's plans unfold in his timing, and we should stay close to those we learn from.
entries.2 kings 2:2: Elijah told Elisha to stay behind, but Elisha refused to leave him. It shows loyal commitment—Elisha wanted to stay with his mentor to the very end.
entries.2 kings 2:3: The young prophets at Bethel asked Elisha if he knew his master would be taken away that day, and he told them to stop talking about it. He knew the truth but didn't want to dwell on the painful parting.
entries.2 kings 2:4: Elijah again tried to leave Elisha behind, and again Elisha swore he would not leave him. His repeated loyalty shows real devotion, not just words.
entries.2 kings 2:5: At Jericho the young prophets asked Elisha the same question about his master being taken, and again he told them to be quiet. He was aware of what was coming but chose not to keep discussing it.
entries.2 kings 2:6: Elijah tried once more to go on alone, and Elisha refused to be separated from him. So the two of them went on together toward the Jordan River.
entries.2 kings 2:7: Fifty young prophets followed at a distance and watched as Elijah and Elisha stood by the Jordan River. They were witnesses to what was about to happen.
entries.2 kings 2:8: Elijah struck the water with his rolled-up cloak, and the river split so the two men could cross on dry ground. This showed God's power working through Elijah.
entries.2 kings 2:9: Across the river, Elijah asked Elisha what he wanted before they parted, and Elisha asked for a double share of Elijah's spirit. He wanted to carry on his mentor's work with real power from God.
entries.2 kings 2:10: Elijah said the request was hard, but if Elisha saw him being taken away, it would be granted. The sign would confirm that God had answered his request.
entries.2 kings 2:11: As they walked and talked, fiery horses and chariots separated them, and Elijah was carried up to heaven in a whirlwind. It was a dramatic, God-given departure unlike any other.
entries.2 kings 2:12: Elisha cried out in grief as he watched, calling Elijah the chariots and horsemen of Israel—meaning his mentor was the nation's real defense. He lost a father figure that day.
entries.2 kings 2:13: Elisha picked up the cloak Elijah had dropped and went back to the edge of the Jordan. He was stepping into his new role.
entries.2 kings 2:14: Elisha struck the water with Elijah's cloak and asked where the God of Elijah was, and the river split for him too. This showed that God's power was now with Elisha.
entries.2 kings 2:15: The young prophets watching from Jericho saw what happened and said Elijah's spirit now rested on Elisha, bowing before him. They recognized God's hand on him.
entries.2 kings 2:16: The prophets offered to send fifty strong men to search for Elijah, thinking God might have set him down somewhere. Elisha told them not to bother.
entries.2 kings 2:17: They kept pressing him until he felt embarrassed to refuse, so he let them send the men. After three days of searching, they found nothing.
entries.2 kings 2:18: The men returned to Elisha at Jericho, and he reminded them he had told them not to go. His word had been right.
entries.2 kings 2:19: The townspeople told Elisha their town was well placed but the water was bad, causing cattle to lose their young. They brought a real problem to God's prophet.
entries.2 kings 2:20: Elisha asked for a new bowl with salt in it, and they brought it to him. He used a simple, ordinary thing to do God's work.
entries.2 kings 2:21: Elisha threw the salt into the spring and declared in God's name that the water was now healed and would no longer cause death or barrenness. God fixed what people could not.
entries.2 kings 2:22: The water stayed pure from that day on, just as Elisha had said. God's word through his prophet proved true and lasting.
entries.2 kings 2:23: On the way to Bethel, some boys mocked Elisha and shouted at him to go up like Elijah did. They were treating God's prophet with contempt.
entries.2 kings 2:24: Elisha cursed them in the Lord's name, and two bears came out of the woods and killed forty-two of them. It was a serious warning about mocking God and his messenger.
entries.2 kings 2:25: Elisha traveled on to Mount Carmel and then back to Samaria. He continued his work across the land.
entries.2 kings 3:1: Jehoram became king of Israel in Samaria during the eighteenth year of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, and he ruled for twelve years. This verse simply fixes the time and length of his reign for the reader.
entries.2 kings 3:2: Jehoram did evil in God's sight, but he was not as bad as his parents because he removed the sacred stone pillar of Baal that his father had set up. It shows that a person can improve on the past and still fall short of doing what is right.
entries.2 kings 3:3: Even so, Jehoram kept committing the same sins that Jeroboam had introduced and led Israel into. The reader sees that bad patterns can be passed down and repeated unless someone deliberately turns from them.
entries.2 kings 3:4: Mesha, the king of Moab, raised sheep and regularly paid the king of Israel a huge amount of wool from his flocks. This shows that Moab was under Israel's control and paying tribute.
entries.2 kings 3:5: After Ahab died, the king of Moab broke free from Israel's control. A change in leadership gave a subject nation the chance to rebel.
entries.2 kings 3:6: At that time Jehoram left Samaria and gathered Israel's fighting men. He was preparing to deal with Moab's rebellion.
entries.2 kings 3:7: Jehoram asked Jehoshaphat of Judah to join him in war against Moab, and Jehoshaphat agreed, treating their peoples and horses as one. The reader sees an alliance formed quickly, with one king promising full support to another.
entries.2 kings 3:8: When asked which route to take, the answer was through the desert of Edom. Their chosen path would prove harsh and dangerous.
entries.2 kings 3:9: The kings of Israel, Judah, and Edom took a long roundabout route for seven days, and then there was no water for the army or their animals. A plan that seemed wise left them in serious trouble.
entries.2 kings 3:10: The king of Israel panicked, saying God had brought the three kings together only to hand them over to Moab. He blamed God for a crisis they had walked into themselves.
entries.2 kings 3:11: Jehoshaphat asked whether there was a prophet of the Lord to consult, and he was told Elisha, who had served Elijah, was there. The reader sees the value of seeking God's direction when things go wrong.
entries.2 kings 3:12: Jehoshaphat said the Lord's word was with Elisha, so the three kings went down to him. A leader's confidence in God's prophet led the whole group to seek guidance.
entries.2 kings 3:13: Elisha told the king of Israel to go to his parents' prophets instead, but the king insisted that God had gathered the three kings to hand them to Moab. Elisha made clear he owed this king nothing.
entries.2 kings 3:14: Elisha swore by the living Lord that he would not even look at the king of Israel if he did not respect Jehoshaphat of Judah. The reader sees that one good person's presence can make a difference for others.
entries.2 kings 3:15: Elisha asked for a musician, and while the man played, the Lord's power came on him so he could speak God's word. Music helped prepare the way for a prophetic message.
entries.2 kings 3:16: Elisha delivered the Lord's message that the valley would be filled with water holes. God was promising a solution before any sign of it appeared.
entries.2 kings 3:17: The Lord said that although they would see no wind or rain, the valley would fill with water for them, their armies, and their animals. God can provide in ways that do not depend on natural conditions.
entries.2 kings 3:18: Elisha said this was only a small thing for the Lord, who would also give the Moabites into their hands. The reader sees that God's help is not limited to one need.
entries.2 kings 3:19: They were told to destroy every fortified town, cut down every good tree, stop up every spring, and cover the good land with stones. The command describes total ruin of the enemy's land.
entries.2 kings 3:20: The next morning, around the time of the offering, water flowed from the direction of Edom until the land was full. God kept his promise at the appointed time.
entries.2 kings 3:21: When all Moab heard the kings had come to fight them, they gathered every man able to bear arms and stood at the border. The whole nation prepared for battle.
entries.2 kings 3:22: Early in the morning, with the sun shining on the water, the Moabites saw it looking red like blood. What God had provided looked like disaster to the enemy.
entries.2 kings 3:23: The Moabites concluded it was blood and that the kings had turned on each other, so they rushed in to collect the plunder. Their mistaken reading of the scene set them up for defeat.
entries.2 kings 3:24: When the Moabites reached the Israelite camp, the Israelites attacked them and drove them back, pressing the attack as they fled. The ambush turned against Moab.
entries.2 kings 3:25: The Israelites tore down towns, covered good fields with stones, stopped up springs, and cut down good trees, driving Moab back until only Kir-hareseth remained, which they surrounded and bombarded. The victory was thorough and devastating.
entries.2 kings 3:26: When the king of Moab saw the battle going against him, he took seven hundred swordsmen to try to break through to the king of Aram, but he failed. A desperate last attempt at escape came to nothing.
entries.2 kings 3:27: The king of Moab then sacrificed his oldest son, his heir, on the wall, and great anger came against Israel, so they withdrew and returned home. The reader sees the horror of the Moabite king's act and how it turned the situation around.
entries.1 kings 22:41: Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king of Judah during the fourth year that Ahab ruled Israel. This dates his reign and shows the two kingdoms were being tracked side by side.
entries.1 kings 22:42: Jehoshaphat was thirty-five when he took the throne and ruled twenty-five years in Jerusalem; his mother was Azubah. These details identify him and mark the length of his reign.
entries.1 kings 22:43: He followed his father Asa's example and did what pleased the Lord, but he left the local worship sites standing, so people kept offering sacrifices there. He was faithful overall, yet his reforms were incomplete.
entries.1 kings 22:44: Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel. This kept the northern and southern kingdoms from fighting each other during his reign.
entries.1 kings 22:45: The other things Jehoshaphat did, including his power and wars, are recorded in the official history of Judah's kings. His full story is preserved elsewhere, not in this book.
entries.1 kings 22:46: He removed from the land the remaining men who had been used in pagan worship, including those left over from his father Asa's time. He carried on cleaning out practices that dishonored God.
entries.1 kings 22:47: At that time Edom had no king of its own. This note sets the political situation around Judah's neighbor.
entries.1 kings 22:48: Jehoshaphat had ships built to sail to Ophir for gold, but they were wrecked at Ezion-geber before they could go. His plan for trade and wealth failed.
entries.1 kings 22:49: Ahaziah son of Ahab offered to send his men along with Jehoshaphat's sailors, but Jehoshaphat refused. He declined the partnership with Israel's king.
entries.1 kings 22:50: Jehoshaphat died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, and his son Jehoram became king after him. His reign ended and passed to the next generation.
entries.1 kings 22:51: Ahaziah son of Ahab became king of Israel in Samaria in Jehoshaphat's seventeenth year, and he ruled only two years. His short reign is dated against Judah's king.
entries.1 kings 22:52: Ahaziah did what was evil in the Lord's sight, following the bad examples of his parents and of Jeroboam, who led Israel into sin. He repeated the same wrong patterns as those before him.
entries.1 kings 22:53: He served and worshiped Baal, which angered the Lord, the God of Israel, just as his father had done. His idolatry provoked God and continued his family's unfaithfulness.
entries.1 kings 8:41: Solomon prays that foreigners who come from far away because they have heard about God will also be welcomed. It means God's care isn't limited to one nation, and outsiders who seek him are heard too.
entries.1 kings 8:42: People from other lands will come because they have heard how powerful and faithful God is. It reminds the reader that God's reputation should draw people in, not push them away.
entries.1 kings 8:43: Solomon asks God to hear and answer the foreigner's prayer from heaven. The point is that when outsiders are treated well by God, everyone on earth can learn who he is.
entries.1 kings 8:44: If God's people go to war at his direction and pray toward the city and temple, they are asking for his help. It means soldiers and nations should look to God, not just their own strength.
entries.1 kings 8:45: Solomon asks God to listen from heaven and give his people justice. It means God is the one who makes things right when his people call on him.
entries.1 kings 8:46: Solomon admits that everyone sins and that defeat and exile can be the result. It's a honest reminder that no one is perfect and that wrongdoing has real consequences.
entries.1 kings 8:47: Even far from home, people can come to their senses and admit they were wrong. It means honest confession is the first step back to God, no matter where you are.
entries.1 kings 8:48: If people turn back to God with their whole heart, even in a foreign land, their prayer still counts. It means repentance isn't about location but about genuinely turning toward God.
entries.1 kings 8:49: Solomon asks God to hear from heaven and act justly for his people in exile. It means distance doesn't stop God from listening or from doing what is right.
entries.1 kings 8:50: Solomon asks God to forgive his people and to soften the hearts of their captors. It means God's mercy can reach even into the worst situations and change how others treat us.
entries.1 kings 8:51: Solomon reminds God that these people belong to him and were rescued from slavery in Egypt. It means God's people are his treasured possession because he saved them.
entries.1 kings 8:52: Solomon asks God to keep his eyes open to the prayers of his servant and his people. It means God is attentive and ready to hear whenever his people cry out.
entries.1 kings 8:53: God set Israel apart from other nations to be his own people, just as he promised through Moses. It means being chosen by God is a privilege that comes with a purpose.
entries.1 kings 8:54: Solomon had been kneeling with his hands raised toward heaven, and then he stood up. It shows that prayer can be earnest and physical, and that it eventually comes to an end.
entries.1 kings 8:55: Solomon stood and blessed the whole assembly of Israel in a loud voice. It means leaders should speak words of blessing and encouragement over the people they serve.
entries.1 kings 8:56: Solomon praises God because every promise he made through Moses came true. It means God keeps his word, and that's a reason for real gratitude.
entries.1 kings 8:57: Solomon prays that God will stay with his people just as he was with their ancestors. It means the reader can ask God to remain close and never abandon them.
entries.1 kings 8:58: Solomon asks God to turn their hearts toward him and guide them to obey his commands. It means we need God's help even to want to follow him.
entries.1 kings 8:59: Solomon wants his prayer to stay before God day and night so God will keep helping his people. It means persistent prayer matters, and God cares about daily needs.
entries.1 kings 8:60: The goal is that everyone on earth will know the Lord is God and there is no other. It means God's people should live in a way that points others to him.
entries.1 kings 8:61: Solomon tells the people to keep their hearts fully committed to God and to obey his laws. It means wholehearted loyalty to God is the right response to everything he has done.
entries.1 kings 8:62: The king and all Israel together presented offerings to the Lord. It means worship is something the whole community does together, not just leaders.
entries.1 kings 8:63: Solomon offered a huge number of animals as peace offerings and the people celebrated the temple's opening. It means the occasion was a big, joyful act of worship and thanksgiving.
entries.1 kings 8:64: There were so many offerings that the bronze altar couldn't hold them all, so the middle of the courtyard was set apart for offerings too. It means the people's response to God was so generous it overflowed the usual arrangements.
