entries.1 kings 8:65: People came from far and wide and the celebration lasted two weeks. It means the whole nation gathered to rejoice before God for an extended time.
entries.1 kings 8:66: On the last day Solomon sent the people home, and they left joyful and grateful for all the good God had done. It means worship should send people away with glad hearts and a sense of God's goodness.
entries.2 kings 7:1: Elisha tells the starving city that by tomorrow food will be so cheap it will seem impossible. God can turn a hopeless shortage into plenty overnight, so don't give up on him.
entries.2 kings 7:2: The king's officer laughs at the promise and doubts God could do it even with a miracle. Elisha says he will see the food arrive but will never eat any of it, because mocking God's word has consequences.
entries.2 kings 7:3: Four men with a skin disease are stuck outside the city gate with no hope. They show that when you have nothing left to lose, it's time to stop waiting and act.
entries.2 kings 7:4: The men weigh their options and realize staying put means certain death, so they risk going to the enemy. Sometimes stepping into danger is the only way to have a chance at life.
entries.2 kings 7:5: They go to the enemy camp at dusk and find it completely empty. What looked like certain capture turned out to be an open door.
entries.2 kings 7:6: God had made the enemy hear the sound of a huge army, so they panicked and ran. God can rescue his people without them lifting a finger, using fear to scatter their enemies.
entries.2 kings 7:7: The enemy soldiers fled in the night, leaving everything behind. God's unseen work sent them running for their lives.
entries.2 kings 7:8: The men eat and grab valuables, hiding them for themselves. It's a natural reaction, but hoarding good fortune while others starve is not the whole story.
entries.2 kings 7:9: They realize it's wrong to keep the good news to themselves while the city starves. When you've been given something good, keeping it quiet is a failure, not safety.
entries.2 kings 7:10: They report to the city guards exactly what they found. Good news is meant to be passed on, not kept secret.
entries.2 kings 7:11: The guards spread the word to the king's household. News of hope travels fast when people are desperate to hear it.
entries.2 kings 7:12: The king assumes it's a trap and suspects the enemy is hiding in the fields. Fear makes it hard to believe good news, even when it's true.
entries.2 kings 7:13: A servant suggests sending a few horses to check, since those men are as good as dead anyway. It's a sensible, low-risk way to find out the truth.
entries.2 kings 7:14: The king sends two riders to follow the enemy's trail. Checking the facts is wise, even when the report sounds too good to be true.
entries.2 kings 7:15: The riders find the road littered with gear the enemy dropped while fleeing, confirming the camp really was abandoned. The evidence backs up the good news.
entries.2 kings 7:16: The people rush out and plunder the camp, and food becomes cheap just as God promised. God's word proved true, and the whole city was saved.
entries.2 kings 7:17: The king puts the doubting officer in charge of the gate, where the crowd tramples him to death. The very man who mocked God's promise saw it happen but never enjoyed it.
entries.2 kings 7:18: The narrator repeats Elisha's prediction to show it came true exactly as spoken. God's promises are reliable, even when they sound impossible.
entries.2 kings 7:19: The officer's mocking question is recalled alongside Elisha's answer that he would see but not taste. Scoffing at God's word doesn't stop it from happening.
entries.2 kings 7:20: The officer dies under the crowd at the gate, just as predicted. What God says will happen, happens, and no one's doubt can prevent it.
entries.2 kings 6:1: The group of prophets training under Elisha had grown too big for the space they were using. When a group or church grows, it may simply need more room rather than being a problem.
entries.2 kings 6:2: They suggested going to the Jordan River to cut timber and build a larger place to live and meet, and Elisha agreed. It's fine for God's people to take practical steps to make room for growth.
entries.2 kings 6:3: One of the men asked Elisha to come along with them, and he said he would. Having a leader present gives people confidence and support in their work.
entries.2 kings 6:4: Elisha went with them, and when they reached the Jordan they began cutting down trees. The leader joined in the ordinary work rather than staying apart from it.
entries.2 kings 6:5: As one man cut wood, the iron head of his axe flew off and sank in the river, and he cried out in distress because the axe was borrowed. Losing something you borrowed is a real worry, since you are responsible for it.
entries.2 kings 6:6: Elisha asked where it fell, threw a stick into the water, and the iron floated up. God cared about a small, ordinary loss and showed his power over nature.
entries.2 kings 6:7: Elisha told him to pick it up, and the man reached out and took it. God's help restored what was lost, and the man simply had to receive it.
entries.2 kings 6:8: The king of Aram was at war with Israel and privately told his officers where he planned to set up camp. Even secret war plans were being made.
entries.2 kings 6:9: Elisha warned the king of Israel to avoid that place because the Arameans were hiding there. God was protecting Israel by revealing the enemy's secret plans.
entries.2 kings 6:10: The king of Israel checked out the warning and stayed away from that spot more than once. Acting on good warning can save you from harm.
entries.2 kings 6:11: The king of Aram was upset and demanded to know which of his own men was leaking information to Israel. He assumed a traitor among his officers.
entries.2 kings 6:12: One officer explained that no one among them was the leak; it was Elisha the prophet, who told Israel's king even the words spoken in the king's bedroom. God knows what is said in secret.
entries.2 kings 6:13: The king ordered his men to find where Elisha was, and he was told Elisha was in Dothan. The king wanted to capture the prophet who was exposing his plans.
entries.2 kings 6:14: He sent a large force with horses and chariots, and they surrounded the town at night. The enemy came in strength and in secret to trap Elisha.
entries.2 kings 6:15: Elisha's servant got up early, saw the army surrounding the town, and panicked, asking what they should do. It is natural to be afraid when trouble looks bigger than you.
entries.2 kings 6:16: Elisha told him not to be afraid, because those on their side were more than those on the enemy's side. God's unseen help is greater than any visible threat.
entries.2 kings 6:17: Elisha prayed, and God opened the young man's eyes so he saw the mountain full of fiery horses and chariots around Elisha. God's protection was there all along, just unseen.
entries.2 kings 6:18: When the Arameans came down toward Elisha, he prayed and God struck them with blindness. God can stop an enemy without any fighting.
entries.2 kings 6:19: Elisha told the blinded soldiers they were at the wrong place and led them to Samaria instead. God used the prophet to guide the enemy army where he wanted them.
entries.2 kings 6:20: Once they were in Samaria, Elisha prayed and their eyes were opened, and they realized they were inside the enemy city. They were completely in Israel's hands.
entries.2 kings 6:21: When Israel's king saw them, he asked Elisha whether he should kill them. He looked to the prophet for direction on what to do with captured enemies.
entries.2 kings 6:22: Elisha said no, since the king had not captured them in battle, and told him to feed them and send them home. Kindness to a defeated enemy is better than revenge.
entries.2 kings 6:23: The king gave them a big meal and sent them back to their master, and after that the Aramean raiding bands stopped coming into Israel. Generosity ended the raids for a time.
entries.2 kings 6:24: Later Ben-hadad, king of Aram, gathered his whole army and surrounded Samaria. The trouble was not over, and a full siege began.
entries.2 kings 6:25: Food became so scarce in the besieged city that an donkey's head and even dove droppings sold for very high prices. A siege could push people to desperate extremes.
entries.2 kings 6:26: As the king walked on the city wall, a woman cried out to him for help. People in desperate need look to those in power for rescue.
entries.2 kings 6:27: The king replied that if the Lord did not help her, he had no help to give, since there was no grain or wine left. He admitted his own helplessness in the crisis.
entries.2 kings 6:28: The king asked what was wrong, and she told him that another woman had proposed they eat her son one day and the other woman's son the next. Hunger had driven people to horrifying acts.
entries.2 kings 6:29: They had boiled and eaten her son, but when she asked for the other woman's son the next day, the woman had hidden him. The story shows how deep the suffering had become.
entries.2 kings 6:30: Hearing this, the king tore his robes, and people saw he was wearing rough haircloth underneath as a sign of grief. He was deeply distressed, though his sorrow did not fix the problem.
entries.2 kings 6:31: The king swore that Elisha would lose his head that very day. In his anger he blamed the prophet for the suffering instead of seeking God.
entries.2 kings 6:32: Elisha was sitting with the town elders and warned them that the king had sent a violent man to kill him, and told them to shut the door against the messenger. God had told Elisha what was coming.
entries.2 kings 6:33: While Elisha was still speaking, the king arrived and said this disaster came from the Lord, asking why he should wait on the Lord any longer. The king was angry at God, yet still came to God's prophet.
entries.2 kings 8:1: God told Elisha to warn the woman whose son he had raised that a seven-year famine was coming, so she should leave home and find somewhere else to live. It shows God cares for ordinary people enough to warn them ahead of trouble.
entries.2 kings 8:2: The woman trusted the prophet's warning and moved her whole household to Philistine territory for the seven years. Her obedience to God's word kept her family safe through the famine.
entries.2 kings 8:3: When the famine ended, she came back and asked the king to restore her house and land, which had likely been taken over while she was gone. She had to appeal to the highest authority to get her property back.
entries.2 kings 8:4: At that very moment, the king happened to be asking Gehazi to tell him about Elisha's great miracles. God was quietly setting up the timing for what came next.
entries.2 kings 8:5: Right as Gehazi was telling the story of the raised son, the woman and her son walked in, and Gehazi pointed them out as living proof. God arranged the timing so her case would be heard favorably.
entries.2 kings 8:6: The king questioned her, believed her story, and ordered that everything be returned to her, including all the crops her land had produced while she was away. God used the king to give her back more than she might have expected.
entries.2 kings 8:7: Elisha traveled to Damascus, and word spread that he had arrived while King Ben-hadad of Aram was sick. Even a foreign king recognized that God's prophet was someone worth paying attention to.
entries.2 kings 8:8: The sick king sent his official Hazael with gifts to ask Elisha whether he would recover. He was looking for a word from God about his future.
entries.2 kings 8:9: Hazael loaded forty camels with the best goods of Damascus and went to Elisha, asking on the king's behalf whether he would get well. The huge gift shows how seriously they took the prophet's answer.
entries.2 kings 8:10: Elisha told Hazael to tell the king he would recover, but God had shown Elisha that the king would actually die. The message was technically true but hid what Hazael himself would do.
entries.2 kings 8:11: Elisha stared at Hazael until he felt uncomfortable, then the prophet broke down crying. He wept because he knew the terrible harm Hazael would bring.
entries.2 kings 8:12: Elisha explained that he was weeping because he foresaw Hazael doing brutal things to Israel: burning cities, killing young men, and violence against children and pregnant women. God's prophet grieved over suffering that was still to come.
entries.2 kings 8:13: Hazael acted shocked, calling himself a nobody who could never do such things, but Elisha told him plainly that God had shown he would become king of Aram. His humble-sounding words did not match what was in his heart.
entries.2 kings 8:14: Hazael went back and told his master only that he would get well, leaving out the part about the king's death. He passed on a partial truth.
entries.2 kings 8:15: The next day Hazael smothered the king with a wet cloth and took the throne for himself. He murdered the man he served to grab power, just as Elisha had foreseen.
entries.2 kings 8:16: This verse marks the start of a new king in Judah, Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat, dated by the reign of Israel's king Joram. It keeps the record of who was ruling where and when.
entries.2 kings 8:17: Jehoram was thirty-two when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for eight years. The verse gives the basic facts of his reign.
entries.2 kings 8:18: Jehoram followed the sinful example of Israel's kings, partly because he married Ahab's daughter, and he did what was evil in God's sight. Bad influences in his closest relationships pulled him away from God.
entries.2 kings 8:19: Even so, God did not destroy Judah, because of his promise to David that his line would always have a lamp. God's faithfulness to his promises held back judgment.
entries.2 kings 8:20: During Jehoram's reign, Edom broke free from Judah's control and set up its own king. Judah's power began to slip as a result of its king's failures.
entries.2 kings 8:21: Jehoram attacked the Edomites at night with his chariots, but they surrounded him and his army, and his people fled home. The battle did not go well for him.
entries.2 kings 8:22: Edom stayed independent from Judah from then on, and Libnah broke away at the same time. The kingdom was losing territory and control.
entries.2 kings 8:23: The rest of Jehoram's deeds are said to be written in the official records of Judah's kings. The writer points readers to the fuller historical record.
entries.2 kings 8:24: Jehoram died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, and his son Ahaziah became king. His reign ended and the throne passed to the next generation.
entries.2 kings 8:25: Ahaziah son of Jehoram became king of Judah in the twelfth year of Israel's king Joram. The verse dates his accession by the northern kingdom's calendar.
entries.2 kings 8:26: Ahaziah was twenty-two when he became king and ruled only one year in Jerusalem; his mother was Athaliah, from the family of Omri. His short reign and his mother's background set the stage for trouble.
entries.2 kings 8:27: Ahaziah followed the evil ways of Ahab's family, since he was related to them by marriage. Family ties again led a king away from God.
entries.2 kings 8:28: Ahaziah joined Joram of Israel in war against Hazael of Aram at Ramoth-gilead, and Joram was wounded. The alliance with Ahab's family drew Judah into Israel's battles.
entries.2 kings 8:29: Joram went back to Jezreel to recover from his wounds, and Ahaziah went to visit him because he was sick. This visit would soon put Ahaziah in the wrong place at the wrong time.
entries.2 kings 4:1: A prophet's widow is left in debt, and the creditor is about to take her two sons as slaves to pay it. It shows how quickly a faithful family can fall into desperate trouble, and that God sees people in that kind of helpless situation.
entries.2 kings 4:2: Elisha asks what she already has, and the answer is only a small jar of oil. God often starts with the little thing a person already has in hand rather than with something they lack.
entries.2 kings 4:3: Elisha tells her to borrow as many empty containers from her neighbors as she can. She has to take a step of faith and gather the containers before anything is poured.
entries.2 kings 4:4: She is to pour the oil into the containers behind a closed door with her sons helping. The miracle happens quietly and privately, in ordinary obedience at home.
entries.2 kings 4:5: She does exactly what she was told, with her sons bringing the containers to her. Simple obedience is the setting where God's provision actually shows up.
entries.2 kings 4:6: The oil keeps flowing until every container is full, then it stops. The supply matched the faith and the preparation, and it stopped only when there was nothing left to fill.
entries.2 kings 4:7: Elisha tells her to sell the oil, pay the debt, and live on the rest with her sons. God's help was practical: it rescued the family and gave them a future, not just a feeling.
entries.2 kings 4:8: A wealthy woman in Shunem keeps urging Elisha to eat at her house whenever he passes by. She shows generous, repeated hospitality to a traveling man of God.
entries.2 kings 4:9: She tells her husband she can see this visitor is a holy man of God. She pays attention to who he is, not just to being kind to a stranger.
entries.2 kings 4:10: The couple builds a small upstairs room with a bed, table, chair, and lamp for Elisha. Their hospitality is thoughtful and practical, meeting his real needs.
entries.2 kings 4:11: One day Elisha comes and rests in the little room they made for him. The room they prepared becomes the place where something important will happen.
entries.2 kings 4:12: Elisha sends his servant Gehazi to call the Shunammite woman to come to him. He wants to respond to her kindness in some way.
entries.2 kings 4:13: Elisha offers to speak to the king or army commander on her behalf, but she says she is content among her own people. She is not looking for favors or advancement.
entries.2 kings 4:14: Elisha asks what can be done for her, and Gehazi points out that she has no son and her husband is old. In that culture, a son meant security and a future, and she had none.
entries.2 kings 4:15: Elisha calls her to the doorway to speak to her directly. He is about to give her a promise about her deepest need.
entries.2 kings 4:16: Elisha promises that in about a year she will hold a son. She begs him not to raise her hopes if it is not true, because the disappointment would be too painful.
entries.2 kings 4:17: The woman becomes pregnant and has a son at the time Elisha named. God kept the promise exactly as it was spoken.
entries.2 kings 4:18: When the boy grows older, he goes out to his father in the harvest field. Ordinary life goes on, and then trouble suddenly arrives.
entries.2 kings 4:19: The boy cries out that his head hurts, and his father has him taken to his mother. A serious illness begins with a small, ordinary complaint.
entries.2 kings 4:20: The boy sits on his mother's lap until midday, and then he dies. The promised child is gone, and the mother is left holding the loss.
entries.2 kings 4:21: She lays the boy on Elisha's bed, closes the door, and goes out. She acts quietly and deliberately, treating the situation as something to bring to God's prophet.
entries.2 kings 4:22: She asks her husband for a servant and a donkey so she can hurry to the man of God and come back. She does not explain the death to him, she just moves toward help.
entries.2 kings 4:23: Her husband wonders why she is going to the prophet on an ordinary day, since it is not a religious festival. She only answers that all is well, keeping her grief to herself for now.
entries.2 kings 4:24: She has the donkey saddled and tells the servant to keep going and not slow down unless she says so. Her urgency shows how much she is depending on reaching Elisha.
entries.2 kings 4:25: She travels to Mount Carmel, and Elisha spots her coming from a distance. He recognizes her but does not yet know what has happened.
entries.2 kings 4:26: Elisha sends Gehazi to ask whether she, her husband, and the child are well, and she answers that all is well. She holds back her grief until she reaches Elisha himself.
entries.2 kings 4:27: She falls at Elisha's feet, and when Gehazi tries to push her away, Elisha stops him because he can see her deep distress. He admits God has not told him what happened, so he is not in control of the situation.
entries.2 kings 4:28: She reminds Elisha that she never asked for a son and had begged him not to raise false hopes. Her pain is that the gift she was given has now been taken away.
entries.2 kings 4:29: Elisha sends Gehazi ahead with his staff, telling him not to stop for greetings along the road, and to lay the staff on the boy's face. It is an urgent errand, but the staff by itself will not be enough.
entries.2 kings 4:30: The mother refuses to leave without Elisha himself, so he gets up and goes with her. She will not settle for a substitute; she wants the man of God present.
entries.2 kings 4:31: Gehazi lays the staff on the boy's face, but nothing happens and the boy does not wake. The prophet's tool alone has no power; the outcome depends on God.
entries.2 kings 4:32: Elisha arrives and finds the child dead, lying on his bed. The situation is exactly as the mother described, with no improvement.
entries.2 kings 4:33: Elisha goes in alone, shuts the door on the two of them, and prays to the Lord. He turns to God privately before doing anything else.
entries.2 kings 4:34: Elisha lies over the child, matching his mouth, eyes, and hands to the child's, and the body grows warm. Life begins to return, and it comes through close, humble contact.
entries.2 kings 4:35: Elisha walks back and forth in the house, then stretches over the child seven times, and the boy opens his eyes. The restoration takes time and repeated effort, but God gives life back.
entries.2 kings 4:36: Elisha calls the Shunammite woman in and simply tells her to pick up her son. The child she lost is restored to her.
entries.2 kings 4:37: She bows at Elisha's feet in gratitude, then takes her son and leaves. Her response is humble thankfulness rather than words.
entries.2 kings 4:38: During a famine, Elisha is at Gilgal with the company of prophets, and he tells his servant to put on the big pot and make soup for them. Even in hard times, he is caring for the needs of the group.
entries.2 kings 4:39: One man gathers wild plants and sliced fruit he does not recognize and adds it to the pot. He acts without knowing what he is putting in, which creates a dangerous situation.
entries.2 kings 4:40: The men taste the soup and cry out that there is death in the pot, and they cannot eat it. Something harmful had been mixed in, and the meal meant to feed them became a threat.
entries.2 kings 4:41: Elisha has flour brought and thrown into the pot, and then the food is safe to eat. God turns a poisoned meal into a nourishing one through the prophet's simple action.
entries.2 kings 4:42: A man brings Elisha bread made from the first grain of the harvest and some fresh grain, and Elisha tells him to give it to the people to eat. The food is brought as an offering to God's servant.
entries.2 kings 4:43: Elisha's servant objects that there is not enough for a hundred men, but Elisha insists on giving it out because the Lord has promised there will be leftovers. The command is to trust God's word over the size of the supply.
entries.2 kings 4:44: The man sets the food before the people, they eat, and there is food left over, just as the Lord had said. God provided more than enough from what looked like far too little.
entries.2 kings 11:1: When Athaliah heard her son the king was dead, she tried to kill every other royal family member so she could keep power. It shows how far someone will go to hold onto control.
entries.2 kings 11:2: Jehosheba, the dead king's sister, secretly rescued her baby nephew Joash and hid him with his nurse so Athaliah could not kill him. One brave person's quick action saved a life.
entries.2 kings 11:3: Joash stayed hidden in the temple for six years while Athaliah ruled the country. God was quietly protecting the rightful heir during a dangerous time.
entries.2 kings 11:4: In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada gathered the military commanders, made a solemn agreement with them, and showed them the hidden king's son. He carefully built support before acting.
entries.2 kings 11:5: Jehoiada gave the guards specific instructions about which groups would stand watch at the palace. Good plans need clear orders so everyone knows their part.
entries.2 kings 11:6: This verse is missing from the text provided, so there is nothing to explain here.
entries.2 kings 11:7: The other divisions of guards were told to watch over the temple. Each group had its own assigned post to keep the plan secure.
entries.2 kings 11:8: The guards were to surround the young king with weapons ready and kill anyone who broke through. Their whole job was to protect the king at all times.
entries.2 kings 11:9: The commanders followed Jehoiada's orders exactly, bringing both the incoming and outgoing guard groups to him. Obedience kept the plan working.
entries.2 kings 11:10: Jehoiada handed out King David's old spears and shields that had been stored in the temple. They used what was available to equip the guards.
entries.2 kings 11:11: The armed men formed a line around the altar and the temple, weapons in hand. They stood between the young king and any threat.
entries.2 kings 11:12: Jehoiada brought out the king's son, crowned him, gave him the royal armbands, anointed him, and everyone clapped and shouted long live the king. The hidden boy was publicly made king.
entries.2 kings 11:13: Athaliah heard the noise of the crowd and came to the temple to see what was happening. Trouble was waiting for her where she least expected it.
entries.2 kings 11:14: She saw the young king standing in his proper place with the commanders and trumpeters beside him while the people celebrated. She tore her clothes and screamed treason, realizing her power was over.
entries.2 kings 11:15: Jehoiada ordered the guards to take her out of the temple grounds and to kill anyone who tried to follow her, but not to kill her inside the Lord's house. Even in judgment he showed respect for the temple.
entries.2 kings 11:16: The guards seized Athaliah and killed her at the palace entrance by the horse gate. Her grab for power ended in her own death.
entries.2 kings 11:17: Jehoiada made a covenant binding the Lord, the king, and the people together as God's own people, and also binding the king and the people to each other. Renewed commitment to God goes hand in hand with loyalty to godly leadership.
entries.2 kings 11:18: The people tore down the temple of Baal, smashed its altars and idols, and killed Baal's priest Mattan. Then Jehoiada set up proper oversight for the Lord's temple. Removing false worship was part of restoring true worship.
entries.2 kings 11:19: Jehoiada led the commanders, guards, and all the people in escorting the king from the temple to the palace, where he took his seat on the throne. The rightful king was now publicly established.
entries.2 kings 11:20: Everyone in the land rejoiced and the city was calm once Athaliah was dead. Peace returned when the usurper was gone and the true king was in place.
entries.2 kings 11:21: Joash was only seven years old when he became king. God can use even a child to carry out his purposes.
entries.2 kings 5:1: Naaman was a powerful, respected army commander whom God had used to bring victory to Aram, but he had a serious skin disease. Even great and successful people carry problems they cannot fix themselves.
entries.2 kings 5:2: A group of Aramean raiders had captured a young Israelite girl and made her a servant to Naaman's wife. God can use even a small, powerless person to set up something important.
entries.2 kings 5:3: The captured girl told her mistress that a prophet in Samaria could cure her master's disease. A simple word of faith from an unlikely person can point someone toward help.
entries.2 kings 5:4: Someone reported the girl's words to Naaman, and he learned what she had said. News of possible healing spread quickly once it was spoken.
entries.2 kings 5:5: The king of Aram told Naaman to go and sent a letter to Israel's king, along with a huge gift of silver, gold, and clothing. People often try to buy or earn what only God can give freely.
entries.2 kings 5:6: The letter asked Israel's king to cure Naaman of his skin disease. The request put the problem in the wrong hands, since no king can heal.
entries.2 kings 5:7: Israel's king panicked, thinking Aram was picking a fight, because only God can give life or death. When we forget who God is, ordinary problems can look like threats.
entries.2 kings 5:8: Elisha told the king to send Naaman to him so Naaman would learn there is a prophet in Israel. God's servants step in when others are afraid.
entries.2 kings 5:9: Naaman arrived at Elisha's door with his horses and chariots, expecting a grand reception. He came with power and status, but healing would not come through those.
entries.2 kings 5:10: Elisha sent a servant out with simple instructions: wash seven times in the Jordan and be healed. God's help often comes in a plain, humble form that we might not expect.
entries.2 kings 5:11: Naaman was furious because he expected Elisha to come out personally and perform an impressive ceremony. We often want God to act on our terms and in our style.
entries.2 kings 5:12: Naaman argued that Damascus rivers were better than any in Israel and stormed off. Pride can make us reject the very thing that would help us.
entries.2 kings 5:13: Naaman's servants pointed out that he would have done some great, hard task if asked, so why not this simple washing? Wise friends can help us see past our pride.
entries.2 kings 5:14: Naaman obeyed, washed seven times in the Jordan, and his skin became like a child's. Humble obedience to God's simple word brought the healing.
entries.2 kings 5:15: Naaman returned and declared that Israel's God is the only God in all the earth, then tried to give Elisha a gift. Real healing leads to real worship and gratitude.
entries.2 kings 5:16: Elisha refused any payment, insisting he served the living Lord. God's gifts are not for sale, and his servants should not profit from them.
entries.2 kings 5:17: Naaman asked for two mule-loads of Israel's soil so he could worship only the Lord from then on. A new believer wanted to carry his new faith home with him.
entries.2 kings 5:18: Naaman asked God's forgiveness for the times he would have to bow in the temple of Rimmon while supporting his king. He was honest about the tension between his new faith and his old duties.
entries.2 kings 5:19: Elisha simply told him to go in peace. God is patient with new believers who are still working out hard situations.
entries.2 kings 5:20: Gehazi, Elisha's servant, decided to chase Naaman and get some of the gifts for himself, using God's name to justify it. Greed can dress itself up as devotion.
entries.2 kings 5:21: Gehazi ran after Naaman, who got down from his chariot to greet him and asked if everything was alright. The trap was set with friendly words.
entries.2 kings 5:22: Gehazi lied, claiming Elisha had sent him to collect silver and clothing for two visiting prophets. Lies often come wrapped in a made-up religious reason.
entries.2 kings 5:23: Naaman gladly gave two talents of silver and the clothing, and sent servants to carry them. Generosity was met with deception.
entries.2 kings 5:24: Gehazi hid the goods in the house and sent the men away. Sin usually involves hiding what we have done.
entries.2 kings 5:25: When Elisha asked where he had been, Gehazi lied and said he had gone nowhere. Lying to God's servant is lying to God.
entries.2 kings 5:26: Elisha said his heart had seen everything, and asked whether this was a time to take money and property. God sees what we do in secret, even when no one else does.
entries.2 kings 5:27: Naaman's skin disease came on Gehazi and his descendants forever, and he left white as snow. Greed and lying brought the very curse Gehazi had tried to profit from.
entries.2 kings 9:1: God's prophet Elisha sends a young prophet on a secret mission with a flask of oil to a military town. It shows God quietly setting his plans in motion through ordinary people.
entries.2 kings 9:2: The young prophet must find a specific army commander named Jehu and take him away from his friends to a private room. God's message is meant for Jehu alone, not for the crowd.
entries.2 kings 9:3: He is to pour the oil on Jehu's head to show God has chosen him as king, then run away quickly. The hurry shows this is dangerous, urgent business.
entries.2 kings 9:4: The young prophet simply obeys and travels to Ramoth-gilead. Faithful obedience, even without seeing the outcome, is the point.
entries.2 kings 9:5: At the army camp the prophet finds the officers sitting together and asks to speak to the commander. Jehu answers, showing he is the one meant.
entries.2 kings 9:6: Privately, the prophet anoints Jehu and tells him God has made him king over Israel. God himself is the one raising up a new leader.
entries.2 kings 9:7: Jehu's job is to wipe out the family of the current king, Ahab, because they killed God's prophets and servants. God is settling accounts for the blood of the innocent.
entries.2 kings 9:8: Every male in Ahab's family will be destroyed, with no exceptions. A family that has defied God will not survive.
entries.2 kings 9:9: Ahab's family will end just like two earlier royal families that God also judged. History shows God keeps his word against evil.
entries.2 kings 9:10: Jezebel, Ahab's wife, will die and be eaten by dogs, with no proper burial. This is a harsh but specific warning of judgment for her cruelty.
entries.2 kings 9:11: When Jehu comes back out, his friends ask what the strange man wanted. Jehu brushes it off at first, not yet ready to tell them.
entries.2 kings 9:12: His friends press him, and Jehu finally tells them the prophet anointed him king. The secret is out among the officers.
entries.2 kings 9:13: The officers immediately spread their cloaks on the steps and blow a horn, declaring Jehu king. They accept God's choice and back him at once.
entries.2 kings 9:14: Jehu begins his plot against King Joram, who is away at war watching for the enemy. The timing works in Jehu's favor.
entries.2 kings 9:15: Joram had gone home to heal from battle wounds, so Jehu orders that no one leave town to warn the king. He moves quickly to keep his plan secret.
entries.2 kings 9:16: Jehu rides to Jezreel where the wounded Joram lies, and King Ahaziah of Judah happens to be visiting. Two kings are unknowingly in Jehu's path.
entries.2 kings 9:17: A lookout sees Jehu's group coming and the king sends a rider to ask if they come in peace. The king is nervous and wants to know their intentions.
entries.2 kings 9:18: The rider asks about peace, but Jehu tells him to fall in behind instead of answering, and he never returns. Jehu refuses to explain himself.
entries.2 kings 9:19: A second rider is sent with the same question and gets the same response. The king's attempts to find out what is happening keep failing.
entries.2 kings 9:20: The lookout reports the second rider also didn't return and notes the driving is wild, like Jehu's. Jehu's reckless style gives him away.
entries.2 kings 9:21: Joram and Ahaziah ride out to meet Jehu and find him at the field that once belonged to Naboth. The meeting happens on the very ground of an old injustice.
entries.2 kings 9:22: Joram asks if Jehu comes in peace, and Jehu answers that peace is impossible while Jezebel's idolatry and witchcraft fill the land. Sin has made peace impossible.
entries.2 kings 9:23: Joram realizes he has been betrayed and turns his horses to flee, shouting a warning to Ahaziah. The trap is sprung.
entries.2 kings 9:24: Jehu shoots Joram with an arrow that pierces his heart, and he collapses in his chariot. The king's reign ends in a single moment.
entries.2 kings 9:25: Jehu tells his officer to throw the body into Naboth's field, reminding him of a prophecy they both heard years before. God's word from long ago is now coming true.
entries.2 kings 9:26: God had promised to repay the blood of Naboth and his sons on that very field, and now it happens. God does not forget injustice, even when it takes years.
entries.2 kings 9:27: Ahaziah flees but is wounded and dies at Megiddo. No one connected to Ahab's evil house escapes.
entries.2 kings 9:28: Ahaziah's servants carry his body to Jerusalem and bury him with his ancestors. Even a king's death ends in an ordinary burial.
entries.2 kings 9:29: A brief note dates when Ahaziah began ruling Judah. It anchors the story in real history.
entries.2 kings 9:30: When Jezebel hears Jehu has arrived, she paints her eyes and fixes her hair, then looks out the window. She faces her end with defiant pride.
entries.2 kings 9:31: Jezebel mocks Jehu by comparing him to Zimri, an earlier man who killed his king. She is taunting him even as she stands in danger.
entries.2 kings 9:32: Jehu looks up and calls for anyone on his side, and a few servants look out at him. Even Jezebel's own household begins to turn.
entries.2 kings 9:33: At Jehu's command the servants throw Jezebel from the window, and she is trampled by horses. Her death is violent and humiliating, as the prophet had said.
entries.2 kings 9:34: Jehu eats and then orders her body buried because she was a king's daughter. He shows a small amount of respect after her death.
entries.2 kings 9:35: When they go to bury her, only a few bones are left, the rest having been eaten by dogs. The prophecy is fulfilled exactly.
entries.2 kings 9:36: Jehu recalls Elijah's words that dogs would eat Jezebel's flesh in Jezreel. God's word through his prophet proved completely true.
entries.2 kings 9:37: Her body will be like dung on the ground, so no one can even point and say it is Jezebel. A proud queen ends with no grave and no memory.
entries.2 kings 10:1: Jehu wrote to the leaders of Samaria who were raising Ahab's seventy sons, setting up his next move against Ahab's family. It shows how a new king went about removing the old royal line.
entries.2 kings 10:2: Jehu pointed out that these leaders had everything needed to defend themselves—chariots, horses, a fortified city, and weapons. He was daring them to act on their strength.
entries.2 kings 10:3: Jehu told them to pick the best of Ahab's sons and fight for their old master's family. He was testing whether they would resist him.
entries.2 kings 10:4: The leaders were terrified because two kings had already fallen to Jehu, and they felt they had no chance against him. Fear kept them from resisting.
entries.2 kings 10:5: The officials in charge gave in completely and offered to obey Jehu instead of setting up another king. They chose survival over loyalty to Ahab's family.
entries.2 kings 10:6: Jehu demanded proof of their loyalty: they must bring him the heads of Ahab's sons by the next day. He forced them to choose sides in a brutal way.
entries.2 kings 10:7: The officials obeyed and killed all seventy of Ahab's sons, sending their heads to Jehu. This shows how far they went to save themselves.
entries.2 kings 10:8: Jehu ordered the heads to be piled at the city gate until morning, a public display of the end of Ahab's line. It was meant to be seen by everyone.
entries.2 kings 10:9: Jehu told the people that he was responsible for killing his master, but the deaths of Ahab's sons were the work of their own guardians. He was shifting blame and justifying himself.
entries.2 kings 10:10: Jehu declared that God's word through Elijah about Ahab's family would certainly come true. He framed the killings as God's judgment being carried out.
entries.2 kings 10:11: Jehu then killed everyone else connected to Ahab in Jezreel—relatives, close friends, and priests. He was wiping out any possible threat or supporter of the old regime.
entries.2 kings 10:12: Jehu continued on his way toward Samaria and stopped at a place where shepherds gathered. The story follows his journey as he secures his rule.
entries.2 kings 10:13: Jehu met relatives of Ahaziah, king of Judah, who were traveling to visit the royal family. They did not know what had happened.
entries.2 kings 10:14: Jehu ordered these forty-two men to be captured and killed at a water-hole. They were caught in the middle of his purge because of their ties to the royal houses.
entries.2 kings 10:15: Jehu met Jehonadab and asked if he was truly on his side; when Jehonadab said yes, Jehu invited him into his chariot. This shows Jehu seeking support from a respected man.
entries.2 kings 10:16: Jehu invited Jehonadab to ride along and see his zeal for the Lord. Jehu wanted his purge to be seen as devotion to God.
entries.2 kings 10:17: When Jehu reached Samaria, he killed the rest of Ahab's family there, just as God had told Elijah. The prophecy was fully carried out.
entries.2 kings 10:18: Jehu gathered the people and claimed he would serve Baal even more than Ahab did. This was not sincere—he was setting a trap.
entries.2 kings 10:19: Jehu called all of Baal's prophets, servants, and priests to a great gathering, threatening death to anyone who stayed away. His real plan was to destroy them all.
entries.2 kings 10:20: Jehu announced a special religious assembly for Baal and had it publicly proclaimed. He used worship as a cover for his plan.
entries.2 kings 10:21: Jehu sent word throughout Israel, and every servant of Baal came, filling the temple from one end to the other. No one suspected the trap.
entries.2 kings 10:22: Jehu told the keeper of the robes to bring out special garments for all the worshippers of Baal. This made the gathering look like a real religious ceremony.
entries.2 kings 10:23: Jehu and Jehonadab entered the temple and ordered a careful check to make sure only Baal's servants were inside, not worshippers of the Lord. He wanted to spare the faithful and trap the rest.
entries.2 kings 10:24: The worshippers began making offerings, while eighty men waited outside with orders to kill anyone who escaped. Jehu had set the trap carefully.
entries.2 kings 10:25: As soon as the offering was finished, Jehu's armed men went in and killed everyone, then dragged out the sacred images. The whole plan was carried out.
entries.2 kings 10:26: They brought out the image of Asherah from Baal's temple and burned it. This was part of removing the false worship.
entries.2 kings 10:27: They tore down Baal's altar and temple and made the place unfit for worship, and it stayed that way. The site was permanently ruined.
entries.2 kings 10:28: Jehu succeeded in ending the worship of Baal in Israel. This was a real reform, even though Jehu himself was not fully faithful.
entries.2 kings 10:29: But Jehu did not turn away from the sins Jeroboam had started—the golden calves at Bethel and Dan were still there. He removed one false worship but kept another.
entries.2 kings 10:30: God told Jehu that because he had carried out God's purpose against Ahab's family, his descendants would rule Israel for four generations. God rewarded him for doing that task.
entries.2 kings 10:31: Yet Jehu did not wholeheartedly follow God's law and kept the sins of Jeroboam. His obedience was partial, not complete.
entries.2 kings 10:32: In those days the Lord began to cut down Israel's territory, and Hazael of Aram attacked throughout the land. Trouble came on Israel from outside.
entries.2 kings 10:33: Hazael took land east of the Jordan, in Gilead, from the tribes of Gad, Reuben, and Manasseh. Israel lost territory as judgment continued.
entries.2 kings 10:34: The rest of Jehu's deeds and his power are recorded in the official history of Israel's kings. The writer points readers to that record for more details.
entries.2 kings 10:35: Jehu died and was buried in Samaria, and his son Jehoahaz became king after him. His rule came to an end like any other king's.
entries.2 kings 10:36: Jehu ruled over Israel in Samaria for twenty-eight years. His reign was long, but it was mixed in its faithfulness to God.
entries.2 kings 12:1: This verse introduces Jehoash as the new king of Judah, noting how long he ruled and who his mother was. It reminds the reader that even kings have a family background and a set time in power.
entries.2 kings 12:2: Jehoash lived in a way that pleased God, largely because the priest Jehoiada taught and guided him. It shows how much a wise, faithful mentor can shape a person's life.
entries.2 kings 12:3: The people kept worshiping at the local shrines instead of the one place God had chosen, and the king did not stop it. Good leadership can still leave some wrong things untouched.
entries.2 kings 12:4: Jehoash told the priests to collect the money people brought to the temple, both required payments and freewill gifts. It shows the king organizing resources for God's house.
entries.2 kings 12:5: Each priest was to gather money from people he knew to pay for repairs to the temple wherever damage was found. The work of maintaining a place of worship was shared among the priests.
entries.2 kings 12:6: By the twenty-third year of his reign, the priests still had not repaired the temple. Good intentions had not turned into action, and the king noticed.
entries.2 kings 12:7: Jehoash confronted Jehoiada and the priests about the delay and told them to stop collecting money personally and instead put it toward the repairs. It shows a leader holding people accountable when a job is not getting done.
entries.2 kings 12:8: The priests agreed to stop taking money from the people and to hand the repair work over to others. Sometimes admitting you are not getting a job done is the honest first step.
entries.2 kings 12:9: Jehoiada set up a chest with a hole in its lid beside the altar so people could drop their money in as they came to the temple. It was a simple, organized way to collect funds for the repairs.
entries.2 kings 12:10: When the chest got full, the king's secretary and the high priest counted the money and bagged it up. Careful record-keeping showed honesty with the money given to God.
entries.2 kings 12:11: The counted money was handed to the supervisors, who paid the carpenters and builders working on the temple. The funds went straight to the people doing the actual work.
entries.2 kings 12:12: The money also paid masons, stonecutters, and suppliers of wood and stone for repairing the temple and restoring it. It shows the practical, ordinary costs of keeping a house of worship in good shape.
entries.2 kings 12:13: None of this money was spent on fancy silver or gold items for the temple. The priority was fixing the building itself rather than buying decorations.
entries.2 kings 12:14: All the money went to the workmen repairing the temple. The needs of the building came before ornamentation.
entries.2 kings 12:15: The workers were trusted without having to submit receipts because they were known to be honest. Trust works best when people have proven themselves reliable.
entries.2 kings 12:16: Money from guilt and sin offerings belonged to the priests and was not put into the temple repair fund. God's law made provision for the priests' support.
entries.2 kings 12:17: Hazael, king of Aram, attacked and captured Gath and then set his sights on Jerusalem. A threat from a powerful neighbor was closing in on Judah.
entries.2 kings 12:18: To save Jerusalem, Jehoash took sacred treasures and gold from the temple and palace and sent them to Hazael, who then withdrew. Fear led the king to buy off an enemy with things dedicated to God.
entries.2 kings 12:19: This note says the rest of Joash's deeds are written in the official royal records. It reminds us that the Bible gives a summary, not every detail, of a king's life.
entries.2 kings 12:20: Joash's own officials plotted against him and killed him at a place called Millo. Even a king can be betrayed by those closest to him.
entries.2 kings 12:21: Two of his servants struck him down, and he was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, with his son Amaziah taking the throne. The story shows that no ruler's power lasts forever.
entries.2 kings 14:1: This verse simply dates when Amaziah became king of Judah, tying it to the reign of the king of Israel. It reminds the reader that these events happened at a real point in history, alongside other rulers.
entries.2 kings 14:2: Amaziah was twenty-five when he took the throne and ruled for twenty-nine years, and his mother's name is recorded. The details show he was a real person with a real family and a set length of rule.
entries.2 kings 14:3: Amaziah generally did what pleased God, but not as wholeheartedly as King David had. It shows that a person can do right yet still fall short of full devotion.
entries.2 kings 14:4: Even though Amaziah did right, he left the local shrines standing, and the people kept offering sacrifices there instead of at the proper place. Good leadership can still leave important things uncorrected.
entries.2 kings 14:5: Once Amaziah's hold on the kingdom was secure, he had the officials who had murdered his father executed. He acted on the wrong done to his family, but he waited until he had the power to do it.
entries.2 kings 14:6: Amaziah did not kill the children of the murderers, because God's law says each person should die for his own sin, not for a parent's. It shows the value God places on fair treatment and personal responsibility.
entries.2 kings 14:7: Amaziah won a major victory over Edom, killing twelve thousand men and capturing a city he renamed. This shows his military success and how he left his mark on the land.
entries.2 kings 14:8: Puffed up by his victory, Amaziah challenged the king of Israel to a face-to-face showdown. Success can make a person bold in ways that lead to trouble.
entries.2 kings 14:9: The king of Israel answered with a little story about a thorn bush that thought it was as great as a cedar tree until an animal trampled it. He was warning Amaziah that he was overestimating himself.
entries.2 kings 14:10: The king of Israel told Amaziah to be satisfied with his win over Edom and stay home, or he would bring disaster on himself and his people. It is a plain warning against pride and picking unnecessary fights.
entries.2 kings 14:11: Amaziah ignored the warning, so the two kings met in battle at Beth-shemesh in Judah. Refusing good advice often leads a person straight into the conflict he was warned about.
entries.2 kings 14:12: Judah's army was beaten by Israel and the soldiers ran home. The proud challenge ended in defeat, showing that confidence alone does not win a fight.
entries.2 kings 14:13: The king of Israel captured Amaziah, marched on Jerusalem, and tore down a long section of its wall. The defeat cost Judah not only the battle but also its security.
entries.2 kings 14:14: The victor looted the temple and the palace treasures and took hostages back to Samaria. The pride of one king brought loss and humiliation to the whole nation.
entries.2 kings 14:15: This verse notes that the rest of Jehoash's deeds and his war with Amaziah are recorded in the official records of Israel's kings. It points the reader to fuller historical accounts for the details.
entries.2 kings 14:16: Jehoash died and was buried with his ancestors in Samaria, and his son Jeroboam took the throne. It marks the end of one reign and the start of the next.
entries.2 kings 14:17: Amaziah outlived the king of Israel by fifteen years. The verse quietly notes that he kept living after the man who had defeated him was gone.
entries.2 kings 14:18: This is a standard note that the rest of Amaziah's deeds are written in Judah's official royal records. It tells the reader where more information could be found.
entries.2 kings 14:19: A plot was formed against Amaziah in Jerusalem, and when he fled to Lachish they followed him there and killed him. Even a king can lose his life when his own people turn against him.
entries.2 kings 14:20: His body was brought back on horseback and buried with his ancestors in Jerusalem. He was given an honorable burial despite his violent death.
entries.2 kings 14:21: The people of Judah made Amaziah's sixteen-year-old son Azariah king in his place. Leadership passed to the next generation, even though he was young.
entries.2 kings 14:22: Azariah rebuilt Elath and restored it to Judah after his father died. He strengthened the nation's territory once he was in charge.
entries.2 kings 14:23: This dates the start of Jeroboam's reign over Israel to the fifteenth year of Amaziah's rule, and notes he reigned forty-one years. It keeps the two kingdoms' timelines lined up for the reader.
entries.2 kings 14:24: Jeroboam did what was evil in God's eyes and never turned away from the idol worship that the earlier Jeroboam had led Israel into. A long reign does not by itself mean a good one.
entries.2 kings 14:25: Jeroboam restored Israel's old borders, just as God had promised through the prophet Jonah. It shows that God kept His word even through a king who did not follow Him.
entries.2 kings 14:26: God saw how bitterly Israel was suffering, with no one left to help and no one to turn to. It shows that God notices the pain of His people even when things look hopeless.
entries.2 kings 14:27: God had not decided to wipe Israel's name off the earth, so He gave them a deliverer through Jeroboam. God's mercy held back the judgment they deserved.
entries.2 kings 14:28: This notes that the rest of Jeroboam's deeds, his power, and his wars, including recovering Damascus, are recorded in Israel's royal records. It points to fuller accounts for the details.
entries.2 kings 14:29: Jeroboam died and was buried with his ancestors, and his son Zechariah became king. It closes his reign and hands the kingdom to the next generation.
entries.2 kings 15:1: Azariah became king of Judah during the reign of Jeroboam of Israel. This marks the start of his rule and shows how the two kingdoms' timelines overlap.
entries.2 kings 15:2: Azariah was only sixteen when he took the throne and ruled for fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His long reign shows stability, and his mother's name is recorded like other kings.
entries.2 kings 15:3: Azariah did what pleased God, following the good example of his father Amaziah. His life shows that a person can choose to follow God's ways.
entries.2 kings 15:4: Even though Azariah was mostly good, he left the local worship sites standing, and people kept offering sacrifices there instead of at the temple. Good leaders can still leave important things undone.
entries.2 kings 15:5: God struck Azariah with a skin disease, so he lived apart from others until he died, while his son Jotham ran the palace and governed the people. Even a good king's life can be marked by hardship and limitation.
entries.2 kings 15:6: The other things Azariah did are written in the official records of Judah's kings. The writer points readers to those records for more detail.
entries.2 kings 15:7: Azariah died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, and his son Jotham took over as king. His death continues the pattern of one king replacing another.
entries.2 kings 15:8: Zechariah, son of Jeroboam, became king over Israel and lasted only six months. His short reign hints at how unstable the northern kingdom had become.
entries.2 kings 15:9: Zechariah did evil in God's sight, continuing the same sinful pattern his father had followed. He failed to break away from the wrong path set before him.
entries.2 kings 15:10: Shallum plotted against Zechariah, killed him publicly in Ibleam, and took the throne for himself. This is a violent takeover, showing the chaos in Israel.
entries.2 kings 15:11: The rest of what Zechariah did is recorded in the official history of Israel's kings. The writer again points to those records.
entries.2 kings 15:12: This fulfilled what God had told Jehu: his descendants would rule Israel for four generations. God's word proved true even in the middle of a violent, unstable time.
entries.2 kings 15:13: Shallum became king of Israel and ruled only one month in Samaria. His very short reign shows how quickly power changed hands.
entries.2 kings 15:14: Menahem came from Tirzah to Samaria, attacked Shallum, killed him, and made himself king. This is another violent seizure of power.
entries.2 kings 15:15: The rest of Shallum's deeds, including his plot, are written in Israel's official records. The writer directs readers there for more.
entries.2 kings 15:16: Menahem destroyed the town of Tappuah and its surrounding area because they refused to let him in, and he committed terrible atrocities there. This shows the cruelty that marked his rise to power.
entries.2 kings 15:17: Menahem became king over Israel and ruled ten years in Samaria. His reign is dated by the years of Azariah of Judah.
entries.2 kings 15:18: Menahem did evil in God's sight and never turned away from the sinful pattern Jeroboam had started. He continued the same wrong path as those before him.
entries.2 kings 15:19: The Assyrian king Pul invaded the land, and Menahem paid him a huge amount of silver to keep his throne secure. He tried to buy safety instead of trusting God.
entries.2 kings 15:20: Menahem raised the money by taxing wealthy men fifty silver pieces each and gave it to Assyria, so the Assyrian king left without staying. The burden of the king's deal fell on the people.
entries.2 kings 15:21: The rest of Menahem's deeds are written in Israel's official records. The writer points to those records for more detail.
entries.2 kings 15:22: Menahem died and was buried with his ancestors, and his son Pekahiah became king. The throne passed to the next generation.
entries.2 kings 15:23: Pekahiah, son of Menahem, became king of Israel in Samaria and ruled only two years. His short reign is dated by Azariah's years in Judah.
entries.2 kings 15:24: Pekahiah did evil in God's sight and did not turn from Jeroboam's sinful pattern. He followed the same wrong path as his predecessors.
entries.2 kings 15:25: Pekah, one of Pekahiah's own officers, plotted against him and killed him in the royal palace with fifty men from Gilead, then took the throne. This is another violent coup within Israel.
entries.2 kings 15:26: The rest of Pekahiah's deeds are written in Israel's official records. The writer again points to those records.
entries.2 kings 15:27: Pekah became king over Israel in Samaria and ruled twenty years. His reign is dated by Azariah's years in Judah.
entries.2 kings 15:28: Pekah did evil in God's sight and did not turn from Jeroboam's sinful pattern. He continued the same wrong path as those before him.
entries.2 kings 15:29: During Pekah's reign, the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser captured many towns and regions and deported the people to Assyria. This was a devastating loss for Israel and a sign of judgment.
entries.2 kings 15:30: Hoshea plotted against Pekah, killed him, and took the throne, during the twentieth year of Jotham of Judah. This is yet another violent takeover in Israel.
entries.2 kings 15:31: The rest of Pekah's deeds are written in Israel's official records. The writer points readers there for more.
entries.2 kings 15:32: Jotham, son of Uzziah, became king of Judah during the second year of Pekah of Israel. His reign is dated by the northern kingdom's king.
entries.2 kings 15:33: Jotham was twenty-five when he became king and ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem; his mother was Jerusha, daughter of Zadok. His age and family background are recorded like other kings.
entries.2 kings 15:34: Jotham did what pleased God, following the good example of his father Uzziah. He chose to walk in the right path his father had set.
entries.2 kings 15:35: Jotham left the local worship sites standing, and people kept sacrificing there; he also built the upper gate of the Lord's temple. Even a good king can leave important reforms undone.
entries.2 kings 15:36: The rest of Jotham's deeds are written in Judah's official records. The writer points to those records for more detail.
entries.2 kings 15:37: During Jotham's time, God began sending Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel against Judah. Trouble was starting to build against the southern kingdom.
entries.2 kings 15:38: Jotham died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, and his son Ahaz became king. The throne passed to the next generation.
entries.2 kings 16:1: This verse simply dates when Ahaz became king of Judah, during the reign of Pekah of Israel. It reminds the reader that these events happened at a real point in history, under real rulers.
entries.2 kings 16:2: Ahaz was young when he took the throne and ruled sixteen years, but he did not follow God the way his ancestor David had. It shows that a good family background does not guarantee a person will stay faithful to God.
entries.2 kings 16:3: Ahaz copied the evil practices of Israel's kings and even sacrificed his own son in fire, imitating the nations God had driven out. This shows how far a leader can fall when he abandons God's ways.
entries.2 kings 16:4: Ahaz offered sacrifices at unauthorized shrines on hills and under trees instead of worshiping at God's chosen place. It warns that worshiping in our own way, rather than God's way, leads people away from him.
entries.2 kings 16:5: Two enemy kings attacked Jerusalem and besieged Ahaz but could not defeat him. Even when trouble surrounds us, God can set limits on what our enemies are allowed to do.
entries.2 kings 16:6: Edom took back the town of Elath and drove out the people of Judah who lived there. This was a real loss for Judah, showing that the nation's troubles were piling up during Ahaz's reign.
entries.2 kings 16:7: Ahaz asked the king of Assyria for help, calling himself his servant and son, which meant placing himself under Assyria's power. It shows the danger of trusting a powerful human ally instead of trusting God.
entries.2 kings 16:8: Ahaz took silver and gold from God's temple and his own treasury and sent it to Assyria as a payment for help. He was using what belonged to God to buy protection, which showed how little he valued God.
entries.2 kings 16:9: The king of Assyria responded by conquering Damascus, deporting its people, and killing Rezin. Ahaz got the help he wanted, but it came at the cost of becoming dependent on a foreign empire.
entries.2 kings 16:10: While in Damascus, Ahaz saw a pagan altar and sent its design back to the priest in Jerusalem. He was letting foreign worship shape God's house, which shows how easily our surroundings can pull us away from God.
entries.2 kings 16:11: The priest Urijah built the new altar exactly as the king ordered and had it ready when Ahaz returned. It shows how even religious leaders can go along with wrong commands from those in power.
entries.2 kings 16:12: When Ahaz came back, he approved the new altar and offered sacrifices on it himself. He was reshaping worship to suit his own preferences rather than following God's instructions.
entries.2 kings 16:13: Ahaz offered the full set of sacrifices on the new altar, including pouring out the blood. Outwardly he was still doing religious acts, but they were directed by his own plans rather than God's commands.
entries.2 kings 16:14: Ahaz moved God's original bronze altar off to the side to make room for his new one. It pictures how people can push God's true worship aside to make room for something they prefer.
entries.2 kings 16:15: Ahaz ordered the priest to use the new altar for all the regular offerings, while keeping the old bronze altar for himself to seek guidance. He was treating worship as something to control and manage for his own purposes.
entries.2 kings 16:16: The priest did exactly what the king commanded. It shows how quickly a whole religious system can be redirected when leaders stop asking what God wants.
entries.2 kings 16:17: Ahaz dismantled parts of the temple furnishings and moved the large water basin off its bronze oxen onto a stone floor. He was altering God's house to suit his own plans and his dealings with Assyria.
entries.2 kings 16:18: Ahaz made changes to the temple because of the king of Assyria. It shows that fear of a powerful foreign ruler, rather than love for God, was driving his decisions.
entries.2 kings 16:19: This verse notes that the rest of Ahaz's deeds are recorded in the official records of Judah's kings. It reminds us that his story is part of a larger history that was carefully kept.
entries.2 kings 16:20: Ahaz died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, and his son Hezekiah became king. Even after a bad king, God continued the line of David and gave Judah another chance through a new ruler.
entries.2 kings 17:1: Hoshea became king of the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Ahaz in Judah, and he ruled for nine years. This sets the time period for the events that follow.
entries.2 kings 17:2: Hoshea did wrong in God's sight, though he was not as bad as the kings before him. Even so, being less bad than others is not the same as being faithful to God.
entries.2 kings 17:3: The king of Assyria attacked Hoshea and made him a subject who had to pay tribute. A powerful enemy was putting pressure on Israel.
entries.2 kings 17:4: Hoshea tried to get help from Egypt and stopped paying tribute, so the Assyrian king found out and threw him in prison. Trusting the wrong ally and breaking his word cost him his freedom.
entries.2 kings 17:5: The Assyrian king then marched through the land and surrounded Samaria, the capital, for three years. The siege was long and devastating for the people.
entries.2 kings 17:6: In Hoshea's ninth year the Assyrians captured Samaria and deported the Israelites to distant lands. This was the end of the northern kingdom as a nation in its own land.
entries.2 kings 17:7: The writer explains that this disaster happened because Israel sinned against the God who had rescued them from slavery in Egypt and had turned to other gods. Their downfall was not bad luck but the result of turning away from the one who saved them.
entries.2 kings 17:8: They copied the customs of the nations God had driven out before them. Adopting the practices of those who rejected God led them away from him.
entries.2 kings 17:9: The Israelites did wrong things in secret against the Lord and built places of worship all over the land, from small watchtowers to walled cities. Their disobedience was widespread and hidden.
entries.2 kings 17:10: They set up stone and wooden pillars for worship on every high hill and under every green tree. They were imitating pagan worship everywhere they went.
entries.2 kings 17:11: They burned offerings at these high places just as the nations God had removed had done, and this made the Lord angry. They were following the very patterns God had warned against.
entries.2 kings 17:12: They served worthless idols even though the Lord had plainly told them not to. God had already made his will clear, so their idolatry was deliberate disobedience.
entries.2 kings 17:13: God repeatedly warned Israel and Judah through his prophets, calling them to turn from their evil ways and obey his law. God was patient and gave them many chances to come back.
entries.2 kings 17:14: But they refused to listen and became stubborn, just like their ancestors who did not trust the Lord. Stubbornness against God's warnings kept them from turning back.
entries.2 kings 17:15: They rejected God's rules and the covenant he made with their ancestors, chasing worthless things and becoming foolish like the nations around them. Rejecting God's word made them empty and confused.
entries.2 kings 17:16: They abandoned all the Lord's commands, made metal idols and an Asherah pole, worshipped the stars, and served Baal. They replaced the worship of God with every kind of false worship.
entries.2 kings 17:17: They even sacrificed their own children in fire and practiced sorcery and divination, doing evil until the Lord was provoked to anger. Their sin had become deeply cruel and corrupt.
entries.2 kings 17:18: So the Lord was very angry with Israel and removed them from his presence, leaving only Judah. Persistent sin finally brought the judgment God had warned about.
entries.2 kings 17:19: Even Judah did not keep the Lord's commands but followed the same practices Israel had made. Judah was not innocent either, despite being spared for a time.
entries.2 kings 17:20: So the Lord rejected all the people of Israel, brought trouble on them, and handed them over to their enemies until he removed them from his sight. God's patience had run out after generations of rebellion.
entries.2 kings 17:21: Israel had split from the house of David and made Jeroboam king, and he led them away from the Lord's laws into great sin. The division became a spiritual disaster that shaped everything after.
entries.2 kings 17:22: The Israelites kept committing the same sins Jeroboam had introduced and never turned away from them. They persisted in the pattern their leaders had set.
entries.2 kings 17:23: Finally the Lord removed Israel from his presence, just as the prophets had said, and they were taken to Assyria, where they remained. The exile was the fulfillment of long-standing warnings.
entries.2 kings 17:24: The Assyrian king brought people from several other nations to settle in the towns of Samaria in place of the Israelites. The land was repopulated with foreigners who did not know the Lord.
entries.2 kings 17:25: At first these new settlers did not worship the Lord, so he sent lions among them and some died. God made it clear that the land belonged to him and demanded reverence.
entries.2 kings 17:26: The settlers told the Assyrian king that they did not know how the god of the land was to be worshipped, and that this was why the lions were killing them. They recognized something was wrong but did not know the true God.
entries.2 kings 17:27: The Assyrian king ordered that one of the exiled Israelite priests be sent back to teach the settlers how to worship the god of the land. Even a pagan ruler acknowledged that the people needed instruction.
entries.2 kings 17:28: So one of the priests taken from Samaria returned and lived in Bethel, teaching the settlers how to worship the Lord. Instruction was given, but it was mixed with the old idolatry.
entries.2 kings 17:29: Each group of settlers made its own gods and placed them in the high places the Samaritans had built, each nation in its own town. Instead of true worship, they added the Lord to their collection of gods.
entries.2 kings 17:30: The people from Babylon made Succoth-benoth, those from Cuth made Nergal, and those from Hamath made Ashima. Each group brought its own idols with it.
entries.2 kings 17:31: The Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burned their children as sacrifices to Adrammelech and Anammelech. Their worship included horrifying practices.
entries.2 kings 17:32: They also worshipped the Lord and appointed priests from among themselves to offer sacrifices at the high places. Their religion was a mixture of devotion to God and to idols.
entries.2 kings 17:33: They worshipped the Lord but also honored their own gods, following the customs of the nations they came from. This divided loyalty was not true worship of God at all.
entries.2 kings 17:34: To this day they continue in their old ways, not truly worshipping the Lord or keeping his commands and law given to the descendants of Jacob. Their religion looked religious but was not obedience to God.
entries.2 kings 17:35: The Lord had made a covenant with them and commanded them to have no other gods, not to worship or serve them or offer sacrifices to them. God's covenant was exclusive and clear.
entries.2 kings 17:36: The Lord, who brought them out of Egypt with great power, is the one they must worship and sacrifice to. He alone had proven himself worthy of their devotion.
entries.2 kings 17:37: They were to keep and obey forever the rules, commands, and law God had written for them, and have no other gods. God's instructions were not optional or temporary.
entries.2 kings 17:38: They were to remember the covenant God made with them and have no other gods. Remembering God's covenant means refusing to give loyalty to anything else.
entries.2 kings 17:39: They were to worship the Lord their God, because he is the one who would save them from all their enemies. Only God could give them real security and deliverance.
entries.2 kings 17:40: But they paid no attention and continued in their old ways. The chapter ends with the sad reality that the people refused to listen to God's clear commands.
entries.2 kings 17:41: These people claimed to worship God while still holding on to their idols, and that mixed loyalty got passed down through the family. It's a warning that what we tolerate in our own lives can become the pattern our children follow.
entries.2 kings 18:1: This verse marks the moment Hezekiah became king of Judah, dated by the reign of Israel's king Hoshea. It reminds the reader that God's story moves through real people and real dates, not vague legend.
entries.2 kings 18:2: Hezekiah was twenty-five when he took the throne and ruled twenty-nine years in Jerusalem; his mother's name is recorded too. The details show he was a real historical king whose life and choices are open before God.
entries.2 kings 18:3: Hezekiah did what was right in God's eyes, following the example of David. It shows that a person's life can be measured by faithfulness to God rather than by success or popularity.
entries.2 kings 18:4: Hezekiah removed the local shrines, smashed the sacred stones, cut down the Asherah pole, and destroyed the bronze snake Moses had made because people were burning offerings to it. Good reform means removing even old religious things that have become objects of worship instead of God.
entries.2 kings 18:5: Hezekiah trusted the Lord, the God of Israel, more than any king of Judah before him. The verse shows that wholehearted trust in God is what makes a life stand out.
entries.2 kings 18:6: He held firmly to the Lord, did not turn away from following him, and kept the commands God gave through Moses. Steady obedience, not just occasional good deeds, is what faithfulness looks like.
entries.2 kings 18:7: The Lord was with Hezekiah, so he prospered, and he rebelled against the king of Assyria instead of serving him. When God is with someone, they can stand up to powers that once controlled them.
entries.2 kings 18:8: He defeated the Philistines all the way to Gaza and its territory. This shows God giving him victory over long-standing enemies of his people.
entries.2 kings 18:9: In Hezekiah's fourth year, the Assyrian king Shalmaneser attacked Samaria and besieged it. The verse sets the stage for judgment on the northern kingdom of Israel.
entries.2 kings 18:10: After three years the siege ended and Samaria fell, in Hezekiah's sixth year and Hoshea's ninth. It shows that God's warnings about judgment came true exactly as stated.
entries.2 kings 18:11: The Assyrian king deported the people of Israel to Assyria and settled them in Halah, Habor by the Gozan River, and the towns of the Medes. Exile was the real consequence of the nation's long rejection of God.
entries.2 kings 18:12: This happened because Israel did not listen to the Lord their God but broke his covenant and disobeyed all that Moses commanded. It is a sober warning that ignoring God's voice has serious results.
entries.2 kings 18:13: In Hezekiah's fourteenth year, Sennacherib of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified towns of Judah. Even a faithful king could still face overwhelming military pressure.
entries.2 kings 18:14: Hezekiah admitted fault and asked the Assyrian king to stop attacking, agreeing to pay whatever was demanded, which was set at three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold. It shows the heavy cost of buying off a powerful enemy.
entries.2 kings 18:15: Hezekiah paid the silver from the Lord's temple and from the royal treasury. The verse shows how a national crisis drained even the resources dedicated to God.
entries.2 kings 18:16: Hezekiah cut the gold off the temple doors and doorposts he had overlaid and gave it to the Assyrian king. It shows how desperate the situation had become, even to the point of stripping the temple.
entries.2 kings 18:17: The Assyrian king sent three high officials with a strong army from Lachish to Jerusalem, and they stationed themselves by the upper pool on the washerman's road. The pressure on Jerusalem was now direct and public.
entries.2 kings 18:18: They called for the king, and three of Hezekiah's officials—Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah—came out to meet them. The verse shows the tense negotiation between a threatened nation and its enemy.
entries.2 kings 18:19: The Assyrian official told them to tell Hezekiah that the great king of Assyria asks what he is relying on. It is a taunt meant to shake the king's confidence.
entries.2 kings 18:20: He says that talk of plans and military strength is empty unless there is someone real to back it up, and asks who Hezekiah is trusting. It exposes the gap between confident words and actual support.
entries.2 kings 18:21: He compares Egypt to a splintered reed that pierces the hand of anyone leaning on it, saying Pharaoh is just as unreliable to those who trust him. It warns against putting hope in powerful allies who cannot deliver.
entries.2 kings 18:22: He claims that if they trust the Lord, Hezekiah has offended him by removing the high places and altars and restricting worship to Jerusalem. The taunt twists the truth, since those removals were actually obedience to God.
entries.2 kings 18:23: He offers a wager: if Hezekiah can supply riders, the Assyrian king will give him two thousand horses. It is mockery of Judah's lack of military strength.
entries.2 kings 18:24: He asks how Judah could even repel the least of Assyria's officers when they are depending on Egypt for chariots and horsemen. The point is to make Judah feel hopelessly outmatched.
entries.2 kings 18:25: He claims he has come to destroy this place with the Lord's own authority, saying the Lord told him to attack the land. It is a bold claim that mixes truth and bluff to intimidate.
entries.2 kings 18:26: Hezekiah's officials asked the Assyrian to speak Aramaic so the people on the wall would not understand. They wanted to keep the frightening threats from spreading panic.
entries.2 kings 18:27: The Assyrian refused, saying he was sent to speak to the men on the wall too, who would suffer hunger and thirst during a siege. He deliberately aimed his words at the ordinary people to break their morale.
entries.2 kings 18:28: He then stood and shouted loudly in Hebrew so everyone could hear the words of the great king of Assyria. The intimidation was now aimed directly at the whole city.
entries.2 kings 18:29: He told the people not to let Hezekiah deceive them, because Hezekiah could not save them. It is a direct attack on the people's trust in their leader.
entries.2 kings 18:30: He warned them not to let Hezekiah make them trust the Lord with promises that the city would be safe. The enemy's strategy was to undermine confidence in God himself.
