entries.2 kings 18:31: He urged them not to listen to Hezekiah but to make peace with Assyria and come out, promising each person could eat from his own vine and fig tree and drink from his own well. It offered a tempting picture of safety in surrender.
entries.2 kings 18:32: He promised to take them to a land like their own, full of grain, wine, bread, olives, and honey, so they would live and not die, and again warned them not to trust Hezekiah's claim that the Lord would save them. The offer sounded generous but meant exile from home and from God's city.
entries.2 kings 18:33: He asked whether any god of the nations had ever kept its land from the Assyrian king. It is an argument from history meant to make the Lord seem no different from powerless idols.
entries.2 kings 18:34: He listed the gods of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah and asked where they were, and whether they had saved Samaria. The taunt assumed all gods were alike and equally defeated.
entries.2 kings 18:35: He asked which of all these gods had saved its country from him, so why should anyone think the Lord would save Jerusalem. It is the climax of the intimidation, directly challenging God's power.
entries.2 kings 18:36: The people stayed silent and gave no answer, because the king had ordered them not to respond. Silence here was disciplined obedience, not agreement with the enemy.
entries.2 kings 18:37: Hezekiah's officials came to him with their clothes torn in grief and told him everything the Assyrian official had said. The verse shows the shock and sorrow the threats caused, and sets up the king's response.
entries.2 kings 20:1: Hezekiah was very sick and close to dying, so the prophet Isaiah told him to get his affairs in order because he would not recover. It reminds readers that death can come sooner than expected, so we should be ready.
entries.2 kings 20:2: Hezekiah turned away to face the wall and prayed to the Lord. It shows that when we are in deep distress, we can turn to God honestly and privately.
entries.2 kings 20:3: Hezekiah asked God to remember how faithfully and wholeheartedly he had lived, and then he cried bitterly. It shows that pouring out our grief and asking God to remember our devotion is a normal part of prayer.
entries.2 kings 20:4: Before Isaiah had even left the area, God gave him a new message. It shows that God can answer prayer quickly, even before we expect it.
entries.2 kings 20:5: God told Isaiah to go back and tell Hezekiah that he had heard his prayer and seen his tears, and that he would be healed and back at the temple in three days. It shows that God notices our sorrow and responds to sincere prayer.
entries.2 kings 20:6: God promised Hezekiah fifteen more years of life and protection for the city from Assyria, for the sake of his own honor and his promise to David. It shows that God's help rests on his own faithfulness, not just on our worthiness.
entries.2 kings 20:7: Isaiah told them to put a fig cake on Hezekiah's wound, and he recovered. It shows that God often works through simple, practical means alongside his promise of healing.
entries.2 kings 20:8: Hezekiah asked Isaiah for a sign confirming that God would heal him and that he would go to the temple on the third day. It shows that asking God for reassurance is not wrong when our faith feels weak.
entries.2 kings 20:9: Isaiah offered Hezekiah a choice of sign: whether the shadow would move forward ten steps or backward. It shows God graciously offering confirmation in a way suited to the person asking.
entries.2 kings 20:10: Hezekiah said moving forward is easy, so let the shadow go backward ten steps instead. It shows he wanted a sign that clearly could not happen by ordinary means.
entries.2 kings 20:11: Isaiah prayed, and God made the shadow go back ten steps on the stairway of Ahaz. It shows that God is sovereign over nature and confirms his word with unmistakable signs.
entries.2 kings 20:12: The king of Babylon sent messengers with a gift to Hezekiah after hearing he had been sick. It shows that news of God's work can reach far places, but also sets up a test of Hezekiah's wisdom.
entries.2 kings 20:13: Hezekiah welcomed the messengers and proudly showed them all his wealth, weapons, and treasures, holding nothing back. It shows how easily success and flattery can lead us to boast instead of giving glory to God.
entries.2 kings 20:14: Isaiah asked Hezekiah what the men had said and where they came from, and Hezekiah answered that they came from distant Babylon. It shows that God was giving Hezekiah a chance to reflect on what he had done.
entries.2 kings 20:15: Isaiah asked what the visitors had seen, and Hezekiah admitted they had seen everything in his house. It shows that his pride had exposed his whole kingdom to a foreign power.
entries.2 kings 20:16: Isaiah told Hezekiah to listen to what the Lord was about to say. It shows that God's word must be heard even when it is unwelcome news.
entries.2 kings 20:17: God said that a time was coming when everything in Hezekiah's house and all his ancestors' treasures would be carried off to Babylon. It shows that pride and careless exposure can lead to serious loss, even generations later.
entries.2 kings 20:18: God also said that some of Hezekiah's own sons would be taken away and made servants in the Babylonian king's palace. It shows that the consequences of a leader's choices can fall on their family.
entries.2 kings 20:19: Hezekiah accepted God's word as good and was relieved that there would be peace and security in his own lifetime. It shows how easy it is to accept judgment when it does not personally cost us much.
entries.2 kings 20:20: The rest of Hezekiah's achievements, including how he built the pool and water channel, are recorded in the official history of Judah's kings. It shows that his practical work for the city was remembered alongside his spiritual life.
entries.2 kings 20:21: Hezekiah died and was buried with his ancestors, and his son Manasseh became king. It shows that even a faithful king's life ends, and the story passes to the next generation.
entries.2 kings 19:1: When the king heard the threats, he was deeply shaken and humbled himself before God, going to the temple to pray. It shows that turning to God in a crisis is the right first response.
entries.2 kings 19:2: Hezekiah sent his top officials and priests, also dressed in mourning, to ask the prophet Isaiah for God's word. It means the leaders sought God's guidance together rather than relying on themselves.
entries.2 kings 19:3: Hezekiah describes the situation as a time of deep distress and disgrace, like a mother too weak to give birth. It means the nation is in desperate trouble and needs God's help to survive.
entries.2 kings 19:4: Hezekiah hopes God will hear the enemy's insults against the living God and act, and he asks Isaiah to pray for the remaining people. It means we can bring insults against God's name to him and ask others to pray with us.
entries.2 kings 19:5: The officials simply did what the king told them and delivered his message to Isaiah. It shows the ordinary step of obeying and seeking God's word in a crisis.
entries.2 kings 19:6: God's answer through Isaiah is that Hezekiah should not be afraid of the insulting words the Assyrian officials spoke. It means God hears threats against him and tells his people not to be shaken by them.
entries.2 kings 19:7: God promises to stir the enemy king to hear alarming news, return home, and be killed there by the sword. It means God himself will deal with the threat and turn the enemy back.
entries.2 kings 19:8: The Assyrian official returned and found his king had moved on to attack another town. It shows the enemy's plans were already shifting, just as God had said.
entries.2 kings 19:9: When the Assyrian king heard that Ethiopia's king was marching against him, he sent another threatening message to Hezekiah. It means pressure came again even after a brief pause, testing the king's trust in God.
entries.2 kings 19:10: The message warns Hezekiah not to let his God give him false hope that Jerusalem will be spared. It means the enemy tries to undermine trust in God's promises by suggesting they are empty.
entries.2 kings 19:11: The king reminds Hezekiah of how Assyria has destroyed every land it attacked and asks why he would be any different. It means the enemy uses fear and past victories to make God's people feel hopeless.
entries.2 kings 19:12: He lists nations whose gods failed to save them from his ancestors. It means he assumes Israel's God is just another powerless god like the rest.
entries.2 kings 19:13: He names more defeated kings and towns, pressing the same point that no one has escaped him. It means the intimidation is repeated to wear down Hezekiah's confidence.
entries.2 kings 19:14: Hezekiah took the letter, read it, then went up to the temple and spread it out before the Lord. It means he brought the threat honestly and openly to God in prayer.
entries.2 kings 19:15: Hezekiah prays to the Lord, who is enthroned above the cherubim, declaring that he alone is God over all kingdoms and made heaven and earth. It means prayer begins by remembering who God truly is.
entries.2 kings 19:16: He asks God to listen and see, and to take note of the insults Sennacherib has spoken against the living God. It means we can ask God to pay attention to the wrong done against his name.
entries.2 kings 19:17: Hezekiah admits the Assyrian kings really have destroyed nations and their lands. It means honest prayer acknowledges the facts rather than pretending the danger isn't real.
entries.2 kings 19:18: He explains those nations' gods were only wood and stone made by human hands, so they could be burned. It means the enemy's gods were never real, unlike the living God.
entries.2 kings 19:19: He asks God to save them so that all the kingdoms of the earth will know that the Lord alone is God. It means the goal of rescue is that God's name be honoured before the world.
entries.2 kings 19:20: Isaiah sends word that God has heard Hezekiah's prayer against Sennacherib. It means God listens when his people pray and answers through his prophet.
entries.2 kings 19:21: God's word says Jerusalem, pictured as a young woman, despises and mocks the Assyrian king. It means the proud enemy who seemed so strong is actually a laughingstock before God's people.
entries.2 kings 19:22: God asks whom the king has insulted and spoken proudly against, and the answer is the Holy One of Israel. It means mocking God's people is really mocking God himself.
entries.2 kings 19:23: The king boasted that with his chariots he had climbed mountains and cut down Lebanon's finest cedars. It means his pride was enormous, claiming power over everything.
entries.2 kings 19:24: He boasted of digging wells in foreign lands and drying up Egypt's rivers with his feet. It means he claimed total control over water and nations, an arrogant exaggeration.
entries.2 kings 19:25: God says he planned all this long ago and now brought it about, using Assyria to turn strong cities into ruins. It means the enemy was only a tool in God's hands, not the real power.
entries.2 kings 19:26: Their people had no strength and were crushed like grass on a roof that dries up quickly. It means the defeated nations were weak and short-lived, not because Assyria was invincible.
entries.2 kings 19:27: God says he knows everything about the Assyrian king, his sitting down and rising up, his coming and going. It means no one is hidden from God, not even the mightiest ruler.
entries.2 kings 19:28: Because of his rage and pride, God will put a hook in his nose and a cord in his lips and send him back the way he came. It means God will restrain and turn back the proud enemy like an animal on a leash.
entries.2 kings 19:29: God gives a sign: for two years the people will eat what grows by itself, and in the third year they will plant and harvest and plant vineyards. It means God will provide for them through the recovery period.
entries.2 kings 19:30: The survivors of Judah will take root again and bear fruit. It means God promises lasting restoration, not just survival.
entries.2 kings 19:31: A remnant will come out of Jerusalem and Mount Zion, and the Lord of armies will accomplish this. It means God's purpose guarantees that his people will continue.
entries.2 kings 19:32: God says the Assyrian king will not enter the city, shoot an arrow at it, or build siege works against it. It means the threat will not touch Jerusalem at all.
entries.2 kings 19:33: He will go back the same way he came and will not enter the city, says the Lord. It means God's word is definite: the enemy's advance stops here.
entries.2 kings 19:34: God will defend the city for his own honour and for the sake of his servant David. It means God's protection rests on his own name and his promises, not on the people's strength.
entries.2 kings 19:35: That night the angel of the Lord struck down 185,000 in the Assyrian army, and in the morning there were only dead bodies. It means God himself defeated the enemy without any battle.
entries.2 kings 19:36: Sennacherib, the Assyrian king, withdrew and went back to Nineveh. It means the threat was over and the enemy retreated just as God had promised.
entries.2 kings 19:37: While he was worshipping his god Nisroch, his own sons killed him with swords and fled, and another son took the throne. It means the proud king met the violent end God had foretold, in the very place of his false worship.
entries.2 kings 22:1: Josiah became king of Judah when he was only eight years old and ruled for thirty-one years. His story shows that even a young person can be given real responsibility and used by God.
entries.2 kings 22:2: Josiah did what pleased the Lord and followed the example of King David, not swerving off the right path. This encourages the reader to stay faithful and consistent in doing right, even from a young age.
entries.2 kings 22:3: In the eighteenth year of his reign, Josiah sent his secretary Shaphan to the temple. This shows a king taking practical steps to care for God's house.
entries.2 kings 22:4: Josiah told Shaphan to have the high priest collect the money that had been gathered from the people at the temple. It shows the king organizing the repair of God's house with the resources people had given.
entries.2 kings 22:5: The money was to be handed to the supervisors so they could pay the workers repairing the temple. Good leadership means making sure resources actually reach the people doing the work.
entries.2 kings 22:6: The funds went to carpenters, builders, and stonecutters, and to buy timber and stone for the repairs. This is ordinary, practical work that keeps a place of worship in good condition.
entries.2 kings 22:7: The workers did not have to account for the money because they were trusted to handle it honestly. This shows the value of trusting people who have proven to be faithful.
entries.2 kings 22:8: The high priest Hilkiah found the Book of the Law in the temple and gave it to Shaphan. It reminds the reader that God's word can be lost or neglected and then rediscovered, changing everything.
entries.2 kings 22:9: Shaphan reported back to the king that the money had been paid out and the work was underway. Honest reporting keeps leaders informed and builds trust.
entries.2 kings 22:10: Shaphan then told the king that Hilkiah had found a book and read it aloud to him. Reading God's word aloud to those in authority can have a powerful effect.
entries.2 kings 22:11: When the king heard the words of the law, he tore his clothes in grief. This shows that God's word should move us deeply when we realize how far we have fallen short.
entries.2 kings 22:12: Josiah gave orders to the priest, his officials, and his servants to act on what had been read. A good response to God's word includes involving others and taking action.
entries.2 kings 22:13: Josiah wanted the Lord's guidance for himself and the whole nation because he feared God's anger over their disobedience. It is wise to seek God's direction when we realize we have been ignoring his word.
entries.2 kings 22:14: The king's men went to Huldah, a woman prophet, to ask the Lord's answer. God can speak through anyone he chooses, and it is right to seek his word humbly.
entries.2 kings 22:15: Huldah told them to take the Lord's message back to the man who sent them. God's word comes with authority and is meant to be delivered faithfully.
entries.2 kings 22:16: The Lord said he would bring disaster on Jerusalem and its people, just as the book warned. Ignoring God's word has real consequences, both for individuals and for a whole society.
entries.2 kings 22:17: The people had abandoned the Lord and worshiped other gods, so his anger would not be turned aside. This shows that turning away from God is serious and brings judgment.
entries.2 kings 22:18: The Lord had a separate message for King Josiah, who had sent them to seek him. God notices when a person sincerely seeks him, even in the middle of a nation's failure.
entries.2 kings 22:19: Because Josiah humbled himself and wept over the warnings, the Lord heard him. God responds with mercy to those who take his word seriously and grieve over sin.
entries.2 kings 22:20: The Lord promised Josiah would die in peace and not see the disaster coming on the city. God's mercy spared him personally, even though judgment on the nation was still certain.
entries.2 kings 21:1: Manasseh became king of Judah at just twelve years old and ruled for fifty-five years, longer than any other king. His long reign shows that God can be patient even when a leader does terrible things.
entries.2 kings 21:2: Manasseh did what God considered evil, copying the wicked practices of the nations God had driven out before Israel. A leader's choices can pull a whole people away from God.
entries.2 kings 21:3: He rebuilt the idol shrines his father Hezekiah had torn down and set up altars to false gods like Baal and the stars. He undid the good his father had done and led people back into idol worship.
entries.2 kings 21:4: He placed idols right inside the Lord's temple, the very place God had chosen for his own name. This shows how far he went in disrespecting God's house.
entries.2 kings 21:5: He built altars to the stars in the temple courtyards, turning God's own courts into places of idol worship. He filled the space meant for worshiping God with worship of false gods.
entries.2 kings 21:6: He sacrificed his own son in fire and practiced fortune-telling and consulted mediums, doing much evil that angered the Lord. This shows how deeply sin can corrupt a person's choices, even toward their own family.
entries.2 kings 21:7: He set up a carved image of the goddess Asherah inside the temple where God had promised his name would remain forever. He directly challenged God's promise by putting an idol where God said he would dwell.
entries.2 kings 21:8: God promised Israel would never again be forced out of their land if they carefully obeyed all his commands. God's blessing was tied to their obedience, not just his promise.
entries.2 kings 21:9: The people refused to listen, and Manasseh led them into worse evil than the nations God had removed before them. A bad leader can make a whole nation worse than those who never knew God.
entries.2 kings 21:10: God spoke to the people through his prophets, his chosen messengers. God does not stay silent about sin; he warns people through those he sends.
entries.2 kings 21:11: God said Manasseh had done worse evil than the Amorites before him and had led Judah into idol worship. God sees and names the sin of leaders who cause others to sin.
entries.2 kings 21:12: God announced he would bring such disaster on Jerusalem and Judah that everyone who heard about it would be stunned. Sin brings real consequences, and God's judgment would be shocking.
entries.2 kings 21:13: God would measure Jerusalem by the same standard he used on Samaria and Ahab's family, wiping it clean like a washed plate turned upside down. God judges all nations by the same standard of justice.
entries.2 kings 21:14: God said he would reject the remnant of his people and hand them over to their enemies, who would plunder them. Persistent sin can lead to losing God's protection.
entries.2 kings 21:15: God said this would happen because his people had done evil and angered him from the day they left Egypt until now. Long patterns of sin, not just one mistake, brought this judgment.
entries.2 kings 21:16: Manasseh also killed many innocent people until Jerusalem was full of blood, on top of his other sins. A leader's evil can cause terrible harm to ordinary, innocent people.
entries.2 kings 21:17: The rest of Manasseh's deeds and sins are recorded in the official history book of Judah's kings. His story was written down, showing that human records keep account of what leaders do.
entries.2 kings 21:18: Manasseh died and was buried in the garden of his palace, and his son Amon became king. Even a long, powerful reign ends in death, and the next generation takes over.
entries.2 kings 21:19: Amon became king at twenty-two and ruled only two years in Jerusalem; his mother was Meshullemeth. His short reign stands in sharp contrast to his father's long one.
entries.2 kings 21:20: Amon did evil in God's eyes, just as his father Manasseh had done. Children often follow the example of their parents, for good or for bad.
entries.2 kings 21:21: He followed all his father's ways, serving and worshiping the same false gods his father had served. He chose to copy his father's idolatry rather than learn from his mistakes.
entries.2 kings 21:22: He turned away from the Lord, the God of his ancestors, and did not walk in God's ways. Rejecting the God your family once knew is a serious choice.
entries.2 kings 21:23: Amon's own servants plotted against him and killed him in his own house. Even a king is not safe from betrayal when his rule is built on evil.
entries.2 kings 21:24: The people of the land executed everyone involved in the plot against the king and made his son Josiah king. Ordinary people stepped in to restore order and set up the next king.
entries.2 kings 21:25: The rest of Amon's deeds are recorded in the official history book of Judah's kings. His actions were written down and remembered, just like his father's.
entries.2 kings 21:26: Amon was buried in the garden of Uzza, and his son Josiah became king in his place. Despite a wicked father, Josiah would become one of Judah's best kings, showing that a person's path is not fixed by their family.
entries.2 kings 24:1: Judah's king Jehoiakim was forced to serve Babylon's king Nebuchadnezzar for three years, then rebelled against him. It shows how quickly a nation's security can collapse when it turns from God.
entries.2 kings 24:2: God used raiding bands from several neighboring nations to attack Judah and destroy it, exactly as his prophets had warned. God's warnings are not empty; ignoring them brings real consequences.
entries.2 kings 24:3: Judah's downfall came by God's own decree because of the sins of King Manasseh, removing the people from his presence. Persistent evil eventually brings judgment, even if it takes generations.
entries.2 kings 24:4: Manasseh had filled Jerusalem with the blood of innocent people, and God would not forgive this. Shedding innocent blood is serious to God and cannot be shrugged off.
entries.2 kings 24:5: The rest of Jehoiakim's deeds are recorded in the official history of Judah's kings. His story is part of a larger record, reminding us that our actions are remembered.
entries.2 kings 24:6: Jehoiakim died and was buried with his ancestors, and his son Jehoiachin became king. Leadership passes on, but the consequences of a king's choices do not disappear.
entries.2 kings 24:7: Egypt's king no longer dared to leave his land because Babylon had taken everything from Egypt's border to the Euphrates River. World powers shift, but God remains in control of history.
entries.2 kings 24:8: Jehoiachin became king at eighteen and ruled only three months; his mother's name is also recorded. A short reign shows how quickly a throne can end when God's judgment comes.
entries.2 kings 24:9: Jehoiachin did evil in God's eyes, just like his father. Children often repeat their parents' sins, and each person is accountable for following that pattern.
entries.2 kings 24:10: Nebuchadnezzar's army surrounded Jerusalem and cut it off completely. When God's judgment arrives, there is no escape route.
entries.2 kings 24:11: Nebuchadnezzar himself came to the city while his troops besieged it. The powerful king personally oversaw Jerusalem's defeat.
entries.2 kings 24:12: Jehoiachin surrendered to Babylon's king along with his mother, officials, and servants, and was taken captive in Babylon's eighth year. Surrender to an earthly king could not undo the judgment that had already come.
entries.2 kings 24:13: Nebuchadnezzar looted the temple treasury and cut up the gold vessels Solomon had made, just as God had said. God's warnings about the temple's destruction came true exactly as spoken.
entries.2 kings 24:14: Babylon carried off Jerusalem's leaders, soldiers, and skilled craftsmen—ten thousand people—leaving only the poorest behind. A nation loses its strength when its capable people are taken away.
entries.2 kings 24:15: Jehoiachin was taken to Babylon with his mother, wives, servants, and the leading men of the land. Exile separated the king from his home and his people.
entries.2 kings 24:16: Seven thousand soldiers and a thousand skilled workers were deported to Babylon. The best and strongest of Judah were removed, leaving the land weak and vulnerable.
entries.2 kings 24:17: Babylon's king made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king in his place and renamed him Zedekiah. The conqueror controlled who ruled, showing that Judah's independence was gone.
entries.2 kings 24:18: Zedekiah became king at twenty-one and ruled eleven years; his mother's name is recorded too. His long reign gave him many chances to turn back to God.
entries.2 kings 24:19: Zedekiah did evil in God's eyes, just as Jehoiakim had done. He repeated the same mistakes instead of learning from them.
entries.2 kings 24:20: God's anger finally led to Jerusalem and Judah being sent away from his presence, and Zedekiah rebelled against Babylon. When people keep refusing God, judgment becomes inevitable, and rebellion only speeds it up.
entries.2 kings 25:1: Babylon's king brought his whole army to surround Jerusalem and built ramps to attack it. It shows how a powerful enemy closed in on God's city, and reminds us that ignoring God's warnings can lead to hard consequences.
entries.2 kings 25:2: The siege lasted about a year and a half, cutting the city off from help. For the reader, it shows that a trapped situation can drag on a long time before it finally breaks.
entries.2 kings 25:3: The food ran out so badly that people had nothing left to eat. It means starvation inside a besieged city, and it shows how desperate life becomes when a crisis goes on too long.
entries.2 kings 25:4: The soldiers broke through the wall and the king escaped at night through a gate by the garden. It means the defense finally collapsed, and it shows that even a king's escape plan can fail.
entries.2 kings 25:5: The Babylonian army chased the king and caught him near Jericho, and his soldiers scattered. It means there was no real escape, and it shows that running from a problem often just delays it.
entries.2 kings 25:6: They captured the king and brought him to the Babylonian king to be judged. It means he had to answer for his rebellion, and it reminds us that leaders are held responsible for their choices.
entries.2 kings 25:7: They killed his sons in front of him, then blinded him and took him to Babylon in chains. It is a brutal picture of loss and humiliation, and it shows how costly it is to turn away from God.
entries.2 kings 25:8: About a month later, the Babylonian king's commander came to Jerusalem. It marks the start of the city's destruction, and it shows that judgment came at a set time, not by accident.
entries.2 kings 25:9: He burned the Lord's temple, the palace, and every important building in Jerusalem. It means the heart of the nation's worship and government was destroyed, and it shows that even sacred places are not safe when people abandon God.
entries.2 kings 25:10: The Babylonian army tore down the walls around Jerusalem. It means the city was left defenseless, and it shows how complete the collapse was.
entries.2 kings 25:11: The commander took most of the remaining people and the skilled workers away as prisoners. It means the city was emptied of its people, and it shows the deep loss of being taken from home.
entries.2 kings 25:12: He left only the poorest people to work the vineyards and fields. It means the land was not completely empty, and it shows that even in judgment God left a small group to keep life going.
entries.2 kings 25:13: The Babylonians broke up the bronze pillars, stands, and large water basin from the temple and carried the bronze to Babylon. It means the temple's beautiful furnishings were looted, and it shows that wealth and beauty do not protect us from loss.
entries.2 kings 25:14: They took all the bronze tools and utensils used in the temple service. It means the equipment for worship was carried off, and it shows how thoroughly the nation's religious life was stripped away.
entries.2 kings 25:15: The commander took the gold and silver bowls and fire pans as well. It means even the precious items were seized, and it shows that nothing valuable was left behind.
entries.2 kings 25:16: The bronze from the two pillars, the water basin, and the stands was too much to weigh. It means the temple had been richly built, and it shows how much was lost in a single day.
entries.2 kings 25:17: Each pillar was about twenty-seven feet tall with a decorative bronze top about four and a half feet high. It means these were impressive structures, and it helps the reader picture the scale of what was destroyed.
entries.2 kings 25:18: The commander arrested the chief priest, the second priest, and the three temple gatekeepers. It means the religious leaders were taken captive, and it shows that no one was exempt from the consequences.
entries.2 kings 25:19: He also took a court official, five of the king's advisers, the army's record keeper, and sixty other leading men. It means the city's leadership was removed, and it shows that a community loses much when its leaders are taken away.
entries.2 kings 25:20: The commander brought all these prisoners to the Babylonian king at Riblah. It means they were handed over for judgment, and it shows that the captives had no say in what happened next.
entries.2 kings 25:21: The Babylonian king had them executed at Riblah in Hamath, and so Judah was taken from its land into exile. It means the nation's leaders were killed and the people were deported, and it marks the sad end of the kingdom of Judah.
entries.2 kings 25:22: Nebuchadnezzar appointed Gedaliah to govern the people who were left in Judah. It means a new local leader was put in charge, and it shows that life went on for those who remained.
entries.2 kings 25:23: The remaining army officers and their men came to Gedaliah at Mizpah to support him. It means the scattered fighters gathered around the new governor, and it shows a moment of possible stability.
entries.2 kings 25:24: Gedaliah swore an oath and told them not to fear the Babylonians, but to settle down and serve the king of Babylon, and things would go well. It means he urged peace and cooperation, and it shows that accepting reality can be the wisest path.
entries.2 kings 25:25: In the seventh month, Ishmael, a member of the royal family, came with ten men and murdered Gedaliah and the Babylonians and Jews with him at Mizpah. It means the peace was shattered by a violent plot, and it shows how one person's ambition can ruin many lives.
entries.2 kings 25:26: Then everyone, from small to great, fled to Egypt out of fear of the Babylonians. It means the people panicked and left the land, and it shows how fear can drive people away from where God had placed them.
entries.2 kings 25:27: In the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's imprisonment, the new Babylonian king Evil-merodach released him from prison. It means a long captivity finally ended, and it shows that even after decades, God can bring a turn for the better.
entries.2 kings 25:28: The king spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and gave him a seat higher than the other kings with him in Babylon. It means he was shown honor, and it shows that God had not forgotten the line of David.
entries.2 kings 25:29: Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes and ate at the king's table every day for the rest of his life. It means he was treated as a guest rather than a prisoner, and it shows a picture of restored dignity.
entries.2 kings 25:30: The king gave him a regular allowance of food every day for the rest of his life. It means his needs were provided for, and it shows that even in exile, God's care continued.
entries.1 chronicles 3:1: This lists the first sons born to David while he ruled from Hebron, naming each son and his mother. It reminds the reader that David's family history was recorded in detail, with real people and real mothers behind each name.
entries.1 chronicles 3:2: This continues the list of David's sons born in Hebron, including Absalom and Adonijah, who would later cause trouble in his family. It shows that even famous leaders had complicated families with many children by different women.
entries.1 chronicles 3:3: This names the fifth and sixth sons born to David in Hebron, along with their mothers. It completes the count of the six sons he had during that period of his rule.
entries.1 chronicles 3:4: This sums up David's time as king: seven and a half years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. It gives the reader a simple timeline of his reign and where his sons were born.
entries.1 chronicles 3:5: This lists four more sons born to David in Jerusalem, all by the same mother, Bath-shua. It shows that his family continued to grow after he moved his capital to Jerusalem.
entries.1 chronicles 3:6: This begins another group of David's sons born in Jerusalem, naming three of them. These names are part of the official record of his household.
entries.1 chronicles 3:7: This adds three more names to the list of David's sons born in Jerusalem. The record keeps track of each child as part of the family line.
entries.1 chronicles 3:8: This finishes the Jerusalem list with three more names and notes the total as nine sons. It shows the writer was careful to count and preserve the family record accurately.
entries.1 chronicles 3:9: This concludes the list of David's sons, noting he also had sons by servant-wives, and mentions his daughter Tamar. It reminds the reader that David's family included daughters too, and that not every detail of his household is recorded.
entries.1 chronicles 3:10: This starts a straight line of kings from Solomon down through Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, and Jehoshaphat. It shows the reader that God kept the royal family line going generation after generation.
entries.1 chronicles 3:11: This continues the royal line with Joram, Ahaziah, and Joash. Each name represents a generation of kings descended from David.
entries.1 chronicles 3:12: This adds Amaziah, Azariah, and Jotham to the family line of kings. It shows the line kept going without a break through many generations.
entries.1 chronicles 3:13: This continues the list with Ahaz, Hezekiah, and Manasseh. It reminds the reader that the royal family included both good and bad kings, yet the line continued.
entries.1 chronicles 3:14: This names Amon and then Josiah as the next kings in the line. It brings the family record closer to the time of the nation's later history.
entries.1 chronicles 3:15: This lists the sons of Josiah in order, from the oldest to the fourth. It shows how the royal family branched out in the next generation.
entries.1 chronicles 3:16: This names the sons of Jehoiakim, including Jeconiah, who would be taken captive. It hints that the family line would continue even through hard times.
entries.1 chronicles 3:17: This notes that Jeconiah was taken prisoner and names his son Shealtiel. It shows the reader that God's family line survived even after defeat and exile.
entries.1 chronicles 3:18: This lists six more sons of Jeconiah born during or after his captivity. It shows the family kept growing even in difficult circumstances.
entries.1 chronicles 3:19: This names the sons of Pedaiah, including Zerubbabel, and lists Zerubbabel's children and their sister. It connects the family line to Zerubbabel, a key figure in the return from exile.
entries.1 chronicles 3:20: This adds five more children to Zerubbabel's family. It shows the family line continuing to expand in the generation after the exile.
entries.1 chronicles 3:21: This traces the descendants of Hananiah through several generations. It shows the family record being kept carefully long after the return from exile.
entries.1 chronicles 3:22: This lists the sons of Shecaniah and then six sons of Shemaiah. It continues the detailed family record into later generations.
entries.1 chronicles 3:23: This names the three sons of Neariah. It keeps the family line moving forward one generation at a time.
entries.1 chronicles 3:24: This ends the list with the seven sons of Elioenai. It shows the family line of David still existed and was still being recorded many years later.
entries.1 chronicles 1:1: This starts a family list with Adam and the first generations after him. It reminds the reader that the story of God's people begins with real people from the very beginning.
entries.1 chronicles 1:2: The list continues with more early ancestors in Adam's family line. It shows the reader that these names were passed down as part of a real family history.
entries.1 chronicles 1:3: More names follow in the same family line, including Enoch and Methuselah. It tells the reader that God's story moves forward through ordinary generations of people.
entries.1 chronicles 1:4: Noah's three sons are named here, the families from whom the nations came. It shows the reader that all peoples trace back to one family.
entries.1 chronicles 1:5: This lists the sons of Japheth, one of Noah's sons. It shows the reader how the nations spread out from Noah's family.
entries.1 chronicles 1:6: These are the grandsons of Japheth through his son Gomer. It keeps showing how different peoples came from one family tree.
entries.1 chronicles 1:7: This names the sons of Javan, another line from Japheth. It reminds the reader that many nations have a shared origin.
entries.1 chronicles 1:8: This lists the sons of Ham, another of Noah's sons. It shows the reader that the nations of the world came from Noah's three sons.
entries.1 chronicles 1:9: These are Ham's grandchildren through Cush and Raamah. It continues tracing how different peoples and regions came to be.
entries.1 chronicles 1:10: Nimrod is singled out as the first great man on earth. It shows the reader that even famous, powerful people fit into God's larger story.
entries.1 chronicles 1:11: This lists peoples that came from Egypt, one of Ham's sons. It shows the reader that whole nations grew from these early families.
entries.1 chronicles 1:12: The list continues with more peoples from Egypt, including the Philistines. It reminds the reader that Israel's neighbors also had a place in this family history.
entries.1 chronicles 1:13: This names Canaan's sons, starting with his oldest, Zidon. It shows the reader where the peoples of Canaan came from.
entries.1 chronicles 1:14: These are more peoples descended from Canaan. It shows the reader that the land Israel would later enter was already filled with related nations.
entries.1 chronicles 1:15: The list of Canaanite peoples continues. It reminds the reader that these groups were all part of one extended family.
entries.1 chronicles 1:16: This finishes the list of Canaan's descendants. It shows the reader that the whole region's peoples trace back to Noah's family.
entries.1 chronicles 1:17: This lists the sons of Shem, the line that leads to Abraham. It shows the reader where God's chosen people came from.
entries.1 chronicles 1:18: The line continues from Arpachshad down to Eber. It shows the reader that the family line was carefully remembered through the generations.
entries.1 chronicles 1:19: Eber's son Peleg was named for a division of the earth in his time. It shows the reader that big events in history were remembered through family names.
entries.1 chronicles 1:20: This lists the sons of Joktan, another line from Eber. It shows the reader how the family spread into many branches.
entries.1 chronicles 1:21: More sons of Joktan are named here. It keeps showing the reader how one family grew into many peoples.
entries.1 chronicles 1:22: The list of Joktan's sons continues. It reminds the reader that these names stood for real families and tribes.
entries.1 chronicles 1:23: This ends the list of Joktan's sons. It shows the reader that this whole branch of the family is accounted for.
entries.1 chronicles 1:24: The focus now narrows to the line from Shem down to Abraham. It shows the reader that God's plan moves through a specific family line.
entries.1 chronicles 1:25: The family line continues through Eber, Peleg, and Reu. It reminds the reader that each generation mattered in God's story.
entries.1 chronicles 1:26: More ancestors are named on the way to Abraham. It shows the reader that Abraham came from a long line of real people.
entries.1 chronicles 1:27: The line reaches Abram, who is also called Abraham. It shows the reader that this is the man God would later make great promises to.
entries.1 chronicles 1:28: Abraham's two sons, Isaac and Ishmael, are named. It shows the reader that both branches of Abraham's family are remembered.
entries.1 chronicles 1:29: This lists Ishmael's sons, starting with his oldest. It shows the reader that Ishmael's family also became many peoples.
entries.1 chronicles 1:30: More of Ishmael's sons are named. It reminds the reader that God's care extended to Abraham's other descendants too.
entries.1 chronicles 1:31: This finishes the list of Ishmael's sons. It shows the reader that Ishmael's family line was fully recorded.
entries.1 chronicles 1:32: This lists the sons Abraham had with Keturah. It shows the reader that Abraham's family spread widely beyond Isaac and Ishmael.
entries.1 chronicles 1:33: These are the sons of Midian, one of Keturah's sons. It reminds the reader that many peoples came from Abraham's household.
entries.1 chronicles 1:34: The line now focuses on Isaac's twin sons, Esau and Israel. It shows the reader that the story is narrowing toward the nation of Israel.
entries.1 chronicles 1:35: This lists the sons of Esau, also called Edom. It shows the reader that Esau's family became its own people group.
entries.1 chronicles 1:36: These are Esau's grandsons through Eliphaz, including Amalek. It shows the reader how Esau's family grew into clans and peoples.
entries.1 chronicles 1:37: This names the sons of Reuel, another of Esau's sons. It continues showing how Esau's descendants spread out.
entries.1 chronicles 1:38: This lists the sons of Seir, the people already living in the region of Edom. It shows the reader that Esau's family mixed with existing local peoples.
entries.1 chronicles 1:39: These are Lotan's children, including his sister Timna. It reminds the reader that the record includes whole families, not just the men.
entries.1 chronicles 1:40: This lists more descendants of Seir's sons. It shows the reader that the peoples of Edom had a detailed, remembered family history.
entries.1 chronicles 2:1: This lists the twelve sons of Israel, the men whose families became the twelve tribes. It reminds the reader that the whole nation traces back to one family.
entries.1 chronicles 2:2: This finishes the list of Israel's twelve sons. Each name stands for a tribe, so the reader sees the full family tree of the nation.
entries.1 chronicles 2:3: Judah had three sons by a Canaanite woman, and his oldest son Er was so wicked that God ended his life. It shows that being born into the right family did not excuse doing evil.
entries.1 chronicles 2:4: Judah's daughter-in-law Tamar gave him two more sons, Perez and Zerah, making five sons in all. It shows God's family line moving forward even through messy family situations.
entries.1 chronicles 2:5: Perez had two sons, Hezron and Hamul. This keeps track of the family line that would become important in Israel's history.
entries.1 chronicles 2:6: Zerah had five sons. The writer is simply recording the branches of Judah's family so later generations know where they came from.
entries.1 chronicles 2:7: Achan, from this family line, brought trouble on Israel by taking things God had said were off-limits. It warns the reader that one person's disobedience can hurt many others.
entries.1 chronicles 2:8: Ethan had a son named Azariah. This is another short link in the family record.
entries.1 chronicles 2:9: Hezron had three sons: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai. The line through Ram will lead to King David.
entries.1 chronicles 2:10: Ram's family line went through Amminadab to Nahshon, a leader of Judah's tribe. It shows God was building a line of leaders over many generations.
entries.1 chronicles 2:11: The family line continued from Nahshon to Salma to Boaz. Boaz is the same man readers meet in the story of Ruth.
entries.1 chronicles 2:12: Boaz was the father of Obed, and Obed was the father of Jesse. The line is getting closer to David.
entries.1 chronicles 2:13: Jesse had several sons, starting with Eliab as the oldest. These brothers are the family David grew up in.
entries.1 chronicles 2:14: This continues the list of Jesse's sons, naming the fourth and fifth. It shows David was not the only son in the family.
entries.1 chronicles 2:15: Jesse's sixth son was Ozem, and the seventh was David. It highlights that David, the great king, was the youngest of many brothers.
entries.1 chronicles 2:16: David had two sisters, Zeruiah and Abigail, and Zeruiah's three sons became famous warriors. It shows David's family included tough, capable men.
entries.1 chronicles 2:17: Abigail's son was Amasa, whose father was an Ishmaelite. It shows the family was connected to people outside Israel as well.
entries.1 chronicles 2:18: Caleb had children with his wife Azubah. The writer keeps tracing the branches of this large family.
entries.1 chronicles 2:19: After Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, and she became the mother of Hur. Life went on, and the family line continued through a second wife.
entries.1 chronicles 2:20: Hur was the father of Uri, and Uri was the father of Bezalel. Bezalel is the craftsman who later helped build the tabernacle.
entries.1 chronicles 2:21: Hezron married a daughter of Machir when he was sixty and had a son named Segub. It shows God giving children even later in life.
entries.1 chronicles 2:22: Segub's son Jair controlled twenty-three towns in Gilead. It shows this family gained real land and influence.
entries.1 chronicles 2:23: Other groups captured sixty of those towns from Jair's family. It reminds the reader that land and power can be lost, not just gained.
entries.1 chronicles 2:24: After Hezron died, his wife had a son named Asshur, who founded Tekoa. The family kept growing even after the father was gone.
entries.1 chronicles 2:25: Jerahmeel, Hezron's oldest son, had five sons, with Ram the oldest. This begins a new branch of the family record.
entries.1 chronicles 2:26: Jerahmeel had a second wife named Atarah, who had a son named Onam. It shows the family had more than one household.
entries.1 chronicles 2:27: Ram, Jerahmeel's oldest son, had three sons. The record keeps naming each generation.
entries.1 chronicles 2:28: Onam had two sons, and Shammai had two sons. This is another step in tracking the family line.
entries.1 chronicles 2:29: Abishur's wife Abihail had two sons by him. The writer includes the wives' names too, showing they mattered in the family story.
entries.1 chronicles 2:30: Nadab had two sons, but Seled died without having children. It shows some family lines came to an end.
entries.1 chronicles 2:31: The line went from Appaim to Ishi to Sheshan to Ahlai. This keeps the record moving forward one generation at a time.
entries.1 chronicles 2:32: Jada had two sons, and Jether died without children. Again, not every branch of the family continued.
entries.1 chronicles 2:33: Jonathan had two sons, and this closes out the list of Jerahmeel's descendants. It marks the end of one section of the family record.
entries.1 chronicles 2:34: Sheshan had only daughters and an Egyptian servant named Jarha. It sets up an unusual turn in the family story.
entries.1 chronicles 2:35: Sheshan gave his daughter in marriage to his servant Jarha, and they had a son named Attai. It shows God's family line continuing through a servant and a daughter, not just through sons.
entries.1 chronicles 2:36: The line went from Attai to Nathan to Zabad. The family kept going through the generations.
entries.1 chronicles 2:37: Zabad's son was Ephlal, and Ephlal's son was Obed. This is another link in the chain.
entries.1 chronicles 2:38: Obed's son was Jehu, and Jehu's son was Azariah. The record continues steadily.
entries.1 chronicles 2:39: Azariah's son was Helez, and Helez's son was Eleasah. Each name shows the family surviving and growing.
entries.1 chronicles 2:40: Eleasah's son was Sismai, and Sismai's son was Shallum. The list keeps tracing the line faithfully.
entries.2 kings 23:1: The king called together all the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem to meet with him. It shows that big changes were about to be announced to the whole nation, not just a few people.
entries.2 kings 23:2: The king went to the temple and read the lost book of God's law out loud to everyone, from important leaders to ordinary people. Everyone, no matter how small, needed to hear what God had said.
entries.2 kings 23:3: The king stood and made a solemn promise to follow the Lord and obey his commands with his whole heart, and the people agreed to do the same. It was a public commitment to take God's word seriously.
entries.2 kings 23:4: The king ordered the priests to remove all the objects used for worshiping false gods from the temple, and he had them burned outside the city. He was cleaning out God's house of everything that dishonored him.
entries.2 kings 23:5: He removed the priests who had been appointed to burn offerings to false gods like Baal, the sun, the moon, and the stars. He stopped the practice of worshiping created things instead of the Creator.
entries.2 kings 23:6: He took the Asherah idol out of the temple, burned it, crushed it to dust, and scattered the dust over graves. He was treating the idol as something worthless and unclean.
entries.2 kings 23:7: He tore down the rooms in the temple where people had been used for sexual worship and where women made robes for the idol. He was removing the shameful practices that had taken over God's house.
entries.2 kings 23:8: He brought the priests from the towns of Judah to Jerusalem and made the places where they had worshiped false gods unfit for use, from one end of the land to the other. He was shutting down the wrong places of worship everywhere.
entries.2 kings 23:9: These priests were not allowed to serve at the Lord's altar in Jerusalem, but they were still given food to eat with the other priests. They were treated fairly even though they could not serve.
entries.2 kings 23:10: He made the place called Topheth unfit for use so that no one could burn their children as offerings to the false god Molech. He was stopping a terrible practice that harmed children.
entries.2 kings 23:11: He removed the horses and chariots that the kings had dedicated to the sun god and burned the chariots. He was getting rid of everything connected to sun worship.
entries.2 kings 23:12: He tore down the altars that earlier kings had built on the roof and in the temple courtyards, crushed them, and threw the dust into the stream. He was undoing the wrong things previous kings had done.
entries.2 kings 23:13: He made unfit the places of worship that Solomon had built for the false gods of other nations. Even a wise king's mistakes had to be corrected.
entries.2 kings 23:14: He broke the stone and wooden pillars used in false worship and filled the places with human bones, which made them ceremonially unclean. He was making sure those places could never be used for worship again.
entries.2 kings 23:15: He destroyed the altar and high place at Bethel that Jeroboam had built, which had led Israel into sin, burning and crushing it to dust. He was removing a long-standing source of idolatry.
entries.2 kings 23:16: Josiah took bones from the nearby graves and burned them on the altar to make it unclean, just as a prophet had predicted long before. This showed that God's words spoken years earlier came true.
entries.2 kings 23:17: Josiah asked whose tombstone he was seeing, and the people told him it belonged to the prophet who had predicted what he was doing. He wanted to know the story behind the grave.
entries.2 kings 23:18: He ordered that the prophet's bones not be disturbed, so they stayed with the bones of another prophet from Samaria. He showed respect for the man who had spoken God's truth.
entries.2 kings 23:19: Josiah also destroyed the high places in the towns of Samaria that the kings of Israel had built, doing the same as he had done at Bethel. He extended the cleanup of false worship beyond Judah.
entries.2 kings 23:20: He put to death all the priests of those high places on their own altars and burned bones on them, then returned to Jerusalem. He dealt harshly with those who had led people into false worship.
entries.2 kings 23:21: The king commanded all the people to celebrate the Passover to the Lord as the book of the law said. He wanted them to obey what God had commanded in the rediscovered book.
entries.2 kings 23:22: No Passover like this one had been kept since the days of the judges or the kings before him. It was an unusually faithful and wholehearted observance.
entries.2 kings 23:23: This Passover was celebrated to the Lord in Jerusalem in the eighteenth year of King Josiah's reign. It marked a high point of his reforms.
entries.2 kings 23:24: Josiah removed all the mediums, fortune-tellers, idols, and detestable things from Judah and Jerusalem so that the words of the law would be carried out. He was making the nation's life match what God's book said.
entries.2 kings 23:25: No king before or after Josiah turned to the Lord with such wholehearted devotion, obeying the law of Moses. He stands out as an example of complete commitment to God.
entries.2 kings 23:26: Even so, the Lord's fierce anger against Judah was not turned away because of all the evil Manasseh had done. The consequences of earlier sin were still coming.
entries.2 kings 23:27: The Lord said he would remove Judah from his presence as he had done with Israel, and he would reject Jerusalem and the temple where his name was. The nation's judgment was already determined.
entries.2 kings 23:28: The rest of Josiah's deeds are recorded in the history book of the kings of Judah. This note points readers to the official records for more details.
entries.2 kings 23:29: In Josiah's days, the king of Egypt marched against Assyria, and Josiah went out to oppose him and was killed at Megiddo. Even a good king's life ended in a tragic battle.
entries.2 kings 23:30: His servants carried his body back to Jerusalem and buried him there, and the people made his son Jehoahaz king in his place. The nation mourned and moved on to a new king.
entries.2 kings 23:31: Jehoahaz was twenty-three when he became king and ruled only three months in Jerusalem; his mother was Hamutal. His reign was very short.
entries.2 kings 23:32: He did evil in the Lord's eyes, following the example of his ancestors. He did not continue his father's good ways.
entries.2 kings 23:33: The king of Egypt put him in chains at Riblah so he could not rule in Jerusalem, and he imposed a heavy tax of silver and gold on the land. Foreign power took control and punished the nation.
entries.2 kings 23:34: Pharaoh made Eliakim king instead of Josiah, changed his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz away to Egypt where he died. The Egyptian king was deciding who ruled Judah.
entries.2 kings 23:35: Jehoiakim taxed the people to pay the silver and gold Pharaoh demanded, with each person paying what was required. The burden fell on ordinary people to satisfy a foreign ruler.
entries.2 kings 23:36: Jehoiakim was twenty-five when he became king and ruled eleven years in Jerusalem; his mother was Zebidah. He had a longer reign than his brother.
entries.2 kings 23:37: He did evil in the Lord's eyes, just as his ancestors had done. Like the kings before him, he turned away from God.
entries.1 chronicles 4:1: This starts a family list for the tribe of Judah, naming Judah's descendants. It reminds the reader that God's story is built through real families and ordinary people.
entries.1 chronicles 4:2: This continues the family line from Shobal down to Jahath and his sons, marking a clan called the Zorathites. It shows how one family grew into a whole community.
entries.1 chronicles 4:3: These are the children of Hur, including a sister named Hazzelelponi. Listing a sister too shows that women were part of the family record, not forgotten.
entries.1 chronicles 4:4: This traces more descendants of Hur, who is linked to the founding of Bethlehem. It quietly connects these old names to a town that later matters greatly in the Bible.
entries.1 chronicles 4:5: Ashhur, connected with the town of Tekoa, had two wives named Helah and Naarah. It simply records a family situation as it was.
entries.1 chronicles 4:6: Naarah had four sons, and they are named here. Each name preserved is a reminder that these were real people, not just numbers.
entries.1 chronicles 4:7: Helah's three sons are listed. The record keeps track of both sides of the family.
entries.1 chronicles 4:8: Koz's sons and another family group are named. These short entries show how the tribe spread into many branches.
entries.1 chronicles 4:9: Jabez was more respected than his brothers, and his mother named him Jabez because she gave birth to him in pain. His name carried the memory of her suffering.
entries.1 chronicles 4:10: Jabez asked God to bless him, enlarge his territory, stay with him, and keep him from harm, and God granted it. It shows that God listens when someone honestly asks him for help and protection.
entries.1 chronicles 4:11: This lists Chelub's family line through Mehir to Eshton. It is another small link in the larger family record.
entries.1 chronicles 4:12: Eshton's sons and a group called the men of Recah are named. The list keeps showing how the clan spread out.
entries.1 chronicles 4:13: Kenaz's sons included Othniel, a well-known leader, and Seraiah. It ties an important figure back to his family roots.
entries.1 chronicles 4:14: Seraiah's line leads to Joab, whose descendants were skilled craftsmen. It honors ordinary workers whose skills helped their community.
entries.1 chronicles 4:15: Caleb's sons and his grandson Kenaz are listed. This keeps the record of a significant family within Judah.
entries.1 chronicles 4:16: Jehallelel's four sons are named. Each entry preserves the memory of a family branch.
entries.1 chronicles 4:17: This lists Ezrah's sons and the children of Bithiah, an Egyptian princess married to Mered. It shows that people from outside Israel were welcomed into the family line.
entries.1 chronicles 4:18: Mered's wife from Judah had three sons who founded towns. The record shows a family's lasting mark on the land.
entries.1 chronicles 4:19: The sons of Hodiah's wife are linked to two towns. It is a brief note connecting families to places.
entries.1 chronicles 4:20: Shimon's and Ishi's sons are named. The list keeps a record of even small family groups.
entries.1 chronicles 4:21: Shelah's sons are listed, including families known for making fine linen. It shows that people's trades were part of their identity.
entries.1 chronicles 4:22: This mentions men who ruled in Moab and later returned to Bethlehem, from very old records. It hints at a history of movement and return that has been carefully preserved.
entries.1 chronicles 4:23: These were potters and gardeners who lived in walled settlements and worked for the king. It reminds us that everyday laborers were part of God's people too.
entries.1 chronicles 4:24: This begins the family list of Simeon, another son of Jacob. It shifts the record to a different tribe.
entries.1 chronicles 4:25: The line continues from Shaul down through Shallum, Mibsam, and Mishma. It traces the family through several generations.
entries.1 chronicles 4:26: Mishma's descendants down to Shimei are named. The record keeps following the family line.
entries.1 chronicles 4:27: Shimei had many children, but his relatives had few, so Simeon's tribe stayed smaller than Judah's. It honestly notes that not every family grows the same.
entries.1 chronicles 4:28: This lists towns where Simeon's people lived, starting with Beersheba. It shows where this tribe actually settled.
entries.1 chronicles 4:29: More of their towns are named here. The list maps out the places they called home.
entries.1 chronicles 4:30: The towns continue, including Hormah and Ziklag. These places later appear elsewhere in Israel's story.
entries.1 chronicles 4:31: The list of towns ends with a note that these were theirs until David became king. It marks a change in how the land was held.
entries.1 chronicles 4:32: Five smaller towns of Simeon are named. It shows the tribe lived in many small settlements, not one big city.
entries.1 chronicles 4:33: This describes the villages around the towns, reaching to Baalath-beer, and notes that family records were kept. It shows the people cared about remembering where they came from.
entries.1 chronicles 4:34: Several family leaders are named here. These were the heads of important households.
entries.1 chronicles 4:35: The list continues with more names and family lines. It builds a record of leadership within the tribe.
entries.1 chronicles 4:36: More leaders are named in this group. Each name represents a family that mattered to the community.
entries.1 chronicles 4:37: Ziza's family line is traced back several generations. It shows careful record-keeping of ancestry.
entries.1 chronicles 4:38: These named men were family chiefs, and their families grew very large. It shows how God had blessed them with numbers.
entries.1 chronicles 4:39: They went toward Gedor to find pasture for their flocks. It shows them acting practically to care for their animals and families.
entries.1 chronicles 4:40: They found rich, peaceful grassland where descendants of Ham had lived before. It describes a good land that had been occupied by others, setting up what comes next.
entries.1 chronicles 5:1: Reuben was Israel's firstborn, but he lost his special firstborn rights because he slept with his father's wife. This shows that being first in line means nothing if you do wrong.
entries.1 chronicles 5:2: Judah became the strongest tribe and produced Israel's rulers, but the firstborn rights still went to Joseph's family. God's plans don't always follow the usual order.
entries.1 chronicles 5:3: This lists the four sons of Reuben, Israel's oldest son. It's a family record showing who came from Reuben.
entries.1 chronicles 5:4: This continues the family line from Joel down through several generations. It's a record of who descended from whom.
entries.1 chronicles 5:5: The family line keeps going through Micah, Reaiah, and Baal. These names trace the family's history.
entries.1 chronicles 5:6: Beerah was the leader of Reuben's tribe when the Assyrian king took him away as a captive. It's a sad reminder that even leaders can be carried off.
entries.1 chronicles 5:7: This lists Reuben's relatives by their family groups, naming Jeiel and Zechariah as leaders. It's a record of the clan's leading men.
entries.1 chronicles 5:8: Bela's family line is traced back through several ancestors, and he lived in the area from Aroer to Nebo and Baal-meon. This shows where this family settled.
entries.1 chronicles 5:9: Their land stretched east to the edge of the desert near the Euphrates River because their herds had grown so large. God had blessed them with growth, so they needed more room.
entries.1 chronicles 5:10: During Saul's reign they defeated the Hagarites and took over the land east of Gilead. This shows God giving them victory in battle.
entries.1 chronicles 5:11: The tribe of Gad lived across from Reuben's people, in the land of Bashan up to Salecah. It's a note about where the Gadites settled.
entries.1 chronicles 5:12: This names the leaders of Gad: Joel first, Shapham second, then Janai and Shaphat. It records who led this tribe in Bashan.
entries.1 chronicles 5:13: This lists seven relatives from Gad's family groups. It's a record of the men who made up their clan.
entries.1 chronicles 5:14: These men are traced back through a long family line to Abihail and beyond. It shows their family heritage.
entries.1 chronicles 5:15: Ahi was the head of these families, and his line is traced through Abdiel and Guni. It identifies who led this group.
entries.1 chronicles 5:16: They lived in Gilead, in Bashan's towns, and across the pasturelands as far as Sirion. This describes the land where they made their home.
entries.1 chronicles 5:17: All these family records were made during the reigns of Jotham of Judah and Jeroboam of Israel. It tells us when this census was taken.
entries.1 chronicles 5:18: The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh had over forty-four thousand fighting men skilled with shields, swords, and bows. They were a strong and well-trained army.
entries.1 chronicles 5:19: They went to war against the Hagarites and three other groups, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab. This shows they faced several enemies at once.
entries.1 chronicles 5:20: God helped them win because they prayed to him and trusted him during the battle. It reminds us that trusting God in hard times brings his help.
entries.1 chronicles 5:21: They captured huge numbers of camels, sheep, donkeys, and people from their enemies. The victory was complete and the spoils were great.
entries.1 chronicles 5:22: Many enemies died because God had decided the battle's outcome, and the tribes then lived in that land until they were later taken captive. God's purpose was fulfilled, but their story didn't end there.
entries.1 chronicles 5:23: The half-tribe of Manasseh grew in number and spread across the land from Bashan to Mount Hermon. God blessed them with growth and territory.
entries.1 chronicles 5:24: This names seven family leaders who were brave warriors and respected men. It honors the leaders of this tribe.
entries.1 chronicles 5:25: But they turned away from God and worshiped the gods of the peoples God had driven out. This shows how easy it is to forget God and follow what's around us.
entries.1 chronicles 5:26: So God stirred up the Assyrian kings to take these tribes captive to distant lands, where they remained. Turning from God led to losing their homeland.
entries.1 chronicles 1:41: This is a family list naming the descendants of Anah through his son Dishon. It reminds the reader that ordinary families and their names mattered to God and were carefully remembered.
entries.1 chronicles 1:42: Another short list of descendants from Ezer and Dishan. These names show that the writer is tracing real family lines, and it encourages us to value the people in our own family history.
entries.1 chronicles 1:43: This begins a list of kings who ruled in Edom before Israel had a king. It shows that God was at work in other nations too, and that history moves forward under his timing.
entries.1 chronicles 1:44: When King Bela died, Jobab took his place as king. It is a simple reminder that leaders come and go, and life continues after them.
entries.1 chronicles 1:45: After Jobab died, Husham from the land of Teman became king. The list keeps showing that each ruler had a turn and then was replaced.
entries.1 chronicles 1:46: Hadad became king after Husham and won a battle against Midian in Moab. It shows that these early kings faced real conflicts and that God allowed them their victories.
entries.1 chronicles 1:47: When Hadad died, Samlah from Masrekah became the next king. The pattern continues, showing that no human king rules forever.
entries.1 chronicles 1:48: After Samlah died, Shaul from Rehoboth by the river took the throne. It is another step in the steady record of Edom's rulers.
entries.1 chronicles 1:49: Baal-hanan became king when Shaul died. The list keeps its simple focus on who ruled next, reminding us that God keeps track of ordinary history.
entries.1 chronicles 1:50: Hadad became king after Baal-hanan, and the writer also names his town and his wife's family. It shows that even personal details like marriage and hometown were worth remembering.
entries.1 chronicles 1:51: Hadad's line ended, and Edom was then led by chiefs rather than kings. This marks a change in how the nation was governed and shows that systems of leadership change over time.
entries.1 chronicles 1:52: This continues the list of Edom's chiefs, naming three more. It reminds the reader that many people shared leadership and each one is recorded.
entries.1 chronicles 1:53: Three more chiefs of Edom are named here. The careful listing shows that God values each person, even those we know nothing else about.
entries.1 chronicles 1:54: The list closes with the last chiefs and says these were the chiefs of Edom. It wraps up the record and reminds us that God remembers whole peoples and their leaders, not just Israel.
entries.1 chronicles 4:41: During King Hezekiah's reign, these named men attacked the Meunim living in that area, destroyed them, and settled there because the land had good pasture for their flocks. It shows God's people taking possession of land they needed, and reminds us that plans and timing matter in how things unfold.
entries.1 chronicles 4:42: Five hundred men from the tribe of Simeon, led by four sons of Ishi, traveled to the hill country of Seir. This is a simple record of a group setting out under clear leaders, showing that organized leadership helped them carry out their mission.
entries.1 chronicles 4:43: They killed the remaining Amalekites who had escaped and settled in that land, where their descendants lived from then on. It describes the end of a long conflict and the people making a permanent home in the place they had taken.
entries.1 chronicles 2:41: This verse simply lists a family line: Shallum was Jekamiah's father, and Jekamiah was Elishama's father. It reminds the reader that God keeps track of ordinary people across the generations, not just famous ones.
entries.1 chronicles 2:42: Caleb's oldest son was Mareshah, and Mareshah's family line led to Ziph and Hebron. These names also became towns in Israel, showing how a family grew into a lasting place among God's people.
entries.1 chronicles 2:43: This lists the four sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem, and Shema. It is a record of a family branch, reminding the reader that each person in God's family history mattered.
entries.1 chronicles 2:44: Shema's line went through Raham to Jorkeam, and Rekem was the father of Shammai. These brief family links show that God remembers people whose names we would otherwise never know.
entries.1 chronicles 2:45: Shammai's son was Maon, and Maon's son was Beth-zur. Again these names became towns, showing how one family's story became part of the land God gave his people.
entries.1 chronicles 2:46: Caleb's servant-wife Ephah had three sons, and one of them, Haran, became the father of Gazez. This shows that even family members with lower status were included in God's record of his people.
entries.1 chronicles 2:47: This lists the six sons of Jahdai. It is a plain family record, reminding the reader that God values each ordinary person in the long story of his people.
entries.1 chronicles 2:48: Caleb's servant-wife Maacah had two sons, Sheber and Tirhanah. The text quietly includes her and her children, showing that God's family record includes people we might overlook.
entries.1 chronicles 2:49: Shaaph's line led to Madmannah, Sheva, Machbena, and Gibea, and Caleb's daughter Achsah is named here too. Women and men alike are part of this family story, and each name points to real people God cared for.
entries.1 chronicles 2:50: This begins the family line of Hur, Ephrathah's oldest son, starting with Shobal, who was the father of Kiriath-jearim. It shows how one branch of the family became linked to a specific town.
entries.1 chronicles 2:51: Salma was the father of Beth-lehem, and Hareph was the father of Beth-gader. These names connect families to towns, showing how God's people settled and grew in the land.
entries.1 chronicles 2:52: Shobal, the father of Kiriath-jearim, had sons, including Haroeh and half of the Manahathites. This records how a family group split and spread out over time.
entries.1 chronicles 2:53: This lists the family groups that came from Kiriath-jearim, including the Zorathites and Eshtaolites. It shows that whole communities grew from these family lines, and God kept track of them all.
entries.1 chronicles 2:54: Salma's descendants included the people of Beth-lehem, the Netophathites, Atroth-beth-joab, and part of the Manahathites and Zorites. This shows how one family's descendants became several recognizable groups in Israel.
entries.1 chronicles 2:55: This names families of scribes living at Jabez who were Kenites descended from Hammath and linked to the Rechabites. It reminds the reader that people with practical jobs like copying records were also part of God's people and his story.
entries.1 chronicles 11:1: The tribes of Israel came to David and publicly declared that they were his own people, sharing the same family and nation. It means the reader should see that unity and shared identity matter when people come together to follow a leader.
entries.1 chronicles 6:1: This lists the three main family groups descended from Levi, the ancestor of Israel's priests and temple workers. It reminds the reader that God's service was passed down through real families and generations.
entries.1 chronicles 6:2: This narrows the family line to Kohath's sons, one of whom was Amram. It shows how the record traces the family branch that would lead to Moses and Aaron.
entries.1 chronicles 6:3: Amram's children were Aaron, Moses, and Miriam, and Aaron's sons are named here too. This connects Israel's great leaders and first priests to one ordinary family line.
entries.1 chronicles 6:4: The family line continues from Eleazar to his son Phinehas and then Abishua. It shows the priestly line carrying on from one generation to the next.
entries.1 chronicles 6:5: The list keeps going with Bukki and then Uzzi. Each name marks another link in the chain of priestly descent.
entries.1 chronicles 6:6: Zerahiah and Meraioth are added to the family record. The writer is carefully preserving who came from whom over many years.
entries.1 chronicles 6:7: Meraioth's son was Amariah, and his son was Ahitub. This continues the steady record of the priestly family through time.
entries.1 chronicles 6:8: Ahitub's son was Zadok, and Zadok's son was Ahimaaz. Zadok became an important priest in Israel's history, and here his place in the family is shown.
entries.1 chronicles 6:9: The line moves from Ahimaaz to Azariah and then Johanan. It keeps tracing the priests generation by generation.
entries.1 chronicles 6:10: Johanan's son Azariah is noted as the priest who served in the temple Solomon built in Jerusalem. This ties the family record to a specific, well-known place of worship.
entries.1 chronicles 6:11: The record continues with Amariah and then Ahitub. It shows the priestly line still active long after earlier generations.
entries.1 chronicles 6:12: Ahitub's son was Zadok, and Zadok's son was Shallum. Another Zadok appears here, showing the family name carried on.
entries.1 chronicles 6:13: Shallum's son was Hilkiah, and Hilkiah's son was Azariah. The list keeps connecting each priest to his father.
entries.1 chronicles 6:14: Azariah's son was Seraiah, and Seraiah's son was Jehozadak. This brings the family line close to the time of exile.
entries.1 chronicles 6:15: Jehozadak was taken away as a captive when Nebuchadnezzar conquered Judah and Jerusalem. It shows that even the priestly family shared in the nation's suffering and exile.
entries.1 chronicles 6:16: The record returns to Levi's three sons: Gershom, Kohath, and Merari. This restates the starting point before listing the other family branches.
entries.1 chronicles 6:17: Gershom's sons are named as Libni and Shimei. It begins to trace the family lines of the other Levite groups.
entries.1 chronicles 6:18: Kohath's sons are listed again: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. This repeats the branch that included the priests.
entries.1 chronicles 6:19: Merari's sons were Mahli and Mushi, and the writer notes these are the Levite family groups named after their fathers. It organizes the people by their ancestral households.
entries.1 chronicles 6:20: This begins a list of Gershom's descendants: Libni, Jahath, and Zimmah. It shows the family line continuing through several generations.
entries.1 chronicles 6:21: The Gershom line continues with Joah, Iddo, Zerah, and Jeatherai. Each name represents another generation of Levite families.
entries.1 chronicles 6:22: This starts the Kohathite line with Amminadab, Korah, and Assir. It traces a different branch of the same Levite family.
entries.1 chronicles 6:23: The line continues with Elkanah, Ebiasaph, and Assir. It shows the family growing and continuing over time.
entries.1 chronicles 6:24: Tahath, Uriel, Uzziah, and Shaul are added to the family record. These names preserve the memory of ordinary people in the service of God.
entries.1 chronicles 6:25: Elkanah's sons are named as Amasai and Ahimoth. The record keeps following the family forward.
entries.1 chronicles 6:26: The line goes through Zophai and Nahath. It is a careful record of who belonged to this family branch.
entries.1 chronicles 6:27: Eliab, Jeroham, Elkanah, and Samuel are listed here. This is the same Samuel who became a prophet and leader in Israel.
entries.1 chronicles 6:28: Samuel's sons are named as Joel the oldest and Abiah the second. It shows that even a great leader's family had its own next generation.
entries.1 chronicles 6:29: This begins the Merari family line with Mahli, Libni, Shimei, and Uzzah. It traces another group of Levites who served in worship.
entries.1 chronicles 6:30: The Merari line ends with Shimea, Haggiah, and Asaiah. These names complete this branch of the family record.
entries.1 chronicles 6:31: David appointed these men to lead the music in the Lord's house after the ark was finally settled in place. It shows that worship through song was an organized and important part of Israel's life.
