entries.1 chronicles 6:32: They led worship with songs at the tent of meeting until Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem, and they served in their assigned turns. It shows faithful service continuing through changing times and places.
entries.1 chronicles 6:33: Heman led the music, and his family line is traced back through Joel to Samuel. This connects the worship leader to the well-known prophet Samuel.
entries.1 chronicles 6:34: The family line continues through Elkanah, Jeroham, Eliel, and Toah. It shows the long heritage behind the man leading worship.
entries.1 chronicles 6:35: Zuph, Elkanah, Mahath, and Amasai are listed in the family line. Each name is a link in the chain of Heman's ancestors.
entries.1 chronicles 6:36: The line goes through Elkanah, Joel, Azariah, and Zephaniah. It keeps tracing the family back through many generations.
entries.1 chronicles 6:37: Tahath, Assir, Ebiasaph, and Korah are named here. This connects Heman's family to the well-known Korah.
entries.1 chronicles 6:38: The line goes back through Izhar, Kohath, Levi, and Israel. This shows Heman was a true descendant of Levi and part of God's chosen people.
entries.1 chronicles 6:39: Asaph, Heman's brother, stood at his right hand in the music service. It shows the worship team was made up of close family members working together.
entries.1 chronicles 6:40: Asaph's family line is traced through Michael, Baaseiah, and Malchijah. It shows that the other worship leader also had a long family heritage.
entries.1 chronicles 6:41: The family line continues with the next names in the record. It keeps showing that these worship leaders came from real, remembered families.
entries.1 chronicles 10:1: The Philistines attacked Israel, and the Israelite soldiers ran away and were wounded or killed on Mount Gilboa. It shows how a battle can turn into a crushing defeat for God's people.
entries.1 chronicles 10:2: The Philistines chased Saul and his sons and killed three of his sons in battle. It means Saul's family lost its heirs in a single day of fighting.
entries.1 chronicles 10:3: The fighting closed in on Saul, and enemy archers hit him with arrows and wounded him badly. It shows Saul trapped and hurting with no way to escape.
entries.1 chronicles 10:4: Saul asked his armor-bearer to kill him so the Philistines would not torture and mock him, but the man was too afraid, so Saul fell on his own sword. It shows Saul choosing death over capture and disgrace.
entries.1 chronicles 10:5: When the armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he killed himself the same way. It shows how deeply loyal and shaken he was by his king's death.
entries.1 chronicles 10:6: Saul and his three sons all died, and his royal family line came to an end. It shows the whole house of Saul falling together in one day.
entries.1 chronicles 10:7: When the Israelites in the nearby valley saw their army run and their king dead, they abandoned their towns and fled, and the Philistines moved in. It shows how one defeat spread fear and cost people their homes.
entries.1 chronicles 10:8: The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the dead, they found Saul and his sons lying dead on Mount Gilboa. It shows the enemy finding the king's body among the fallen.
entries.1 chronicles 10:9: The Philistines stripped Saul's armor, cut off his head, and sent messengers around their land to announce the news to their gods and their people. It shows them treating Israel's king as a trophy of their victory.
entries.1 chronicles 10:10: They placed Saul's armor in the temple of their gods and hung his head in the temple of Dagon. It shows them crediting their gods with the win and publicly shaming Saul.
entries.1 chronicles 10:11: When the people of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, they responded. It shows that some Israelites still cared about honoring their king.
entries.1 chronicles 10:12: Their fighting men traveled to retrieve the bodies of Saul and his sons, buried their bones under a tree in Jabesh, and fasted for seven days. It shows them giving the king an honorable burial and mourning his death.
entries.1 chronicles 10:13: Saul died because he sinned against the Lord by disobeying his word and by consulting a medium instead of seeking God. It shows that rejecting God's guidance has serious consequences.
entries.1 chronicles 10:14: Saul did not ask the Lord for direction, so God ended his life and gave the kingdom to David, Jesse's son. It shows that God removed Saul and raised up David as king in his place.
entries.1 chronicles 11:41: This is a list of David's mighty warriors, including Uriah the Hittite, a foreigner who served him faithfully. It reminds readers that God values loyalty and courage in ordinary people, even outsiders.
entries.1 chronicles 11:42: Adina was a leader from the tribe of Reuben who brought thirty men with him to support David. It shows that good leadership means bringing others along to serve a worthy cause.
entries.1 chronicles 11:43: Hanan and Joshaphat are named among David's fighting men. Each name matters, showing that God remembers the contributions of people we might otherwise overlook.
entries.1 chronicles 11:44: Uzzia, Shama, and Jeiel were among David's warriors, coming from different towns. Their inclusion shows that people from many places joined together to support God's chosen king.
entries.1 chronicles 11:45: Jediael and his brother Joha are listed as part of David's fighting force. It reminds us that family members can serve side by side and that faithfulness is worth recording.
entries.1 chronicles 11:46: This verse names several more warriors, including Ithmah from Moab, a nation often at odds with Israel. It shows that commitment to David, and to God's purposes, mattered more than a person's background.
entries.1 chronicles 11:47: The list ends with Eliel, Obed, and Jaasiel, closing out the roll of David's mighty men. It reminds readers that every person who serves faithfully plays a part, even if their name is only briefly mentioned.
entries.1 chronicles 7:1: This lists the four sons of Issachar, one of Israel's tribes. It reminds the reader that each family line was remembered and recorded.
entries.1 chronicles 7:2: Tola's descendants were organized by family and counted as fighting men, numbering over twenty-two thousand in David's time. It shows how large and structured these family groups had become.
entries.1 chronicles 7:3: Uzzi's line produced five sons, all described as chiefs. It shows that leadership in these families was passed down through specific people.
entries.1 chronicles 7:4: These families had many wives and children, which produced thirty-six thousand fighting men. It reflects how family size and marriage shaped a tribe's strength.
entries.1 chronicles 7:5: In total, Issachar's families counted eighty-seven thousand strong fighting men. The writer is showing the tribe's overall size and military strength.
entries.1 chronicles 7:6: This begins the record of Benjamin's three sons. It marks a shift to a new tribe in the family list.
entries.1 chronicles 7:7: Bela's five sons were family heads and fighting men, numbering over twenty-two thousand. It again ties family leadership to military strength.
entries.1 chronicles 7:8: This names the nine sons of Becher. It simply preserves the family line for later generations.
entries.1 chronicles 7:9: Becher's descendants were counted as family heads and fighting men, over twenty thousand in all. It shows the size of this branch of Benjamin.
entries.1 chronicles 7:10: This lists Jediael's grandson Bilhan and his seven sons. It continues tracing the family line in detail.
entries.1 chronicles 7:11: Jediael's descendants totaled seventeen thousand two hundred fighting men fit for war. It shows this family's contribution to the tribe's army.
entries.1 chronicles 7:12: This briefly names Shuppim, Huppim, and Dan's son Hushim. It keeps these smaller family lines in the record.
entries.1 chronicles 7:13: This lists Naphtali's four sons, noting their mother was Bilhah. It connects the tribe to its family origins.
entries.1 chronicles 7:14: This begins Manasseh's line through his servant-wife, naming Machir as Gilead's father. It shows that family lines could run through secondary wives too.
entries.1 chronicles 7:15: This notes Gilead's wife Maacah, his sister Hammoleketh, and his brother Zelophehad, who had only daughters. It fills in the family connections around Gilead.
entries.1 chronicles 7:16: Maacah bore Peresh and Sheresh, and Sheresh's sons were Ulam and Rakem. It continues the family line through Gilead's household.
entries.1 chronicles 7:17: Ulam's son was Bedan, all traced back through Gilead, Machir, and Manasseh. It shows how the writer links each person to the larger tribe.
entries.1 chronicles 7:18: Gilead's sister Hammoleketh had three sons. It shows that women in these records could also be named as mothers of family lines.
entries.1 chronicles 7:19: This names Shemida's four sons. It adds another branch to the family record.
entries.1 chronicles 7:20: This traces Ephraim's line through several generations, with repeated names like Tahath. It shows the family tree continuing over time.
entries.1 chronicles 7:21: Ezer and Elead were killed by men of Gath when they tried to take their cattle. It is a sad reminder that these families faced real danger and loss.
entries.1 chronicles 7:22: Ephraim mourned his sons for a long time, and his brothers came to comfort him. It shows grief and family support even among these ancient ancestors.
entries.1 chronicles 7:23: Ephraim later had another son and named him Beriah because trouble had come to his family. The name itself carried the memory of their sorrow.
entries.1 chronicles 7:24: Ephraim's daughter Sheerah built several towns. It shows that women could play a significant role in establishing places.
entries.1 chronicles 7:25: This continues Ephraim's line through Rephah, Resheph, Telah, and Tahan. It keeps the family tree moving forward.
entries.1 chronicles 7:26: The line continues through Ladan, Ammihud, and Elishama. Each generation is linked to the next.
entries.1 chronicles 7:27: The line ends here with Nun and his son Joshua, the famous leader. It shows that Joshua came from this same family line.
entries.1 chronicles 7:28: This describes the towns and lands where these families lived, from Bethel to Gezer and Shechem. It grounds the family record in real places.
entries.1 chronicles 7:29: Manasseh's descendants lived near towns like Beth-shean, Taanach, Megiddo, and Dor. It shows the tribes of Joseph settling across a wide area.
entries.1 chronicles 7:30: This lists Asher's sons and his daughter Serah. It begins the record of another tribe.
entries.1 chronicles 7:31: Beriah's sons were Heber and Malchiel, who was Birzaith's father. It continues Asher's family line.
entries.1 chronicles 7:32: Heber's sons are named, along with their sister Shua. It shows sisters were sometimes included in these records.
entries.1 chronicles 7:33: This names Japhlet's three sons. It adds another branch to Asher's family tree.
entries.1 chronicles 7:34: Shomer's sons are listed here. It keeps track of each family within the tribe.
entries.1 chronicles 7:35: Hotham's four sons are named. It continues the detailed family record.
entries.1 chronicles 7:36: This begins a longer list of Zophah's sons. It shows how large some of these families became.
entries.1 chronicles 7:37: The list of Zophah's sons continues with six more names. It completes that branch of the family.
entries.1 chronicles 7:38: Jether's three sons are named. It adds another line to Asher's descendants.
entries.1 chronicles 7:39: Ulla's three sons are listed. It finishes this section of the family record.
entries.1 chronicles 7:40: All these were Asher's descendants, strong fighting men and leaders, numbering twenty-six thousand in the army. It summarizes the tribe's strength and closes the record.
entries.1 chronicles 8:1: This starts a family list for the tribe of Benjamin, naming Bela as the firstborn and his brothers in order. It reminds the reader that God kept track of ordinary families through generations.
entries.1 chronicles 8:2: The list of Benjamin's sons continues with Nohah and Rapha. Each name shows that real people, not just numbers, made up this family line.
entries.1 chronicles 8:3: Here the record moves to Bela's own sons, including Gera, who was the father of Ehud. It shows how one generation leads into the next in this family.
entries.1 chronicles 8:4: More of Bela's sons are named: Abishua, Naaman, and Ahoah. The writer is carefully preserving the family's memory.
entries.1 chronicles 8:5: The last of Bela's sons listed are Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram. These names may seem unimportant, but they show that every person in the family was counted.
entries.1 chronicles 8:6: This lists the sons of Ehud, who were leaders of family groups living in Geba. It shows that some of these families settled in a particular town.
entries.1 chronicles 8:7: Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera are named, and Gera's sons Uzza and Ahihud are mentioned. The record keeps following the family branches.
entries.1 chronicles 8:8: Shaharaim had children in Moab after he sent away his wives Hushim and Beerah. This is a brief note about a complicated family situation in a foreign land.
entries.1 chronicles 8:9: With his wife Hodesh, Shaharaim had sons named Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, and Malcam. The list continues to show how his family grew.
entries.1 chronicles 8:10: Jeuz, Shachia, and Mirmah are named as Shaharaim's sons, and they became heads of family groups. This means they were leaders within their extended families.
entries.1 chronicles 8:11: Hushim, one of Shaharaim's earlier wives, had sons named Abitub and Elpaal. The record keeps track of each branch of the family.
entries.1 chronicles 8:12: Elpaal's sons included Eber, Misham, and Shemed, who built the towns of Ono and Lod and their surrounding villages. This shows that some in this family were builders and settlers.
entries.1 chronicles 8:13: Beriah and Shema were family leaders in Aijalon who drove out the people of Gath. This tells the reader that these men were known for a military victory.
entries.1 chronicles 8:14: Shashak and Jeremoth are named as brothers of the previous men. The family record continues with another branch.
entries.1 chronicles 8:15: Zebadiah, Arad, and Eder are listed next. These are more names in the growing family tree.
entries.1 chronicles 8:16: Michael, Ishpah, and Joha are identified as sons of Beriah. The writer is showing which father each man belonged to.
entries.1 chronicles 8:17: Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, and Heber are named here. The list keeps moving through the family's generations.
entries.1 chronicles 8:18: Ishmerai, Izliah, and Jobab are named as sons of Elpaal. This connects them to the earlier mention of Elpaal's line.
entries.1 chronicles 8:19: Jakim, Zichri, and Zabdi appear next in the record. Each name adds to the picture of this tribe's families.
entries.1 chronicles 8:20: Elienai, Zillethai, and Eliel are listed. The writer is carefully working through the family groups.
entries.1 chronicles 8:21: Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath are named as sons of Shimei. This shows another branch of the family.
entries.1 chronicles 8:22: Ishpan, Eber, and Eliel are listed next. The record continues without comment, just preserving the names.
entries.1 chronicles 8:23: Abdon, Zichri, and Hanan are named here. These are more members of the tribe of Benjamin.
entries.1 chronicles 8:24: Hananiah, Elam, and Anathothijah appear in the list. The writer is making sure none of these family members are forgotten.
entries.1 chronicles 8:25: Iphdeiah and Penuel are named as sons of Shashak. This ties them back to an earlier family leader.
entries.1 chronicles 8:26: Shamsherai, Shehariah, and Athaliah are listed. The family record keeps growing with each verse.
entries.1 chronicles 8:27: Jaareshiah, Elijah, and Zichri are named as sons of Jeremoth. This closes out one section of the family list.
entries.1 chronicles 8:28: These men were heads of families and chief men, and they lived in Jerusalem. This tells the reader that some of Benjamin's descendants settled in the important city of Jerusalem.
entries.1 chronicles 8:29: Jeiel, called the father of Gibeon, lived in Gibeon, and his wife was Maacah. This introduces a new family line connected to another town.
entries.1 chronicles 8:30: Jeiel's oldest son was Abdon, followed by Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, and Nadab. The list shows the order of sons in this family.
entries.1 chronicles 8:31: Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth are named next. These are more sons in Jeiel's family line.
entries.1 chronicles 8:32: Mikloth's son was Shimeah, and these families lived in Jerusalem alongside their relatives. This shows family groups settling near each other.
entries.1 chronicles 8:33: Ner was the father of Abner, and Kish was the father of Saul, Israel's first king, whose sons included Jonathan and Eshbaal. This connects the family list to well-known figures in Israel's history.
entries.1 chronicles 8:34: Jonathan's son was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal's son was Micah. This continues the royal family line after Saul and Jonathan.
entries.1 chronicles 8:35: Micah's sons were Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz. The record keeps following the descendants of Saul's family.
entries.1 chronicles 8:36: Ahaz was the father of Jehoaddah, whose sons included Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri, and Zimri was the father of Moza. This shows the family line continuing through several generations.
entries.1 chronicles 8:37: Moza was the father of Binea, and the line continued through Raphah, Eleasah, and Azel. Each generation is named in order.
entries.1 chronicles 8:38: Azel had five sons: Azrikam the oldest, then Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. This completes the record of Azel's immediate family.
entries.1 chronicles 8:39: Eshek, Azel's brother, had sons named Ulam, Jeush, and Eliphelet. This adds a side branch to the family tree.
entries.1 chronicles 8:40: Ulam's sons were warriors who used bows, and his family grew to a hundred and fifty descendants. The chapter ends by saying all these were sons of Benjamin, tying the whole list back to one ancestor.
entries.1 chronicles 9:1: This verse sums up that all Israel's families were recorded in official royal records, and it notes that Judah was carried off to Babylon as punishment for their sin. It reminds the reader that God keeps account of His people and that sin has real consequences.
entries.1 chronicles 9:2: After the exile, the first people to resettle their family lands were ordinary Israelites along with the priests, Levites, and temple servants. It shows that restoring worship and community life was the priority for those returning home.
entries.1 chronicles 9:3: Some people from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh settled in Jerusalem. It shows that people from different tribes came together to rebuild life in the holy city.
entries.1 chronicles 9:4: This lists Uthai's family line back to Perez, son of Judah. It shows that even ordinary residents of Jerusalem had a clear, remembered heritage.
entries.1 chronicles 9:5: This names Asaiah, the oldest of the Shilonite clan, and his sons. It simply records which family group lived in Jerusalem.
entries.1 chronicles 9:6: This counts 690 men from the Zerah clan living in Jerusalem. It shows the city was repopulated by specific, numbered families.
entries.1 chronicles 9:7: This begins listing the men from the tribe of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem, starting with Sallu. It shows Benjamin's families were part of rebuilding the city.
entries.1 chronicles 9:8: This continues naming Benjaminite men and their family lines. It shows the careful record-keeping of who lived where after the return.
entries.1 chronicles 9:9: These men's relatives totaled 956, all heads of families listed by their fathers' names. It shows the community was organized by family and that leaders were clearly identified.
entries.1 chronicles 9:10: This lists the priests living in Jerusalem: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, and Jachin. It shows that priestly families were settled in the city to serve at the temple.
entries.1 chronicles 9:11: This traces Azariah's line back to Zadok and Ahitub and notes he was the ruler of the house of God. It shows a qualified leader was put in charge of temple affairs.
entries.1 chronicles 9:12: This names more priests and their family lines. It shows the priestly work was shared among several established families.
entries.1 chronicles 9:13: These priests' relatives totaled 1,760 capable men who did the work of God's house. It shows a large, organized group was dedicated to temple service.
entries.1 chronicles 9:14: This begins listing the Levites living in Jerusalem, starting with Shemaiah from the Merari clan. It shows the Levites were also settled and organized for service.
entries.1 chronicles 9:15: This names more Levites, including Mattaniah from the family of Asaph. It shows the temple staff included people from well-known worship families.
entries.1 chronicles 9:16: This names Obadiah and Berechiah, whose families lived in the villages of the Netophathites. It shows even Levites in outlying towns were part of the temple workforce.
entries.1 chronicles 9:17: This lists the gatekeepers, with Shallum as their chief. It shows that guarding the entrances was an organized, important job.
entries.1 chronicles 9:18: These gatekeepers had served at the king's gate on the east side and had guarded the entrances of the Levites' tents. It shows their role had a long history of protecting holy places.
entries.1 chronicles 9:19: Shallum and his Korahite relatives were responsible for the worship order and guarding the tent's doors, as their ancestors had done. It shows faithfulness in service was passed down through generations.
entries.1 chronicles 9:20: In earlier times Phinehas son of Eleazar had been their leader, and the writer adds a blessing asking the Lord to be with him. It shows respect for godly leadership from the past.
entries.1 chronicles 9:21: Zechariah son of Meshelemiah was the gatekeeper at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. It shows a specific person was assigned to guard the place of worship.
entries.1 chronicles 9:22: There were 212 gatekeepers, listed by family, whom David and Samuel had appointed to their posts. It shows that orderly, trustworthy appointments were made for temple service.
entries.1 chronicles 9:23: These men and their sons guarded the doors of the Lord's house, the tent, as watchmen. It shows guarding God's house was a serious, ongoing family responsibility.
entries.1 chronicles 9:24: The gatekeepers stood guard on all four sides—east, west, north, and south. It shows the house of God was carefully protected from every direction.
entries.1 chronicles 9:25: Their relatives in nearby villages came in every seven days to join them on duty. It shows the gatekeeping work was shared on a rotating schedule.
entries.1 chronicles 9:26: The four chief gatekeepers, who were Levites, had the special job of overseeing the rooms and storehouses of God's house. It shows trusted leaders handled the temple's resources.
entries.1 chronicles 9:27: They slept around the house of God because they were responsible for guarding it and opening it each morning. It shows their devotion involved being present day and night.
entries.1 chronicles 9:28: Some of them were in charge of the worship utensils, keeping count of what went in and came out. It shows careful accountability was part of serving God.
entries.1 chronicles 9:29: Others were responsible for the holy items and supplies like flour, wine, oil, incense, and spices. It shows even practical supplies for worship were handled by assigned people.
entries.1 chronicles 9:30: Some of the priests' sons were responsible for mixing the spices. It shows specific tasks in worship were given to specific people.
entries.1 chronicles 9:31: Mattithiah, a Levite and oldest son of Shallum the Korahite, was in charge of baking the flat cakes. It shows humble, practical work was part of temple service.
entries.1 chronicles 9:32: Some Kohathite Levites were responsible for preparing the holy bread and setting it out before the Lord every Sabbath. It shows regular, faithful preparation was needed for worship.
entries.1 chronicles 9:33: These Levite family heads led the music and singing, living in the temple rooms and free from other work because their duty continued day and night. It shows worship through music was a full-time, devoted calling.
entries.1 chronicles 9:34: These were the chief Levite family heads, and they lived in Jerusalem. It shows the leaders of worship and service were settled in the city.
entries.1 chronicles 9:35: Jeiel, the father of Gibeon, lived in Gibeon, and his wife was named Maacah. It introduces a family line connected to Saul's ancestry.
entries.1 chronicles 9:36: This lists Jeiel's sons, beginning with Abdon his oldest, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, and Nadab. It records the family line leading toward Saul.
entries.1 chronicles 9:37: This continues the list with Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth. It simply records more members of this family line.
entries.1 chronicles 9:38: Mikloth was the father of Shimeam, and these families lived in Jerusalem alongside their relatives. It shows family groups were settled close together.
entries.1 chronicles 9:39: This traces the line from Ner to Kish to Saul, and names Saul's sons Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal. It connects the record to Israel's first king and his family.
entries.1 chronicles 9:40: Jonathan's son was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal was the father of Micah. It continues Saul's family line, showing the record was kept even after the monarchy ended.
entries.1 chronicles 13:1: David didn't act alone; he talked things over with his military leaders and other officials first. It shows that good leadership listens to others before making big decisions.
entries.1 chronicles 13:2: David shared his plan to bring everyone together to move the ark, but he checked whether the people agreed and whether it fit God's will. It reminds us to include others and seek God's direction in our plans.
entries.1 chronicles 13:3: David wanted to bring back the ark, the special chest that represented God's presence, because it had been neglected during Saul's reign. It's a call to put God back at the center of life after a time of ignoring him.
entries.1 chronicles 13:4: The people agreed with the plan because it seemed right to them. When a good plan is clearly explained, people can unite behind it.
entries.1 chronicles 13:5: David gathered people from across the whole land to join in bringing the ark back. It shows how important this moment was to the whole nation, not just to David.
entries.1 chronicles 13:6: They went to Kiriath-jearim to fetch the ark, which was known as the place where God's name is called on and where he sits between the winged figures. It was treated as something holy and set apart for God.
entries.1 chronicles 13:7: They moved the ark on a new cart with two men driving it. This detail matters because later it becomes clear this wasn't the way God had said the ark should be carried.
entries.1 chronicles 13:8: David and the whole nation celebrated with loud music and singing before God. Their joy was real, but joyful worship still needs to be done God's way.
entries.1 chronicles 13:9: When the oxen stumbled, Uzza reached out to steady the ark. His instinct was to protect it, but touching the ark was forbidden.
entries.1 chronicles 13:10: God struck Uzza dead for touching the ark, because God had said the ark must not be handled. It shows that God takes his instructions seriously, even when our intentions seem good.
entries.1 chronicles 13:11: David was upset and angry about what happened, and the place was named after it. Even a man after God's own heart could be confused and troubled by God's actions.
entries.1 chronicles 13:12: David became afraid of God and wondered how the ark could ever safely come to him. Awe and fear of God can make us cautious about how we approach him.
entries.1 chronicles 13:13: Instead of taking the ark to Jerusalem, David had it taken to the house of Obed-edom. Fear made him pause and rethink his plan.
entries.1 chronicles 13:14: The ark stayed three months at Obed-edom's house, and God blessed him and everything he had. God's presence brings blessing, and this showed David that the ark could be handled rightly.
entries.1 chronicles 9:41: This lists the sons of a man named Micah, continuing a family record. It reminds the reader that ordinary families and their names mattered to God and were remembered.
entries.1 chronicles 9:42: This traces the family line from Ahaz down through Jarah to Zimri and Moza. It shows that each generation passed the family story on, and that God keeps track of ordinary people across time.
entries.1 chronicles 9:43: The family line continues from Moza to Binea and then down to Azel. It is a simple record of generations, showing that faithfulness carries on quietly from parent to child.
entries.1 chronicles 9:44: Azel had five sons, and all their names are recorded here. The list ends with this family, reminding the reader that every person in a family line is known and valued, not just the famous ones.
entries.1 chronicles 14:1: A foreign king sent David building materials and skilled workers to help build his house. It shows that God was helping David gain respect and support from other nations.
entries.1 chronicles 14:2: David understood that God had made him king and had strengthened his kingdom. It reminds the reader that success and position come from God, not just from our own effort.
entries.1 chronicles 14:3: While living in Jerusalem, David married more women and had more children. This was common for kings then, but it also shows how his family grew during this time.
entries.1 chronicles 14:4: This begins a list of the sons David had while in Jerusalem, starting with Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. It records David's growing family as part of his story.
entries.1 chronicles 14:5: The list of David's sons continues with Ibhar, Elishua, and Elpelet. These names simply record the children born to him in Jerusalem.
entries.1 chronicles 14:6: The list adds Nogah, Nepheg, and Japhia. It is a plain record of David's sons and shows his family expanding.
entries.1 chronicles 14:7: The list ends with Elishama, Beeliada, and Eliphelet. Together these names show the full set of sons born to David in Jerusalem.
entries.1 chronicles 14:8: When the Philistines heard David was now king over all Israel, they came looking for him, and David went out to meet them. Trouble came because of his new position, and he responded by facing it.
entries.1 chronicles 14:9: The Philistines spread out across the valley of Rephaim. This sets the scene for the battle David was about to face.
entries.1 chronicles 14:10: David asked God whether he should attack and whether God would give him victory, and God said yes. It shows David asking God for guidance before acting, and God answering clearly.
entries.1 chronicles 14:11: David defeated the Philistines there, and he named the place Baal-perazim because God had broken through his enemies like rushing water breaks down a wall. It reminds the reader to give God the credit for victories.
entries.1 chronicles 14:12: The Philistines left their idols behind when they fled, and David ordered them to be burned. It shows David removing the false gods of his defeated enemies.
entries.1 chronicles 14:13: The Philistines came out again and spread across the valley. The enemy returned, so David had to face the same threat a second time.
entries.1 chronicles 14:14: David asked God again, and this time God gave him a different plan: don't go straight at them, but circle around and face them near the spice trees. It shows that God's guidance can change from one situation to the next.
entries.1 chronicles 14:15: God told David to attack when he heard the sound of footsteps in the tops of the trees, because God himself was going ahead of him to defeat the Philistines. It teaches that God leads and fights for his people, and they should follow his signal.
entries.1 chronicles 14:16: David did exactly what God said, and the Israelites defeated the Philistines all the way from Gibeon to Gezer. Obeying God's instructions led to the victory he had promised.
entries.1 chronicles 14:17: David became famous in all the lands, and God made all the nations afraid of him. It shows that God can give a person honor and respect among others.
entries.1 chronicles 15:1: David built a place for himself in the city and prepared a special tent to house the ark of God. It shows the reader that David made careful plans to honor God.
entries.1 chronicles 15:2: David said only the Levites should carry the ark, because God had chosen them for this job permanently. It reminds the reader that God's work should be done God's way.
entries.1 chronicles 15:3: David gathered all the people of Israel in Jerusalem to bring the ark to the place he had prepared. It shows the reader that this was a shared, public event for the whole community.
entries.1 chronicles 15:4: David also assembled the priests and the Levites for the task. It shows the reader that he included the right people God had set apart for this work.
entries.1 chronicles 15:5: This verse lists the first group of Levites, the family of Kohath, with their leader and 120 relatives. It shows the reader that the families were organized and counted for the job.
entries.1 chronicles 15:6: This lists the family of Merari, with their leader and 220 relatives. It shows the reader that each family group had its own place in the work.
entries.1 chronicles 15:7: This lists the family of Gershom, with their leader and 130 relatives. It shows the reader that every branch of the Levites was included.
entries.1 chronicles 15:8: This lists the family of Elizaphan, with their leader and 200 relatives. It shows the reader that the preparations involved many people working together.
entries.1 chronicles 15:9: This lists the family of Hebron, with their leader and 80 relatives. It shows the reader that even smaller groups had a part to play.
entries.1 chronicles 15:10: This lists the family of Uzziel, with their leader and 112 relatives. It shows the reader that the whole tribe was gathered for the task.
entries.1 chronicles 15:11: David called the two leading priests and the leaders of the Levite families to come to him. It shows the reader that he gave clear instructions to those in charge.
entries.1 chronicles 15:12: David told these leaders to set themselves apart for God and to bring the ark to the place he had prepared. It reminds the reader that coming near to God calls for being made clean and ready.
entries.1 chronicles 15:13: David said the earlier attempt failed and brought punishment because they did not seek God's direction properly. It warns the reader that good intentions are not enough if we ignore what God has said.
entries.1 chronicles 15:14: The priests and Levites set themselves apart for God so they could carry the ark. It shows the reader that they took God's instructions seriously this time.
entries.1 chronicles 15:15: The Levites carried the ark on its poles, just as God had commanded Moses. It shows the reader that obeying God's exact instructions brought things back in line.
entries.1 chronicles 15:16: David told the Levite leaders to appoint singers and musicians to play instruments and sing joyful songs. It shows the reader that worship and celebration were part of honoring God.
entries.1 chronicles 15:17: The Levites appointed Heman, Asaph, and Ethan to lead the music. It shows the reader that skilled, named people were given responsibility for leading worship.
entries.1 chronicles 15:18: A second group of Levites joined them, including men who served as gatekeepers. It shows the reader that many people with different roles worked together.
entries.1 chronicles 15:19: Heman, Asaph, and Ethan were assigned to play loud brass instruments. It shows the reader that the music was bold and joyful.
entries.1 chronicles 15:20: Zechariah and several others were assigned to play stringed instruments for a particular part of the music. It shows the reader that the worship was carefully organized.
entries.1 chronicles 15:21: Another group played stringed instruments to lead the singing. It shows the reader that the music had structure and leadership.
entries.1 chronicles 15:22: Chenaniah led the music and gave directions because he was skilled at it. It shows the reader that expertise was valued in serving God.
entries.1 chronicles 15:23: Berechiah and Elkanah were assigned to guard the ark. It shows the reader that protecting what was holy was treated as a serious job.
entries.1 chronicles 15:24: Seven priests played horns in front of the ark, and two men guarded it. It shows the reader that both praise and careful protection surrounded God's presence.
entries.1 chronicles 15:25: David, the leaders, and the army captains went with joy to bring the ark from Obed-edom's house. It shows the reader that this was a happy, united celebration.
entries.1 chronicles 15:26: When God helped the Levites carrying the ark, they offered seven oxen and seven sheep as a sacrifice. It shows the reader that they responded to God's help with gratitude and worship.
entries.1 chronicles 15:27: David and all the Levites carrying the ark wore fine linen, and David also wore a linen priestly garment. It shows the reader that everyone dressed specially for this holy occasion.
entries.1 chronicles 15:28: All Israel brought up the ark with shouts and loud music from horns and instruments. It shows the reader that the whole nation joined in joyful worship.
entries.1 chronicles 15:29: Michal, Saul's daughter, watched David dancing from a window and thought he looked foolish. It shows the reader that wholehearted worship can be misunderstood by others.
entries.1 chronicles 6:42: The family line continues with more names of ancestors. Each name matters because it shows this person belonged to a real family with a history of faith.
entries.1 chronicles 6:43: The list ends by tracing the line back to Levi, the ancestor of all the temple workers. It shows the reader that this family's role in worship went back a very long way.
entries.1 chronicles 6:44: This starts a matching list for the other group of temple workers, the family of Merari, naming their ancestors. It shows that every group of servants had its own place and history.
entries.1 chronicles 6:45: More names continue the family line of these temple workers. The reader sees that God's work was carried on by many ordinary families over many years.
entries.1 chronicles 6:46: The list keeps going back through the generations. It reminds the reader that faithfulness was passed down from parents to children.
entries.1 chronicles 6:47: This line also ends at Merari and then Levi, the ancestor of the temple workers. It shows these people had a clear, God-given place among his servants.
entries.1 chronicles 6:48: The rest of the temple workers were given the job of doing all the practical work around the tent where God was worshiped. It shows the reader that behind-the-scenes service for God is real and important work.
entries.1 chronicles 6:49: Only Aaron and his descendants were allowed to offer the sacrifices and do the most sacred duties, including dealing with Israel's sin. It shows the reader that God set up a specific way for people to be forgiven and to approach him.
entries.1 chronicles 6:50: This begins a list of Aaron's descendants, the priests, from one generation to the next. It shows the reader that the priestly role was handed down in a family line.
entries.1 chronicles 6:51: The priestly family line continues with more names. Each generation took its turn serving God in the same sacred role.
entries.1 chronicles 6:52: More names carry the priestly line forward. It reminds the reader that God's worship was kept going steadily, generation after generation.
entries.1 chronicles 6:53: The list ends with Zadok and Ahimaaz, well-known priests in Israel's history. It shows the reader that this family line produced faithful leaders in worship.
entries.1 chronicles 6:54: This begins a list of the towns where these priestly families were to live. The descendants of Aaron got first pick because of their special role. It shows the reader that God made sure his servants had homes and places to live.
entries.1 chronicles 6:55: The priests were given Hebron and the land around it in Judah. It shows the reader that God provided specific, real places for the people who served him.
entries.1 chronicles 6:56: The open fields around Hebron went to Caleb and his family instead. It shows the reader that God's provision was carefully arranged so different families each got what they needed.
entries.1 chronicles 6:57: The priests received Hebron, a city of refuge where someone could flee for safety, along with several other towns. It shows the reader that God cares about both worship and justice and safety for people in trouble.
entries.1 chronicles 6:58: More towns are named as belonging to the priests. It shows the reader that God's servants were spread out among the people, not crowded into one place.
entries.1 chronicles 6:59: The list of priestly towns continues. Each town gave the priests a place to live and serve among the wider community.
entries.1 chronicles 6:60: Three towns from the tribe of Benjamin are added, making thirteen towns in all for the priests. It shows the reader that God kept his promise to provide for those who served him.
entries.1 chronicles 6:61: The other families of temple workers received ten towns from several other tribes. It shows the reader that God made sure every group of his servants had a place to live.
entries.1 chronicles 6:62: The family of Gershom received thirteen towns from four different tribes. It shows the reader that God's care reached every family that served him.
entries.1 chronicles 6:63: The family of Merari received twelve towns from three tribes. It shows the reader that God provided fairly for each group of temple workers.
entries.1 chronicles 6:64: The people of Israel gave these towns and their surrounding land to the temple workers. It shows the reader that supporting those who serve God was a shared responsibility of the whole community.
entries.1 chronicles 6:65: These towns were assigned from the land of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin. It shows the reader that God's plan for his servants was worked out in real places and real land.
entries.1 chronicles 6:66: The families of Kohath received towns from the tribe of Ephraim. It shows the reader that God placed his servants among different tribes so they could serve the whole nation.
entries.1 chronicles 6:67: Shechem, another city of refuge, was given to them along with Gezer. It shows the reader that God cared about providing safety for people as well as places for worship.
entries.1 chronicles 6:68: Two more towns are named for these temple workers. It shows the reader that God's provision was detailed and specific, not vague.
entries.1 chronicles 6:69: The list of towns for the Kohath families ends with two more names. It shows the reader that God made sure his servants had enough places to live and work.
entries.1 chronicles 6:70: The rest of the Kohath families received two towns from the half-tribe of Manasseh. It shows the reader that even the smaller groups of God's servants were not forgotten.
entries.1 chronicles 6:71: The family of Gershom received two towns from the half-tribe of Manasseh. It shows the reader that God provided for each family group according to its needs.
entries.1 chronicles 6:72: Two towns from the tribe of Issachar were given to the Gershom families. It shows the reader that God's servants were spread across the land to serve the people.
entries.1 chronicles 6:73: Two more towns are added to their list. It shows the reader that God's care for his servants was steady and complete.
entries.1 chronicles 6:74: Two towns from the tribe of Asher were given to them. It shows the reader that God's provision reached into every part of the country.
entries.1 chronicles 6:75: Two more towns are named for these temple workers. It shows the reader that God's plan included homes and land for everyone who served him.
entries.1 chronicles 6:76: Three towns from the tribe of Naphtali completed their share. It shows the reader that God kept his promise to provide for the families who served at his tent.
entries.1 chronicles 6:77: The remaining Merari families received two towns from the tribe of Zebulun. It shows the reader that God made sure even the last group of temple workers had a place to live.
entries.1 chronicles 6:78: Four towns east of the Jordan River were given to them from the tribe of Reuben. It shows the reader that God's care extended to his servants on both sides of the river.
entries.1 chronicles 6:79: Two more towns are named for these families. It shows the reader that God's provision was complete and carefully recorded.
entries.1 chronicles 6:80: Two towns from the tribe of Gad are listed for them. It shows the reader that God provided for his servants all across the land, and every family had a home.
entries.1 chronicles 12:1: These were skilled fighting men who came to join David at Ziklag while Saul was still hunting him. It shows that even in hard, dangerous times, people were willing to stand with David and help him.
entries.1 chronicles 12:2: These men were experts with bows and could shoot or sling stones with either hand, and they came from Saul's own tribe of Benjamin. Their skill and their choice to back David made them especially valuable.
entries.1 chronicles 12:3: This verse simply lists the names of the leaders and men in that group. It reminds us that each person who helped David is remembered by name.
entries.1 chronicles 12:4: Ishmaiah was a notable warrior among David's elite fighters and led them, along with several other named men. Even the leaders were willing to serve alongside others.
entries.1 chronicles 12:5: This is another short list of men who joined David. The record of their names shows that ordinary individuals mattered in building his support.
entries.1 chronicles 12:6: These men came from the Korahite family line. Their inclusion shows that support for David came from many different family groups.
entries.1 chronicles 12:7: Two more men from Gedor are named here. The list keeps growing, showing steady, broad support for David.
entries.1 chronicles 12:8: Some tough, experienced soldiers from the tribe of Gad left their homes to join David in the wilderness. They were fierce and fast, the kind of loyal fighters any leader would want.
entries.1 chronicles 12:9: This begins a list of the Gadite leaders in order of rank. It shows their group was well organized under clear leadership.
entries.1 chronicles 12:10: The list of Gadite commanders continues with the fourth and fifth men. Each leader had his place in the order.
entries.1 chronicles 12:11: The sixth and seventh commanders are named here. The orderly record shows how these fighting men were structured.
entries.1 chronicles 12:12: The eighth and ninth commanders are listed. The count keeps going, showing a full and organized force.
entries.1 chronicles 12:13: The tenth and eleventh commanders complete the list. Every leader is named, showing none were forgotten.
entries.1 chronicles 12:14: These Gadite leaders were officers over large groups, from a hundred up to a thousand men. Even the least important among them carried real responsibility.
entries.1 chronicles 12:15: These men crossed the flooded Jordan River in the spring and drove off the people living in the valleys on both sides. Their courage in a dangerous crossing showed how capable they were.
entries.1 chronicles 12:16: Some men from Benjamin and Judah also came to David at his hideout. Support for David was coming from several tribes, not just one.
entries.1 chronicles 12:17: David met them and spoke honestly: if they came as friends, he would welcome them, but if they came to betray him, he trusted God to judge them. He was open but also careful, and he left justice in God's hands.
entries.1 chronicles 12:18: God's Spirit came on Amasai, who declared that they were truly on David's side and that God was with him. David accepted their pledge and made them officers in his army.
entries.1 chronicles 12:19: Some men of Manasseh came to David when he was with the Philistines, but the Philistine leaders distrusted him and sent him away, fearing he would turn back to Saul. Even when others doubted him, God was quietly protecting David.
entries.1 chronicles 12:20: When David returned to Ziklag, several Manassite commanders came over to his side. These were men of high rank, and their support strengthened him.
entries.1 chronicles 12:21: These men helped David against raiding bands because they were strong warriors and army officers. Their help came at a time when David needed it.
entries.1 chronicles 12:22: More and more people joined David every day until his army was huge, like an army sent by God. Steady, growing support showed that God was behind David's rise.
entries.1 chronicles 12:23: This begins a count of the armed men who came to Hebron to make David king, just as the Lord had promised. It shows God's plan being carried out by real people.
entries.1 chronicles 12:24: Judah sent almost seven thousand armed spearmen. The tribe closest to David gave strong military support.
entries.1 chronicles 12:25: Simeon sent over seven thousand experienced fighting men. Their numbers added real strength to David's cause.
entries.1 chronicles 12:26: The tribe of Levi sent four thousand six hundred men. Even the priestly tribe took part in supporting David as king.
entries.1 chronicles 12:27: Jehoiada, a leader from Aaron's family, came with three thousand seven hundred men. The religious leadership stood behind David too.
entries.1 chronicles 12:28: Zadok, a young but capable warrior, came with twenty-two captains from his family. Young men with ability were also part of David's support.
entries.1 chronicles 12:29: Benjamin, Saul's own tribe, sent three thousand men, though most of that tribe had stayed loyal to Saul until then. Support for David was growing even among his rival's relatives.
entries.1 chronicles 12:30: Ephraim sent over twenty thousand famous fighting men. Large, well-known families threw their weight behind David.
entries.1 chronicles 12:31: The half-tribe of Manasseh sent eighteen thousand men, each listed by name, to make David king. Their coming was deliberate and personal, not just a crowd.
entries.1 chronicles 12:32: The men of Issachar understood the times and knew what Israel should do, and two hundred of their leaders came. Wise people who understand what is happening are a great gift to any nation.
entries.1 chronicles 12:33: Zebulun sent fifty thousand loyal, well-trained soldiers ready for battle with all kinds of weapons. They came wholeheartedly, not half-heartedly.
entries.1 chronicles 12:34: Naphtali sent a thousand officers leading thirty-seven thousand spearmen. Their organized numbers showed serious commitment to David.
entries.1 chronicles 12:35: Dan sent over twenty-eight thousand men skilled in battle order. Good organization made their support effective.
entries.1 chronicles 12:36: Asher sent forty thousand trained soldiers ready for war. Their large contribution added to the growing force at Hebron.
entries.1 chronicles 12:37: The tribes east of the Jordan sent a hundred and twenty thousand armed men. Even those far away joined in making David king.
entries.1 chronicles 12:38: All these trained soldiers came to Hebron determined to make David king, and the rest of Israel agreed. The whole nation was united behind God's chosen leader.
entries.1 chronicles 12:39: They stayed with David for three days, eating and drinking what their fellow Israelites had prepared. It was a time of celebration and shared joy.
entries.1 chronicles 12:40: People from nearby tribes brought abundant food on animals—bread, figs, grapes, wine, oil, cattle, and sheep—because there was joy in Israel. When God's plan comes together, it is right to celebrate.
entries.1 chronicles 6:81: This verse lists two more towns, Heshbon and Jazer, along with the pastureland around them, that were given to the Levites. It's a reminder that God made sure the people who served in worship had places to live and land to support them.
entries.1 chronicles 18:1: David defeated the Philistines and captured their city of Gath along with its surrounding towns. This shows God giving David success against Israel's long-time enemies.
entries.1 chronicles 18:2: David defeated the Moabites and made them subject to him, paying him tribute. It shows his kingdom growing stronger under God's help.
entries.1 chronicles 18:3: David defeated Hadadezer, the king of Zobah, as he was trying to extend his power toward the Euphrates River. God gave David victory over a powerful opponent.
entries.1 chronicles 18:4: David captured a huge number of chariots, horses, and soldiers, and disabled most of the horses so they couldn't be used against him. He was making sure his enemies could not rebuild their strength.
entries.1 chronicles 18:5: When Syrian forces from Damascus came to help Hadadezer, David's army killed twenty-two thousand of them. This shows how far David's victories reached.
entries.1 chronicles 18:6: David stationed troops in Damascus and made the Syrians subject to him, and the Lord gave him victory wherever he went. The writer makes clear that David's success came from God, not just from his own skill.
entries.1 chronicles 18:7: David took the gold shields carried by Hadadezer's officers and brought them to Jerusalem. These valuable items became part of the wealth dedicated to God.
entries.1 chronicles 18:8: David took large amounts of bronze from two of Hadadezer's towns, and later his son Solomon used it to make the temple's bronze furnishings. What was taken in war was eventually used for worship.
entries.1 chronicles 18:9: When Tou, the king of Hamath, heard that David had defeated Hadadezer's whole army, he took notice. News of David's victories was spreading to neighboring kings.
entries.1 chronicles 18:10: Tou sent his son to greet David and congratulate him, since Hadadezer had been Tou's enemy, and he brought gifts of gold, silver, and bronze. Other nations were seeking peace with David because of his success.
entries.1 chronicles 18:11: David set apart these gifts to the Lord, along with the silver and gold he had taken from many other nations. He treated his victories as a way to honor God rather than just enrich himself.
entries.1 chronicles 18:12: David's army killed eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. This was another major victory that secured his borders.
entries.1 chronicles 18:13: David placed troops throughout Edom and made the Edomites subject to him, and the Lord gave him victory everywhere he went. The repeated phrase stresses that God was the source of his success.
entries.1 chronicles 18:14: David ruled over all Israel and made fair and right decisions for his people. Good leadership meant not just winning battles but treating people justly.
entries.1 chronicles 18:15: Joab commanded the army and Jehoshaphat kept the official records. David surrounded himself with capable people to run the kingdom.
entries.1 chronicles 18:16: Zadok and Ahimelech served as priests, and Shavsha was the secretary. The kingdom was organized with both religious and administrative leaders.
entries.1 chronicles 18:17: Benaiah commanded the king's special guard, and David's sons held high positions close to the king. David's government included trusted warriors and family members in key roles.
entries.1 chronicles 17:1: David notices that he lives in a fine cedar house while God's sacred chest sits in a tent, and he wants to do something about it. It's a good impulse to want to honor God better than we currently do.
entries.1 chronicles 17:2: Nathan the prophet tells David to go ahead with his plan because God seems to be with him. But even wise, well-meaning advice can be wrong if it hasn't been checked with God first.
entries.1 chronicles 17:3: That same night God speaks to Nathan and corrects the plan. God can redirect our good intentions, and we should stay open to being corrected.
entries.1 chronicles 17:4: God tells Nathan to stop David from building him a house. Not every good idea we have is actually what God wants us to do.
entries.1 chronicles 17:5: God points out that he has never lived in a building since he brought Israel out of Egypt; he has always moved with his people in a tent. God cares more about being with his people than about having an impressive building.
entries.1 chronicles 17:6: God asks whether he ever demanded a cedar house from any of Israel's leaders. We shouldn't assume God wants what we think would look impressive for him.
entries.1 chronicles 17:7: God reminds David where he came from, taking him from watching sheep to leading his people. Remembering our humble beginnings helps us stay grateful rather than proud.
entries.1 chronicles 17:8: God says he has been with David everywhere, defeated his enemies, and will make his name great. God's presence and help, not our own strength, are what lift us up.
entries.1 chronicles 17:9: God promises a safe, settled home for Israel where they will no longer be uprooted or harmed. God's people can rest in his promise to protect and establish them.
entries.1 chronicles 17:10: God recalls Israel's history under the judges and promises to defeat David's enemies and give him a lasting royal line. God's plans reach beyond one person to future generations.
entries.1 chronicles 17:11: God promises that after David dies, one of his own sons will take the throne and his kingdom will be made strong. God's promises continue past our own lifetime.
entries.1 chronicles 17:12: God says this son will build the temple, and his rule will be made secure forever. What David wanted to do, God would accomplish through someone else in his timing.
entries.1 chronicles 17:13: God promises to be a father to this king and never withdraw his mercy from him. God's commitment to his people is steady and loving, not conditional on their perfection.
entries.1 chronicles 17:14: God promises this king a permanent place in his house and kingdom, with a throne that will never be overthrown. This points to a lasting kingdom that ultimately finds its fulfillment in Jesus.
entries.1 chronicles 17:15: Nathan passes on to David everything God had said in the vision. Faithful messengers tell the whole truth, even when it changes the original plan.
entries.1 chronicles 17:16: David sits before God and humbly asks who he is to receive such kindness. Realizing how much God has done should make us humble and grateful.
entries.1 chronicles 17:17: David says God's promises go far beyond anything he deserved, even speaking about his family's distant future. God often gives far more than we could ask or imagine.
entries.1 chronicles 17:18: David admits he has nothing more to say, because God already knows him completely. We can be honest and quiet before God, who knows us fully.
entries.1 chronicles 17:19: David credits God's own heart and purpose for all these great things, not his own worth. Our blessings come from God's generosity, not our merit.
entries.1 chronicles 17:20: David declares that no one is like God and there is no other God. Everything he has heard and seen confirms that God alone is worthy of our trust.
entries.1 chronicles 17:21: David marvels that no other nation had a god who rescued them, made them his own, and drove out their enemies. God's rescue of his people is unique and worth remembering.
entries.1 chronicles 17:22: David affirms that God made Israel his own people forever and became their God. God's commitment to his people is permanent, not temporary.
entries.1 chronicles 17:23: David asks God to keep the promise he just made about David and his family. It's right to pray back to God what he has already promised.
entries.1 chronicles 17:24: David prays that God's name will be honored and his promise to David's family will stand. We can want God's reputation and faithfulness to be seen by others.
entries.1 chronicles 17:25: David says that because God revealed his promise, he now feels bold enough to pray. Knowing God's promises gives us confidence to come to him in prayer.
entries.1 chronicles 17:26: David acknowledges that God is God and that he has promised this good thing. Trusting God's character goes hand in hand with trusting his words.
entries.1 chronicles 17:27: David rests in the fact that God has chosen to bless his family forever. When God blesses, it lasts, and we can rest in that.
entries.1 chronicles 19:1: The king of Ammon died and his son Hanun took over as king. This is just setting the scene for what happens next.
entries.1 chronicles 19:2: David wanted to show kindness to Hanun because Hanun's father had been kind to David, so he sent messengers to comfort him about his father's death. It shows David's loyalty to old friends.
entries.1 chronicles 19:3: Hanun's advisors convinced him that David's messengers were really spies looking for a way to conquer the land. Suspicion turned a friendly gesture into a threat.
entries.1 chronicles 19:4: Hanun humiliated David's messengers by shaving off half their beards and cutting their clothes short, then sent them away. This was a public insult meant to shame them.
entries.1 chronicles 19:5: When David heard how ashamed his men were, he told them to stay in Jericho until their beards grew back before returning. He was protecting them from further embarrassment.
entries.1 chronicles 19:6: The Ammonites realized they had made David an enemy, so they paid a huge amount of silver to hire chariots and soldiers from neighboring lands. They prepared for war out of fear.
entries.1 chronicles 19:7: They hired a massive army of chariots and troops and gathered their forces for battle. The conflict was growing much bigger than a simple insult.
entries.1 chronicles 19:8: When David heard about the army gathering, he sent his general Joab with all his fighting men. David responded to the threat with force.
entries.1 chronicles 19:9: The Ammonites lined up at the city gate while the hired kings set up their forces in the open field. The enemy was positioned for battle on two fronts.
entries.1 chronicles 19:10: Joab saw he was surrounded, with enemies in front and behind, so he picked his best soldiers to face the Arameans. He made a smart plan for a difficult situation.
entries.1 chronicles 19:11: Joab put his brother Abishai in charge of the rest of the troops to face the Ammonites. The army was split to handle both threats at once.
entries.1 chronicles 19:12: Joab and his brother agreed to help each other if either side was struggling. They worked as a team and looked out for one another.
entries.1 chronicles 19:13: Joab encouraged his men to be brave and fight for their people and their God's cities, while leaving the outcome to God. We can do our best and trust God with the results.
entries.1 chronicles 19:14: Joab and his men attacked the Arameans, who ran away in defeat. The battle went well for Israel's side.
entries.1 chronicles 19:15: When the Ammonites saw their allies running, they also fled back into the city, and Joab returned to Jerusalem. The victory was complete for that day.
entries.1 chronicles 19:16: The defeated Arameans regrouped and brought in more troops from beyond the river under a new commander. They weren't ready to give up yet.
entries.1 chronicles 19:17: David gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and faced the Arameans in battle. This time David himself led the army.
entries.1 chronicles 19:18: Israel defeated the Arameans badly, killing thousands of chariot soldiers and footmen and their commander. It was a decisive victory.
entries.1 chronicles 19:19: The Arameans made peace with David and became subject to him, and they stopped helping the Ammonites. The conflict ended with Israel on top.
entries.1 chronicles 16:1: They brought God's special chest into the tent David had set up for it and offered sacrifices to God there. This shows the people making a serious, joyful effort to honor God in the right place.
entries.1 chronicles 16:2: After finishing the sacrifices, David blessed the people in the Lord's name. A leader's words can be a gift that sends people home encouraged.
entries.1 chronicles 16:3: David gave every man and woman in Israel a loaf of bread, some meat, and a raisin cake. Everyone got the same share, showing that the celebration was for all the people, not just the important ones.
entries.1 chronicles 16:4: David assigned some Levites to serve in front of the ark by thanking, praising, and honoring the Lord. Worship was given a regular, organized place in the life of the community.
entries.1 chronicles 16:5: This lists the musicians and leaders, with stringed instruments and loud brass, leading the music. Music was a key way the people expressed praise together.
entries.1 chronicles 16:6: Two priests blew trumpets constantly before the ark of God's covenant. The sound reminded everyone that God was present among them.
entries.1 chronicles 16:7: On that day David started the practice of giving thanks to the Lord through Asaph and his fellow musicians. This was the beginning of an ongoing habit of praise.
entries.1 chronicles 16:8: Give thanks to the Lord, honor his name, and tell other people what he has done. Your gratitude is meant to be shared, not kept to yourself.
entries.1 chronicles 16:9: Sing to him and let your mind dwell on the amazing things he has done. Praise involves both your voice and your thoughts.
entries.1 chronicles 16:10: Be proud of belonging to the Lord's holy name, and let everyone who seeks him be glad. Looking for God should bring joy, not gloom.
entries.1 chronicles 16:12: Remember the great things God has done, his miracles, and the rulings he has given. Remembering keeps your faith strong when life gets hard.
entries.1 chronicles 16:13: This speaks to Israel, the descendants of Jacob, whom God loves. God's people are addressed as his servants and his beloved.
entries.1 chronicles 16:14: The Lord is our God, and he rules over all the earth. He is not a local deity but the judge of everyone.
entries.1 chronicles 16:15: God never forgets his covenant promise; it stands for a thousand generations. You can trust that his commitments to his people do not expire.
entries.1 chronicles 16:16: This recalls the covenant God made with Abraham and the promise he swore to Isaac. God's faithfulness runs through family lines and history.
entries.1 chronicles 16:17: God confirmed that promise to Jacob as a lasting agreement for Israel. What began with one person became a permanent commitment to a whole people.
entries.1 chronicles 16:18: God promised to give them the land of Canaan as their inheritance. He made a specific, concrete promise about real land.
entries.1 chronicles 16:19: This was when they were few in number and living as foreigners. God's care mattered most when they were small and vulnerable.
entries.1 chronicles 16:20: They wandered from nation to nation and kingdom to kingdom. Even while unsettled, they were not forgotten by God.
entries.1 chronicles 16:21: God protected them from harm and even rebuked kings on their behalf. God defends his people when they are weak and exposed.
entries.1 chronicles 16:22: God warned others not to touch his anointed ones or harm his prophets. He takes personally any harm done to those he has set apart.
entries.1 chronicles 16:23: Sing to the Lord, all the earth, and announce his salvation every day. Good news about God is meant to be told continually, not just on special occasions.
entries.1 chronicles 16:24: Declare his glory and wonders among the nations and all peoples. God's greatness is for everyone, not just one group.
entries.1 chronicles 16:25: The Lord is great and deserves great praise, and he is to be revered above all other gods. Worship should match how great God truly is.
entries.1 chronicles 16:26: The gods of the nations are worthless, but the Lord made the heavens. Only the Creator deserves to be worshiped.
entries.1 chronicles 16:27: Splendor and majesty surround him, and strength and joy are in his dwelling. Being near God means being near real joy and power.
entries.1 chronicles 16:28: All families of the peoples are called to give the Lord glory and strength. Worship is not limited to one nation but open to everyone.
entries.1 chronicles 16:29: Give the Lord the glory his name deserves, bring an offering, and worship him in holy attire. Worship involves both what you bring and how you come.
entries.1 chronicles 16:30: Stand in awe of him, all the earth, because the world is firmly set and cannot be shaken. God's order gives stability to everything.
entries.1 chronicles 16:31: Let heaven and earth rejoice and let the nations hear that the Lord reigns. The whole creation is invited to celebrate God's kingship.
entries.1 chronicles 16:32: Let the sea roar and the fields and everything in them be glad. All of nature is pictured joining in praise to God.
entries.1 chronicles 16:33: Let the trees sing for joy before the Lord, because he is coming to judge the earth. Even creation looks forward to God setting things right.
entries.1 chronicles 16:34: Give thanks to the Lord because he is good and his mercy never ends. God's kindness is constant, which is a steady reason for gratitude.
entries.1 chronicles 16:35: Ask God to save us, gather us back from the nations, so we can honor his holy name and boast in his praise. Rescue from trouble is meant to lead to worship.
entries.1 chronicles 16:36: Praise the Lord, the God of Israel, forever, and all the people agreed and praised him. Worship becomes complete when the whole community joins in.
entries.1 chronicles 16:37: David arranged for Asaph and his relatives to serve before the ark every day, doing what was needed. Regular, daily service keeps worship going beyond one big event.
entries.1 chronicles 16:38: Obed-edom, Hosah, and sixty-eight relatives were appointed as gatekeepers. Even the practical jobs like guarding doors were part of serving God.
entries.1 chronicles 16:39: Zadok the priest and his fellow priests served at the high place in Gibeon. Worship was happening in more than one location, each with its own duties.
entries.1 chronicles 16:40: They offered burnt offerings to the Lord morning and evening every day, as the law required. Faithful daily worship was the backbone of Israel's life with God.
entries.1 chronicles 16:41: Heman, Jeduthun, and others chosen by name were there to praise the Lord because his mercy lasts forever. Specific people were set apart to keep reminding everyone of God's enduring kindness.
entries.1 chronicles 20:1: Spring was the usual season for kings to lead their armies to war, but this time David stayed home in Jerusalem while his commander Joab fought and captured the Ammonite capital. It reminds readers that even great leaders can step back from their duties, and that choices made at such times can matter greatly.
entries.1 chronicles 20:2: David took the heavy gold crown, set with precious stones, from the Ammonite king's head and wore it himself, and he carried off large amounts of valuable goods from the city. This shows the complete victory and plunder that followed the capture of Rabbah.
entries.1 chronicles 20:3: David forced the people of the captured towns into hard labor with saws, iron picks, and axes, then he and his army returned to Jerusalem. The verse records the harsh treatment defeated peoples received in that era of warfare.
entries.1 chronicles 20:4: Later, war broke out again with the Philistines at Gezer, and Sibbecai killed Sippai, one of the giant descendants of Rapha, and the Philistines were defeated. It shows that Israel's victories continued through individual soldiers, not only through David.
entries.1 chronicles 20:5: In another battle with the Philistines, Elhanan killed Lahmi, the brother of Goliath from Gath, whose spear shaft was as thick as a weaver's beam. This recalls the famous defeat of Goliath and shows that other giant warriors also fell to Israel's fighters.
entries.1 chronicles 20:6: In another battle at Gath there was an unusually tall man with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all, also descended from the giants. The text presents him as a remarkable physical specimen among Israel's enemies.
entries.1 chronicles 20:7: When this giant insulted Israel, Jonathan, the son of David's brother Shimea, killed him. It shows that courage against mockery of God's people was rewarded, even from within David's own family.
entries.1 chronicles 20:8: These giant warriors from Gath were all descendants of Rapha, and they were killed by David and his men. The verse sums up that the feared giants were defeated through David and his loyal soldiers.
entries.1 chronicles 16:42: These men were given the job of playing loud horns and other instruments for the worship songs, while others guarded the doorway. It shows that even practical and musical tasks in worship were assigned and taken seriously.
entries.1 chronicles 16:43: After the worship ended, everyone went home, and David went back to bless his own household. It reminds the reader that caring for your family at home matters just as much as public worship.
entries.1 chronicles 22:1: David points to the place where God's house and altar will be, marking it as the chosen site. For the reader, it shows that worship of God has a set, serious place in the life of his people.
entries.1 chronicles 22:2: David gathers foreign workers living in Israel and sets stonecutters to prepare building stones for God's house. It shows David organizing practical labor so the temple project can move forward.
entries.1 chronicles 22:3: David stockpiles huge amounts of iron for nails and fittings and bronze beyond weighing. The reader sees that preparing well for God's work includes gathering ordinary materials in abundance.
entries.1 chronicles 22:4: Cedar wood arrives in vast quantities from the Sidonians and Tyrians for David. It shows neighboring peoples contributing resources to the building of God's house.
entries.1 chronicles 22:5: David explains that Solomon is young and untested while the temple must be magnificent, so he prepares materials before he dies. For the reader, it models planning ahead and preparing for work you may not finish yourself.
entries.1 chronicles 22:6: David summons Solomon and instructs him to build the house for the Lord, Israel's God. It shows a father passing on a serious responsibility to his son.
entries.1 chronicles 22:7: David tells Solomon that he himself had wanted to build a house for the Lord. The reader sees that good desires can be sincere even when God does not let us carry them out.
entries.1 chronicles 22:8: God told David he could not build the house because he had shed much blood in great wars. It shows that God sets the terms for his own worship, and past violence disqualified David from this task.
entries.1 chronicles 22:9: God promises David a son who will live in rest, named Solomon, and Israel will have peace in his time. For the reader, it shows God giving peace and rest as gifts that make his work possible.
entries.1 chronicles 22:10: God says Solomon will build the house, and God will be a father to him and establish his rule forever. It shows God personally adopting the builder and promising lasting stability.
entries.1 chronicles 22:11: David blesses Solomon, praying the Lord will be with him and that he will succeed in building God's house. The reader sees encouragement and prayer passed from one generation to the next.
entries.1 chronicles 22:12: David prays that God will give Solomon wisdom and understanding so he can obey God's law for Israel. It shows that wisdom and obedience matter even more than building skill.
entries.1 chronicles 22:13: David says things will go well if Solomon carefully keeps God's laws, and tells him to be strong and courageous without fear. For the reader, success is tied to faithful obedience and courage rather than to worry.
entries.1 chronicles 22:14: David reports that despite his own limitations he has prepared enormous amounts of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone, and Solomon can add more. It shows generous, costly preparation for God's house.
entries.1 chronicles 22:15: David notes that Solomon has many skilled workers—stonecutters, woodworkers, and experts in every kind of craft. The reader sees that God's work needs many different hands and skills.
entries.1 chronicles 22:16: David says the gold, silver, bronze, and iron are beyond counting, then urges Solomon to get up and work with the Lord's help. It shows that after preparation comes the call to act, trusting God's presence.
entries.1 chronicles 22:17: David commands all Israel's leaders to help Solomon his son. It shows that a big task needs the support of the whole community, not just one person.
entries.1 chronicles 22:18: David reminds the leaders that God is with them and has given them rest and victory over the land. For the reader, it calls people to recognize God's help and respond with cooperation.
entries.1 chronicles 22:19: David urges the leaders to commit themselves wholeheartedly to worship and to start building so the ark and holy objects can be placed in God's house. It shows that wholehearted devotion should lead to concrete action.
entries.1 chronicles 21:1: Satan pushed David to count his army, hoping to cause harm to Israel. It reminds us that tempting thoughts can come from outside us and lead to trouble.
entries.1 chronicles 21:2: David ordered his commanders to count all the fighting men across the whole country so he would know his exact strength. He wanted to measure his power by numbers.
entries.1 chronicles 21:3: Joab warned the king that this count could bring guilt on Israel, even while wishing God would multiply the people far more. A wise friend may question a decision that seems spiritually dangerous.
entries.1 chronicles 21:4: The king overruled Joab, so Joab obeyed and traveled through the whole land before returning to Jerusalem. Authority won out even when the order was unwise.
entries.1 chronicles 21:5: Joab reported the total: about 1.1 million fighting men in Israel and 470,000 in Judah. The huge numbers showed the nation's military strength.
entries.1 chronicles 21:6: Joab refused to count Levi and Benjamin because he was disgusted by the king's command. Even a partial obedience revealed his unease with what was happening.
entries.1 chronicles 21:7: God was displeased with the census and brought punishment on Israel. Actions that seem merely practical can still matter greatly to God.
entries.1 chronicles 21:8: David admitted his sin and begged God to forgive him, calling his own action very foolish. Honest confession is the right response when we realize we have done wrong.
entries.1 chronicles 21:9: God spoke to Gad, the prophet who served David, giving him a message for the king. God often uses trusted messengers to confront us.
