entries.1 chronicles 21:10: God told Gad to offer David a choice among three punishments, and David had to pick one. Consequences for sin can be real and unavoidable.
entries.1 chronicles 21:11: Gad came to David and presented the options just as the Lord had said. The decision was now in David's hands.
entries.1 chronicles 21:12: The choices were three years of famine, three months of fleeing from enemies, or three days of disease and the angel of the Lord bringing destruction. David had to weigh which judgment to accept.
entries.1 chronicles 21:13: David said the choice was hard but chose to fall into the Lord's hands rather than human hands, trusting God's mercy. It is better to trust God's mercy than to face enemies without it.
entries.1 chronicles 21:14: The Lord sent disease on Israel, and seventy thousand men died. The punishment was severe and the cost was real.
entries.1 chronicles 21:15: As the angel was about to destroy Jerusalem, the Lord relented and stopped him, and the angel stood by Ornan's threshing floor. God's mercy limited the destruction.
entries.1 chronicles 21:16: David saw the angel with a drawn sword over Jerusalem, and he and the leaders fell face down in mourning and fear. A vision of judgment should move us to humble ourselves.
entries.1 chronicles 21:17: David confessed that he was the one who sinned by ordering the count, and he asked God to punish him and his family rather than the innocent people. A true leader takes responsibility for his own wrong.
entries.1 chronicles 21:18: The angel told Gad to have David build an altar to the Lord on Ornan's threshing floor. God provided a specific place for worship and restoration.
entries.1 chronicles 21:19: David went up to the threshing floor just as Gad had instructed in the Lord's name. Obedience followed the message.
entries.1 chronicles 21:20: Ornan was threshing grain when he turned and saw the angel, and his four sons hid themselves. The sight of the angel terrified the family.
entries.1 chronicles 21:21: When Ornan saw David approaching, he left the threshing floor and bowed low before the king. He showed respect to the king who had come to him.
entries.1 chronicles 21:22: David asked to buy the threshing floor at full price so he could build an altar and stop the disease among the people. He wanted to make things right with God.
entries.1 chronicles 21:23: Ornan offered to give David the land, oxen, tools, and grain for free. He was generous and willing to help the king worship.
entries.1 chronicles 21:24: David refused to take it for nothing, insisting on paying the full price because he would not offer God something that cost him nothing. Worship and sacrifice should involve real cost.
entries.1 chronicles 21:25: David paid Ornan six hundred shekels of gold for the site. He honored his word and gave a substantial price.
entries.1 chronicles 21:26: David built an altar, offered burnt and peace offerings, and prayed, and God answered by sending fire from heaven on the altar. God responded to sincere worship with visible acceptance.
entries.1 chronicles 21:27: The Lord commanded the angel, and the angel put his sword back in its sheath. The judgment was over and peace was restored.
entries.1 chronicles 21:28: When David saw that the Lord had answered him at Ornan's threshing floor, he continued making offerings there. He responded to God's mercy with worship.
entries.1 chronicles 21:29: At that time the Lord's tabernacle made by Moses and the altar of burnt offering were at the high place in Gibeon. The old place of worship was still standing elsewhere.
entries.1 chronicles 21:30: David was afraid to go to Gibeon to seek God because he was terrified of the angel's sword. Fear kept him from going to the usual place of worship.
entries.1 chronicles 21:31: David said that the Lord's house and the altar for Israel's burnt offerings should be at Ornan's threshing floor. He wanted the place of God's mercy to become the place of ongoing worship.
entries.1 chronicles 23:1: David was very old and near the end of his life, so he made his son Solomon king to take over from him. It reminds readers that good leaders plan ahead for who comes next.
entries.1 chronicles 23:2: David gathered Israel's leaders, priests, and temple workers together for an important announcement. It shows he wanted everyone involved and informed as the leadership passed to Solomon.
entries.1 chronicles 23:3: They counted all the Levite men who were thirty or older, and there were 38,000 of them. This shows how many people were available to serve in the temple.
entries.1 chronicles 23:4: Of those men, 24,000 were assigned to supervise the temple work and 6,000 served as judges and officials. It shows the work was organized and shared among many people.
entries.1 chronicles 23:5: Another 4,000 men were gatekeepers, and 4,000 played instruments David had made to praise the Lord. It shows that worship and practical service were both important parts of the temple.
entries.1 chronicles 23:6: David organized the Levites into groups based on Levi's three sons: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. It shows that structure and order helped the work run smoothly.
entries.1 chronicles 23:7: This begins listing the family lines within the Gershonite group, starting with Ladan and Shimei. It shows that each family had its place in the larger organization.
entries.1 chronicles 23:8: Ladan's sons were Jehiel, who was the head, along with Zetham and Joel, three in all. It records who led this part of the family.
entries.1 chronicles 23:9: Shimei's sons were Shelomoth, Haziel, and Haran, and these men led the families of Ladan. It shows how leadership was passed down through families.
entries.1 chronicles 23:10: Shimei also had four sons: Jahath, Zizah, Jeush, and Beriah. It simply records the next generation of this family line.
entries.1 chronicles 23:11: Jahath was the oldest and Zizah the next, but because Jeush and Beriah had few sons, they were counted together as one family group. It shows the count was adjusted to fit real circumstances.
entries.1 chronicles 23:12: Kohath had four sons: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. It lists the family lines that came from this branch of Levi.
entries.1 chronicles 23:13: Aaron and Moses were Amram's sons, and Aaron and his descendants were set apart forever to handle the most holy things, offer sacrifices, and bless the people in God's name. It shows that some roles were special and lasting.
entries.1 chronicles 23:14: Moses' sons were counted as part of the tribe of Levi. It shows that even Moses' family served among the ordinary temple workers.
entries.1 chronicles 23:15: Moses' two sons were named Gershom and Eliezer. It records the next generation of Moses' family.
entries.1 chronicles 23:16: Gershom's oldest son was Shebuel. It names the leader of that family line.
entries.1 chronicles 23:17: Eliezer's oldest son was Rehabiah, and Eliezer had no other sons, but Rehabiah had many descendants. It shows how one family line grew large over time.
entries.1 chronicles 23:18: Izhar's oldest son was Shelomith. It names the head of that family group.
entries.1 chronicles 23:19: Hebron's sons were Jeriah, Amariah, Jahaziel, and Jekameam, in that order of seniority. It records the leaders of this family line.
entries.1 chronicles 23:20: Uzziel's sons were Micah, the oldest, and Isshiah. It names the heads of this family group.
entries.1 chronicles 23:21: Merari's sons were Mahli and Mushi, and Mahli's sons were Eleazar and Kish. It lists the family lines from this branch of Levi.
entries.1 chronicles 23:22: Eleazar died without sons, only daughters, and their cousins, the sons of Kish, married them. It shows how the family line was kept going when there were no male heirs.
entries.1 chronicles 23:23: Mushi's sons were Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth, three in all. It records the next generation of this family.
entries.1 chronicles 23:24: These were the Levites listed by family, all twenty years old and up who did the work of the Lord's house. It shows the age for service was lowered, meaning more people could help.
entries.1 chronicles 23:25: David said the Lord had given Israel rest and had made Jerusalem his permanent dwelling place. It explains why the temple work could now be settled and stable.
entries.1 chronicles 23:26: From then on, the Levites would no longer need to carry the Lord's house and its equipment from place to place. It shows a change from a traveling worship system to a fixed one.
entries.1 chronicles 23:27: Counting the Levites from age twenty was one of David's final acts. It shows he was still organizing God's work even near the end of his life.
entries.1 chronicles 23:28: The Levites worked alongside Aaron's descendants in the temple, caring for the courtyards, rooms, and cleansing of holy things. It shows their job was practical support for the priests.
entries.1 chronicles 23:29: They were responsible for the holy bread, the grain offerings, and all the weights and measures. It shows they handled the everyday details that kept worship running correctly.
entries.1 chronicles 23:30: They stood every morning and every evening to praise and make music to the Lord. It shows that regular, daily worship was a central part of their job.
entries.1 chronicles 23:31: They also helped with burnt offerings on Sabbaths, new moons, and festivals, following the law exactly. It shows their service was tied to the regular rhythm of Israel's worship.
entries.1 chronicles 23:32: They took care of the Tent of Meeting and the holy place, working under the direction of Aaron's sons. It shows they served in support roles, following the priests' leadership.
entries.1 chronicles 24:1: This verse starts a list of how Aaron's descendants, the priestly family, were divided into work groups. It reminds the reader that serving God was organized by family lines.
entries.1 chronicles 24:2: Two of Aaron's sons died before their father and left no children, so the remaining two sons carried on the priestly work. It shows that the job of serving God continued even after tragedy.
entries.1 chronicles 24:3: King David, working with the leading priests, arranged these men into their assigned duties. It shows that planning and cooperation were part of setting up worship.
entries.1 chronicles 24:4: One branch of the family had more family leaders than the other, so it received more groups. The division was made fairly according to how many leaders each side had.
entries.1 chronicles 24:5: The groups were assigned by casting lots, which was seen as letting God decide. Both branches of the family shared in the important work of the temple.
entries.1 chronicles 24:6: A scribe wrote down the names as the king and the priests watched, alternating between the two family lines. It shows the assignments were official and carefully recorded.
entries.1 chronicles 24:7: This begins the list of the twenty-four groups in the order they were chosen. The first group was named after Jehoiarib.
entries.1 chronicles 24:8: The list continues with the third and fourth groups chosen. Each name stands for a group that would take its turn serving.
entries.1 chronicles 24:9: The fifth and sixth groups are named here. The orderly list shows each group had its own place and turn.
entries.1 chronicles 24:10: The seventh and eighth groups are listed, including Abijah, a name later connected with a priestly division in the New Testament. Each group had a set turn to serve.
entries.1 chronicles 24:11: The ninth and tenth groups are named. The careful numbering shows that every group was counted and given its turn.
entries.1 chronicles 24:12: The eleventh and twelfth groups are recorded. The list keeps moving steadily through all the assigned groups.
entries.1 chronicles 24:13: The thirteenth and fourteenth groups are named here. Each one had its own identity and responsibility in temple service.
entries.1 chronicles 24:14: The fifteenth and sixteenth groups are listed. The rotation ensured that the work was shared among many families.
entries.1 chronicles 24:15: The seventeenth and eighteenth groups are named. The list shows the full set of groups being completed in order.
entries.1 chronicles 24:16: The nineteenth and twentieth groups are recorded. Each group would serve in its assigned turn at the temple.
entries.1 chronicles 24:17: The twenty-first and twenty-second groups are named. The numbering shows the plan was nearly complete.
entries.1 chronicles 24:18: The twenty-third and twenty-fourth groups finish the list. With all twenty-four named, the schedule for priestly service was set.
entries.1 chronicles 24:19: These groups were assigned to take their turns serving in the Lord's house, following the rules God had given through Aaron. It shows that worship was done God's way, in an orderly rotation.
entries.1 chronicles 24:20: The list now turns to the other Levite families who were not priests. It names the family leaders from the line of Amram.
entries.1 chronicles 24:21: This names a leader from the family of Rehabiah. It continues recording the Levite family heads.
entries.1 chronicles 24:22: The family leaders from the Izharite branch are named here. The record keeps track of who led each Levite family.
entries.1 chronicles 24:23: The sons of Hebron are listed in order of rank. It shows how leadership passed down within this family.
entries.1 chronicles 24:24: This names leaders from the family of Uzziel. The list continues to document the Levite family structure.
entries.1 chronicles 24:25: Another leader from Micah's family line is named. The record carefully notes each branch of the family.
entries.1 chronicles 24:26: The list moves to the family of Merari, naming its sons and their descendants. It shows the Levites were organized by their family lines.
entries.1 chronicles 24:27: This names more descendants from the Merari family through Jaaziah. The record keeps track of each branch.
entries.1 chronicles 24:28: One man named Eleazar had no sons, which is noted because it affected how his family line continued. It shows the record paid attention to real family situations.
entries.1 chronicles 24:29: This names the family of Kish and its descendant Jerahmeel. The list continues documenting the Levite families.
entries.1 chronicles 24:30: The sons of Mushi are named, closing out this section of Levite families. It summarizes that these were all Levites by family.
entries.1 chronicles 24:31: The non-priest Levites were also assigned their duties by casting lots, just like the priests, with the king and leaders present. It shows that every family, older or younger, had an equal share in serving God.
entries.1 chronicles 25:1: David and the leaders set apart certain men from three families to serve God by prophesying with music, playing stringed and brass instruments. It shows that music was a serious, organized act of worship, not just background noise.
entries.1 chronicles 25:2: Asaph's sons worked under their father's direction, and Asaph himself served as a prophet under the king's authority. This means worship was done in an orderly way, with clear leadership and obedience.
entries.1 chronicles 25:3: Jeduthun's six sons served under their father, who led them in praising God with stringed instruments as a prophet. It shows a father passing on the work of worship to his children.
entries.1 chronicles 25:4: This verse simply lists the fourteen sons of Heman by name. It reminds us that each person in God's service is known and named, not just a number.
entries.1 chronicles 25:5: All these were Heman's sons, and God blessed Heman, the king's seer, with many children to strengthen his work. It shows that God can give a person a large family as part of their calling and support.
entries.1 chronicles 25:6: All these men made music in the Lord's house under their fathers' direction, with the three fathers under the king's orders. It shows worship in God's house was carefully organized with clear lines of responsibility.
entries.1 chronicles 25:7: Along with their relatives, 288 men were trained and skilled in making music to the Lord. It shows that serving God with music took real training and effort, not just good intentions.
entries.1 chronicles 25:8: They cast lots to assign the work, giving everyone an equal chance, whether important or unimportant, teacher or student. It shows that in God's work, everyone is treated fairly and no one is favored over another.
entries.1 chronicles 25:9: The first lot fell to Joseph of Asaph's group, and the second to Gedaliah, each with twelve family members. It shows the assignments were decided by lot, leaving the outcome in God's hands.
entries.1 chronicles 25:10: The third lot went to Zaccur and his family group of twelve. Each group got its turn and its place in the work.
entries.1 chronicles 25:11: The fourth lot went to Izri and his group of twelve. This continues the orderly, fair division of duties among the musicians.
entries.1 chronicles 25:12: The fifth lot went to Nethaniah and his group of twelve. Each family received its assigned role in serving God.
entries.1 chronicles 25:13: The sixth lot went to Bukkiah and his group of twelve. The list keeps showing that every group had a real part to play.
entries.1 chronicles 25:14: The seventh lot went to Jesharelah and his group of twelve. The work was shared out step by step, with no group left out.
entries.1 chronicles 25:15: The eighth lot went to Jeshaiah and his group of twelve. Each assignment came in its proper order.
entries.1 chronicles 25:16: The ninth lot went to Mattaniah and his group of twelve. The pattern continues, showing fairness and order in God's service.
entries.1 chronicles 25:17: The tenth lot went to Shimei and his group of twelve. Every group had its own place and turn in the work.
entries.1 chronicles 25:18: The eleventh lot went to Azarel and his group of twelve. The list shows the work was divided evenly among many families.
entries.1 chronicles 25:19: The twelfth lot went to Hashabiah and his group of twelve. Halfway through the list, the same fair pattern holds.
entries.1 chronicles 25:20: The thirteenth lot went to Shubael and his group of twelve. Each group was given its own responsibility in worship.
entries.1 chronicles 25:21: The fourteenth lot went to Mattithiah and his group of twelve. The assignments kept coming in order, with no confusion.
entries.1 chronicles 25:22: The fifteenth lot went to Jeremoth and his group of twelve. Every family had a turn and a task in serving God.
entries.1 chronicles 25:23: The sixteenth lot went to Hananiah and his group of twelve. The work continued to be shared out fairly.
entries.1 chronicles 25:24: The seventeenth lot went to Joshbekashah and his group of twelve. Each group received its own place in the rotation.
entries.1 chronicles 25:25: The eighteenth lot went to Hanani and his group of twelve. The list shows that even the later groups mattered just as much.
entries.1 chronicles 25:26: The nineteenth lot went to Mallothi and his group of twelve. The orderly division of work kept going to the end.
entries.1 chronicles 25:27: The twentieth lot went to Eliathah and his group of twelve. Each family was counted and given its role.
entries.1 chronicles 25:28: The twenty-first lot went to Hothir and his group of twelve. The pattern of fair assignment continues.
entries.1 chronicles 25:29: The twenty-second lot went to Giddalti and his group of twelve. Every group was included in the work of worship.
entries.1 chronicles 25:30: The twenty-third lot went to Mahazioth and his group of twelve. The list is nearly complete, with each group given its turn.
entries.1 chronicles 25:31: The twenty-fourth and last lot went to Romamti-ezer and his group of twelve. The list ends showing that all 24 groups were assigned fairly, and everyone had a part to play.
entries.1 chronicles 26:1: This verse starts a list of the men who served as gatekeepers at the temple, beginning with the family of Meshelemiah. It shows that even guarding doors was an organized, honorable job in God's house.
entries.1 chronicles 26:2: Meshelemiah's sons are named in order, starting with his oldest. The text simply records who they were, showing that families were counted and organized for service.
entries.1 chronicles 26:3: The list of Meshelemiah's sons continues to the seventh. Each name mattered because each man had a place in the work.
entries.1 chronicles 26:4: Now the sons of Obed-edom are listed in order. Like the others, his family was organized for service at the temple.
entries.1 chronicles 26:5: Obed-edom had eight sons, and the writer notes that God had blessed him. His many children are seen as a sign of God's favor.
entries.1 chronicles 26:6: Shemaiah's sons became leaders in their family because they were capable men. Ability and responsibility went together in this service.
entries.1 chronicles 26:7: Shemaiah's sons are named, and some of their relatives are described as strong fighting men. The point is that these were capable, sturdy men suited for the work.
entries.1 chronicles 26:8: All these descendants of Obed-edom, sixty-two in total, were able and strong for the work. The large, capable family was a real asset to the temple service.
entries.1 chronicles 26:9: Meshelemiah's group totaled eighteen capable men. The numbers show the work was taken seriously and staffed properly.
entries.1 chronicles 26:10: Hosah's son Shimri was made chief even though he was not the firstborn. It shows that leadership could be given by choice rather than only by birth order.
entries.1 chronicles 26:11: Hosah's sons are listed, thirteen in all. Again the record shows a family set apart for temple duty.
entries.1 chronicles 26:12: These gatekeeper groups were men of authority, assigned responsible roles in serving at the house of the Lord. Their job was important, not minor.
entries.1 chronicles 26:13: Assignments to each gate were made by casting lots, and small and large families had equal chance. It shows the decision was left to God rather than favoritism.
entries.1 chronicles 26:14: Shelemiah was given the east gate, and his son Zechariah, a wise counselor, got the north gate. Wisdom was valued alongside the practical work.
entries.1 chronicles 26:15: Obed-edom received the south gate, and his sons were put in charge of the storehouse. Each family had its own specific post.
entries.1 chronicles 26:16: Hosah was assigned the west gate and the road going up, with guards posted in shifts. The temple was watched carefully from every side.
entries.1 chronicles 26:17: The number of guards on duty each day is given for each side. This shows the gatekeeping was a well-planned, round-the-clock operation.
entries.1 chronicles 26:18: More guards were posted at the western colonnade and pathway. Every entrance and approach was covered.
entries.1 chronicles 26:19: This summarizes the gatekeeper divisions from the Korahite and Merarite families. The list closes by naming the two family groups involved.
entries.1 chronicles 26:20: Other Levites were put in charge of the temple treasuries and the holy items. Money and sacred objects were handled by trusted men.
entries.1 chronicles 26:21: The family line of Ladan the Gershonite is introduced, with Jehieli named as a head of family. The record traces who was responsible for what.
entries.1 chronicles 26:22: Jehieli's sons Zetham and Joel were given charge of the treasuries of the Lord's house. This was a position of real trust.
entries.1 chronicles 26:23: The verse lists several Levite clans: Amramites, Izharites, Hebronites, and Uzzielites. These groups are being organized for temple duties.
entries.1 chronicles 26:24: Shebuel, a descendant of Moses, was the officer in charge of the treasuries. Even Moses' family line had a specific assigned role.
entries.1 chronicles 26:25: The family line of Eliezer is traced down to Shelomoth. This shows how the responsibility for the treasuries passed through generations.
entries.1 chronicles 26:26: Shelomoth and his relatives were responsible for the holy things given by King David, family leaders, and army officers. Gifts dedicated to God were carefully guarded.
entries.1 chronicles 26:27: Some of the goods captured in war were dedicated as holy offerings for building the Lord's house. Even spoils of war were given to God's work.
entries.1 chronicles 26:28: Everything dedicated by Samuel, Saul, Abner, Joab, and others was kept under Shelomoth's care. Gifts given to God over many years were preserved and managed.
entries.1 chronicles 26:29: Some Izharites, led by Chenaniah and his sons, handled public affairs for Israel, including judging and administration. Their service was outside the temple as well.
entries.1 chronicles 26:30: Seventeen hundred capable Hebronites were made overseers west of the Jordan, handling both the Lord's work and the king's business. This shows the Levites helped govern daily life, not just temple rituals.
entries.1 chronicles 26:31: In David's fortieth year, a search found capable Hebronite men at Jazer in Gilead, and Jerijah was their chief. The record shows careful checking of who was fit for service.
entries.1 chronicles 26:32: Twenty-seven hundred family heads from Jerijah's group were made overseers over the tribes east of the Jordan, for God's work and the king's business. This shows the Levites were trusted with both spiritual and civil responsibilities.
entries.1 chronicles 27:1: This lists David's officials and the army divisions that served one month at a time, each with 24,000 men. It shows that David organized the country carefully and shared the work among many people.
entries.1 chronicles 27:2: Ishbaal led the soldiers who served in the first month, and his unit had 24,000 men. It is a simple record of who was in charge and how many men he commanded.
entries.1 chronicles 27:3: Ishbaal came from the family of Perez and was the top commander for the first month. His family background is noted to show he was a respected leader.
entries.1 chronicles 27:4: Eleazar led the second month's division, also 24,000 strong. The pattern continues of naming each leader and the size of his unit.
entries.1 chronicles 27:5: Benaiah, a priest's son, commanded the third month's division of 24,000 men. Even religious leaders' families took part in defending the nation.
entries.1 chronicles 27:6: This Benaiah was a famous warrior among David's mighty men, and his son Ammizabad served in his unit. It shows that ability and family service were both valued.
entries.1 chronicles 27:7: Asahel, Joab's brother, led the fourth month's division, and his son took over after him. The army was organized so leadership could pass down within a family.
entries.1 chronicles 27:8: Shamhuth led the fifth month's division of 24,000 men. This is another entry in the list of monthly army commanders.
entries.1 chronicles 27:9: Ira from Tekoa commanded the sixth month's division of 24,000 men. The record keeps track of each leader and his men in turn.
entries.1 chronicles 27:10: Helez from Pelon, an Ephraimite, led the seventh month's division of 24,000 men. His tribe is mentioned to show the army drew from all parts of Israel.
entries.1 chronicles 27:11: Sibbecai led the eighth month's division of 24,000 men. The list continues to show a well-ordered rotation of troops.
entries.1 chronicles 27:12: Abiezer from Anathoth, a Benjamite, commanded the ninth month's division of 24,000 men. Each month had its own leader and unit ready to serve.
entries.1 chronicles 27:13: Maharai led the tenth month's division of 24,000 men. The same careful pattern of monthly service is repeated here.
entries.1 chronicles 27:14: Benaiah from Pirathon, an Ephraimite, led the eleventh month's division of 24,000 men. The army was drawn from many different towns and tribes.
entries.1 chronicles 27:15: Heldai led the twelfth month's division of 24,000 men. With this, all twelve months of the year are covered by organized units.
entries.1 chronicles 27:16: This begins a list of leaders over each tribe of Israel, starting with Reuben and Simeon. It shows David had people responsible for every part of the nation.
entries.1 chronicles 27:17: Hashabiah led the tribe of Levi, and Zadok led the priests. Both religious and civil matters had their own leaders.
entries.1 chronicles 27:18: Elihu, one of David's brothers, led Judah, and Omri led Issachar. Family members and trusted men were given responsibility over tribes.
entries.1 chronicles 27:19: Ishmaiah led Zebulun and Jerimoth led Naphtali. Each tribe had a specific person in charge.
entries.1 chronicles 27:20: Hoshea led Ephraim and Joel led half of Manasseh. The large tribes were also organized under named leaders.
entries.1 chronicles 27:21: Iddo led the other half of Manasseh in Gilead, and Jaasiel led Benjamin. Even tribes split across regions had their own overseers.
entries.1 chronicles 27:22: Azarel led Dan, and this closes the list of tribal leaders. It shows that every tribe had someone accountable for it.
entries.1 chronicles 27:23: David did not count men under twenty because God had promised to make Israel as numerous as the stars. The promise mattered more than a full census.
entries.1 chronicles 27:24: Joab began the counting but never finished, and it brought God's anger on Israel, so the number was left out of the official records. Some actions, even well-intentioned, can go against God's will and cause harm.
entries.1 chronicles 27:25: Azmaveth managed the king's property, and Jonathan managed the storehouses in the countryside and towns. Good administration meant someone was responsible for every resource.
entries.1 chronicles 27:26: Ezri was in charge of the field workers and farmers. Even ordinary farm labor was organized and overseen.
entries.1 chronicles 27:27: Shimei managed the vineyards and Zabdi managed the wine produced and stored. Each part of the economy had a trusted person in charge.
entries.1 chronicles 27:28: Baal-hanan looked after the olive and sycamore trees, and Joash looked after the oil supplies. The king's wealth came from careful management of land and crops.
entries.1 chronicles 27:29: Shitrai managed the herds in Sharon and Shaphat managed those in the valleys. Livestock was spread out and needed local overseers.
entries.1 chronicles 27:30: Obil, an Ishmaelite, managed the camels and Jehdeiah managed the donkeys. People from outside Israel were trusted with important work.
entries.1 chronicles 27:31: Jaziz managed the flocks, and all these men were in charge of David's property. The list ends by summarizing that the king's resources were well organized.
entries.1 chronicles 27:32: Jonathan, David's uncle, was a wise adviser and scribe, and Jehiel cared for the king's sons. Wise counsel and care for family were both important roles.
entries.1 chronicles 27:33: Ahithophel was the king's adviser and Hushai was the king's close friend. A ruler needs both good advice and loyal friendship.
entries.1 chronicles 27:34: After Ahithophel came Jehoiada and Abiathar as advisers, and Joab commanded the army. The chapter closes by naming the top advisers and military leader around David.
entries.2 chronicles 1:1: God was with Solomon and made his kingdom strong and great. It shows that success comes from God's presence, not just our own effort.
entries.2 chronicles 1:2: Solomon gathered all the leaders and officials of Israel together. He was organizing the nation and speaking to those in charge.
entries.2 chronicles 1:3: Solomon and the people went to Gibeon, where the original Tent of Meeting made by Moses was kept. They went there to seek God.
entries.2 chronicles 1:4: David had already moved the ark of God to Jerusalem and set up a tent for it there. So the ark was in Jerusalem while the old tent was still at Gibeon.
entries.2 chronicles 1:5: The bronze altar made by Bezalel was at Gibeon in front of the Lord's Tent. Solomon and the people went there to worship God.
entries.2 chronicles 1:6: Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on the bronze altar at the Tent of Meeting. It was a huge act of devotion and seeking God.
entries.2 chronicles 1:7: That night God appeared to Solomon and invited him to ask for whatever he wanted. God was giving him an open door to request anything.
entries.2 chronicles 1:8: Solomon reminded God of the great mercy shown to his father David and thanked God for making him king. He was acknowledging God's kindness.
entries.2 chronicles 1:9: Solomon asked God to keep the promise made to David, since he now ruled a vast number of people. He was relying on God's word to be faithful.
entries.2 chronicles 1:10: Solomon asked for wisdom and knowledge to lead the people well. He wanted to govern fairly rather than seek personal gain.
entries.2 chronicles 1:11: God noted that Solomon did not ask for riches, honor, revenge, or long life, but for wisdom to judge God's people. God was pleased with what was in his heart.
entries.2 chronicles 1:12: God granted Solomon wisdom and knowledge, and also gave him wealth and honor beyond any king before or after him. God rewards those who seek what matters most.
entries.2 chronicles 1:13: Solomon returned from Gibeon to Jerusalem and ruled over Israel. He went back to his duties as king after worshiping God.
entries.2 chronicles 1:14: Solomon built up a large army of chariots and horsemen, keeping them in chariot cities and with him in Jerusalem. He was strengthening his military power.
entries.2 chronicles 1:15: Silver and gold became as common as stones in Jerusalem, and cedar wood was plentiful. Solomon's wealth was extraordinary.
entries.2 chronicles 1:16: Solomon's horses were imported from Egypt, and his traders bought them from Kue. His wealth allowed him to trade for valuable animals.
entries.2 chronicles 1:17: Chariots and horses had set prices, and Solomon's traders sold them to the kings of the Hittites and Aram as well. His trading network reached beyond Israel.
entries.1 chronicles 28:1: David gathered all Israel's leaders, officials, and fighting men in Jerusalem for an important announcement. It shows that what he was about to say mattered to the whole nation, not just a few people.
entries.1 chronicles 28:2: David told the people he had wanted to build a temple as a resting place for the ark of God's covenant. He had already prepared materials, showing his sincere desire to honor God.
entries.1 chronicles 28:3: God told David he could not build the temple because he was a warrior who had shed blood. Even a good desire can be set aside by God for reasons we may not fully understand.
entries.1 chronicles 28:4: David recalled how God chose his family, then him, to be king over Israel forever. He was reminding the people that his position came from God, not from himself.
entries.1 chronicles 28:5: God gave David many sons and chose Solomon to sit on Israel's throne. This showed that God was directing the succession of leadership.
entries.1 chronicles 28:6: God told David that Solomon would build the temple, and God would treat him as a son. This was a promise of close relationship and special purpose for Solomon.
entries.1 chronicles 28:7: God promised to establish Solomon's kingdom forever if he remained faithful and obedient. The blessing was conditional on Solomon's ongoing loyalty to God.
entries.1 chronicles 28:8: David urged the people, in front of the whole assembly, to obey God's commands so they and their children could keep the good land. Obedience was tied to their long-term security and inheritance.
entries.1 chronicles 28:9: David told Solomon to know God personally and serve him wholeheartedly, because God sees every heart and thought. If Solomon sought God he would find him, but turning away would bring serious consequences.
entries.1 chronicles 28:10: David reminded Solomon that God had chosen him to build the temple and told him to be strong and get to work. The task was clear, and courage was needed to carry it out.
entries.1 chronicles 28:11: David gave Solomon detailed plans for the temple's rooms, storerooms, and the place for the mercy seat. He was passing on careful preparation so the building would be done properly.
entries.1 chronicles 28:12: David shared the plans he had in mind for the courtyards, surrounding rooms, and storerooms for holy things. Every part of the temple was thoughtfully planned out.
entries.1 chronicles 28:13: The plans included how the priests and Levites would be organized and how worship and its equipment would be handled. Good order was important for honoring God.
entries.1 chronicles 28:14: David specified exact amounts of gold and silver for the various temple objects. This shows careful stewardship of valuable materials meant for God's house.
entries.1 chronicles 28:15: He gave precise weights of gold and silver for the lampstands and their utensils. Even the smallest details of the temple's furnishings were planned with care.
entries.1 chronicles 28:16: He specified gold for the tables holding the holy bread and silver for other tables. The temple's everyday furnishings were to be made with quality materials.
entries.1 chronicles 28:17: He gave exact amounts of pure gold for the hooks, bowls, and cups. Nothing in the temple service was left to chance or done carelessly.
entries.1 chronicles 28:18: He designated the finest gold for the incense altar and for the cherubim that spread their wings over the ark. The most sacred parts of the temple received the most precious materials.
entries.1 chronicles 28:19: David said the Lord had given him the written plan for all these things. He believed God himself guided the design, not just human imagination.
entries.1 chronicles 28:20: David encouraged Solomon to be strong and courageous and not to fear, because God would be with him until the work was finished. God's presence was the reason Solomon could face such a big task.
entries.1 chronicles 28:21: David pointed out that the priests, Levites, skilled workers, and all the people were ready to help Solomon. He would not have to do the work alone.
entries.1 chronicles 29:1: David tells the people that his son Solomon is young and untested, but the temple he must build is not for people—it is for God. It reminds readers that God's work is bigger than any one person's experience.
entries.1 chronicles 29:2: David says he has given everything he could toward building God's house—gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and costly stones. It shows that giving to God's work starts with using what you actually have.
entries.1 chronicles 29:3: Because David deeply loves God's house, he gives his own personal gold and silver on top of what he already provided. It shows that real devotion goes beyond the minimum.
entries.1 chronicles 29:4: David names the huge amounts of gold and silver he is giving to cover the temple walls. It shows his gift was specific and generous, not vague good intentions.
entries.1 chronicles 29:5: David explains the gold and silver are for the craftsmen's work, then asks who will step forward to dedicate themselves to the Lord today. It invites the reader to consider volunteering for God's work.
entries.1 chronicles 29:6: The family leaders, tribal chiefs, army commanders, and royal officials responded by giving themselves freely. It shows that leaders set an example when they give willingly.
entries.1 chronicles 29:7: The people gave enormous amounts of gold, silver, bronze, and iron for the Lord's house. It shows that when many people give together, the total can be far greater than any one gift.
entries.1 chronicles 29:8: Those who owned precious stones handed them over to be stored for the temple under a trusted official. It shows that every kind of resource has a place in God's work.
entries.1 chronicles 29:9: The people rejoiced because their giving was voluntary and sincere, and David was full of joy too. It shows that cheerful, willing giving brings joy to both giver and leader.
entries.1 chronicles 29:10: David praises the Lord in front of everyone, calling him the God of Israel forever. It shows that public gratitude to God is fitting when people have given generously.
entries.1 chronicles 29:11: David says power, glory, authority, and honor all belong to God, because everything in heaven and earth is his. It reminds readers that God is above all and owns everything.
entries.1 chronicles 29:12: Wealth and honor come from God, and he holds power and strength to make people great. It reminds readers that success and ability are gifts from God, not self-made achievements.
entries.1 chronicles 29:13: David responds to all this by simply praising God and honoring his glorious name. It shows that recognizing who God is should lead to gratitude.
entries.1 chronicles 29:14: David asks who he and his people are to give so freely, since everything comes from God and they are only giving back what is already his. It reminds readers that our giving is returning what God first gave us.
entries.1 chronicles 29:15: David says people are like foreigners and temporary residents before God, and their days pass like a shadow. It reminds readers that life is short and everything we have is temporary.
entries.1 chronicles 29:16: David acknowledges that all the material gathered for God's house came from God's own hand and belongs to him. It keeps readers from pride about what they give.
entries.1 chronicles 29:17: David knows God looks at the heart and delights in honesty, and he says he gave willingly with a sincere heart and rejoiced to see the people do the same. It reminds readers that God cares about why we give, not just what we give.
entries.1 chronicles 29:18: David prays that God will keep this willingness in the hearts of the people and keep their hearts loyal to him. It shows that lasting devotion is something we need God to sustain.
entries.1 chronicles 29:19: David asks God to give Solomon a wholehearted commitment to obey God's commands and to finish building the temple. It shows that a good heart before God matters more than skill or resources.
entries.1 chronicles 29:20: David tells the people to praise the Lord, and they bow down and worship both the Lord and the king. It shows that worship and respect for God's chosen leader went together in Israel.
entries.1 chronicles 29:21: The next day the people offered sacrifices to the Lord—a thousand each of oxen, sheep, and lambs, plus drink offerings and many other gifts. It shows their worship was costly and wholehearted.
entries.1 chronicles 29:22: The people feasted with great joy and anointed Solomon as king a second time, and Zadok as priest. It shows that obeying God's plan brought celebration and unity.
entries.1 chronicles 29:23: Solomon took the throne as the Lord's king in David's place, and everything went well for him, with all Israel under his rule. It shows that God establishes leaders and blesses those who follow his plan.
entries.1 chronicles 29:24: All the officials, soldiers, and even David's other sons submitted to Solomon's authority. It shows that God-given leadership is honored when people willingly follow it.
entries.1 chronicles 29:25: The Lord made Solomon greatly respected and gave him glory and honor greater than any king of Israel before him. It shows that God himself lifts up those he chooses.
entries.1 chronicles 29:26: This verse simply states that David, Jesse's son, was king over all Israel. It marks the summary of his reign.
entries.1 chronicles 29:27: David ruled Israel for forty years—seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem. It gives a plain record of the length and places of his reign.
entries.1 chronicles 29:28: David died at a good old age, with long life, wealth, and honor, and his son Solomon took over as king. It shows a life that ended well after faithful service.
entries.1 chronicles 29:29: The record says all David's deeds, from beginning to end, were written down by Samuel, Nathan, and Gad. It shows that David's life was remembered and recorded for later generations.
entries.1 chronicles 29:30: These records included David's reign, his power, and the events of his time in Israel and in surrounding kingdoms. It reminds readers that God's work through a leader touches the wider world, not just one nation.
entries.2 chronicles 3:1: Solomon began building the Lord's temple on Mount Moriah in Jerusalem, at the spot his father David had set apart on Ornan's threshing floor. This shows God keeps his promises across generations, and our preparations can pave the way for others.
entries.2 chronicles 3:2: The work started in the second month of the fourth year of Solomon's reign. It reminds us that big undertakings for God have a real starting point in time and history.
entries.2 chronicles 3:3: Solomon laid the foundation of the temple, which measured sixty cubits long and twenty cubits wide by the old standard. The careful measurements show that worship of God was planned with order and care.
entries.2 chronicles 3:4: The porch in front of the temple was twenty cubits long, as wide as the building, and a hundred and twenty cubits high, covered inside with fine gold. The grandeur was meant to reflect how much God deserves honor.
entries.2 chronicles 3:5: The main hall was paneled with cypress wood, overlaid with fine gold and decorated with palm tree and chain designs. Beauty in worship can point the heart toward God's worth.
entries.2 chronicles 3:6: The temple was adorned with precious stones, and the gold used was of the finest kind, called Parvaim gold. Giving God the best, not the leftovers, is the pattern here.
entries.2 chronicles 3:7: The whole temple—beams, thresholds, walls, and doors—was covered in gold, and the walls were carved with figures of winged beings. Every part was treated as sacred, not just the visible front.
entries.2 chronicles 3:8: Solomon built the Most Holy Place, a twenty-cubit square room like the main hall, and covered it with six hundred talents of fine gold. The innermost room was the most costly, showing that closeness to God is the greatest treasure.
entries.2 chronicles 3:9: Even the nails weighed fifty shekels of gold, and the upper rooms were overlaid with gold. No detail was too small to be done with excellence for God's house.
entries.2 chronicles 3:10: In the Most Holy Place Solomon made two large winged figures and covered them with gold. These images marked the place of God's presence and reminded worshipers of the heavenly realm.
entries.2 chronicles 3:11: The wings of the two figures stretched out twenty cubits in total, one wing of each touching the temple wall and the other wings meeting in the middle. The design shows unity and covering around the place of God's presence.
entries.2 chronicles 3:12: The second figure's wings were arranged the same way, one touching the wall and one meeting the first figure's wing. Symmetry and order marked the holy space.
entries.2 chronicles 3:13: Together the figures' wings spanned twenty cubits, and they stood upright on their feet facing the inner room. They stood ready to serve, facing toward the heart of the temple.
entries.2 chronicles 3:14: Solomon made a curtain of blue, purple, and red fine linen, woven with figures of winged beings. This veil set apart the Most Holy Place, teaching that access to God's presence was guarded and precious.
entries.2 chronicles 3:15: In front of the temple he set up two pillars thirty-five cubits high, each with a capital of five cubits on top. These pillars stood as a visible marker of the temple's entrance and strength.
entries.2 chronicles 3:16: He made chain-like ornaments for the tops of the pillars and attached a hundred pomegranate shapes to them. Decorative details like these showed care and celebration in God's house.
entries.2 chronicles 3:17: He set the pillars in front of the temple, one on the right and one on the left, naming them Jachin and Boaz. The names mean 'he establishes' and 'in him is strength,' reminding worshipers that God is the one who makes his people firm and strong.
entries.2 chronicles 5:1: Solomon finished building God's temple and stored the silver, gold, and other sacred items his father David had dedicated inside it. It reminds readers that finishing a task for God and honoring what earlier generations gave are both part of faithful service.
entries.2 chronicles 5:2: Solomon gathered Israel's leaders in Jerusalem to bring the ark of the covenant up from the City of David. It shows that important spiritual moments were shared publicly by the whole community, not handled by one person alone.
entries.2 chronicles 5:3: All the people of Israel assembled before the king during the feast held in the seventh month. This tells the reader that worship and celebration brought the whole nation together around God.
entries.2 chronicles 5:4: The elders of Israel arrived, and the Levites lifted up the ark to carry it. It shows that God's holy things were handled with care by the people appointed to do that work.
entries.2 chronicles 5:5: The priests and Levites carried the ark, the Tent of Meeting, and all the holy objects that belonged in the Tent. It reminds readers that worship involves respecting and caring for what has been set apart for God.
entries.2 chronicles 5:6: Solomon and the whole assembly sacrificed so many sheep and oxen before the ark that they could not be counted. It shows how seriously and joyfully the people honored God's presence among them.
entries.2 chronicles 5:7: The priests placed the ark in the innermost room of the temple, the Most Holy Place, beneath the wings of the cherubim. This shows that God's presence was given the most honored place in the whole building.
entries.2 chronicles 5:8: The cherubim's outstretched wings spread over the ark and its carrying poles. It pictures God's presence being sheltered and honored in the place prepared for it.
entries.2 chronicles 5:9: The carrying poles were long enough that their ends could be seen from the holy place in front of the inner room, though not from outside. This detail shows the ark was set in its proper place and stayed there.
entries.2 chronicles 5:10: Inside the ark were only the two stone tablets Moses had placed there at Horeb, where God made his covenant with Israel after the exodus from Egypt. It reminds readers that God's agreement with his people was the heart of what the ark stood for.
entries.2 chronicles 5:11: The priests came out of the holy place, and all of them had made themselves holy without following their usual rotation. It shows that on this special occasion the priests set aside normal routines to prepare for God's presence.
entries.2 chronicles 5:12: The Levite musicians, dressed in fine linen, stood with cymbals and stringed instruments east of the altar, joined by 120 priests blowing trumpets. It shows that many people used their skills together to lead the nation in worship.
entries.2 chronicles 5:13: When the trumpeters and singers praised God together in one voice, saying he is good and his mercy lasts forever, a cloud filled the temple with God's glory. It shows that wholehearted, unified praise is met by God's real presence among his people.
entries.2 chronicles 5:14: The cloud was so thick that the priests could not stay at their places to do their work, because God's glory filled the temple. It shows that God's presence can be so overwhelming that it stops ordinary activity and leaves people in awe.
entries.2 chronicles 4:1: Solomon built a large bronze altar where sacrifices would be offered to God. It reminds readers that worship involves giving something up to honor God.
entries.2 chronicles 4:2: He made a huge round metal tank for water, about fifteen feet across and over seven feet tall. This was a major piece of the temple equipment used for cleansing.
entries.2 chronicles 4:3: Decorative flower shapes were cast all around the tank in two rows. The care taken shows that the place of worship was meant to be beautiful, not just useful.
entries.2 chronicles 4:4: The giant tank rested on twelve metal ox statues facing the four directions. The number twelve likely recalls the twelve tribes of Israel, tying the temple to the whole nation.
entries.2 chronicles 4:5: The tank's rim was as thick as a hand and shaped like a lily, and it held thousands of gallons. Its huge size shows how much water was needed for the priests' cleansing.
entries.2 chronicles 4:6: Ten smaller basins were made for washing the parts of burnt offerings, while the big tank was for the priests to wash themselves. Being clean before God was treated as serious business.
entries.2 chronicles 4:7: He made ten gold lampstands and placed them inside the temple, five on each side. These gave light in the house of God, following the pattern Moses had been given.
entries.2 chronicles 4:8: He made ten tables and a hundred gold bowls for the temple. These supported the regular offerings and service carried out there.
entries.2 chronicles 4:9: He built a courtyard for the priests and a larger outer courtyard, with doors covered in bronze. The layout set apart space for worship and for the people.
entries.2 chronicles 4:10: The great water tank was placed at the southeast corner of the temple. Its position kept it handy for the priests' washing.
entries.2 chronicles 4:11: Huram finished making all the pots, shovels, and bowls for King Solomon's temple. His skilled work completed a huge job done for God's house.
entries.2 chronicles 4:12: The list names the two bronze pillars with their decorative tops and the meshwork around them. These stood at the temple entrance as impressive markers of God's house.
entries.2 chronicles 4:13: Four hundred pomegranate-shaped decorations in two rows adorned the tops of the pillars. The detail shows the craftsmanship poured into honoring God.
entries.2 chronicles 4:14: He made ten stands and ten basins that sat on them. These movable basins helped with washing during the temple rituals.
entries.2 chronicles 4:15: The great water tank and the twelve oxen beneath it are named again. Together they formed a striking centerpiece for the priests' cleansing.
entries.2 chronicles 4:16: All the pots, shovels, meat hooks, and other utensils were made of polished bronze by Huram, described as a father figure to Solomon. Even ordinary tools for the temple were made well.
entries.2 chronicles 4:17: The bronze items were cast in clay molds in the Jordan Valley between Succoth and Zeredah. The location shows this was a large-scale manufacturing effort.
entries.2 chronicles 4:18: Solomon had so many bronze objects made that no one bothered to weigh the metal. The abundance reflects the wealth and grandeur of the temple project.
entries.2 chronicles 4:19: Solomon also made the gold altar and the tables that held the sacred bread. These were the furnishings for the temple's ongoing worship.
entries.2 chronicles 4:20: The lampstands and their lamps were made of pure gold to burn regularly before the inner room. Steady light symbolized constant devotion to God.
entries.2 chronicles 4:21: The floral decorations, lamps, and tools were all made of the finest gold. Nothing but the best was used in the place of worship.
entries.2 chronicles 4:22: Even the small tools and the doors into the most holy place were covered in the best gold. The most sacred space was treated with the greatest honor.
entries.2 chronicles 8:1: After twenty years Solomon had finished building both the Lord's temple and his own palace. It reminds us that big projects take time and steady effort.
entries.2 chronicles 8:2: Solomon rebuilt some towns that King Huram had given him and settled Israelites there. He made use of what he was given to provide homes for his people.
entries.2 chronicles 8:3: Solomon went to war against Hamath-zobah and defeated it. This shows his kingdom growing strong through military victory.
entries.2 chronicles 8:4: Solomon built up Tadmor in the desert and all the supply towns in the region of Hamath. He strengthened his country's infrastructure and storage.
entries.2 chronicles 8:5: He fortified both Upper and Lower Beth-horon, making them walled towns with gates and bars. He was securing his land against attack.
entries.2 chronicles 8:6: Solomon built Baalath, all his storage towns, towns for his chariots and horses, and anything else he wanted in Jerusalem, Lebanon, and across his kingdom. He used his wealth and power to develop the whole land.
entries.2 chronicles 8:7: This lists the remaining peoples in the land who were not Israelites. They were the descendants of the nations Israel had not fully removed.
entries.2 chronicles 8:8: Solomon forced the surviving members of these peoples into labor, and this continued long after. It shows how defeated peoples were put to hard work.
entries.2 chronicles 8:9: Solomon did not force Israelites into slave labor; they served as soldiers, officers, and chariot commanders. His own people held positions of honor and responsibility.
entries.2 chronicles 8:10: Solomon had two hundred and fifty chief officials overseeing the people. He organized his government with clear leaders in charge.
entries.2 chronicles 8:11: Solomon moved Pharaoh's daughter from David's city to a house he built for her, because he considered the places where the ark had been to be holy. He wanted to honor God's holy things even in his marriage arrangements.
entries.2 chronicles 8:12: Solomon offered burnt offerings to the Lord on the altar he had built in front of the temple porch. He personally led worship at the place dedicated to God.
entries.2 chronicles 8:13: He offered the sacrifices Moses had commanded every day, on Sabbaths, at new moons, and at the three yearly festivals. He followed God's instructions for worship carefully and regularly.
entries.2 chronicles 8:14: Solomon assigned the priests and Levites their duties just as his father David had arranged, including praise and guarding the doors. He kept the worship system organized and faithful to David's plan.
entries.2 chronicles 8:15: The priests and Levites carefully carried out every order the king gave them about their work and the temple supplies. They were diligent and obedient in their service.
entries.2 chronicles 8:16: All of Solomon's work was completed, from laying the temple's foundation to finishing it. He saw the Lord's house through to the end.
entries.2 chronicles 8:17: Solomon then traveled to Ezion-geber and Eloth, ports on the sea in Edom. He expanded his reach to the coast for trade.
entries.2 chronicles 8:18: Huram sent Solomon ships and skilled sailors, who sailed with Solomon's men to Ophir and brought back four hundred and fifty talents of gold. This shows how partnerships and trade brought great wealth to the kingdom.
entries.2 chronicles 2:1: Solomon decided to build a temple for the Lord and also a palace for himself as king. It shows that honoring God was a priority in his plans, and it invites readers to make room for God in their own plans.
entries.2 chronicles 2:2: Solomon counted out workers for the building project: many to carry materials, many to cut stone, and thousands to supervise. Large tasks for God still need organization and willing workers, and every role matters.
entries.2 chronicles 2:3: Solomon asked Huram, the king of Tyre, for help, reminding him of the cedar wood he had supplied for David's building. It is fine to ask others for help and to build on good relationships from the past.
entries.2 chronicles 2:4: Solomon explains that the temple is set apart for God, where incense, sacred bread, and sacrifices will be offered regularly according to God's command. Worship involves steady, faithful practice, not just occasional moments.
entries.2 chronicles 2:5: The temple is meant to be grand because the God it honors is greater than every other god. What we build or do for God should reflect how highly we think of him.
entries.2 chronicles 2:6: Solomon admits that no building can contain God, since even the heavens cannot hold him; he builds only as a place to burn incense before him. God is far greater than anything we can make for him, so our efforts are humble offerings, not favors to him.
entries.2 chronicles 2:7: Solomon asks for a skilled craftsman in metals, fabrics, and decorative carving to work alongside the craftsmen already in Judah. Good work for God uses real skill and teamwork, bringing different talents together.
entries.2 chronicles 2:8: Solomon requests cedar, cypress, and sandalwood from Lebanon, knowing Huram's men are expert woodcutters, and says his own men will work with them. Asking for the right materials and cooperating with skilled people helps a good project succeed.
entries.2 chronicles 2:9: Solomon needs a huge amount of timber because the house he is building will be great and impressive. Big goals for God's honor require big, practical preparation.
entries.2 chronicles 2:10: Solomon promises to pay the woodcutters generously with grain, barley, wine, and oil. Fair payment for work is part of doing things rightly, and generosity supports those who labor.
entries.2 chronicles 2:11: Huram replies in writing that God made Solomon king because he loves his people. Even an outside ruler can recognize God's care, reminding readers that God's love is often shown through the leaders and circumstances he provides.
entries.2 chronicles 2:12: Huram praises the Lord as maker of heaven and earth for giving David a wise son to build the temple and the palace. It is good to thank God for wisdom and for the people he raises up to do his work.
entries.2 chronicles 2:13: Huram says he is sending a wise and skilled man named Huram, described as like a father to him. Experienced, trustworthy people are a gift to any project, and it is wise to send your best.
entries.2 chronicles 2:14: This craftsman has a mixed background but wide skills in metals, stone, wood, fabrics, and design, and he is to join Solomon's craftsmen and David's. God-given ability matters more than someone's family background, and skilled people should be welcomed and put to work.
entries.2 chronicles 2:15: Huram agrees to the deal and asks Solomon to send the promised grain, oil, and wine to his workers. Keeping agreements and supplying what was promised builds trust between people.
entries.2 chronicles 2:16: Huram's men will cut as much wood as needed in Lebanon and float it by sea to Joppa, from where it can be taken up to Jerusalem. A big job gets done through cooperation and practical planning, step by step.
entries.2 chronicles 2:17: Solomon counted the foreigners living in Israel, as his father David had done, and found a hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred. Careful counting and record-keeping help leaders manage large responsibilities well.
entries.2 chronicles 2:18: Solomon assigned seventy thousand to transport, eighty thousand to cut stone, and three thousand six hundred to supervise the work. A large task runs smoothly when people are given clear roles, and faithful supervision helps everyone work well.
entries.2 chronicles 7:1: As soon as Solomon finished praying, fire came down from heaven and burned up the sacrifices, and God's presence filled the temple. It showed the people that God had truly accepted their worship and was with them.
entries.2 chronicles 7:2: God's presence was so overwhelming that the priests could not even go inside the temple. It reminds us that God is holy and far greater than we are.
entries.2 chronicles 7:3: When the people saw the fire and God's glory, they knelt down and worshiped, thanking God because he is good and his love lasts forever. Seeing God at work should move us to humble thanks and praise.
entries.2 chronicles 7:4: The king and all the people responded by offering sacrifices to the Lord. Worship that recognizes God's greatness naturally leads to giving him our best.
entries.2 chronicles 7:5: Solomon offered a huge number of animals, and the whole nation celebrated the dedication of God's house. It was a joyful, wholehearted celebration of what God had done.
entries.2 chronicles 7:6: The priests and musicians took their places, playing the instruments David had arranged, while the people stood and praised God for his lasting love. Music and worship helped the whole community honor God together.
entries.2 chronicles 7:7: There were so many sacrifices that the bronze altar could not hold them all, so Solomon set apart the middle of the courtyard to offer them. The people gave so generously that the normal setup was not enough.
entries.2 chronicles 7:8: Solomon and all Israel held a seven-day celebration, and people came from far away across the land. It was a huge gathering of the whole nation rejoicing together.
entries.2 chronicles 7:9: On the eighth day they held a special holy gathering, after seven days of dedicating the altar and seven days of feasting. The celebration was carefully ordered around worship of God.
entries.2 chronicles 7:10: After the celebration, Solomon sent the people home, and they went full of joy because of all the good God had done. Remembering God's goodness fills our hearts with gladness.
entries.2 chronicles 7:11: Solomon finished building both the Lord's temple and his own palace, and everything he had planned was completed well. God had blessed his work, and he finished what he set out to do.
entries.2 chronicles 7:12: God appeared to Solomon at night and told him he had heard his prayer and chosen the temple as the place for sacrifices. God listens when we pray and responds to us.
entries.2 chronicles 7:13: God describes times when he may withhold rain, send locusts, or bring disease on the land. Hard times can come, and God is sovereign even over them.
entries.2 chronicles 7:14: If God's people humble themselves, pray, seek him, and turn from their wrong ways, he will hear from heaven, forgive them, and restore their land. This is a clear promise that humble repentance brings God's forgiveness and healing.
entries.2 chronicles 7:15: God says his eyes will be open and his ears attentive to the prayers made at this place. He promises to watch over and listen to the prayers of his people.
entries.2 chronicles 7:16: God has chosen and set apart this temple so his name will be there forever, and he will keep his eyes and heart on it always. God commits himself to be present with his people.
entries.2 chronicles 7:17: God tells Solomon that if he walks faithfully before him like David did, obeying all his commands and laws, then blessing will follow. Faithfulness to God is a personal choice that matters.
entries.2 chronicles 7:18: God promises to establish Solomon's royal throne, keeping his promise to David that Israel would always have a ruler from his line. God keeps the promises he makes.
entries.2 chronicles 7:19: But if Solomon or the people turn away from God, disobey his laws, and worship other gods, there will be serious consequences. Turning from God to other things always carries a cost.
entries.2 chronicles 7:20: God warns that he will remove the people from the land and reject the temple he made holy, making it a warning and a disgrace among the nations. Disobedience can lead to losing what God has given.
entries.2 chronicles 7:21: The ruined temple will astonish everyone who passes by, and they will ask why the Lord did this to the land and the house. God's judgment becomes a visible lesson to others.
entries.2 chronicles 7:22: People will answer that it happened because the people turned away from the Lord who brought them out of Egypt and worshiped other gods instead. The disaster is explained as the result of abandoning the God who saved them.
entries.2 chronicles 9:1: A foreign queen heard how wise Solomon was and traveled a long way with rich gifts to test him with hard questions. It shows that a good reputation draws people to see the truth for themselves.
entries.2 chronicles 9:2: Solomon answered every question she had and hid nothing from her. God's wisdom given to him was complete enough to meet every honest seeker.
entries.2 chronicles 9:3: The queen saw both his wisdom and the buildings he had made. What she observed matched what she had heard, so his whole life backed up his reputation.
entries.2 chronicles 9:4: She saw his food, his well-ordered servants, their fine clothes, and his worship at the temple, and it left her breathless. The order and devotion of his court overwhelmed her.
entries.2 chronicles 9:5: She told the king that the reports she had heard in her own country were true. Seeing for herself confirmed what others had said about him.
entries.2 chronicles 9:6: She admitted she had not believed the reports until she came, and even then the reality was far greater than what was told her. Hearing about something great is never as convincing as seeing it.
entries.2 chronicles 9:7: She called his wives and servants happy because they were always near him and heard his wisdom. Being close to wisdom is a privilege worth valuing.
entries.2 chronicles 9:8: She praised the Lord for delighting in Solomon and placing him on the throne, and she saw God's love for Israel behind it. A good ruler is a sign of God's care for his people.
entries.2 chronicles 9:9: She gave him a huge amount of gold, spices, and jewels, more spices than anyone had ever seen. Her generosity matched the greatness she had witnessed.
entries.2 chronicles 9:10: Huram's servants and Solomon's servants brought back gold from Ophir along with sandalwood and jewels. Trade and cooperation brought wealth and rare materials into the kingdom.
entries.2 chronicles 9:11: The sandalwood was used for steps in the temple and palace and for musical instruments, unlike anything seen before in Judah. Rare gifts were turned into beauty and worship.
entries.2 chronicles 9:12: Solomon gave the queen everything she asked for, beyond what she had brought him, and she returned home with her servants. Generosity flowed both ways between them.
entries.2 chronicles 9:13: The gold that came to Solomon in a single year weighed six hundred and sixty-six talents. His wealth was enormous and steady, year after year.
entries.2 chronicles 9:14: On top of what traders brought, all the kings of Arabia and local rulers gave him gold and silver. His riches came from many directions, not just one source.
entries.2 chronicles 9:15: He made two hundred large shields of hammered gold, each using six hundred shekels of gold. Even his weapons and armor were made of precious metal.
entries.2 chronicles 9:16: He made three hundred smaller gold shields and stored them in a special palace building. His wealth was displayed in ceremonial armor kept in a showplace.
entries.2 chronicles 9:17: He made a large throne of ivory covered with the finest gold. The throne showed his high position and the value placed on his rule.
entries.2 chronicles 9:18: The throne had six steps, a gold footrest, and armrests with lions beside them. Every detail was designed to show dignity and strength.
entries.2 chronicles 9:19: Twelve lions stood on the steps, six on each side, and nothing like it existed in any other kingdom. His throne was unique and unmatched.
entries.2 chronicles 9:20: All his drinking cups and the vessels in the special palace were gold, and silver was not even valued in his day. His wealth was so great that ordinary precious metal seemed common.
entries.2 chronicles 9:21: His ships sailed with Huram's servants and returned every three years with gold, silver, ivory, monkeys, and peacocks. Long-distance trade brought exotic goods and great riches.
entries.2 chronicles 9:22: Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in both wealth and wisdom. God had given him a place above every other ruler of his time.
entries.2 chronicles 9:23: Kings from everywhere came to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart. His gift drew the world to him and pointed back to God as its source.
entries.2 chronicles 9:24: Each visitor brought gifts year after year: silver, gold, robes, armor, spices, horses, and transport animals. His wisdom and position made him the center of international respect.
entries.2 chronicles 9:25: He had four thousand stalls for horses and chariots and twelve thousand horsemen stationed in chariot cities and in Jerusalem. His military strength was vast and well organized.
entries.2 chronicles 9:26: He ruled over all the kings from the Euphrates River to Philistia and as far as Egypt's border. His kingdom stretched over a huge region.
entries.2 chronicles 9:27: He made silver as common as stones in Jerusalem and cedar as plentiful as sycamore trees in the lowlands. His wealth changed what was ordinary in the land.
entries.2 chronicles 9:28: Horses were brought to Solomon from Egypt and from every land. Even his supply of animals came from far and wide.
entries.2 chronicles 9:29: The rest of Solomon's deeds are recorded in the writings of the prophets Nathan, Ahijah, and Iddo. His story was written down by people who watched it happen.
entries.2 chronicles 9:30: Solomon ruled over Israel in Jerusalem for forty years. His reign was long and stable.
entries.2 chronicles 9:31: Solomon died and was buried in the city of David, and his son Rehoboam became king in his place. Even the wisest and richest king came to an end, and his kingdom passed to the next generation.
entries.2 chronicles 6:1: Solomon says that God has chosen to dwell in a thick cloud, a hidden and mysterious presence. It reminds the reader that God is real and near, yet far beyond what we can see or control.
entries.2 chronicles 6:2: Solomon has built a grand house for God to dwell in among his people forever. For the reader, it shows the desire to give God a lasting place of honor in the community.
entries.2 chronicles 6:3: Solomon turns to the whole crowd of Israelites and blesses them while they stand to listen. It shows a leader caring for his people and a community standing together before God.
entries.2 chronicles 6:4: Solomon praises God for keeping the promise he made to his father David and for making it happen by his own power. Readers are reminded that God's words can be trusted and that he acts to fulfill them.
entries.2 chronicles 6:5: God recalls that since bringing Israel out of Egypt he had never picked a particular town for his house or a particular man to lead his people. It shows that this new choice of Jerusalem and David's line was God's own initiative.
entries.2 chronicles 6:6: God has now chosen Jerusalem as the place for his name and David as the ruler over Israel. For the reader, it shows that God chooses specific people and places to carry out his purposes.
entries.2 chronicles 6:7: Solomon remembers that his father David deeply wanted to build a house for God. It shows that good desires to honor God matter, even when we are not the ones who complete them.
entries.2 chronicles 6:8: God told David that his desire to build the house was good. Readers learn that God sees and values our intentions to honor him, even if he has different plans for how they unfold.
entries.2 chronicles 6:9: God explained that David would not build the house; his son would do it instead. It teaches that God's plans often pass from one generation to the next, and that is not a failure but his design.
entries.2 chronicles 6:10: Solomon says God has kept his promise: he now sits on David's throne and has built the house for God. It shows that God's promises come true in real, visible ways.
entries.2 chronicles 6:11: Solomon has placed the ark, which holds God's covenant with Israel, inside the house. It reminds the reader that God's promises and his presence go together.
entries.2 chronicles 6:12: Solomon stands before the altar in front of all the people. It shows a leader praying publicly, inviting the whole community to witness his dependence on God.
entries.2 chronicles 6:13: Solomon had a bronze platform made, and he knelt on it with his hands raised toward heaven in front of everyone. It shows humble, earnest prayer and reminds the reader that kneeling before God is fitting even for a king.
entries.2 chronicles 6:14: Solomon prays that there is no God like the Lord, who keeps his faithful love toward those who wholeheartedly follow him. Readers are invited to trust a God whose character and commitment never change.
entries.2 chronicles 6:15: Solomon thanks God for keeping the promise he spoke to David and for making it happen. It encourages the reader to notice and thank God when his words prove true.
entries.2 chronicles 6:16: Solomon asks God to keep his promise that David's line would always have a ruler, as long as his descendants obey God's law. It shows that God's promises often come with the call to faithful obedience.
entries.2 chronicles 6:17: Solomon prays simply that God will do what he said. It models a plain, trusting prayer that holds God to his own promises.
entries.2 chronicles 6:18: Solomon marvels that God, whom even the vast heavens cannot contain, would dwell with people on earth, let alone in this house. It reminds the reader how astonishing and gracious it is that God comes near to us.
entries.2 chronicles 6:19: Solomon asks God to pay attention to his prayer and plea for mercy. It shows that ordinary people can boldly ask God to listen and care.
entries.2 chronicles 6:20: Solomon asks God to watch over this house day and night and to hear prayers made toward it. Readers learn that God invites people to bring their prayers to a place set apart for him.
entries.2 chronicles 6:21: Solomon asks God to hear the prayers of his people when they turn toward this place, and to forgive from heaven. It shows that God hears from his dwelling place and responds with mercy.
entries.2 chronicles 6:22: Solomon describes a case where someone wrongs a neighbor and comes to God's altar to swear an oath about it. It shows that God's house is a place where serious matters and truth are brought before him.
entries.2 chronicles 6:23: Solomon asks God to judge fairly from heaven, punishing the guilty and clearing the innocent. It reminds the reader that God sees the truth and cares about justice.
entries.2 chronicles 6:24: Solomon prays for the case where Israel is defeated in war because of sin, then turns back to God and prays in this house. It shows that turning back to God is always the right response to failure.
entries.2 chronicles 6:25: Solomon asks God to forgive his people and bring them back to their land. It reminds the reader that God's forgiveness includes restoration, not just pardon.
entries.2 chronicles 6:26: Solomon describes drought coming because of sin, and the people turning toward this place, honoring God and repenting. It shows that hardship can lead people back to God.
entries.2 chronicles 6:27: Solomon asks God to forgive, teach the right way to live, and send rain on the land. Readers see that God's forgiveness and his guidance go together, and that he cares about daily needs like rain.
entries.2 chronicles 6:28: Solomon lists many kinds of trouble: famine, disease, crop damage, locusts, and enemies surrounding towns. It shows that no hardship is outside the reach of prayer.
entries.2 chronicles 6:29: Solomon says that whatever trouble any person has, if they stretch out their hands toward this house in prayer, God should hear. It reminds the reader that personal pain is always welcome before God.
entries.2 chronicles 6:30: Solomon asks God to hear from heaven, forgive, and give each person what their ways deserve, since only God knows every heart. It shows that God sees what others cannot and judges with full knowledge.
entries.2 chronicles 6:31: Solomon prays that people will worship God and walk in his ways for as long as they live in the land. It reminds the reader that answered prayer should lead to a life that honors God.
