entries.2 chronicles 6:32: Solomon includes foreigners who come from far away because they have heard of God's greatness, and who pray toward this house. It shows that God's welcome is not limited to one nation.
entries.2 chronicles 6:33: Solomon asks God to give the foreigner what he asks, so that all peoples may know God's name and worship him. It reminds the reader that God's blessing is meant to draw others to himself.
entries.2 chronicles 6:34: Solomon prays for soldiers sent out to war who turn toward this city and house in prayer. It shows that even in conflict, people are invited to depend on God.
entries.2 chronicles 6:35: Solomon asks God to hear their prayer from heaven and to see that justice is done for them. It reminds the reader that God cares about fairness and the outcome of hard situations.
entries.2 chronicles 6:36: Solomon admits that no one is without sin, and describes the people being defeated and taken captive to a distant land. It shows an honest view of human failure and the real consequences sin can bring.
entries.2 chronicles 6:37: Solomon pictures the captives coming to their senses in that far land, turning back to God, and confessing that they have sinned and done wrong. It shows that honest confession is the first step back to God.
entries.2 chronicles 6:38: Solomon describes the captives turning back to God with all their heart and soul, praying toward their land, city, and this house. It reminds the reader that wholehearted repentance reaches God even from far away.
entries.2 chronicles 6:39: Solomon asks God to hear from heaven, act justly, and forgive his people who have sinned against him. It shows that God's forgiveness is available even after serious failure.
entries.2 chronicles 6:40: Solomon closes by asking God to keep his eyes open and his ears attentive to the prayers made in this place. It reminds the reader that God is not distant or deaf but attentive to those who pray.
entries.2 chronicles 10:1: Rehoboam, Solomon's son, traveled to Shechem where the people of Israel had gathered to crown him as their new king. This was the moment he would officially take over from his father.
entries.2 chronicles 10:2: Jeroboam had fled to Egypt earlier to escape King Solomon, and when he heard what was happening in Israel, he returned home. His return set him up to become a leader among the people.
entries.2 chronicles 10:3: The people sent for Jeroboam to come, and he joined all of Israel in approaching the new king Rehoboam together. They came as a united group with a request.
entries.2 chronicles 10:4: The people told Rehoboam that his father Solomon had made their lives very hard, and they asked him to lighten the load; if he did, they promised to serve him loyally. They were offering their loyalty in exchange for fairer treatment.
entries.2 chronicles 10:5: Rehoboam told them to come back in three days, so the people left to wait. He wanted time to think about his answer before responding.
entries.2 chronicles 10:6: Rehoboam asked the older men who had advised his father Solomon what answer he should give the people. He was seeking wisdom from those with long experience.
entries.2 chronicles 10:7: The older men advised him to be kind and speak gently to the people, because that would win their lasting loyalty. Their advice was that kindness builds a stronger kingdom than harshness.
entries.2 chronicles 10:8: Rehoboam ignored the older men's advice and instead turned to the young men he had grown up with, who now served him. He chose to listen to people his own age rather than those with experience.
entries.2 chronicles 10:9: Rehoboam asked the young men what answer he should give to the people's request to lighten the heavy burden his father had placed on them. He was looking for their opinion on the same question.
entries.2 chronicles 10:10: The young men told him to answer the people with a boast: that his little finger was thicker than his father's whole body, meaning he would be even stronger and harsher than Solomon. Their advice was arrogant and designed to intimidate.
entries.2 chronicles 10:11: The young men told him to threaten the people with even harder treatment than his father gave, saying his father punished them with whips but he would punish them with scorpions. This was a cruel and threatening answer.
entries.2 chronicles 10:12: Jeroboam and all the people came back to Rehoboam on the third day, just as the king had told them to. They were expecting his answer to their request.
entries.2 chronicles 10:13: The king answered the people harshly and ignored the wise advice of the older men. He chose confrontation over kindness.
entries.2 chronicles 10:14: Rehoboam gave the people the answer the young men had suggested, threatening to make their burden heavier and to punish them more severely than his father did. He followed the arrogant advice instead of the wise counsel.
entries.2 chronicles 10:15: The king refused to listen to the people, and this happened because God was carrying out what he had already announced through the prophet Ahijah to Jeroboam. Even the king's bad decision fit into God's larger plan.
entries.2 chronicles 10:16: When the people saw the king would not listen to them, they rejected the family of David, declaring they had no share in him, and they went home. This was the moment the kingdom split apart.
entries.2 chronicles 10:17: Rehoboam continued to rule only over the Israelites who lived in the towns of Judah. His kingdom was now much smaller than his father's had been.
entries.2 chronicles 10:18: Rehoboam sent Adoniram, the official in charge of forced labor, to the people, but they stoned him to death; Rehoboam quickly fled in his chariot to Jerusalem. The situation had turned violent and the king barely escaped.
entries.2 chronicles 10:19: From that time on, Israel has been separated from the family of David. The division between the northern tribes and David's line became permanent.
entries.2 chronicles 12:1: Once Rehoboam felt secure and strong as king, he and the whole nation stopped following God's law. It warns that success can make us careless about God.
entries.2 chronicles 12:2: Five years into his reign, Egypt's king Shishak attacked Jerusalem because the people had sinned against God. It shows that turning from God can bring real trouble.
entries.2 chronicles 12:3: Shishak came with a huge army of chariots, horsemen, and countless soldiers from several nations. The forces against them were overwhelming, showing how serious the threat was.
entries.2 chronicles 12:4: Shishak captured the fortified towns of Judah and advanced all the way to Jerusalem. The enemy was now at the capital's doorstep.
entries.2 chronicles 12:5: The prophet Shemaiah told the king and leaders that because they had abandoned God, God had let them fall into Shishak's hands. It is a direct explanation of why they were in danger.
entries.2 chronicles 12:6: The king and leaders humbled themselves and admitted that God was right. Admitting we were wrong is the first step toward mercy.
entries.2 chronicles 12:7: When God saw their humility, he told them he would not destroy them but would soon rescue them. God responds with mercy to genuine humility.
entries.2 chronicles 12:8: Still, they would serve Shishak for a time, so they could learn how much better God's rule is than serving foreign kings. Hard lessons can teach us the value of belonging to God.
entries.2 chronicles 12:9: Shishak took all the treasures of the temple and the palace, including the gold shields Solomon had made. Sin cost them the wealth and glory they had enjoyed.
entries.2 chronicles 12:10: Rehoboam replaced the gold shields with bronze ones and gave them to his guards. The cheaper substitute showed how far the kingdom's glory had fallen.
entries.2 chronicles 12:11: The guards carried the bronze shields whenever the king went to the temple and then returned them to storage. It became a regular reminder of what had been lost.
entries.2 chronicles 12:12: Because Rehoboam humbled himself, God held back his anger and did not destroy him completely, since there was still some good in Judah. God's judgment is tempered by mercy.
entries.2 chronicles 12:13: Rehoboam grew strong again and ruled in Jerusalem for seventeen years, starting at age forty-one; his mother was Naamah from Ammon. God had chosen Jerusalem as his special city.
entries.2 chronicles 12:14: Rehoboam did evil because his heart was not truly committed to the Lord. Outward success means little if the heart is not loyal to God.
entries.2 chronicles 12:15: The rest of Rehoboam's record was written by the prophets Shemaiah and Iddo, and he was at war with Jeroboam throughout his reign. His story is preserved honestly, both good and bad.
entries.2 chronicles 12:16: Rehoboam died and was buried in the city of David, and his son Abijah became king. One king's reign ends and another begins, but God's plan continues.
entries.2 chronicles 6:41: Solomon asks God to come and dwell among his people, bringing his saving help to the priests and joy to those who belong to him. It invites the reader to welcome God's presence and to want his goodness to shape their life and worship.
entries.2 chronicles 6:42: Solomon pleads with God not to reject the king he has chosen, and asks him to remember the faithful love he promised to David. For the reader, it is a reminder to rely on God's promises and to trust that he keeps his word.
entries.2 chronicles 11:1: Rehoboam gathered a huge army from Judah and Benjamin to fight the northern tribes and win back the kingdom he had lost. It shows how quickly people reach for war when they feel wronged.
entries.2 chronicles 11:2: God spoke to a prophet named Shemaiah and gave him a message to deliver. God still steps into human plans and speaks through people.
entries.2 chronicles 11:3: The message was addressed to King Rehoboam and to all the people of Judah and Benjamin. God's word came to the whole nation, not just the king.
entries.2 chronicles 11:4: God told them not to fight their own relatives, because what had happened was his doing, and they obeyed and went home. Sometimes the right response is to stop and trust God instead of forcing our own way.
entries.2 chronicles 11:5: Rehoboam stayed in Jerusalem and put his effort into building up fortified towns in Judah. After giving up the war, he focused on protecting what he still had.
entries.2 chronicles 11:6: This lists the first towns he fortified, including Bethlehem and Tekoa. These were real places where people lived and needed protection.
entries.2 chronicles 11:7: The list continues with more towns he strengthened. Each name represents a community he was responsible to defend.
entries.2 chronicles 11:8: More towns are named as part of his building program. The detail shows he worked steadily across the region.
entries.2 chronicles 11:9: The list of fortified towns goes on. Rehoboam was preparing for trouble rather than being caught off guard.
entries.2 chronicles 11:10: The final towns are named, in both Judah and Benjamin. He strengthened his whole territory, not just one area.
entries.2 chronicles 11:11: He made the towns strong, put commanders in them, and stocked them with food, oil, and wine. Good leadership prepares for hard times.
entries.2 chronicles 11:12: He also stored weapons in every town and made them very strong, and Judah and Benjamin stayed loyal to him. Preparation and loyalty went together.
entries.2 chronicles 11:13: Priests and Levites from all over Israel came to him. People will move toward a place where God is honored.
entries.2 chronicles 11:14: The Levites left their homes and property and came to Judah because Jeroboam had pushed them out and wouldn't let them serve as priests. Standing for God can cost you, but it is worth it.
entries.2 chronicles 11:15: Jeroboam appointed his own priests for shrines and for idols shaped like goats and calves. When people reject God's way, they invent substitutes.
entries.2 chronicles 11:16: People from every tribe who were truly devoted to the Lord followed the Levites to Jerusalem to worship the God of their ancestors. Real faith shows itself in what people are willing to leave behind.
entries.2 chronicles 11:17: For three years they strengthened the kingdom of Judah and helped Rehoboam, and during that time they followed the ways of David and Solomon. Good leadership grows when people walk with God.
entries.2 chronicles 11:18: Rehoboam married Mahalath, who was from David's family line. Marriages like this were often about keeping family and tribal ties strong.
entries.2 chronicles 11:19: She gave him three sons. The record of his family shows how his household grew.
entries.2 chronicles 11:20: He then married Maacah, Absalom's daughter, and she had four sons by him. Family connections kept shaping his reign.
entries.2 chronicles 11:21: Rehoboam loved Maacah more than all his other wives, and he had many wives and children. Having many wives was common for kings then, but it brought complications.
entries.2 chronicles 11:22: He made Maacah's son Abijah the chief among his brothers because he intended him to be king. A father's favoritism shaped who would lead next.
entries.2 chronicles 11:23: He wisely spread his sons among the fortified towns, gave them plenty of supplies, and found wives for them. He acted shrewdly to keep his family settled and loyal.
entries.2 chronicles 14:1: Abijah died and was buried in Jerusalem, and his son Asa took over as king. During Asa's early years the country had peace for ten years, which sets up the story that follows.
entries.2 chronicles 14:2: Asa lived in a way that God saw as good and right. The writer is telling us that this king's choices lined up with what God wanted.
entries.2 chronicles 14:3: Asa removed the places and objects used to worship other gods, including stone and wooden idols. He cleared out the things that had been pulling people away from God.
entries.2 chronicles 14:4: Asa urged the people of Judah to seek the Lord, the God their ancestors had followed, and to obey his commands. He wanted the whole nation to turn back to God.
entries.2 chronicles 14:5: Asa also removed the local shrines and sun idols from the towns of Judah. Because of this, the kingdom had peace while he ruled.
entries.2 chronicles 14:6: Asa built up fortified towns in Judah while the land was peaceful and no wars were happening, since God had given him rest. Peace gave him room to prepare and strengthen the country.
entries.2 chronicles 14:7: Asa told the people to build walls, towers, and gates around their towns while they still had the land. He said God had given them rest because they had stayed faithful to him, so the building work went well.
entries.2 chronicles 14:8: Asa had a large army: 300,000 from Judah with shields and spears, and 280,000 from Benjamin with shields and bows. These were all trained fighting men.
entries.2 chronicles 14:9: Zerah the Ethiopian came against them with a huge army of a million men and 300 chariots, advancing to Mareshah. The odds against Asa were enormous.
entries.2 chronicles 14:10: Asa went out to meet him, and the two armies lined up for battle in the valley north of Mareshah. The stage was set for a fight.
entries.2 chronicles 14:11: Asa prayed to God, admitting that only God can help the weak against the strong. He said their hope was in God and asked him to keep mere human power from winning over him.
entries.2 chronicles 14:12: God struck fear into the Ethiopians in front of Asa and Judah, and they ran away. God answered the prayer and turned the battle around.
entries.2 chronicles 14:13: Asa and his men chased them as far as Gerar and destroyed so many that the enemy army could not regroup, because they were broken before the Lord and his army. The men of Judah carried off a great deal of plunder.
entries.2 chronicles 14:14: They also captured all the towns around Gerar, because God had put fear of them on those places. From those towns they took a large amount of goods.
entries.2 chronicles 14:15: They attacked the camps where the cattle owners lived and took many sheep and camels, then returned to Jerusalem. The victory God gave them brought great wealth as well.
entries.2 chronicles 15:1: God's Spirit came upon Azariah, giving him a message to deliver. This shows God still speaks through people to guide His followers.
entries.2 chronicles 15:2: Azariah told King Asa that God stays close to those who stay close to Him, but turns away from those who abandon Him. The same choice faces every reader: seek God and find Him near.
entries.2 chronicles 15:3: For a long time Israel had lived without God, without priests to teach them, and without His law. Life without God's guidance leaves people spiritually lost.
entries.2 chronicles 15:4: Whenever the people turned back to God in their trouble and looked for Him, He let them find Him. No matter how far someone has drifted, God welcomes those who turn back.
entries.2 chronicles 15:5: In those days travel was unsafe and trouble was everywhere. When people abandon God, life becomes chaotic and unstable.
entries.2 chronicles 15:6: Nations and towns were torn apart by conflict, and God allowed this trouble as discipline. Division and strife are the fruit of turning away from Him.
entries.2 chronicles 15:7: Azariah urged Asa to be strong and not give up, promising that his effort would be rewarded. Faithful work for God is never wasted.
entries.2 chronicles 15:8: Encouraged by the prophet's words, Asa removed the idols from his land and repaired the Lord's altar. Hearing God's word should move us to clean up our lives and restore our devotion.
entries.2 chronicles 15:9: Asa gathered Judah, Benjamin, and many from Israel who had moved to him because they saw God was with him. When God's presence is evident in a life, others are drawn toward it.
entries.2 chronicles 15:10: The people assembled in Jerusalem in the fifteenth year of Asa's reign. This was a planned national gathering to seek God together.
entries.2 chronicles 15:11: They sacrificed animals captured in war as offerings to the Lord. They gave back to God from what they had gained, honoring Him with their success.
entries.2 chronicles 15:12: The people committed themselves to follow the Lord wholeheartedly. A real commitment to God involves the heart and the will, not just words.
entries.2 chronicles 15:13: Anyone who refused to be loyal to the Lord was to be put to death, showing how seriously this agreement was taken. In that era, loyalty to God was treated as a matter of life and death for the whole community.
entries.2 chronicles 15:14: They sealed their promise to God with a loud oath, accompanied by trumpets and horns. Publicly declaring commitment to God strengthens resolve and unites people.
entries.2 chronicles 15:15: All Judah rejoiced over the oath because they had made it sincerely and sought God with all their desire, and He gave them peace. Wholehearted seeking of God brings joy and rest.
entries.2 chronicles 15:16: Asa removed his own grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she had made an idol for Asherah, and he destroyed the image. Loyalty to God must come before family ties, even when it is costly.
entries.2 chronicles 15:17: The high places were not removed from Israel, yet Asa's heart remained fully devoted to the Lord throughout his life. God looks at the heart's direction even when a person's reforms are incomplete.
entries.2 chronicles 15:18: Asa brought into God's house the silver, gold, and articles that had been dedicated to God by his father and by himself. Honoring God with valuable gifts is a way of showing devotion.
entries.2 chronicles 15:19: There was no war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa's reign. His faithfulness to God brought a long period of peace to the nation.
entries.2 chronicles 16:1: Baasha, king of the northern kingdom, attacked Judah and built a town to block traffic in and out, cutting Asa off. It shows how a threat can close in on us and push us to look for a way out.
entries.2 chronicles 16:2: Instead of asking God for help, Asa took money from the temple and his own treasury to buy an ally. We can be tempted to solve problems with money or deals rather than trusting God.
entries.2 chronicles 16:3: Asa asked the king of Aram to break his treaty with Baasha and side with him, offering silver and gold as payment. It is a reminder that relying on human deals can replace relying on God.
entries.2 chronicles 16:4: Ben-hadad agreed and sent his armies to attack northern Israel's towns, doing what Asa wanted. The plan worked, but it was built on a bargain rather than on God.
entries.2 chronicles 16:5: When Baasha heard his towns were under attack, he stopped building and left. The pressure eased, but not because Asa had trusted God.
entries.2 chronicles 16:6: Asa and the people of Judah took the leftover stones and wood from Baasha's project and used them to build two of their own towns. What was meant to trap them became useful material.
entries.2 chronicles 16:7: A prophet named Hanani told Asa that because he trusted the king of Aram instead of God, he lost the chance to defeat that king. Trusting the wrong thing can cost us a victory God wanted to give.
entries.2 chronicles 16:8: Hanani reminded Asa of the huge Ethiopian army God had once helped him defeat because he trusted God then. Remembering past help from God can show us what we should do now.
entries.2 chronicles 16:9: God is always watching, ready to strengthen people whose hearts are fully his, and Hanani told Asa he had acted foolishly and would face wars from then on. God looks for wholehearted trust, and our choices have real consequences.
entries.2 chronicles 16:10: Asa got angry at the prophet and put him in prison, and he also treated some of the people harshly. Being corrected can make us defensive, but lashing out only makes things worse.
entries.2 chronicles 16:11: This notes that the rest of Asa's life was written down in the official records of the kings. It reminds us that our whole life story is recorded and matters.
entries.2 chronicles 16:12: In his later years Asa got a severe foot disease but looked only to doctors and did not turn to the Lord. Seeking medical help is fine, but leaving God out of our troubles is a mistake.
entries.2 chronicles 16:13: Asa died and was buried with his ancestors after ruling forty-one years. Even a long reign ends, and how we finish matters.
entries.2 chronicles 16:14: He was buried in a tomb he had prepared, laid on a bed of fragrant spices, and the people held a great fire in his honor. The honor shown at his burial contrasts with the sad way his trust in God had faded.
entries.2 chronicles 17:1: Jehoshaphat took over as king after his father and made his position strong against the northern kingdom of Israel. It reminds readers that new leaders must secure their footing, but true strength comes from God.
entries.2 chronicles 17:2: He stationed troops in Judah's fortified cities and appointed officials throughout Judah and in the Ephraimite towns his father had captured. Good leadership means protecting your people and organizing responsibly.
entries.2 chronicles 17:3: God was with Jehoshaphat because he followed his father's early example of faith and did not worship the false gods called Baals. Following good examples and staying loyal to God brings his presence.
entries.2 chronicles 17:4: Instead he sought the God of his father, obeyed his commands, and refused to copy the sinful ways of Israel. Each person must choose to follow God rather than imitate bad examples.
entries.2 chronicles 17:5: Because of his faithfulness, God strengthened his kingdom, and the people gave him gifts so that he became very rich and respected. God honors those who honor him, often with stability and blessing.
entries.2 chronicles 17:6: He was deeply committed to the Lord's ways and even removed the illegal worship sites and sacred poles from Judah. Real devotion shows itself in action, including getting rid of things that lead people away from God.
entries.2 chronicles 17:7: In his third year as king, he sent five of his officials out to teach in the towns of Judah. A good leader invests in teaching people what is right.
entries.2 chronicles 17:8: He sent Levites and priests along with those officials to help with the teaching. Teaching works best when people with different skills work together.
entries.2 chronicles 17:9: They traveled through all Judah teaching the people and carrying the book of the Lord's law with them. God's word should be shared widely so everyone can learn how to live.
entries.2 chronicles 17:10: The surrounding kingdoms became afraid of the Lord and did not attack Jehoshaphat. When God is with someone, even enemies are held back.
entries.2 chronicles 17:11: Some Philistines brought him gifts and silver, and Arabians brought him thousands of sheep and goats. God can turn former enemies into sources of blessing.
entries.2 chronicles 17:12: Jehoshaphat grew stronger and stronger, building fortresses and storage cities in Judah. Steady growth and careful preparation are wise, as long as God remains the source.
entries.2 chronicles 17:13: He had large supplies in Judah's towns and a strong army stationed in Jerusalem. A wise leader prepares resources and protection for the people he serves.
entries.2 chronicles 17:14: The army was organized by family groups, starting with Adnah who commanded three hundred thousand soldiers. Order and clear leadership make any group effective.
entries.2 chronicles 17:15: Next was Jehohanan with two hundred eighty thousand men. Each leader had a defined role, showing that teamwork requires structure.
entries.2 chronicles 17:16: Then came Amasiah, who volunteered himself willingly to the Lord, with two hundred thousand soldiers. God values people who serve him eagerly, not just out of duty.
entries.2 chronicles 17:17: From Benjamin came Eliada, a mighty warrior, with two hundred thousand men armed with bows and shields. Courage and readiness matter, but they should be offered to God.
entries.2 chronicles 17:18: After him was Jehozabad with a hundred eighty thousand men trained for battle. Training and discipline are important parts of serving well.
entries.2 chronicles 17:19: These troops served the king in Jerusalem, in addition to those he stationed in the fortified towns throughout Judah. Strong defense requires both a central force and local protection.
entries.2 chronicles 19:1: Jehoshaphat returned home safely to Jerusalem after being involved in a battle. It shows God brought him back unharmed even though he had made a bad choice.
entries.2 chronicles 19:2: A prophet named Jehu confronted the king for helping wicked King Ahab, who hated God, and told him God was angry about it. It reminds us that who we team up with matters to God.
entries.2 chronicles 19:3: Even so, God saw real good in Jehoshaphat because he had removed idols from the land and set his heart on worshiping God. God notices the good we do, even when we fail in other ways.
entries.2 chronicles 19:4: Jehoshaphat stayed in Jerusalem and traveled throughout the land, urging people to turn back to the God of their ancestors. Leaders can help people find their way back to God.
entries.2 chronicles 19:5: He appointed judges in every fortified town of Judah to settle disputes. Good leadership means making sure people have fair and honest people to decide their cases.
entries.2 chronicles 19:6: He told the judges to be careful because they were deciding cases for God, not just for people, and God was with them. Whatever work we do for others should be done remembering God is watching.
entries.2 chronicles 19:7: He urged them to honor God and work carefully, because God is fair and shows no favoritism and takes no bribes. We can trust God to be perfectly fair, and we should aim to be fair too.
entries.2 chronicles 19:8: Jehoshaphat also set up Levites, priests, and family leaders in Jerusalem to handle cases involving God's law and disputes among the people. Having trustworthy people in place helps a community run justly.
entries.2 chronicles 19:9: He ordered them to serve with respect for God, faithfully and with whole hearts. Doing our work honestly and sincerely is what God asks of us.
entries.2 chronicles 19:10: He warned them to handle serious cases carefully so no one would be guilty before God, which would bring trouble on everyone. Careless decisions can hurt many people, so we should take our responsibilities seriously.
entries.2 chronicles 19:11: He put the high priest in charge of religious matters and a family leader over the king's affairs, with Levites as helpers, and told them to be strong because God is with those who do right. We can work boldly when we know God stands with those who are honest.
entries.2 chronicles 13:1: This verse simply dates when Abijah became king of Judah, during the reign of Israel's king Jeroboam. It reminds the reader that these events happened at a real point in history, with two kings ruling at the same time.
entries.2 chronicles 13:2: Abijah ruled in Jerusalem for only three years, and his mother was Maacah; a war broke out between him and Jeroboam. It shows that his short reign was marked by conflict from the start.
entries.2 chronicles 13:3: Abijah marched out with 400,000 trained soldiers, while Jeroboam lined up 800,000 against him. The reader sees that Abijah was badly outnumbered, setting up the story of how the battle would be won.
entries.2 chronicles 13:4: Abijah stood on a hill in the territory of Ephraim and called out to Jeroboam and all Israel to listen to him. He wanted to make his case publicly before the fighting began.
entries.2 chronicles 13:5: Abijah says it should be obvious that God gave the throne of Israel to David and his descendants permanently, under a binding agreement. He is arguing that fighting against David's line means fighting against what God set up.
entries.2 chronicles 13:6: Abijah points out that Jeroboam, who had served Solomon, rebelled against his own king. He is framing Jeroboam as a traitor rather than a legitimate ruler.
entries.2 chronicles 13:7: Abijah says worthless, reckless men gathered around Jeroboam and overpowered Rehoboam when he was young and inexperienced. He claims Jeroboam's rise came through force, not through God's choice.
entries.2 chronicles 13:8: Abijah accuses Jeroboam of planning to resist the authority God gave to David's descendants, trusting in his huge army and in the golden calves he had made as gods. He is saying their strength and their idols are no match for God's rightful king.
entries.2 chronicles 13:9: Abijah charges that Jeroboam had thrown out God's real priests and let anyone become a priest just by bringing an animal sacrifice, like the nations around them. He is pointing out that their worship had been replaced with something man-made.
entries.2 chronicles 13:10: In contrast, Abijah says Judah has not abandoned the Lord, and still has the proper priests from Aaron's family and the Levites serving in their places. He presents Judah as the side still faithful to God.
entries.2 chronicles 13:11: Abijah describes the daily worship in Judah: sacrifices every morning and evening, the sacred bread on the table, and the lamps lit each evening, all done as God commanded. He is saying Judah kept God's instructions while Israel walked away from them.
entries.2 chronicles 13:12: Abijah declares that God himself leads Judah, with priests blowing trumpets against the enemy, and warns Israel not to fight against the Lord. He is telling them that opposing Judah means opposing God and will end badly.
entries.2 chronicles 13:13: While Abijah was speaking, Jeroboam had secretly sent troops around behind Judah, so Judah was surrounded front and back. It shows the enemy used a sneaky trap rather than fair, open battle.
entries.2 chronicles 13:14: When Judah realized they were attacked from both sides, they cried out to the Lord while the priests blew their trumpets. In a desperate moment, their first move was to call on God.
entries.2 chronicles 13:15: As the men of Judah shouted, God threw Jeroboam and all Israel into panic before Abijah and Judah. The victory came from God's action, not just from Judah's shouting.
entries.2 chronicles 13:16: The Israelites ran away from Judah, and God handed them over to Judah's army. The text makes clear that God gave the victory.
entries.2 chronicles 13:17: Abijah's army struck down 500,000 of Israel's best soldiers in a massive defeat. The huge number shows how complete the rout was.
entries.2 chronicles 13:18: Israel was defeated that day and Judah won because they trusted in the Lord, the God of their ancestors. The writer names their trust in God as the reason for the outcome.
entries.2 chronicles 13:19: Abijah chased Jeroboam and captured several of his towns, including Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron with their surrounding villages. The victory was not just on the battlefield but also in taking territory.
entries.2 chronicles 13:20: Jeroboam never regained his strength during Abijah's lifetime, and the Lord struck him down. It shows that the one who fought against God's chosen line did not recover.
entries.2 chronicles 13:21: Abijah grew powerful and had fourteen wives, twenty-two sons, and sixteen daughters. In that culture, a large family was a sign of strength and blessing.
entries.2 chronicles 13:22: The rest of Abijah's deeds, his conduct, and his words were written down in the records of the prophet Iddo. It tells the reader that more about him was recorded elsewhere, even if not included here.
entries.2 chronicles 18:1: Jehoshaphat was very rich and respected, and he tied his family to wicked King Ahab by marrying his son to Ahab's daughter. Good things in life can quietly pull us into bad company and bad choices.
entries.2 chronicles 18:2: After some years Jehoshaphat visited Ahab, who threw a huge feast and then talked him into joining a war at Ramoth-gilead. Being treated well can make us agree to things we should think about first.
entries.2 chronicles 18:3: Ahab asked Jehoshaphat to fight with him, and Jehoshaphat promised they and their armies were as one. It is easy to promise too much to the wrong person.
entries.2 chronicles 18:4: Jehoshaphat wisely said they should first ask the Lord what to do. Before big decisions, we should ask God rather than just go along with others.
entries.2 chronicles 18:5: Ahab gathered four hundred prophets, and they all told him to go and fight because God would give him victory. A large crowd saying the same thing does not make it true.
entries.2 chronicles 18:6: Jehoshaphat asked if there was another prophet of the Lord they could ask. It is wise to look for someone who truly speaks for God, not just people who agree with us.
entries.2 chronicles 18:7: Ahab admitted there was one prophet, Micaiah, but he hated him because he never predicted good things for him. We should not reject truth just because it is not what we want to hear.
entries.2 chronicles 18:8: Ahab sent an official to bring Micaiah quickly. The king wanted God's answer, but only on his own terms.
entries.2 chronicles 18:9: The two kings sat in their royal robes at the city gate while all the prophets performed before them. It looked impressive, but appearance is not the same as truth.
entries.2 chronicles 18:10: Zedekiah made iron horns and declared that with them the king would crush the Arameans. People can act very confident and dramatic while still being wrong.
entries.2 chronicles 18:11: All the prophets agreed: go up and win, because the Lord will give victory. Everyone agreeing does not mean God is behind it.
entries.2 chronicles 18:12: The messenger told Micaiah that all the prophets were saying good things, so he should say the same. There is pressure to just go along with the crowd, but that is not always right.
entries.2 chronicles 18:13: Micaiah said that as surely as the Lord lives, he would say only what God told him. We should be committed to telling the truth even when it is unpopular.
entries.2 chronicles 18:14: At first Micaiah gave the same answer as the other prophets: go up and succeed. The king could tell he was not speaking sincerely.
entries.2 chronicles 18:15: The king made Micaiah swear to tell him only the truth in the Lord's name. Ahab wanted the truth, but only after he had tried to avoid it.
entries.2 chronicles 18:16: Micaiah saw Israel scattered like sheep with no shepherd, and the Lord said to send them home in peace. The vision meant the king would be gone and the people left without a leader.
entries.2 chronicles 18:17: Ahab told Jehoshaphat that Micaiah never prophesied anything good for him. He heard the truth but only complained about it.
entries.2 chronicles 18:18: Micaiah told them to listen to the Lord's word: he saw the Lord on his throne with all heaven's army standing around him. God is the true ruler over everything that happens.
entries.2 chronicles 18:19: The Lord asked how Ahab could be persuaded to go to Ramoth-gilead and die there, and different suggestions were made. Even the death of a king is under God's control.
entries.2 chronicles 18:20: A spirit came forward and offered to trick Ahab, and the Lord asked how it would do it.
entries.2 chronicles 18:21: The spirit said it would put lies in the mouths of all Ahab's prophets, and the Lord told it to go and do so. The false prophets were speaking lies, and God allowed it as judgment on Ahab.
entries.2 chronicles 18:22: Micaiah told Ahab that the Lord had put a lying spirit in his prophets' mouths and had declared disaster against him. The comfortable words Ahab wanted were actually leading him to ruin.
entries.2 chronicles 18:23: Zedekiah slapped Micaiah in the face and mocked him, asking where the Lord's spirit had gone. People often attack the messenger when they cannot stand the message.
entries.2 chronicles 18:24: Micaiah answered that Zedekiah would find out on the day he hid in an inner room for safety. The truth would be proven when disaster came.
entries.2 chronicles 18:25: Ahab ordered Micaiah taken back to the city officials. The king punished the man who told him the truth.
entries.2 chronicles 18:26: Ahab ordered Micaiah put in prison on bread and water until he returned safely. He was sure he would come back, but God had said otherwise.
entries.2 chronicles 18:27: Micaiah said that if Ahab returned safely, then the Lord had not spoken through him. He staked everything on God's word being true.
entries.2 chronicles 18:28: So Ahab and Jehoshaphat went up to Ramoth-gilead to fight. They went ahead even after hearing the warning.
entries.2 chronicles 18:29: Ahab disguised himself so he would not look like the king, and told Jehoshaphat to wear his royal robes. Ahab tried to protect himself by putting his ally in danger.
entries.2 chronicles 18:30: The king of Aram ordered his chariot commanders to attack only the king of Israel. The enemy focused on the one man they thought mattered most.
entries.2 chronicles 18:31: When the commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they thought he was the king of Israel and surrounded him, but he cried out and the Lord helped him and turned them away. God rescued Jehoshaphat even though he was in the wrong place.
entries.2 chronicles 18:32: When the commanders realized Jehoshaphat was not the king of Israel, they stopped chasing him. God's help came at just the right moment.
entries.2 chronicles 18:33: A soldier shot an arrow at random, and it struck Ahab between the parts of his armor, badly wounding him. What seemed like a random shot fulfilled God's word.
entries.2 chronicles 18:34: The battle went on all day, and Ahab stayed propped up in his chariot facing the Arameans until he died at sunset. The disguise did not save him; God's word came true.
entries.2 chronicles 22:1: Ahaziah became king of Judah because raiders had killed all his older brothers. This shows how quickly a family's plans can be overturned by violence.
entries.2 chronicles 22:2: Ahaziah was only twenty-two and ruled just one year; his mother Athaliah came from the family of Omri. It reminds us that a person's family background shapes them, for good or bad.
entries.2 chronicles 22:3: Ahaziah followed the wicked example of his mother's family, because his mother taught him to do evil. Parents have great power to lead their children toward right or wrong.
entries.2 chronicles 22:4: Ahaziah did what was evil in God's eyes because he took advice from his father's wicked relatives. The people we listen to can lead us toward our own harm.
entries.2 chronicles 22:5: Following their advice, Ahaziah joined Israel's king in a war against Aram, and the king of Israel was wounded. Bad counsel led him into a dangerous alliance.
entries.2 chronicles 22:6: Ahaziah went to visit the wounded king of Israel at Jezreel. A simple visit set him on a path he did not expect.
entries.2 chronicles 22:7: God had arranged that this visit would bring Ahaziah down, since he joined Jehoram against Jehu, whom God had chosen to destroy Ahab's family. God's purposes move forward even through ordinary decisions.
entries.2 chronicles 22:8: While Jehu was carrying out God's judgment on Ahab's family, he also killed Judah's princes and Ahaziah's relatives. Being tied to a doomed family brought them down too.
entries.2 chronicles 22:9: Ahaziah was found hiding in Samaria and was killed, but was buried with respect because of his good grandfather Jehoshaphat. His death left his family unable to hold the kingdom.
entries.2 chronicles 22:10: When Athaliah saw her son was dead, she ordered the killing of the rest of the royal family so she could take power. Ambition drove her to terrible cruelty.
entries.2 chronicles 22:11: Jehoshabeath, the king's daughter, secretly rescued baby Joash from the massacre and hid him with his nurse. One brave, quiet act saved the royal line.
entries.2 chronicles 22:12: Joash was hidden in God's house for six years while Athaliah ruled the land. God protected the child who would one day restore the throne.
entries.2 chronicles 21:1: Jehoshaphat died and was buried in Jerusalem, and his son Jehoram took over as king. This reminds us that leaders come and go, and each new generation inherits both the position and the choices that come with it.
entries.2 chronicles 21:2: Jehoshaphat had several other sons besides Jehoram. Knowing their names shows they were real people with a real stake in the family, which makes what happens next even more shocking.
entries.2 chronicles 21:3: Their father gave the younger sons generous gifts and some fortified towns, but he kept the throne for Jehoram because he was the firstborn. A father can provide for his children, but the eldest still carried the main responsibility.
entries.2 chronicles 21:4: Once Jehoram felt secure on the throne, he had his own brothers killed, along with some other leaders. Greed for power can turn a person against even their closest family, and that is a warning about what ambition can do to us.
entries.2 chronicles 21:5: Jehoram became king at thirty-two and ruled for eight years. The short record of his reign is a reminder that how long we live matters less than how we live.
entries.2 chronicles 21:6: Jehoram copied the evil practices of the northern kings, partly because he married into Ahab's family. The people we tie our lives to can pull us away from what is right, so our closest relationships matter more than we think.
entries.2 chronicles 21:7: God did not wipe out David's family line, because he had promised David that his descendants would always have a lasting place. God keeps his promises even when the people involved do not deserve it.
entries.2 chronicles 21:8: While Jehoram was king, the country of Edom broke free from Judah's control and set up its own king. Weak or bad leadership often leads to losses that affect everyone, not just the leader.
entries.2 chronicles 21:9: Jehoram took his army and chariots and attacked the Edomites at night, but they surrounded him. Even a bold plan can fail when God is not on your side.
entries.2 chronicles 21:10: Edom stayed free from then on, and another town, Libnah, also broke away, because Jehoram had turned away from the Lord. Turning from God can cost us things we never expected to lose.
entries.2 chronicles 21:11: Jehoram set up places for false worship in the hills and led the people of Jerusalem and Judah away from God. A leader's wrong choices can drag a whole community down with them.
entries.2 chronicles 21:12: The prophet Elijah sent Jehoram a letter from God, pointing out that he had not followed the good example of his father or grandfather. God notices when we ignore the good examples set before us.
entries.2 chronicles 21:13: The letter said Jehoram had copied the evil kings of the north and had killed his own brothers, who were better men than he was. Doing wrong and then hurting better people to protect yourself makes the wrong even worse.
entries.2 chronicles 21:14: God announced that disaster would come on Jehoram's people, his children, his wives, and everything he owned. A leader's choices do not stay contained; they affect the people closest to him.
entries.2 chronicles 21:15: Jehoram himself would suffer from a painful, ongoing stomach disease. The judgment was personal, and it would be slow and hard to ignore.
entries.2 chronicles 21:16: God stirred up the Philistines and the Arabs to attack Jehoram. When we set ourselves against God, trouble can come from directions we never saw coming.
entries.2 chronicles 21:17: The attackers broke into Judah and carried off the king's wealth, his sons, and his wives, leaving him only his youngest son. Jehoram lost almost everything he had built his life around.
entries.2 chronicles 21:18: After all that, the Lord struck Jehoram with a stomach disease that could not be cured. Some consequences cannot be reversed, which is why it matters to turn from wrong early.
entries.2 chronicles 21:19: After two years of terrible suffering, Jehoram died, and his people did not honor him with the usual funeral fire given to kings. A life lived badly can end without the respect that others receive.
entries.2 chronicles 21:20: Jehoram was thirty-two when he became king and ruled eight years, and when he died no one was sorry; he was buried in the city of David but not with the kings. How we treat people while we live shapes how we are remembered after we are gone.
entries.2 chronicles 23:1: After years of waiting, the priest Jehoiada finally took bold action and teamed up with five army commanders. It shows that sometimes doing the right thing means stepping forward with courage and trusted allies.
entries.2 chronicles 23:2: The commanders traveled through Judah and gathered the Levites and family leaders from every town to come to Jerusalem. It means the plan was spreading and people were being brought together for something important.
entries.2 chronicles 23:3: Everyone in God's house agreed to make the king's son the true king, just as God had promised David's family. It reminds the reader that God keeps his promises, even when things look hopeless.
entries.2 chronicles 23:4: Jehoiada gave the priests and Levites specific guard duties, with one group watching the doors. It shows that careful organization and each person doing their part matters in serving God.
entries.2 chronicles 23:5: Other groups were placed at the palace and the horse gate, while the people stayed in the courtyards. It means everyone had a clear position so the plan would work safely.
entries.2 chronicles 23:6: Only the priests and Levites on duty were allowed inside the temple, because they were set apart for that work. It teaches that God's house is to be treated with respect and order.
entries.2 chronicles 23:7: The Levites formed an armed ring around the king and were told to protect him at all costs. It shows how seriously they took their duty to guard the rightful king.
entries.2 chronicles 23:8: The Levites and the people of Judah followed Jehoiada's orders exactly, and no group was sent home. It shows the value of obedience and everyone staying at their post.
entries.2 chronicles 23:9: Jehoiada handed out King David's old spears and shields that had been stored in the temple. It means they used what was already available to them rather than waiting for something new.
entries.2 chronicles 23:10: Jehoiada arranged all the armed men in position around the king, from one side of the temple to the other. It shows how thoroughly they prepared to protect the young king.
entries.2 chronicles 23:11: They brought out the king's son, crowned him, gave him the royal symbols, and anointed him king while everyone shouted for his long life. It was the moment the rightful king finally took his place.
entries.2 chronicles 23:12: Athaliah heard the noise of the crowd running and cheering for the king and came to see what was happening. It shows that the truth was about to catch up with her.
entries.2 chronicles 23:13: She saw the young king standing in his proper place with the leaders and musicians celebrating, and she tore her clothes and cried out that they had betrayed her. It shows how someone in the wrong can see rightful joy as a threat.
entries.2 chronicles 23:14: Jehoiada ordered the guards to take her out of the temple area and to kill anyone who tried to follow her, but not to kill her inside God's house. It shows that justice was carried out, but with respect for God's house.
entries.2 chronicles 23:15: They seized her and took her to the palace by the horse gate, where she was put to death. It marks the end of her attempt to hold onto power that was never hers.
entries.2 chronicles 23:16: Jehoiada led the people and the king in a solemn agreement to belong to the Lord. It means the whole nation was recommitting themselves to God together.
entries.2 chronicles 23:17: The people then tore down the temple of Baal, smashed its altars and idols, and killed its priest. It shows they were serious about removing false worship from their lives.
entries.2 chronicles 23:18: Jehoiada restored the proper order of worship in the Lord's house, with priests and Levites offering sacrifices as Moses' law directed, with joy and singing. It means worship was put back the way God intended it.
entries.2 chronicles 23:19: He placed gatekeepers at the doors to keep out anyone who was ceremonially unclean. It shows that access to God's house was to be handled with care and reverence.
entries.2 chronicles 23:20: Jehoiada led the leaders and all the people in escorting the king from the temple down to the palace and seating him on the royal throne. It was the public, joyful moment the rightful king took charge.
entries.2 chronicles 23:21: Everyone in the land celebrated and the city was peaceful because Athaliah was gone. It shows that removing what was wrong brought calm and joy to the whole community.
entries.2 chronicles 20:1: A coalition of enemy nations declared war on King Jehoshaphat of Judah. It reminds the reader that trouble can come even to people who are trying to do right.
entries.2 chronicles 20:2: Messengers brought Jehoshaphat alarming news that a huge army was already close by, marching in from across the Dead Sea. The threat was real and near, not distant.
entries.2 chronicles 20:3: Jehoshaphat was afraid, but instead of panicking he turned to God for guidance and called the whole country to fast and pray. Fear can be the starting point for seeking God rather than giving up.
entries.2 chronicles 20:4: People from every town in Judah gathered to ask the Lord for help. When danger is great, it is good for a whole community to pray together.
entries.2 chronicles 20:5: Jehoshaphat stood publicly in the temple area in front of the people. He led them openly in prayer rather than hiding his dependence on God.
entries.2 chronicles 20:6: He prayed by recalling that God rules over heaven and every nation, and that no power can stand against him. Remembering who God is gives courage when we feel outmatched.
entries.2 chronicles 20:7: He reminded God that he had given this land to Israel, the descendants of his friend Abraham, as a lasting possession. Recalling God's past faithfulness strengthens faith in the present.
entries.2 chronicles 20:8: God's people had settled in the land and built a house there for his name. They had made a lasting commitment to worship him in that place.
entries.2 chronicles 20:9: They believed that if disaster, war, disease, or famine came, they could cry out to God at his house and he would hear and save them. It is right to bring our worst troubles to God.
entries.2 chronicles 20:10: He pointed out that the attacking nations were the very peoples God had once spared Israel from destroying. The enemy was now repaying kindness with aggression.
entries.2 chronicles 20:11: Instead of gratitude, these nations were trying to drive God's people out of the land he had given them. Jehoshaphat laid the injustice honestly before God.
entries.2 chronicles 20:12: He admitted they had no strength to face the army and did not know what to do, so they were looking to God for help. It is honest and wise to admit our limits and fix our eyes on God.
entries.2 chronicles 20:13: The whole community stood waiting before the Lord, including wives and small children. Everyone, young and old, shared in depending on God.
entries.2 chronicles 20:14: In the middle of the gathering, God's Spirit came upon a Levite named Jahaziel. God can speak through ordinary people to guide his people.
entries.2 chronicles 20:15: God's message through Jahaziel was to not be afraid, because the battle belonged to God, not to them. We can release our fear when we trust that God is the one who fights for us.
entries.2 chronicles 20:16: God told them to go out and face the enemy the next day at a specific place. Faith means moving forward in obedience, even when the danger is still there.
entries.2 chronicles 20:17: They were told they would not need to fight; they only had to take their position, stand still, and watch God rescue them. Sometimes trusting God means waiting and watching rather than striving.
entries.2 chronicles 20:18: Jehoshaphat bowed face down to the ground, and all the people worshiped the Lord. Their response to God's promise was humble worship.
entries.2 chronicles 20:19: The Levites stood up and praised the God of Israel with loud voices. Praise was their natural response to God's reassuring word.
entries.2 chronicles 20:20: Early the next morning, as they set out, Jehoshaphat urged the people to trust the Lord and his prophets, promising they would be safe and succeed. Trusting God's word is the key to standing firm.
entries.2 chronicles 20:21: Jehoshaphat arranged for singers to walk ahead of the army, praising God for his enduring mercy. They put worship in front of the battle rather than behind it.
entries.2 chronicles 20:22: As soon as the singing and praise began, the Lord caused confusion among the enemy armies and they were defeated. God acted in response to their worship and trust.
entries.2 chronicles 20:23: The enemy nations turned on each other and destroyed themselves. God defeated the threat without Judah lifting a weapon.
entries.2 chronicles 20:24: When Judah reached the lookout point, they saw only dead bodies and no living enemy. God had done exactly what he promised.
entries.2 chronicles 20:25: The people spent three days collecting huge amounts of supplies, wealth, and clothing from the enemy camp. God's rescue came with more than they could carry.
entries.2 chronicles 20:26: On the fourth day they gathered in a valley to bless the Lord, and it was named the Valley of Blessing. God's deliverance turned a place of danger into a place of praise.
entries.2 chronicles 20:27: Jehoshaphat led the people back to Jerusalem full of joy because the Lord had given them victory over their enemies. Gratitude and joy are the right response to God's help.
entries.2 chronicles 20:28: They entered the Lord's house with stringed and wind instruments. Their worship was loud, joyful, and public.
entries.2 chronicles 20:29: When the surrounding kingdoms heard how the Lord had fought for Israel, fear of God fell on them all. God's deliverance protected his people and made his power known.
entries.2 chronicles 20:30: Jehoshaphat's kingdom was peaceful because the Lord gave him rest on every side. God's help brought lasting calm, not just a one-time victory.
entries.2 chronicles 20:31: This verse gives Jehoshaphat's age, length of reign, and his mother's name. It grounds the story in real history and a real person.
entries.2 chronicles 20:32: Jehoshaphat followed the good example of his father Asa and did what was right in God's eyes. A faithful example in a family can shape a faithful life.
entries.2 chronicles 20:33: However, the pagan worship sites were not removed, and the people's hearts were not fully devoted to God. Even a good leader cannot force every heart to be faithful.
entries.2 chronicles 20:34: The rest of Jehoshaphat's deeds were written down in other historical records. His story was remembered and recorded for later generations.
entries.2 chronicles 20:35: Later Jehoshaphat made an alliance with Ahaziah, the king of Israel, who did much evil. Even good people can make unwise partnerships.
entries.2 chronicles 20:36: Together they built ships at Ezion-geber to sail to Tarshish. They joined resources for a trading venture, but the partnership was with a wicked king.
entries.2 chronicles 20:37: A prophet named Eliezer told Jehoshaphat that because he joined with Ahaziah, God would destroy his work, and the ships were wrecked. Wrong partnerships can bring loss, and God is not indifferent to whom we join ourselves with.
entries.2 chronicles 27:1: This verse gives the basic facts about Jotham: he became king at twenty-five, ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem, and his mother was Jerushah. It reminds the reader that even kings had ordinary family details and a set time to rule.
entries.2 chronicles 27:2: Jotham did what was right before God, following his father's good example, but he did not enter the Temple himself, and the people kept on doing wrong. It shows that a good leader can still fall short and that people don't automatically change just because their king does right.
entries.2 chronicles 27:3: Jotham repaired and built up parts of the Temple and the city wall. His faith showed itself in practical work on the places where people worshiped and lived.
entries.2 chronicles 27:4: He also built towns in the hills and forts and towers in the wooded areas. He was preparing and protecting his country, not just sitting still as king.
entries.2 chronicles 27:5: Jotham defeated the Ammonites in war, and they paid him a large amount of silver and grain for three years in a row. This shows that God gave him success and that his victory brought real benefit to the nation.
entries.2 chronicles 27:6: Jotham grew strong because he made the Lord his guide in everything he did. The reader learns that lasting strength comes from depending on God, not just from hard work or good plans.
entries.2 chronicles 27:7: The rest of Jotham's deeds and wars were written down in the official records of the kings. It reminds us that this short account is only a summary of a whole life.
entries.2 chronicles 27:8: This repeats that Jotham was twenty-five when he began to rule and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. It frames his story with simple, factual details.
entries.2 chronicles 27:9: Jotham died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, and his son Ahaz took the throne. It shows that every reign ends and the next generation takes over, so each king's choices matter beyond his own lifetime.
entries.2 chronicles 24:1: Joash became king when he was only seven years old and ruled for forty years in Jerusalem; his mother was Zibiah. This reminds readers that God can use even a young person to lead and do important work.
entries.2 chronicles 24:2: Joash did what pleased the Lord, but only while the priest Jehoiada was alive to guide him. It shows how much our choices can depend on the good influences around us, and warns us to hold to what is right even when those influences are gone.
entries.2 chronicles 24:3: Jehoiada arranged two wives for Joash, and he had sons and daughters. This was a normal way in that culture to secure a family line for the king.
entries.2 chronicles 24:4: Joash wanted to repair the Lord's temple, which had fallen into disrepair. It shows a good desire to honor God by restoring what was broken.
entries.2 chronicles 24:5: Joash told the priests and Levites to collect money from across Judah each year to fix God's house, and to do it quickly, but they were slow to act. Good intentions need follow-through, and delay can keep important work from getting done.
entries.2 chronicles 24:6: The king asked Jehoiada why the Levites had not collected the tax that Moses had set up for the tent of worship. It shows that leaders are accountable for making sure God's work is funded and carried out.
entries.2 chronicles 24:7: Athaliah and her sons had damaged the Lord's temple and given its sacred things to false gods. This explains why the repairs were so badly needed and shows how bad leadership can harm worship.
entries.2 chronicles 24:8: At the king's command they made a chest and placed it outside the entrance of the Lord's house. This was a simple, practical way to collect money for the repairs.
entries.2 chronicles 24:9: A proclamation went out through Judah and Jerusalem for people to bring the tax Moses had commanded in the wilderness. It called the whole community to take part in supporting God's house.
entries.2 chronicles 24:10: All the leaders and people came gladly and gave their money until everyone had contributed. Their willing generosity is a picture of people giving cheerfully for God's work.
entries.2 chronicles 24:11: The chest was brought to the king's officials whenever it was full, the money was emptied out, and the chest was returned; this happened daily and a large sum was raised. Steady, organized effort added up to a great result.
entries.2 chronicles 24:12: The king and Jehoiada gave the money to those in charge of the work, who hired builders and craftsmen to restore the Lord's house. Good leadership put the funds to work where they were needed most.
entries.2 chronicles 24:13: The workers repaired the damage and rebuilt God's house until it was strong and beautiful again. Faithful labor can restore what has been broken down.
entries.2 chronicles 24:14: When the work was finished, the leftover money was used to make vessels for the temple, and regular offerings continued as long as Jehoiada lived. The people's generosity provided not only repairs but also what was needed for ongoing worship.
entries.2 chronicles 24:15: Jehoiada grew old and died at the age of 130. His long life was a sign of God's blessing on a faithful servant.
entries.2 chronicles 24:16: He was buried among the kings in the city of David because he had done good for Israel and for God's house. His faithful service was honored even though he was not a king.
entries.2 chronicles 24:17: After Jehoiada died, the leaders of Judah came and bowed before the king, and he listened to them. This marks a turning point where Joash began to follow bad advice instead of godly guidance.
entries.2 chronicles 24:18: The people abandoned the Lord's house and worshiped wooden pillars and idols, and because of this sin judgment came on Judah and Jerusalem. Turning away from God brings serious consequences.
entries.2 chronicles 24:19: The Lord sent prophets to call the people back to him, and the prophets warned them, but they refused to listen. God is patient and keeps calling people back, but we must actually respond.
entries.2 chronicles 24:20: God's Spirit came on Zechariah, who stood before the people and warned them that because they had abandoned the Lord, he had abandoned them. Rejecting God's warnings leads to trouble, not freedom.
entries.2 chronicles 24:21: The people plotted against Zechariah and, by the king's order, stoned him to death in the courtyard of the Lord's house. This shows how far they had fallen, killing the very messenger God sent to help them.
entries.2 chronicles 24:22: Joash forgot the kindness Jehoiada had shown him and killed his son, and as he died Zechariah asked the Lord to see it and repay. God does not ignore injustice done to the innocent.
entries.2 chronicles 24:23: In the spring the Aramean army attacked Joash, killed the leaders of the people, and sent the plunder to the king of Damascus. The judgment Zechariah asked for began to come upon them.
entries.2 chronicles 24:24: Even though the Aramean army was small, the Lord gave them victory over a much larger army because Judah had abandoned him. This shows that no army is strong enough when God is against it.
entries.2 chronicles 24:25: The Arameans left Joash badly diseased, and his own servants plotted against him because of the murder of Jehoiada's son, killing him in his bed; he was buried in the city of David but not in the royal tombs. His failure to honor God cost him honor in death.
entries.2 chronicles 24:26: The two men who plotted against Joash were Zabad, son of an Ammonite woman, and Jehozabad, son of a Moabite woman. The text names them to show the plot was real and specific.
entries.2 chronicles 24:27: The record of Joash's sons, the prophet's words against him, and the rebuilding of the Lord's house are written in the book of the kings, and his son Amaziah became king after him. This closes the account and points forward to the next king.
entries.2 chronicles 25:1: This verse gives basic facts about Amaziah: he became king at twenty-five, ruled twenty-nine years in Jerusalem, and his mother was Jehoaddan. It reminds us that every leader has a real family and a real span of time to use well.
entries.2 chronicles 25:2: Amaziah generally did what God said was right, but his heart was not fully committed to God. It is possible to do many right things outwardly while holding back part of your heart, and God cares about that part too.
entries.2 chronicles 25:3: Once Amaziah felt secure as king, he had the men who had murdered his father executed. He used his new strength to deal with old wrongs, which shows how power can be used for justice or for revenge.
entries.2 chronicles 25:4: Amaziah followed God's law by not killing the children of the murderers, since each person should die only for his own sin. God's justice does not punish people for crimes they did not commit.
entries.2 chronicles 25:5: Amaziah organized the men of Judah and Benjamin into units and counted those twenty and older, finding three hundred thousand trained soldiers. Good preparation and order are wise, but they are not the same as trusting God.
entries.2 chronicles 25:6: Amaziah also hired a hundred thousand experienced soldiers from Israel for a large amount of silver. He was adding human strength to his army, which would soon become a problem.
entries.2 chronicles 25:7: A prophet of God warned Amaziah not to take the Israelite army with him, because God was not with those people. Help from the wrong source can do more harm than good, even when it looks strong.
entries.2 chronicles 25:8: The prophet told Amaziah to go and fight with courage, but warned that God alone decides who wins or falls. Your success does not depend only on your strength; it depends on God.
entries.2 chronicles 25:9: Amaziah worried about the money he had already spent on the hired soldiers, and the prophet answered that God can give far more than that. Do not let fear of losing money keep you from obeying God.
entries.2 chronicles 25:10: Amaziah obeyed and sent the hired Israelite soldiers home, which made them furious with Judah. Doing the right thing can cost you and can make people angry, but it is still the right thing.
entries.2 chronicles 25:11: Encouraged, Amaziah led his army out and defeated ten thousand men of Seir in the Valley of Salt. God gave him a real victory, showing that obedience was the better path.
entries.2 chronicles 25:12: The men of Judah captured another ten thousand and threw them from the top of a rock, killing them. This was a brutal act of war, and the Bible reports it plainly without calling it good.
entries.2 chronicles 25:13: The Israelite soldiers Amaziah had sent home attacked towns in Judah, killing three thousand people and taking much loot. The rejected help turned into a real threat, showing how costly it can be to get tangled with the wrong allies.
entries.2 chronicles 25:14: After defeating the Edomites, Amaziah brought their idols home and began to worship them. It is strange and sad to win a battle and then bow down to the gods of the people you defeated.
entries.2 chronicles 25:15: God was angry and sent a prophet to ask Amaziah why he was worshiping gods that could not even save their own people from him. It makes no sense to trust something that has already proved powerless.
entries.2 chronicles 25:16: When Amaziah threatened to kill him, the prophet stopped and said it was clear God had decided to destroy the king because he would not listen. Refusing correction is a serious step toward ruin.
entries.2 chronicles 25:17: Amaziah, following advice from his officials, challenged the king of Israel to a face-to-face fight. Pride after a victory pushed him to pick a fight he did not need.
entries.2 chronicles 25:18: The king of Israel answered with a story about a thorn bush that asked a cedar for a marriage alliance and was then trampled by a wild animal. The point is that a small, proud person who picks a fight with someone much stronger will get crushed.
entries.2 chronicles 25:19: The king of Israel told Amaziah that his victory over Edom had made him proud and that he should stay home instead of bringing trouble on himself and Judah. Success can make us overconfident and lead us into needless danger.
entries.2 chronicles 25:20: Amaziah would not listen, and God allowed this stubbornness so that he would be defeated, because Judah had followed the gods of Edom. Sometimes God lets people face the results of their own choices.
entries.2 chronicles 25:21: So the king of Israel came, and he and Amaziah met in battle at Beth-shemesh in Judah. The challenge was accepted, and the two armies faced each other.
entries.2 chronicles 25:22: Judah was beaten by Israel, and the soldiers ran away to their homes. The proud challenge ended in a humiliating defeat.
entries.2 chronicles 25:23: The king of Israel captured Amaziah at Beth-shemesh, took him to Jerusalem, and broke down a large section of the city wall. The defeat was not only on the battlefield; it damaged the capital itself.
entries.2 chronicles 25:24: The king of Israel took the gold, silver, and temple articles, along with the king's wealth and hostages, and returned to Samaria. The treasures that belonged to God were carried off because of Amaziah's foolishness.
entries.2 chronicles 25:25: Amaziah outlived the king of Israel by fifteen years. Even after a crushing defeat, he continued to live, which shows that God's mercy gives people time.
entries.2 chronicles 25:26: This verse notes that the rest of Amaziah's deeds are written in the official records of the kings. It reminds us that the Bible gives a summary, not every detail, of a person's life.
entries.2 chronicles 25:27: After Amaziah turned away from following the Lord, people plotted against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish, where he was killed. Turning away from God led to a life that ended in betrayal and death.
entries.2 chronicles 25:28: His body was brought back on horseback and buried with his ancestors in the city of David. Even a king who ended badly was given a proper burial, closing the story of his life.
entries.2 chronicles 30:1: Hezekiah invited people from all across Israel and Judah to come to Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover. It shows a leader urging people to worship God together, and reminds readers that God welcomes people to come to him.
entries.2 chronicles 30:2: The king and his officials agreed to hold the Passover a month later than usual. It shows that when plans don't work out, leaders can adjust timing while still honoring God.
entries.2 chronicles 30:3: They couldn't celebrate on the normal date because not enough priests were ready and the people hadn't gathered yet. It reminds readers that preparation matters when approaching God.
entries.2 chronicles 30:4: The king and the people agreed the plan was good. It shows that wise decisions are often made together rather than by one person alone.
entries.2 chronicles 30:5: They sent word throughout the whole land inviting everyone to come celebrate the Passover in Jerusalem, since it hadn't been done properly for a long time. It shows the value of inviting others back to worship.
entries.2 chronicles 30:6: Messengers carried the king's letter urging the people to return to the Lord so he would restore the few who had survived Assyria's attacks. It reminds readers that turning back to God brings hope even after hard times.
entries.2 chronicles 30:7: The letter warned the people not to copy their ancestors, who turned from God and brought ruin on themselves. It encourages readers to learn from past mistakes instead of repeating them.
entries.2 chronicles 30:8: They were told not to be stubborn but to give themselves to God and serve him, so his anger would turn away. It invites readers to soften their hearts and commit to God rather than resist him.
entries.2 chronicles 30:9: If the people returned to God, even their captured relatives would be treated kindly and allowed home, because God is gracious and merciful. It assures readers that God does not turn away those who come back to him.
entries.2 chronicles 30:10: The messengers traveled through the northern tribes, but many people just laughed and mocked them. It reminds readers that sharing God's invitation will not always be welcomed.
entries.2 chronicles 30:11: Some people from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem. It shows that even when most refuse, some will respond, and humility opens the way to God.
entries.2 chronicles 30:12: In Judah, God united the people to obey the king's orders as his own word. It shows that God can bring people together in a common purpose when they follow him.
entries.2 chronicles 30:13: A huge crowd gathered in Jerusalem to celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month. It shows how a sincere call to worship can draw many people together.
entries.2 chronicles 30:14: The people removed the pagan altars in Jerusalem and threw the incense equipment into the Kidron Valley. It reminds readers that turning to God often means clearing out things that dishonor him.
entries.2 chronicles 30:15: They sacrificed the Passover lambs on the set day, and the priests and Levites, feeling ashamed, prepared themselves and brought offerings to God's house. It shows that shame can lead to renewed devotion and service.
entries.2 chronicles 30:16: The priests and Levites took their proper places as Moses' law directed, with priests handling the blood the Levites gave them. It shows the importance of following God's instructions carefully in worship.
entries.2 chronicles 30:17: Many people hadn't properly prepared themselves, so the Levites killed the Passover lambs for them to set them apart to the Lord. It shows God making a way for people who weren't fully ready.
entries.2 chronicles 30:18: Many from the northern tribes ate the Passover without the required cleansing, so Hezekiah prayed that God would show mercy to them. It reminds readers that God's mercy covers honest hearts even when rules weren't fully kept.
entries.2 chronicles 30:19: Hezekiah prayed for those who sincerely set their hearts on God even without the proper cleansing ritual. It shows that God looks at the heart's direction, not just outward correctness.
entries.2 chronicles 30:20: The Lord listened to Hezekiah's prayer and healed the people. It encourages readers that God hears sincere prayers for mercy and responds with grace.
entries.2 chronicles 30:21: The people celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with great joy, while the Levites and priests praised God daily with loud music. It shows that wholehearted worship brings deep joy.
entries.2 chronicles 30:22: Hezekiah encouraged the Levites who understood worship well, and they celebrated seven more days with peace offerings and praise. It reminds readers that encouraging those who serve God strengthens worship.
entries.2 chronicles 30:23: The whole assembly agreed to extend the celebration another seven days, and they did so with joy. It shows that genuine joy in worship makes people want more of it.
entries.2 chronicles 30:24: Hezekiah donated a thousand oxen and seven thousand sheep, the officials gave even more, and many priests prepared themselves. It shows generous giving supporting worship and encouraging others to serve.
entries.2 chronicles 30:25: Everyone present—Judah's people, priests, Levites, visitors from Israel, and foreigners living in the land—rejoiced greatly. It shows that worshiping God can unite very different people in shared joy.
entries.2 chronicles 30:26: Jerusalem hadn't seen joy like this since the days of Solomon. It reminds readers that renewed devotion to God can bring a joy that surpasses what people remember.
entries.2 chronicles 30:27: The priests and Levites blessed the people, and their prayer reached God's holy dwelling in heaven. It assures readers that sincere prayers and blessings are heard by God.
entries.2 chronicles 28:1: Ahaz became king at twenty and ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem, but unlike his ancestor David he did not do what pleased God. The reader sees that a good family history does not guarantee a good life; each person must choose to follow God.
entries.2 chronicles 28:2: Ahaz copied the sinful practices of the kings of the northern kingdom and made metal idols for false gods. It means he deliberately turned away from God to follow the wrong example of others.
entries.2 chronicles 28:3: Ahaz even burned his own children as offerings in a valley near Jerusalem, copying the horrible customs of the nations God had driven out. This shows how far people can fall when they reject God, and it warns the reader against letting evil become normal.
entries.2 chronicles 28:4: Ahaz offered sacrifices and burned incense at many shrines on hills and under trees. He was worshiping anywhere and everywhere except where God had said, showing a heart that wanted religion on its own terms.
entries.2 chronicles 28:5: Because of Ahaz's sin, God allowed the king of Aram to defeat him and take many people captive, and then the king of Israel also crushed him. The reader learns that turning from God brings real consequences, often through other people.
entries.2 chronicles 28:6: Pekah of Israel killed 120,000 fighting men of Judah in a single day because they had abandoned the Lord. It is a sober picture of how serious it is to forsake God, and a warning to take faithfulness seriously.
entries.2 chronicles 28:7: A strong soldier from Ephraim killed the king's son, the palace manager, and the king's second-in-command. This shows that when a nation falls under judgment, even its leaders and royal family are not protected.
