entries.2 chronicles 28:8: The Israelites captured 200,000 of their own relatives from Judah, along with many women and children and much property, and took them to Samaria. It shows how sin had turned brothers into enemies and caused terrible suffering.
entries.2 chronicles 28:9: A prophet named Oded met the returning army and told them that God had allowed Judah to be defeated because of their sin, but that Israel had killed them with excessive, cruel anger. The reader sees that God notices not only what we do but how we do it.
entries.2 chronicles 28:10: Oded warned the Israelites that they planned to make their own relatives slaves, and asked whether they themselves were free from sin against God. It reminds the reader not to be proud when judging others, since we also fail.
entries.2 chronicles 28:11: The prophet told them to send the captives back home, because God's anger was burning against Israel for what they had done. It shows that God calls people to stop doing wrong and make it right, even when they have already won.
entries.2 chronicles 28:12: Some leaders from Ephraim stood up against the soldiers returning from the war. It shows that courage to oppose wrongdoing is important, even when it means standing against your own people.
entries.2 chronicles 28:13: These leaders refused to let the captives be brought in, saying that keeping them would add to Israel's own sin and guilt before God. The reader learns that doing wrong to others only adds to our own guilt.
entries.2 chronicles 28:14: The armed soldiers handed over the prisoners and the goods they had taken to the leaders and the assembled people. It shows that good leadership can stop a wrong action before it goes further.
entries.2 chronicles 28:15: The named leaders took care of the captives, giving clothes, shoes, food, drink, and oil to those who had nothing, and carried the weak on donkeys back to Jericho. This is a picture of mercy: treating even enemies and captives with kindness and dignity.
entries.2 chronicles 28:16: At that time King Ahaz asked the king of Assyria for help. Instead of turning to God in his trouble, he looked to a powerful foreign nation, which the reader can see is a mistake.
entries.2 chronicles 28:17: The Edomites attacked Judah again and carried people away as prisoners. This shows that trouble kept coming on Judah from every side because of the nation's sin.
entries.2 chronicles 28:18: The Philistines pushed into towns in the lowlands and the south of Judah and settled there. It shows how a nation that turns from God loses its security and land.
entries.2 chronicles 28:19: God humbled Judah because of Ahaz, who had led the people into reckless sin against the Lord. The reader sees that leaders have real influence, and that leading others into sin is serious.
entries.2 chronicles 28:20: Tiglath-pileser of Assyria came to Ahaz but brought him trouble instead of the help he wanted. It shows that trusting in powerful people rather than God often makes things worse.
entries.2 chronicles 28:21: Ahaz took wealth from the temple, from his own palace, and from the leading men and gave it to the Assyrian king, but it did not help him. The reader learns that you cannot buy your way out of trouble you brought on yourself by sin.
entries.2 chronicles 28:22: When Ahaz was in trouble, he did even more evil against the Lord instead of repenting. It shows that hardship can either turn a person toward God or make them harder, and warns the reader to choose the first.
entries.2 chronicles 28:23: Ahaz sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, thinking those gods were helping his enemies, but they led to his downfall and Israel's. It shows the foolishness of worshiping what seems powerful instead of the true God.
entries.2 chronicles 28:24: Ahaz gathered up and cut apart the temple vessels, shut the doors of the Lord's house, and set up altars all over Jerusalem. He was actively shutting down worship of God and replacing it with his own religion.
entries.2 chronicles 28:25: In every town of Judah Ahaz set up shrines for burning incense to other gods, making the Lord angry. It shows how one leader's sin can spread through a whole nation.
entries.2 chronicles 28:26: The rest of Ahaz's deeds, from beginning to end, are written in the record of the kings of Judah and Israel. It reminds the reader that our actions are remembered and recorded, even when no one seems to notice.
entries.2 chronicles 28:27: Ahaz died and was buried in Jerusalem, but not in the royal tombs, and his son Hezekiah became king. It shows that a life of unfaithfulness leaves a tarnished legacy, even in death.
entries.2 chronicles 29:1: This verse gives basic facts about Hezekiah: he became king at 25, ruled 29 years in Jerusalem, and his mother was Abijah. It reminds the reader that real people with real families and lifespans stood behind these events.
entries.2 chronicles 29:2: Hezekiah did what was right in God's eyes, following the example of his ancestor David. The reader is shown that a good leader is measured by whether he does right before God.
entries.2 chronicles 29:3: In his very first month as king, Hezekiah opened the temple doors that had been shut and repaired them. It shows he made worship of God his first priority.
entries.2 chronicles 29:4: He gathered the priests and temple workers together in an open area on the east side. He was calling the people responsible for worship to come and hear him.
entries.2 chronicles 29:5: Hezekiah told the Levites to make themselves clean and to clean out the temple, removing anything unclean. The reader sees that coming near to God requires dealing with what is wrong first.
entries.2 chronicles 29:6: Hezekiah admits that earlier generations had turned away from God and abandoned his temple. It is an honest confession of the past rather than pretending everything was fine.
entries.2 chronicles 29:7: He describes how the temple doors had been shut, the lamps put out, and no incense or offerings made. Worship of God had completely stopped.
entries.2 chronicles 29:8: Because of this, God's anger had come on Judah and Jerusalem, making them a shocking and shameful sight. The reader sees that ignoring God has real consequences.
entries.2 chronicles 29:9: He points out that their fathers had died by the sword and their families had been taken captive. The past failure had cost them dearly.
entries.2 chronicles 29:10: Hezekiah says he intends to make a covenant with the Lord so that his fierce anger will turn away from them. It shows a leader taking the initiative to restore the relationship with God.
entries.2 chronicles 29:11: He urges the Levites not to be careless, because God had chosen them to serve him and offer sacrifices. The reader is reminded that being set apart for God's service is a serious calling.
entries.2 chronicles 29:12: This lists the Levite leaders from different family groups who responded and took their places. It shows that the work of restoring worship began with specific people stepping up.
entries.2 chronicles 29:13: More Levite leaders from other families are named as they joined the effort. The list shows the response was broad, not just a few individuals.
entries.2 chronicles 29:14: Still more Levite leaders from additional families are named. The reader sees a whole community getting involved in the cleanup and restoration.
entries.2 chronicles 29:15: They gathered their fellow Levites, made themselves clean, and went in to clean the temple as the king had commanded according to God's word. Obedience to God's instruction is the focus here.
entries.2 chronicles 29:16: The priests cleaned the inside of the temple and carried the unclean things out to the courtyard, where the Levites took them to the Kidron Valley. It shows a thorough, organized removal of what didn't belong.
entries.2 chronicles 29:17: They began making the temple holy on the first day of the first month and finished the whole job by the sixteenth day. The work took time and was done step by step.
entries.2 chronicles 29:18: They reported to Hezekiah that the temple, the altar, and the table for the holy bread were all cleaned. The reader sees that the job was completed and verified.
entries.2 chronicles 29:19: They also restored the items King Ahaz had thrown out in his sin and put them back in their proper places before the altar. Things that had been wrongly discarded were made right again.
entries.2 chronicles 29:20: Hezekiah got up early, gathered the city officials, and went up to the temple. He led the way personally rather than just giving orders.
entries.2 chronicles 29:21: They brought seven each of oxen, rams, lambs, and goats as a sin offering for the kingdom, the temple, and Judah, and the priests were told to offer them. It shows a serious, organized effort to make things right with God.
entries.2 chronicles 29:22: The animals were killed and their blood was poured out on the altar by the priests. This was the prescribed way to deal with sin before God.
entries.2 chronicles 29:23: The goats for the sin offering were brought before the king and the assembled people, who laid their hands on them. This showed the people identifying with the offering made on their behalf.
entries.2 chronicles 29:24: The priests killed the goats and made a sin offering on the altar to take away the sin of all Israel, as the king had ordered. The reader sees that the offering was meant for the whole nation, not just individuals.
entries.2 chronicles 29:25: Hezekiah stationed the Levites in the temple with musical instruments, following the instructions God had given through David, Gad, and Nathan. Music in worship was part of God's own plan, not an afterthought.
entries.2 chronicles 29:26: The Levites stood ready with David's instruments and the priests with their trumpets. Everyone was in place for worship to begin.
entries.2 chronicles 29:27: When Hezekiah gave the signal, the burnt offering began, and at the same moment the song of the Lord started with trumpets and instruments. Worship in music and sacrifice went together.
entries.2 chronicles 29:28: All the people worshiped while the songs played and the trumpets sounded, until the burnt offering was finished. The whole congregation participated in honoring God.
entries.2 chronicles 29:29: When the offering was over, the king and everyone with him bowed their heads in worship. It shows that the response to what God had done was humble reverence.
entries.2 chronicles 29:30: Hezekiah and the officials told the Levites to praise God using the words of David and Asaph, and they did so joyfully, bowing their heads. Praise was expressed both in words and in posture.
entries.2 chronicles 29:31: Hezekiah invited the people, now dedicated to the Lord, to bring offerings and thank offerings into the temple, and those whose hearts were willing brought burnt offerings too. Giving was voluntary and came from the heart.
entries.2 chronicles 29:32: The people brought seventy oxen, a hundred rams, and two hundred lambs as burnt offerings to the Lord. The reader sees a generous, wholehearted response from the people.
entries.2 chronicles 29:33: They also dedicated six hundred oxen and three thousand sheep. The scale of giving shows how seriously the people took this restoration.
entries.2 chronicles 29:34: There weren't enough priests to skin all the animals, so the Levites helped until the work was done, and the Levites were more eager to make themselves clean than the priests were. It shows that willingness matters, and that cooperation got the job done.
entries.2 chronicles 29:35: There were many burnt offerings along with the fat of peace offerings and drink offerings, and so the work of the temple was put back in order. The reader sees that proper worship was fully restored.
entries.2 chronicles 29:36: Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced because God had prepared the people, and it had all happened suddenly. It shows that joy follows when people respond to God, and that God can bring about change quickly.
entries.2 chronicles 31:1: After the big religious cleanup, the people went through Judah and even into Ephraim and Manasseh smashing the stone and wooden idols and tearing down the shrines and altars until none were left, then everyone went home to their own property. It means real change showed up in their actions, not just their feelings, and it invites the reader to ask whether their own commitments actually change how they live.
entries.2 chronicles 31:2: Hezekiah organized the priests and Levites into groups, each with its own assigned work, including the burnt offerings, peace offerings, worship, and praise at the doors of the Lord's house. It means good worship needs good order, and it reminds the reader that serving God well usually takes planning and clear roles.
entries.2 chronicles 31:3: Hezekiah paid for the regular burnt offerings out of his own wealth, covering the morning and evening sacrifices plus the Sabbath, new moon, and festival offerings as the law of the Lord required. It means the king put his own money behind what he believed in, and it challenges the reader to support good work with real resources, not just words.
entries.2 chronicles 31:4: Hezekiah told the people of Jerusalem to give the priests and Levites their rightful share so the priests could stay strong in carrying out the law of the Lord. It means the people's giving kept the worship going, and it reminds the reader that those who serve God full-time depend on the support of others.
entries.2 chronicles 31:5: As soon as the order went out, the Israelites brought generous amounts—the firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, honey, and field produce—and a tenth of everything, piling up a huge store. It means the people responded quickly and generously, and it shows the reader that giving can be joyful and abundant rather than grudging.
entries.2 chronicles 31:6: The people of Israel and Judah living in the towns of Judah brought a tenth of their oxen and sheep and a tenth of the holy things dedicated to the Lord, stacking them in great heaps. It means whole communities joined in giving, and it reminds the reader that generosity grows when people do it together.
entries.2 chronicles 31:7: The first pile of goods was started in the third month, and by the seventh month the collections were complete. It means the giving happened steadily over months, and it shows the reader that faithful generosity is a habit built over time, not a one-time burst.
entries.2 chronicles 31:8: When Hezekiah and the officials saw the huge store of goods, they praised the Lord and blessed the people of Israel. It means the leaders recognized the abundance as God's goodness and honored the people who gave, and it encourages the reader to notice and thank God when generosity shows up.
entries.2 chronicles 31:9: Hezekiah asked the priests and Levites about the stored goods. It means the king checked in on how the giving was being handled, and it reminds the reader that good stewardship includes asking honest questions about money and resources.
entries.2 chronicles 31:10: Azariah the chief priest answered that ever since the people began bringing offerings, there had been more than enough food, because the Lord had blessed his people and left a great surplus. It means God's blessing showed up in practical abundance, and it reassures the reader that God's provision often exceeds what is strictly needed.
entries.2 chronicles 31:11: Hezekiah ordered storerooms to be prepared in the house of the Lord, and they were made ready. It means the king made sure there was a proper place to keep the gifts, and it reminds the reader that good intentions need practical organization to be useful.
entries.2 chronicles 31:12: They faithfully put all the offerings, tithes, and holy things into the storerooms, with Conaniah the Levite in charge and his brother Shimei as second. It means the goods were handled honestly and with accountability, and it shows the reader why trustworthy people matter when handling shared resources.
entries.2 chronicles 31:13: Ten named men served as overseers under Conaniah and Shimei, appointed by King Hezekiah and Azariah, the ruler of God's house. It means the work was shared and supervised by many people, and it reminds the reader that teamwork and clear authority keep important work from going wrong.
entries.2 chronicles 31:14: Kore, a Levite who guarded the east gate, was put in charge of the freewill offerings and of distributing the Lord's offerings and the most holy things. It means someone trustworthy was assigned to hand out what came in, and it shows the reader that generosity only helps when the gifts actually reach the people who need them.
entries.2 chronicles 31:15: Under Kore, six named men in the priests' towns were responsible for giving shares to their fellow priests by division, to small and great alike. It means the distribution reached everyone fairly, and it reminds the reader that fairness matters when sharing resources among people.
entries.2 chronicles 31:16: The shares also went to every male three years old and up who was listed by family and who came to the Lord's house for the daily work of their divisions. It means even the youngest were counted and cared for, and it shows the reader that a community's support should include everyone, not just the important people.
entries.2 chronicles 31:17: The priests' families were listed by their fathers' names, and the Levites twenty years old and up were listed according to their work in their divisions. It means careful records were kept so the right people got the right support, and it reminds the reader that good record-keeping is part of caring for people well.
entries.2 chronicles 31:18: The lists included all the little ones, wives, sons, and daughters of the whole community, because they had set themselves apart for the positions they were given. It means whole families were provided for, and it shows the reader that serving God is a family matter, not just an individual one.
entries.2 chronicles 31:19: For the priests, the sons of Aaron, living in the countryside around their towns, men were named in each town to give shares to all the males among the priests and to everyone listed among the Levites. It means no one was forgotten just because they lived far from the temple, and it reminds the reader that fair support should reach people wherever they are.
entries.2 chronicles 31:20: Hezekiah did this throughout all Judah, doing what was good, right, and true before the Lord his God. It means his wholehearted obedience showed in his actions, and it encourages the reader that integrity is measured by what you actually do, not just what you say.
entries.2 chronicles 31:21: In everything he undertook for God's house, God's law, and God's commands, Hezekiah sought God and worked with serious purpose, and things went well for him. It means wholehearted effort paired with seeking God led to success, and it encourages the reader to put real heart into what they do for God.
entries.2 chronicles 32:1: Right after Hezekiah had faithfully done good work, a powerful enemy king invaded his land and threatened his cities. Doing right does not mean trouble will never come, so we should not be surprised when hard times follow good efforts.
entries.2 chronicles 32:2: Hezekiah realized the enemy had come with the specific goal of attacking Jerusalem. Facing a real threat, he paid attention to the danger instead of pretending it was not there.
entries.2 chronicles 32:3: Hezekiah discussed a plan with his officials and military leaders to cut off the water sources outside the city, and they agreed to help. Wise leaders ask for advice and work together with others rather than acting alone.
entries.2 chronicles 32:4: A large crowd worked together to block up the springs and the stream running through the land, so the enemy army would have no water. Practical preparation, done by many hands, can make a real difference in a crisis.
entries.2 chronicles 32:5: Hezekiah took courage and repaired the broken walls, built taller towers and an outer wall, strengthened a key part of the city, and stored up weapons. Faith and practical effort go together, so we should prepare as best we can while trusting God.
entries.2 chronicles 32:6: He appointed military leaders over the people and gathered them in a public place at the city gate, then spoke to encourage them. Good leaders bring people together and speak courage into them when they are afraid.
entries.2 chronicles 32:7: Hezekiah told the people to be strong and brave, not afraid of the huge enemy army, because a greater power was with them. Our courage can rest on the fact that God is greater than any threat we face.
entries.2 chronicles 32:8: The enemy king had only human strength, but Hezekiah said God was with them to help and fight for them, and the people trusted his words. We can rely on God's help rather than measuring our chances by human strength alone.
entries.2 chronicles 32:9: The Assyrian king, camped with his army at another city, sent messengers to Jerusalem to deliver a message to Hezekiah and the people. Pressure often comes through words and threats, not only through direct attack.
entries.2 chronicles 32:10: The message mocked the people, asking what they were trusting in while trapped inside their walled city. Fear works by making us doubt what we are relying on.
entries.2 chronicles 32:11: The enemy claimed Hezekiah was misleading the people, saying God would save them while they starved inside the city. Lies often twist good leadership into something that sounds foolish or harmful.
entries.2 chronicles 32:12: The enemy pointed to Hezekiah's removal of local shrines and altars, claiming this had offended God. The truth was the opposite, but the enemy used half-truths to create doubt.
entries.2 chronicles 32:13: The king boasted about what he and his ancestors had done to other nations, asking whether those nations' gods had saved them. Pride loves to list past victories and use them to intimidate.
entries.2 chronicles 32:14: He challenged the people to name any god among the defeated nations who had rescued his people from his power, then asked why their God would be any different. The enemy treats the living God as just one more powerless idol.
entries.2 chronicles 32:15: He warned the people not to be fooled or trust Hezekiah, arguing that since no other god had saved anyone, their God certainly would not. This is the same old lie, dressed up with confident words.
entries.2 chronicles 32:16: The king's servants went even further, speaking against the Lord God and against Hezekiah his servant. Mockery of God and his people often grows bolder when it is not answered.
entries.2 chronicles 32:17: He also sent letters insulting the Lord, the God of Israel, repeating that the gods of other nations had failed and so would Hezekiah's God. Written words can carry the same poison as spoken threats.
entries.2 chronicles 32:18: The messengers shouted all this in the people's own language to those standing on the wall, trying to frighten and unsettle them so the city could be captured. Fear is a weapon, and we should recognize when words are aimed at shaking our trust.
entries.2 chronicles 32:19: They spoke of the God of Jerusalem as if he were just like the idols of other nations, made by human hands. The living God is not a handmade object, and treating him that way is a serious mistake.
entries.2 chronicles 32:20: Hezekiah the king and Isaiah the prophet prayed about the situation, crying out to heaven. When threats and insults come, turning to God in prayer is the right response.
entries.2 chronicles 32:21: The Lord sent an angel who killed the enemy's soldiers and commanders, so the king went home in disgrace and was later killed by his own sons in his god's temple. God can defeat an enemy in ways no army could, and human pride ends in shame.
entries.2 chronicles 32:22: The Lord rescued Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem from the Assyrian king and from all their enemies, giving them peace on every side. God's rescue brings rest, not just survival.
entries.2 chronicles 32:23: Many people brought offerings to the Lord and valuable gifts to Hezekiah, and he was honored among the nations from then on. When God delivers, others take notice, and honor comes to those he helps.
entries.2 chronicles 32:24: In those days Hezekiah became very sick and near death, and he prayed to the Lord, who answered him with a sign. God hears prayer even in our weakest moments.
entries.2 chronicles 32:25: Hezekiah did not respond rightly to the kindness shown him, because his heart became proud, and this brought judgment on him and on Judah and Jerusalem. Pride after blessing is a real danger, and it affects more than just the person who is proud.
entries.2 chronicles 32:26: Hezekiah humbled himself and turned from his pride, and so did the people of Jerusalem, so the Lord's judgment did not fall during his lifetime. Admitting pride and humbling ourselves can turn away trouble.
entries.2 chronicles 32:27: Hezekiah became very wealthy and honored, and he built storehouses for his gold, silver, jewels, spices, shields, and fine objects. God can bless generously, and it is wise to manage what he gives.
entries.2 chronicles 32:28: He also built storehouses for grain, wine, and oil, and shelters for all kinds of livestock. Good stewardship includes planning and providing for the future.
entries.2 chronicles 32:29: He built towns for himself and acquired many flocks and herds, because God had given him great wealth. Prosperity is a gift from God, and it should be received with gratitude.
entries.2 chronicles 32:30: Hezekiah redirected the upper spring of Gihon to bring water down to the west side of the City of David, and he did well in everything he undertook. Practical improvements that help people are part of doing good.
entries.2 chronicles 32:31: When representatives from Babylon came to ask about the miraculous sign in the land, God left Hezekiah to himself to test what was in his heart. Even good people are tested, and God sometimes lets us act on our own to reveal what we truly trust.
entries.2 chronicles 32:32: The rest of Hezekiah's deeds and his good works are written down in the vision of the prophet Isaiah and in the records of the kings of Judah and Israel. Faithful lives are remembered, and their stories are preserved for others.
entries.2 chronicles 32:33: Hezekiah died and was buried in the honored place among David's descendants, and all Judah and Jerusalem honored him at his death, and his son Manasseh became king. A life that honors God can be honored by others at its end, and leadership passes on to the next generation.
entries.2 chronicles 33:1: Manasseh became king at just twelve years old and ruled for fifty-five years. It shows that even a long reign can be spent badly, so length of time is not the same as faithfulness.
entries.2 chronicles 33:2: Manasseh did what God considered evil, copying the wicked customs of the peoples God had driven out before Israel. The reader is warned that following the crowd's bad example leads away from God.
entries.2 chronicles 33:3: He rebuilt the shrines his father had torn down and set up altars to false gods, including worship of the stars. This shows how quickly good work can be undone when someone turns from God.
entries.2 chronicles 33:4: He even built altars to false gods inside the Lord's own temple, the place God had chosen for his name. It is a picture of disrespecting what God has set apart for himself.
entries.2 chronicles 33:5: He filled the temple courtyards with altars for star worship. The place meant for worship of the true God was crowded with things that dishonored him.
entries.2 chronicles 33:6: He sacrificed his own children in fire and practiced fortune-telling and spiritism. This verse shows how far evil can go when a person rejects God completely.
entries.2 chronicles 33:7: He placed a carved idol inside God's temple, the very house God had promised to honor forever. It shows the seriousness of putting something else in the place that belongs to God.
entries.2 chronicles 33:8: God promised Israel would stay in their land if they carefully obeyed all he commanded through Moses. The blessing was tied to obedience, not just to God's past promises.
entries.2 chronicles 33:9: Manasseh led Judah so far astray that they became worse than the nations God had removed from the land. A bad leader can drag a whole people down with him.
entries.2 chronicles 33:10: God spoke to Manasseh and the people, but they refused to listen. Ignoring God's warnings does not make them go away; it only leads to consequences.
entries.2 chronicles 33:11: So God allowed the Assyrian army to capture Manasseh, bind him with chains, and take him to Babylon. Trouble came as a direct result of ignoring God's warnings.
entries.2 chronicles 33:12: In his distress Manasseh cried out to the Lord and humbled himself before the God of his ancestors. Even a very wicked person can turn to God when they are broken.
entries.2 chronicles 33:13: God heard his prayer and brought him back to Jerusalem and his throne, and then Manasseh knew the Lord was truly God. This shows that God is willing to answer a humble cry for help.
entries.2 chronicles 33:14: Afterward he strengthened Jerusalem's defenses and stationed army commanders throughout Judah. His change of heart showed itself in practical action to protect his people.
entries.2 chronicles 33:15: He removed the foreign gods, the idol, and the altars he had built, and threw them out of the city. Real repentance means getting rid of the wrong things, not just feeling sorry.
entries.2 chronicles 33:16: He repaired the Lord's altar, offered sacrifices on it, and told all Judah to serve the Lord, the God of Israel. His restored devotion led him to call others back to God too.
entries.2 chronicles 33:17: The people still offered sacrifices at the local shrines, but now only to the Lord their God. Their worship was sincere but not fully in line with how God had said to worship.
entries.2 chronicles 33:18: The rest of Manasseh's story, including his prayer and what the prophets said to him, is recorded in the records of the kings of Israel. It reminds us that God's dealings with people are remembered and written down.
entries.2 chronicles 33:19: His prayer, God's answer, and his sins before he humbled himself are all recorded in the prophets' history. This shows that both our wrongs and our turning to God matter and are remembered.
entries.2 chronicles 33:20: Manasseh died and was buried in his own house, and his son Amon became king. Even a long, eventful life ends, and the next generation takes over.
entries.2 chronicles 33:21: Amon became king at twenty-two and ruled only two years in Jerusalem. His short reign is a reminder that we are not guaranteed a long time to change our ways.
entries.2 chronicles 33:22: Amon did evil like his father had done, worshiping and serving the idols his father had made. He copied his father's sins but not his father's later repentance.
entries.2 chronicles 33:23: Unlike his father, Amon never humbled himself before the Lord but kept sinning more and more. Pride and refusal to repent led him further into wrongdoing.
entries.2 chronicles 33:24: Amon's own servants plotted against him and killed him in his house. His evil and arrogance ended in betrayal by those closest to him.
entries.2 chronicles 33:25: The people of the land executed those who had plotted against King Amon and made his son Josiah king. The people upheld justice and the royal line continued, setting the stage for Josiah's reign.
entries.2 chronicles 26:1: The people of Judah chose Uzziah, a sixteen-year-old, to be king after his father died. It shows that leadership can pass to someone young, and that God can use people of any age.
entries.2 chronicles 26:2: Uzziah rebuilt and reclaimed the town of Eloth for Judah after his father's death. This shows he worked to restore what had been lost and to strengthen his country.
entries.2 chronicles 26:3: Uzziah became king at sixteen and ruled in Jerusalem for fifty-two years; his mother was Jechiliah. His long reign reminds us that God can give someone many years to do good work.
entries.2 chronicles 26:4: Uzziah did what was right in God's eyes, following the example of his father Amaziah. A good example from a parent can help a person choose to do right.
entries.2 chronicles 26:5: Uzziah sought God while Zechariah taught people to respect God, and as long as he stayed faithful, God made things go well for him. Seeking God and listening to wise teaching brings blessing.
entries.2 chronicles 26:6: Uzziah fought the Philistines, broke down their city walls, and built towns in their territory. God can give a person success in hard struggles when they trust him.
entries.2 chronicles 26:7: God helped Uzziah against the Philistines, the Arabians in Gur-baal, and the Meunim. Success in battle came because God was the one giving the help.
entries.2 chronicles 26:8: The Ammonites brought gifts to Uzziah, and his fame spread as far as Egypt because he became very powerful. God can make a person's influence grow far beyond what they expected.
entries.2 chronicles 26:9: Uzziah built and fortified towers at key gateways and corners of Jerusalem's walls. Wise preparation and defense help protect what matters.
entries.2 chronicles 26:10: Uzziah built towers in the wilderness and dug storage places for water, because he had many cattle and loved farming. Caring for land and animals is a good and practical way to serve.
entries.2 chronicles 26:11: Uzziah had a fighting army organized in divisions, listed by his officials under Hananiah's authority. Good organization helps people work together effectively.
entries.2 chronicles 26:12: There were 2,600 heads of families who were strong fighting men. Strong leadership at the family level supported the whole army.
entries.2 chronicles 26:13: Under these leaders was a trained army of 307,500 strong soldiers who helped the king against his enemies. A well-trained and united force can accomplish a lot.
entries.2 chronicles 26:14: Uzziah equipped all his soldiers with shields, spears, helmets, armor, bows, and slings for stones. Preparing people well is part of being a responsible leader.
entries.2 chronicles 26:15: In Jerusalem Uzziah had skilled men make machines on the towers to shoot arrows and large stones, and his fame spread because God helped him greatly. God-given skill and help can make someone strong and respected.
entries.2 chronicles 26:16: Once Uzziah became strong, pride led him to ruin; he went into the Lord's temple to burn incense, which was not his job. Success can tempt us to overstep our place and dishonor God.
entries.2 chronicles 26:17: Azariah the priest went in after Uzziah with eighty brave priests of the Lord. Godly people sometimes need courage to confront wrong, even when it comes from a powerful person.
entries.2 chronicles 26:18: The priests told Uzziah that burning incense was their holy work, not his, and warned him he had done wrong. Some roles are set apart for specific service, and ignoring that brings dishonor.
entries.2 chronicles 26:19: Uzziah became angry at the priests, and while he was raging with the incense vessel in his hand, leprosy appeared on his forehead in the Lord's house. Anger against God's correction can lead to serious consequences.
entries.2 chronicles 26:20: Azariah and the priests saw the leprosy on Uzziah's forehead and hurried him out, and he left quickly because the Lord had struck him. God's judgment can come suddenly, and even a king cannot escape it.
entries.2 chronicles 26:21: Uzziah remained a leper until he died, living apart and cut off from the Lord's house, while his son Jotham managed the palace and judged the people. Pride cost Uzziah his place of worship and his active role as king.
entries.2 chronicles 26:22: The rest of Uzziah's deeds, from first to last, were written down by the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz. God remembers and records the whole story of a person's life, both good and bad.
entries.2 chronicles 26:23: Uzziah died and was buried with his ancestors in the kings' burial field, but they noted he was a leper, and his son Jotham became king. Even a long, successful reign ends, and our final legacy is shaped by how we finish.
entries.ezra 1:1: God had promised through Jeremiah that the exile would end, and he moved the Persian king Cyrus to act so that promise came true. It shows God keeps his word and can use even a foreign ruler to do it.
entries.ezra 1:2: Cyrus credits the God of heaven with giving him his vast empire and says he has been given the job of building God a house in Jerusalem. It reminds the reader that God is over all nations, not just one.
entries.ezra 1:3: Cyrus lets any of God's people go back to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple and says God be with them. It shows God making a way for his people to return and worship him again.
entries.ezra 1:4: People staying behind in other places are told to help the returning exiles with silver, gold, supplies, and animals for the temple. It shows that those who cannot go can still share in God's work by giving.
entries.ezra 1:5: The family leaders of Judah and Benjamin, along with priests and Levites, got ready to go because God stirred their hearts. It shows that real willingness to serve comes from God moving inside a person.
entries.ezra 1:6: Their neighbors pitched in with silver and gold articles, supplies, animals, and valuable things, plus freewill offerings. It shows how God provides for his work through the generosity of ordinary people around them.
entries.ezra 1:7: Cyrus brought out the temple articles that Nebuchadnezzar had stolen from Jerusalem and put in his own god's temple. It shows God had not forgotten his house, and what was taken would be restored.
entries.ezra 1:8: Cyrus had his treasurer Mithredath count out these articles and hand them to Sheshbazzar, the leader of Judah. It shows careful, orderly handling of what was dedicated to God.
entries.ezra 1:9: This verse begins listing the exact numbers of the gold and silver articles being returned. It shows the record was kept precisely, so nothing dedicated to God was lost or overlooked.
entries.ezra 1:10: The list continues with gold and silver bowls and a thousand other articles. It shows the huge scale of what was being given back for God's house.
entries.ezra 1:11: In total 5,400 gold and silver articles were brought back by Sheshbazzar when the exiles returned from Babylon to Jerusalem. It shows God fully restored what had been taken, down to the last item.
entries.2 chronicles 36:1: After King Josiah died, the people chose his son Jehoahaz to be the next king. It shows that leadership passed to a new generation, but the people made the choice themselves.
entries.2 chronicles 36:2: Jehoahaz was only twenty-three and lasted just three months as king. His short reign hints that his time in power was cut off quickly.
entries.2 chronicles 36:3: The king of Egypt removed him from the throne and forced the country to pay heavy taxes in silver and gold. Judah was no longer free but under a foreign power's control.
entries.2 chronicles 36:4: Egypt's king picked Jehoahaz's brother Eliakim to rule instead, renamed him Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz away to Egypt. The nation's king was now chosen by a foreign ruler.
entries.2 chronicles 36:5: Jehoiakim ruled eleven years starting at twenty-five, and the writer says plainly that he did evil before God. Long rule did not mean a good heart.
entries.2 chronicles 36:6: The king of Babylon attacked Jehoiakim and dragged him away in chains to Babylon. Judah's trouble was now coming from the east as well.
entries.2 chronicles 36:7: Nebuchadnezzar also carried off some of the temple's sacred objects and put them in his own god's temple. It looked like the God of Israel had been defeated along with his people.
entries.2 chronicles 36:8: The writer sums up Jehoiakim's reign as full of shameful deeds and points readers to the royal records for more. His son Jehoiachin took the throne after him.
entries.2 chronicles 36:9: Jehoiachin became king at eighteen and lasted only three months and ten days, and he too did evil before the Lord. Even a very short reign is judged by how the king treated God.
entries.2 chronicles 36:10: When spring came, Nebuchadnezzar sent for Jehoiachin and took him and more temple treasures to Babylon, then installed Zedekiah as king. The exile was tightening its grip on Judah.
entries.2 chronicles 36:11: Zedekiah became king at twenty-one and ruled for eleven years. Like the kings before him, his long reign would be measured by his faithfulness to God.
entries.2 chronicles 36:12: Zedekiah did evil and refused to humble himself before the prophet Jeremiah, who spoke God's word to him. Ignoring God's messenger is the same as ignoring God.
entries.2 chronicles 36:13: Zedekiah broke a solemn promise he had sworn before God and rebelled against Babylon, hardening his heart against the Lord. Breaking your word, especially a promise made before God, is serious.
entries.2 chronicles 36:14: The leaders, priests, and people all joined in copying the disgusting practices of other nations and defiled the temple God had set apart. When leaders and people sin together, the whole community is affected.
entries.2 chronicles 36:15: God kept sending prophets again and again because he felt sorry for his people and his temple. God's warnings come from compassion, not from a desire to punish.
entries.2 chronicles 36:16: The people mocked God's messengers and laughed at his prophets until there was no remedy left. Making fun of God's warnings closes the door on help.
entries.2 chronicles 36:17: So God brought the Babylonians, who killed young and old alike without mercy, even in the temple. When people refuse every warning, judgment finally comes.
entries.2 chronicles 36:18: The Babylonians carried off all the temple treasures, large and small, along with the wealth of the king and his officials. Nothing sacred or valuable was left behind.
entries.2 chronicles 36:19: They burned God's temple, broke down Jerusalem's walls, and destroyed its fine buildings. The city that seemed secure was left in ruins.
entries.2 chronicles 36:20: Those who survived the sword were taken as prisoners to Babylon and served its kings until Persia took over. God's people became slaves in a foreign land.
entries.2 chronicles 36:21: The land lay empty for seventy years, resting the way God had commanded, just as Jeremiah had said. God's word proved true even when it took decades to happen.
entries.2 chronicles 36:22: In Cyrus of Persia's first year, God stirred him to make a public proclamation so Jeremiah's words would come true. God can move even a foreign king to carry out his plans.
entries.2 chronicles 36:23: Cyrus announced that God had given him all the kingdoms and told him to build a temple in Jerusalem, and he invited God's people to go back. After judgment, God opened a door for his people to return home.
entries.2 chronicles 35:1: King Josiah had the people celebrate the Passover, remembering how God rescued Israel from Egypt, and they killed the lamb on the set day. It shows the reader that honoring God's commands was central to Josiah's leadership.
entries.2 chronicles 35:2: Josiah organized the priests into their assigned roles and encouraged them for their work in the temple. Good leaders help people know their part and feel supported in serving God.
entries.2 chronicles 35:3: The Levites, who taught Israel and were set apart for God, were told the sacred chest now had a permanent home, so they could focus on serving God and the people instead of carrying it. It reminds the reader that settled worship frees us to serve faithfully.
entries.2 chronicles 35:4: The Levites were told to get ready for service in their assigned groups, following the plans handed down from David and Solomon. Preparation and order help worship run well.
entries.2 chronicles 35:5: They were to stand in the temple in their family groups, with Levites assigned to help each group of the people. It shows the value of organizing people so everyone is cared for.
entries.2 chronicles 35:6: They were to kill the Passover lambs, prepare themselves, and get things ready for the people so everything would follow God's instructions through Moses. Obedience to God's directions was the goal.
entries.2 chronicles 35:7: Josiah personally donated thousands of lambs and oxen from his own wealth so everyone present could share in the Passover. Generous leaders give from what they have to help others worship.
entries.2 chronicles 35:8: The king's officials and the temple leaders also gave freely, providing animals for the priests' Passover offerings. When leaders give generously, it encourages worship for everyone.
entries.2 chronicles 35:9: The heads of the Levite families gave thousands of animals to supply the Levites' Passover offerings. Each group helped provide what was needed for the whole celebration.
entries.2 chronicles 35:10: Everything was arranged, and the priests and Levites took their assigned places just as the king had directed. Careful planning made the worship orderly and complete.
entries.2 chronicles 35:11: The lambs were killed, the priests handled the blood, and the Levites skinned the animals. Each person did their part so the whole service could be carried out.
entries.2 chronicles 35:12: They set aside the burnt offerings to give to each family group, following what was written in the law of Moses, and did the same with the oxen. The reader sees that worship was done according to God's written word.
entries.2 chronicles 35:13: The Passover lamb was roasted over fire as the law required, and the other holy offerings were boiled and quickly served to all the people. The people were fed promptly and according to God's instructions.
entries.2 chronicles 35:14: After preparing for the people, the Levites prepared for themselves and the priests, because the priests were busy offering sacrifices until night. Serving others came first, and no one was left without what they needed.
entries.2 chronicles 35:15: The singers and gatekeepers stayed at their posts as David had arranged, and the Levites prepared food for them too. Everyone's role mattered, and others made sure they were cared for.
entries.2 chronicles 35:16: All the worship for that day was fully prepared, both the Passover and the burnt offerings on the altar, just as Josiah had ordered. Complete obedience made the day's worship possible.
entries.2 chronicles 35:17: All the Israelites who were there celebrated the Passover and the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread. It was a time of shared remembrance and joy for the whole community.
entries.2 chronicles 35:18: No Passover like this one had been kept since the prophet Samuel's time, and no king of Israel had ever matched it, with priests, Levites, Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem all taking part. It shows how seriously Josiah led the nation back to God.
entries.2 chronicles 35:19: This remarkable Passover took place in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign. The date marks a high point in his efforts to restore faithful worship.
entries.2 chronicles 35:20: After Josiah had restored the temple, King Neco of Egypt marched to fight at Carchemish, and Josiah went out to oppose him. A good king's story can still take a dangerous turn.
entries.2 chronicles 35:21: Neco sent messengers telling Josiah he had no quarrel with Judah and that God had told him to hurry, warning Josiah to stay out of the way or be destroyed. It reminds the reader to listen carefully, even when a warning is unexpected.
entries.2 chronicles 35:22: Josiah refused to turn back, ignored Neco's words that came from God, and went into battle at Megiddo. Even a faithful person can make a costly mistake by not listening.
entries.2 chronicles 35:23: Archers shot King Josiah, and he told his servants to get him away because he was badly hurt. The battle turned against him in a moment.
entries.2 chronicles 35:24: His servants moved him from his chariot to another and took him to Jerusalem, where he died and was buried with his ancestors, and all Judah and Jerusalem mourned deeply. A beloved leader's death brought the whole nation to grief.
entries.2 chronicles 35:25: The prophet Jeremiah composed a lament for Josiah, and singers, men and women, have remembered him in their songs ever since, which became a custom in Israel. It shows how deeply a faithful life can be remembered.
entries.2 chronicles 35:26: The rest of Josiah's deeds and his faithful obedience to what was written in the law of the Lord are recorded. His life is summed up by his loyalty to God's word.
entries.2 chronicles 35:27: All his deeds, from first to last, are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah. The record of his life was kept for later generations to read.
entries.2 chronicles 34:1: Josiah became king of Judah when he was only eight years old, and he ruled for thirty-one years. Even someone young can be given big responsibility, and God can work through people of any age.
entries.2 chronicles 34:2: Josiah did what pleased God, following the good example of his ancestor David and not swerving off the path. His life shows that it's possible to stay faithful when you commit to doing right.
entries.2 chronicles 34:3: While still a young man, Josiah began sincerely seeking the God of David, and a few years later he started removing the idols and shrines from Judah and Jerusalem. Turning to God early can lead to real changes in your life and surroundings.
entries.2 chronicles 34:4: Josiah personally supervised the destruction of the altars to false gods, cutting down and crushing the idols to powder and scattering the dust on the graves of those who had worshiped them. This shows how seriously he took removing things that dishonored God.
entries.2 chronicles 34:5: He burned the bones of the false priests on their own altars, which cleansed Judah and Jerusalem from idol worship. Cleaning out wrong practices completely, not halfway, was central to his reform.
entries.2 chronicles 34:6: He extended this cleanup to towns in the territories of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and as far as Naphtali, leaving ruins around them. His concern for right worship reached beyond his own kingdom.
entries.2 chronicles 34:7: Throughout the land of Israel he tore down altars and wooden poles, crushed the idols, and cut down the sun-images, then returned to Jerusalem. He was thorough in removing every trace of false worship.
entries.2 chronicles 34:8: In the eighteenth year of his reign, after the land and temple had been cleansed, Josiah sent officials to repair the damage to the house of the Lord. Good reform includes restoring what has been neglected.
entries.2 chronicles 34:9: The officials collected the money brought to God's house from the people of Manasseh, Ephraim, the remnant of Israel, and all Judah, Benjamin, and Jerusalem, and gave it to the high priest. The people's giving supported the work of God's house.
entries.2 chronicles 34:10: The money was handed to the supervisors of the temple work, who passed it on to the workers repairing and rebuilding the house. Organized, honest handling of resources made the repair possible.
entries.2 chronicles 34:11: The funds went to carpenters and builders for cut stone and timber to restore the structures the kings of Judah had let fall into ruin. Skilled labor and materials were needed to undo years of neglect.
entries.2 chronicles 34:12: The workers did their jobs faithfully, supervised by Levites from the Merari and Kohath clans, while other Levites who were skilled musicians also served. Faithful work and good oversight go together in serving God.
entries.2 chronicles 34:13: The Levites directed the laborers and oversaw all kinds of work, and some served as scribes, officers, and gatekeepers. Everyone had a role, and each role mattered for the work to succeed.
entries.2 chronicles 34:14: While the money was being brought out of the temple, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law of the Lord given through Moses. Sometimes an important discovery happens in the middle of ordinary duties.
entries.2 chronicles 34:15: Hilkiah told Shaphan the secretary that he had found the Book of the Law in the temple and handed it to him. Finding God's word is worth telling others about.
entries.2 chronicles 34:16: Shaphan brought the book to the king and reported that the servants were carrying out everything they had been assigned. Honest reporting keeps leaders informed about what is actually happening.
entries.2 chronicles 34:17: He explained that all the money in the Lord's house had been collected and handed over to the supervisors and workers. The account was clear and complete.
entries.2 chronicles 34:18: Shaphan then told the king that Hilkiah had given him a book, and he began reading from it to the king. Reading God's word aloud to those in authority can change hearts.
entries.2 chronicles 34:19: When the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes as a sign of deep grief. God's word confronted him with how far his people had strayed, and he responded with real sorrow.
entries.2 chronicles 34:20: The king gave orders to Hilkiah, Ahikam, Abdon, Shaphan, and Asaiah. A serious response to God's word includes seeking wise guidance.
entries.2 chronicles 34:21: He told them to ask the Lord for direction for himself and for the people left in Israel and Judah, because God's anger was great since their ancestors had not obeyed this book. When you realize you've fallen short, the right move is to seek God.
entries.2 chronicles 34:22: Hilkiah and the king's men went to Huldah, a woman prophet living in Jerusalem, and talked with her about the matter. God sometimes speaks through unexpected people, and wise leaders listen.
entries.2 chronicles 34:23: She told them that the Lord, the God of Israel, had a message for the man who sent them. God's word came clearly through her to the king.
entries.2 chronicles 34:24: The Lord said he would bring disaster on that place and its people, all the curses written in the book read before the king. Ignoring God's word for generations brings serious consequences.
entries.2 chronicles 34:25: Because the people had abandoned God, burning offerings to other gods and angering him with what they made, his anger was poured out and would not be quenched. Turning to false gods provokes real judgment.
entries.2 chronicles 34:26: But to the king who sent them to seek the Lord, God said that because he had listened to his words, there was good news for him. God notices when someone truly listens to him.
entries.2 chronicles 34:27: Because Josiah's heart was tender and he humbled himself before God, weeping and grieving over what he heard, God said he had heard him. Humility and sorrow over sin move God's heart.
entries.2 chronicles 34:28: God promised Josiah would die in peace and be buried with his ancestors, not seeing the disaster coming on the place and its people, and they brought this answer back to the king. God showed mercy to a faithful king even while judgment loomed for the nation.
entries.2 chronicles 34:29: The king summoned all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem to gather. A leader's response to God's word should involve the whole community.
entries.2 chronicles 34:30: Josiah went up to the Lord's house with all the people, great and small, priests and Levites, and read the Book of the Law to them. God's word is meant to be shared with everyone, not kept to yourself.
entries.2 chronicles 34:31: Standing by the pillar, the king made a covenant before the Lord to follow him and keep his commands and laws with all his heart and soul, and to obey the words of the book. Real commitment involves the whole heart, not just outward actions.
entries.2 chronicles 34:32: He had everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin pledge themselves to the covenant, and the people of Jerusalem kept their agreement with the God of their ancestors. Leaders can call people to faithfulness, and the people must choose to follow.
entries.2 chronicles 34:33: Josiah removed all the detestable things from all the land of Israel and made everyone serve the Lord their God, and they remained faithful as long as he lived. One faithful leader can influence a whole nation toward God.
entries.ezra 3:1: The Israelites had returned from exile and were living in their own towns, and in the seventh month they all gathered in Jerusalem with one shared purpose. It shows how God's people come together to worship and rebuild, and it invites the reader to join others in seeking God rather than staying isolated.
entries.ezra 3:2: The leaders and priests rebuilt the altar for burnt offerings, following what Moses' law had commanded. They started with worship before anything else, showing the reader that putting God first is the right foundation for any new beginning.
entries.ezra 3:3: Even though they were afraid of the surrounding peoples, they set the altar in place and offered sacrifices every morning and evening. It means faith can act despite fear, and the reader can keep worshiping and doing what is right even when surrounded by threats.
entries.ezra 3:4: They celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles and kept up the daily offerings exactly as the law required. It shows obedience in worship, and it reminds the reader that regular, ordered devotion to God matters, not just occasional big moments.
entries.ezra 3:5: After the feast they continued with the regular offerings, new moon offerings, and all the appointed feasts, plus freewill gifts anyone wanted to give. It means worship became a steady habit, and the reader is encouraged to give and worship consistently, not only when they feel like it.
entries.ezra 3:6: They began offering sacrifices on the first day of the seventh month, even though the temple foundation had not yet been laid. It shows that worship can start before everything is finished, and the reader can begin honoring God now rather than waiting for perfect conditions.
entries.ezra 3:7: They paid workers and supplied food, drink, and oil to the people of Tyre and Sidon so cedar wood could be shipped from Lebanon to Joppa, as King Cyrus had permitted. It shows practical planning and generosity in God's work, and the reader learns that faith involves real effort and resources, not just words.
entries.ezra 3:8: In the second year after arriving, the leaders, priests, Levites, and returned exiles began the temple work and put Levites twenty and older in charge of supervising it. It shows organized, shared responsibility in serving God, and the reader sees that everyone has a part to play in building up God's work.
entries.ezra 3:9: Jeshua, Kadmiel, Hodaviah's sons, and Henadad's sons with their relatives all worked together to oversee the laborers in God's house. It means teamwork and shared leadership matter, and the reader is encouraged to cooperate with others rather than work alone.
entries.ezra 3:10: When the foundation was laid, the priests in their robes with trumpets and the Levites with cymbals praised the Lord, following David's instructions. It shows that milestones in God's work should be marked with praise, and the reader can celebrate and thank God when progress is made.
entries.ezra 3:11: They sang back and forth, praising God because he is good and his mercy to Israel lasts forever, and all the people shouted with joy over the foundation. It means God's goodness and lasting mercy deserve loud gratitude, and the reader can trust that his kindness does not run out.
entries.ezra 3:12: Many older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the first temple wept loudly when they saw the new foundation, while others shouted for joy. It shows that people can feel deep grief and joy at the same time, and the reader learns to make room for both in others and in themselves.
entries.ezra 3:13: The joyful shouting and the weeping mixed together so loudly that the sound carried far away. It means big moments in God's work can stir mixed emotions, and the reader can accept that worship and rebuilding may bring both sorrow and celebration.
entries.ezra 2:1: This lists the Jews that the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar had taken captive, and who now came back to their own towns in Jerusalem and Judah. It means God brought his people home after years of exile, and it reminds the reader that God keeps his promises to restore.
entries.ezra 2:2: These are the leaders who traveled back with the returning exiles, starting with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. It shows the return was organized under named leaders, and it reminds the reader that God works through ordinary people to carry out his plans.
entries.ezra 2:3: This begins a long list of family groups and how many men were in each, starting with the family of Parosh at 2,172. It shows that every returning family was counted and remembered, and it reminds the reader that God values each person and family among his people.
entries.ezra 2:4: The family of Shephatiah numbered 372 men. It is one more entry in the record of those who came back, showing that each family group had its place in the return.
entries.ezra 2:5: The family of Arah numbered 775 men. The careful counting shows the return was a real, organized event, and it reminds the reader that God knows and keeps track of his people.
entries.ezra 2:6: The family of Pahath-moab, through Jeshua and Joab, numbered 2,812 men. This large group shows how many descendants of one family line returned together to rebuild their lives.
entries.ezra 2:7: The family of Elam numbered 1,254 men. Each number in this list records real people who made the journey home, showing that God's restoration involved specific, named families.
entries.ezra 2:8: The family of Zattu numbered 945 men. The list keeps counting the returning exiles family by family, showing that no group was left out of the record.
entries.ezra 2:9: The family of Zaccai numbered 760 men. This is another entry in the census of those who returned, showing the care taken to record who came back.
entries.ezra 2:10: The family of Bani numbered 642 men. The record continues, showing that the return involved many different family groups, each with its own place among God's people.
entries.ezra 2:11: The family of Bebai numbered 623 men. Each family's number is listed, showing that the returning community was made up of many ordinary households.
entries.ezra 2:12: The family of Azgad numbered 1,222 men. The list keeps showing how many people from each family line chose to leave Babylon and return home.
entries.ezra 2:13: The family of Adonikam numbered 666 men. This is one more family group counted among those who came back to Judah.
entries.ezra 2:14: The family of Bigvai numbered 2,056 men. This was one of the larger family groups in the return, showing how many people from one line made the journey.
entries.ezra 2:15: The family of Adin numbered 454 men. The record continues to list each family and its size, showing the return was carefully documented.
entries.ezra 2:16: The family of Ater, through Hezekiah, numbered 98 men. Even small family groups are listed, showing that every returning household mattered in the record.
entries.ezra 2:17: The family of Bezai numbered 323 men. This is another entry in the list of families who came back from exile to rebuild their homes.
entries.ezra 2:18: The family of Jorah numbered 112 men. The list keeps counting the returning families, showing that the community was rebuilt one household at a time.
entries.ezra 2:19: The family of Hashum numbered 223 men. Each family's number is recorded, showing the care taken to know who made up the returning people.
entries.ezra 2:20: The family of Gibbar numbered 95 men. This small group is still named and counted, showing that no returning family was too small to be remembered.
entries.ezra 2:21: The people of Bethlehem numbered 123 men. The list now includes towns as well as families, showing that people returned to specific places to rebuild their communities.
entries.ezra 2:22: The men of Netophah numbered 56. This small town's returning men are recorded, showing that even small places had people who came home.
entries.ezra 2:23: The men of Anathoth numbered 128. This town's returning men are listed, showing that the return reached many different local communities.
entries.ezra 2:24: The people of Azmaveth numbered 42 men. Even a very small group is recorded, showing that every returning community was noted.
entries.ezra 2:25: The people of Kiriath-arim, Chephirah, and Beeroth together numbered 743 men. Several nearby towns are grouped together, showing how returning families settled back into their local areas.
entries.ezra 2:26: The people of Ramah and Geba together numbered 621 men. These towns' returning people are counted together, showing the return involved whole communities, not just individuals.
entries.ezra 2:27: The men of Michmas numbered 122. This town's returning men are recorded, showing that the list covers many small local places.
entries.ezra 2:28: The men of Bethel and Ai together numbered 223. These two towns' returning people are counted together, showing that people went back to rebuild in their old home areas.
entries.ezra 2:29: The family of Nebo numbered 52 men. This small group is still named, showing that even the smallest returning families were remembered.
entries.ezra 2:30: The family of Magbish numbered 156 men. This is another small family group recorded among those who came back from exile.
entries.ezra 2:31: The other family of Elam numbered 1,254 men. A second group with the same family name is listed, showing the record was detailed enough to tell apart different branches of a family.
entries.ezra 2:32: The family of Harim numbered 320 men. This family group is counted among the returning exiles, adding to the record of who came home.
entries.ezra 2:33: The people of Lod, Hadid, and Ono together numbered 725 men. Three towns are grouped together, showing how returning families settled back into their local regions.
entries.ezra 2:34: The people of Jericho numbered 345 men. This town's returning people are recorded, showing that the return included people from many different places.
entries.ezra 2:35: The family of Senaah numbered 3,630 men. This was one of the largest groups in the return, showing how many people from one family line came back to rebuild.
entries.ezra 2:36: This starts a separate list of the priests, beginning with the family of Jedaiah through Jeshua at 973 men. It shows that priests were among the returning exiles, and it reminds the reader that worship and service to God were being restored.
entries.ezra 2:37: The priestly family of Immer numbered 1,052 men. The priests are counted separately, showing that the returning community made sure its religious leadership was restored.
entries.ezra 2:38: The priestly family of Pashhur numbered 1,247 men. This large priestly group is recorded, showing that many priests returned to serve in the rebuilt temple.
entries.ezra 2:39: The priestly family of Harim numbered 1,017 men. The list of priests continues, showing that the returning community carefully organized who would lead worship.
entries.ezra 2:40: This lists the Levites, the temple helpers, starting with the family of Jeshua and Kadmiel through Hodaviah at 74 men. It shows that the people who assisted the priests also returned, and it reminds the reader that every role in serving God matters.
entries.ezra 6:1: King Darius ordered a search of the royal records kept in Babylon to find the original decree. It shows that official records were checked to settle a dispute fairly.
entries.ezra 6:2: The search turned up a scroll in the king's palace at Achmetha in Media, and it contained an official written record. This means the evidence they needed was found and written down.
entries.ezra 6:3: The scroll recorded that King Cyrus had ordered the temple in Jerusalem to be rebuilt, with its foundations laid and set dimensions. It confirmed the Jews had royal permission to rebuild.
entries.ezra 6:4: The decree specified the building materials and said the cost would be paid from the king's treasury. This meant the project had official financial backing.
entries.ezra 6:5: Cyrus also ordered that the gold and silver temple items taken by Nebuchadnezzar be returned to their proper place in Jerusalem. This corrected an old wrong and restored what had been taken.
entries.ezra 6:6: Darius told the regional officials to stay away from the building site and stop interfering. It means the opponents of the Jews were ordered to back off.
entries.ezra 6:7: The officials were told to let the temple work continue and not hinder the Jewish leaders. This gave the builders freedom to keep going.
entries.ezra 6:8: Darius ordered that the building costs be paid from royal tax money collected in the region, given promptly so the work would not stop. It meant the project was funded and protected by the king.
entries.ezra 6:9: Whatever the priests needed for sacrifices—animals, grain, salt, wine, and oil—was to be supplied every day without fail. This ensured worship could continue regularly.
entries.ezra 6:10: The supplies were so the priests could offer sacrifices and pray for the king and his sons. It shows the king wanted the blessing of prayers on his behalf.
entries.ezra 6:11: Darius set a harsh penalty for anyone who changed his order: their house would be destroyed and they would be punished severely. It shows how seriously the king protected the decree.
entries.ezra 6:12: Darius called on God, who had chosen Jerusalem for his name, to destroy any king or people who tried to alter the order or harm the temple. It placed the project under God's protection as well as the king's.
entries.ezra 6:13: The regional officials obeyed Darius's order and carried it out carefully. It shows the opposition stopped once the king's command was clear.
entries.ezra 6:14: The Jewish leaders kept building and succeeded, encouraged by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, until the work was finished as God had said and the kings had ordered. It shows God's word and human authority working together.
entries.ezra 6:15: The temple was completed on the third day of the month Adar in the sixth year of Darius's reign. It marks the finish of a long, hard rebuilding project.
entries.ezra 6:16: The returned Israelites, priests, and Levites celebrated the dedication of the temple with joy. It was a happy moment of thanksgiving for what God had allowed them to finish.
entries.ezra 6:17: At the dedication they offered hundreds of animals, plus twelve male goats as a sin offering for all Israel, one for each tribe. It showed they were asking forgiveness and giving thanks for the whole nation.
entries.ezra 6:18: They organized the priests and Levites into their assigned groups for temple worship, following what was written in the book of Moses. It means worship was set up again in an orderly way.
entries.ezra 6:19: The returned people celebrated Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. It was a key festival remembering how God had rescued them.
entries.ezra 6:20: The priests and Levites had all purified themselves, so they were able to kill the Passover lamb for everyone who had returned, including the priests. It shows careful preparation for worship.
entries.ezra 6:21: The returned Israelites, along with others who had turned from the sinful ways of the surrounding peoples to serve the Lord, ate the Passover meal together. It shows that anyone willing to follow God could join the community.
entries.ezra 6:22: They celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with joy, because the Lord had made the king favorable to them and helped them with the temple work. It reminds the reader that God can move even powerful rulers to help his people.
entries.ezra 4:1: The enemies of the returning Jews heard that they were rebuilding the temple. This shows that doing God's work often attracts opposition from people who don't want it to succeed.
entries.ezra 4:2: These opponents offered to help build, claiming they worshiped the same God. But their offer was false, and it reminds us that not everyone who claims to be on our side really is.
entries.ezra 4:3: The Jewish leaders refused the offer and said only they would build, as the king had commanded. They were right to protect the work from people whose help would have compromised it.
entries.ezra 4:4: The people around them tried to discourage the builders and make them afraid. This shows that opposition can come through fear and discouragement, not just direct attacks.
entries.ezra 4:5: They even paid people to work against the Jews and block their plans for years. This reminds us that opposition to good work can be persistent and last a long time.
entries.ezra 4:6: Later, under a new king, the enemies formally accused the people of Judah. This shows they kept looking for ways to cause trouble over many years.
entries.ezra 4:7: Under another king, a group of officials sent a letter against the Jews in the official language of the region. This was an organized effort to turn the government against God's people.
entries.ezra 4:8: Two officials, Rehum and Shimshai, sent their own letter against Jerusalem to the king. This shows how people in power can use their position to oppose God's work.
entries.ezra 4:9: The letter came from a whole group of officials and peoples settled in the area. Many voices joined together to accuse the Jews.
entries.ezra 4:10: These were the peoples that a great Assyrian king had resettled in Samaria and the region beyond the river. They were outsiders who had been planted there by a foreign empire.
entries.ezra 4:11: This is the opening of their letter to King Artaxerxes, identifying themselves as his servants in the province. They presented themselves as loyal subjects while working against the Jews.
entries.ezra 4:12: They told the king that the Jews were rebuilding Jerusalem, calling it a rebellious and wicked city, and claimed its walls were nearly finished. This was an exaggerated and hostile report meant to alarm the king.
entries.ezra 4:13: They warned that once the city was rebuilt, the Jews would stop paying taxes, which would cost the king money. This was a calculated appeal to the king's financial interests.
entries.ezra 4:14: They claimed they were acting out of loyalty to the king and did not want to see him dishonored. This shows how opposition is often dressed up as concern for the ruler's good.
entries.ezra 4:15: They asked the king to check his own records, claiming history would show Jerusalem had always been rebellious. This was a selective and misleading use of the past to justify their accusation.
entries.ezra 4:16: They warned that if the city was rebuilt, the king would lose control of the whole province. This was the real threat they wanted the king to fear.
entries.ezra 4:17: The king sent his reply to the officials and their associates in Samaria and the province. The king had listened to their accusations.
entries.ezra 4:18: The king confirmed that he had read and understood their letter. Their accusations had reached the highest authority.
entries.ezra 4:19: The king ordered a search, and the records did show that Jerusalem had rebelled against kings in the past. The enemies' claims had enough truth in them to seem convincing.
entries.ezra 4:20: The records also showed that powerful kings had once ruled from Jerusalem and collected taxes from the whole region. This made the king nervous about the city's potential.
entries.ezra 4:21: The king ordered the work stopped until he gave further permission. The rebuilding was halted by royal command.
entries.ezra 4:22: He told them to act carefully and quickly so the problem would not grow. The king was determined to protect his own interests.
entries.ezra 4:23: The officials went to Jerusalem at once and forced the Jews to stop building. The opposition succeeded, and the work was halted by force.
entries.ezra 4:24: So the rebuilding of God's temple stopped until the second year of King Darius. God's work was paused for a time, but it was not abandoned forever.
entries.ezra 7:1: This introduces Ezra and traces his family line back through important priests. It shows the reader that Ezra came from a respected priestly heritage.
entries.ezra 7:2: The family list continues, linking Ezra to well-known priestly ancestors. It reminds the reader that Ezra's background was rooted in Israel's worship tradition.
entries.ezra 7:3: More names in Ezra's family tree are given. Each name connects him further back to the established priesthood.
entries.ezra 7:4: The list keeps going, showing an unbroken line of ancestors. This matters because it proves Ezra's right to serve as a priest.
entries.ezra 7:5: The family line ends with Aaron, the first high priest. This confirms that Ezra was a genuine descendant of Israel's original priesthood.
entries.ezra 7:6: Ezra traveled from Babylon and was highly skilled in God's law, and the king granted his requests because God was with him. It shows the reader that God can open doors through powerful people when he is at work.
entries.ezra 7:7: A group of Israelites, including priests, temple workers, and singers, went with Ezra to Jerusalem. It shows that this was a community effort, not just one man's journey.
entries.ezra 7:8: Ezra arrived in Jerusalem in the fifth month of the king's seventh year. It simply marks the timing of his arrival.
entries.ezra 7:9: The trip from Babylon took about four months, and Ezra made it safely because God helped him. It encourages the reader that God can guide and protect long, difficult journeys.
entries.ezra 7:10: Ezra committed himself to studying God's law, obeying it, and then teaching it to others. It gives the reader a model: learn God's word, live it out, then share it.
entries.ezra 7:11: This begins a copy of the official letter King Artaxerxes gave Ezra. It shows that Ezra's mission had royal backing.
entries.ezra 7:12: The king addresses Ezra with a grand title and wishes him peace. It shows how highly the king regarded Ezra and his God.
entries.ezra 7:13: The king decreed that any Israelite in his kingdom who wanted to go to Jerusalem with Ezra was free to do so. It shows the reader that God can move even foreign rulers to support his people.
entries.ezra 7:14: The king and his advisors sent Ezra to investigate how things were in Judah and Jerusalem according to God's law. It shows that Ezra's task was to check and guide the community by God's standards.
entries.ezra 7:15: Ezra was to carry silver and gold given by the king and his advisors as offerings to Israel's God in Jerusalem. It shows that even outsiders contributed to God's work.
entries.ezra 7:16: He was also to collect additional gifts from the people and priests in Babylon for God's temple. It reminds the reader that giving toward God's work came from many sources.
entries.ezra 7:17: The money was to be used carefully to buy animals and offerings for the temple altar. It shows the reader that resources given to God should be used purposefully and honestly.
entries.ezra 7:18: Ezra and his companions could decide how to use the remaining money as long as it honored God. It shows that God gives freedom in how we manage resources, guided by what pleases him.
entries.ezra 7:19: The temple items entrusted to Ezra were to be delivered to God's house in Jerusalem. It reminds the reader to handle what has been dedicated to God with care.
