entries.ezra 7:20: Any further needs for the temple could be paid from the king's treasury. It shows that God can provide for his work through unexpected sources.
entries.ezra 7:21: The king ordered all his treasurers to supply whatever Ezra needed without delay. It shows the reader that God can command widespread cooperation for his purposes.
entries.ezra 7:22: The king set generous limits on silver, grain, wine, oil, and unlimited salt for the temple. It shows that God's work was given abundant provision.
entries.ezra 7:23: The king insisted that everything God required be done fully, so that trouble would not come on his kingdom. It shows the reader that honoring God brings blessing, while neglecting him brings risk.
entries.ezra 7:24: Temple workers were exempted from taxes and fees. It shows that the king wanted those serving God to be free to do their work.
entries.ezra 7:25: Ezra was to appoint judges and teach God's laws to those who did not know them. It reminds the reader that leadership and teaching go together in guiding people rightly.
entries.ezra 7:26: Anyone who disobeyed God's law or the king's law faced serious punishment. It shows the reader that living under God's authority has real consequences.
entries.ezra 7:27: Ezra praised God for moving the king to honor the temple in Jerusalem. It encourages the reader to thank God when he stirs people to support his work.
entries.ezra 7:28: Ezra recognized that God's kindness before the king gave him strength, and he gathered leaders to go with him. It shows the reader that God's help can embolden us to lead and act.
entries.ezra 5:1: God sent two prophets, Haggai and Zechariah, to encourage the Jews by speaking to them in God's name. It reminds the reader that God speaks to people through faithful messengers to keep them going.
entries.ezra 5:2: The leaders Zerubbabel and Jeshua responded by restarting the work on God's temple, and the prophets supported them. It shows that hearing God's word should lead to action, and that God's messengers stand with those who obey.
entries.ezra 5:3: A regional governor and his officials came and challenged the Jews, asking who had authorized them to rebuild the temple and its wall. It shows that doing God's work can bring official opposition and hard questions.
entries.ezra 5:4: The officials also asked for the names of the men in charge of the building work. It shows that those who oppose God's work often want to identify and target its leaders.
entries.ezra 5:5: God was watching over the Jewish leaders, so the work was not stopped while the matter was sent to King Darius for a decision. It reminds the reader that God protects his people and his work even when authorities must be consulted.
entries.ezra 5:6: This verse introduces the official letter that the governor and his associates sent to King Darius. It shows that the challenge to the building was handled through proper channels rather than by force.
entries.ezra 5:7: The letter opens with a respectful greeting of peace to King Darius. It shows that God's people can deal honestly and respectfully with governing authorities.
entries.ezra 5:8: The officials reported that they had visited Judah and found the temple being rebuilt with large stones and timber, and the work was progressing well. It shows that even outsiders could see the serious effort being made.
entries.ezra 5:9: The officials told the king they had asked the builders who had given them authority to rebuild. It shows they were investigating whether the work was legally permitted.
entries.ezra 5:10: They also asked for the leaders' names so they could report them to the king. It shows the matter was being documented and passed up to the highest authority.
entries.ezra 5:11: The Jews answered that they served the God of heaven and earth and were rebuilding the temple that a great king of Israel had built long ago. It shows they were honest about their identity and their historic right to build.
entries.ezra 5:12: They explained that their ancestors had angered God, so he allowed Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon to destroy the temple and take the people captive. It shows that they accepted their past failure as the reason for their trouble.
entries.ezra 5:13: They noted that King Cyrus of Babylon had issued an order to rebuild God's temple. It shows that the current work was backed by a previous royal decree.
entries.ezra 5:14: Cyrus had taken back the gold and silver temple articles that Nebuchadnezzar had seized and given them to Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed as governor. It shows that God can use even pagan kings to restore what was lost.
entries.ezra 5:15: Cyrus instructed Sheshbazzar to take the articles to Jerusalem and rebuild God's temple on its original site. It shows the king's order was specific and honored the temple's proper place.
entries.ezra 5:16: Sheshbazzar laid the temple foundations in Jerusalem, and the work had continued from then until now, though not yet finished. It shows the rebuilding was a long, ongoing effort rather than a quick success.
entries.ezra 5:17: The officials asked the king to search the royal records in Babylon to confirm Cyrus's order and then tell them his decision. It shows that verifying the facts and waiting for proper authority is a wise way to handle opposition.
entries.ezra 9:1: The leaders told Ezra that the returned exiles, including priests, had intermarried with the surrounding peoples and adopted their detestable practices. It means God's people had blurred the line between faith and the culture around them, and the reader is warned that compromise often starts at the top.
entries.ezra 9:2: They had married foreign women, mixing the holy people with the surrounding nations, and the leaders were the worst offenders. It means those with the most responsibility set the bad example, so readers should be careful that their own influence doesn't lead others astray.
entries.ezra 9:3: Ezra was so devastated by the report that he tore out his hair and beard and sat down stunned. It means real grief over sin is physical and honest, and the reader is invited to take sin seriously rather than shrug it off.
entries.ezra 9:4: Everyone who trembled at God's word gathered around Ezra, and he sat there appalled until the evening sacrifice. It means those who honor God's word will be drawn together in shared concern, and the reader can find comfort in not grieving alone.
entries.ezra 9:5: At the evening sacrifice Ezra got up from his humiliation and knelt with hands spread out to God. It means prayer is the right response to a crisis, and the reader can bring heavy situations to God openly and humbly.
entries.ezra 9:6: Ezra was too ashamed to look up, confessing that the people's sins had piled up beyond their heads and reached heaven. It means sin is serious and needs honest confession, and the reader is encouraged to name their wrongs plainly before God.
entries.ezra 9:7: From their ancestors' days until now the people had sinned greatly, and their sins had brought defeat, captivity, plunder, and disgrace. It means sin has real consequences that can last generations, and the reader is reminded to learn from the past rather than repeat it.
entries.ezra 9:8: God had shown brief grace by letting a remnant return and giving them a firm foothold in his holy place, bringing light and renewed life. It means God's mercy gives fresh starts even after failure, and the reader can look for God's kindness in hard times.
entries.ezra 9:9: Though still servants, God had not abandoned them in their bondage but showed mercy before the Persian kings, enabling them to rebuild his house and giving them a wall in Judah and Jerusalem. It means God can work through powerful outsiders to help his people, and the reader can trust that God is present even in difficult circumstances.
entries.ezra 9:10: Ezra asks what can be said now, since the people had failed to keep God's commands. It means there are no excuses left for disobedience, and the reader is invited to be honest about their own failures instead of defending them.
entries.ezra 9:11: God had told them through the prophets that the land was unclean because of the detestable practices of its peoples. It means God had warned them clearly in advance, and the reader is reminded that God's warnings are meant to protect, not to spoil.
entries.ezra 9:12: God had commanded them not to intermarry or seek the peace and prosperity of these peoples, so that they could be strong and pass the land to their children. It means loyalty to God matters more than convenient alliances, and the reader should guard their closest commitments.
entries.ezra 9:13: Ezra acknowledges that their punishment was less than their sins deserved and that God had spared a remnant from death. It means God's discipline is mixed with mercy, and the reader can be grateful that God does not treat us as our sins deserve.
entries.ezra 9:14: Ezra asks whether they should again break God's commands by marrying into these peoples, which would bring total destruction with no survivors. It means repeating known sin invites serious consequences, and the reader is warned not to presume on God's patience.
entries.ezra 9:15: Ezra confesses that God is righteous while they are a spared remnant standing before him in guilt, and no one can stand on their own merit. It means we depend entirely on God's mercy, and the reader is pointed toward humility rather than self-justification.
entries.ezra 8:1: This begins a list of the family leaders who traveled back to Jerusalem from Babylon with Ezra, during the reign of King Artaxerxes. It reminds the reader that this return was a real, organized journey led by named people.
entries.ezra 8:2: This continues the list, naming specific men from important priestly and royal family lines who made the trip. It shows that people from Israel's most significant families were part of the return.
entries.ezra 8:3: Here the list names Zechariah from the family of Parosh, along with 150 men traveling with him. It shows the group was made up of whole family groups, not just individuals.
entries.ezra 8:4: This names Eliehoenai from the family of Pahath-moab, who brought 200 men with him. Each entry shows how the returning community was counted family by family.
entries.ezra 8:5: This lists another group of 300 men traveling under a leader from the family of Shecaniah. It continues the careful record of who was making the journey.
entries.ezra 8:6: Ebed from the family of Adin is named here with 50 men. Even the smaller groups were recorded, showing that every family mattered in the return.
entries.ezra 8:7: Jeshaiah from the family of Elam is listed with 70 men. The record keeps showing that the returning group was made up of many different families.
entries.ezra 8:8: Zebadiah from the family of Shephatiah is named with 80 men. The list continues to document each family's contribution to the journey.
entries.ezra 8:9: Obadiah from the family of Joab is listed with 218 men. This larger group shows that some families sent many people back to Jerusalem.
entries.ezra 8:10: A leader from the family of Shelomith is named with 160 men. The list keeps counting the people who committed to the return.
entries.ezra 8:11: Zechariah from the family of Bebai is listed with only 28 men. Even a small group is included, showing that no one was overlooked.
entries.ezra 8:12: Johanan from the family of Azgad is named with 110 men. The record continues to show the size and makeup of each family group.
entries.ezra 8:13: The last sons of Adonikam are named here with 60 men. This shows that even the remaining members of a family were included in the return.
entries.ezra 8:14: Uthai and Zabbud from the family of Bigvai are listed with 70 men. This ends the list of families who traveled back with Ezra.
entries.ezra 8:15: Ezra gathered the people by a river and camped there for three days, then noticed that no Levites had come. This matters because Levites were needed to serve in the temple.
entries.ezra 8:16: Ezra sent for a group of respected and wise leaders to help solve the problem of the missing Levites. It shows he acted carefully by involving capable men.
entries.ezra 8:17: Ezra sent these leaders to Iddo, a chief in Casiphia, asking him to send temple workers to join them. It shows Ezra actively recruiting the people needed for God's house.
entries.ezra 8:18: With God's help, the group brought back a Levite named Ish-sechel along with Sherebiah and his relatives, eighteen men in all. It shows that their effort to find temple workers succeeded because God helped them.
entries.ezra 8:19: Hashabiah and Jeshaiah from the family of Merari are named with twenty of their relatives and sons. This adds more Levites to the group needed for temple service.
entries.ezra 8:20: They also brought 220 temple servants, whose families had long been assigned to help the Levites. These workers were all listed by name, showing they were valued and organized.
entries.ezra 8:21: Ezra called for a time of fasting and prayer by the river, asking God to guide them and protect their families and belongings on the journey. It shows they depended on God rather than on their own strength.
entries.ezra 8:22: Ezra had told the king that God protects his servants, so he was ashamed to ask for soldiers to guard them. He chose to trust God's protection instead of looking inconsistent about his faith.
entries.ezra 8:23: So they fasted and prayed, and God answered their prayer. It shows that their humble dependence on God was met with a real response.
entries.ezra 8:24: Ezra set apart twelve leading priests, along with Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brothers. He chose trusted men to take charge of the valuable offerings.
entries.ezra 8:25: Ezra handed over the silver, gold, and temple vessels that had been donated for God's house. This shows careful handling of gifts meant for worship.
entries.ezra 8:26: He weighed out large amounts of silver and gold into their hands. Weighing it shows the value was carefully measured and accounted for.
entries.ezra 8:27: He also gave them gold basins and fine bronze vessels worth as much as gold. These valuable items were part of the offering for God's house.
entries.ezra 8:28: Ezra told these men that they and the vessels were set apart for the Lord, and that the silver and gold were a freewill offering to God. It reminds the reader that what is given to God is holy and must be treated with care.
entries.ezra 8:29: Ezra told them to guard everything until they could weigh it out in Jerusalem before the priests, Levites, and family leaders. It shows the importance of honesty and accountability with what belongs to God.
entries.ezra 8:30: The priests and Levites accepted the weighed silver, gold, and vessels to carry them to God's house in Jerusalem. They took on the responsibility of transporting holy things safely.
entries.ezra 8:31: They left the river on the twelfth day of the first month and traveled to Jerusalem, and God protected them from enemies along the way. It shows that their trust in God was rewarded with safe travel.
entries.ezra 8:32: When they arrived in Jerusalem, they rested for three days. This simple detail shows the journey was completed and they took time to recover.
entries.ezra 8:33: On the fourth day, the silver, gold, and vessels were weighed out in God's house and handed to trusted priests and Levites. It shows the gifts were delivered and accounted for exactly as planned.
entries.ezra 8:34: Everything was checked by number and weight, and the amounts were written down at that time. This shows careful record-keeping so nothing was lost or misused.
entries.ezra 8:35: The returned exiles offered burnt offerings and sin offerings to the God of Israel. It shows they began their new life in the land by worshiping God and seeking forgiveness.
entries.ezra 8:36: They delivered the king's orders to the royal officials and governors in the region, and those leaders gave support to the people and God's house. It shows the king's decree helped the returned community get the help they needed.
entries.nehemiah 2:1: Nehemiah served wine to the king, and this time he looked sad, which he had never dared to do before. It means he was about to take a risk by showing his true feelings.
entries.nehemiah 2:2: The king noticed Nehemiah's sad face and guessed it was inner sorrow, not sickness, which made Nehemiah very afraid. It shows that being honest about our pain can feel dangerous.
entries.nehemiah 2:3: Nehemiah respectfully told the king he was sad because his ancestral city lay in ruins with its gates burned. It means grief over broken places is natural and worth naming.
entries.nehemiah 2:4: The king asked what Nehemiah wanted, and before answering he silently prayed to God. It means a quick prayer for help is a wise first move in a big moment.
entries.nehemiah 2:5: Nehemiah asked the king to send him to rebuild the city where his ancestors were buried. It means he turned his sorrow into a clear, specific request.
entries.nehemiah 2:6: The king, with the queen beside him, asked how long the trip would take, and Nehemiah gave him a set time. It means good plans include realistic timelines.
entries.nehemiah 2:7: Nehemiah asked for official letters so the regional rulers would let him travel safely to Judah. It means wise preparation includes getting the permissions you need.
entries.nehemiah 2:8: Nehemiah also asked for wood from the king's forest to rebuild the gates, wall, and his own house, and the king granted it because God was with him. It means God can move powerful people to supply what we need.
entries.nehemiah 2:9: Nehemiah delivered the king's letters to the regional rulers, and the king had also sent army officers and horsemen with him. It means God's help often comes through practical protection and support.
entries.nehemiah 2:10: Two local officials were upset that someone had come to help the Israelites. It means doing good can stir up opposition from people who don't want things to change.
entries.nehemiah 2:11: Nehemiah arrived in Jerusalem and rested there for three days. It means it's wise to pause and settle in before starting a big task.
entries.nehemiah 2:12: Nehemiah got up at night with a few men and told no one what God had put in his heart to do for Jerusalem. It means some God-given plans need quiet time before they're shared.
entries.nehemiah 2:13: By night he inspected the broken walls and burned gates of the city. It means seeing a problem up close helps you understand what needs fixing.
entries.nehemiah 2:14: He continued to the fountain gate and the king's pool, but the rubble was so bad his animal couldn't get through. It means real damage can block progress and must be faced honestly.
entries.nehemiah 2:15: He went up the valley by night, inspecting the wall, then returned through the valley gate. It means careful, quiet assessment comes before public action.
entries.nehemiah 2:16: The leaders didn't know where he had gone or what he was doing, because he hadn't yet told anyone. It means it's okay to keep plans private until you're ready.
entries.nehemiah 2:17: Nehemiah told the people plainly that the city was in bad shape and urged them to rebuild the wall so they would no longer be ashamed. It means naming the problem honestly can motivate people to act.
entries.nehemiah 2:18: He told them how God had helped him and what the king had said, and they responded by getting ready to work. It means sharing evidence of God's help builds courage in others.
entries.nehemiah 2:19: Three opponents mocked the builders and accused them of rebelling against the king. It means criticism and false accusations often come when good work begins.
entries.nehemiah 2:20: Nehemiah answered that God would help them succeed, and told the opponents they had no share or claim in Jerusalem. It means trust in God's help lets you keep working despite mockery.
entries.nehemiah 4:1: Sanballat was furious that the Jews were rebuilding the wall and made fun of them. It shows that doing good work can bring mockery from others.
entries.nehemiah 4:2: Sanballat mocked the Jews in front of his friends and army, saying their effort was weak and hopeless. He tried to make them feel foolish for even trying.
entries.nehemiah 4:3: Tobiah added his own insult, saying the wall was so flimsy a fox could knock it down. Mockery often piles on when people want to discourage you.
entries.nehemiah 4:4: Nehemiah asked God to hear how they were being mocked and to turn the insults back on the mockers. He brought his hurt to God instead of fighting back himself.
entries.nehemiah 4:5: Nehemiah asked God not to overlook the wrong these men had done, since they had insulted God's people while they worked. He trusted God to deal with them justly.
entries.nehemiah 4:6: The people kept building, and the wall reached half its height because they worked hard. Steady effort in spite of opposition gets real results.
entries.nehemiah 4:7: When the enemies heard the wall was actually being repaired, they were furious. Success often makes opponents angrier.
entries.nehemiah 4:8: All the enemies plotted together to attack Jerusalem and stir up trouble. The threat was now real, not just words.
entries.nehemiah 4:9: The people prayed to God and also set guards day and night. Faith and practical action went together.
entries.nehemiah 4:10: The workers in Judah were wearing out, and the rubble was piling up, so they felt the job was impossible. Discouragement from within can be as hard as enemies outside.
entries.nehemiah 4:11: The enemies planned a surprise attack to kill the workers and stop the building. The danger was serious and hidden.
entries.nehemiah 4:12: Jews living near the enemies kept warning them over and over that attacks were coming from every side. Repeated warnings showed how real the threat was.
entries.nehemiah 4:13: Nehemiah stationed people by families in the exposed low spots, armed with swords, spears, and bows. He organized them for defense where they were most vulnerable.
entries.nehemiah 4:14: Nehemiah told the leaders and people not to be afraid but to remember the great and awesome Lord, and to fight for their families and homes. Courage comes from remembering who God is.
entries.nehemiah 4:15: When the enemies learned their plot was known and God had foiled it, everyone returned to work on the wall. God's protection let them get back to the task.
entries.nehemiah 4:16: From then on, half the servants worked while half stood guard with weapons, and the leaders stayed behind the people of Judah. They balanced work and watchfulness.
entries.nehemiah 4:17: The builders and carriers worked with one hand while holding a weapon in the other. They had to be ready for danger even while doing their job.
entries.nehemiah 4:18: Each builder kept his sword at his side, and a man stood by Nehemiah ready to sound the alarm. Readiness was built into the work.
entries.nehemiah 4:19: Nehemiah told the leaders and people that the work was large and spread out, so they were far apart on the wall. He was honest about the difficulty of staying connected.
entries.nehemiah 4:20: Nehemiah said that wherever they heard the horn, they should gather there, and that God would fight for them. They had a clear signal and a clear source of hope.
entries.nehemiah 4:21: They kept working, with half holding spears from dawn until the stars came out. They stayed committed through long, dangerous days.
entries.nehemiah 4:22: Nehemiah told everyone to stay inside Jerusalem at night with their servants, so they could guard at night and work by day. He arranged their lives around the crisis.
entries.nehemiah 4:23: Nehemiah, his brothers, servants, and guards never took off their clothes, and each kept his weapon even at the water. The whole group stayed constantly ready.
entries.ezra 2:41: This verse counts the temple musicians who returned from exile, listing 128 descendants of Asaph. It shows that worship through music was an important part of the community's life and was carefully organized.
entries.ezra 2:42: This lists the gatekeepers and their families, 139 in all, who were responsible for guarding the temple. It reminds us that even behind-the-scenes jobs mattered in serving God.
entries.ezra 2:43: This begins a list of the temple servants, a group who assisted the priests and Levites with practical work. Their inclusion shows that ordinary service was valued alongside more visible roles.
entries.ezra 2:44: This continues the list of temple servants by naming more family groups. Each name represents real people who played a part in restoring worship.
entries.ezra 2:45: More families of temple servants are named here. The detailed record shows that every worker's contribution was remembered and counted.
entries.ezra 2:46: This verse adds more names to the list of temple servants. It shows the community kept careful records of who belonged to which family group.
entries.ezra 2:47: The list of temple servant families continues. These were people who supported the work of the temple in practical ways.
entries.ezra 2:48: More temple servant families are listed here. Their presence in the record shows they were part of the returning community and its mission.
entries.ezra 2:49: This continues naming the families of temple servants. It reflects how the returning exiles were organized by family and role.
entries.ezra 2:50: More families of temple servants appear in this verse. The long list shows that many people shared in the support work of the temple.
entries.ezra 2:51: The list of temple servant families goes on. Each group had its own identity and place in the community's service.
entries.ezra 2:52: This verse names more temple servant families. It shows the record was kept in an orderly way, family by family.
entries.ezra 2:53: More families of temple servants are listed. Their work, though less prominent, was part of the community's worship life.
entries.ezra 2:54: This closes the list of temple servant families. It shows that even the last names on the list were important enough to be recorded.
entries.ezra 2:55: This begins a list of the descendants of Solomon's servants, another group attached to the temple. They were part of the community that returned to rebuild.
entries.ezra 2:56: More families of Solomon's servants are named here. The record shows these groups were counted and included in the return.
entries.ezra 2:57: This verse adds the final families of Solomon's servants to the list. It shows the community carefully tracked everyone who came back.
entries.ezra 2:58: This gives the total number of temple servants and Solomon's servants together, 392. It summarizes the size of this support group in the returning community.
entries.ezra 2:59: Some people returned from certain towns but could not prove their family line was Israelite. It shows that belonging to the community was taken seriously and needed evidence.
entries.ezra 2:60: This lists the families of those who could not prove their ancestry, 652 people in all. They were still part of the return, even with uncertain records.
entries.ezra 2:61: Some priests also could not prove their family line, including one whose ancestor had married into the family of Barzillai. It shows that family identity and records mattered for priestly service.
entries.ezra 2:62: When their names could not be found in the family records, these priests were treated as unfit for priestly work. It shows the community applied its rules carefully, even when it was painful.
entries.ezra 2:63: The governor told them not to eat the most holy food until a priest could decide their case using the Urim and Thummim. It shows they were not permanently rejected but waited for a proper decision.
entries.ezra 2:64: This gives the total number of the whole returning community, 42,360 people. It shows the return from exile was a large, organized movement of people.
entries.ezra 2:65: Besides the main group, there were 7,337 servants and 200 musicians. It shows the community included many workers and people who contributed to its life.
entries.ezra 2:66: This lists the horses and other transport animals the people brought with them. It shows the return involved real practical needs and resources for the journey and new life.
entries.ezra 2:67: This adds camels and donkeys to the count of animals. It shows the community had the livestock needed to travel and settle in the land.
entries.ezra 2:68: When some family leaders arrived at the temple site in Jerusalem, they gave freely toward rebuilding God's house. It shows that generosity and commitment to worship were part of the return.
entries.ezra 2:69: Each person gave what they could, and the total was a large amount of gold, silver, and priestly robes. It shows that everyone's giving, according to ability, added up to something significant.
entries.ezra 2:70: The priests, Levites, musicians, gatekeepers, temple servants, and the rest of the people settled in their own towns. It shows the community was reestablished in the land, each group in its place.
entries.ezra 10:1: Ezra was praying and openly admitting the people's wrong, crying and lying down in front of God's house. A large crowd of men, women, and children gathered around him, all weeping bitterly, showing how deeply the sin had hurt the community.
entries.ezra 10:2: Shecaniah spoke up and admitted that the people had sinned against God by marrying women from the surrounding peoples. Even so, he said there was still hope for Israel, showing that confession can open the door to change.
entries.ezra 10:3: Shecaniah proposed making a solemn promise to God to send away these wives and their children, if Ezra and the others who respected God's word agreed, and to do it according to the law. This was a serious step to correct a serious wrong.
entries.ezra 10:4: Shecaniah urged Ezra to take action, promising that the people would stand behind him. He encouraged Ezra to be strong and get the job done, since it was his responsibility to lead.
entries.ezra 10:5: Ezra stood up and made the leading priests, the Levites, and all Israel swear an oath to carry out this plan. They agreed and bound themselves by that promise.
entries.ezra 10:6: Ezra left the area in front of God's house and went into a room belonging to Jehohanan. He ate and drank nothing there because he was still grieving over the sin of the returned exiles.
entries.ezra 10:7: A public notice went out through all Judah and Jerusalem telling everyone who had returned from exile to gather in Jerusalem.
entries.ezra 10:8: Anyone who failed to show up within three days would lose all his property and be excluded from the community of returned exiles, as the leaders had decided. This showed how serious the matter was.
entries.ezra 10:9: Within the three days, the men of Judah and Benjamin gathered in Jerusalem on the twentieth day of the ninth month. They sat in the open square before God's house, trembling because of the issue at hand and because of heavy rain.
entries.ezra 10:10: Ezra stood up and told the people plainly that they had sinned by marrying foreign women, which added to Israel's guilt. He named the wrong directly rather than softening it.
entries.ezra 10:11: Ezra called the people to confess to the Lord, the God of their ancestors, and to do what pleased him. Specifically, they were to separate themselves from the surrounding peoples and from these foreign wives.
entries.ezra 10:12: The whole assembly answered in a loud voice, agreeing that Ezra was right and that they should do as he said.
entries.ezra 10:13: The people pointed out that there were too many of them, it was raining heavily, and they could not stand outside any longer. They also noted that this problem was too big to settle in a day or two because their sin was great.
entries.ezra 10:14: They suggested that their leaders act on behalf of everyone, and that those in each town who had married foreign women come at scheduled times with the town's elders and judges. This would continue until God's fierce anger over the matter was turned away.
entries.ezra 10:15: Only Jonathan and Jahzeiah opposed this plan, and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite backed them up. So the proposal did not have unanimous support.
entries.ezra 10:16: The returned exiles carried out the plan. Ezra and chosen heads of families, listed by name, were set apart, and on the first day of the tenth month they began carefully investigating the matter.
entries.ezra 10:17: By the first day of the first month they had finished dealing with all the men who had married foreign women. The process took about three months to complete.
entries.ezra 10:18: Among the priests who had married foreign women were men from the family of Jeshua son of Jozadak, along with his brothers: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah.
entries.ezra 10:19: These men pledged to send their wives away, and to make things right for their sin they offered a ram from the flock as a guilt offering.
entries.ezra 10:20: From the family of Immer, the men involved were Hanani and Zebadiah.
entries.ezra 10:21: From the family of Harim, the men listed were Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah.
entries.ezra 10:22: From the family of Pashhur, the men named were Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah.
entries.ezra 10:23: Among the Levites, the men listed were Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah (also called Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer.
entries.ezra 10:24: Among the singers, Eliashib was named, and among the gatekeepers, Shallum, Telem, and Uri.
entries.ezra 10:25: From the rest of Israel, the family of Parosh included Ramiah, Izziah, Malchijah, Mijamin, Eleazar, Malchijah, and Benaiah.
entries.ezra 10:26: From the family of Elam, the men named were Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi, Jeremoth, and Elijah.
entries.ezra 10:27: From the family of Zattu, the men listed were Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad, and Aziza.
entries.ezra 10:28: From the family of Bebai, the men named were Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai.
entries.ezra 10:29: From the family of Bani, the men listed were Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Jeremoth.
entries.ezra 10:30: From the family of Pahath-moab, the men named were Adna, Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezalel, Binnui, and Manasseh.
entries.ezra 10:31: From another branch of the family of Harim, the men listed were Eliezer, Isshijah, Malchijah, Shemaiah, and Shimeon.
entries.ezra 10:32: Also from that group were Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah.
entries.ezra 10:33: From the family of Hashum, the men named were Mattenai, Mattattah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei.
entries.ezra 10:34: From the family of Bani, the men listed were Maadai, Amram, and Uel.
entries.ezra 10:35: Continuing that list were Benaiah, Bedeiah, and Cheluhi.
entries.ezra 10:36: Also named were Vaniah, Meremoth, and Eliashib.
entries.ezra 10:37: The list continues with Mattaniah, Mattenai, and Jaasu.
entries.ezra 10:38: Also included were Bani, Binnui, and Shimei.
entries.ezra 10:40: The list ends with Machnadebai, Shashai, and Sharai.
entries.nehemiah 5:1: The poorer Jews cried out against their own wealthy countrymen who were treating them badly. It means unfair treatment within a community is a real wrong that should be noticed, not ignored.
entries.nehemiah 5:2: Some families were so large they simply needed grain to survive. It means basic needs like food can become a desperate struggle, and that struggle deserves a hearing.
entries.nehemiah 5:3: Others had to mortgage their land and homes just to buy food. It means debt can strip people of what they need to live, and poverty often forces hard choices.
entries.nehemiah 5:4: Still others had borrowed money to pay the king's taxes, putting their property at risk. It means heavy taxes and debt together can push ordinary people to the edge.
entries.nehemiah 5:5: They pointed out they were just as human as their rich neighbors, yet their children were being sold into slavery and they could do nothing. It means treating people as less valuable than yourself is deeply unjust.
entries.nehemiah 5:6: When Nehemiah heard these complaints he became very angry. It means anger at injustice can be right, and it can move someone to act.
entries.nehemiah 5:7: After thinking it over, he confronted the officials for charging interest to their own people and called a large public meeting. It means leaders should think carefully and then openly challenge wrongs, especially among their own group.
entries.nehemiah 5:8: He reminded them they had worked to free fellow Jews from slavery abroad, and now they were enslaving each other. It means it makes no sense to rescue people and then turn around and oppress them yourself.
entries.nehemiah 5:9: He told them their behavior was wrong and would bring shame on them before other nations and before God. It means how we treat people affects our reputation and our witness to others.
entries.nehemiah 5:10: He admitted that he and his men had also been charging interest and said they should all stop. It means real leadership includes owning your own faults and changing course.
entries.nehemiah 5:11: He demanded they return the land, houses, and money they had taken, right away. It means making things right usually requires giving back what was wrongly taken, not just saying sorry.
entries.nehemiah 5:12: The officials agreed to do it, and Nehemiah had the priests make them swear an oath to keep their promise. It means a public commitment before God helps people follow through on doing right.
entries.nehemiah 5:13: Nehemiah shook out his robe as a symbol that anyone who broke the promise would be shaken out and left with nothing, and the people agreed and praised God. It means serious promises deserve serious consequences, and doing right should be celebrated.
entries.nehemiah 5:14: For twelve years as governor, Nehemiah never took the food allowance he was entitled to. It means leaders can choose to give up their rights for the good of the people they serve.
entries.nehemiah 5:15: Earlier governors had burdened the people heavily, but Nehemiah didn't, because he respected God. It means power should not be used to squeeze people, and fear of God should shape how leaders treat others.
entries.nehemiah 5:16: He kept working on the wall and didn't acquire land for himself, and all his servants helped with the work. It means staying focused on the task and not using your position for personal gain.
entries.nehemiah 5:17: On top of everything, he fed about a hundred and fifty people at his table, including visitors from other nations. It means generosity and hospitality are part of good leadership.
entries.nehemiah 5:18: He provided large daily meals but still refused the governor's food allowance because the people were already heavily burdened. It means true leaders consider what people can bear and don't add to their load.
entries.nehemiah 5:19: Nehemiah asked God to remember all he had done for the people. It means it's right to want God to see your good efforts, and to find your reward in him.
entries.nehemiah 3:1: The high priest and his fellow priests led the way by repairing the Sheep Gate themselves. It shows that leaders should be first to pitch in, not just give orders.
entries.nehemiah 3:2: Ordinary men from Jericho worked right alongside the priests on the wall. Rebuilding is a shared job where people from different places do their part.
entries.nehemiah 3:3: A group of builders repaired the Fish Gate, fitting its beams and hanging its doors with locks and bars. Each team took full responsibility for finishing its section properly.
entries.nehemiah 3:4: Several men, named with their family lines, repaired stretches of wall next to each other. The work moved forward because each person did the part in front of them.
entries.nehemiah 3:5: The people of Tekoa worked, but their leaders refused to help. It's a warning that those with authority can let everyone down by holding back.
entries.nehemiah 3:6: Two men repaired the Old Gate, setting its beams and hanging its doors with locks and bars. Faithful, unglamorous repair work keeps a city safe.
entries.nehemiah 3:7: Men from Gibeon and Mizpah worked beside others on the wall. People from outside the city also shared in the effort.
entries.nehemiah 3:8: A goldsmith and a perfume-maker worked on the wall next to each other. Ordinary tradespeople used their hands for the common good, not just their own trade.
entries.nehemiah 3:9: A local official in charge of half of Jerusalem repaired his section. Leaders were expected to get their hands dirty too.
entries.nehemiah 3:10: Jedaiah repaired the wall right across from his own house. Working near home gave people a personal stake in doing a good job.
entries.nehemiah 3:11: Two men repaired another section plus the Tower of the Ovens. Big projects get done when people take on extra pieces beyond the obvious.
entries.nehemiah 3:12: A ruler of half of Jerusalem repaired the wall with his daughters. Whole families, including women, joined the work.
entries.nehemiah 3:13: Hanun and the people of Zanoah rebuilt the Valley Gate and a long stretch of wall. Some teams simply covered a lot of ground.
entries.nehemiah 3:14: A local leader repaired the Dung Gate and hung its doors. Even the gate named for waste mattered and was worth fixing well.
entries.nehemiah 3:15: A district leader repaired the Fountain Gate and the wall by the king's garden and the steps. Careful, detailed work protected the city's water and access.
entries.nehemiah 3:16: Nehemiah repaired the wall as far as the royal tombs and the soldiers' quarters. Each person took a defined stretch and finished it.
entries.nehemiah 3:17: The Levites, the temple workers, joined the building too. Religious duties didn't excuse them from practical labor for the community.
entries.nehemiah 3:18: More men from Keilah and their leader repaired the next section. Neighboring groups kept the work moving in order.
entries.nehemiah 3:19: A district leader repaired the wall opposite the armory at the bend in the wall. Strategic spots like weapons storage got attention.
entries.nehemiah 3:20: Baruch worked hard on another section, from the bend to the high priest's house. Some workers are noted for real effort, not just showing up.
entries.nehemiah 3:21: Meremoth repaired a second section near the high priest's house. Doing more than one part shows commitment beyond the minimum.
entries.nehemiah 3:22: Priests from the nearby lowlands repaired the next stretch. Even those from outside the city came to help.
entries.nehemiah 3:23: Benjamin, Hasshub, and Azariah repaired the wall right by their own homes. People naturally care most about what's close to them.
entries.nehemiah 3:24: Binnui repaired the section from Azariah's house to the corner of the wall. The work continued steadily, piece by piece.
entries.nehemiah 3:25: Palal and Pedaiah repaired the wall near the palace tower and the guard area. Protecting the king's house and the watch post mattered for the city's safety.
entries.nehemiah 3:26: The temple servants living on the hill repaired the area near the Water Gate and the tower. Even the lowest-status workers had a real part in the project.
entries.nehemiah 3:27: The men of Tekoa repaired a second section near the great tower. Despite their leaders' earlier refusal, the ordinary people kept working.
entries.nehemiah 3:28: Past the Horse Gate, the priests each repaired the wall opposite their own house. Personal responsibility made the work concrete and accountable.
entries.nehemiah 3:29: Zadok and Shemaiah, the east gatekeeper, repaired sections near their homes and post. People fixed what they knew and used daily.
entries.nehemiah 3:30: Hananiah, Hanun, and Meshullam repaired more sections, one right opposite his own room. Small, personal assignments added up to a whole wall.
entries.nehemiah 3:31: A goldsmith repaired the wall near the inspection gate and the corner. Skilled craftsmen kept contributing to the shared building project.
entries.nehemiah 3:32: Goldsmiths and merchants finished the last stretch between the corner and the Sheep Gate. The whole circuit was completed because everyone did their piece.
entries.nehemiah 6:1: Nehemiah's enemies heard the wall was rebuilt with no gaps left, though the gates weren't set up yet. Progress on good work often gets noticed by those who oppose it.
entries.nehemiah 6:2: His enemies invited him to a meeting in a nearby village, but they really planned to harm him. Not every friendly invitation is sincere.
entries.nehemiah 6:3: Nehemiah refused to come, saying he was doing important work and wouldn't stop it to meet with them. Some work is too important to interrupt for distractions.
entries.nehemiah 6:4: They asked the same thing four times and got the same answer each time. Staying consistent is a good way to handle repeated pressure.
entries.nehemiah 6:5: Sanballat tried a fifth time, sending a servant with an unsealed letter anyone could read. The pressure escalated but the tactic was still a trap.
entries.nehemiah 6:6: The letter accused Nehemiah and the Jews of planning a rebellion and making him their king. False rumors are often used to scare people into reacting.
entries.nehemiah 6:7: The letter claimed prophets were proclaiming him king and that the king would hear of it, then urged him to come talk. It was a threat dressed up as concern.
entries.nehemiah 6:8: Nehemiah replied plainly that none of it was true and that Sanballat had made it all up. A simple, honest denial is often the best answer to lies.
entries.nehemiah 6:9: Their real goal was to frighten the workers so the wall would never be finished, so Nehemiah prayed for strength. Fear is a tool, and prayer is the answer to it.
entries.nehemiah 6:10: A man named Shemaiah, who was confined to his house, urged Nehemiah to hide inside the Temple because of a supposed plot to kill him. Even advice from religious people can be wrong.
entries.nehemiah 6:11: Nehemiah refused to run away or hide in the Temple, saying that wasn't fitting for someone in his position. Courage means not abandoning your post out of fear.
entries.nehemiah 6:12: Nehemiah realized God had not sent this man; he was prophesying against him because Tobiah and Sanballat had paid him. Not every spiritual-sounding message comes from God.
entries.nehemiah 6:13: They paid him so Nehemiah would be scared into doing something wrong, giving them grounds to ruin his reputation. Fear can push people into sin, which is exactly what enemies want.
entries.nehemiah 6:14: Nehemiah asked God to remember the harmful deeds of Tobiah, Sanballat, and the prophets who tried to frighten him. It's right to bring unfair attacks to God rather than take revenge yourself.
entries.nehemiah 6:15: The wall was finished in just fifty-two days. Steady work, despite opposition, can accomplish a lot in a short time.
entries.nehemiah 6:16: When the surrounding nations heard the wall was done, they were afraid and humbled, recognizing God had done it. God's work done faithfully can silence and awe those who opposed it.
entries.nehemiah 6:17: During this time, the leading men of Judah were exchanging many letters with Tobiah. Even inside the community, some people were aligned with the enemy.
entries.nehemiah 6:18: Many in Judah were bound to Tobiah by oath because of family ties through marriage. Loyalty to relatives can sometimes pull people away from what is right.
entries.nehemiah 6:19: People kept telling Nehemiah how good Tobiah was and reporting Nehemiah's words back to him, and Tobiah kept sending letters to intimidate him. Flattery and fear were both used against him, but he stayed focused on his work.
entries.ezra 10:41: This verse just lists three more men by name among a larger group. It reminds the reader that these were real individuals, each counted in what the community was dealing with.
entries.ezra 10:42: Three more names are added to the same list. The point is simply that every person was named and accounted for, not lost in a crowd.
entries.ezra 10:43: This verse names a group of men from the family of Nebo. It continues the same record, showing that several families were involved in the same situation.
entries.ezra 10:44: These men had all married women from outside their people, and some of those marriages had produced children. It shows the situation was serious and had real family consequences, not just a rule being broken.
entries.nehemiah 8:1: Everyone gathered together in one place and asked Ezra to read them God's law. It shows that coming together to hear God's word is something people should want to do.
entries.nehemiah 8:2: Ezra read the law to the whole crowd, including women and anyone old enough to understand. God's word is for everyone, not just leaders or men.
entries.nehemiah 8:3: Ezra read from morning until midday and the people listened carefully the whole time. It shows how much they valued hearing God's word.
entries.nehemiah 8:4: Ezra stood on a wooden platform built for the occasion, with leaders standing on both sides of him. They made careful arrangements so everyone could hear and see.
entries.nehemiah 8:5: Ezra opened the book where everyone could see, and the people stood up out of respect. Standing showed they treated God's word as something important.
entries.nehemiah 8:6: Ezra praised God and the people responded by raising their hands and bowing down to worship. Hearing God's word led them straight into worship.
entries.nehemiah 8:7: A group of Levites helped the people understand the law while everyone stayed in their places. Others were there to help people grasp what was being read.
entries.nehemiah 8:8: They read God's law out loud and explained what it meant so people could understand it. Understanding what God says is the goal, not just hearing it.
entries.nehemiah 8:9: The leaders told the people to stop crying, because hearing the law had made them weep. Being convicted is good, but that day was meant for joy, not grief.
entries.nehemiah 8:11: The Levites calmed the people and told them not to be sad because the day was holy. God's word can correct us without crushing us.
entries.nehemiah 8:12: The people went home to eat, drink, share food, and celebrate because they had understood what was read. Understanding God's word should produce real joy.
entries.nehemiah 8:13: The next day the family leaders, priests, and Levites came back to Ezra to study the law more closely. Real understanding makes people want to learn even more.
entries.nehemiah 8:14: They discovered in the law that God had commanded Israel to live in tents during the feast of the seventh month. Reading the Bible carefully helps us find things we had missed.
entries.nehemiah 8:15: They were told to announce everywhere that people should gather branches from the hills to build tents, just as the law said. Obedience meant following God's instructions exactly.
entries.nehemiah 8:16: The people went out, collected branches, and built tents on their roofs and in the public squares. They put God's command into practice right where they lived.
entries.nehemiah 8:17: The returned exiles lived in the tents and celebrated with great joy, something Israel had not done since Joshua's time. Obeying God brought them a joy they had not known for generations.
entries.nehemiah 8:18: Ezra read from the law every day of the feast, and they held a solemn assembly on the last day as the law required. Steady, daily time in God's word shaped the whole celebration.
entries.nehemiah 7:1: Once the wall was finished and the gates were in place, Nehemiah assigned guards, singers, and temple workers to their duties. It means that finishing a big job includes organizing the people who will keep it running.
entries.nehemiah 7:2: Nehemiah put two trusted men in charge of Jerusalem, choosing them because they were faithful and truly respected God. It means that good leadership starts with character and trustworthiness, not just skill.
entries.nehemiah 7:3: Nehemiah gave careful security instructions: open the gates late, close and lock them early, and have residents guard the areas near their own homes. It means that even after success, it's wise to stay alert and protect what you've built.
entries.nehemiah 7:4: The city was large, but few people lived in it and most of the houses were still in ruins. It means that a big project can look finished on the outside while the real work of filling it with life is still ahead.
entries.nehemiah 7:5: God prompted Nehemiah to gather the leaders and people and record them by family, and he found an old list of the first returning exiles. It means that keeping good records helps a community know who they are and where they came from.
entries.nehemiah 7:6: This begins a list of the people groups who had been taken captive to Babylon and later returned to their own towns in Jerusalem and Judah. It means that God brought his people home after a long, hard exile.
entries.nehemiah 7:7: This names the leaders who came back with Zerubbabel, followed by the total count of Israelite men. It means that the return was organized under clear leadership, and every person counted mattered.
entries.nehemiah 7:8: This records that 2,172 men from the family of Parosh returned. It means that ordinary families, not just famous leaders, were part of rebuilding the community.
entries.nehemiah 7:9: This records that 372 men from the family of Shephatiah returned. It means that each family group, however small, was remembered and counted.
entries.nehemiah 7:10: This records that 652 men from the family of Arah returned. It means that the list preserves the memory of everyday people who helped restore their homeland.
entries.nehemiah 7:11: This records that 2,818 men from the family of Pahath-moab, through Jeshua and Joab, returned. It means that large family groups played a big part in the nation's recovery.
entries.nehemiah 7:12: This records that 1,254 men from the family of Elam returned. It means that the record keeps track of each group so no one's contribution is forgotten.
entries.nehemiah 7:13: This records that 845 men from the family of Zattu returned. It means that the community was rebuilt family by family, each one adding to the whole.
entries.nehemiah 7:14: This records that 760 men from the family of Zaccai returned. It means that even a simple count shows real people with real homes to rebuild.
entries.nehemiah 7:15: This records that 648 men from the family of Binnui returned. It means that faithfulness in small numbers still counted in the life of the nation.
entries.nehemiah 7:16: This records that 628 men from the family of Bebai returned. It means that the list honors ordinary families who made the long journey home.
entries.nehemiah 7:17: This records that 2,322 men from the family of Azgad returned. It means that a large group of people shared the same hope of starting over.
entries.nehemiah 7:18: This records that 667 men from the family of Adonikam returned. It means that each family's return was part of a bigger story of restoration.
entries.nehemiah 7:19: This records that 2,067 men from the family of Bigvai returned. It means that the community was strong enough to include many different family groups.
entries.nehemiah 7:20: This records that 655 men from the family of Adin returned. It means that the record values each family's place in rebuilding the nation.
entries.nehemiah 7:21: This records that 98 men from the family of Ater, through Hezekiah, returned. It means that even a small family group was worth naming and remembering.
entries.nehemiah 7:22: This records that 328 men from the family of Hashum returned. It means that every returning family had a part to play in the new community.
entries.nehemiah 7:23: This records that 324 men from the family of Bezai returned. It means that the list keeps a careful account of the people who came back.
entries.nehemiah 7:24: This records that 112 men from the family of Hariph returned. It means that small numbers still represented real households with real futures.
entries.nehemiah 7:25: This records that 95 men from Gibeon returned. It means that even the smallest groups were included in the record of God's people.
entries.nehemiah 7:26: This records that 188 men from Bethlehem and Netophah returned. It means that people from specific towns came back to rebuild their own local communities.
entries.nehemiah 7:27: This records that 128 men from Anathoth returned. It means that each town's returning people helped restore the land piece by piece.
entries.nehemiah 7:28: This records that 42 men from Beth-azmaveth returned. It means that even a very small group was counted and valued.
entries.nehemiah 7:29: This records that 743 men from Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth returned. It means that neighboring towns worked together to resettle the region.
entries.nehemiah 7:30: This records that 621 men from Ramah and Geba returned. It means that the return involved many local communities, not just one big city.
entries.nehemiah 7:31: This records that 122 men from Michmas returned. It means that each small town's people were part of the larger restoration.
entries.nehemiah 7:32: This records that 123 men from Bethel and Ai returned. It means that places with deep history were being repopulated by their own people.
entries.nehemiah 7:33: This records that 52 men from the other Nebo returned. It means that even a tiny group was named and remembered in the record.
entries.nehemiah 7:34: This records that 1,254 men from the other Elam returned. It means that families with the same name were distinguished and counted separately.
entries.nehemiah 7:35: This records that 320 men from the family of Harim returned. It means that each family line contributed to the rebuilding of the nation.
entries.nehemiah 7:36: This records that 345 men from Jericho returned. It means that an ancient city's people came back to restore their home.
entries.nehemiah 7:37: This records that 721 men from Lod, Hadid, and Ono returned. It means that several towns together made up a significant part of the returning community.
entries.nehemiah 7:38: This records that 3,930 men from the family of Senaah returned. It means that one of the largest groups came from an ordinary family line, showing that everyday people carried the work.
entries.nehemiah 7:39: This begins the list of priests, starting with 973 men from Jedaiah's family through Jeshua. It means that worship and spiritual leadership were carefully restored alongside the city.
entries.nehemiah 7:40: This records that 1,052 men from the family of Immer served as priests. It means that a large number of priests returned, showing how important worship was to the rebuilt community.
entries.nehemiah 7:41: This is a count of one family group that came back from exile, numbering 1,247 people. It reminds the reader that every family mattered in rebuilding the community.
entries.nehemiah 7:42: This lists another returning family group with 1,017 people. It shows the record keepers carefully tracked who came back.
entries.nehemiah 7:43: This counts the Levites, the temple helpers, who returned, totaling 74. Even small groups had a role in restoring worship.
entries.nehemiah 7:44: This counts the temple musicians from Asaph's family, 148 in all. Their presence shows that praise and music were part of rebuilding.
entries.nehemiah 7:45: This counts the gatekeepers who guarded the temple, 138 people from several families. Their job reminds us that protecting what is holy matters.
entries.nehemiah 7:46: This begins a list of the Nethinim, temple servants who assisted the Levites. These workers were valued enough to be recorded by name.
entries.nehemiah 7:47: This continues the list of temple servant families. Each name shows that ordinary workers were part of the restored community.
entries.nehemiah 7:48: More temple servant families are named here. The record shows that even behind-the-scenes roles were remembered.
entries.nehemiah 7:49: This adds more families of temple servants to the list. It shows the community included many who served in practical ways.
entries.nehemiah 7:50: The list of temple servant families continues. These names remind the reader that every contribution to the temple's work counted.
entries.nehemiah 7:51: More temple servant families are recorded. The careful listing shows the community valued all its members.
entries.nehemiah 7:52: This continues naming temple servant families. It shows the return was organized and each group was accounted for.
entries.nehemiah 7:53: More families of temple servants are listed. Their inclusion shows that service, not status, defined their place.
entries.nehemiah 7:54: The list of temple servant families goes on. It reminds the reader that faithfulness in small roles is worth recording.
entries.nehemiah 7:55: This adds more temple servant families to the record. The community kept track of everyone who served.
entries.nehemiah 7:56: This ends the list of temple servant families. It shows the record was thorough and no group was forgotten.
entries.nehemiah 7:57: This begins a list of the descendants of Solomon's servants, another group of temple workers. Their family history was preserved too.
entries.nehemiah 7:58: More families of Solomon's servants are named. It shows the community included people with a long history of service.
entries.nehemiah 7:59: This finishes the list of Solomon's servant families. The record shows care for every group in the returning community.
entries.nehemiah 7:60: This gives the total of the temple servants and Solomon's servants together: 392. It shows the community counted its workers as a whole.
entries.nehemiah 7:61: Some people returned but could not prove their family was Israelite. It reminds the reader that belonging was important and records mattered.
entries.nehemiah 7:62: This counts 642 people from three families whose ancestry was uncertain. It shows honesty about what the community did not know.
entries.nehemiah 7:63: Some priests could not prove their family line, including one whose ancestor took a foreign name. It shows that priestly status depended on clear records.
entries.nehemiah 7:64: These priests were removed from priestly service because their family records could not be found. It shows the community took holiness and order seriously.
entries.nehemiah 7:65: The governor ruled they could not eat the holiest food until a priest could decide their case. It shows patience and respect for God's rules when answers were unclear.
entries.nehemiah 7:66: The total number of returning people was 42,360. It gives a sense of the size of the community that rebuilt Jerusalem.
entries.nehemiah 7:67: Besides the main group, there were 7,337 servants and 245 musicians. It shows the community included many workers and worshipers.
entries.nehemiah 7:68: They brought 736 horses and 245 other pack animals. These animals helped the people travel and carry supplies.
entries.nehemiah 7:69: They also had 435 camels and 6,720 donkeys. This shows the return was a large, practical move of people and goods.
entries.nehemiah 7:70: Some family leaders gave money and supplies for the temple work, and the governor gave a large amount too. It shows leaders led by giving generously.
entries.nehemiah 7:71: Other family leaders gave gold and silver for the work. It shows that many people shared the cost of rebuilding.
entries.nehemiah 7:72: The rest of the people also gave gold, silver, and priestly robes. It shows that ordinary people contributed alongside the leaders.
entries.nehemiah 7:73: Once the work was set up, the priests, helpers, guards, musicians, servants, and all the people settled in their own towns. It shows the community returned to normal life with everyone in place.
entries.nehemiah 9:1: The people gathered to fast and show sorrow by wearing rough cloth and putting dust on themselves. It shows that admitting wrong before God can involve real, humble grief.
entries.nehemiah 9:2: The Israelites separated themselves from foreign peoples and openly confessed their own sins and the sins of their ancestors. It means being honest about wrong, including wrong passed down in a family or nation.
entries.nehemiah 9:3: They spent part of the day reading God's law aloud and part of it confessing sin and worshipping. It shows that hearing God's word and responding to it belong together.
entries.nehemiah 9:4: A group of Levites stood on the steps and cried out loudly to the Lord. It shows that prayer can be passionate and public, not always quiet and private.
entries.nehemiah 9:5: The Levites told the people to stand up and praise the Lord, whose name is above all praise. It means we should actively, deliberately give God the honor he deserves.
entries.nehemiah 9:6: This prayer praises God as the only Lord, who made everything and keeps it all going. It reminds the reader that everything that exists belongs to God and depends on him.
entries.nehemiah 9:7: The prayer recalls how God chose Abram and led him out of Ur, giving him a new name. It shows God takes the initiative in a person's life and guides them step by step.
entries.nehemiah 9:8: God saw that Abraham's heart was faithful and made a promise to give his descendants the land, and God kept it. It means God notices real faithfulness and keeps his promises.
entries.nehemiah 9:9: God saw the suffering of the Israelites in Egypt and heard their cries. It means God is not blind to the pain of his people; he notices and listens.
entries.nehemiah 9:10: God performed miracles against Pharaoh because he saw how cruelly Egypt treated his people. It shows God stands against those who oppress others and defends the helpless.
entries.nehemiah 9:11: God split the sea so the people walked through on dry ground, while their pursuers sank like a stone. It means God can make a way for his people even when escape looks impossible.
entries.nehemiah 9:12: God led them visibly, with a cloud by day and fire by night, to light the way. It means God doesn't leave his people guessing; he guides them along the road.
entries.nehemiah 9:13: God came down at Mount Sinai and spoke good and true laws from heaven. It means God's rules are not arbitrary but are right and good for those who follow them.
entries.nehemiah 9:14: God made his holy Sabbath known to them and gave his laws through Moses. It means God himself teaches his people how to live, including setting aside rest.
entries.nehemiah 9:15: God gave them bread from heaven and water from a rock when they were hungry and thirsty, and told them to go take the land. It means God provides for real needs while also calling people to step forward in trust.
entries.nehemiah 9:16: But the people, including their ancestors, became proud and stubborn and ignored God's commands. It means pride can make a person refuse to listen, even to God.
entries.nehemiah 9:17: They refused to obey and forgot God's wonders, even choosing a leader to take them back to Egypt, yet God forgave them anyway. It shows God is patient and merciful even when people turn away.
entries.nehemiah 9:18: Even when they made a metal calf and called it their god, they still had done wrong against the God who rescued them. It means people can replace the true God with something made by their own hands.
entries.nehemiah 9:19: Even then, God in his mercy did not abandon them in the desert; the cloud and fire kept leading them. It means God's mercy keeps guiding people even after they fail badly.
entries.nehemiah 9:20: God gave them his good Spirit to teach them and kept supplying manna and water. It means God not only provides for physical needs but also teaches and guides by his Spirit.
entries.nehemiah 9:21: For forty years in the desert God sustained them so that their clothes didn't wear out and their feet didn't swell. It means God's care can be quiet and constant over a very long time.
entries.nehemiah 9:22: God gave them victory over kingdoms and peoples and handed them land to possess. It means God can give his people what they could never take for themselves.
entries.nehemiah 9:23: God made their children as numerous as the stars and brought them into the land he had promised. It means God keeps promises across generations, not just to one person.
entries.nehemiah 9:24: Their children entered and took the land, and God subdued the Canaanites before them. It means God goes ahead of his people and makes a way for them.
entries.nehemiah 9:25: They captured walled cities and rich land with houses, wells, vineyards, and orchards, and they enjoyed the good things God gave. It means God's gifts can be abundant, and enjoying them is part of his goodness.
entries.nehemiah 9:26: But they became stubborn, turned from God's law, and killed the prophets who tried to bring them back. It means people can reject even those who are trying to help them return to God.
entries.nehemiah 9:27: When enemies oppressed them and they prayed, God heard from heaven and sent rescuers. It means God listens when people in trouble call to him, even after they've wandered.
entries.nehemiah 9:28: When they had rest they did evil again, and the cycle repeated, yet God kept rescuing them in mercy. It means God's mercy is persistent, even when people keep repeating the same mistakes.
entries.nehemiah 9:29: God warned them to return to his law, but they proudly refused and turned away. It means ignoring God's warnings is a choice, and it has consequences.
entries.nehemiah 9:30: God patiently put up with them for years and spoke through his prophets, but they wouldn't listen, so they were handed over to other nations. It means God's patience is long, but refusing to listen still has results.
entries.nehemiah 9:31: Even so, God in his great mercy did not destroy them completely or abandon them. It means God's mercy sets a limit on judgment; he does not give up on his people.
entries.nehemiah 9:32: The prayer asks the great and faithful God not to ignore the long trouble that has come on the people from the days of Assyria until now. It means it's okay to bring long-standing pain honestly before God.
entries.nehemiah 9:33: They admit that God has been right in everything that happened, and that they were the ones who did wrong. It means real repentance agrees with God's view of things instead of blaming him.
entries.nehemiah 9:34: Their kings, leaders, priests, and ancestors all failed to keep God's law or pay attention to his warnings. It means failure to follow God isn't limited to ordinary people; leaders fail too.
entries.nehemiah 9:35: Even while enjoying God's good gifts in their own kingdom, they did not serve him or turn from their evil ways. It means blessings can be enjoyed without gratitude, and that is a real danger.
entries.nehemiah 9:36: They confess that they are slaves today, even in the very land God gave their ancestors. It means sin can turn a gift into a burden, and honesty about that is the first step.
entries.nehemiah 9:37: The land's produce goes to kings set over them because of their sins, and those kings control their bodies and animals. It means the consequences of wrongdoing can affect everyday life and freedom.
entries.nehemiah 9:38: Because of all this, they make a written agreement in good faith and their leaders sign it. It means when people recognize their need, they can respond with a concrete, serious commitment.
entries.nehemiah 11:1: The leaders settled in Jerusalem, and the rest of the people cast lots so that one family in ten would move into the holy city while the other nine stayed in their own towns. It shows that living in Jerusalem was a sacrifice people were asked to share fairly.
entries.nehemiah 11:2: The people blessed those who volunteered to move to Jerusalem. It means the community honored those willing to give up their home towns for the good of the city.
entries.nehemiah 11:3: This lists the leaders of the provinces who lived in Jerusalem, while the rest of the people, including priests, Levites, temple servants, and Solomon's servants, lived on their family land in the towns of Judah. It shows how the returning exiles were organized by family and role.
entries.nehemiah 11:4: Some members of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin lived in Jerusalem, and here the family line of one Judahite named Athaiah is traced back several generations. It shows that real, named families made up the city's population.
entries.nehemiah 11:5: This continues the family record with Maaseiah, another man from Judah whose ancestors are listed. It shows the careful record-keeping that helped confirm who belonged to each family.
entries.nehemiah 11:6: The descendants of Perez living in Jerusalem numbered 468 able men. It shows that a sizable group from one family line settled in the city.
entries.nehemiah 11:7: This begins the list of Benjamin's descendants living in Jerusalem, tracing Sallu's family line. It shows that both major tribes were represented in the city.
entries.nehemiah 11:8: After Sallu came Gabbai and Sallai, with 928 men in their group. It shows the number of Benjaminites who made Jerusalem their home.
entries.nehemiah 11:9: Joel son of Zichri was their leader, and Judah son of Hassenuah was second in command over the city. It shows that the settlers had organized leadership.
entries.nehemiah 11:10: This starts the list of priests living in Jerusalem, naming Jedaiah, Joiarib, and Jachin. It shows that worship at the temple was supported by priests who actually lived nearby.
entries.nehemiah 11:11: Seraiah's family line is traced back to Zadok and Ahitub, and he is called the ruler of the house of God. It shows that the temple's top official came from a long-established priestly line.
entries.nehemiah 11:12: The priests' relatives who did the work of the temple numbered 822, and Adaiah's family line is listed. It shows how many priests were needed to keep the temple running.
entries.nehemiah 11:13: Adaiah's relatives, who were heads of families, numbered 242, and another priest named Amashsai is listed with his ancestors. It shows the temple staff was organized by family groups.
entries.nehemiah 11:14: Their relatives, fighting men, numbered 128, led by Zabdiel son of Haggedolim. It shows that the priests' group also included men able to defend the city.
entries.nehemiah 11:15: This begins the list of Levites living in Jerusalem, starting with Shemaiah's family line. It shows that the Levites, who assisted the priests, were also settled in the city.
entries.nehemiah 11:16: Shabbethai and Jozabad were Levite leaders in charge of the work outside the temple. It shows that some Levites handled the practical business that supported worship.
entries.nehemiah 11:17: Mattaniah led the singing of praise and prayer, with Bakbukiah next to him and Abda also named. It shows that music and prayer were a planned, organized part of temple life.
entries.nehemiah 11:18: All the Levites in the holy city numbered 284. It shows the size of the group dedicated to helping the priests.
entries.nehemiah 11:19: The gatekeepers Akkub, Talmon, and their relatives numbered 172 and guarded the temple doors. It shows that protecting the house of God was a serious assigned duty.
entries.nehemiah 11:20: The rest of Israel, including priests and Levites, lived in the towns of Judah on their own family land. It shows that most people stayed in their inherited places rather than moving to Jerusalem.
entries.nehemiah 11:21: The temple servants lived in the Ophel area of Jerusalem, with Ziha and Gishpa in charge of them. It shows that even the lowest-ranking temple workers had leaders and a place to live.
entries.nehemiah 11:22: Uzzi, from the family of Asaph the musicians, was overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem and managed the work of God's house. It shows that worship and temple business were under one trusted leader.
entries.nehemiah 11:23: The king had given orders about the musicians and provided a set amount for their daily needs. It shows that the government officially supported those who led worship.
entries.nehemiah 11:24: Pethahiah, from the family of Zerah in Judah, served the king in all matters concerning the people. It shows there was a Jewish representative handling the community's affairs with the king.
entries.nehemiah 11:25: Some men of Judah lived in towns like Kiriath-arba, Dibon, and Jekabzeel and their surrounding villages. It shows where the people settled across the countryside.
entries.nehemiah 11:26: This continues the list of towns where Judahites lived, naming Jeshua, Moladah, and Beth-pelet. It shows the wide spread of settlements across the land.
entries.nehemiah 11:27: The list continues with Hazar-shual, Beer-sheba, and its surrounding villages. It shows that people resettled the southern areas of Judah.
entries.nehemiah 11:28: Ziklag and Meconah with its villages are added to the list. It shows more towns where the people made their homes.
entries.nehemiah 11:29: En-rimmon, Zorah, and Jarmuth are named next. It shows the careful record of where each community lived.
entries.nehemiah 11:30: Zanoah, Adullam, Lachish, and Azekah with their villages are listed, and the people lived from Beer-sheba to the valley of Hinnom. It shows the full extent of Judahite settlement in the south.
entries.nehemiah 11:31: The Benjaminites lived from Geba to Michmash, Aija, and Bethel with its villages. It shows where the tribe of Benjamin settled in the north.
entries.nehemiah 11:32: Anathoth, Nob, and Ananiah are named as Benjaminite towns. It shows the specific places where these families lived.
entries.nehemiah 11:33: Hazor, Ramah, and Gittaim are added to the list. It shows the continuing record of Benjaminite settlements.
entries.nehemiah 11:34: Hadid, Zeboim, and Neballat are named next. It shows more towns where the people resettled.
entries.nehemiah 11:35: Lod and Ono are listed, along with the valley of craftsmen. It shows that skilled workers also had their own communities.
entries.nehemiah 11:36: Some divisions of the Levites in Judah were assigned to Benjamin. It shows that the Levites were distributed among the tribes to serve them.
entries.nehemiah 12:1: This starts a list of the priests and Levites who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. It reminds the reader that real, named people did the hard work of rebuilding.
entries.nehemiah 12:2: This continues the list of priests who came back from exile. Each name shows that the restored community was made up of specific families, not just a crowd.
entries.nehemiah 12:3: More names of returning priests are recorded here. The writer is keeping careful records so later generations would know who served.
entries.nehemiah 12:4: The list of returning priests continues. These names matter because they show the community was organized and its history preserved.
entries.nehemiah 12:5: Still more priests who returned from exile are named. The detail shows that every family's part in the return was remembered.
entries.nehemiah 12:6: The list of priests continues with two more names. The record keeps the past clear for the people who came after them.
entries.nehemiah 12:7: This closes the list, saying these were the leading priests and their relatives in Jeshua's time. It shows the community had clear leaders who guided the return.
entries.nehemiah 12:8: Here the Levites are listed, including Mattaniah, who led the singers. It shows that music and worship were part of the community's life from the start.
