entries.job 6:28: Job asks them to look him in the eye, because he will not lie to their faces. He wants them to see he is speaking honestly.
entries.job 6:29: Job urges them to change their minds and stop judging him wrongly, because he is still in the right. He asks them to reconsider their harsh opinion of him.
entries.job 6:30: Job asks whether there is any evil in what he says, and whether he doesn't clearly know his own trouble. He insists he understands his situation and is not speaking wickedness.
entries.job 7:1: Job is saying that human life on earth is like hard labor, with trouble assigned to us and days spent like a hired worker waiting for pay. It reminds the reader that suffering is a normal part of life, not always a sign that something is uniquely wrong with you.
entries.job 7:2: A servant longs for the cool evening and a worker waits for his wages, just as people long for relief from their labor. The reader can see that longing for rest and reward is a natural human feeling.
entries.job 7:3: Job says his inheritance has been empty months of pain and nights of exhausting weariness. He is describing his suffering honestly, showing the reader that it is okay to name how hard life feels.
entries.job 7:4: When Job lies down, he wonders when it will be time to get up, and the night drags on while he tosses and turns until dawn. This captures the misery of sleepless nights and the feeling that time moves painfully slowly when you are suffering.
entries.job 7:5: Job describes his body as covered with worms and dirt, with skin that crusts over and then cracks open again. He is expressing how completely his illness has worn him down, body and spirit.
entries.job 7:6: Job says his days fly by faster than a weaver's thread and end without any hope. He feels his life is short and slipping away with nothing good to look forward to.
entries.job 7:7: Job asks God to remember that his life is like a breath, and he believes he will never see good again. He is pleading to be noticed in his pain, showing how deep despair can feel.
entries.job 7:8: Job says that once he is gone, no one will see him anymore, and even God's eyes will search for him but he will be gone. He is expressing the fear that death ends everything and that he will be forgotten.
entries.job 7:9: Just as a cloud disappears and never returns, Job says a person who goes down to the grave does not come back up. He is voicing the finality of death as he understands it.
entries.job 7:10: Job says the dead person never returns home, and his place no longer knows him. This shows his sense of being cut off from life and from everything familiar.
entries.job 7:11: Job decides he will not stay silent but will pour out his bitter feelings and complain in the pain of his spirit. The reader learns that honest, raw prayer to God is allowed, even when it sounds like complaint.
entries.job 7:12: Job asks God whether he is a sea or a sea monster that needs to be guarded and restrained. He feels God is watching him too closely, as if he were a dangerous force to be contained.
entries.job 7:13: Job thinks that lying in bed might bring him comfort and rest from his sickness. He is looking for even a small relief from his suffering.
entries.job 7:14: But instead of rest, God sends frightening dreams and terrifying visions. Job feels that even sleep offers him no escape from fear.
entries.job 7:15: Job says he would rather be strangled to death than keep living with his pain. This shows how extreme his suffering has become and how honestly he expresses it.
entries.job 7:16: Job says he has no desire to live and does not want to live forever, asking God to leave him alone because his days are like a breath. He is worn out and wants his suffering to end.
entries.job 7:17: Job asks what a human being is that God would make him so important and keep such close attention on him. He is puzzled and overwhelmed that God seems so focused on him.
entries.job 7:18: Job says God checks on him every morning and tests him every moment. He feels constantly examined and watched, with no relief.
entries.job 7:19: Job asks how long it will be before God looks away and gives him even a moment to breathe. He is begging for a small break from the pressure he feels.
entries.job 7:20: Job asks that if he has sinned, what has he done to God, the watcher of people, and why God has made him a target so that he is a burden to himself. He is questioning why his suffering feels so personal and unrelenting.
entries.job 7:21: Job asks why God does not just forgive his sin and remove his guilt, since he will soon be dead and God will search for him but he will be gone. He is longing for forgiveness and relief before his life ends.
entries.job 11:1: Zophar from Naamah speaks up as the third friend to answer Job. This marks a new voice joining the argument.
entries.job 11:2: Zophar asks whether Job's many words should go unchallenged and whether talking a lot proves someone is right. He is accusing Job of assuming he is correct just because he talks so much.
entries.job 11:3: He asks whether Job's boastful talk should silence everyone and whether Job can mock without anyone correcting him. He thinks Job is being arrogant and needs to be called out.
entries.job 11:4: Zophar quotes Job's claim that his conduct is pure and he is innocent before God. He is setting up his argument against Job's insistence on his own innocence.
entries.job 11:5: Zophar wishes God would speak directly and argue with Job. He believes God's words would settle the matter against Job.
entries.job 11:6: He wishes God would reveal the hidden depths of wisdom, showing that God's purposes are beyond what Job understands. He hints that God may be punishing Job less than he deserves.
entries.job 11:7: Zophar asks whether Job can fully understand God or grasp the limits of the Almighty. The point is that God is far beyond human understanding.
entries.job 11:8: God's wisdom is higher than the heavens and deeper than the grave, beyond Job's reach. Zophar is saying Job cannot possibly figure God out.
entries.job 11:9: God's wisdom is longer than the earth and wider than the sea. It is far too vast for any person to measure.
entries.job 11:10: If God moves to arrest someone or bring them to death, no one can stop him. Zophar is stressing that God's power cannot be resisted.
entries.job 11:11: God sees through people and notices evil without effort. Nothing wicked escapes his attention.
entries.job 11:12: Zophar says a foolish person will gain wisdom only when a wild donkey is born tame, meaning it will never happen. He is calling Job foolish and hopeless to change on his own.
entries.job 11:13: Zophar tells Job to set his heart right and reach out to God in prayer. He is offering Job a way to fix his situation.
entries.job 11:14: He says Job must remove any wrongdoing from his hands and not let evil stay in his home. Repentance, in Zophar's view, is the condition for things to improve.
entries.job 11:15: Then Job could lift his face without shame and stand firm without fear. Zophar promises confidence and security if Job cleans up his life.
entries.job 11:16: Job would forget his troubles as water flows away. The pain of the past would fade from memory.
entries.job 11:17: Job's life would become brighter than noon, and even darkness would turn into morning. Zophar pictures a complete turnaround from gloom to light.
entries.job 11:18: Job would feel safe because there is hope, and he could rest peacefully after looking around. Security and calm would return to his life.
entries.job 11:19: Job would lie down without fear of danger, and people would seek his favor. He would be respected and at peace.
entries.job 11:20: But the wicked will wear out their eyes looking for help, find no escape, and have only death to hope for. Zophar ends by warning that evil people come to ruin.
entries.job 10:1: Job is so worn down by suffering that he no longer wants to live, and he decides to stop holding back and pour out his bitter feelings in words. It shows that honest grief can be spoken out loud, even when it sounds raw.
entries.job 10:2: Job speaks directly to God, asking him not to treat him as guilty without showing him what he is being charged with. It reflects the pain of feeling accused and not knowing why.
entries.job 10:3: Job asks whether God gains anything by being harsh toward the work he himself made, while seeming to favor those who do wrong. It voices the confusion of someone who feels God is against him unfairly.
entries.job 10:4: Job asks whether God sees and judges the way a human being does, limited by human eyes. He is appealing to the idea that God must see more truly than people do.
entries.job 10:5: Job asks whether God's life is as short as a human's, so that he has to hurry to catch wrongdoing. He is questioning why God seems to be pressing him so hard and so quickly.
entries.job 10:6: Job suggests that God is hunting for his sin and keeping close track of any wrong he might do. It expresses the feeling of being watched and examined without mercy.
entries.job 10:7: Job insists that he is not a wrongdoer, yet no one can rescue him from God's power. He feels trapped between his innocence and God's seeming hostility.
entries.job 10:8: Job points out that God made him with his own hands, yet now seems to have turned against him and is tearing him down. It is the painful question of why the maker would destroy what he made.
entries.job 10:9: Job asks God to remember that he was formed from dust, and pleads that he not be sent back to dust so soon. He is asking for mercy based on how fragile he is.
entries.job 10:10: Job pictures his own beginning in the womb as something like milk being poured out and thickened into cheese. He is describing how God carefully formed him from soft, formless material.
entries.job 10:11: Job describes how God gave him skin, flesh, bones, and muscles, knitting him together piece by piece. He is acknowledging that his whole body is God's careful work.
entries.job 10:12: Job remembers that God showed him kindness, kept him alive by grace, and watched over his spirit. Even in his pain, he admits that his life has been sustained by God's care.
entries.job 10:13: Job believes God had a hidden plan all along, keeping these thoughts secret in his heart. He is struggling with the feeling that God's kindness was hiding something harder underneath.
entries.job 10:14: Job suspects that God was watching for any wrong he did and would never let him off the hook. It shows how exhausting it feels to live under constant suspicion.
entries.job 10:15: Job says that if he is guilty, he is doomed, and if he is innocent, he still cannot hold his head up because he is overwhelmed with shame and trouble. He feels there is no way to win.
entries.job 10:16: Job imagines that if he showed any strength or pride, God would hunt him like a lion and keep showing his power against him. He feels constantly targeted and overpowered.
entries.job 10:17: Job feels that God keeps bringing new charges and fresh attacks against him, as if sending one army after another. It describes the sense of being worn down by wave after wave of trouble.
entries.job 10:18: Job asks why he was even born, saying it would have been better to die at birth and never be seen. He is expressing deep despair about his existence.
entries.job 10:19: Job wishes he had gone straight from the womb to the grave, as though he had never existed. It is a cry of someone who feels his life has brought only pain.
entries.job 10:20: Job asks God to look away from him for a moment, since his life is short, so he can have a little relief. He is pleading for a brief break from constant scrutiny and suffering.
entries.job 10:21: Job is thinking about the grave, the place he will not return from, a land of darkness and gloom. He is facing the nearness of death and the sadness of it.
entries.job 10:22: Job describes the grave as a land of deep darkness and confusion, where even the light is dark. It shows how bleak and hopeless death feels to him in his suffering.
entries.job 12:1: Job begins his reply to his friends. He is about to answer what they just said to him.
entries.job 12:2: Job says this sarcastically: his friends act as if they know everything and are the only wise people left. It warns the reader against being smug about having all the answers.
entries.job 12:3: Job insists he understands as much as they do and is not inferior to them. His point is that the obvious truths they keep repeating are things everyone already knows.
entries.job 12:4: Job feels like a joke to his neighbors, even though he prays to God and has lived uprightly. It shows that being mocked does not mean a person has done wrong.
entries.job 12:5: People who are comfortable look down on those who are struggling, as if trouble were always the sufferer's own fault. The reader is cautioned against contempt for people who are hurting.
entries.job 12:6: Job observes that those who do violence and provoke God often live securely and prosper. This is his honest complaint that life does not always reward the good and punish the bad.
entries.job 12:7: Job tells his friends to learn from animals and birds. Even creatures can teach a lesson about who really controls life.
entries.job 12:8: He extends the invitation to creatures that crawl on the ground and to fish in the sea. The whole created world can tell the same story if people will pay attention.
entries.job 12:9: Anyone can see from all these creatures that the Lord's hand made and governs them. Creation itself points to God's power.
entries.job 12:10: Every living creature's life and every human breath are held in God's hand. The reader can take comfort that life itself rests with God, not with chance.
entries.job 12:11: Just as the mouth tastes food, the ear tests what it hears. Job is saying his friends should weigh his words fairly instead of dismissing them.
entries.job 12:12: People assume that age brings wisdom and long life brings understanding. Job states this common belief before going on to qualify it.
entries.job 12:13: Real wisdom and strength belong to God, and power and understanding are his. Human wisdom is not the final authority.
entries.job 12:14: What God tears down cannot be rebuilt, and no one can release whom God shuts in. God's decisions are not overturned by human effort.
entries.job 12:15: God can hold back the waters so land dries up, or release them so the earth is flooded. He has authority over nature itself.
entries.job 12:16: Strength and sound judgment are with God, and both the deceiver and the deceived are in his hands. Nothing, not even error, escapes his control.
entries.job 12:17: God can strip advisers of their wisdom and make judges look foolish. Human expertise is not guaranteed to succeed.
entries.job 12:18: God can remove kings' authority and bind them instead. Earthly rulers are not beyond his reach.
entries.job 12:19: God can bring priests to ruin and overturn those who seemed securely established. Position and status offer no protection from him.
entries.job 12:20: God can silence trusted spokesmen and take away the good judgment of elders. Even respected voices can be shown to be wrong.
entries.job 12:21: God humbles leaders and removes power from the strong. Strength and rank do not impress him.
entries.job 12:22: God brings hidden things out of darkness and makes deep shadows bright. Nothing is too obscure for him to see or reveal.
entries.job 12:23: God can make nations great and then bring them down, expanding peoples and then dispersing them. The rise and fall of nations is in his hands.
entries.job 12:24: God can take away the understanding of the earth's rulers and leave them wandering in trackless waste. Leaders can be left without direction when God removes their insight.
entries.job 12:25: Such rulers grope in darkness with no light and stagger like drunkards with no one to help. It pictures how helpless human leaders become without God's guidance.
entries.job 13:1: Job is saying he has seen and heard these things for himself, so he really knows what he is talking about. It reminds the reader that personal experience can give real understanding.
entries.job 13:2: Job tells his friends that he understands as much as they do and is not beneath them. It means the reader should not assume someone who is suffering is ignorant or foolish.
entries.job 13:3: Job would rather speak directly to God and argue his case with him than keep debating with his friends. It shows that bringing honest questions straight to God is allowed.
entries.job 13:4: Job accuses his friends of covering up the truth and offering help that does not actually help. It warns the reader that comfort given with false or careless words does no good.
entries.job 13:5: Job says his friends would show more wisdom by staying silent. It means sometimes saying nothing is wiser than speaking.
entries.job 13:6: Job asks his friends to listen carefully to his argument and weigh his words. It shows he wants a fair hearing rather than being dismissed.
entries.job 13:7: Job asks whether they will speak wrongly on God's behalf and put false words in his mouth. It warns against defending God with lies or unfair claims.
entries.job 13:8: Job asks if they will show favoritism toward God and act as his defenders in this case. It means being partial in an argument is not the same as being right.
entries.job 13:9: Job asks whether it will go well for them when God examines them, since they cannot trick God like a man. It reminds the reader that God sees through our pretense.
entries.job 13:10: Job says God will correct them if they secretly show favoritism. It means hidden bias will not escape God's notice.
entries.job 13:11: Job asks whether God's greatness and fear should not make them tremble. It means God's majesty should make us humble and careful in what we say.
entries.job 13:12: Job calls their wise sayings dust and their defenses mere earth, meaning they are weak and worthless. It warns against trusting in impressive but empty words.
entries.job 13:13: Job tells them to be quiet and let him speak, whatever happens to him as a result. It shows his honesty and courage to speak his mind.
entries.job 13:14: Job says he will risk his own body and life to make his case. It means he is willing to take a real risk for the sake of honesty.
entries.job 13:15: Even if God kills him, Job says he will still argue his case before him and not back down. It shows remarkable trust that keeps talking to God even in despair.
entries.job 13:16: Job believes this bold approach will actually save him, because a wicked person would not dare come before God. It means honesty before God is safer than hiding.
entries.job 13:17: Job asks them to listen closely and store up his words in their minds. It means pay careful attention to what someone is really saying.
entries.job 13:18: Job says he has prepared his case and is confident he will be proven right. It shows his firm belief in his own innocence.
entries.job 13:19: Job asks if anyone can argue against him, because if so he would be silent and die. It means he is so sure of his case that he stakes his life on it.
entries.job 13:20: Job asks God for just two things before he comes to speak with him. It shows he is setting terms for a direct conversation with God.
entries.job 13:21: Job asks God to stop punishing him and to stop terrifying him with fear. It means he wants to talk freely without being overwhelmed.
entries.job 13:22: Job offers God a choice: God can call and Job will answer, or Job can speak and God can reply. It shows Job wants a real two-way conversation.
entries.job 13:23: Job asks God to tell him exactly what his wrongdoings and sins are. It means he wants to know the specific charge against him.
entries.job 13:24: Job asks why God hides his face and treats him like an enemy. It expresses the pain of feeling abandoned by God.
entries.job 13:25: Job asks if God will keep chasing something as weak as a leaf blown by the wind or a dry stick. It means he feels God is being harsh with someone already fragile.
entries.job 13:26: Job says God records bitter charges against him and makes him pay for the sins of his youth. It shows how past mistakes can feel like they are still being held against us.
entries.job 13:27: Job says God puts his feet in chains, watches all his paths, and limits his steps. It means he feels trapped and closely watched with no freedom.
entries.job 13:28: Job describes a person wearing away like rotten wood or a moth-eaten robe. It pictures how suffering makes a person feel worn down and fragile.
entries.job 16:1: Job speaks up again in reply to his friends. This simply marks the start of his answer to them.
entries.job 16:2: Job says he has heard this kind of talk many times before, and calls his friends comforters who only add to his pain. It reminds us that bad advice or harsh words can hurt more than help someone who is suffering.
entries.job 16:3: Job asks whether their endless windy speeches will ever stop, and what makes them keep arguing with him. He is pushing back against words that pile on instead of soothing.
entries.job 16:4: Job says he could easily talk the same way if their situations were swapped, and he could gang up on them with words and mocking gestures. He is pointing out how easy it is to criticize when you are not the one hurting.
entries.job 16:5: Job says that if he were in their place, he would use his words to strengthen them and offer real comfort. He is describing the kind of friend he wishes they had been to him.
entries.job 16:6: Job says that speaking his mind does not ease his pain, and staying silent does not make it go away either. He feels trapped with no way to find relief.
entries.job 16:7: Job says God has worn him out and left him gripped by trouble. He feels completely drained and overwhelmed by his suffering.
entries.job 16:8: Job says his own wasted body stands as evidence against him, as if his thinness testifies to his guilt. He feels that even his appearance is being used to accuse him.
entries.job 16:9: Job describes God as attacking him in anger, and says onlookers glare at him with cruelty. He feels surrounded by hostility from every side.
entries.job 16:10: Job says people open their mouths against him, strike him in the face with insults, and crowd together to oppose him. He feels ganged up on and humiliated.
entries.job 16:11: Job believes God has handed him over to wicked people and thrown him into their power. He feels abandoned to those who mean him harm.
entries.job 16:12: Job says he was once at ease, but God has shattered him, grabbed him by the neck, and set him up as a target. He feels his life has been turned from peace to being a bullseye.
entries.job 16:13: Job pictures attackers surrounding him and piercing him without mercy until his life drains away. He feels his suffering is relentless and deadly.
entries.job 16:14: Job says he is broken again and again, and that God charges at him like a warrior. He feels the blows keep coming with no letup.
entries.job 16:15: Job says he has worn rough sackcloth against his skin and laid his strength in the dust. These are outward signs of deep grief and humiliation.
entries.job 16:16: Job says his face is red from crying and his eyes grow dark. His grief is visible on his body and wearing him down.
entries.job 16:17: Job insists he has done nothing violent and that his prayer is sincere. He is claiming his suffering is not a fair punishment for wrongdoing.
entries.job 16:18: Job cries out that the earth should not hide his blood or silence his cry. He desperately wants his innocence and his suffering to be remembered and heard.
entries.job 16:19: Even now Job says his witness and defender is in heaven. In the middle of his pain he holds on to the hope that God above will speak for him.
entries.job 16:20: Job says his friends mock him while his eyes pour out tears to God. He feels misunderstood by people and turns his weeping toward God.
entries.job 16:21: Job longs for someone to argue his case with God, like a mediator between a person and God. He wants a fair hearing for his situation.
entries.job 16:22: Job says that soon he will set out on a journey from which he will not return, meaning death is near. He speaks as someone who feels his time is running short.
entries.job 14:1: Human life is brief and filled with hardship. This reminds the reader that trouble is a normal part of being human, not a sign that something is uniquely wrong with them.
entries.job 14:2: A person appears briefly like a flower and then is gone, fading like a shadow. It means our time is short, so life should be taken seriously.
entries.job 14:3: Job asks God why he would closely watch and judge a creature as weak and fleeting as a human being. It expresses the feeling that God's scrutiny seems too heavy for someone so fragile.
entries.job 14:4: A person who is already unclean cannot produce something clean on their own. It means we cannot fix our own moral brokenness by ourselves.
entries.job 14:5: God has set a fixed number of days and months for each person, with a limit they cannot pass. It means our lifespan is in God's hands, not fully under our control.
entries.job 14:6: Job asks God to look away and leave him alone so he can enjoy his short life like a hired worker who looks forward to his pay. It is a plea for relief from constant pressure.
entries.job 14:7: A tree that is cut down still has hope of growing again. This sets up a contrast: nature can recover, but humans seem not to.
entries.job 14:8: Even when a tree's root is old and its stump is dead in the ground, there is still hope. It means apparent death is not always the end for a tree.
entries.job 14:9: Just a little water makes the stump sprout and grow like a young plant. It shows how quickly life can return when conditions are right.
entries.job 14:10: A person who dies is gone, and no one knows where they are. It expresses the finality and mystery of death from a human viewpoint.
entries.job 14:11: Water drains from a pool and a river dries up. This picture shows how something can disappear completely and not come back.
entries.job 14:12: A person lies down in death and does not rise until the heavens end. It reflects the belief that the dead sleep and are not active.
entries.job 14:13: Job wishes God would hide him safely in the grave until his anger passes, then remember him at a set time. It is a longing for relief and a second chance.
entries.job 14:14: Job asks whether a dead person can live again, and says he would wait through all his hardship if release would come. It voices hope mixed with deep uncertainty.
entries.job 14:15: Job imagines God calling and him answering, and God longing for the work he made. It expresses a desire for restored relationship with God.
entries.job 14:16: Job feels God is counting his every step and not letting his sin go unnoticed. It conveys the feeling of being watched and held accountable.
entries.job 14:17: Job pictures his wrongdoing sealed up in a bag and his sin kept safe, meaning it is stored up and not forgotten. It shows his fear that his sins are being held against him.
entries.job 14:18: Mountains crumble and rocks shift from their place. This shows that even the most solid things in nature eventually break down.
entries.job 14:19: Water wears down stones and washes away soil, and in the same way God brings human hope to an end. It pictures how forces beyond our control can destroy what we count on.
entries.job 14:20: God overcomes a person permanently, and death changes their face and sends them away. It describes death as a final defeat that no one can resist.
entries.job 14:21: A dead person does not know whether their children are honored or humbled. It means death cuts people off from the ongoing life of their family.
entries.job 14:22: Even in death, the person's flesh still feels pain and their soul is sad. It expresses Job's sense that suffering does not simply stop at the grave.
entries.job 15:1: Eliphaz speaks up to answer Job. This is the start of his second speech to Job.
entries.job 15:2: Eliphaz asks whether a wise person would answer with empty talk that helps no one. He is saying Job's words are like hot air with no value.
entries.job 15:3: He asks whether anyone should argue using words that do no good. For the reader, it is a warning that talk without substance helps nobody.
entries.job 15:4: Eliphaz accuses Job of undermining respect for God and cutting short quiet worship. He claims Job's loud complaints are damaging his devotion to God.
entries.job 15:5: He says Job's own sin is driving what he says, and that he has learned to speak like a liar. In other words, Eliphaz thinks Job's words come from a bad heart.
entries.job 15:6: Eliphaz says he does not need to prove Job wrong, because Job's own words condemn him. The reader sees that words can testify against the one who speaks them.
entries.job 15:7: Eliphaz sarcastically asks if Job was the first person ever born or existed before the hills. He is mocking Job for acting as if he alone knows everything.
entries.job 15:8: He asks if Job sat in on God's private council and grabbed all wisdom for himself. The point is that no human has God's full knowledge.
entries.job 15:9: Eliphaz asks what Job knows that he and his friends do not. He is claiming they are just as wise as Job.
entries.job 15:10: He points to older, grey-haired men among them who are older than Job's father. He is saying age and tradition are on their side.
entries.job 15:11: Eliphaz asks whether God's comfort and gentle words are not enough for Job. He suggests Job is ignoring the kindness God has shown.
entries.job 15:12: He asks why Job's heart is out of control and his eyes look proud. He is accusing Job of arrogance and losing his temper.
entries.job 15:13: Eliphaz says Job is turning his spirit against God and letting angry words pour out. He sees Job's speech as rebellion against God.
entries.job 15:14: He asks how any human can be pure or upright. The point is that no person is perfectly clean before God.
entries.job 15:15: Eliphaz says God does not even trust his holy ones, and the heavens are not pure in his sight. He means that if even heavenly beings fall short, humans surely do.
entries.job 15:16: He says it is far worse for a person who is disgusting and unclean and drinks evil like water. The reader is meant to see how low Eliphaz thinks humans are.
entries.job 15:17: Eliphaz asks Job to listen, and says he will tell what he has seen. He is about to give his own observation as evidence.
entries.job 15:18: He says these are things wise men received from their fathers and did not hide. He is appealing to handed-down wisdom as reliable.
entries.job 15:19: He notes that the land was given only to those wise men, with no outsider among them. He is stressing that this teaching is pure and uncontaminated.
entries.job 15:20: Eliphaz claims the wicked suffer pain all their days and the cruel get only a few years. He is saying bad people always pay in this life.
entries.job 15:21: He says a wicked man hears sounds of terror, and destruction hits him even when things seem peaceful. The point is that the wicked never feel safe.
entries.job 15:22: He says the wicked have no hope of escaping the darkness, and the sword is waiting for them. Eliphaz is describing a doomed fate for evildoers.
entries.job 15:23: He pictures the wicked wandering around looking for bread and certain that trouble is coming. The reader sees a picture of constant anxiety.
entries.job 15:24: Eliphaz says fear of dark days overwhelms the wicked, and trouble and pain defeat him. He is saying the wicked live under constant dread.
entries.job 15:25: He explains this happens because the wicked shakes his fist at God and defies the Almighty. The suffering is presented as the result of proud rebellion.
entries.job 15:26: He describes the wicked charging at God like a soldier in heavy armor, like a king ready for battle. It pictures stubborn, defiant resistance to God.
entries.job 15:27: Eliphaz says the wicked man's face is covered with fat and his body has grown thick. He means the wicked lives in luxury and self-indulgence.
entries.job 15:28: He says the wicked settles in ruined towns and houses no one should live in, which are falling apart. The point is that his home is under judgment.
entries.job 15:29: He says the wicked will not get rich or keep what he has, and his crops will not flourish. Eliphaz claims prosperity will not last for the wicked.
entries.job 15:30: He says the wicked will not escape the darkness, and fire and wind will destroy his branches and buds. It is a picture of total loss.
entries.job 15:31: Eliphaz warns the wicked not to trust in what is false, because he will get deceit as his reward. The reader is warned that false hope pays back in disappointment.
entries.job 15:32: He says the wicked's branch is cut off before its time and its leaf stops being green. It means his life is cut short and loses its freshness.
entries.job 15:33: He compares the wicked to a vine whose grapes never ripen or an olive tree that drops its flowers. The point is that his life produces nothing good.
entries.job 15:34: Eliphaz says groups of evildoers bear no fruit, and the tents of those who take bribes will burn. He is saying corruption ends in ruin.
entries.job 15:35: He says evil people conceive trouble and give birth to it, and what comes from them is shame. The reader sees that sin produces its own bad results.
entries.job 9:1: Job begins his reply to his friend. He is about to answer what was just said to him.
entries.job 9:2: Job agrees that God is just, but asks how any ordinary person could ever prove themselves right in front of God. It means we can't win an argument with God on our own.
entries.job 9:3: If someone tried to argue their case with God, they couldn't answer even one question out of a thousand. God knows far more than we do.
entries.job 9:4: God is deeply wise and very powerful, and no one who has fought against him has ever come out ahead. It's foolish to think we can resist God and win.
entries.job 9:5: God can move or remove mountains without anyone even noticing, and he does it in his anger. Nothing in creation is too big for him to overturn.
entries.job 9:6: God can shake the earth out of its place so that even its foundations tremble. The whole world is under his control.
entries.job 9:7: God can command the sun to stop shining and the stars to go dark. Even the sky obeys his orders.
entries.job 9:8: God stretched out the heavens and walks on the waves of the sea. He rules over everything above and below.
entries.job 9:9: God made the constellations—the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades—and the far southern skies. He is the maker of all the stars.
entries.job 9:10: God does great things we can't figure out and wonders too many to count. We should be humble before a God like that.
entries.job 9:11: God can pass right by us and we won't even see or notice him. He is at work whether we are aware of it or not.
entries.job 9:12: If God decides to take something away, no one can stop him or ask him what he's doing. He has the right to do as he pleases.
entries.job 9:13: God's anger can't be turned aside, and even the strongest helpers were crushed under him. No power can stand against God.
entries.job 9:14: So how could Job possibly argue his case or find the right words to answer God? We are far too small to debate with him.
entries.job 9:15: Even if Job were in the right, he couldn't answer God; he could only beg for mercy from the one who seems to be against him. Being right doesn't guarantee winning with God.
entries.job 9:16: Even if God came when Job called, Job wouldn't be sure God would listen to him. It feels to him like God may not hear.
entries.job 9:17: Job feels God would crush him with a storm and multiply his wounds for no reason. He feels overwhelmed by suffering he didn't deserve.
entries.job 9:18: Job feels God won't even let him catch his breath, but fills him with bitter grief. His suffering feels constant and suffocating.
entries.job 9:19: If it comes down to strength, God is far stronger; if it comes to a legal case, no one can make God show up for trial. We can't force God to answer us.
entries.job 9:20: Even if Job were right, God would declare him wrong; even if innocent, God would call him guilty. Job feels he can never win.
entries.job 9:21: Job insists he is innocent, but he no longer cares what happens to him and has lost his will to live. Deep suffering can make life feel pointless.
entries.job 9:22: Job says it makes no difference to him—God destroys both the guilty and the innocent alike. It feels to him like good and bad people meet the same fate.
entries.job 9:23: When disaster strikes suddenly, Job feels God laughs at the suffering of innocent people. He is expressing raw pain, not a settled belief about God.
entries.job 9:24: Job says the world is handed over to wicked people and its judges are blinded; if God isn't behind it, then who is? He is wrestling with why evil seems to win.
entries.job 9:25: Job's days run by faster than a runner and vanish without any good coming to him. Life feels short and empty of hope.
entries.job 9:26: His days rush past like fast boats or an eagle swooping down on its prey. Time is slipping away quickly.
entries.job 9:27: Job considers trying to forget his grief, put on a happy face, and cheer up. He thinks about trying to move on.
entries.job 9:28: But he is still afraid of all his pain, certain that God will not treat him as innocent. Fear keeps pulling him back down.
entries.job 9:29: Job feels God will never clear him, so he wonders why he should bother trying at all. When you feel condemned no matter what, effort seems pointless.
entries.job 9:30: Even if Job washed himself with snow water and scrubbed his hands with soap, it wouldn't help. He feels no amount of cleansing could make him acceptable.
entries.job 9:31: Job feels God would still push him into the mud until even his clothes were disgusted with him. He feels utterly unclean and rejected.
entries.job 9:32: God isn't a man like Job, so Job can't answer him or meet him in court as an equal. There's a huge gap between God and us.
entries.job 9:33: There is no neutral judge between Job and God who could lay a hand on both of them. Job feels he has no one to settle the dispute fairly.
entries.job 9:34: Job wishes God would take away his punishing rod and stop terrifying him. He longs to be free from fear of God's punishment.
entries.job 9:35: Then Job would speak his mind without fear of God, because he doesn't believe he deserves this fear. He wants to speak freely without being crushed.
entries.job 17:1: Job feels completely crushed and believes his life is over, with nothing left but the grave. It means the reader should not be quick to judge someone who speaks this way in deep suffering.
entries.job 17:2: Job is surrounded by people who mock him, and their cruel laughter wears him down. It reminds the reader how much pain careless ridicule adds to someone already hurting.
entries.job 17:3: Job asks God himself to stand surety for him, because no human friend will take his side. It means when everyone else fails us, we can still bring our case directly to God.
entries.job 17:4: Job believes God has kept his accusers from understanding the truth, so they will not be honored. It means we should be careful about judging before we truly understand a situation.
entries.job 17:5: Job warns that a person who betrays a friend for personal gain brings trouble on his own family. It means loyalty matters, and betraying friends for profit has real consequences.
entries.job 17:6: Job has become a public joke, a byword and a target of mockery among the people. It shows how painful it is when a person's suffering becomes entertainment for others.
entries.job 17:7: Job's grief has drained his eyes and wasted his body until he is only a shadow. It means deep sorrow affects a person physically, not just emotionally.
entries.job 17:8: Good people are shocked and shaken when they see what is happening to Job. It means even the faithful can be disturbed when the innocent suffer.
entries.job 17:9: Despite everything, the upright person keeps going and grows stronger in doing right. It means hardship does not have to stop us from staying faithful.
entries.job 17:10: Job challenges his friends to come back, but says none of them has shown real wisdom. It means comforters who only criticize are not truly wise.
entries.job 17:11: Job feels his life is over and all his plans and hopes have been cut off. It means when plans collapse, it is honest to grieve what is lost.
entries.job 17:12: Job's friends keep insisting things will brighten, but he sees only darkness ahead. It means false optimism can feel like a denial of real pain.
entries.job 17:13: Job pictures death as his only home, with his bed made in darkness. It shows how completely hopeless he feels about his future.
entries.job 17:14: Job speaks of the grave and worms as his closest family, since death seems all he has left. It means he feels utterly abandoned by life itself.
entries.job 17:15: Job asks where his hope has gone and who will ever see what he longed for. It means when hope seems gone, the question of where to look next is real and painful.
entries.job 17:16: Job asks whether his hope will go down with him into the grave and the dust. It means he wonders if anything he hoped for can survive death.
entries.job 19:1: Job begins to speak again in response to his friends. This reminds the reader that he is still in the middle of the argument and is about to answer them directly.
entries.job 19:2: Job asks his friends how long they will keep hurting him and wearing him down with their words. It shows how much their constant criticism has hurt him.
entries.job 19:3: Job says they have insulted him many times and feel no shame about treating him badly. The reader sees that repeated harsh words do real damage.
entries.job 19:4: Job says that if he really has done something wrong, it only affects him, not them. He is pushing back on their claim to be his judges.
entries.job 19:5: Job points out that they are acting superior to him and using his suffering as proof he is guilty. It warns against assuming someone's pain means they did wrong.
entries.job 19:6: Job insists that it is God who has treated him unfairly and trapped him like an animal in a net. He is honest about feeling that God is against him.
entries.job 19:7: Job cries out that violence is being done to him, but no one answers or defends him. It shows the pain of calling for help and getting silence.
entries.job 19:8: Job says God has blocked his path and made his road dark so he cannot move forward. He feels trapped with no way out.
entries.job 19:9: Job says God has stripped him of his honor and taken away his dignity. He has lost the respect and standing he once had.
entries.job 19:10: Job feels broken down on every side and says his hope has been pulled up like a dead tree. It pictures total collapse and loss of hope.
entries.job 19:11: Job believes God's anger is burning against him and treats him like an enemy. He is expressing how personal and painful this feels.
entries.job 19:12: Job describes God's forces closing in on him like an army surrounding his tent. He feels completely besieged and helpless.
entries.job 19:13: Job says God has pushed his brothers far away, and they now treat him like a stranger. Suffering has left him isolated even from family.
entries.job 19:14: Job's relatives and close friends have abandoned him, and even his household has forgotten him. It shows how quickly people can disappear when someone suffers.
entries.job 19:15: Job says even his servants treat him like a foreigner. He has lost his place and status in his own home.
entries.job 19:16: Job calls his servant but gets no answer, and has to beg him for attention. It shows how far his authority and dignity have fallen.
entries.job 19:17: Job says his breath is offensive to his wife and he is repulsive to his own family. His suffering has made even those closest to him pull away.
entries.job 19:18: Job says even young children disrespect him and turn their backs when he stands up. He feels mocked by everyone, even the least expected.
entries.job 19:19: Job says all his close companions avoid him and those he loved have turned against him. It shows the deep loneliness of being rejected by friends.
entries.job 19:20: Job describes himself as skin and bones, barely escaping with his life. It pictures how severe and wasting his suffering has become.
entries.job 19:21: Job begs his friends to show him pity because God's hand has come down hard on him. He asks for compassion instead of more judgment.
entries.job 19:22: Job asks why his friends are cruel to him, as if they were God, and keep speaking against him. He is hurt that they pile on more pain.
entries.job 19:23: Job wishes his words could be written down and recorded. He wants his side of the story to be preserved.
entries.job 19:24: Job wishes his words were carved into rock with iron and lead so they would last forever. It shows how much he wants his complaint remembered.
entries.job 19:26: Even after his body is destroyed, Job expects to see God. This is a striking statement of hope beyond his suffering.
entries.job 19:27: Job says he will see God for himself, not as a stranger, and his heart longs for it. It shows a deep personal hope of meeting God.
entries.job 19:28: Job warns that if they claim he is being punished because sin is at his root, they are wrong. He is defending himself against their accusations.
entries.job 19:29: Job warns them to fear the sword of judgment, because there is a judge who sees what they are doing. It is a reminder that God will hold people accountable for how they treat others.
entries.job 20:1: Zophar speaks up next in the argument. He is one of Job's friends who thinks he knows why Job is suffering.
entries.job 20:2: Zophar says his thoughts are restless and pushing him to answer. He feels he has to speak up because he is upset.
entries.job 20:3: Zophar says Job's words insult him and are just empty talk. He is offended and thinks Job's answers make no sense.
entries.job 20:4: Zophar asks if Job knows what has been true since people were first put on earth. He appeals to old, common wisdom.
entries.job 20:5: Zophar claims that a wicked person's pride and happiness only last a short time. He is saying that evil people always get cut down quickly.
entries.job 20:6: Even if a wicked person rises very high and seems great, it will not last. Zophar pictures someone lifted up to the sky.
entries.job 20:7: The wicked person will vanish forever like dung that is thrown away. People who saw him will wonder where he went.
entries.job 20:8: He will disappear like a dream you forget when you wake up. He will be gone like a vision in the night that leaves nothing behind.
entries.job 20:9: No one will see him again, and the place where he lived will not remember him. He will be completely forgotten.
entries.job 20:10: His children will have to beg from the poor, and he will have to give back the wealth he took. His family will suffer for his wrongs.
entries.job 20:11: His body is full of youthful strength now, but it will die and turn to dust with him. His energy will not save him from death.
entries.job 20:12: Even though doing evil tastes sweet to him and he hides it in his mouth like a treat. He enjoys his sin and keeps it secret.
entries.job 20:13: He holds on to his evil and refuses to let it go. He keeps it close because he likes it.
entries.job 20:14: But that sweet evil turns bitter in his stomach and becomes like snake poison inside him. What he enjoyed ends up hurting him.
entries.job 20:15: He swallows down wealth, but God makes him vomit it back up. He cannot keep what he gained by doing wrong.
entries.job 20:16: He drinks in snake poison, and it kills him. The evil he took in destroys him.
entries.job 20:17: He will never enjoy the good things of life, like streams of honey and milk. His wrongdoing cuts him off from blessings.
entries.job 20:18: He has to give back what he worked for and cannot enjoy it. He gets no pleasure from his profits.
entries.job 20:19: He did this because he was cruel to the poor and ignored them when they were in trouble. He also took houses by force that he did not build.
entries.job 20:20: His wealth gives him no peace, and the things he loved cannot save him. He is restless and unsafe.
entries.job 20:21: He was never satisfied with what he had. Because of his greed, his good times will end quickly.
entries.job 20:22: Even when he is rich, he is full of worry because everyone in trouble turns against him. His abundance brings him anxiety, not safety.
entries.job 20:23: God gives him what he wants, but then pours out his anger on him like rain. His desires become the doorway to judgment.
entries.job 20:24: He may run from an iron weapon, but a bronze arrow will strike him. There is no escape from the danger coming for him.
entries.job 20:25: The arrow goes through his body, and he is overcome with fear. He is struck down and terrified.
entries.job 20:26: Darkness is kept for all his wealth, and a fire not made by human hands destroys him and everything in his tent. Total ruin comes on him and his home.
entries.job 20:27: The heavens reveal his sin, and the earth itself testifies against him. His wrongdoing is exposed and cannot be hidden.
entries.job 20:28: His household's goods are carried off to another land, taken away on the day of wrath. His family loses everything.
entries.job 20:29: This is what Zophar says the wicked receive from God. He believes this is the fate God gives to evil people.
entries.job 21:1: Job speaks up in reply to his friends. He is about to answer what they have said to him.
entries.job 21:2: Job asks his friends to listen closely to what he is saying. He says that simply listening would be a real comfort to him.
entries.job 21:3: Job wants a chance to speak his mind without being interrupted. After that, he says, they can mock him if they want.
entries.job 21:4: Job asks whether his complaint is really aimed at people. If his spirit is troubled, he feels he has good reason for it.
entries.job 21:5: Job tells them to look at him and be shocked. He wants them to cover their mouths in silence rather than keep arguing.
entries.job 21:6: Just thinking about his situation makes Job's body tremble with fear. His distress is deep and physical, not just words.
entries.job 21:7: Job asks a hard question: why do wicked people often live long and grow powerful? It bothers him that bad people seem to do well.
entries.job 21:8: The wicked see their children grow up around them. Their families stay close and thrive before their eyes.
entries.job 21:9: Their homes are safe and free from fear. They don't seem to suffer the punishment God is supposed to bring.
entries.job 21:10: Even their farm animals prosper. Their cattle breed successfully and don't lose their young.
entries.job 21:11: Their children run around happily like a flock of sheep. The young ones play and dance together.
entries.job 21:12: They sing and celebrate to music. They enjoy life and are glad when they hear instruments playing.
entries.job 21:13: Their lives end peacefully without long suffering. Then suddenly they die and go down to the place of the dead.
entries.job 21:14: Yet these same people tell God to leave them alone. They say they don't want to know his ways.
entries.job 21:15: They ask what God is that they should serve him. They see no benefit in praying to him.
entries.job 21:16: Job admits their success seems to be in their own hands. But he says he wants nothing to do with their way of life.
entries.job 21:17: Job asks how often the wicked really do get cut off. How often does trouble or God's anger actually fall on them?
entries.job 21:18: He wonders how often they are blown away like chaff or straw in a storm. In his experience, it doesn't happen often.
entries.job 21:19: Some say God stores up punishment for a wicked man's children. Job thinks the man himself should suffer so he learns the lesson.
entries.job 21:20: Job wants the wicked to see their own ruin. He wants them to feel God's anger for themselves.
entries.job 21:21: Once a man is dead, what does he care about what happens to his family? His months are over and he is gone.
entries.job 21:22: No one can teach God anything. He is the judge over even the highest powers.
entries.job 21:23: One person dies while still comfortable and at peace. Life ends well for him.
entries.job 21:24: His body is well fed and strong. He has plenty and loses none of his strength.
entries.job 21:25: Another person dies bitter and unhappy. He never got to enjoy anything good in life.
entries.job 21:26: Both of them end up in the dust of the grave. The same worms cover them both.
entries.job 21:27: Job says he knows what his friends are thinking. He sees the cruel plans they have against him.
entries.job 21:28: He quotes their question: where is the house of the ruler, and where is the tent of the wicked? They assume the wicked lose everything.
entries.job 21:29: Job tells them to ask people who have traveled and seen the world. They should pay attention to what those travelers report.
entries.job 21:30: Travelers know that wicked people often escape trouble. They are spared on the day of disaster and wrath.
entries.job 21:31: No one confronts a wicked man to his face. No one repays him for the wrongs he has done.
entries.job 21:32: He is carried to his grave and a watch is kept over his tomb. He gets an honorable burial.
entries.job 21:33: The soil of the valley is sweet to him, and crowds follow him to the grave. Many went before him and many will come after.
entries.job 21:34: Job asks why they offer comfort that helps nothing. Their answers are empty and misleading, and he sees right through them.
entries.job 23:1: Job speaks up again in reply. This simply marks the start of his answer to his friends.
entries.job 23:2: Job says his complaint is still bitter and that God's hand presses hard on his pain. He feels crushed and wants the reader to know his suffering is real.
entries.job 23:3: Job wishes he knew where to find God so he could go straight to him. He longs to bring his case directly to God instead of talking past him.
entries.job 23:4: Job would lay out his case in order and fill his mouth with arguments. He wants a fair hearing where he can state his side fully.
entries.job 23:5: Job wants to hear God's answer and learn what God would say to him. He is looking for a real response, not silence.
entries.job 23:6: Job doubts God would use raw power to crush him, but believes God would actually listen to him. He hopes for a fair hearing rather than being overpowered.
entries.job 23:7: Job believes an honest man could argue his case there and be cleared by God for good. He trusts that truth would win if he could only reach God's court.
entries.job 23:8: Job looks forward and backward but cannot find God anywhere. He feels God is absent no matter which way he turns.
entries.job 23:9: Job searches on the left and right but sees no sign of God. His sense of God's hiddenness grows in every direction.
entries.job 23:10: Job is sure God knows the path he walks, and that after testing he will come out like refined gold. Even in pain, he holds hope that the trial will prove his integrity.
entries.job 23:11: Job claims he has followed God's steps and stayed on God's way without swerving. He insists his life has been faithful, which is why his suffering confuses him.
entries.job 23:12: Job says he has not disobeyed God's commands and has treasured God's words in his heart. He points to his obedience as evidence that his suffering is not deserved.
entries.job 23:13: Job says God's purpose is fixed and cannot be changed, and God does whatever he desires. He feels small before a God whose mind will not be swayed.
entries.job 23:14: Job believes God will carry out to the end whatever he has planned for him. He expects more of the same appointed hardship, not relief.
entries.job 23:15: Because of this, Job is afraid before God and overwhelmed by thoughts of him. God's power and fixed purpose leave him shaken rather than comforted.
entries.job 23:16: Job says God has made his heart weak and his mind troubled. He names God directly as the source of his inner collapse.
entries.job 23:17: Job feels swallowed by darkness and black night covering his face. His suffering has left him in deep gloom with no light in sight.
entries.job 25:1: This line introduces Bildad, one of Job's friends, as the next person to speak. It simply marks a change in the conversation, reminding the reader that these are the words of a human friend, not God.
entries.job 25:2: Bildad says that God holds all authority and power, and that he keeps order and peace even in the heavens above. For the reader, it means God is in charge of everything, far beyond what we can see.
entries.job 25:3: Bildad asks who could ever count God's vast forces, and points out that his light reaches everyone everywhere. The point for the reader is that God's reach and knowledge are unlimited, so nothing is hidden from him.
entries.job 25:4: Bildad asks how any human being could possibly be pure and right in God's sight. It reminds the reader that no one measures up to God's perfect standard on their own.
entries.job 25:5: Bildad says that even the moon and stars look dim and impure compared to God's brightness. The reader is meant to feel how great God's purity is next to everything else.
entries.job 25:6: Bildad concludes that humans, compared to God, are as small as insects or worms. It's a strong picture of how humble and dependent we are before a holy God.
entries.job 26:1: This line simply introduces Job's reply, marking the start of a speech. It tells the reader to pay attention to what Job is about to say.
entries.job 26:2: Job is being sarcastic, asking his friends what help they have actually given to someone weak and helpless. It reminds the reader that harsh words to a suffering person help no one.
entries.job 26:3: Job continues the sarcasm, saying his friends have offered no real wisdom to someone who lacks it. It warns the reader that advice can sound wise yet still miss the point.
entries.job 26:4: Job asks whose words his friends are really speaking and where their ideas come from. It invites the reader to question whether their own words come from God or from themselves.
entries.job 26:5: Job pictures the dead in the underworld trembling before God's power. It shows that nothing, not even the realm of the dead, is outside God's control.
entries.job 26:6: God sees the hidden place of the dead and the place of destruction with nothing hidden from him. It means the reader can trust that no secret or dark place is beyond God's sight.
entries.job 26:7: God stretched out the northern sky and hangs the earth on nothing. It points to God as the one who holds the whole world in place.
entries.job 26:8: God holds the waters inside thick clouds without the clouds breaking under their weight. It shows God's careful control over the forces of nature.
entries.job 26:9: God covers his throne with cloud, hiding his glory from view. It means God is real and present even when we cannot see him clearly.
entries.job 26:10: God draws a boundary on the sea, marking where light and darkness meet. It shows that God sets limits on the world he made.
entries.job 26:11: Even the pillars that hold up the sky shake at God's rebuke. It means God's word is powerful enough to make the strongest things tremble.
entries.job 26:12: By his power God calms the sea and by his wisdom he defeats the sea monster Rahab. It shows God's strength and wisdom winning over chaos.
entries.job 26:13: God's breath clears the skies, and his hand strikes down the fleeing serpent. It pictures God bringing order and light out of disorder.
entries.job 26:14: Job says all this is only the edge of what God does, and we hear just a whisper of it. It reminds the reader that God is far greater than anything we can fully understand.
entries.job 18:1: Bildad, one of Job's friends, speaks up next in the argument. He is about to give his own opinion about why Job is suffering.
entries.job 18:2: Bildad tells Job to stop talking so much and to listen and learn wisdom. He is frustrated that Job keeps defending himself instead of accepting their advice.
entries.job 18:3: Bildad feels insulted, as if Job treats him and his friends like stupid animals. He is saying Job is acting as though they know nothing.
entries.job 18:4: Bildad asks Job why the whole world should change just to suit him, and warns that Job is only hurting himself with his anger. He thinks Job is being unreasonable and self-centered.
entries.job 18:5: Bildad begins describing what he believes happens to wicked people: their success and happiness are snuffed out like a lamp. He is hinting that this is what has happened to Job.
entries.job 18:6: He pictures the wicked person's home going dark, with every source of light put out. In other words, trouble and ruin come to the wicked.
entries.job 18:7: The wicked person's strength fails and his own plans bring him down. Bildad is saying that evil people trip themselves up.
entries.job 18:8: He compares the wicked to someone who walks into a hidden trap without realizing it. Disaster catches them when they are not looking.
entries.job 18:9: The trap closes on the wicked person's foot and holds him fast. Bildad is saying that bad people cannot escape the consequences of their actions.
entries.job 18:10: A hidden snare waits in the path of the wicked person. Trouble is set up ahead of them, ready to catch them.
entries.job 18:11: The wicked person is surrounded by terrors that chase him at every step. Bildad describes a life of constant fear and dread.
entries.job 18:12: Hunger drains the wicked person's strength while disaster waits to strike him. His ruin is pictured as close and certain.
entries.job 18:13: Disease eats away the wicked person's skin and body. Bildad is describing sickness as part of the punishment that comes on evil people.
entries.job 18:14: The wicked person is dragged out of the safety of his home and brought to death, called here the king of fears. He loses everything he trusted in.
entries.job 18:15: Strangers take over the wicked person's home, and fire falls on his house. His property is destroyed and taken from him.
entries.job 18:16: The wicked person is like a plant whose roots dry up underground and whose branches are cut off above. Nothing of him is left growing or alive.
entries.job 18:17: The wicked person is forgotten completely, and no one remembers his name. His memory disappears from the world.
entries.job 18:18: He is driven out of the light into darkness and pushed out of the world. Bildad pictures total removal and disgrace.
entries.job 18:19: The wicked person has no children or family left among his people, and no one remains in his home to carry on his name. His family line comes to an end.
entries.job 18:20: People from east and west are shocked and terrified when they see what happened to the wicked person. His downfall becomes a warning to everyone.
entries.job 18:21: Bildad concludes that this is what happens to the homes of sinners and to those who ignore God. He is implying that Job's disaster proves Job is such a person.
entries.job 24:1: Job asks why God, who rules everything, doesn't set clear times for judging evil, and why people who know him never see justice happen. It gives voice to the frustration of waiting for God to act while wrong seems to go unpunished.
entries.job 24:2: Wicked people move boundary markers to steal land and drive off whole flocks along with the shepherds who watch them. It shows how the powerful take what isn't theirs and leave others with nothing.
entries.job 24:3: They take the donkey that belongs to an orphan and seize a widow's ox as payment for a debt. The most vulnerable people are stripped of the little they depend on to survive.
entries.job 24:4: The poor are pushed off the road and forced to hide together out of sight. Those with no power are treated as if they have no right to be seen.
entries.job 24:5: Like wild donkeys in the desert, the poor search hard for food and scrape a living from barren land to feed their children. It pictures people working desperately just to keep their families alive.
entries.job 24:6: They gather leftover grain from other people's fields and pick the last grapes from the vineyards of the rich. The poor survive on what is left behind by those who own the land.
entries.job 24:7: At night they sleep with no clothes and nothing to keep them warm in the cold. It shows how deep poverty leaves people without even basic shelter and covering.
entries.job 24:8: They are soaked by mountain rain and huddle in cracks in the rocks for shelter. People with no home are left exposed to the weather and take refuge wherever they can.
entries.job 24:9: A fatherless baby is torn from its mother to be taken as payment for a debt, and poor people's children are seized. Even the youngest and most helpless are treated as things to be collected.
entries.job 24:10: People walk around with no clothes and, though starving, still harvest grain from the fields. They do the hard work that feeds others while going hungry themselves.
entries.job 24:11: They press olives for oil and tread grapes, yet they have nothing to drink. The workers produce plenty for others but are denied even the basics they make.
entries.job 24:12: From the city come the groans of the dying and the cries of the wounded, yet God does not respond to their prayer. It names the raw pain of suffering people who feel unheard by God.
entries.job 24:13: Some people hate the light and refuse to learn its ways or walk in them. These are people who choose darkness because they don't want their deeds seen.
entries.job 24:14: A murderer gets up before dawn to kill the poor and needy. Evil doesn't wait; it rises early to prey on those who cannot defend themselves.
entries.job 24:15: An adulterer waits for evening, thinking no one will see him, and covers his face; the thief also moves about at night. People doing wrong count on darkness to hide what they do.
entries.job 24:16: Thieves break into houses in the dark and shut themselves away by day, having nothing to do with the light. They arrange their whole lives around avoiding being seen.
entries.job 24:17: For them the middle of the night feels like morning, and the terrors of darkness don't frighten them. They have grown so used to the dark that it no longer bothers them.
entries.job 24:18: They are swept away quickly like something floating on water; their land is cursed and no one returns to their vineyard. Their success is brief and their place in the world is soon gone.
entries.job 24:19: Just as snow water dries up in the heat, so sinners disappear down into the grave. However strong they seem, death dries them up like everything else.
entries.job 24:20: Their own town forgets them, their name fades from memory, and they are pulled up like a dead tree. In the end the wicked leave nothing behind that lasts.
entries.job 24:21: Such a man shows no kindness to a widow and no pity for her child. Cruelty to the helpless is the mark of the person Job is describing.
entries.job 24:22: But God by his power keeps the strong alive, and they rise again even when they had no hope of living. God's power is what sustains people, even those who don't deserve it.
entries.job 24:23: God gives them a sense of safety and support, yet his eyes are watching everything they do. Even when the wicked feel secure, God sees their ways clearly.
entries.job 24:24: They are lifted up for only a little while, then they are gone, brought low and cut off like grain. Their greatness is short-lived and ends suddenly.
entries.job 24:25: Job challenges anyone to prove his words false or show that what he says is worthless. He is confident that what he has described is true and dares his friends to refute it.
entries.job 22:1: Eliphaz speaks up to answer Job. This is the start of his third speech to Job.
entries.job 22:2: A person cannot really give God anything God needs, since whatever good we do mainly helps us. So being good is not a favor we do for God.
entries.job 22:3: God does not gain anything from our being good or lose anything from our sin. Eliphaz is saying Job's goodness does not put God in his debt.
entries.job 22:4: Eliphaz asks whether God is punishing Job because Job has been so devoted to him. He doubts that is the reason.
entries.job 22:5: Eliphaz accuses Job of great wickedness and countless sins. He assumes Job's suffering must be proof of hidden wrongdoing.
entries.job 22:6: Eliphaz claims Job took pledges from people for no reason and stripped poor people of their clothing. These are serious accusations against Job's character.
entries.job 22:7: He says Job refused water to the weary and withheld bread from the hungry. In other words, Job is accused of being stingy and heartless.
entries.job 22:8: Eliphaz says Job used his power and status to claim the land for himself. He pictures Job as someone who used influence for personal gain.
entries.job 22:9: He accuses Job of sending widows away empty-handed and crushing orphans. These are charges of neglecting the most vulnerable people.
entries.job 22:10: Because of these supposed sins, Eliphaz says Job is trapped and suddenly overwhelmed with fear. He sees Job's troubles as a direct result of wrongdoing.
entries.job 22:11: He describes Job as surrounded by darkness so he cannot see, and flooded with trouble. This is his picture of Job's present misery.
entries.job 22:12: Eliphaz points out that God is high in the heavens, far above the stars. He is building toward the idea that God is too distant to notice small details.
entries.job 22:13: He claims Job has said God does not know what is happening and cannot judge from behind the dark clouds. Eliphaz is putting words in Job's mouth.
entries.job 22:14: He says Job thinks thick clouds hide God so he cannot see, and that God only walks on the edge of the sky. This is Eliphaz's version of Job's view.
entries.job 22:15: Eliphaz asks whether Job will keep following the old path that wicked people walked. He warns Job not to copy their way of life.
entries.job 22:16: He recalls how such wicked people were swept away before their time, destroyed by a flood. Their sudden end is meant as a warning to Job.
entries.job 22:17: Those wicked people told God to leave them alone and mocked what God could do to them. Eliphaz says this is the attitude Job should avoid.
entries.job 22:18: Even though God had filled their homes with good things, Eliphaz says he wants no part of their plans. He distances himself from the wicked.
entries.job 22:19: Good people saw the downfall of the wicked and were glad, and those who did no wrong laughed at them. Eliphaz says the righteous celebrate when evil is punished.
entries.job 22:20: They said the wicked surely lose everything, and their wealth is burned up. The point is that evil people do not last.
entries.job 22:21: Eliphaz urges Job to make peace with God and submit to him, promising that then things will go well. He offers this as the path back to blessing.
entries.job 22:22: He tells Job to accept instruction from God's mouth and treasure his words in his heart. In other words, listen to God and take it seriously.
entries.job 22:23: If Job returns to God, humbles himself, and removes evil from his home, then restoration can follow. Eliphaz makes repentance the condition for things getting better.
entries.job 22:24: He tells Job to treat his finest gold as worthless dust and throw it among the rocks. This means letting go of reliance on wealth.
entries.job 22:25: Then God himself will be Job's treasure, and God's teaching will be his silver. The point is that knowing God is worth more than riches.
entries.job 22:26: When that happens, Job will find delight in God and be able to lift his face to him without shame. Eliphaz promises renewed confidence before God.
entries.job 22:27: Job will pray and God will answer, and Job will be able to keep his promises to God. Prayer and faithfulness will be restored.
entries.job 22:28: Whatever Job plans will succeed, and light will shine on his path. Eliphaz promises a bright future if Job follows his advice.
entries.job 22:29: God brings down the proud but saves those who are humble in spirit. Eliphaz says humility is the way to be lifted up.
entries.job 22:30: God rescues even the guilty, and if Job's hands are clean he too will be saved. Eliphaz ends by tying rescue to clean hands and right living.
entries.job 27:1: Job begins speaking again, starting a new part of his argument. This reminds the reader that Job is still in the middle of making his case.
entries.job 27:2: Job swears by the living God, even though he feels God has denied him justice and made his life bitter. He is being honest that he feels wronged by God while still addressing God as the Almighty.
entries.job 27:3: Job says that as long as he still has breath and God's spirit gives him life, he will keep speaking. He sees his very life as coming from God.
entries.job 27:4: Job insists that he will not lie or speak deceitfully. He is claiming that his words have been honest and true.
entries.job 27:5: Job firmly refuses to agree that his friends are right about him. He would rather die than admit to being guilty of what they accuse him of.
entries.job 27:6: Job holds tightly to his claim of being in the right and refuses to let it go. His conscience is clear, and he does not believe his life deserves blame.
entries.job 27:7: Job wishes that his enemy would end up like the wicked and the sinner. He wants those who oppose him to face the same fate he believes wrongdoers receive.
entries.job 27:8: Job asks what hope a wicked person has when God cuts his life short and demands his soul back. The point is that the wicked have nothing to look forward to at the end.
entries.job 27:9: Job asks whether God will listen to a wicked person's cry when trouble comes. The implied answer is no, because such a person did not turn to God before.
entries.job 27:10: Job asks whether a wicked person will truly enjoy God and pray to him regularly. The expected answer is no, since the wicked do not delight in God.
entries.job 27:11: Job offers to teach his friends about how God acts and what the Almighty has in mind. He is confident he understands something they are missing.
entries.job 27:12: Job points out that his friends have seen the same things he has, yet they are talking nonsense. He is frustrated that they are not making sense of what they observe.
entries.job 27:13: Job describes the fate that God gives to the wicked and to cruel people. He is laying out what he believes happens to those who do evil.
entries.job 27:14: Job says that even if a wicked man has many children, they will die by the sword or go hungry. His family will not escape trouble.
entries.job 27:15: Job says the wicked man's surviving family will die of disease and not even get a proper burial, and their widows will not mourn them. This shows total disgrace and loss.
entries.job 27:16: Job pictures a wicked man piling up silver like dust and storing up piles of clothes. He may become very rich in this life.
entries.job 27:17: But Job says the upright and innocent will end up wearing those clothes and owning that silver. The wicked man's wealth will pass to good people.
entries.job 27:18: Job compares the wicked man's house to something as flimsy as a spider's web or a temporary watchman's shelter. It looks like a home but has no real strength.
entries.job 27:19: The wicked man lies down rich, but when he wakes, his wealth is gone. He loses everything in a single night.
entries.job 27:20: Terror comes over the wicked man like a flood, and a storm carries him away at night. His downfall comes suddenly and violently.
entries.job 27:21: The east wind lifts the wicked man up and sweeps him away from his place. He is forcibly removed from everything he had.
entries.job 27:22: Job says God shoots at the wicked man without mercy, and he tries to run away. There is no escape from God's judgment.
entries.job 27:23: People clap and hiss as the wicked man is driven from his place. Others celebrate his downfall rather than mourn it.
entries.job 29:1: Job continues his speech here. He is about to look back on the good old days before his suffering began.
entries.job 29:2: Job longs to be the way he was in the past, when he felt God was protecting him. It is natural to miss seasons when life felt safe and blessed.
entries.job 29:3: Job remembers when God's light seemed to guide him, even through dark times. He misses that sense of God leading him.
entries.job 29:4: Job recalls his younger, thriving years when he felt God's hand of blessing over his home. He is grieving the loss of that season.
entries.job 29:5: Job remembers when God felt close and his children were around him. The loneliness of his present loss makes the memory painful.
entries.job 29:6: Job describes his past prosperity with picture language of abundance—milk and oil flowing freely. He once had more than enough.
entries.job 29:7: Job recalls going to the town gate, where important business and decisions were made. He had a respected place there.
entries.job 29:8: Young men stepped aside and old men stood up when Job arrived. He was shown great respect by everyone.
entries.job 29:9: Even rulers quieted down and covered their mouths when Job spoke. His words carried real weight.
entries.job 29:10: The leading men fell silent and held back their words in Job's presence. He was listened to with awe.
entries.job 29:11: People who heard about Job called him blessed, and those who saw him spoke well of him. His reputation was good.
entries.job 29:12: Job helped the poor who cried out, orphans, and anyone with no one to defend them. He used his position to protect the vulnerable.
entries.job 29:13: People on the edge of ruin blessed Job, and he brought joy to widows. His kindness changed lives.
entries.job 29:14: Job made doing right his way of life, like clothes he always wore. Fairness was part of who he was.
entries.job 29:15: Job helped those who could not see or walk, guiding and supporting them. He stepped in for people who couldn't manage alone.
entries.job 29:16: Job cared for the poor like a father and looked into cases involving strangers to make sure they got justice. He took responsibility for people outside his own circle.
entries.job 29:17: Job stopped violent people and made them give back what they had taken. He stood up against wrongdoing.
entries.job 29:18: Job expected to live a long life and die surrounded by his family. He thought his future was secure.
entries.job 29:19: Job pictures himself as a well-watered tree with fresh dew on its branches. He expected to keep growing and thriving.
entries.job 29:20: Job believed his honor would stay strong and his strength would remain ready for use. He felt confident about the future.
entries.job 29:21: People listened to Job and waited quietly for his advice. His opinion mattered to them.
entries.job 29:22: After Job spoke, people stayed quiet and took his words to heart. They valued what he said.
entries.job 29:23: People waited for Job's words like farmers waiting for rain. They were eager for his guidance.
